games.name: The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth
games.short_description: The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth is a randomly generated action RPG shooter with heavy Rogue-like elements. Following Isaac on his journey players will find bizarre treasures that change Isaac’s form giving him super human abilities and enabling him to fight off droves of mysterious creatures, discover secrets and fight his way to safety.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: The Binding of Isaac is the top-down roguelite that helped bring the genre back to modern gaming, and he calls it probably the most packed roguelite around. He says it is the one game he could play forever because it never gets old. He has over 300 hours in it and notes it keeps receiving new content. He places it in S tier without hesitation and tells viewers who haven't played it to go play it.
praise: Enormous amount of content: many characters, items and things to do
Level designs are amazing
Characters play very differently from one another
Huge item pool that still feels balanced despite the power-fantasy moments
Plenty of depth to master and endless replayability
Still being updated with new content after all these years
criticism: No real criticisms; he says there is nothing left to say that has not already been said
Admits he has not played much of the newest content
unique_points: Helped revive roguelikes and roguelites in the modern era
Makes the player feel overpowered at times yet retains mastery depth
Sheer density of content makes it feel like the most packed roguelite available
commentary.quote: it never gets old you can always come back to it
design_criteria: Content volume: characters, items and secrets in huge quantity
Level design: praised as amazing
Character diversity: each character plays distinctly
Balance and power fantasy: feels overpowered sometimes but still balanced
Replayability: never gets old, long-term play
Ongoing support: continued new content

community.one_liner: A twin-stick, room-by-room dungeon crawler by Edmund McMillen where Isaac descends through randomly generated floors collecting hundreds of synergistic items, wrapped in grotesque religious-horror imagery.
community.consensus_summary: Regarded as one of the defining roguelikes: Steam shows 96.8% positive across about 459k reviews (Overwhelmingly Positive) and critics landed in the high 80s for Rebirth (Metacritic 88 on 15 reviews, OpenCritic 87 with 92% recommending). Players praise near-endless replayability from 700+ items and 34 characters, tight shooting, and the bleak-funny identity. The recurring complaints are RNG swings, opaque item text, a long unlock and completion grind, and steep difficulty for newcomers. The game is fully released and very much alive: Repentance is the final expansion and the community keeps it going with mods and Workshop content, and a 2026 patch triggered some DLC-loading complaints on Steam.
best_things: Huge replayability: 700+ items, 188 trinkets, 34 characters (with Tainted versions) and thousands of hours are cited by long-time players
Item synergies produce wildly different builds each run (Brimstone, Tech X and similar combos are commonly named as highlights)
Tight, responsive twin-stick combat with a fast, addictive 'one more run' loop
Strong, committed dark and gross aesthetic with a memorable soundtrack and a story told through endings and secrets
Repentance rebalanced overpowered and weak items, added new routes, bosses and thousands of rooms; one review gave the DLC 9.5/10
Very good value, especially on sale, given the content volume; Steam Workshop mods extend it further
Hidden secrets and discoverable mechanics reward curiosity and community knowledge-sharing
worst_things: Item effects are poorly explained in-game, so many players rely on mods or the wiki to know what pickups do
Heavy RNG: item pools are bloated, so bad rolls and unwinnable seeds are common, and top players restart early floors until they find a strong first item
Hostile onboarding: new players report difficulty even learning controls and the game's systems, with little guidance
Some content gates are harsh: powerful items like Godhead and Death Certificate require beating hard late bosses, sometimes with one-hit characters like The Lost
Repentance-era balance: trap rooms and sudden damage can ruin runs regardless of knowledge; Delirium is described as broken by teleporting onto the player
Multiplayer/co-op reportedly desyncs, and you cannot rejoin mid-floor
Darker themes (child abuse, religious extremism) and crude humor put some players off; content is not for younger players
Recent patches reportedly broke DLC loading or launch (Afterbirth+/Repentance), with some players rolling back to older versions and unable to refund
improvements: Better in-game item descriptions or an optional info display (the most popular mod simply tells you what items do)
A gentler tutorial/onboarding so new players learn controls and core systems
Less RNG dependence and tighter item pool curation so runs feel less dependent on early luck
Fewer time-gated and grindy completion requirements (daily challenges, repeated hard-mode clears)
More reliable online co-op and better patch QA so DLC does not break after updates
unique_things: Extremely dense item-interaction system with 700+ items, giving emergent builds no other roguelike matches in raw variety
Shoot-in-four-directions dungeon crawl structure with Zelda-style rooms instead of continuous levels
Uncompromising religious-horror and body-horror theme paired with cartoon visuals and dark comedy
Completion meta with 34 characters, dozens of endings and a 'Dead God' 100% achievement that can take 500+ hours
Shaped the modern roguelite genre; the series originated from a Flash game in 2011 and was remade in Rebirth in 2014
tedious_or_disliked: 100% completion and unlocks are a long grind, cited as 500+ hours, including killing final bosses repeatedly across many characters
Daily challenges act as real-calendar time gates for certain unlocks, which players compare to mobile-game design
Restarting early floors or rerolling until the item pool looks promising, and slower clears when pools are diluted (a reported habit, not a top review theme)
Hard-mode requirements for best unlocks feel punishing for casual players
Some players dislike specific characters or modes (Jacob and Esau, Curse of the Blind, Lazarus, Tainted Lost are named in reviews)
Four-way shooting and enemy design feel restrictive or boring to a minority, with hitbox or movement complaints in a few reviews
Forced modes for unlocks, e.g. Greed Mode, are said to stall enjoyment of the core game
divisive_points: RNG versus skill: critics call it luck-driven, while defenders point to long win streaks by top players as proof skill dominates
Repentance: many see a masterpiece of content and balance, others feel it added chores and pushed difficulty toward hardcore players
Low-information design: some love discovering item effects by experiment, others find it poor design
Art style and tone: praised as distinctive and funny by fans, dismissed as teenage-edgy or off-putting by others
community.reception_notes: The 2011 Flash original sold about 700k copies in under a year and passed 2 million by late 2012 (per news reports), which funded the Rebirth remake by McMillen and Nicalis (Nov 2014, new engine, co-op, hundreds of new items). Afterbirth, Afterbirth+ and the 2021 Repentance expansion followed (OpenCritic 88, 82 and 83 per search results). Steam-revenue-calculator estimates for Rebirth are about $225M gross and about $66M net (Boxleiter-style, order-of-magnitude only); SteamSpy lists 5 to 10 million owners. Metacritic page re-fetched: Metascore 88 on 15 reviews, user 8.2 on 1,154 ratings. Current Steam reviews (2026) are still overwhelmingly positive, with many ironic 'I hate this game' recommendations from 1000+ hour players, a few complaints about a recent patch breaking DLC loading, and multiplayer desync complaints.

games.name: Dead Cells
games.short_description: Dead Cells is a roguelite, metroidvania inspired, action-platformer. You'll explore a sprawling, ever-changing castle... assuming you’re able to fight your way past its keepers in 2D souls-lite combat. No checkpoints. Kill, die, learn, repeat.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Dead Cells is a fast-paced action roguelite where you always play the same character and build each run around the weapons and gear you find. He considers it very popular for good reason, with distinct weapons, great balance and superb game feel. He also praises the developers' constant stream of updates and DLC. He disputes the metroidvania label but still calls it one of the best action roguelikes and places it in S tier.
praise: Every weapon feels distinct, with its own animations and clearly careful design
Excellent balance: almost any weapon is viable for a successful run
Game feel is outstanding; you are fast and feel powerful, cutting through enemies
Each run feels unique even with few passives, since weapons carry the variety
Developers keep releasing updates and DLC, adding bosses, biomes and weapons
Developers published a talk explaining how they designed it to feel good
criticism: Marketed as a metroidvania, which he disagrees with; it is effectively a standard roguelite once the traversal abilities are unlocked
Only three to four hours of ability unlocking gate the world traversal, after which the metroidvania element fades
Few unique passives, so variety relies almost entirely on weapons
unique_points: Variety comes from weapon design rather than passives or differing characters
Weapon animations and feel are individually designed, making each one a different playstyle
Ongoing content updates keep the game fresh for years
commentary.quote: in terms of like action roguelikes it's one of the best it's an easy s tier
comparisons: Metroidvania games (as a genre label he rejects)
design_criteria: Game feel: speed and power fantasy make combat satisfying
Weapon diversity: each weapon has unique animations and behaviour
Balance: nearly all weapons are viable
Run variety: runs feel unique despite few passives
Content updates: ongoing DLC, bosses, biomes and weapons
Genre honesty: metroidvania label seen as marketing rather than design

community.one_liner: A 2D roguelite action-platformer with Metroidvania-style exploration and fast, souls-lite combat, where each run through a procedurally assembled castle ends in permadeath and permanent unlocks.
community.consensus_summary: Dead Cells is one of the most acclaimed roguelites ever made: 97% positive across about 184k Steam reviews (Overwhelmingly Positive), Metacritic 89 and OpenCritic 89 from 150+ critics, plus multiple Best Action/Indie awards in 2018. Players and critics agree the combat feel, movement, art, music and build variety are best in class. Complaints center on the unlock grind, same-y repeat runs, hard-to-read hitboxes and two-hit deaths at high difficulty, and especially the way DLC content is visibly gated inside the base game. It left Early Access in August 2018 and has sold over 10 million copies. Content updates ended with Update 35 'The End is Near' in 2024 after Motion Twin cancelled further Evil Empire work; the game is now in bug-fix-only maintenance, which still draws some community resentment.
best_things: Fluid, responsive combat with very tight controls and animation; often cited as the genre benchmark for game feel
Huge weapon, skill and mutation variety that supports many distinct builds (e.g. crit, brutality, tactics scaling) and run-to-run experimentation
Strong roguelite loop: each death unlocks blueprints, runes, and shortcuts so failure feels like progress
Exploration with rune-gated secret areas and hidden details that reward curiosity, blending Metroidvania ideas into runs
Beautiful, vibrant pixel art with fluid animation, and a well-regarded soundtrack
Boss Cell difficulty tiers (BC 0-5) let players scale challenge and add new enemies and mechanics, giving endgame replay value
Assist Mode lets players tune difficulty without disabling achievements; widely praised as true accessibility
Runs well on low-end hardware and Steam Deck; many free updates and cheap, well-liked DLC (Queen and the Sea, Return to Castlevania)
worst_things: DLC zones, doors and achievements appear inside the base game with buy prompts, which many reviewers see as pushy and as making the base game feel incomplete
Unlock grind: weapons and blueprints must be bought with cells/souls repeatedly across runs, so the grind is seen as the content
Fixed early structure means the first biomes are replayed constantly, so runs feel repetitive despite procedural layouts
Hitbox and move-cancel inconsistencies: weapon visuals larger than actual hit areas, tiny enemy hitboxes, and attack animation lock-in make some deaths feel unfair
Enemies attacking from offscreen or through walls and occasional glitches are reported as cheap damage sources in later difficulties
Weak, sparse narrative and lore that many players find underdeveloped
Some weapons feel weak, gimmicky or are hard to make viable, narrowing the builds that actually work at high difficulty
Controller rebinding limitations and achievement restrictions on some options cited by a few reviewers
Some players find combat floaty and the game simple or shallow in build composition, with rewards for successful runs not satisfying enough to keep grinding
improvements: Less intrusive DLC presentation (or hiding DLC content/prompts for non-owners)
Faster or less repetitive unlock economy so the meta progression feels less like a grind
More variety in early-game biomes and route structure so runs diverge earlier
Clearer, more consistent hitboxes and animation-cancel rules
Better balance for underused weapons and more build-defining synergies at high Boss Cell levels
Deeper story and lore delivery and more bosses (base game has few bosses, per critics)
unique_things: Roguelite and Metroidvania fusion: permanent movement runes open new routes in later runs instead of a fixed world map
No checkpoints, no level-up stats: power comes from picking weapons and three-color scroll upgrades within a run (brutality, tactics, survival)
Player-controlled route choice between biomes each run, with a nonlinear branching castle
Curse mechanic (one hit kills until you clear enough kills) as a voluntary risk-reward system
Originally designed as a 3D project by Motion Twin and reworked into pixel-art 2D, which fans credit for its animation quality
Long post-launch life: five years of free updates, crossovers (Castlevania, Hollow Knight, Hades, etc.) and mobile/console ports
tedious_or_disliked: Repeatedly grinding the same early biomes just to fund blueprint unlocks
Dying at high Boss Cell difficulty to two hits after a long run, where a single mistake wipes the run
Buy prompts for DLC content interrupting fast runs, including timed door challenges
Luck-dependent weapon drops that can leave a run without a workable build
Runs that feel deflating after the early game: ramping back up after each death feels barely worth it to some players
divisive_points: Difficulty: many call it fair and skill-based, while others feel two-hit deaths and Curse make higher tiers frustrating
Grind and repetition: fans feel constant progression, while critics feel the core run structure barely changes after 30+ hours
DLC and monetization: many say DLC is cheap and optional, others feel base game is gated and incomplete
Motion Twin vs Evil Empire after update cancellation: some players negative-review to protest the studio, others defend the decision or praise the game regardless
community.reception_notes: Launched in Steam Early Access in May 2017 and quickly passed 1 million sales; 1.0 launched August 2018 on PC and consoles with very strong reviews and Golden Joystick Best Indie and Game Award wins. Motion Twin later sold over 10 million copies (announced at GDC) helped by 34 free updates and a mobile release; third-party revenue estimates (Steam-only, Boxleiter method) give roughly $178M gross / $52M net. Publishing duties shifted to Evil Empire for live ops from 2019 and they produced the DLC (Rise of the Giants, Bad Seed, Fatal Falls, Queen and the Sea, Return to Castlevania). In 2024 Update 35 'The End is Near' became the last content update; Motion Twin said it wanted to avoid 'more of the same', but co-creator Sebastien Benard publicly called the explanation misleading and pointed to an economic cut in favor of Motion Twin's new game Windblown. Recent Steam reviews show a small wave of protest negatives against Motion Twin and notes that the final update shipped unfinished from beta. Metacritic page cites platforms PC, PS4, Xbox One, Switch, iOS.

community.one_liner: A gun-themed bullet-hell dungeon crawler from Dodge Roll (published by Devolver Digital, 2016) in which quirky Gungeoneers dodge-roll through procedurally generated chambers to reach the gun that can kill the past.
community.consensus_summary: Enter the Gungeon is widely regarded as a genre standard-bearer for action roguelikes. It holds an Overwhelmingly Positive Steam rating (about 95% of roughly 90k reviews) and Metacritic critic scores in the low-to-mid 80s (PC 84, PS4 82, Xbox One 85, Switch 87), with a more lukewarm Metacritic user score of 7.7. Players and critics praise the weapon variety, tight dodge-roll combat, pixel art, theming and humour, and the huge depth of secrets. Complaints centre on its punishing difficulty, heavy RNG, unlock-only (no permanent stat) progression and weak-gun clutter. It is not early access; the last major content patch (A Farewell to Arms, April 2019) ended development, although it reached mobile in 2025 and Steam reviews show players still active in 2026. The sequel Enter the Gungeon 2 has since been announced/released on Steam.
best_things: Huge, whimsical roster of guns and items packed with pop-culture references, and a consistent gun-pun theme (Chambers, Gundead, Blanks, Ammonomicon)
Tight, responsive dodge-roll and bullet-hell combat that rewards skill over stacking overpowered builds
Polished pixel art, music and charm; reviewers say the love for gaming culture is obvious
Enormous endgame of secrets: hidden floors, secret bosses, secret characters and quests that keep players returning for hundreds of hours
Fair-feeling difficulty curve in the eyes of fans: deaths feel earned and improvement is tangible
Local co-op, pause-and-save, free DLC updates and a very low price for the content
Bosses are memorable and distinct, with no-hit bonuses that reward mastery
worst_things: Progression is almost entirely item unlocks; you always restart with the same stats, so meta-progression feels thin compared with Hades-style rogue-lites
Runs are heavily RNG-dependent; a run can hinge on getting a decent boss-killing gun and a second room-clearing gun
Many guns and items are considered weak or useless, and unlocked items still have to drop by chance
Limited variety in room layouts and enemy encounters; players who master it say rooms become memorisable and content after beating the Lich is sparse
Characters often feel similar, with some commonly described as near re-skins apart from special ones such as the Bullet and Robot
Normal rooms feel like a long runback to the boss fights; any damage taken in a boss fight (no-hit bonus) can feel demoralizing, and some reviewers call normal fights spammy or filler
Cryptic item descriptions and steep learning curve for newcomers
Some players report the camera/screen motion causes dizziness, high GPU usage, and an occasional co-op soft-lock with no settings fix
improvements: Add a way to ban or filter weak guns/items from the loot pool
More meaningful permanent progression or build-shaping choices at chests and shops
Online co-op (only local co-op exists), ideally with separate screens
More variety in room layouts, enemies and late-game challenge content
Camera and accessibility options (one reviewer reports motion-sickness dizziness and no fix in settings) and GPU usage tuning
More clarity on what unlocks and items do before selecting them
unique_things: Fully committed gun theme: floors, enemies, currency-like items and UI are all bullet or gun puns
Dodge roll with invincibility frames in a bullet-hell context, which divides hardcore shmup fans
Reward system for no-damage boss fights (extra heart containers/currency) that pushes skill play
Unusually large secret ecosystem: Rat fight, secret floors, secret NPC quests, alternate chambers, extra characters
Weapons with bizarre mechanics and references (for example a T-shirt cannon), with guns treated as characters
No permanent stat upgrades; progression is sideways, via unlocks, so skill remains the main variable
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding for the last unlockable characters and 100% achievements, including NPC quest chains that some find irritating (e.g. Frifle's quests, finding the Lost Adventurer)
Slow, sideways meta progression that never makes you stronger
Thieving rat stealing saved ammo, plus key and chest shortages frustrating runs
Runs ruined by ammo starvation or only having the starter pistol at the first boss
Long repetitive room-clearing stretches to reach the short, high-stakes boss fights
divisive_points: Difficulty: fans see it as fair and skill-based; others find it too punishing and unrewarding for those who struggle
RNG: some praise the huge synergy space, others say gear luck decides too much of each run
Dodge roll: loved for accessibility of movement, criticised by some bullet-hell purists as undercutting the genre
Content depth: fans cite hundreds of hours of secrets, while others say there is little post-game challenge and little run-to-run variety
community.reception_notes: Launch week sold over 200,000 copies (about 75% on Steam), 800,000+ by January 2017 and 3+ million across platforms by January 2020 (Wikipedia). SteamSpy lists 2-5 million Steam owners, and steam-revenue-calculator estimates roughly $67.6M gross and $20M net on Steam (Boxleiter-method estimate, not audited). Free content updates followed: Supply Drop (Jan 2017), Advanced Gungeons & Draguns (Jul 2018) and A Farewell to Arms (Apr 2019), after which development ended; some recent Steam reviewers note no updates since 2019. Critics at launch compared it favourably with The Binding of Isaac and Nuclear Throne, and PC Gamer called the bosses among the hardest things the reviewer had met. Nintendo Switch is the best-rated version on Metacritic (87); console reviewers noted controller aiming is less precise than mouse. A mobile release arrived in August 2025 and a 3D sequel, Enter the Gungeon 2, followed. Steam lists Windows and Linux, no native Mac. The 10th anniversary in April 2026 prompted renewed positive reviews.

community.one_liner: Supergiant Games' isometric action roguelite in which Zagreus, son of Hades, fights out of the Greek Underworld, with story and dialogue woven into the run-and-die loop.
community.consensus_summary: Hades is treated as a landmark of the genre by both critics and players: Metacritic 93 from 58 critic reviews with no mixed or negative ones, Steam 'Overwhelmingly Positive' at about 98% of roughly 309k reviews, and Wikipedia reports 99% of critics recommending it on OpenCritic. It swept Game of the Year at BAFTA, DICE, GDC and other ceremonies and became the first video game to win a Hugo. It spent almost two years in early access (from Dec 2018) and then launched in full in Sept 2020 to very strong sales. The main dissent comes from players who bounce off the roguelite structure itself (repetition, fixed biomes and bosses, RNG, meta-grind), not from the craft. Metacritic user score is lower than critics at 8.5, with Metacritic's summary citing RNG frustration and repetitive restarts.
best_things: Story is delivered through the run loop: each death brings new hub dialogue, so failure advances the narrative and feels rewarding rather than punishing
Fast, fluid, responsive combat with six distinct weapons and several aspects each, praised as weighty and satisfying
Boon system from the Olympian gods gives build variety and synergies (duo boons) while staying compact enough to understand
Writing, voice acting and characterisation are repeatedly singled out, including Zagreus's politeness and the gods' interplay and relationships
Art direction by Jen Zee and the soundtrack are near-universal praise
Accessible for roguelike newcomers: God Mode quietly boosts you after each death, and the hub and mirror upgrades soften early losses
Heat / Pact of Punishment gives scalable endgame difficulty and long replay value
Many reviewers who dislike the genre say this was the one that hooked them
worst_things: Only four biomes and a fixed set of bosses, so runs feel samey after a few dozen hours
Final boss fight against Hades is a big difficulty spike, frustrating to some players on the True Ending route
RNG in boon and reward offers can make runs feel unfair or throttle progress
Reviewers who want Binding of Isaac style emergent builds find boons mostly stat bonuses and percentages with few memorable or wild builds
Reaching full narrative closure (epilogue) takes very many clears; only a small share of players get there
Some players find the combat button-mashy, with heavy area damage, projectile spam and particle clutter (the lava biome and its bombers are a named pain point)
improvements: More biomes, bosses and enemy variety to reduce repetition (partly answered by Hades II)
Stronger, more game-changing boons or build-defining items for wilder synergies
A less grindy route to the epilogue and to late resources such as Titan Blood
Heat system that adds new mechanics rather than mostly limiting options or raising numbers
Clearer tracking of upgrade shop contents and rewards; several negative reviewers complain that remembering every god's offerings is hard
Finer-grained difficulty and assist options than God Mode's fixed ramp; one reviewer wanted an initial armour setting like Hades II
unique_things: Narrative-first roguelite: dialogue, relationships and plot progress are the meta-progression alongside stat unlocks
Greek mythology cast reinterpreted with personality-driven, sympathetic gods
Protagonist who is meant to die: death returns you to a living hub home with characters who react to how you died
God Mode accessibility that scales up with each failure, so the story is reachable for anyone
Pact of Punishment and heat let you tailor difficulty with many modifiers and unlock cosmetic rewards
Release-quality polish from a two-year early access that shipped with full voice acting and music
tedious_or_disliked: Running the same four regions and bosses many times to reach the story's ending
Grinding for meta resources such as Titan Blood and diamonds late in the game, described as a chore
Dodging heavy AoE and projectile spam in the later rooms, called monotonous by some
Heat-stacking runs where the added difficulty feels like restricted options rather than fresh play
Story interruptions and hub trips feel like hurdles to players who just want to start the next run; some later realise they are the point
Some users compare the loop to habit-forming or gambling-style design
divisive_points: Roguelite meta-progression: many find it a gentle learning curve, purists feel it hides whether they are actually improving
Story gating and repetition: praised as integrated and rewarding by most, but a slog by others (e.g. 70+ hours with little left to see)
Boon depth: fans praise clear synergies, critics say few builds are memorable compared with Isaac or Slay the Spire
Difficulty: hard at first, then manageable for most players, but the final boss and high heat frustrate some
community.reception_notes: Early access began 6 Dec 2018 after a Game Awards reveal; Wikipedia cites about 700k copies during nearly two years of early access and another 300k in three days after the 17 Sept 2020 full release (over 1M total then; later third-party estimates are far higher). Launch on PC (Windows, macOS) and Switch; PS4/PS5 and Xbox arrived 13 Aug 2021; a Netflix Games mobile version ran from March 2024 until it was removed in July 2025. Cross-save between Windows and Switch came via a Dec 2020 patch. Won GOTY at BAFTA, DICE, GDC, New York Game Awards and SXSW, plus a Hugo. Current Steam reviews are still highly positive, with the sequel Hades II drawing players back to the original. Note: OpenCritic's exact average was not retrievable in this session (WebSearch budget exhausted and the game page could not be located), so it is left null.

games.name: Inscryption
games.short_description: Inscryption is an inky black card-based odyssey that blends the deckbuilding roguelike, escape-room style puzzles, and psychological horror into a blood-laced smoothie. Darker still are the secrets inscrybed upon the cards...

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm gonna put this one as an easy s tier

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Inscryption is a story-driven deck-building roguelike from the creator of Pony Island. He treats it as the biggest campaign-style game on the list, something to experience once, and he avoids spoilers. He thinks the story, puzzles and exploration are superb and calls the game a masterpiece even though the card gameplay is its weakest part. He places it in S tier, close to Enter the Gungeon.
praise: Story and plot twists are absolutely amazing
Unusual mix of elements that combine very well
Puzzle elements and exploration with secrets to uncover
Works even for people who are not deck-building fans
Memorable one-time adventure that blew his mind
criticism: Card gameplay is the weakest part of the game
Very easy to break
Not very well balanced, though he says it is not meant to be

A deck-builder that does not require deck-building expertise to enjoy
Mixes deck building, puzzles, exploration and narrative reveals
Designed to be played once, not replayed for hundreds of hours
commentary.quote: I'm gonna put this one as an easy s tier
design_criteria: Story and narrative: the main strength, with twists and secrets
Uniqueness of combinations: several genres blended effectively
Gameplay and balance: weakest aspect, easy to break and unbalanced
Puzzle and exploration: adds discovery beyond card battles
Replayability: meant to be played about once, unlike Gungeon
Accessibility: enjoyable without being a deck-building fan

community.one_liner: A deckbuilding roguelike from Daniel Mullins Games (published by Devolver Digital) that starts as a sacrifice-based card battler in a creepy cabin and keeps changing genre, blending escape-room puzzles, psychological horror and a meta-narrative across three acts.
community.consensus_summary: Inscryption is one of the best-reviewed indie games of 2021: Steam shows Overwhelmingly Positive (about 96.8% of roughly 149k reviews), Metacritic critics score it 85 with users at 8.5, and it swept major awards (GDC Game of the Year and the IGF Seumas McNally Grand Prize, a first for both). Praise centres on atmosphere, the blood/bones sacrifice card system, inventive puzzles and a story that constantly subverts expectations. The consistent dissent is that Act 1 is the peak: Acts 2 and 3 and the ARG-style meta-story are seen by a minority as a pacing drop, a bait-and-switch from the store page, or repetitive. It is a finished game (not early access); the free Kaycee's Mod (Mar 2022) added an endless roguelike mode, and it later shipped on Mac/Linux and consoles. Most players urge going in blind.
best_things: Act 1 atmosphere: the dark cabin, Leshy as a menacing card-game opponent, sound design and art style are repeatedly called one of a kind
Constant surprise: the game shifts genre, rules and format, and players say it is far more than the store page suggests
Sacrifice card system (blood, bones, scales) and sigils: easy to learn but with depth; the scale/tug-of-war damage mechanic was singled out by critics
Escape-room style puzzles and hidden secrets woven into the deckbuilding, with a stupid amount of detail according to players
Fourth-wall-breaking, meta storytelling and memorable characters (the four Scrybes); the ending handshake sequence is a fan favourite
Replay value: Kaycee's Mod gives an endless roguelike mode, plus challenges, achievements and ARG content; some players report hundreds of hours
Soundtrack and visual design: a twisted take on 90s floppy-disc adventure aesthetics (Eurogamer) and a well-loved OST
Teaches mechanics through play rather than tutorials, making it approachable even for people who dislike deckbuilders
worst_things: Many say the game peaks in Act 1; Act 2 (8-bit 2D) and Act 3 (sci-fi factory with P03) lose the horror tension and charm
Store page, trailer and demo show only Act 1, which a number of negative reviewers call a bait-and-switch
The meta-narrative / ARG (Karnoffel code, live-action video footage, real-world references) is called convoluted, hard to take seriously or not worth the time
Act 3 is seen by some as repetitive: map backtracking, many similar fights, and little downside to dying or save-scumming
Acts 2 and 3 are felt to have low stakes since the game is linear and failure barely sets you back, unlike Act 1
Tonal and mechanical whiplash: critics like PC Gamer said the eerie delight fades well before the end, and Destructoid said later chapters gripped less than the first
Overall length and pacing: some find the later parts a test of endurance with too many new mechanics introduced at once

The ending and overall story payoff disappoint some players: they expected branching outcomes or a stronger conclusion and felt the story was told shallowly or through a forgettable live-action framing
improvements: Make Act 1 (the most loved part) longer or offer more content in that format, or a stand-alone mode built around it (Kaycee's Mod was the partial answer)
Fully fleshed-out worlds and playable stories for Magnificus and Grimora, which fans say feel underdeveloped compared with Leshy and P03
Make Acts 2 and 3 carry real consequences for failure, and trim repetitive map traversal and filler fights in Act 3
Market the game more accurately, since store screenshots and trailers only show Act 1
Clearer or more optional delivery of the lore; some reviewers wanted the story told more directly rather than through ARG-style puzzles
Allow more player agency or alternate endings; some players expected branching outcomes that do not exist
unique_things: A deckbuilder wrapped in a horror escape room: you get up from the table, inspect the cabin and solve puzzles that change your cards and rules
Sacrifice-based costs (blood, bones, energy, gems) on a lane-based board with a scale for damage instead of player health
Each act is effectively a different game with a different look and card economy, all framed by a fictional 'game within a game' mystery
Meta-narrative that reaches outside the game (file manipulation, live-action footage, ARG codes, callbacks to Mullins' earlier games)
Grew from a Ludum Dare 43 prototype (Sacrifices Must Be Made) and won both GDC Game of the Year and the IGF Grand Prize, a first
tedious_or_disliked: Act 3's travel-fight-upgrade loop over a map, with back and forth between areas and many similar battles
Act 2 mechanics that feel underexplained or exploitable, leading some to ignore the puzzle of deck building
Decoding the ARG and Karnoffel code to understand the full story, which some find exhausting or unnecessary
divisive_points: The meta-story and ARG: fans call it brilliant and the reason to play; detractors call it a pretentious or creepypasta-like grab bag that hurts the game
Act 2: some love the puzzles and music, others call it the slog that kills the horror pacing
Whether Inscryption is a roguelike at all beyond Act 1 and Kaycee's Mod, versus a narrative puzzle game that uses deckbuilding
Replay value: Act 1 and Kaycee's Mod support replay, but the main story is linear and many consider it a one-time experience best played blind
community.reception_notes: Launched Oct 19, 2021 on Windows to strong reviews; Metacritic critic score 85 (49 critic reviews on the PC page; 1,107 user ratings) and user score 8.5. Won the GDC Game of the Year and IGF Seumas McNally Grand Prize (2022), plus a BAFTA for game design and many best-of-2021 lists. Wikipedia reports over 1 million copies sold by January 2022; a third-party Boxleiter-method estimate puts Steam owners at 2-5 million and gross revenue around 118M USD, which is an order-of-magnitude guess and not audited. Free Kaycee's Mod launched Mar 17, 2022. Platform releases: Linux/macOS Jun 2022, PS4/PS5 Aug 2022, Switch Dec 2022, Xbox Apr 2023. Not early access; no notable abandonment or controversy found. OpenCritic score could not be retrieved (the direct page and API were unavailable) so it is left null. Web search quota was exhausted, so community themes draw mainly on Steam reviews plus Metacritic and Wikipedia.

games.name: Peglin
games.short_description: Peglin is a Pachinko Roguelike - Fight enemies by collecting special orbs and popping pegs to deal damage. Acquire special relics that radically change the game and ensure no two runs are the same. Aim carefully to survive in this unique turn-based RPG!

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Peglin is a Peggle-style roguelike where you launch a ball at pegs and the result damages enemies. He calls it a great example of someone taking a unique idea and making it a roguelike. He has put hundreds of hours into it over several years and keeps returning as it gets regular updates. He places it in S tier, while saying it is not quite the masterpiece of the other S tier games.
praise: Every run feels very different thanks to varied builds, characters and relics
Many unique orbs and events keep fights fun and engaging
Strong blend of RNG and skill, with deserved broken runs now and then
Continuous updates add new characters and orbs roughly monthly
Good pacing, helped by an option to speed up the game
Well-executed roguelike design overall
criticism: Gameplay looks a bit old or slow at first glance, though speed-up mitigates it
Not quite as masterful as the top S tier games
Needs more attention and visibility
unique_points: Fuses Peggle-style ball physics with roguelike build-crafting
Player skill matters alongside RNG, unusual for a luck-based genre
commentary.quote: it has no right being this good it is an absolute s tier for me
design_criteria: Run variety: builds, characters, relics make each run distinct
Synergies and broken runs: rare overpowered runs feel earned
Skill vs RNG: a balanced blend
Content and support: frequent updates with new characters and orbs
Pacing: speed-up option keeps runs moving
Event and orb diversity: many unique options keep fights engaging

community.one_liner: A Peggle-style pachinko roguelite from Red Nexus Games where you launch orbs at pegs to damage enemies while collecting relics and upgrading orbs across a run.
community.consensus_summary: Peglin is well liked by players (Steam 'Very Positive', about 84% of roughly 17.7k reviews) and mixed-to-favorable among the few critics who covered it (Metacritic 76 from 8 reviews on Switch, user score 6.9 from 29 ratings). The core loop of bouncing orbs around a peg board and building synergies with relics is widely called addictive and great for short sessions, including on Steam Deck, Switch and mobile. The recurring complaints are heavy RNG, only three acts for most of the game's life, steep late-game (Cruciball) difficulty and repetition. It launched in Early Access in April 2022, hit 1.0 and Switch on Aug 27, 2024, and is still being updated; a 2.0 update in March 2026 reportedly added a fourth act, new items, enemies and music.
best_things: The Peggle-meets-Slay-the-Spire premise is fresh and the core loop of aiming, bouncing and watching damage numbers climb is described as satisfying and dopamine-heavy
Easy to learn and pick up; runs are short (one reviewer averages about 50 minutes) and the game can be saved and resumed, which suits casual or chill play
Build variety through orbs and relics; finding a combination that clicks and improvising around what you are offered is a common highlight
Multiple characters and the Cruciball difficulty ladder give replay value and let players choose between relaxed and punishing runs
Charming pixel art and music, and a developer team that keeps patching and is praised for listening to feedback
Works well on handheld and mobile (Steam Deck, Switch); Metacritic critics singled out the Switch version
Very high playtimes among fans (several reviewers report 250 to over 2,000 hours)
worst_things: Heavy RNG: orb trajectories are hard to control, so luck can outweigh skill, which critics and many negative Steam reviews cite
Limited content for a long stretch: only three acts plus a final boss, so runs feel samey and players can see everything quickly (the 2026 fourth act is meant to address this)
Uneven option balance: some relics and orbs are seen as near-useless while others are mandatory at higher difficulty
Cruciball levels add nerfs and tougher enemies rather than new mechanics, which some see as lazy difficulty scaling
Some enemy types and encounters (long-range damage you cannot avoid, the Wall boss, lines of exploding goblins) are cited as run-ending regardless of build
Unlocking characters and the true ending relies on grinding large counters such as debuffs applied or coins spent
Synergy traps: boss orbs with negative damage can silently break builds if you do not know how items interact
Price ($19.99) is questioned by some given the amount of content; many recommend buying on sale
improvements: More acts, areas, enemies, characters, orbs and relics; a recurring request even from positive reviewers
An endless or post-final-boss mode so players can keep testing builds and see new orbs without risking them early in a run
Let players choose map routes instead of having to shoot a ball and hope it lands on the desired path
Rework the late-game difficulty so it comes from interesting enemy design rather than stat nerfs and unavoidable damage
Better balance and clearer communication of item interactions and effect names for new players
Revisit the anti-save-scum behavior added in late Oct 2025 that, per a top negative review, counts quitting and resuming after a short session as save scumming and can ruin the run
unique_things: Pachinko/Peggle physics as the combat system in a turn-based roguelite, where you aim at enemies and pegs rather than play cards
Orbs act as the deck: you add and upgrade orbs, and relics modify how pegs and damage behave
Board layout and peg interaction matter more than a typical deckbuilder, yet the goal is damage accumulation rather than clearing the board like Peggle
Cruciball difficulty system for scaling challenge after winning
Began as a 48-hour game jam prototype ('Goblin Drop') and later won Best Design at the 2022 Taipei Game Show per Wikipedia
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding character unlocks and the true ending via large cumulative counters
Repetition of the same three biomes and similar boss encounters across many runs
Navigating the map by shooting a ball and hoping it lands on the path you want
Late-game frustration at Cruciball 5+, where reviewers report physics feeling erratic, refresh orbs in awkward spots, and enemies that counter common builds
Runs that go badly snowball with little chance to recover, which some find miserable
Anti-save-scum rule after Oct 2025 interfering with short stop-and-resume sessions
divisive_points: RNG: fans see it as part of the fun and improvisation, detractors see gambling-like luck that undermines build planning
Difficulty: patches are said by some to make the game easier while others say higher Cruciball levels are unfairly stacked
Value: some call it one of the best games for the price, others say it is only worth it on sale due to limited content
Whether it plays like Peggle: some love the nostalgia, others note it plays quite differently and do not get the Peggle feel
community.reception_notes: Early Access on PC began April 25, 2022; mobile followed April 11, 2023; 1.0 and the Nintendo Switch release came Aug 27, 2024 (Steam lists this date). Wikipedia says it sold about 400,000 copies in its first year in Early Access. Steam-revenue-calculator estimates about $14.9M gross and $4.4M net revenue, and SteamSpy-style data gives 500k to 1M owners; both are estimates, not audited. Version 2.0 (March 16, 2026) reportedly added a fourth act, items, enemies and music. Steam reviews from late 2025 include a controversy over anti-save-scum changes, and recent reviews remain mostly positive with ongoing developer support. Metacritic has few scores (8 critic, 29 user) so they are a weak signal. Steam lists Windows and Mac only; Switch and mobile exist separately. No OpenCritic listing could be confirmed; the web search budget was exhausted, so Reddit and outlet reviews could not be fetched (Reddit fetch was blocked).

games.name: Revita
games.short_description: In this fast paced twin-stick roguelite platformer, you play as an unnamed child ascending an ominous clocktower in pursuit of their lost memories. Harvest and sacrifice souls to grow your power in order to challenge procedural encounter rooms and intimidating bosses!

placements.verbal_evidence: none

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Revita is a 2D action dungeon-crawler roguelike where your health doubles as currency, so every purchase costs HP. He loves it and calls it one of his favorite roguelikes these days, plans a 100 percent achievement run, and thinks it deserves far more attention. He stresses it is packed with content and builds, but is not for everyone since it demands comfort with action roguelikes. Bugs and broken item interactions hold it back from topping Gungeon. No tier letter is spoken in this segment.
praise: Health-as-currency gimmick creates a strong risk/reward loop that rewards skilled players
Huge amount of content: many builds, items, guns and customizations
Every run feels different from the start and ends differently
Hub world with purchasable options, plenty of secrets and hidden worlds
Builds can feel genuinely overpowered, with good balance of skill and luck
Strong Gungeon inspiration; he keeps returning to it and calls it a new favorite
criticism: Many bugs, including ones that blocked achievements during his completion attempt
Many item combinations do not interact as expected (e.g. laser beam and split bullets)
Health-as-currency is risky design: struggling players snowball downward and cannot buy anything
Not recommendable to players uncomfortable with action roguelikes
Promised update still not released
unique_points: Health is the currency; everything you do costs HP
Design snowballs in both directions: comfortable players get easier runs, strugglers get harder ones
commentary.quote: it's still one of my favorite new roguelikes out there
design_criteria: Risk vs reward: health as currency rewards mastery but punishes strugglers
Content volume: many items, guns, builds and secrets
Build variety: each run starts and ends differently
Synergies: powerful builds feel good, but some combos are unimplemented
Polish/bugs: bugs and broken interactions cost it against Gungeon
Accessibility: requires comfort with action roguelikes
Meta-progression: hub world with purchasable things

community.one_liner: A twin-stick, pixel-art roguelite platformer by BenStar in which an amnesiac child climbs a clocktower and spends their own health as currency for relics and upgrades.
community.consensus_summary: Revita is well liked by the players who stick with it: Steam sits at Very Positive (about 81% of roughly 2,400 reviews) and Metacritic shows 78 from 11 critics, with a user score of 8.1 from only 14 ratings. Praise centres on the tight twin-stick feel, the risk/reward health-as-currency loop, the art and music, and deep unlock-driven replayability. Detractors find the rooms claustrophobic, the weapons short-ranged, items weak or flat stat bumps, and progression slow and RNG-heavy. The game is effectively abandoned: the planned 2.0 update was halted in late 2023 due to money problems, but a 2.0 beta branch on Steam contains much of the finished work and is widely recommended. It is a recognized hidden gem that rarely appears on big roguelite lists.
best_things: Health-as-currency loop: you pay HP for chests, relics and upgrades, which makes every hit and every purchase a real risk/reward decision
Tight, responsive twin-stick movement and shooting that several reviewers say feels snappy and satisfying
Pixel art, atmosphere and soundtrack are repeatedly called beautiful; some compare the mood to Hollow Knight
Steady drip-feed of unlocks, relics, tickets and secrets, plus relic synergies that keep runs unpredictable
Ticket system lets you opt into more difficulty for more power, plus ascension-style (shard) difficulty ramping
Cryptic, interesting lore and a true ending that keeps some players hooked across many runs
Polish and respect for player time: snappy transitions, light hardware demands (runs on integrated graphics), very cheap on sale
Critics (GameCritics, GamingTrend, Nintendo World Report, PLAY! Zine at 80) praised balance, satisfying combat, smooth platforming and fresh-feeling runs
worst_things: Claustrophobic, chokepointed rooms; some later rooms and boss arenas make enemies hard to reach or avoid
Short weapon range, bullet spread and self-knockback make aiming feel imprecise and damage feel cheap
Poor visual clarity: semi-transparent foreground elements hide bullets, traps blend into levels, and some enemy attacks have weak tells
Many items and upgrades are flat stat boosts (a few percent damage or fire rate) that do not change gameplay
Heavy RNG and snowballing: chests reveal contents only after you pay HP, and taking damage early can leave you unable to buy anything
Controller support criticised: right-stick aiming feels off, confirm/back buttons follow Nintendo layout, reported gamepad complaints on PC

Bugs and rough edges reported: cannot quit from main menu, accidental return-to-metro wipes a run with no confirmation, some max-health mechanic reports, a startup-screen ad for a plush no longer sold
Development abandoned, so these issues will not get official fixes beyond what is in the beta
improvements: Faster early meta-progression so varied, powerful builds arrive sooner (several positive reviewers also say this)
More interesting, gameplay-altering items and more distinct weapons instead of small numeric boosts; more than one character and few choices per run is a recurring gripe
Open up rooms and boss arenas and improve visual clarity and enemy telegraphing (the 2.0 beta reportedly addresses claustrophobic rooms)
Better guidance on secret progression, such as the post-Shard-5 alternate biome unlock conditions that players say they only found by googling
Polish controller aim and button mapping, and add confirmation before abandoning a run or quitting
Faster transitions and loading between rooms; some players call the lift/loading/spawn waits too long, though others praise the transitions
unique_things: Your health bar is your currency: you convert souls into permanent max HP, then spend HP on relics, chests and upgrades
Twin-stick shooter combined with 2D platforming and wall jumps in a roguelite structure
Soul-harvesting and sacrifice theme in a clocktower tied to the five stages of grief, with cryptic lore and a bleak true ending
Ticket system that trades extra difficulty for power before each run, plus shard-based ascension difficulty
Secret alternate biomes unlocked by obscure conditions (for example breaking hidden beehives), plus a fishing minigame
Curses you can stack that restrict you only in specific, circumventable ways
tedious_or_disliked: Slow meta-currency accumulation; most run items are locked behind it, so early runs feel limited
Getting the true ending requires repeated clears, which some find exhausting
Obscure, niche secret-unlock requirements for late content that feel undiscoverable without a guide
Being starved of HP or starved of items; any damage reduces what you can buy, so careful no-hit play is required to progress
Boss fights described as health sponges, and difficulty ramps slowly for some players who quit around shard 2
Bleak ending in which the player character dies, which one reviewer found off-putting
divisive_points: Health-as-currency: praised as the defining hook and depth of the game by many, called frustrating and a gamble by others who compare it unfavourably to Isaac devil deals
Difficulty: some say it is challenging but fair and finished a run on the second attempt, others find it punishing or tedious; both views appear in the same Steam reviews
Abandonment: some reviewers mark the game down because updates stopped, while long-time players say it already feels complete and the beta adds plenty
Run variety: fans cite synergies and constant unlocks, critics cite one character, one style of weapon and samey stat-boost items
community.reception_notes: Launched April 21, 2022 on Switch and Windows; PlayStation and Xbox versions followed April 20, 2023, and Red Art Games released a physical edition in late 2023. A major 2.0 update was announced in April 2023 but development stopped around October 2023 because of financial difficulties, and the developer reportedly said in Discord that the project was abandoned for budget reasons. The last official update was in 2024, and a Steam 2.0 beta branch holds much of the finished content and tweaks. Several reviewers mention a wish that BenStar would return. One reviewer mentions unspecified political issues around the developer. Steam price $16.99, frequently discounted to about $5. Steam-revenue-calculator estimates roughly $1.0M gross and about $296k net, with SteamSpy owners at about 200k to 500k; these are rough estimates, not audited figures. OpenCritic score not found (page could not be retrieved); Steam lists no Metacritic score in its data. Reddit and Push Square fetches were blocked, and web search budget was exhausted, so community coverage relies mainly on Steam reviews and forum topics.

games.name: Risk of Rain 2

other_scores.source: Steam DLC: Seekers of the Storm

placements.verbal_evidence: "going to be an easy s tier for me ... it's still going to be an S tier that's for sure"

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Risk of Rain 2 is the 3D third-person shooter sequel to the 2D original, widely popular and heavily updated with patches and DLC. He loves it: the core shooting is so fun that it never gets old even though runs start fairly similarly. The constant stream of items keeps the character feeling steadily stronger. He places it in S tier, noting he plays it less these days than Peglin or Ravenous-style favourites, but it still earns the top spot.
praise: Core gameplay is so enjoyable it does not get old despite few starting customizations
Constant item drops (roughly five to ten per level) keep the player feeling rewarded and increasingly powerful
Huge item pool means steady power growth with core abilities even if individual items are not game-changing
The jump from 2D to 3D works amazingly well as a shooter
Many secrets, areas, biomes and bosses to discover
Varied characters with slight ability customization at the start
Visually pleasing, great multiplayer, and lots of updates and DLC
criticism: Runs start fairly similarly from run to run with few early customizations
Many items do not drastically change gameplay
unique_points: Rare case of a sequel moving from 2D to 3D successfully
Always-flowing reward loop from items compensates for limited starting variety
Easy to pick up, hard to master
commentary.quote: it's going to be an easy S tier for me
design_criteria: Core gameplay feel: fun enough to carry the game on its own
Item frequency and rewards: constant drops drive a sense of power growth
Item diversity: large pool, though individually modest
Starting variety: limited, but judged not to matter
Content and exploration: secrets, biomes, bosses
Accessibility: easy to play, hard to master
Level length: levels last several minutes
Visuals and multiplayer: noted as positives but not affecting the rating
commentary.rerank_note: Rated with the new content and DLC factored in; no explicit move from a prior tier stated.

community.one_liner: A 3D third-person co-op action roguelite by Hopoo Games in which you fight through escalating waves on an alien planet, stacking hundreds of items into absurd power builds before the difficulty clock overwhelms you.
community.consensus_summary: Risk of Rain 2 is widely regarded as one of the defining action roguelites: Steam lists it at about 94% positive across roughly 353k reviews, Metacritic critics give it 85, and outlets called it among the best roguelikes, especially in co-op. Praise centers on the item-stacking power fantasy, the character roster and the soundtrack. It left early access (March 2019) for 1.0 in August 2020 and has kept receiving paid expansions (Survivors of the Void 2022, Seekers of the Storm 2024, Alloyed Collective Nov 2025). The main friction today is less the game than its ownership: after Gearbox bought the IP in 2022 and 2K/Take-Two's EULA (mandatory arbitration) was added, many long-time players leave negative reviews while still praising gameplay.
best_things: Item stacking snowballs builds from a plain pistol into screen-filling chain reactions; the power-fantasy and 'one more run' loop is the core praise
Huge item pool and synergies reward experimentation and produce very different runs
Survivor roster plays distinctly, each with unlockable skill variants and alternate loadouts that add mastery depth
Co-op with friends (up to 4) is cited as the best way to play and the main reason people buy it
Stylish cel-shaded look and a widely loved soundtrack
Difficulty scales continuously in real time, so pacing and risk/reward (when to open chests versus finish the stage) stay tense
Lots of unlockables, artifacts, Eclipse difficulties and mods give hundreds of hours of replay; reviewers report 100-300+ hours
Post-launch support over several years, with Alloyed Collective seen by some as repairing the goodwill lost by Seekers of the Storm
worst_things: One-shot deaths from enemies or bosses (Brass Contraption, Elder Lemurian, Void Reavers) feel unfair when you are otherwise stacked with defence
Late-game screens fill with particles and effects until they are unreadable, and huge item counts can tank FPS
Repetitive environments and limited story, which critics flagged in reviews
Enemy variety feels thin to some players, and runs can feel like searching for the teleporter
Multiplayer desyncs, lobby failures and mid-run crashes reported since the Gearbox-era updates, with no reconnect option
Gearbox/2K ownership: a later EULA with mandatory arbitration and the console-port codebase drove waves of negative Steam reviews despite high playtime
Seekers of the Storm launched buggy and unbalanced (DLC alone sits around 54% positive on Steam)
No mid-run save, so long runs are all-or-nothing
improvements: Reduce or add options to tone down visual clutter and performance drops in late-game item-heavy runs
Better onboarding: new players report struggling to find the teleporter and learn mechanics, and only discover helper settings by accident
Fix long-standing multiplayer desync, lobby and reconnect issues
Add mid-run saving or suspend to support 1-2 hour runs
Address one-shot mechanics and tune balance so defence builds are not negated by single attacks
Revert or clarify the EULA changes and give players a way to report bugs in-game
unique_things: 3D third-person shooter take on a roguelite, unlike 2D top-down peers like Isaac or Hades
No fixed run timer, but difficulty scales continuously with time spent: enemies get stronger the longer you stay, so pace is part of strategy
Items are almost all passive and stack without a cap, creating emergent build chaos rather than fixed builds
Looping the game (continuing past the final boss) and the Void, Lunar and Eclipse layers give it a long endgame
Lunar items are deliberate risk/reward trade-offs that can cost you mobility or your whole inventory
Teleporter boss fights plus an open-ended hunt for chests, shrines and multishops in each stage
tedious_or_disliked: Hunting for the hidden teleporter on each stage can eat time; many players rely on the indicator settings
Shrine of Chance and other gambling objects feel punishing with low success rates
Unlocking all artifacts, skins and challenges can be grindy and repeats risky deaths
Long late-game loops where screens are unreadable and performance drops
Some find the game never clicks; a negative reviewer said they never felt like continuing despite good music, visuals and pacing
divisive_points: Difficulty and one-shot deaths: lovers call it fair rule-mastery, others call it cheap
Simple environments and visuals: praised as gameplay-first clarity by some, called tech-demo-like by others
Whether the paid expansions (especially Seekers of the Storm) improved or diluted the game
Whether to recommend the game at all, given the Gearbox/Take-Two EULA, with many positive-playtime reviewers voting down on principle
community.reception_notes: Early access launched March 2019 and drew over 650,000 players in week one and over a million sales in the first month; PC sales passed 4 million by March 2021 (Wikipedia). Full 1.0 release was Aug 11, 2020, consoles Oct 2020, PS5/Xbox Series in Aug 2024. SteamSpy estimates 5-10 million owners and the steam-revenue-calculator estimate is around $264M gross / $78M net (rough Boxleiter-method estimates, not audited). Gearbox acquired the IP in Nov 2022 and Hopoo Games went on hiatus in Sept 2024 when key developers joined Valve. Steam now shows wave of negative reviews tied to a newer EULA with mandatory arbitration and to multiplayer desync, even from players with hundreds of hours. Some sources saw web-search limits: OpenCritic page could not be fetched, so the opencritic score is null (Wikipedia mentions 93% recommend). Steam store page fetch showed 95% of 163k reviews, apparently a cached older number; local data shows 93.8% of 353k.

games.name: Slay the Spire
games.short_description: We fused card games and roguelikes together to make the best single player deckbuilder we could. Craft a unique deck, encounter bizarre creatures, discover relics of immense power, and Slay the Spire!

other_scores.score: Overwhelmingly Positive, 97.5% positive of about 218,968 reviews

placements.verbal_evidence: even without mods uh this is still a masterpiece that's an S tier for me

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Slay the Spire is the deck-building roguelike that kicked off the whole genre, and most later deck-builders descend from it. He calls it the most perfectly designed deck-builder and says it is his favorite roguelike right now, with more Steam playtime than any other game. He also thinks it is the ideal entry point to the genre because it is the simplest yet best-designed of them all. The huge modding scene adds to his love, but he says it is an S-tier masterpiece even without mods.
praise: Cards are very well balanced: none feels overpowered or useless, and each can be played several ways
Many characters with many different builds
Relics act as run-long passives that change how you play, so every run feels different
Unlocking a new card pick after the first run makes runs feel unique early on
Huge modding community adds new characters, worlds and DLC-like content; he plays almost only modded now
Simplest and best-designed deck-builder, so ideal for introducing newcomers to the genre
Lasting appeal: he has played since release and followed every update
criticism: Visuals are not especially impressive
Music is merely fine
No new official updates or DLC at this point
You cannot customize your starting deck
unique_points: It pioneered the deck-building roguelike genre and inspired nearly every game in it
Modding scene is among the biggest in roguelikes, with a recent expansion built by roughly 70 modders over years
Card and relic balance keeps variety high without any dominant or dead options
commentary.quote: this is still a masterpiece that's an S tier for me
design_criteria: Balance: no card is overpowered or useless
Build diversity: many characters and many viable builds
Synergies and run variety: relics change playstyle each run
Replayability and longevity: years of play, mod support
Accessibility: simple, good for newcomers
Visuals and audio: acknowledged as average but not important to him
Meta-progression: new card choices unlock after first run
Community and modding: huge, though he tries not to let it sway the rating

community.one_liner: A single-player roguelike deckbuilder by Mega Crit where you climb a three-act tower with one of four characters, building a fresh deck from card, relic and potion rewards each run.
community.consensus_summary: Slay the Spire is widely treated as the genre-defining roguelike deckbuilder. Critics were near-unanimous (Metacritic PC 89 from 24 reviews, all positive; a 98% critic-recommend figure is cited via Wikipedia (OpenCritic page not re-verified)) and Steam players rate it Overwhelmingly Positive at about 97.5% across roughly 219k reviews. Praise centres on tight card design, readable decisions and enormous replayability. The recurring dissent, mostly from a small negative minority on Steam, is about RNG and loss feeling undeserved. It launched in Early Access in Nov 2017 and hit 1.0 in Jan 2019, then spread to consoles and mobile. Its sequel, Slay the Spire 2, entered Early Access in March 2026 .
best_things: Card and relic synergies reward experimentation; players report discovering new builds after hundreds or thousands of hours
Highly addictive one-more-run loop: top-voted reviews show players at 150-680 hours and joking about losing sleep and study time
Four characters (Ironclad, Silent, Defect, Watcher) play very differently and each has multiple archetypes
Branching map with visible elites, shops, rest sites and events turns pathing into a clear risk-versus-reward decision that many later roguelikes copied
Enemies telegraph their intents, so combat is puzzle-like and deaths can usually be traced to a decision
Ascension levels (20 of them) plus the Heart ending give a very deep difficulty curve that keeps veterans challenged
Fast, pick-up-and-stop session format: no timers, save anytime, works offline and on handhelds, and easy to play in short bursts
Reviewers say it is accessible to people with no card-game experience while still having high depth
Strong value: frequently discounted heavily, and cited in reviews as a bargain for the hours delivered
worst_things: RNG in card rewards, relic offers and boss/elite draws can doom a run early, which is the dominant complaint in Steam negative reviews
Some bosses and encounters hard-counter certain decks; the final act and Heart fight demand specific setups that can feel like a check against the build you drew
Losses after long runs can feel undeserved or like gambling rather than skill, per several negative reviews
Characters are felt to be unevenly strong by some players, with some bosses being harsh on particular characters
Visual style is functional rather than beautiful; even positive reviews call the art plain
Console and mobile versions stopped receiving updates after Humble Games' publishing arm shut down in July 2024
No undo button, which players say makes misclicks and misreads costly
improvements: More randomness mitigation or reroll-type tools in normal runs (the Custom/constructed style modes are said to build decks that feel like cheating)
An undo or take-back option for accidental plays
Better balance between characters and against specific boss matchups
Less punishing early difficulty scaling and a gentler on-ramp to ascensions for newer players
Faster, more satisfying unlock progression, since players find unlocking cards via slow XP on each run dull
unique_things: Helped define the roguelike deckbuilder genre; its map, relic and card-reward structure was widely imitated
Enemy intent display turns each fight into a deterministic puzzle layered on top of draw randomness
Permanent meta progression is only unlocks, not stat upgrades, so every run starts equal
Deck thinning and deck-size control as a core skill: adding cards is often a mistake
A deep ascension ladder plus an optional Heart fight extend the game far beyond a first win
Has a robust mod and Workshop scene, including large fan expansions such as Downfall
tedious_or_disliked: Runs that blur together for some players; a few say the loop lacked the one-more-run pull after the first dozens of hours
Slow unlock XP that gates cards per character, which some call grindy
High win-rate grind to climb ascensions, with some players stuck near a 20% win rate and reporting frustration
Losing a long run to one bad draw or burst boss attack and having to restart from floor 1
Having to build towards the final boss while surviving the regular fights on the way up
divisive_points: RNG versus skill: fans say good play mitigates bad draws, critics say randomness overwhelms the strategy
Difficulty and ascension grind: veterans love the ceiling, newcomers find the learning curve steep
No run-to-run power progression: praised as pure skill, disliked as a lack of persistent reward by some reviewers
Endgame Heart and act 4 requirements: considered a great climax by some and an annoying build check by others
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched Nov 2017 with slow initial sales (around 2,000 copies), then took off after a large Chinese streamer featured it; it reached Steam's second best-selling slot in Jan 2018, passed 1 million copies by June 2018 and 1.5 million by March 2019. 1.0 released Jan 23, 2019, followed by PS4 (May 2019), Switch (June 2019), Xbox One (Aug 2019), iOS (June 2020) and Android (Feb 2021). It won or was nominated for multiple 2019 awards (IGN Best Strategy Game of 2019, PC Gamer Best Design 2019). Third-party estimates put Steam gross revenue near $200M and developer net near $59M (Boxleiter-style estimate, not audited), and SteamSpy-style data puts owners at 5-10 million. Steam concurrent players still around 15k per the data file. Slay the Spire 2 entered Early Access on March 5, 2026 (co-op up to 4 players, Godot engine). Console and mobile ports stopped being updated after Humble Games' publishing division shut in July 2024.
