games.name: Balatro
games.short_description: The poker roguelike. Balatro is a hypnotically satisfying deckbuilder where you play illegal poker hands, discover game-changing jokers, and trigger adrenaline-pumping, outrageous combos.

other_scores.source: Steam user reviews (97.8% positive, ~199k reviews, Overwhelmingly Positive)

placements.verbal_evidence: that's why it's going to be an S tier for me

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Balatro is a solo-developed poker-themed deck-building roguelike that exploded in popularity seemingly out of nowhere. He argues the hype is justified: it is extremely simple to understand yet strategically deep, and it is intensely satisfying thanks to multiplicative score scaling. He recommends it to nearly anyone and places it in S tier. His main reservation is that it is currently unbalanced, though a joker-rebalancing update was imminent.
praise: Among the simplest deck builders: few keywords, quick poker tutorial, no poker knowledge needed
Simple mechanics combined with deep strategy, which he sees as the best kind of design
Extremely satisfying multiplicative combos and huge exploding numbers
Fast deck changes, frequent discards, and quick access to jokers make every run differ early
Rewards game-breaking builds without making them trivial, since you must understand the mechanics
Normal difficulty goes effectively infinite so you can keep scaling until the game catches up
Quick-paced runs that are easy to restart over and over
criticism: Currently pretty unbalanced, with lots of tweaking still possible
Some runs feel normal and unremarkable unless you find and plan around a build
Score beyond the target gives no extra reward, so huge numbers are purely for fun
unique_points: Poker hands as the core deck-building twist, making it approachable to anyone
Exponential multiplier scaling as a central satisfaction engine
Endless mode on normal difficulty means players chase breaking the game rather than higher difficulties
Design lesson: approachability plus strategic depth drove its broad appeal
commentary.quote: it's one of the easier games out there to break and yet still feel rewarding
design_criteria: Simplicity and approachability: few keywords, easy onboarding for any audience
Strategic depth: easy to learn but hard to master
Satisfaction/feel: multiplicative combos and big numbers
Synergies and build diversity: jokers and deck changes create varied runs
Balance: currently unbalanced, patch incoming
Run length and pacing: fast runs with quick deck churn keep replays fresh
Difficulty scaling: infinite normal mode rewards game-breaking
Risk vs reward: breaking the game is rewarding but requires mechanical understanding

commentary.label: Top 10 of 2024 (#1)
commentary.summary: Balatro is a poker-based deck-building roguelike where you play poker hands to beat score targets across eight antes, modifying your deck, upgrading hands and collecting Jokers. He calls it simple to learn but hard to master, and names it his favorite roguelike of the year, placing it at number one. He especially values the variety of builds, the earned feeling of a powerful run, and a well-balanced endless mode with huge numbers.
praise: Simple mechanics with deep strategy, which he sees as the foundation of a great strategy roguelike
Every Joker is unique, enabling many builds so runs feel different from each other
Powerful builds feel earned through knowledge and timing, like in The Binding of Isaac
Endless mode is enjoyable and addicting, and achievements still unlock there
Exponential score growth is implemented well and stays balanced despite many ways to multiply points
Audio-visual feedback is very satisfying: the point-counting sound and the score catching fire at high numbers
Varied starting decks and difficulty options give replayability and challenge
criticism: Reaching huge scores requires luck plus a lot of game knowledge
Not every run ends in a monstrous build, though he says the gameplay remains fun regardless
unique_points: Poker deck-builder hybrid where Jokers act as passive abilities driving build variety
Exponential growth is notoriously hard to balance in roguelikes, yet Balatro handles it better than anything he has seen
Endless mode that is genuinely fun, with achievements still unlockable
commentary.quote: this is my favorite rogl I've played this year
design_criteria: Simplicity vs depth: easy to understand, hard to master
Build diversity: unique Jokers give a wide range of strategies
Synergies and scaling: exponential growth balanced well
Earned power fantasy: overpowered runs feel earned by knowledge
Endless mode: enjoyable and keeps achievements active
Audio/visual feedback: satisfying counting sound and flaming score
Replayability: varied starting decks and difficulty options

community.one_liner: A poker-themed roguelike deckbuilder by solo dev LocalThunk in which you play (deliberately illegal) poker hands and stack Joker modifiers to beat escalating score targets.
community.consensus_summary: Balatro is one of the most acclaimed indie releases of the decade: Metacritic 90 from 32 critics (100% positive), OpenCritic 92 with 100% of critics recommending, and Steam shows about 97.8% positive across roughly 199k reviews (Overwhelmingly Positive). Critics compared it directly to Slay the Spire and called it extremely addictive and easy to pick up; players echo this and most of the negativity is about RNG-heavy high difficulties rather than the base game. It is not early access, but the long-promised 1.1 content update was delayed into 2026 (developer declined a 2025 date to avoid crunch), which some players read as the game being slow-moving or abandoned. It sold over 5 million copies by January 2025, and later won multiple awards (Game Developers Choice GOTY, Game Awards indie and debut categories, BAFTA Debut).
best_things: Extremely addictive 'one more run' loop: short runs, instant restarts, and big satisfying score cascades
Joker synergies and combo-building (retriggers, scaling jokers, Blueprint/DNA-style engines) create wildly different runs and 'broken build' payoffs
Easy to learn even for people who do not know poker; the run-info screen teaches hands visually and the game pulls in non-roguelike players
Juicy presentation: screen feel, animations, sound design and the chill, catchy soundtrack are repeatedly praised
Distinct pixel-art joker designs and overall CRT-like style give it a strong identity
Great value at about $15 with hundreds of hours of play for many, plus a huge unlock list (decks, vouchers, stakes) for completionists
Low system requirements and wide availability (PC, Mac, mobile, consoles); short runs suit mobile and handheld play
Made by one person, which reviewers and players treat as part of its appeal
worst_things: Luck dominates at higher stakes: players say skill matters less and run quality is decided by shop and joker RNG, with stacked RNG layers (shop, boss blinds, draws, probabilistic cards like Wheel of Fortune)
All-or-nothing blinds: missing a target by a hair ends the run, so losing is abrupt and feels bad rather than a slow, engaging struggle
Higher stakes remove resources (fewer discards, less income, stickers) which pushes players toward a narrow set of viable builds (high card, pairs) and away from straights and flushes
Some players find few meaningful decisions after the first few rounds once a build direction is locked in
Joker pool dilution as more jokers unlock: many weak or non-synergistic jokers clog shops, with no way to banish or curate them
Some find it designed to be compulsive rather than rewarding, leaving a flat or guilty feeling after wins
Progress does not sync between platforms (for example mobile and Steam), forcing players to unlock everything twice
Famously time-consuming: top Steam reviews joke about losing hours, 3 AM sessions and being unable to stop
improvements: Cross-platform progression sync (promised on a roadmap per Steam reviewers, still requested)
A way to curate the joker pool or banish unwanted jokers to fight dilution
Rework higher stakes and challenge decks so they demand skill and adaptation rather than more RNG and restarts
Reduce the grind of unlocking every stake on every deck (15 decks, many stakes)
More frequent content updates and communication about the delayed 1.1 update; the Matador joker and Blue Stake tweaks were previewed
Better balance of boss blinds, since a few are seen as run-killers with no time to pivot
unique_things: Takes poker hands as the combat system rather than fantasy combat, then breaks poker rules with jokers, so 'illegal poker' is the hook
Score is a chips-times-mult multiplication, so scaling comes from stacking multiplicative jokers into exponential numbers (players joke about e-notation scores)
Planet cards upgrade hand types, tarot and spectral cards edit the deck, so the deck itself is reshaped in play
Interest-based economy rewards saving money, creating constant spend-versus-save tension
Appeals to non-roguelike fans: reviewers called it a roguelike for people who do not like roguelikes
Cultural crossover reach: free Friends of Jimbo cosmetic packs (Witcher 3, Slay the Spire, Stardew Valley, etc.) and a cameo in a Black Mirror episode
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding stakes: players say one deck across all stakes, times 15 decks, means dozens of hours; one estimate cited 72 wins for the remaining decks' middle stakes
Gold Stake and above described as a slot-machine grind of rerolling the shop and restarting until a good joker appears
Restarting repeatedly on hard challenge decks when shops offer no scoring jokers early
100% completion and some achievements are seen as requiring RNG luck more than mastery
divisive_points: Whether higher stakes are satisfying challenge (risk and planning) or just RNG tedium; some love Gold Stake, others call it the game's weakest part
Is it deep strategy or a shallow dopamine machine? Critics praise layered systems while some Steam negatives call it not that deep
The addictive design: celebrated as pure fun by most, described as manipulative or guilt-inducing by a minority
Developer cadence: praised for avoiding crunch, but some players are frustrated by the delayed 1.1 update
community.reception_notes: Launched Feb 20, 2024 on PC and quickly became a breakout hit (over $1M in the first 8 hours and 1M copies in the first month, 5M+ by January 2025 per Wikipedia). Steam revenue estimator puts gross revenue at about $95M (Boxleiter-style estimate, not audited) and the Steam-owner estimate at 2-5M. Mobile launched Sept 2024 and Nintendo Switch 2 version Feb 2026; Metacritic platform scores are 90 (PC, PS5, Switch) and 95 (Xbox). Controversies: PEGI raised it to 18+ for gambling imagery (later appealed to 12+ in Feb 2025), and YouTube age-restricted many Balatro videos in March 2025. Patch 1.0.1c made the game easier. The promised 1.1 update slipped out of 2025 and the dev says it will be done when it is done. Steam page shows ongoing strong review scores through 2026.

games.name: Into the Breach
games.short_description: Control powerful mechs from the future to defeat an alien threat. Each attempt to save the world presents a new randomly generated challenge in this turn-based strategy game.

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put into the breach as an easy s tier; that is an easy s tier for me

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Into the Breach is a turn-based, board-centric tactics roguelike from the makers of FTL, where you control a small squad of mechs to defend cities from monsters. Mechanics are extremely simple, but the strategic depth is huge, to the point of spending many minutes on a single turn. He is blown away by how well designed it is and sees it as a staple of turn-based games. He places it in S tier and considers it better than FTL, possibly above Balatro.
praise: Very simple, easy-to-understand mechanics (shoot, jump, push) that still produce enormous strategic depth
Many meaningful options each turn even with only three or four mechs
Lots of different mechs, so squad formations make every run feel different
Unique little events and multiple difficulty levels give a lot of content for such a simple game
Accessible strategy for people who like turn-based games but lack patience for complex rulesets like Civilization
Does everything it sets out to do perfectly; masterful design
criticism: He acknowledges others may not consider it S tier; no real design flaws are named
A single turn can take up to ~10 minutes of deliberation (framed as a consequence of depth)
unique_points: Simple mechanics combined with simple enemy behavior yield near-limitless strategic options
Squad composition variety drives run-to-run freshness
Shows that great design can achieve huge depth with minimal rules
commentary.quote: this is a phenomenal game... design wise it's perfect
design_criteria: Simplicity of mechanics: individual effects and enemy behaviors are easy to understand
Strategic depth: many options per turn despite simple rules
Diversity: many mechs and squad formations change each run
Content/replayability: events and multiple difficulties
Accessibility: approachable for non-hardcore strategy players
Overall design polish: executes its goals perfectly

community.one_liner: A turn-based tactics roguelite from Subset Games (makers of FTL) where you pilot a squad of three mechs on tiny 8x8 grids to protect city buildings from insectoid Vek, with every enemy attack telegraphed in advance.
community.consensus_summary: Into the Breach is treated as a modern classic of the tactics and roguelite space. Critics gave it a Metacritic score of 90 on PC (89 on Switch), and it won Best Strategy Game at The Game Awards 2018, among other awards. Steam players agree, with about 94% positive across roughly 22,400 reviews (Very Positive). The praise centres on perfect-information combat, compact puzzle-like turns and squad variety. The main dissent is from players who find it more of a rigid puzzle game than a tactics game, and from those who still feel unavoidable spawn RNG can doom a run. It is not early access or abandoned. The free Advanced Edition update shipped in July 2022 alongside the Netflix mobile release, and players still ask for more content or a sequel.
best_things: Enemy attacks are telegraphed, so there are no hit-chance rolls. Losses feel like your own mistakes, which reviewers often contrast with XCOM.
Each turn is a self-contained micro-puzzle: pushing, pulling, blocking spawns and redirecting attacks, with depth coming from very simple rules.
Protecting the Power Grid (city buildings) rather than just killing everything is a fresh objective that changes how you evaluate every move.
Large variety of mech squads, pilots and weapon upgrades. Each squad teaches a different way to think about the game, and squad achievements hint at how to play them.
Short runs and short battles (roughly 10-15 minutes each) make it easy to pick up and put down, and it works well on Steam Deck and with a gamepad.
Economy of design: small maps, no filler, clean pixel art and a well-regarded soundtrack by Ben Prunty.
Difficulty ramps gradually, with Easy through Unfair settings, so players report steadily improving on squads that once beat them.
Runs are short enough that a blunder costs about 3 hours rather than a 15-hour XCOM-style campaign.
worst_things: Some players say it plays like a rigid puzzle game rather than a tactical one, with the board state mattering more than player choice.
Enemy spawn positions and targeting can create situations that feel unwinnable without grid damage, especially on the first turn of a mission or in the final island.
Losing a run discards upgrades. Some players find the penalty harsh when a poor upgrade choice only shows up an hour later.
Missions share the same core puzzle despite varied objectives, and some players report repetitiveness after a while.
The tutorial is thin and the legibility of threats and solutions is hard for newcomers, who often need external guides.
The unlock system (squads and pilots tied to achievements) is criticised by some as an FTL-style chore.
Steep difficulty: several negative reviewers say even Normal wipes them out repeatedly and the game is not for players who dislike punishing roguelikes.
Legibility of puzzles is hard: players struggle to tell whether a bad board needs a tradeoff or was set up wrong at the start.
improvements: Players keep asking for more content or a sequel, and several recent Steam reviewers say they return hoping for an update.
Better onboarding or in-game explanation of mechanics and enemy behaviour.
Some want more flexible undo, for example allowing a turn reset when it is the last unit's action.
More build and upgrade variety, and more map or mission variety, to reduce repetition.
Reduced luck in spawn placement, or more tools to recover from a bad spawn.
unique_things: Fully deterministic combat with visible enemy intentions: a tactics game built like a chess puzzle.
Health bar is the city Power Grid, so victory means damage mitigation rather than total elimination.
Time-travel framing: losing a run sends a chosen pilot back into a new timeline with their experience, giving a light meta-progression.
Enemy and environmental interactions such as water, ice, fire and mountains are central, and enemies can kill or block each other.
8x8 boards and five-turn missions give it a compactness unlike XCOM-style or Fire Emblem-style tactics games.
tedious_or_disliked: Restarting entire runs after a late failure, with upgrades lost.
Unlocking squads and pilots via achievements, which some find grindy.
Having to spend minutes planning single turns, which can feel like homework to people expecting a relaxed strategy game.
Learning curve where players feel they are being punished for not knowing enemy behaviour yet.
Once mechanics are 'solved', some reviewers feel runs become a repeated puzzle with the same base and little novelty.
divisive_points: Whether the RNG is a problem: fans say the game is essentially deterministic, while critics say spawns and targeting can make puzzles unsolvable.
Puzzle versus tactics: some see it as a perfect blend, others feel it lacks the tactical freedom they wanted.
Difficulty: some beat Unfair, others report never finishing Normal.
Run length and permadeath: fans value short restarts, detractors dislike losing progress.
community.reception_notes: Launched Feb 27, 2018 on Windows to acclaim and became Metacritic's best-reviewed PC game of 2018. It came to macOS and Switch in August 2018 and Linux in April 2020. The free Advanced Edition (July 19, 2022) added squads, pilots, enemies and an Unfair difficulty, and Netflix released iOS and Android versions the same day. Awards include Best Strategy Game at The Game Awards 2018, Best Design at the 2019 GDC Awards and Best Original Property at the BAFTA Games Awards. Steam Spy estimates 1-2 million owners, and steam-revenue-calculator estimates about $4.4M gross (a rough Boxleiter-method estimate, not audited). Metacritic user score of 7.8 is notably lower than the critic score, reflecting a minority who bounce off the puzzle feel and difficulty. OpenCritic score could not be retrieved (page lookup failed and the search budget was exhausted), so it is null.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Spiritfall is a 2D action roguelike with a Hades-style boon structure that plays like a platform fighter. He played it in Early Access and was excited for the full release. As a former competitive Smash player, he found the combat a natural fit and considers the gameplay outstanding. He calls it an easy S tier but says he would still put Hades above it, and admits some Smash bias.

Every weapon feels like a different character with its own moveset
Hades-style boons from gods, with fusions and combo boons, change how each weapon plays
Strong roguelike layer on top of excellent core gameplay, which is rare for combat-focused games
High replayability from different weapons, blessings and approaches each run
Good sense of progression, with visually distinct worlds and awesome bosses
Plenty to unlock and secrets, including a very hard secret true boss

Copies Hades' boon framework but applies it to a very different kind of combat
Each god's blessings drastically change how weapons are played

Replayability: weapon and boon combinations create different runs
Synergies and boons: fusion/combo boons exist but are less impactful than Hades
Meta-progression and content: lots to unlock and secrets, but wants more

commentary.label: Top 10 of 2024 (#4)
commentary.summary: Spiritfall is a 2D action roguelike heavily inspired by Hades, with the twist of being one of the few true fighting-game roguelikes. He recommends it to Smash Brothers fans, calling the combat crisp, deep and very satisfying. Runs vary a lot thanks to weapon and aspect choices plus blessing-driven builds. He ranks it fourth of the year and calls it one of his favorite games played that year, hoping for ongoing updates with more content.
praise: Crisp, extensive, very satisfying fighting-game-style combat with combos and a wide range of abilities
Surprising run-to-run variety; different ways to approach each encounter depending on enemy, boss and build
Weapons and aspects each feel like a brand new character, with strong move sets from the start of a run
Items and boons transform the core gameplay into unique builds with many synergies
Divine spirits offer three blessings each that enhance core mechanics with good variety and synergy
Fantastic audiovisuals; each biome feels unique and immersive, with great bosses and an amazing final encounter
criticism: Wants more content: secrets, different encounters and additional bosses
Hopes the developers keep updating the game, implying current content is limited

Character variety comes from weapons and aspects rather than selecting different characters
commentary.quote: spiritfall is one of my favorite games I've played this year
design_criteria: Combat feel: crisp, satisfying fighting-game combos and abilities
Build variety: weapons and aspects act as distinct characters
Synergies: boons and blessings create many build combinations
Run variety: encounters can be approached in different ways
Audiovisuals: unique, immersive biomes

community.one_liner: A 2D action roguelite by Gentle Giant (published by Team17) whose combat borrows from platform fighters like Smash Bros and Brawlhalla, wrapped in a Hades-style blessings-and-hub structure.
community.consensus_summary: Players like it a lot: Steam sits at Very Positive (about 93% of roughly 2,000 reviews, 92% of the most recent 30 days' small sample). Metacritic user score is 7.5 on only 15 ratings, and there are just 3 critic reviews, so no Metascore and no meaningful critic consensus exists. The dominant take is 'Hades meets Smash Bros', with praise for combat feel, weapons and the difficulty options. The recurring complaint is limited content: same bosses every run, few blessings, a solved feeling after several runs, and a 5-clear structure to see the real ending. It left Early Access (started Apr 2023) and launched 1.0 on Feb 28, 2024; there is no sign of abandonment, since reviews continue into late 2026, though the player base is small (steamspy est. 50k-100k owners, ~16 CCU).
best_things: Combat feels like a platform fighter: launching, wall-splatting and comboing enemies is described as satisfying, with very polished animation and hit feedback
Weapons are distinct from each other and have alternate forms (e.g. Sisterhood Gauntlets, scythe) that change playstyle
150+ blessings, elemental upgrades and assist/bolt abilities that synergise; reviewers say few feel unimpactful
Adjustable difficulty and accessibility options are praised, letting weaker players finish the story
Hand-drawn, Miyazaki-flavoured art and a strong soundtrack (though one critic found the music forgettable)
Permanent upgrades between runs feel meaningful without being mandatory; hidden rifts and secrets reward exploration
Scope is reasonable and what is there is polished; $19.99 price viewed as fair, especially on sale
worst_things: Low content: the same bosses on the same levels every run and every clear, so it feels repetitive after roughly 6-10 hours
Finishing requires about 5 full clears, and the final payoff is reported as just one extra boss phase, which many call anticlimactic
Only a limited number of blessings/relics and repeated active abilities and status effects; some feel they have solved the game after a couple of runs
Much of the combat is 'ragdolling' enemies in hitstun; true platform-fighter play (knockoffs, edge-guarding) mostly appears only in rifts or the last area
Crowds of overlapping 2D enemies are hard to read, leading to cheap hits and spam-the-dash/projectile play
Enemy telegraphs reported as mismatched with real attack timing; some mobs ignore hitstun to add artificial difficulty
Weak plot and sparse lore; story is minimal and sprinkled in

Reported bugs: credits freeze/loop on completion, brief freezes, enemies attacking before level entry, a boss path glitch, new saves granting achievements; Steam Deck black-screen at launch per ImpulseGamer

Weapon quality is uneven per several negative reviews: outside the fists many weapons are called slow and clunky, with combos that do not mesh with most blessings; the top negative review says knockoff play only appears in the final area or bonus fights
Some players report launch/graphics problems (black screen on Steam Deck, graphics glitching on launch, one refund over it), so performance is not universally smooth
improvements: More bosses, more rooms/biome variety and procedural variation so runs differ more
More blessings, weapon movesets and build synergies to avoid the feeling of solving the game
Make movement/tech (e.g. wavedash and other advanced platform-fighter mechanics) available earlier instead of behind skill unlocks
Better enemy readability and clearer, consistent telegraphs in crowded fights
Smarter difficulty curve: late-tier modifiers are said to spike damage; first two bosses can be harder than the last
A more rewarding ending and stronger narrative for the multi-clear structure; ability to reset permanent upgrades; clearer info on secrets
unique_things: Combat built on platform-fighter ideas (knockback, launching, wall-splat, sweet spots) rather than standard hack-and-slash
Hades-like structure with Slay-the-Spire-style node map for choosing rooms and shared HP across a run
Weapons with alternate forms that change inputs and moveset
Hidden rift rooms that turn into one-on-one knockback duels for extra loot
Hard versions of bosses and Pact-like challenge modifiers after the first clear, plus a boss-rush room
Runs on Mac (no Linux build) and offers granular difficulty adjustment
tedious_or_disliked: Repeating the same boss lineup five times to reach the ending
Grinding skill points and permanent upgrades after the first clear; unlock gating of core moves
Long stretches of low-threat filler rooms before a boss, since shared HP makes small rooms unchallenging
Shielded bosses that do not flinch, which negates the combo-heavy combat exactly where challenge lives
High-tier modifier runs needing a precise build, making 10-skull clears feel unreachable for some
Visual clutter and cheap damage when many enemies and effects are on screen
divisive_points: Whether it truly delivers platform-fighter depth: fans of Smash/Brawlhalla call it a great fit, while competitive fighter players call it bare-bones with no real shield/dodge/grab
Responsiveness and movement: praised as fluid by many, described as sluggish or non-responsive by others
Derivative vs fresh: labelled 'Hades clone' by some critics/users, called one of the most innovative roguelites by others
Value: fine at $19.99 for some, only worth it on discount for others given the content volume
Weapon feel: praised as distinct and build-changing by many, called clunky and poorly synergised with blessings by others
community.reception_notes: Metacritic has only 3 critic reviews (95, 90, 66), so no Metascore; Metacritic user score is 7.5 from 15 ratings. No OpenCritic page could be confirmed (search was unavailable and the guessed page belonged to another game), so opencritic is null. Early Access ran from Apr 3, 2023 to the 1.0 launch on Feb 28, 2024. Steam revenue-calculator estimate is about $1.2M gross / $353k net (Boxleiter-style, unaudited). Platforms: Windows and Mac on Steam, no Linux. Some copies were distributed via the Jingle Jam charity bundle, which can inflate owner counts relative to sales. Steam reviews keep arriving through 2026, suggesting continued trickle of players; the 30-day sample is tiny (11 reviews). Web search budget was exhausted during this task, so Reddit and other community threads were not read directly; community sentiment here rests on Steam reviews plus Metacritic user reviews and three outlet reviews.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: The Void Rains Upon Her Heart is a story-heavy 2D bullet hell boss rush roguelike built around the idea of loving your enemies. He calls it possibly the most interesting of the 130+ roguelikes he has played and is considering a dedicated video on it. He loves the slow-bullet, precision-based gameplay, the enormous amount of boss content and the discovery-driven unlock structure. His main gripe is that panic attacks can be stockpiled to trivialise final bosses. He places it in S tier and says it deserves more love than any other game on the list.
praise: Bullet hell feel is among the best he has played: slower bullets, readable screen, precision over reflex, not punishing
Huge content volume: roughly 100 monsters/bosses, each with unique move sets that change by difficulty level
Bosses scale per level in bullet speed, health, damage and also attack patterns
Unlocks are informational (revealing monster and ability info) rather than stat upgrades, giving a two-phase game of discovery then planning builds
Abilities gained from each boss can meaningfully change how you play
Dark, gloomy visuals and a love-themed story contrast deliberately; strong story emphasis with cutscenes and characters
Final bosses are awesome, and he keeps finding new bosses, abilities, modes and events after ~20 hours
criticism: Panic attack system (bullet-clearing resource) can be stacked, e.g. ~18 saved for the final boss, making it too easy
Final bosses were easy for him even on higher difficulty because of hoarded panic attacks
Many abilities are fairly unimpactful and just trigger automatically
Roguelike elements take a back seat to core gameplay
Early hours are all question marks, which may feel odd when you want to build toward something
unique_points: Love-your-enemies gimmick and heavy narrative in a bullet hell boss rush
Unlockables reveal information instead of upgrading the character, so progression is knowledge-based
Two-stage structure: long discovery phase, then deliberate build planning once abilities are identified; he says he has not seen another game do this successfully
Boss move sets change per difficulty level, multiplying content
commentary.quote: this game deserves more love than any other game on this list
design_criteria: Core gameplay feel: bullet speed and readability give fair, precision-based dodging
Content volume: ~100 bosses with level-dependent move sets
Meta-progression: unlocks reveal information rather than power
Discovery vs planning: unknown items early, strategic builds later
Ability impact: some abilities change play, many are automatic and minor
Balance/difficulty: stackable panic attacks undermine final boss challenge
Story and visuals: dark tone contrasting love theme, heavy cutscenes
Uniqueness: rare concept and execution among roguelikes

commentary.summary: The Void Reigns Upon Her Heart is a 2D shoot-'em-up boss rush roguelike that he ranks second in his 2024 list. community.one_liner: A solo-developed bullet-hell boss-rush roguelite where you play an alien girl who befriends randomly chosen monsters, each giving gifts that power up her heart, leading up to a final battle.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players treat it as a hidden gem: about 99% positive across roughly 2,000 reviews (Overwhelmingly Positive), with very high playtimes in the top reviews (many 80-400 hours). It is still in Early Access since Feb 2018, but the developer says about 90% of content is done and ships near-monthly patches (v8.37h landed Sep 26, 2026), so it is actively maintained, not abandoned. Reviewers say it has more content than many finished games, with Isaac-style unlock depth. The main friction is the art style and nudity, plus a long-standing wish for the unfinished story content. Mainstream critic coverage is essentially absent: the Metacritic page exists but has no scores, and I could not locate an OpenCritic entry. Note: web search quota was exhausted during this task, so community detail comes mainly from Steam reviews and store data rather than Reddit or outlet reviews.
best_things: Huge content depth for the price ($12.99): about 110 boss battles, 600+ gifts, 80+ events, 4 playable characters, 5 modes and 750+ achievements per the store page
Isaac-style unlock loop: the more you unlock, the more there is to unlock; reviewers compare the volume to Binding of Isaac's Dead God save
Gentle difficulty ramp with lots of player control over difficulty, so newcomers to bullet hell can learn patterns and eventually beat bosses that once seemed impossible
Short runs, easy resets and a satisfying feedback loop make the game feel meditative and very replayable
Only around 8 monsters and a similar number of gifts appear per run, yielding varied builds; gifts are described as well balanced and interlocking without needing a wiki
Strong music and varied, charming enemy/boss designs
Solo developer with visible passion and frequent updates, responsive to feedback (e.g. added options to invert the victory and heartbreak flash colours after a player reported headaches)
Emotional story themes of persevering when you want to give up resonate with players
worst_things: Nudity and sexualised-looking monster girl art make some players uncomfortable; even with the nudity blur option, one negative reviewer said it was still unpleasant, and fans admit they cannot recommend it to friends
Bright white flashes on heartbreak and victory caused headaches for at least one player before an invert option was added
Still Early Access after years; some abilities and story entries carry placeholder or coming-soon text
Controls and camera described as a bit slippery or wonky by an otherwise enthusiastic reviewer
Some characters are less fun; the charge-beam twin character is called tiring to hold and low damage by one long-time player
Items skew toward passive stat upgrades rather than functionality-changing effects, per a 113-hour reviewer
Very low player counts (often about 30 or fewer concurrent) limit community and discoverability
improvements: Finish the story content and story-related boss battles, which the developer names as the main missing piece
Add more accessibility options for flashes and effects (partly addressed with inverted flash colours), and possibly an option to reduce small victory flashes
Rebalance weaker characters such as the charge-beam twin and make charge input less tiring
Add more items that change how you play rather than plain stat boosts
Polish controls and camera feel, and complete placeholder text or abilities before a 1.0 release
Make lore and story reachable without requiring extremely high difficulty
unique_things: Boss-rush structure with a roguelite gift-progression layer, combining bullet hell with Isaac-like meta-unlocks
Love and befriending framing: you calm cursed monsters instead of just killing them, and they reward you with gifts
Scale of about 750 achievements that unlock further content in an Early Access game built by one person
Flexible difficulty and practice tools so the same game works for casual and hardcore bullet-hell players
Mental-health-driven narrative (anxiety, depression, suicide themes, with a content warning) inside a bright, cute aesthetic
Nearly all-female cast of alien monster girls with distinctive art direction
tedious_or_disliked: Holding the charge button for the twin character's attack is tiring (settings exist to change input style or auto-fire)
Early hours are hard for players new to bullet hell, before patterns are learned
Grinding the meta-progression currency (tetrid) and chasing 700+ achievements can become a long commitment, though fans mostly enjoy it
Screen flashes at heartbreak and victory are unpleasant for light-sensitive players
divisive_points: Art style and nudity: some call it the only thing keeping the game from being considered one of the best bullet hells, others say the aesthetics are adorable or simply do not matter
Difficulty: fans praise its approachability while others find early bosses seem impossible at first
Early Access: some see it as effectively complete with more content than finished games, while a few highlight unfinished story and placeholder text
community.reception_notes: Released into Steam Early Access Feb 14, 2018 by Veyeral Games (publisher The Hidden Levels) and has stayed there, with the developer stating about 90% of content is complete and roughly monthly updates; the newest patch notes seen are v8.37h on Sep 26, 2026 (crash fixes), following v8.37f (Sep 24) that added elemental reactions to Shanx forms and gift duration display. Recent Steam reviews were 100% positive in the sample shown, and several 2025-2026 reviews mention discovering it through a streamer (Olexa) and a winter sale, suggesting a recent visibility bump. The Steam page carries a content warning for anxiety, depression and suicide themes and optional non-sexual nudity. Windows only on Steam (no Mac or Linux); the Metacritic page lists PC and Nintendo Switch but has no reviews yet. No notable controversies found beyond one negative review calling the developer a scam over a requirements change and another over nudity. Only 2 negative reviews were in the local sample (19 negative out of 2,012 total). Limitation: web search was out of budget, so no Reddit threads or editorial reviews were read.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Hades II is the early-access sequel to Supergiant's Hades, starring Melinoe, a magic-wielding protagonist fighting to save her family from Kronos. He considers the original a masterpiece and finds the sequel a true sequel rather than DLC, keeping the feel while twisting the mechanics. He calls the current early access build fantastic, and even bigger than Hades 1. It becomes his first S tier of the night, and he likes it more than the original, though he is pausing until full release and suggests newcomers may want to wait.
praise: Keeps the original Hades feel while feeling like a real sequel, not a DLC
Melinoe as a magic user changes pacing: longer dash, running, mana, chargeable attacks
Arcana cards replace the mirror with far more build and permanent-ability customization
Two full paths (surface and underground) with entirely different biomes and monsters, both feeling full
Developers actively take player feedback and change mechanics in each update
Voice acting, art and a deeper, more serious story with flashbacks are excellent
Wider resource/crafting currencies (seeds, minerals, fishing) that tie into route choice
criticism: More complicated mechanics than Hades 1, losing some of the first game's simplicity
Wonders whether building two paths was necessary versus one path with double the content
Many currencies and systems are hard to grasp without seeing them
Still in early access, so he recommends newcomers consider waiting for the full release
unique_points: Two entirely separate paths with no reused biomes or monsters, effectively two games in one
Route choice driven by which craftable materials you want to bring back to the hub
Arcana card system with unlock-by-filling-slots progression is a richer meta-progression than the mirror
Sequel design that adds complexity yet stays playable even when tired
commentary.quote: I really like Hades 2 more than the first
design_criteria: Sequel identity: distinct enough from the first game to justify existing
Mechanical complexity vs simplicity: more depth but still approachable
Meta-progression: Arcana cards and many crafting currencies versus the simple mirror
Content breadth: two paths with unique biomes and enemies
Developer responsiveness: feedback-driven iteration during early access

commentary.label: Top 10 of 2024 (#3)
commentary.summary: Hades II is Supergiant's action roguelite sequel, still in early access in 2024, where Melinoe fights to rescue her family from Kronos. He calls it one of his top games of the year and keeps the original as a long-time favourite. He finds it slightly slower and more complex than the first game, and more reliant on meta-progression and grind, which he enjoys. He is unsure the dual-path (underworld or surface) split was necessary, but finds it an impressive inclusion and praises the developers for listening to feedback.

Hack-and-slash combat that still feels good despite Melinoe being more of a magic user
Hub full of NPCs, permanent upgrades and cosmetic options that keep players engaged between runs
Story is more serious, which he prefers

Start-of-run choice between underworld and surface, each a complete world with its own biomes, enemies and bosses

Meta-progression needs multiple ingredient types, making it more grindy and longer to finish
Unsure the two-path split was needed versus doubling content on one path

Additional dash/sprint mechanic, extra Omega weapon moves, and Arcana cards that are more intricate than the Mirror
Heavier meta-progression tied to the increased importance of story
commentary.quote: Hades 2 is one of my top games of the year

Combat feel: slower but still satisfying hack and slash
Hub and between-run activities: keep players engaged

Content volume: multiple full paths with unique biomes, enemies and bosses

Developer responsiveness to feedback during early access

community.one_liner: Supergiant Games' isometric action roguelite sequel to Hades, in which Melinoe, witch princess of the Underworld, fights through Underworld and Surface routes to kill the Titan of Time, Chronos.
community.consensus_summary: Hades II is received as a near-universal success. Steam shows roughly 95.7% positive (about 123.7k reviews, Overwhelmingly Positive), PC Metacritic is 94 from 46 critic reviews with no mixed or negative scores, and Wikipedia cites 99% of critics recommending it on OpenCritic. Most players and critics say it improves on the original in combat depth, build variety, content volume, art and music. It left Early Access (launched May 2024) for a full release on Sep 25, 2025, then came to PS5 and Xbox in April 2026. The main fault line is the story ending and some repetition or grind in the late game, not the moment-to-moment gameplay. Third-party estimates put it at 2-5 million Steam owners and over $100M gross revenue (estimates, not audited).
best_things: Combat is praised as faster, deeper and more skill-driven than Hades 1, with critics calling it some of the best action combat in games
Weapon variety (multiple distinct weapon types with aspects) plus the Magick bar and Omega moves give many viable build styles
Boons, Hexes and the Arcana (tarot) system combine into varied, experimental builds; progression is allocated after a run, which pulls you into the next one
Art direction, character design, Darren Korb's music and the voice acting are singled out by both critics and players
The witchy, tarot and Greek-myth setting feels fresh rather than a reskin; Melinoe has a distinct feel from Zagreus
Huge content volume and replayability, with reviewers reporting hundreds of hours and still seeing new dialogue
Story and dialogue are woven into the run loop, with witty characters and reactive bosses (e.g. Chronos and Scylla reacting to pausing or muting music)
Supergiant's polish and responsiveness to feedback, from a long Early Access period to post-launch ending patches, is widely appreciated
worst_things: The ending is the most criticised element: Rock Paper Shotgun noted the game did not end with Chronos being killed as advertised, and Final Weapon called it extremely disappointing
Many Steam negative reviews call the narrative resolution weak or an anticlimax, even while praising the gameplay
Players complained that Zagreus and the Hades 1 cast overshadow Melinoe in her own game
Some feel the boon system is less tightly tuned for synergies than in Hades 1, with some weapons or builds feeling weaker or too limited
Several users feel it is a polished more-of-the-same iteration rather than a leap, with a familiar boon, weapon and gifting loop
Some negative reviewers find the progression loop hollow or unrewarding after long play
Several negative reviewers say the supporting characters feel static, with little growth or plot twists compared with Hades 1
improvements: A more satisfying, better-paced story conclusion and payoff for Melinoe specifically (Supergiant added extra scenes and an option to revert to the pre-ending state about a month after launch)
Less reliance on returning Hades 1 characters; more focus on Melinoe's own arc
Tighter boon and weapon balance so every weapon feels worthwhile and build synergies are clearer
Reduce the resource farming and number of runs needed to reach the true ending
More variation in levels and boss encounters to cut down repetition over long playtime
unique_things: Two separate routes, an Underworld path and a Surface path, instead of one descent (Erebus/Oceanus/Fields of Mourning/Tartarus vs Ephyra/Thessaly Rift/Mount Olympus/Summit)
Magick bar that recharges by attacking, used for casts and Omega moves that pin or control enemies
Witchcraft systems: Hexes channelling Selene's power, plus a tarot-style Arcana deck with Fear-style difficulty
Gathering and crafting resources in the Crossroads and between runs, with a larger hub and overworld feel
Story told through run-by-run reactive dialogue, with a sequel that took years of Early Access updates (Olympic, Warsong, Unseen)
tedious_or_disliked: Resource farming and the many runs required to reach the true ending are called padding by some Metacritic users
Repetitive boss encounters and limited level variety over long playtime
Some players dislike specific weapons as too limited or uninteresting, and feel the loop wears thin after 100+ hours
divisive_points: The ending and Zagreus's role: praised story depth from some, called a nothingburger or emotional letdown by others
Whether it is a huge improvement over Hades 1 or a safe refinement of the same formula
Late-game grind for the true ending: seen as satisfying replay value by some, padding by others
Boon balance: some like the varied viable options, others miss the tuned synergies of the original
community.reception_notes: Early Access began May 5, 2024 (Windows), with macOS in Oct 2024; updates included Olympic (Oct 2024), Warsong (Feb 2025, final boss and expanded story) and Unseen (Jun 2025). Version 1.0 launched Sep 25, 2025 on Windows, macOS, Switch and Switch 2; PS5 and Xbox Series X/S followed Apr 14, 2026, including Game Pass. Launch reception was overwhelmingly positive, with backlash on Steam focused on the ending; Supergiant responded roughly a month later with added scenes and an option to revert to the pre-conclusion state. The game won Best Action Game at The Game Awards 2025 and several audio and Steam Deck awards, and was nominated for Game of the Year at several ceremonies. Steam price is $20.99 (Mac supported, no Linux build). Revenue and ownership figures are third-party estimates: Steam-revenue-calculator estimates about $109.7M gross and $32.4M net to the developer; SteamSpy lists 2-5M owners. The OpenCritic integer score could not be retrieved because web search budget was exhausted and the OpenCritic page fetch failed.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Blue Prince is a first-person puzzle roguelike where you draft rooms to build a new mansion each day, hunting for hints to hundreds of persistent, knowledge-based puzzles. He was initially skeptical that puzzles and roguelikes could mix, but thinks the game blends the two counterintuitive genres into something unique and amazing. He calls it kind of a masterpiece and an 'escape room roguelike', and names it an obvious S tier knowledge-based progression game. He has a few wishes: a save feature, an in-game camera, clearer signalling of puzzle solvability, and less punishing handling of RNG and of the room 46 ending.
praise: Room drafting gives a fresh house every run, with secrets and hints in every room
Hundreds of puzzles with huge depth; still not all uncovered, and solutions persist once solved
Design pushes players to chase many mysteries at once rather than fixate on one
Roguelike structure actually improves the game for patient players
Accessible to non-gamers, puzzle fans and roguelike fans alike
Skilled players can manipulate the draft, so there is real skill despite RNG
Amazing community of puzzle solvers, lore channels and challenge runs
criticism: No save feature, and a day can last 10 minutes or 90 minutes
Players must photograph puzzles on their phone to track everything; an in-game camera would be better
Late-game puzzles are so obscure that they are nearly impossible without looking them up, and there is no hint which are doable
RNG can block you from reaching the room a hint points to, which frustrates some
Reaching room 46 the first time ends the run, and a follow-up quest there is easy to miss, which soured his late game
Game does not reassure players that ending a day early or a bad day is fine
unique_points: Fuses roguelike repetition with puzzle aha moments via persistent knowledge that carries between runs
He calls this genre knowledge-based progression and says few games manage it because it is so hard
Randomly generated minor puzzles coexist with large fixed puzzles requiring knowledge
Design lesson: tell players that information gained matters more than a single day's RNG outcome
commentary.quote: Blueprints is a pretty obvious S tier game.
design_criteria: Puzzle and roguelike blend: how well repeated runs coexist with aha moments
Knowledge-based progression: persistent discoveries rather than stat unlocks
Depth and mystery: layers of puzzles and lore that keep going deeper
RNG handling: room draft randomness versus player agency and communication
Quality of life: no save, phone-photo note-taking, and puzzle solvability signalling
Run length: unpredictable day length
Accessibility: appeals to non-gamers and gamers
Community and longevity: ongoing discoveries and challenge runs

community.one_liner: A first-person puzzle-mystery game by Dogubomb (published by Raw Fury) in which you draft a shifting 45-room manor each day, roguelite-style, hunting for the hidden Room 46 and the estate's many secrets.
community.consensus_summary: Blue Prince is one of the best-reviewed games of 2025: Metacritic 92 (critics), OpenCritic about 89 with roughly 96% of critics recommending it, and a Steam rating of Very Positive (about 86% of roughly 20,000 reviews). Critics and fans praise the puzzle depth, atmosphere, environmental storytelling and the feeling of obsessive note-taking discovery. Player opinion is noticeably cooler than critic opinion, though: Metacritic user score is 7.7 and the Steam negatives cluster around RNG-gated puzzle testing, lack of mid-run saves, and diminishing returns in the long endgame. It is a finished, released game (PC April 10 2025, PS5/Xbox, Switch 2 in March 2026), not early access.
best_things: Deep, layered puzzle design where nearly every room hides clues connecting to other puzzles across the manor
Addictive draft-a-room core loop: choosing from three room options and planning routes through the grid feels strategic and fresh
Atmosphere, art direction and music; Mt. Holly has a distinct early-20th-century fictional-world identity
Environmental storytelling told through notes, photos and letters that players piece together themselves
Rewards curiosity and obsessive note-taking; players report spreadsheets, notebooks and screenshot folders and sharing it with a partner or community
Easy to start but hundreds of hours deep; many Steam reviewers report 100-270 hours and call it a favorite game ever
Randomness is woven into the fiction (e.g. frequently-seen family members show up more in the house) and into tactical decisions
worst_things: RNG gates testing of solved puzzles: you can know the answer yet wait many runs/days for the needed rooms or items to be offered
No real mid-run save; 'Save and Quit' effectively abandons the run, and runs can take an hour or more, which drives refunds and negative reviews
Diminishing returns: the early game feels great, the late game narrows toward one big endgame goal where luck dominates
Little permanent meta-progression compared with Hades, Isaac or Balatro; upgrades are sparse and many purchases vanish at day's end
Quality-of-life friction: unskippable animations, slow walking speed, intro and day-start sequences, slow item pickup, and reports of crashes or softlocks
Some late puzzles are very cryptic or contrived, and word-play or pronunciation-based clues disadvantage non-native English speakers
Story payoff / cliffhanger ending leaves some players unsatisfied after very long playtimes
improvements: Add a true suspend-and-resume save, possibly as an accessibility option
Give more ways to manipulate or influence room RNG earlier, or let players lock in already-achieved progress
Speed up or allow skipping animations, intros and traversal, and raise baseline movement speed
Reduce reliance on luck in the endgame so players who know the solution can execute it without waiting for lucky runs
Add more lasting between-run upgrades so repeated days feel cumulative
Better in-game notes or hint-tracking tools to reduce reliance on external notebooks
unique_things: Combines a roguelite room-drafting loop (drafting rooms onto a grid) with a 3D first-person Myst/Outer Wilds-style mystery
Meta-progression is knowledge, not stats: the real unlock is what the player learns and writes down
Every day the manor layout is reshuffled, and puzzles often span multiple rooms and multiple runs
Room 46 goal framed by a will whose rules (take nothing in, take nothing out, leave by night) define the mechanics
Puzzle design that expects the player to keep external notes, photos and even math
tedious_or_disliked: Repeating known steps over many runs just to get the rooms needed to execute one solved puzzle
Post-game and endgame grinding for coins, crafting and filling the room gallery, which feels luck-dependent
Long unskippable animations and slow movement that compound across hundreds of days
Needing one-hour-plus uninterrupted sessions because of the no-save design
Bad-luck streaks where the draft offers dead ends or none of the rooms you need
divisive_points: RNG: one camp says it is strategy and planning you can learn to manage, the other says it is an unfair barrier; experience tracks luck and playstyle
The roguelite + puzzle fusion: praised as innovative by critics but, per many players, the two genres pull against each other (aha moment vs. waiting to implement it)
Note-taking requirement: delightful for some, homework for others
Endgame and ending: rewarding obsession for completionists, anticlimactic or cliffhanger-ish for others
community.reception_notes: Launched April 10 2025 to near-universal critical acclaim and strong Steam sales; it was nominated/awarded across major 2025 awards (The Game Awards, DICE, Game Developers Choice, Golden Joystick and others). The Steam audience rating has drifted down to about 86% positive as long-term players reported RNG fatigue, missing saves and endgame diminishing returns, and Metacritic user score (7.7, about 66% positive) is much lower than the critic score. Ports followed on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S and on Nintendo Switch 2 (shadow-dropped March 3 2026 after an Indie World showcase); a physical edition via iam8bit is listed for October 2026. Steam price is $29.99. No credible official copies-sold figure was found; revenue and owner numbers are third-party estimates.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Elden Ring Nightreign is FromSoftware's co-op-focused soulslike roguelike spin-off, built on Elden Ring's combat with faster mobility, ultimates, distinct characters and a closing-zone battle-royale structure. He covered it at launch and has since revised his opinion upward thanks to updates, including better single-player support and a hard mode. He still has real complaints about repeated map content, the relic system and the lack of pause, but the core loop is so satisfying that he calls it an easy S tier. He also credits the lower-than-AAA price and a AAA studio trying something different and listening to feedback.
praise: Crisp, satisfying FromSoftware combat; every sword swing feels great
Weapons feel distinct, as in Elden Ring
Distinct characters and added mobility, ultimates and faster pacing
Zone-closing, time-limited run structure ending in a big final boss
Quick runs: a full adventure in under an hour
Final bosses and semi-weekly enhanced boss events with unique third phases
Active post-launch support, single-player improvements, and a reduced non-AAA price

Single map with repeated location layouts and not fully random; needs more content and bosses
Easy once experienced in Souls games; gets repetitive before the hard mode

commentary.label: Top 10 of 2025 (#4)
commentary.summary: Elden Ring Nightreign is a fast-paced cooperative soulslike roguelike where players race a shrinking map, collecting loot and levels to defeat the run's Night Lord. He admits it has the most nitpicks of any game on his list, yet the core FromSoftware combat is so satisfying that it lands at number four. He finds the solo experience surprisingly excellent despite the co-op marketing. He calls it a must-play for anyone craving top-notch Elden Ring gameplay, with the caveat that its format is not for every Soulslike fan.

Roguelike elements/meta-progression: minor but nice; long-term progression differs

Co-op vs solo: solo experience fantastic

community.one_liner: A standalone FromSoftware co-op action spin-off that compresses Elden Ring combat into ~40-minute, three-day expeditions for up to three players, ending in a Nightlord boss fight, with randomized maps, loot and bosses and roguelite-style run resets.
community.consensus_summary: Nightreign sold very well (2M units in 24 hours, 3.5M in five days, 5M+ by July 2025) and is rated Very Positive on Steam (about 82 percent of roughly 192k reviews). Critics were warmer than the Metacritic user base: Metascore 77 versus a mixed 6.8 user score, and 76-77 percent of OpenCritic critics recommended it. Praise centers on fast, addictive combat, movement, character variety and the Nightlord boss fights, especially with friends. Complaints center on heavy asset reuse from Elden Ring, RNG-driven loot, a weak solo and random-matchmaking experience, and a thin roguelite meta layer. Post-launch, the Steam crowd has soured on content cadence: the single Forsaken Hollows DLC (Dec 2025) was received less favorably (33 percent of OpenCritic critics recommended it), and recent negative reviews describe the game as abandoned or stale.
best_things: Fast, responsive Elden Ring combat plus a much-improved movement and traversal system that Steam reviewers say fixes the base game's clunkiness
Ten-ish distinct Nightfarer classes (8 at launch, Undertaker and Scholar added by DLC) that play very differently and support many build styles
Nightlord bosses, their stronger Everdark versions, and the soundtrack and arena presentation are frequently singled out as highlights
Co-op with friends is the core strength; Metacritic users and Steam reviewers call it addictive and very replayable
Condensed run length (around 40-45 minutes) gives a bite-sized, replayable take on Souls combat with randomized bosses, points of interest and Shifting Earth map variants
No PvP, no microtransactions and no difficulty-locked paywalls; the roguelite loop drives players to hundreds or even 1000+ hours
Good value perceived by fans at $39.99 given the hours logged, with long-term players reporting the game is in a better state than at launch
worst_things: Heavy reuse of enemies, weapons, bosses and environments from base Elden Ring; some call it a mode that should have been free or a mini-game for $40
Solo play is widely described as frustrating because many bosses and the Deep of Night update feel tuned for a party
Playing with randoms is chaotic: teammates quit after going down, and Deep of Night leaver penalties punish the remaining players
Cheated or modded relics reportedly appear in higher-depth lobbies, with no ban or reporting system that players trust
Loot is a roulette: players describe 40-minute runs with mostly irrelevant drops (boost incantations, weapon skills), making progression luck over skill
Content drought: Steam reviews in 2026 say months passed with only two new characters, two new Nightlords and one new map, and the developer is accused of abandoning the game
Deep of Night update drew complaints about the win/loss point ratio, enemy stat scaling at high Depths, and reskinned mutated enemies that mostly one-shot players
improvements: More regular content: additional Nightlords, maps, characters and unused Elden Ring assets (fans explicitly ask for Shadow of the Erdtree weapons and the Everdark versions of remaining bosses)
A real matchmaking and leaver system: penalties for quitting, reporting/bans for cheating, and fixes to the Deep of Night point loss when teammates leave
In-game communication (voice or text chat) and better tools for playing with randoms
Reworked loot so runs feel less RNG-dependent, with more varied and meaningful drops
Solo balancing and better scaling for duo/solo, plus pausing or a safer way to handle interrupted runs (players note no pause in online runs)
Broader map variety and event frequency, since enemy spawns and POIs become predictable
unique_things: Souls-like combat reframed as a session-based co-op run: three in-game days, each ending in a boss, with a shrinking storm-like circle ('the Night') that forces movement
Fixed roster of heroes with unique passives and ultimates rather than a blank-slate character, giving it a hero-shooter feel inside an action RPG
Extraction-style pressure: limited time to level and gather gear before each night, no shopping or long exploration like Elden Ring
Shifting Earth map variants and randomized points of interest/bosses layered onto a recognizable Limveld map
Two distinct versions of each Nightlord (Everdark Sovereign), with a difficulty-escalating Deep of Night ranked mode added later
Meta progression through relics and a hub (Roundtable Hold) instead of the usual Souls-like level-and-weapon grind
tedious_or_disliked: Runs are long (up to about 40-60 minutes) and cannot be paused online, which is hard for players with limited time, especially in duo or trio
Deep of Night penalties and leavers can force players to grind matches solo to advance
Searching for a useful weapon or relic across a run is seen as repetitive and luck-driven
Rushing to the next objective prevents reading abilities or comparing items, so the game feels hectic rather than tactical
Content repetition: once the roster and map pool are exhausted, long-time players say runs blur together
No in-game voice chat or cross-play make it harder to coordinate with friends or randoms (duo mode was missing at launch)
divisive_points: Whether it is a good roguelite: some reviewers call it a good spinoff but a weak roguelite compared with indie genre peers, while others love the loop
Solo play: some players say the base game was workable solo, others say recent updates made it effectively unviable
Design direction: fans who love combat praise the focus, while fans who want world-building and exploration find it stripped down
Whether the price and reused assets are acceptable for a $40 standalone title
community.reception_notes: Launched May 29-30, 2025 at $39.99 on PC, PS4/PS5 and Xbox. Sales were strong (2M in 24 hours, 3.5M in 5 days, 5M+ by July 2025; 14th best-selling game of 2025 in the US per Wikipedia; SteamSpy-style estimate 2-5M owners on Steam alone; steam-revenue-calculator estimates about $223M gross on Steam, an order-of-magnitude figure). Critic scores are mostly favorable (GameSpot 9/10, VG247 5/5, Destructoid 8.5, PC Gamer 80, Eurogamer 4/5, IGN 7/10, NME and Guardian 3/5, PCGamesN 6/10), with lower marks for asset reuse and the roguelike structure. Metacritic user score is notably mixed at 6.8 from 1,404 ratings (56 percent positive). June 2025 updates added harder Everdark Sovereign bosses; the Deep of Night ranked mode and later balance changes divided the community. The Forsaken Hollows DLC (Dec 4, 2025) added two expedition bosses, a new map variant and the Undertaker and Scholar but was received less favorably than the base game; recent (2026) negative Steam reviews accuse the publisher of neglect. Awards include Japan Game Awards Excellence and nominations for Golden Joystick, The Game Awards 2025 and BAFTA Games Awards 2026 (Multiplayer). The OpenCritic page could not be fetched directly (my guessed page IDs were wrong and the web search budget was exhausted), so OpenCritic top critic average is null.

games.name: Monster Train 2
games.short_description: Monster Train returns with all new clans, new enemy factions, new challenges, new modes and more! Defend your Pyre in the classic three-tiered, vertical gameplay that made the original roguelike deckbuilder a hit.

other_scores.source: Steam DLC Destiny of the Railforged

placements.verbal_evidence: Monster Train is an easy S tier. I'm going to put this as my top of S tiers.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Monster Train 2 is the sequel to a deck-building roguelike with an auto-battler flavor, where you place units across three floors and fight waves up a train, Slay the Spire style. He considers the original one of his favorite deck builders ever and judges the sequel better, calling it possibly his favorite deck builder of all time. It keeps the core formula but adds quality-of-life changes, new card types and a big hidden reveal that multiplies build diversity. He gives it an easy S tier and puts it at the top of S.
praise: Deployment phase: drawing all units at the start of each fight and placing them freely cuts RNG, while energy limits keep fights from feeling identical
Huge build diversity from the clan system (two clans per run, two champions each), massively expanded by the spoiler reveal that restores the first game's clans, giving roughly 180 combinations
New additions like equipment cards, room cards, unit abilities and a selectable Pyre feel like simple, well-judged layers of customization
Ascension-style difficulty scaling makes early runs easy to jump into and have fun with crazy combos, without overwhelming the player
Visuals, animation, art style and soundtrack are standout and instantly recognizable
Rewind and restart-battle options help with mistakes and reveal how strategic and mathematical positioning and spell choices are
criticism: Spell-focused clan is the weakest: gimmicky and poor at fusing with other clans, even worse than in the first game
Story element and joke dialogue on units feel unnecessary, though minor
Pyre of Dominion is slightly overpowered and some balance tweaks are still wanted
Deployment phase can make fights a bit consistent, and the rewind button can be used to cheat or feels slow and cheap
Wants more boss variety and more content; community challenges don't interest him
unique_points: The hidden reveal that unlocks all clans from the first game inside the sequel, doubling build diversity, is one of the coolest things he has seen in a roguelike
Deployment phase as a design fix for unit-draw RNG in an auto-battler deck builder
Restart battle option teaches how much tiny positioning and spell choices matter
commentary.quote: Monster Train is an easy S tier.
design_criteria: Build diversity: clan combinations and roguelike elements let decks transform each run
RNG control: deployment phase reduces unit-draw randomness
Difficulty scaling: easy start with ascension-style ramp
Synergies: crazy deck combinations across clans
Clan balance: spell clan weak, Pyre of Dominion too strong
Visuals and audio: distinctive art, smooth animation, great music
Quality of life: rewind and restart battle options
Replayability: every run feels unique, more content and bosses desired
Sequel iteration: small additions rather than drastic change

community.one_liner: A sequel to Shiny Shoe's roguelike deckbuilder in which you defend a Pyre atop a three-floor vertical train by pairing two of the clans, drafting units and spells, and snowballing them against Titan-led enemy waves.
community.consensus_summary: Monster Train 2 is received as one of the best roguelike deckbuilders, praised by both critics and players as the original refined and expanded. It holds 87 on Metacritic (31 critic reviews), 'Overwhelmingly Positive' on Steam (about 95% of roughly 10,200 reviews) and a 7.8 Metacritic user score that is noticeably lower than the Steam figure. Critics and fans tend to describe it as a 'safe' but confident sequel that obsoletes the first game, with huge content depth and replayability. The main pushback is about boom-or-bust RNG, enemies and bosses that hard-counter specific builds, a cluttered and oversized UI, and weak story writing. It released May 21, 2025 (full release, not early access), and has kept receiving updates, including a paid expansion (Destiny of the Railforged) in February 2026.
best_things: Huge replay value: 10 clans with a main-plus-ally pairing, plus covenant ranks, challenges, daily runs and Soul Savior mode; reviewers report hundreds of hours without boredom.
Snowballing combat feels explosive and satisfying; assembling a broken build and steamrolling bosses is the recurring highlight.
New systems (equipment, room cards, Pyre Hearts, the deployment phase) add build depth; IGN and Metacritic critics singled out equipment cards.
Clan reworks and new clans are widely liked; original clans were rebuilt and are unlockable without extra cost, and the mushroom-themed Underlegion is a fan favourite.
Strong soundtrack that keeps getting called out by both critics and players.
Visual clarity aids such as the damage preview and improved quality-of-life over the first game.
Good value and respectful monetisation: $24.99 base game, a free demo, and players note first-game content was not locked behind DLC.
Accessible enough for newcomers to deckbuilders while still deep; some players who bounced off Slay the Spire say this one clicked.
worst_things: Heavy RNG and boom-or-bust runs: several reviewers say fights are either trivial or unwinnable, with few tight, close matches.
Enemy and boss design can hard-counter a build (incant enemies, floor silence, sweep, cleave, magic shield, resurrection), punishing experimental builds.
Post-launch bosses were criticised by some long-time players as overtuned and too dominant.
UI is busy and oversized: players say it feels designed for mobile, is hard to read on PC, and everything flashes and shakes.
Story, dialogue and cutscenes are widely regarded as weak (described as laughably or charmingly bad depending on the reviewer).
Some feel it is expansion-sized rather than a true second game, and that the first game has better bosses, writing or polish.
Status effects and card interactions pile up to the point where units carry too many effects to track.
Some long-time players argue it lacks the difficulty and challenge options of Monster Train 1 and is too easy at the top if you know the tricks.
improvements: Reduce hard-counter encounters or let players see or influence upcoming enemy types so experimental builds are not blindsided.
Add a UI or graphics simplification option and a less cluttered, more PC-friendly layout (whole train visible without scrolling).
Restore first-game features some miss: a bigger boss pool, the Divine Temple shard system, and a mid-fight restart option.
Rebalance or add toggles for overtuned post-launch bosses and weak clans (Awoken, Luna, Stygian and Gilda are mentioned as struggling).
Improve the story and writing, or make cutscenes skippable or removable.
Expand challenge and difficulty options and strengthen endless mode, which a Metacritic user called poorly designed.
unique_things: Three-floor vertical train with a Pyre: you position units on floors while enemies advance floor by floor, unlike Slay the Spire's single lane.
Main clan plus allied clan pairing across 10 clans creates very many combinations, each with alternate starting champions.
Deployment phase lets you place units across floors, making decks more spell-heavy and adding positioning decisions.
Room cards, equipment and selectable Pyre Hearts layer extra scaling systems on top of the deck.
Destiny of the Railforged adds the Railforged clan with a Forge mechanic plus a Soul Savior mode with upgradeable soul enhancements.
Daily challenges with leaderboards and handcrafted Dimensional Challenges, plus a free unlimited demo.
tedious_or_disliked: Long unlock grind: levelling every clan to 10 and unlocking all cards and relics reportedly takes around 100 hours before the full game opens up.
Having to repeat the same answer to recurring enemy mechanics (silence, sweep, incant) reduces build variety.
Covenant (difficulty) climbing can feel like a loop of chasing a scaling multistriker or other high-roll engine.
divisive_points: Whether it is a perfect evolution of the first game or merely a big expansion; some players prefer Monster Train 1's polish and boss design.
Difficulty and balance: some find it too easy with broken events and builds, while others find bosses and enemy counters punishing.
Art direction and presentation: many love the art style and mushroom or cat designs, while some users describe the art as inconsistent or bad.
Destiny of the Railforged is liked (83% positive on Steam, about 325 reviews) but notably less loved than the base game, with some complaining about balance of its new mode.
community.reception_notes: Launched May 21, 2025 to strong reviews (Metascore 87 from 31 critics; top scores from Hey Poor Player, Screen Rant and Try Hard Guides at 100, Noisy Pixel 95, Game Informer 93, PC Gamer 91, IGN, GamesRadar+, Shacknews and Siliconera at 90; one mixed outlet called it slot-machine-like RNG). Steam ratings have held at Overwhelmingly Positive, with some very high-hour reviewers (hundreds of hours, one at 880 hours). Post-launch content includes the paid expansion Destiny of the Railforged (February 2, 2026; new Railforged clan with Forge mechanic plus Soul Savior mode) and newly added bosses that some veterans found overtuned. A demo with unlimited playtime exists. Platforms on Steam: Windows and Mac. SteamSpy estimates 200,000 to 500,000 owners (order-of-magnitude only; the revenue-calculator site returned $0 so no usable revenue figure). The OpenCritic score could not be verified: the OpenCritic page IDs tried resolved to unrelated games and web search quota was exhausted, so it is reported as null. Metacritic user score rests on only about 77 ratings (71% positive, 22% mixed, 6% negative).
