games.name: Mewgenics
games.short_description: Build the ultimate cat army through tactical breeding and send them into deep, challenging turn-based adventures. Draft abilities, collect items, and manipulate genetics across generations in this roguelike tactics game from the creators of The Binding of Isaac and The End is Nigh.

other_scores.source: OpenCritic (percent recommend, via Wikipedia; top critic average not retrieved)

placements.verbal_evidence: I think Mugenics is an easy S tier. No question.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Mewgenics is Edmund McMillan's follow-up to The Binding of Isaac: a board-centric, turn-based strategy roguelike where you command a squad of cats with very different play styles. He treats it as deserving its hype, with enormous content (100+ hours and he still hasn't hit the true ending), endlessly varied fights, and runs that feel fresh every time. He still has gripes about breeding opacity, shops and equipment restrictions, but they matter less after 100 hours. He calls it an easy S tier.
praise: Huge amount of content, arguably more than any other roguelike including Isaac, for the price
Every board looks different thanks to the many abilities, items and enemies, like shuffling a deck of cards
Strategic depth rewarded by knowledge, with relatively little RNG so skilled players win most runs confidently
Game-breaking combos are hard to earn, so being overpowered feels rewarding rather than trivial
Losing cats does not feel terrible since new ones are easy to get and best cats only go on adventures once
Pre-run setup (picking cats, roles, items) takes 10+ minutes and makes the start of each run unique
Long main quest, many side quests and meta progression that unlocks options rather than raw stat boosts
criticism: Breeding system is complicated and confusing, and takes too long to teach the player how it works
Equipment placement limits and curses can lock a cool item away from a character
Questionable quality of life such as pathing that sends cats through spikes
Choice events should let you pick which cat (or between two cats) handles them
In-run shops are boring, mostly just buying level-ups, so money feels less exciting than in Isaac
Instant-death or run-ruining effects like charm can feel unfair, though they have been reduced
unique_points: A completely different genre (turn-based tactics board) from Isaac yet with similar content density and knowledge-driven design
Pre-run team building solves the common roguelike problem of repetitive run openings
Permanent cat loss is softened by breeding and easy replacement, unlike punishing losses in Darkest Dungeon
Meta progression is about breeding systems and options, not plain stat upgrades
commentary.quote: I think Mugenics is an easy S tier. No question.
design_criteria: Content volume: hundreds of hours with a long main quest and side quests
Gameplay variety: abilities, items and enemies combine so each board differs
Strategy and knowledge: skill and game knowledge beat RNG
Risk vs reward: overpowered builds are earned, and losses are softened
Run start variety: extensive customization before each run
Meta progression: unlocks options and breeding rather than raw power, but slow
Quality of life: pathing, event cat choice and equipment limits
Fairness: instant-death and charm effects can ruin runs
Economy: shops and money feel less meaningful than in Isaac
Onboarding: breeding information arrives too slowly
commentary.rerank_note: Re-evaluation: he previously made an in-depth review at about 30 hours; now at about 100 hours his early complaints still apply but bother him less.

community.one_liner: A turn-based tactics roguelite from Edmund McMillen and Tyler Glaiel where you breed mutant cats across generations, equip them with class-based abilities and items, and send them on long, permadeath-flavored runs.
community.consensus_summary: Mewgenics launched on Steam on Feb 10, 2026 (full release, not early access) to very strong reception: Steam sits around 90% positive (Very Positive, ~54k reviews in the local data) and Metacritic shows a Metascore of 88 from critics with a user score of about 8.1. Critics (Eurogamer Germany, Games.cz, Multiplayer.it, Siliconera and others) call it dense, endlessly varied and addictive, with early game-of-the-year talk; Wikipedia reports over 1 million copies and roughly $23M in the first week. Player criticism concentrates on the meta-layer rather than the combat: house/breeding management has little sorting or filtering, UI and ability descriptions are inconsistent, and Act 3 difficulty and run length feel punishing to some. The developers have kept patching (a 1.1 balance and breeding update, four new languages, console ports on Sept 8, 2026, and a small free update and first DLC in progress), so it is actively supported.
best_things: Extremely deep tactical combat with 1,000+ abilities and 900+ items, producing wild synergies and build variety; players compare it to Final Fantasy Tactics crossed with Magic-style drafting and combo-building
The cat breeding and genetics layer (mutations, birth defects, inherited traits) creates emergent stories and strange, hilarious builds
Soundtrack widely singled out as a highlight, in some Steam reviews the best part of the game
Huge content volume: 200+ hour campaign, 100+ bosses, many unique enemies that each demand a specific plan; reviewers with 60+ hours say they had seen under a third of it
Strong Edmund McMillen personality: grotesque humour, charming art style, and a true Binding-of-Isaac-style sense of discovery
Highly addictive loop; multiple reviewers describe ragequitting then sinking dozens of hours anyway
Acts 1 and 2 are frequently described as engaging and easy to jump back into
worst_things: House and cat management is clunky: no way to sort or filter cats by stat, no simple way to clear accumulating poop, and extra rooms unlock very late
UI problems in battle: easy to misclick, cannot see other cats' items and abilities mid-fight when it is not their turn, and ability descriptions are inconsistent or omit ranges
Act 3 is a difficulty spike; several reviewers say runs turn stressful rather than fun, and losing a run can mean losing cats you spent a long time breeding
Hidden or unclear information forces knowledge checks in a turn-based game, which some find fair in Isaac but annoying in a tactics game
Some events offer a trivial upside against severe downsides (for example money versus injuring a cat), which reads as unfair
Humour does not land for everyone: a KonsoliFIN critic called it often grating and dated, and another reviewer called it criminally unfunny
Display options at launch: no borderless fullscreen and no 16:10 aspect ratio support, per a popular positive Steam review
Heavy RNG can frustrate players wanting a purely skill-based challenge (noted in critic consensus)
Drafting abilities without being told what you are choosing between or what they do in context, which several top negative reviews cite as poor onboarding for TBS players
improvements: Add sorting, filtering, labeling or renaming tools for cats and a faster way to handle the house (breaking poop, bulk actions)
Streamline the post-run breeding/management loop so it takes less time between runs
Improve battle UI clarity: safer click targets, view all allies' abilities and items on any turn, consistent ability text with stated ranges
Let players preserve or test more items or builds so late-game is not fully at the mercy of roguelike drops and stockpiling broken items
Smooth Act 3 balance and reduce the feeling that hidden content is gated behind borderline annoying runs
Better display support (borderless fullscreen, more aspect ratios); the developers have since added four languages and console ports
unique_things: Fuses Isaac-style chaotic item roguelite design with a FFT-like tactics grid, a deck-building-flavored ability draft, and a genetic breeding sim
Permanent cat lineages carry traits, mutations and defects between runs, so your breeding house is effectively the meta-progression
Every cat has a voice and personality, and disorders, parasites and injuries are mechanical features with absurd effects (for example a corpse-eating trait that also eats teammates)
Ridiculon soundtrack and performances tie into the marketing, with live Gamescom performance
Long gestation: announced in 2012 as a Super Meat Boy follow-up, cancelled, then rebooted in 2018 with Tyler Glaiel into the current tactics design
tedious_or_disliked: Managing a growing population of cats in the house: clicking through every cat to compare stats, with no list or filter
Runs that last an hour or more, then a long management step after each run
Stockpiling items to take into later runs, which some see as a cop-out to justify harder late enemies
Grindiness noted by several reviewers, especially chasing unlocks and finishing the later acts
Losing a run late can erase many hours of breeding progress, which makes Act 3 feel stressful
Sorting which items to keep after each run via a large grid with very limited filtering
divisive_points: Humour and tone: some call it the heart of the game, others find the crude and dated jokes grating
Difficulty and chaos over balance in Act 3: some love breaking the game with synergies, others find the required game-break every run unfun
Breeding system changes in patch 1.1 (stimulation, inbreeding, mutation tweaks): intended as balance and depth but some players say it made management more of a pain
Amount of hidden or discoverable information: praised as Isaac-like discovery by some, criticised as bad UX for a tactics game by others
community.reception_notes: Full release Feb 10, 2026 on Windows, with Nintendo Switch 2, PS5 and Xbox Series versions on Sept 8, 2026 (cloud saves link to Steam; keyboard and mouse supported). Wikipedia reports over 150,000 copies in the first 6 hours and over 1 million copies with about $23M in the first week; revenue-estimator sites returned zero for this title, so treat third-party sales figures as unavailable. Metacritic lists 54 critic reviews (52 positive, 2 mixed), none negative. Steam recent reviews (about 86% positive over the last 30 days) are slightly lower than all-time, consistent with late-game and QoL complaints. Patch 1.1 reworked breeding and stimulation mechanics, altered events and many class abilities; new Japanese, Korean, Russian and Simplified Chinese localisations went live after a beta; a small free update with a new way to play plus the first small DLC are in development. Some minor backlash over certain voice cameos was mentioned on Wikipedia. OpenCritic numeric score could not be fetched (page lookup failed and web search budget was exhausted), so it is recorded as null.

games.name: Slay the Spire 2
games.short_description: The iconic roguelike deckbuilder returns. Craft a unique deck, encounter bizarre creatures, and discover relics of immense power in Slay the Spire 2!

placements.verbal_evidence: right now obviously an S ... currently I'm just going to put Sledspire 2 above [Slay the Spire 1]

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Slay the Spire 2 is the sequel to the game that popularized roguelike deckbuilders, reviewed here while still in early access. He has cleared Ascension 10 with every character and sees it as a proper sequel that refines the original rather than reinventing it. He calls the card design a master class and praises the variety, visuals and multiplayer. His complaints are thin content in places, unfinished art and a disliked meta-progression system. He places it in S, slightly above the first game.
praise: Card design is a master class: cards work across many decks and no single card is mandatory
Huge variety across relics, characters and cards makes every run feel very different
Kept what players loved from the first game and cut disliked characters and cards (the Watcher)
Big visual upgrade, with unique animations for many cards and every enemy, making it very satisfying to watch
Ancients replace boss relics, and the new relics are more niche and polarizing, with less guaranteed energy
Multiplayer is well integrated and fun, with real-time visibility and map drawing
Developers balance actively and listen to community feedback, such as cutting early infinites
criticism: Early access content is a bit light: the final boss lacks animation and much art is unfinished
Meta-progression (the epoch system) is visually messy, confusing and uninvolving; he wants a full revamp
Acts 2, 3 and 4 still need work, and he worries about a very long early access
Multiplayer lacks teammate deck visibility, relic exchange and unique multiplayer events
Harder and more complex for casual players because energy is scarcer
unique_points: Deliberately a straightforward sequel with no new gimmick mechanic, which he sees as the right call for the genre's originator
Two complete biomes on the first act, each with distinct events, enemies and bosses
Multiplayer chest-picking mechanic and drawing on the map
Builds are not locked to one archetype, unlike the poison-focused approach in the first game
commentary.quote: This is how you do a sequel in my eyes.
design_criteria: Card design and balance: cards viable in many decks, no mandatory cards
Variety and replayability: characters, relics and cards producing different runs
Synergies: multiple build paths per character rather than one archetype
Visuals and animation: unique enemy and card animations matter in a low-motion genre
Meta-progression: epoch system judged confusing and unfinished
Difficulty and complexity: scarcer energy and polarizing boss relics add depth
Content completeness: early access gaps in acts, art and animation
Multiplayer design: cooperative features and missing unique interactions
Developer responsiveness: balance patches and community feedback
commentary.rerank_note: Places Slay the Spire 2 above Slay the Spire 1 in S tier, saying both are game of the year worthy.

community.one_liner: Mega Crit's sequel to the genre-defining roguelike deckbuilder, adding two new characters, a redesigned Ancients/Epochs structure, and up to 4-player co-op; currently in Steam Early Access.
community.consensus_summary: Slay the Spire 2 launched in Early Access on March 5, 2026 to huge hype, record concurrency and near-universal critic praise (full-marks reviews from outlets such as PCGamesN), and early Steam reviews were glowing about visuals, content volume and co-op. Since then Steam sentiment has slid to Mixed (about 61% positive across roughly 203k reviews), driven by a long run of balance patches that many players feel made enemies, elites and the Act 3 bosses more punishing and less varied, plus review-bombing waves (including heavily negative Simplified Chinese reviews). Even many negative reviewers say the core card game, art and animation are top-notch and that they are leaving thumbs-down only on the current state of balance and direction. The game is still Early Access with no Act 4 announced as of the latest update notes I could read; Mega Crit is teasing big secret features after its September break.
best_things: The core deckbuilding loop stays as compelling as the original, with many reviewers saying it feels even deeper and more polished
New art style, animations and game feel are widely called a clear upgrade over Slay the Spire 1
Up to 4-player co-op that translates the single-player experience well, including multiplayer-specific cards; players use it to play with friends and family
Large amount of content already in Early Access: two new characters (Regent, Necrobinder), new enemies, bosses, events, lore and music
Ancients replacing boss relics give three-way choices each act and add build variety
Epochs/unlock progression and richer events with real risk make runs feel more rewarding and story-connected
Fair pricing ($24.99, same as the first game) with content updates promised as free rather than DLC
Steam Workshop mod support, Bestiary and ongoing developer communication
worst_things: Repeated patches that nerf strong cards and buff enemies; many long-time fans say each update made runs harder and less fun

Act 3 third-boss slot has been a flashpoint: the boss was redesigned several times then replaced (Doormaker removed, Aeonglass added), with reviewers saying the fights counter whole archetypes or feel unfinished
Elites and bosses often feel like raw number checks (block X now, huge HP pools, regen, strength scaling) with less identity than in the first game
Difficulty is front-loaded and punishing at high Ascension, with little margin for error so runs can end without an obvious lesson learned
Balance is uneven across characters; some builds feel almost irrelevant against the third boss
Accessibility gaps: incomplete keyboard navigation, which a disabled player cited as a reason for a negative review
Some negative reviewers question Mega Crit's Early Access management and direction after rapid boss changes
improvements: Finish Act 4 and the remaining act variants (only Act 1 had multiple variants early on)
Make elite and boss fights more varied and puzzle-like instead of damage races, and stabilise the Act 3 boss pool
Rebalance difficulty curve and Ascension scaling so it does not hinge on a strong Act 1 or a 'god run'
Full keyboard and controller-style navigation/accessibility support
unique_things: Co-op deckbuilding for up to 4 players inside a Slay the Spire framework
Ancients: a choice of three rewards at each act's end instead of a single boss relic
Epochs meta-progression and a stronger lore/story layer than the original
Two new characters, The Regent and The Necrobinder, alongside returning Ironclad, Silent and Defect
Rebuilt RNG system meant to decorrelate random elements, and a Bestiary showing enemy moves and animations
Shift from Unity to Godot after Unity's fee controversy, costing the team around two years of rework
tedious_or_disliked: Long, high-hour grinds through Ascension where build options get narrowed by enemy checks and infinite/engine decks feel forced
Enemies that chip through block or slam 30+ damage, making many fights feel like the same damage race
Frequent balance churn means good strategies can be invalidated between patches
Solo play feeling less fun to some players than co-op after recent changes
Perceived developer responsiveness to a few high-level streamers rather than casual players
divisive_points: Difficulty: some critics and players find it easier than the original (PCGamesN noted easier infinites and dangers), while a large share of patched-era Steam reviewers find it harshly difficult
Whether the balance patches are necessary corrections to infinites and homogenised play or an over-correction that removed fun builds
Geographic split: English Reddit and reviews skew positive while Simplified Chinese Steam reviews skew much more negative
Whether the sequel is a big leap or feels like an expansion of the original (noted by some critic reviews)
community.reception_notes: Launched March 5, 2026 in Early Access at $24.99 on Windows, macOS and Linux after a delay from 2025. Per Wikipedia it hit over 177,000 concurrent players on day one and passed 3 million sales within a week, with over 25 million runs played. The Metacritic page shows a pending Metascore with 9 critic reviews compiled and no user reviews yet; no OpenCritic page could be reached. Steam reception started extremely positive and declined to Mixed overall after balance patches (v0.100 through 1.0 and later betas) and several review-bombing incidents: two over balance changes, largely from China, and one in May 2026 tied to a consultant credit. Latest notes show the last major update on June 18, 2026 (v0.107.1), Steam Workshop support, a new Act 3 boss (Aeonglass), bi-weekly beta patches, and big unannounced features teased for after the September 2026 break; Act 4 is not yet announced. Steam revenue estimator sites show zero for this title, so use the Wikipedia 3M-in-a-week figure instead.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Across the Obelisk is a co-op-style deck-building roguelike where you control four characters at once. PepperHead uses it as the first deck builder of the list and talks about how the genre shares common gimmicks, so each game must build its own identity. He finds it complex and overwhelming for newcomers, but praises its engaging overworld and charming presentation. He rates it a solid A tier while cautioning that it is not for people new to deck builders.
praise: Controlling four characters at once is its unique hook
Outside-of-combat world and exploration feel engaging and immersive, like a real adventure
Cute, fun art and animations, more lively than typical minimalistic deck-builder animations
Many characters, cards and build possibilities once you have played a few hours
Good balance between combat gameplay and the overworld/events layer
One of the best deck-building games in his view
criticism: Pretty complicated with a lot of information, overwhelming for beginners
Managing four characters and their placement adds to the overload
Not recommended if you are not used to deck-building games
unique_points: Four characters played simultaneously, with placement management a big part of play
Design lesson: deck builders need a good balance between card combat and the outside world; this one nails the outside world
commentary.quote: this one does a really really good job
design_criteria: Identity within genre: how a deck builder differentiates itself from similar card mechanics
Unique gimmick: four simultaneous characters with placement
Balance of combat and overworld: both layers need to be good
World immersion: exploration and events feel like an adventure
Art and animation: charm beyond the genre's usual minimalism
Build diversity: many characters, cards and builds
Accessibility/complexity: high information load, unfriendly to newcomers

community.one_liner: A co-op (1-4 player) roguelite deckbuilder/RPG by Dreamsite Games where you run a party of four heroes through a branching campaign map, crafting decks and stacking buffs against tactical enemies.
community.consensus_summary: Steam shows Mostly Positive (about 80% of roughly 13,000 reviews). The base game is widely loved for its depth, co-op and replayability, and critics who reviewed it were favourable (3.5/5 to 4/5, 7/10 to 8.5/10) but noted that it is a solid genre entry rather than a genre great. The dominant recent complaint, in the most helpful negative reviews, is not the gameplay but Paradox's DLC monetisation: pricey DLC, locked DLC nodes and cards appearing in the base game, plus ongoing bugs and desyncs. It is not abandoned (a DLC-heavy release cadence continues), but several long-time players say meaningful free content and fixes have dried up and there is no sequel or mod support.
best_things: Very deep deck and party customisation: 16 base heroes across four roles, 500+ cards and 300+ items, with card crafting/upgrading and traits that enable many builds
Co-op is a standout: each player controls a hero, which spreads the deck-building load and makes it a rare strong multiplayer deckbuilder; players report 250+ hours with friends
Huge replayability from branching map paths, events with hero-specific options, Madness difficulty levels, extra modes and sandbox
Distinctive art style and appealing original cast; lighthearted tone
Big amount of content in the base game (100+ hours to see it all per multiple reviewers), so the $20 base is considered good value
Meta-progression (unlocking cards, perks, heroes and their mini-quests) keeps runs feeling rewarding
worst_things: Aggressive DLC monetisation since the Paradox takeover: some DLC costs as much as the base game for a small amount of content, and new characters/skins are priced separately; full set is often quoted around $90+
DLC content is baked into the map and card pools: flashing DLC-locked nodes that lead to a purchase prompt, and DLC cards offered as dead, unselectable rewards in the base game
Stability problems: long-standing random crashes, reset resolution, and desyncs in co-op (card dragging, boss tactics, shopping) reported after newer DLC
Balance is lopsided: buff/debuff stacking and scaling builds dominate, raw-damage and off-meta comps (e.g. 3 healers or 3 scouts) struggle, and some heroes have clearly optimal paths
Campaign acts are largely fixed, so it is only semi-random; some players feel it is easier than Slay the Spire and lacks true roguelite variance
Perceived lack of effort on the base game: no mod support and little substantial free content for years, with calls for a properly reworked sequel
Character select UI redesign seen as clunky, and attempts to push the Paradox launcher drew complaints

Recent DLC is criticised for heavy power creep, a clash in art style and arbitrary design that do not mesh with the base game, while the game is also described as having received no meaningful content for about 4 years

Paradox-era business practices beyond DLC price: an unnecessary launcher and complaints about data collection, cited by long-time players (hundreds of hours) as the reason they no longer recommend the game
improvements: Bundle or cut prices of DLC, or make updates free, and stop promoting DLC inside the base game's map and card rewards
Stop showing unselectable DLC cards in reward screens for non-owners
Fix persistent crashes and co-op desyncs with proper testing before DLC releases
Rebalance so that more than buff-stacking builds are viable and early-game starting heroes are less limited
Add mod support and more free base-game content or a true sequel focused on core cards and classes
Improve the character-select UI so all hero info can be seen without scrolling
unique_things: One of the first multiplayer roguelike deckbuilders, with every player piloting their own hero and deck
Party-of-four RPG structure with Darkest Dungeon-style hero roles (warrior, scout, mage, healer) combined with Slay the Spire-style card play
Energy carries over between turns (up to 10) rather than resetting, and heroes have equipment, traits and player-level perks
Card crafting and upgrading with shards at the start of each act, plus hero unlock mini-quests and Obelisk corruption challenges
Branching campaign map with persistent, semi-fixed content and Madness difficulty levels and sandbox modifiers
tedious_or_disliked: Early-game grind: starting heroes are weak with limited deckbuilding until enough cards and heroes are unlocked, which one reviewer called a long and painful early game
Building a deck solo takes a long time; several players recommend at least 2 players
Constant reminders of missing DLC (flashing exclamation marks, locked characters) interrupting play
Runs can become stale after a long time since acts are fixed and buff stacking trivialises content
Bug-related interruptions such as crashes and desyncs, and the Paradox launcher push
divisive_points: Whether the DLC is fair: some say it is optional, improving over time and worth buying on sale; others say it feels predatory and unavoidable because the holes show in the game
Difficulty and roguelite-ness: some find it easier and more controllable than Slay the Spire, which they like, while others find the fixed maps and stacking too easy
Whether it beats Slay the Spire: a few prefer it, others say it does some things better and some worse
Whether the base game alone is worth $20 without DLC: many say yes, at least one reviewer with 300 hours says no
community.reception_notes: Launched into Steam early access in 2021 (GamingOnLinux covered it in April 2021) and released 1.0 on Aug 16, 2022, praised as an engrossing co-op deckbuilder, with early balance and grind complaints. Publisher Paradox (Arc) took over and the game now has many DLC packs (Sands of Ulminin, Shores of Sahti, Sigrun the Valkyrie, Bernard the Alchemist and others); recent reviews skew negative about DLC monetisation even from long-time fans, dragging the overall rating to around 80%. Also on Switch and PlayStation/Xbox. Metacritic has no Metascore yet (it needs 4 critic reviews; only 2 shown), and OpenCritic lists 4 reviews without a displayed aggregate in what I could fetch. Revenue and owner numbers are third-party estimates, not audited.

commentary.summary: Arcanium is a deck-building roguelike with a huge roster of playable characters, played as a party of three on a board-game-like map. He finds it very strategic, challenging and replayable, with the fun coming from discovering new character combinations. The outside-world layer is minimal and events repeat, and the animation bothers him a little. He places it in A tier, but only recommends it to people already used to deck builders because of the amount to track.

community.one_liner: An open-world, single-player roguelite deckbuilder by Supercombo in which you lead a party of three anthropomorphic-animal heroes across a semi-open procedural map to stop Akhan the Calamity.
community.consensus_summary: Players rate it Very Positive on Steam (about 82% of roughly 817 reviews), with praise for its hero variety, the three-character party and the editable deck, and a polished cartoon-animal look. Critics covered it only lightly: the two OpenCritic reviews (6.5 and 6 out of 10) call it enjoyable but complex, difficult and sometimes restrictive. Recurring complaints are a long grind to unlock everything, a slow UI and run pace, uneven hero balance, weak tutorialisation, and cards that turn out to be samey. It left early access on 22 September 2022 with three new heroes and an Arena mode, and later came to Epic, iOS and Netflix Games. It is a niche, low-volume title today, with only a handful of concurrent players on Steam.
best_things: Party of three heroes with a hand and deck for each, so every turn is a puzzle of splitting action points between characters
Lots of heroes to play with and many party and difficulty combinations, which keeps things feeling fresh
Deck is fully editable outside and between fights, with no forced bloat as in Slay the Spire style games
Semi-open map you can roam freely, choosing which regions to hit for rewards or XP instead of following a fixed node tree
Appealing cartoon-animal art style that draws people in
Lots of unlockables (cards, artifacts, ability customization) and multiple difficulty levels give long-term replay; reviewers with 80 to 110+ hours report it
Fun, approachable casual deckbuilder that is easy to pick up for relaxed sessions
Items and artifacts can be reused after battle, which players found a pleasant surprise
worst_things: Heavy unlock and achievement grind; meta-progression needs a huge number of runs
Slow UI and very large maps make a single run take a long time, so it is hard to fit in a session
Hero balance is uneven, with some characters strong and others near useless
Explanations are poor: artifacts and effects like Burn are unclear or lack audio feedback, and the game is hard to learn
Card pool per hero is narrow, so builds get samey and depth can be false
UI pain points: artifacts are hard to look up, and cards must be dragged rather than click-and-target
Some boss mechanics (removing action points, damage immunity after a threshold) feel like turn denial instead of interactive challenge
Bugs reported: quest rewards not granted, map nodes becoming undiscovered on reload
improvements: Add click-to-target card play and controller support (currently drag and drop only; no controller)
Add an undo option for mistaken moves
Improve tutorials and in-game tooltips or an artifact compendium, and add audio/visual feedback for status effects
Speed up the UI and offer smaller or faster run formats; rebalance the unlock grind
Expand card pools and rebalance weak heroes so builds are more varied
Let players change their ultimate ability mid-run, possibly at a cost, to adapt to found artifacts and cards
unique_things: Three-hero party with three separate decks and hands, instead of the usual single-character deckbuilder
Open-world semi-open procedural 3D map where you can travel anywhere and start from any point, and enemies get harder the longer you linger in a province
Completely editable deck with a collection you swap cards in and out of, inverting the no-removal convention of the genre
Hero leveling and ability card unlocks persist between runs, giving it an RPG progression flavour
Arena mode focused purely on combat against corrupted versions of the world's heroes
Distinct anthropomorphic animal setting mixing magic and technology
tedious_or_disliked: Unlock grind for heroes, cards and achievements described as abysmal by some players
Runs are long and the UI is slow, so even one run per sitting is hard
Dragging cards on every play is fiddly
Having to manage three hands and many factors per turn is demanding and at times confusing because of poor explanation
Late bosses can shut down your plan through AP loss or damage immunity, which feels unfair to some
Lack of controller support and no undo irritate some players
divisive_points: Depth: some find unending combinations and a lot to learn, others call it false depth with few viable builds per hero
Difficulty and complexity: praised as a challenge by some and cited by critics as limiting its audience to hardcore players
Editable deck: seen as freeing by some and as undermining deckbuilding tension by others
community.reception_notes: Metacritic has only one critic review and no user ratings, so no Metascore; OpenCritic has two reviews and no aggregate average. Early access began before 2021 (Gaming Professors reviewed in 2021); it launched 1.0 on Steam 21/22 September 2022 at $24.99 (now $19.99) after adding three heroes, new final bosses, a new enemy type and an Arena mode, with translations into 15 languages. It has since appeared on Epic Games Store, iOS and Netflix Games. Steam is Windows only. Third-party estimates (Steam Spy range 50k to 100k owners; steam-revenue-calculator about 133k USD gross, about 39k net) are order-of-magnitude figures only. Steam reviews extend through 2026, so it still has a small but active player base.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Astral Ascent is a fast 2D action roguelite with a Hades-like structure: room-by-room runs with chosen rewards, a character-driven story and a hub world full of upgrades. It was still in early access when he recorded, which is unusual for him, but a large update drew him in. He is very enthusiastic about the animation, art, and the flashy, satisfying combat. He places it in what the ASR renders as 'an eighth', most likely A tier, just above Arcanum.
praise: Stunning animation, visuals and art with lots of care put into characters
Hades-style approach: attention to plot and characters alongside gameplay
Gameplay feels awesome: quick, flashy, every spell and hit is satisfying
Wizard/ninja power fantasy
Rooms offer different rewards at the end, like Hades
Big hub world with many upgrades and new characters to talk to after each run
criticism: Not fully released yet, so he is unsure how the final version will turn out
The volume of hub upgrades can feel overwhelming, though he dismisses this as a minor concern
unique_points: Hades-like structure combined with a fast ninja/wizard combat feel
Hub world keeps unlocking new characters and upgrade paths after each run
commentary.quote: it feels so good it just feels amazing playing
design_criteria: Charm/visuals: animation and art are a major highlight
Game feel: fast, flashy, satisfying spells and hits
Meta-progression: extensive hub upgrades and characters
Room/reward structure: Hades-style rewards per room
Narrative/characters: care put into plot and characters
commentary.rerank_note: Early-access game he would not normally rate; verdict is provisional pending full release.

community.one_liner: A fast 2D action-platformer roguelite by Hibernian Workshop where you pick one of four heroes (solo or local co-op) and fight through the Garden, an astral prison, to defeat twelve Zodiac bosses using a cycling set of four spells.
community.consensus_summary: Astral Ascent is very well regarded: Steam shows roughly 94.6% positive across about 8,600 reviews (Very Positive), Metacritic critic score is 86 and OpenCritic is 84 with 100% of critics recommending. Critics and players call the combat fast, responsive and satisfying, the pixel art and boss fights outstanding, and the build variety deep, often comparing it to Dead Cells (and Hades for meta-progression and cast). Complaints cluster around an overwhelming, poorly explained upgrade/meta system, a confusing hub, a derivative or cliched story with cringey dialogue, and samey non-boss rooms. Metacritic user score is lower (7.4 on few ratings), reflecting a minority who find the combat shallow. It spent about 18 months in Steam Early Access and launched 1.0 on 14 Nov 2023 (also PS4/PS5/Switch); it has kept receiving updates (2.0 Outer Reaches, Celestial Haven DLC, Dead Cells crossover).
best_things: Fast, fluid, responsive combat with no spell cooldowns; mana from basic attacks powers very strong spells that can melt enemies, which players find refreshing
Zodiac boss fights are consistently called memorable, well designed and visually striking, often the highlight of a run
Gorgeous hand-crafted pixel art, animations, anime-style cutscenes and strong music/voice work
Huge build variety: four equipped spells each with augments (gambits), imprints and affinities, plus a signature spell and different characters that play distinctly
Destiny Levels give a scalable difficulty ladder and strong endgame replay value
Local co-op is praised as the best way to play; several reviewers said it only clicked in co-op
Good polish and Steam Deck performance, and a developer that keeps supporting the game with free and paid content
The 'spells must be cast in order' system makes you think about your whole loadout rather than one favorite skill
worst_things: Upgrade and meta-progression systems are overwhelming and poorly explained; some players say it took many runs (one said ~30) before things clicked
Story and dialogue are widely described as derivative of Hades, stereotypical or cringey, with wasted potential; several positive reviewers still say the writing is the weak spot
Non-boss rooms feel easy, samey and like filler compared to the bosses; some find the ambient music sleepy there
Some players find combat lacks impact/feedback: weak-feeling basic attacks, enemies that barely react, and spamming spells in order regardless of which spells are equipped
The hub area and finding upgrade merchants is confusing
Build depth is questioned by a minority: cheap high-hit spells outperform expensive ones and modifiers matter more than the spell itself, so characters feel less different than advertised
Visual busyness bothers some: screen noise, colorful enemies blending into the background, and a cluttered interface
A few technical issues mentioned: long first-boot load on Steam Deck, high-refresh-rate (240Hz) problems, controller prompt mismatches, tooltips needing work
Cheap-feeling hits: some enemies and projectiles track or teleport onto you regardless of dodge timing, costing perfect-room rewards
improvements: A better onboarding/intro that shows combat potential early (e.g. a stronger starting experience or a companion) since the opening almost made some players quit
Clearer tooltips and explanations for spells, gambits, imprints and how to actually finish/clear the game (Destiny system is not obvious)
More meaningful differences between spells and more viable expensive spells so builds feel less homogeneous
More varied room/level generation; reviewers of the Outer Reaches DLC said new lands use very similar level generation and offer little incentive beyond reward choices
Stronger writing and deeper character interactions so the cast and Zodiac lore pay off the setup
More hit feedback (knockback, enemy reactions) to make basic attacks feel punchier
unique_things: Four-spell rotation: spells are used one at a time in a fixed cycle, so you are only as strong as your weakest spell
Mana-driven combat with no spell cooldowns, plus separate cooldown-based 'echo' abilities
Zodiac-themed cast and bosses, each hero having personal storylines and a signature spell and weapon
Perfect-room clear rewards that push players to avoid damage, tied to rewards and progression
Two-player local co-op with distinct heroes, and a scalable Destiny Level difficulty system
Imprints and affinities layered on augmented spells (added/expanded in 2.0), and a crossover with Dead Cells
tedious_or_disliked: Learning the many overlapping upgrade systems and reading lots of skill text before builds make sense
Meta-progression with many unlocks and lots of tutorial hand-holding, which some find grindy or intrusive
Repeating easy, similar non-boss rooms after the first ~10 runs
Needing to clear rooms without taking damage to maximize rewards, which punishes tanky or chip-damage playstyles
Hub navigation and hunting for the right merchant or NPC
Some players report run length feels random because enemies scale alongside you, making progression feel weak in places
Grindy, repetitive loop for some: players report boredom after extended playtime (one at ~20 hours) with empty or sparse stages
divisive_points: Combat feel: most praise it as fast and satisfying, a vocal minority finds it shallow, low-impact and spam-heavy
Story and characters: some call it a surprise highlight that hooked them, others call it cringey, derivative of Hades and forgettable
Art direction: widely called stunning, but a few find it busy or bland/ADHD-overload
Difficulty: base game described as easy by some, while higher Destiny Levels and modifiers are very hard; some see that as great scaling, others as slow to ramp
community.reception_notes: Launched in Steam Early Access in 2022 and praised early as a potential next great roguelike; 1.0 released 14 Nov 2023 on PC, Mac, Linux, PS4, PS5 and Switch to strong reviews (OpenCritic top 7% per its percentile ranking, 100% of critics recommend). Steam reviews stay very high years later. Post-launch support includes the 2.0 update with The Outer Reaches DLC (new worlds, enemies, imprint mechanic, optional Andromeda boss), a Dead Cells crossover, the Celestial Haven DLC (a critter shelter), and further character DLC. Estimated Steam revenue from third-party calculator is about 4.2M gross / 1.2M net (Boxleiter estimate, not audited); SteamSpy lists 200k-500k owners. Metacritic user score (7.4 on ~51 ratings) is noticeably lower than critics. Price is $24.99.

praise: 40+ characters that play drastically differently, each with big upsides and downsides
Shop items also come with tradeoffs, so build management is constantly interesting
Huge amount of build customization even with the same items and enemies
Easy to pick up and play; auto-firing weapons make it great on Steam Deck
Sound design and music are great
Minimalistic animation and enemy visuals fit the game fine
Everything is focused on the gameplay itself
criticism: Wishes there were a bit more enemy variation
Minimalistic visuals and animation (accepted as a fitting choice)
Looser roguelike: you unlock characters and items but not upgrades

Item upsides and downsides create meaningful choices in the shop

community.one_liner: A top-down arena shooter roguelite from Blobfish in which a potato auto-fires up to six weapons at alien hordes across short 20-90 second waves, buying items between rounds to craft builds.
community.consensus_summary: Brotato is one of the best-liked survivors-like games on Steam, at 95.9% positive across about 119k reviews (Overwhelmingly Positive), and it has sold an estimated 2-5 million copies at a $4.99 price. Critics are warmer than lukewarm but more reserved than players (Metacritic 76, OpenCritic Top Critic Average 76), mostly praising the addictive short-run loop and build variety while noting limited enemy variety and repetition. It is a full release (early access ended June 2023) that has been actively updated. Development moved from Blobfish to Evil Empire (Dead Cells studio) in 2025, which brought the New Dawn update and later the May 2026 All Pain No Gain update with the Nightmare difficulty. That update drew a wave of negative reviews from long-time players, though the overall score stayed very high.
best_things: Huge build variety: dozens of potatoes (characters), lots of weapons and items, and stat-stacking synergies that make each run feel like a different recipe
Very short waves and quick runs give a strong 'one more run' pull and suit short sessions
Characters change how you play rather than just tweaking stats, and some only make sense once you figure out their gimmick
Between-wave shop, rerolls, economy and positioning add real strategy on top of simple auto-aim shooting
Excellent optimisation: runs on low-end hardware and is praised on Steam Deck, with auto-aim suiting handhelds and the ability to pause/resume a run across devices
Local split-screen co-op is widely appreciated
Exceptional value at about $5 with hundreds of hours of replay and cheap DLC
No grind-heavy meta progression, so new players can start playing the real game immediately (cited by Niche Gamer as a good roguelike entry point)
Highly addictive, low-friction loop: top-voted positive reviews describe logging hundreds of hours and marathon co-op sessions with friends
worst_things: Low enemy variety: several players say build combinations far outnumber enemy types, and the brown arenas and purple aliens feel samey over time
Repetition and a half-baked endless mode are the most common long-session complaints in aggregated review analysis
Balance: some characters, weapons and item archetypes are seen as overpowered or near-useless; higher difficulties funnel toward meta builds
Heavy RNG in shop offers: a run can be decided by whether the shop gives you what your build needs, which feels bad after a 40-60 minute run
Too many stats to track; losing a long run because a stat like speed or regen was slightly low frustrates some players
Critics and some players find it light on lore, exploration and traditional roguelite progression, more a 'mini-game' than a full campaign
Achievements locked behind DLC annoy completionists, and DLC is seen by some as not matching base-game quality

improvements: Add native online co-op; Steam Remote Play Together is reported as poor or unplayable
More enemy types and arena/biome variety, plus a stronger endless mode
Clearer item descriptions and better in-game explanation of stats and scaling
Rebalance Nightmare and the shop so it is not dominated by glass-cannon builds and shop luck, or offer a less punishing way to engage with the new content
Quality-of-life additions such as co-op item exchange, more picks when luck is high, and better save safety between versions

Manual movement only with auto-aimed weapons, combined with a six-weapon-slot limit and stat-based scaling (armor, dodge, harvesting, engineering, etc.)
Potato characters with bizarre constraints, such as a one-hit-death character (The Wounded) or builds around turrets and pets

Endless mode and post-Danger 5 play, which some call pointless or repetitive once everything is unlocked
Chasing 100% achievements, especially those requiring DLC and new achievements added with each update
Nightmare difficulty: tripled enemy health, environmental projectiles from screen edges and fog, widely described by unhappy long-time players as bullet-hell spam that makes shop RNG decide runs
Sifting through a bloated shop and item pool, which the new pets feature is said to have made worse by some players
divisive_points: The All Pain No Gain update: many veteran reviewers feel Evil Empire pushed the game toward a bullet hell and made it exhausting, while others welcome the extra challenge and note the base game had become too easy
Depth versus accessibility: some want more meta-progression and long-term goals, others value the clean, quick, no-grind structure
Comparison with Vampire Survivors: fans call Brotato the better, faster game, while critics say it has less skill expression
Whether DLC is good value for the price

community.one_liner: An isometric, Hades-adjacent action roguelite from Passtech Games where a treasure hunter delves procedurally generated Mesoamerican-themed temples, using parry-and-dodge combat, torch light management and a corruption/curse system.
community.consensus_summary: Generally well received: Steam sits at Very Positive (about 83% of roughly 9,200 reviews), critics land in the high 70s to low 80s, and the combat is the near-universal highlight. The dissent is about structure rather than feel: a repetitive, grindy loop, limited enemy/room/weapon variety, slow meta-progression, and a punishing, RNG-heavy final temple. It spent about a year in Early Access (from March 2020) and launched fully on 23 Feb 2021 on PC, Switch, PS4 and Xbox One; post-launch support included a Dead Cells crossover in April 2021. Players often describe it as Hades on hard mode, but with much less story and personality, and it tends to be recommended to people who already like skill-based action more than to genre newcomers.
best_things: Crunchy, responsive combat built on parry, perfect dodge and weapon combos; many reviewers (critic and player) rate it above Hades for feel and fairness
Skill-first design: limited randomness in weapons and synergies means learning enemies and patterns, not build luck, decides runs
Light and darkness system: braziers and the torch reveal traps and reduce danger, and fire can turn enemies into light sources, adding a tactical layer
Curse/corruption mechanic creates risk-reward decisions (taking curses or trading blood for loot) and runs with real tension
Bosses with thematic, readable patterns, each tied to a god's domain (power, knowledge, etc.)
Strong atmosphere and art direction for the Aztec/Maya-inspired temples, with good sound design (for example the death-whistle perfect-dodge cue)
Large weapon roster (claws, swords, hammers, etc.) with different movesets, plus pleasant pick-up-and-put-down run length
Polished after a long Early Access period; performs well and is playable on controller and Switch
worst_things: Repetition: the same limited set of rooms, traps, enemies and bosses are learned by heart within roughly 15 hours, and the structure forces replaying earlier temples to reach later ones
Story and characters are thin to non-existent, so there is little narrative pull to keep running
Late-game difficulty feels cheap to many: teleporting, briefly invulnerable enemies, area attacks and health-sponge elites in the last temples
Final temple is long and grindy, with heavy gold requirements for final sacrifices and a DPS-check final boss that players call a wall
Weapon balance is uneven; some players feel fast weapons like claws dominate and other weapons are technically viable but worse
Curses often feel weak or randomly punishing: some reviewers say they rarely affect a run, while in the last temple the health-draining curse can leave you one hit from death
Slow, low-value meta-progression: unlocks cost a lot of crystal skulls for marginal gains
Achievements (including memoir-style completionist ones) are seen as grindy for 100% runs
Heavy reliance on RNG (starting items, late-game luck) makes the back half feel slow and unfair, and several reviewers say the final boss is a chore rather than a challenge
improvements: More enemy, room, boss and weapon variety so later runs feel different
Faster or more meaningful meta-progression, and fewer repeat traversals of earlier temples
Better tuning of the final temple: less elite health-sponge padding, more viable dexterity/damage builds, and a fairer gold requirement
More story, characters or lore payoff to give a reason to keep running
More reliable tools for managing corruption, so the curse system feels like a choice and not a dice roll
Clearer or more predictable handling of tanky/unparryable enemies in large mixed-enemy rooms
unique_things: Torch and brazier light management that changes both visibility and damage, rather than being just cosmetic lighting
Corruption meter that builds from room transitions and blood trades, spawning rule-changing curses instead of only giving buffs
Souls-like, turn-taking combat rhythm (strike then defend) in an isometric roguelite instead of Hades-style fast aggression
Parry-centred weakening/stun mechanic tied to blessings, with the sense of a slower, more deliberate run
Temple-by-temple structure with tiered boss sections and a distinctive Mesoamerican-inspired setting
Crossover content such as the Dead Cells weapon pack (April 2021)
tedious_or_disliked: Re-clearing the first section of each temple to reach deeper boss tiers, then repeating the whole structure for the final temple and hard mode
Grinding crystal skulls for weapons, blessings, rerolls and better starting gear, with some players saying normal difficulty feels gated by those hours
Rooms packed with five or more enemies, many tanky or unparryable, which slow the pace and undermine the parry mechanic
Teleporting/invulnerable enemies and screen-filling attacks in later temples that feel more like waiting than skill
Elite health-sponge enemies and high gold costs in the final temple
divisive_points: Whether it is a good roguelike or just a good action game: some say slow, methodical combat suits a run-based loop, others say it is a poor fit because runs are slow and repetitive
Difficulty and curses: some love the skill ceiling and risk-reward tension, others find late difficulty and RNG curses cheap
Progression pace: fans like slow unlocks that preserve weapon preferences, critics of it call the grind a chore
Hades comparison: praised as better combat and fairer, but clearly behind on story, art style and character
community.reception_notes: Metacritic PC critic score is 78 from 20 critic reviews (user score 6.9 from 112 ratings), verified on the Metacritic page. OpenCritic shows a Top Critic Average of 81 from 50 reviews with 86% recommending (Strong tier). IGN called it a standout roguelite; Nintendo Life compared the combat favorably to Hades; Game Informer felt it went stale after several runs. Launched from Early Access (March 2020, initially only the Jaguar section) to full release on 23 Feb 2021 on Windows, Switch, PS4 and Xbox One (no Mac/Linux). Steam price $19.99, SteamSpy owners estimate 500K-1M, about 84 concurrent players at time of data, and recent Steam reviews are still being posted, so it has an active if small audience. No major controversies found.

community.one_liner: A 2D side-scrolling, mouse-aimed action roguelite by TEAM HORAY (Steam, Feb 2018) where you dash and jump through procedurally assembled dungeons, collect weapons and accessories, manage a hunger/food system, and buy permanent stat upgrades between runs.
community.consensus_summary: Dungreed is a long-running indie favourite on PC: Steam shows roughly 9,600 reviews at about 93% positive (Very Positive), and the positive reviews come from players with very high playtime (often 50-250 hours) who praise weapon and build variety, snappy dash-based combat and the Workshop mods. Critic coverage is thin: Metacritic has no Metascore (only one Nintendo Life review of the Switch port, 80) and a tiny Switch user score of 7.2 from 5 ratings. The complaints are consistent: awkward keyboard/mouse and controller handling, repeated items and thin area variety, RNG-driven balance where lucky builds trivialise the game and unlucky ones are stuck, and bullet-hell late bosses. Steam reviewers say the developer has moved on to Sephiria, so content updates appear to have slowed, but the modding scene keeps it alive. Note: this research was done with WebSearch unavailable (session search budget exhausted), so critic/community coverage relies on Steam data, Metacritic, and the Steam community pages rather than Reddit or major outlets.
best_things: Huge weapon and accessory pool that synergises into many different builds; several reviewers cite 'god runs' from item combinations
Fast, snappy dash-based movement and combat that feels good once a build comes together (one reviewer likens the movement approach to Rogue Legacy)
Character customisation per run, with many valid playstyles and a difficulty curve that adds new content gradually
Food/hunger system: buying food for buffs fills a hunger meter that drains, forcing you to budget stat gains against saving room for better food
No contact damage from enemies, which one reviewer singled out as a relief
Active Steam Workshop: custom weapons, characters and even items imported from Sephiria extend replay value (reviewers call the Workshop community 'legends')
Strong value at about $10 and good long-tail engagement, with many players returning every few months
Pixel-art style and movement praised by several reviewers (one calls it a personal favourite 2D roguelike)
worst_things: Controls draw the harshest complaints: aiming and dashing follow the mouse pointer so keyboard players dash the wrong way, and keybinding/settings menus were reported as broken by some
Controller support is inconsistent: one PS5-controller user reports the game flipping between Xbox and 'Undefined' input mid-run; others say it plays best on a gamepad
Item and loot rotation feels repetitive: the same items recur in shops and chests, so the large library feels smaller than it is, and there is low visual variety across areas

Balance is swingy: lucky weapon/evasion/block combos make you near-invincible while a poor-loot run leaves you with weak items; some legendary items are reported weaker than commons and some characters feel underpowered

Late bosses are bullet sponges that flood the screen with projectiles; one complaint notes a boss using red/orange/brown projectiles in a red/orange/brown hell stage where attacks blend into the background
Enemy attack timings feel slow compared with the very fast player and spam-attack weapons, making dodging feel jarring (detailed in one long negative review)
Bland, minimal story and lore according to several reviewers
improvements: Better input handling: a working rebinding menu and reliable controller detection (PS controllers especially)
More permanent upgrades or meta-progression to help struggling players, since progression tops out and later success is skill plus RNG
Better item rotation/pool management so shops and chests do not keep showing the same items
More area and visual variety, and more enemy/boss diversity to reduce repetitiveness
Rebalancing rarity and weak characters so legendary items and unorthodox builds are not punished; clearer guaranteed healing rather than mostly RNG healing
Fix or clarify achievement bugs (one 100% player reports the final food-eating achievement not unlocking) and quest progress not carrying across a single run
unique_things: Food/hunger meter as a build-management resource: buffs are bought and limited by stomach capacity, which is unusual for the genre
2D mouse-aimed shooter/melee hybrid platformer with a dash-centred movement kit and no contact damage
Town-rebuilding and training meta layer: permanent stat training plus unlockable vendors and NPCs rescued from the dungeon
Active Steam Workshop scene adding custom characters and weapons to a game with a simple pixel-art pipeline
Available on PC, Switch, PS4 and iOS
tedious_or_disliked: Achievement hunting and the optional true final boss: reviewers describe completion as long, repetitive and in places annoying (one says the true boss looked more annoying than satisfying)
Repeated runs through the same few areas, with a lack of area variety, leads to fatigue after dozens of runs
Spending runs with only low-rarity gear and no healing is frustrating once meta-progression is maxed out
Bullet-hell late stages and projectile-spamming bosses become a slog rather than a skill test for some
Keyboard controls and cursor-relative dashing cause cheap hits, making the keyboard experience a chore
divisive_points: Difficulty and balance: some call it 'pretty easy' and relaxing, others call it punishing and skill-only with poorly balanced RNG
Depth and longevity: fans put in 100-250 hours and call it a gold-standard roguelite, while others see a generic, shallow, cheap-feeling roguelite that falls flat after 15-20 runs
Controls and game feel: praised as crisp and snappy (especially on controller) by many, described as awkward or unintuitive by others, partly due to the 2.5D perspective and mouse-relative aiming
Item pool: 'massive loot library' versus 'same items keep showing up'
community.reception_notes: Launched on Steam on Feb 14, 2018 from a small Korean indie team and built a durable audience through word of mouth and content updates; later ports reached Nintendo Switch, PS4 and iOS (per Metacritic). Critics barely covered it: Metacritic shows only one critic review (Nintendo Life, 80), so no Metascore, and the Switch user score of 7.2 is based on 5 ratings. Steam's all-time rating sits around 93% positive on roughly 9.6k reviews, with recent reviews also positive. Reviewers in 2025-2026 say updates have largely stopped as the developer shifted to Sephiria, but the Workshop community continues to add content. Recurring technical issues reported in negative reviews include input/keybinding bugs and controller misdetection. SteamSpy-style data in the local file lists roughly 200k-500k owners, which, together with the revenue estimate, is order-of-magnitude only. No OpenCritic page could be found (OpenCritic fetches failed or returned an unrelated game).

Player control of pacing via pause and repair

Historical influence and age

community.one_liner: A real-time-with-pause spaceship management roguelike-like where you run a Federation cruiser and its crew through eight procedurally generated sectors, fleeing a rebel fleet to deliver intel to the fleet before permadeath ends the run.
community.consensus_summary: FTL is widely regarded as a genre-defining indie classic: Steam shows about 95% positive across roughly 78.9k reviews (Overwhelmingly Positive), Metacritic critics score it 84 and users 8.3. Critics praised the way it makes players feel like starship captains, the tense system and crew juggling, and the ten-dollar value; the main critical knock (for example Edge at 70) is how much survival depends on random loot and dice rolls. Players who love it talk about hundreds or thousands of hours and the Multiverse mod, while the most common negative Steam reviews are from people who bounced off the RNG and the difficulty, including on Easy. It is a finished game (Advanced Edition free update in 2014), not early access, and Steam reviewers still describe it as beloved 14 years on.
best_things: Tense real-time-with-pause combat where you manage power between weapons, shields, engines, oxygen and other subsystems, and can pause to plan frame by frame
Crew micromanagement creates emotional stories: losing a favourite crew member to fire, boarders or vacuum stings and drives 'one more run'
Deep build variety from weapons, drones, augments and ship layouts (ten ships plus unlockable alternate layouts) with tactics that reward learning enemy and weapon matchups
Skill-based progression rather than power unlocks: reviewers note runs get easier because the player improves, not because of meta upgrades
Atmospheric soundtrack and lonely, vast space mood that many reviewers single out
Strong random-event writing and choose-your-own-adventure style text encounters that make each run feel like a new story
Tiny footprint, cheap price and runs on very low-end hardware (Mac, Windows, Linux)
Huge replay value and mod scene, especially the Multiverse mod, which reviewers describe as an enormous expansion in the spirit of the original
worst_things: RNG-heavy evasion and hit chances: bad streaks of misses or enemy volleys on key systems can end a run no matter how well you play (the most common complaint in negative Steam reviews)
Early game snowballing: a weak scrap or weapon start, or a bad early sector, compounds and dooms later sectors
Final boss (the Rebel flagship) is seen as a sharp difficulty and mechanic spike; several reviewers say it demands specific builds plus luck after hours of runs
Boarding and fire mechanics can feel like harsh pass/fail minigames, and fires can snowball quickly and kill crew
Difficulty labels feel misleading: multiple reviewers say 'Easy' is still very hard, and one cited only about a quarter of players having beaten the game on Easy
Crew and click handling in the heat of combat can feel fiddly, with crew reaction and pathing occasionally frustrating
Some weapon classes and droids feel weak or poorly balanced versus others, per reviewers
improvements: Rename or rebalance difficulty modes so Easy is truly approachable for casual players, as many negative reviews request
Reduce reliance on evasion dice and punishing streaks, or give players more tools to mitigate bad luck, especially in the final sector
Better teaching of hazards so players understand why a run collapsed early (one reviewer wanted clearer feedback on what went wrong)
Better balance for droids, anti-personnel options and weaker weapons, and smoother crew task handling (auto-repair priority ideas appeared in reviews)
Smoother final boss ramp: a reviewer said the flagship introduces multi-stage mechanics not seen earlier, and wanted a more refined successor or second version
More official content or a sequel beyond Advanced Edition: fans say they want more from Subset Games
unique_things: You fly no ship directly; you run its systems and crew as a bridge-level commander, blending roguelike structure with real-time tactics and ship management
Permadeath runs with no persistent power upgrades, only unlocked ships and layouts, so player knowledge is the progression
Star Trek and Firefly flavour with six alien crew races whose traits (rock, mantis, engi, slug, zoltan, crystal) change tactics
Designed explicitly as a 'suicide mission' with the developers reportedly targeting roughly a 10% win rate
Pause-anytime, frame-by-frame spatial planning of fires, breaches, boarders and oxygen across a cutaway ship layout
Tiny two-person team (Matthew Davis and Jay Ma) that turned a Kickstarter ask of $10,000 into over $200,000 and helped kick off the indie roguelike wave
tedious_or_disliked: Long runs, often 2-3 hours by reviewers' accounts, so a loss in the last sector feels costly
Early-game scrap scrounging and node-by-node exploration when a start is weak can feel grindy and repetitive
Repeated restarts when a run is crippled early by bad luck, without meta progression to soften it
Fire and boarding micromanagement in crises can feel stressful rather than fun
Guessing where the rebel fleet advance will catch you can create dead-end paths that feel unfair
Constant vigilance: one reviewer called it both slow and the most stressful strategy roguelike they had played
divisive_points: RNG versus skill: fans say losses teach you and truly unwinnable runs are rare, while critics and many players say luck decides too many runs
Difficulty: celebrated 'suicide mission' design for some, unfair and mislabeled difficulty modes for others
Whether it still holds up against modern roguelites with meta progression; one long-time completionist gave it 7.5/10 for this reason
community.reception_notes: Launched September 2012 after a Kickstarter that raised over $200,000 against a $10,000 goal, and was immediately a critical and commercial breakout for a two-person studio; it won IGF Excellence in Design and Audience awards, the GDC Best Debut award for 2013 and PC Gamer's Short-form Game of the Year 2012. The free Advanced Edition (April 3, 2014) added races, weapons, ships, drones, music and events, and a Hard difficulty; it also launched on iPad the same year to strong reviews. Estimated Steam gross revenue is about $10.6M (net about $3.1M to the developer) per the Steam Revenue Calculator, which is a Boxleiter-style estimate and SteamSpy puts owners at 2-5 million. OpenCritic has no FTL entry that I could find (the game predates the site), so OpenCritic is null. Available on Windows, Mac and Linux, with iPad and Steam Remote Play noted.

community.one_liner: A colourful first-person roguelite looter-shooter with RPG-style characters, scroll-based builds and 1-4 player co-op, made by Duoyi Games' Gunfire Reborn Studio.
community.consensus_summary: Players love it: Steam shows about 93% positive across roughly 104k reviews (Very Positive), and Steam Spy puts owners at 2-5 million. Praise centres on satisfying gunplay, character and weapon variety, and strong co-op. Critics are more lukewarm: the Metacritic page (Xbox version) has a 75 critic score from 10 reviews and a 7.1 user score from 64 ratings. It launched in early access in May 2020, reached 1.0 in Nov 2021 and later came to consoles and mobile. It is still updated, with seasonal content and paid DLC characters about every six months. Recent Steam negatives focus on DLC power creep, machine-translated text, dead co-op matchmaking, suspected AI-generated art and an EULA change.
best_things: Gunplay is fun and satisfying, often compared to Borderlands and Immortal Redneck, with an addictive run loop
Large roster of characters, each with two skills and an ultimate, that change how a run plays, especially in co-op
Wide variety of weapons and scrolls allows many build experiments, including lucky-shot and elemental builds
Bosses are distinct and fluid, each with readable mechanics
Great character designs, from cool to cute, in a colourful art style
Co-op networking is smooth, and each player gets their own drops that can be traded
Seasonal mechanics are all kept available so players avoid FOMO, and support continues years after release
worst_things: English localization is widely described as machine-translated, with confusing or wrong descriptions and some text left in Chinese
DLC characters are much stronger than base ones, making runs on the highest difficulty very easy and creating power creep
Build variety becomes stale, with each character reduced to a few optimal weapon and skill combos, and seasonal mechanics feel similar
Online co-op matchmaking is described as dead, so co-op needs friends
Balance swings in high difficulty, where enemies either die in one hit or barely take damage
Recent reviews cite undisclosed AI-generated art in official artwork and emotes, which drove a wave of negative reviews
Some players report worsening performance, crashes and lost save data over time
New EULA added forced arbitration and deletion of data after 365 days of inactivity, drawing the most-upvoted recent negative reviews even from fans
improvements: Add more bosses per stage and new stage areas, since current boss variety is limited
Make updates meatier, because long-term players say a year of patches can be seen in a few hours and maxing meta progression is quick
Improve English localization and tooltips so item and scroll interactions are clear
Rebalance DLC versus base characters and give hard difficulties a real challenge ceiling
Fix matchmaking or add a lobby or social hub for co-op players
Offer a clearer dodge (short distance and unclear i-frames) and possible third-person or mod support, both requested by players
unique_things: Hades-and-Borderlands-style mix: FPS shooting with hero abilities, scroll (passive) builds and Chinese mythology-inspired anthropomorphic characters
Scroll system lets players assemble synergies, with each character having a different preferred approach (cat for elements, owl for scrolls, fox for frontal assault)
Seasons as switchable, permanently available mechanics with a free battle pass rather than limited-time FOMO
Each co-op player has individual drops, guns and scrolls that can still be exchanged
Runs are long, skill-based dungeon crawls where player skill and enemy knowledge matter more than level-ups
tedious_or_disliked: Runs can feel repetitive in the short term, and veterans say restarting becomes a chore once builds feel samey
Waiting for co-op matches, or never finding one
Getting key scrolls matters for some builds, so a run can be lost to luck of drops
Reading unclear tooltips and untranslated text to understand mechanics
Meta-progression is quickly maxed, leaving little to chase between updates
Dodge feels awkward and the game can feel laggy even solo for some players
divisive_points: DLC model: some see it as fair funding for a live-service game with no FOMO, others see paid characters as power creep and pay-to-win-feeling
Difficulty: early runs feel unfair and punishing, yet experienced players find builds trivial on the hardest difficulty
Comparison to Roboquest, Deadzone Rogue and Abyssus: some say gunplay is weaker but content is larger, others feel its builds are shallower
Update cadence and nerfs: fans praise ongoing support while others call updates thin and dislike character nerfs
community.reception_notes: Early access started May 22, 2020, with 1.0 on Nov 2021 (Steam lists Nov 17, 2021). It had passed 2 million copies by Nov 2021 per Wikipedia, and third-party estimates (Steam Spy 2-5M owners, steam-revenue-calculator about $65.7M gross and about $19.4M net, Boxleiter-method estimates) suggest a large hit. It reached mobile in May 2022, Xbox and PC Game Pass in Oct 2022 and PlayStation in June 2023. Metacritic's 75 and 7.1 come from the console-era page with few ratings. Wikipedia lists the PS and Switch releases, while Metacritic also lists Switch. The Metacritic critic score is based on only 10 reviews. OpenCritic could not be retrieved (web search budget was exhausted and guessed URLs were wrong), so it is left null. Recent Steam reviews (2025-2026) show a mix of long-time fans praising seasons and continued support, and negative reviews over alleged undisclosed AI art, a new EULA with forced arbitration and inactive-data deletion, DLC power creep and nerfs, plus a report that the game pinged a domain the developers no longer control. Steam community threads also mention crashes and data loss. Steam lists Windows only, despite other platforms.
