community.one_liner: A 2D side-scrolling action roguelite from Magic Design Studios in which you play an overworked Death, CEO of Death Inc., fighting rogue employees across office-themed departments with scythes, spells and curses.
community.consensus_summary: Have a Nice Death is well liked but not a genre-topper: Steam sits at Very Positive (about 86% of roughly 10.8k reviews), Metacritic critics at 81 (26 reviews, Generally Favorable) and Metacritic users at a lukewarm 7.3 from only 117 ratings. Nearly everyone praises the hand-drawn art, music, dark office humour and snappy combat. The recurring complaints are brutal boss and mob damage, scarce healing, slow and stingy unlock drops, and level and enemy repetition. It spent a year in Early Access (from March 2022), hit 1.0 on PC and Switch on 22 March 2023 with the Inevitable Time Department, and reached PlayStation and Xbox in December 2023. Critics tend to compare it to Dead Cells (and Hades/Hollow Knight) and call it a strong but derivative entry; Steam's recent reviews are still 81% positive, so it retains a steady but small audience (about 91 concurrent players in the snapshot).
best_things: Hand-drawn, muted gothic-corporate art direction with distinct, animated character designs, often compared to Hollow Knight
Fast, precise, responsive movement and combat; some players say it plays well even with mouse and keyboard
Dark-comedy office-culture setting with witty bosses and NPCs who trash-talk you based on how you played
Soundtrack that mixes elevator-music and corporate-chill hub tracks with upbeat boss themes
Large build variety: 70+ weapons and spells, cloaks (cooldown-based), and risk/reward curses that act as run-long power-ups
Boss fights that reward pattern recognition and feel satisfying to beat
Fast retry loop and a sense of real skill growth: players report first-difficulty runs becoming easy after practice
worst_things: Healing is scarce, and the grey-zone (recoverable damage) health system confuses players and is called unintuitive; one Metacritic user said they could rarely find healing items
Bosses and even regular mobs deal huge damage, creating frustrating difficulty spikes
Boss fights are visually cluttered: effects cover the player character, so some deaths feel cheap and artificial
Levels and enemies repeat: maps are rearrangements of the same rooms and the enemy roster is small, so runs feel samey over time
Combat depth is called shallow by some, mostly mashing attack with few real combos, and many in-run upgrades feel low-impact
Weapon, spell and food unlocks drop rarely, so players never see most of the content; progression feels restrictive (IGN made a similar point about progression)
Reported bugs: crashes/freezes, input delay and achievement-tracking issues raised on Steam forums (minor relative to other complaints in top reviews)
Systems are explained poorly; reviewers say the UX is confusing and they never understood what half the things do
Value is debated: top critical reviews say it may not justify $25 at full price and suggest waiting for a sale
improvements: Explain the systems (curses, grey health, cloaks, unlock paths) better instead of leaving players to work them out
Improve enemy, room and level variety so floors stop feeling like reshuffled walls
Make healing and permanent unlocks more accessible and raise drop rates for weapons and food so more of the content gets seen
Rebalance difficulty so normal rooms and bosses are closer in challenge, with better scaling across the easy and normal modes
Reduce boss visual clutter so the player model stays readable
Deeper combat with more weapon interactions and combos; fix crashes and input delay
unique_things: Premise that satirises work culture and burnout: Death as an overworked CEO dealing with rogue employees in corporate departments
Hollow Knight-style movement and art in a roguelite, often described as Dead Cells with more Hollow Knight-like controls
Curse system of risk/reward, run-long power-ups sitting alongside scythes, spells and cooldown cloaks
Bosses that comment on your damage taken, kills and gear, making fights feel personal and funny
Floor structure based on office departments, with a story that concludes in the 1.0 Inevitable Time Department
tedious_or_disliked: Dozens of failed runs before reaching the first ending; one 36-hour reviewer stopped caring about continuing the grind
Feeling of little progress because most unlocks rarely show up, so you always feel like you just started
Same maps and platforming sections start feeling samey; the map is simple enough that you always know where to go
Repeating the first-floor boss fight and the rest of the boss gauntlet; some players say the game is the same down to the end
Healing scarcity turning long runs into attrition between bosses
divisive_points: Difficulty: some call it punishing in a satisfying way and got much better, others call bosses unbalanced and artificially hard
Combat depth: praised as fluid with plentiful builds by some, and as basic button-mashing by others
Whether it is a true roguelike or roguelite is debated on the Steam forums, and some players find the graphic violence jarring; one Steam thread on it got 49 comments
Polygon objected to presenting the cruel protagonist sympathetically, while other critics loved the humour and setting
community.reception_notes: Early Access began March 2022 (Steam store lists March 8, 2022); 1.0 launched 22 March 2023 on PC and Switch with the Inevitable Time Department (new boss, mini-boss, enemies and a story conclusion). PlayStation and Xbox versions followed 5 December 2023. Wikipedia credits Gearbox Publishing as publisher while Steam currently lists Arc Games, so the publisher changed or the sources lag. Steam is Windows-only, with no Mac or Linux build. Price $24.99. Critics were warm at launch (Metascore 81, no negative reviews, 81% positive / 19% mixed), while Metacritic users are more mixed. Current Steam sentiment is stable at Very Positive. No OpenCritic score could be retrieved: web search was out of budget and the OpenCritic page I tried was the wrong game.

community.one_liner: A 2020 roguelike deckbuilder from Shiny Shoe in which you defend a multi-floor demon train's pyre from angel invaders by placing units on vertical floors, pairing two clans per run.
community.consensus_summary: Monster Train is broadly regarded as one of the best roguelike deckbuilders after Slay the Spire. Steam shows about 96% positive across roughly 23k reviews (Overwhelmingly Positive), Metacritic critic score is 86 from 27 reviews (all positive), and the Metacritic user score is 7.9 (lower and more mixed than Steam). Critics and players praise the floor-placement tactics, clan mixing and snowball-into-broken-combo runs. Criticism centres on the small enemy/boss roster, a long unlock grind, balance at top Covenant ranks, and dated art. It is not early access; it has had free content updates and a paid DLC (The Last Divinity), and since 2025 many reviewers steer newcomers to Monster Train 2 instead.
best_things: Multi-floor train layout adds spatial tactics (what goes on which floor, floor-wide effects, hit-point math) that Slay the Spire lacks; critics called it its own kind of puzzle
Pairing a main clan with a secondary clan produces many synergy combinations and encourages experimentation
Each clan has a distinct signature mechanic, which keeps runs feeling different
Snowballing into an over-the-top 'exodia' deck and steamrolling enemies is deeply satisfying; some players say it feels more empowering than Slay the Spire
Boss challenges are telegraphed up front, so you can draft toward them; several reviewers like this clarity
Runs are fairly short and playable in bursts; the game is accessible to genre newcomers and ramps up via the Covenant difficulty system
Upbeat soundtrack, and strong replay value (players report hundreds of hours and 100% achievements)
Steady free updates added champions, mutators, run records and Steam Workshop mod support
worst_things: Very small enemy and boss variety: players say you see essentially every enemy within a single run, and encounters feel like repetitive bullet sponges
Runs are short and deckbuilding feels cut off just as it gets interesting; only about 10 fights per run compared with dozens in Slay the Spire
High Covenant ranks (around 20-25) scale enemies so aggressively that many cards and some clan pairings become unviable, forcing the same 'broken' combos
Some complain drafted cards are not much better than starters, or that picks are obvious, so choices feel less meaningful
Art style and animation are polarising: several call it mobile-game or Hearthstone-like, cheap looking or ugly
Reported crashes or hangs on startup linked to the intro video (AVProVideo/Unity errors) that some say persist years later
With Monster Train 2 containing the first game's clans and more, a number of recent negative reviews say not to buy the original at $25
improvements: Add more enemy types and bosses (Metacritic users and critics such as Softpedia asked for more boss variety)
Fine-tune Covenant scaling and clan balance at the top ranks so more cards and clan combinations stay viable
Reduce or streamline the unlock grind, since factions and content are gated behind repeated runs of the same short campaign
Give players more ways to reduce variance (starting-hand or loadout options) rather than rerolling setups
Lengthen or deepen the drafting phase so deck building feels less rushed
Fix the persistent startup crash and improve Steam Deck and other platform stability
unique_things: Vertical multi-floor battlefield with a pyre you must protect, mixing deckbuilding with tower-defence-style positioning
Two-clan deck construction (main plus allied clan) with a champion choice defining the strategy
Units persist and level up across fights via upgrades, making the deck feel like an army that grows stronger
Covenant ladder, with a campaign structure where bosses are known in advance and players draft toward them
Playing the demons defending hell against angels gives it a goofier, lighter tone than Slay the Spire; one reviewer calls it Slay the Spire's chiller, goofier cousin
Competitive PvP multiplayer mode, unusual for the genre, and later Steam Workshop mod support
tedious_or_disliked: Unlocking all clans, cards and Covenant levels means replaying the same handful of stages many times, and some reviewers describe it as more grind than strategy
Low Covenant ranks are seen as too easy, and reaching meaningful difficulty takes 15-20 runs
Late-game balance feels restrictive: players can sense at the start of a run whether it is doomed, and failing is less fun than in Slay the Spire
Repetitive encounters and bloated card mechanics make runs feel samey after the first dozens of hours
Weak narrative, so there is little story motivation between runs
Drafted cards often feel only marginally better than the starter cards, so some players feel drafting choices matter little and the meta-progression is outrageously long
divisive_points: Versus Slay the Spire: many say Monster Train is deeper and more empowering, while others find it less tightly balanced and more luck-dependent or 'braindead'
Difficulty: some call it much easier than Slay the Spire and relaxing, others call high Covenants punishing and unfun
Art direction and music: praised as slick and upbeat by some, called dated, ugly or only serviceable by others
Whether to buy the original or go straight to Monster Train 2, which many see as strictly better for the same price
community.reception_notes: Launched May 2020 to strong reviews (IGN 9/10, Game Informer 9/10, Rock Paper Shotgun called it possibly the best deckbuilder since Slay the Spire; Northernlion dubbed it 2020's best deckbuilder) and was nominated for IGN Best Strategy/Tactics and a D.I.C.E. strategy/simulation award. Ported to Xbox One (Dec 2020), Switch (Aug 2021, later the First Class complete edition), iOS (Oct 2022) and PS5 (July 2024). Post-launch free updates include Friends & Foes (champions, bosses, run records), Wild Mutations (35 mutators) and Herzal's Workshop (Steam Workshop mods); paid DLC is The Last Divinity. Steam's all-time rating stays around 96% but the recent 30-day sample was 88% (small sample), partly reflecting negative reviews urging buyers toward Monster Train 2 (released May 21, 2025). Steam shows Windows only. Revenue estimate is approximate: steam-revenue-calculator.com estimates about $23.6M gross and $7.0M net on Steam (Boxleiter-style estimate, not audited), and SteamSpy lists 500k-1M owners. OpenCritic could not be retrieved (search budget exhausted and the page was not located), so opencritic is null.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Noita is a roguelike where every pixel/particle is physically simulated, and you descend a huge mountain-like world as deep as you can. He calls it extremely punishing, possibly one of the hardest roguelikes ever, with a wand-building spell system that produces wild and often lethal interactions. He admires the depth of hidden secrets and the dedicated community, and he met the developers at GDC years ago. He places it in A tier but wouldn't recommend it widely because it demands serious commitment.
praise: Fully simulated particles make fire, water and other materials behave in distinctive, realistic ways
Enormous number of secrets and things to discover, with a very committed community
Wand crafting where spells interact in unexpected, creative ways
Difficulty is deliberate and part of the design
Permadeath feels less painful than in Darkest Dungeon since you never get attached to a character
Fans love it intensely
criticism: Extremely punishing and brutal, which limits who it suits
Experimenting with an untested spell combo can kill you instantly, even 30 minutes into a run
Demands a big time commitment, so he won't recommend it to many people
The simulation concept alone could not carry a whole game (implied need for other layers)
unique_points: Every particle in the world is simulated, enabling emergent physics interactions
Around a hundred secrets intended to be nearly undiscoverable, taking years to understand
Dying to your own spell experiments is an accepted, expected part of the loop
commentary.quote: this game is great it is one of the only a tier games
design_criteria: Uniqueness of core gimmick: particle simulation is distinctive
Depth and secrets: huge discoverability and community mystery
Difficulty: brutal by design
Synergies: spell and wand combinations interact in crazy ways
Risk vs reward: experimentation can instantly kill you
Accessibility/commitment: not for casual players, playtime ranges from 45 minutes to 2000 hours

community.one_liner: A physics-sim action roguelite from Nolla Games where every pixel is a simulated material and you build your own spell wands to fight and dig through a procedurally generated underworld.
community.consensus_summary: Players rate Noita extremely highly (Steam: Overwhelmingly Positive, about 95% of roughly 89k reviews, with recent reviews still around 92%), and many long-time players call it one of the deepest games ever made. Critics were favorable but more mixed than players: Metacritic sits at 76 from 20 reviews, with scores ranging from 95 down to 45, mostly split on whether the randomness and lethality are a feature or a flaw. The recurring split is between admiration for the wand-building and pixel-physics depth and frustration with one-shot deaths, hidden knowledge and slow early-game loops. It left early access on 15 Oct 2020 (early access began 24 Sep 2019); the developers shipped the Epilogue update in March 2021 and a second Epilogue update in April 2024, plus ongoing bug fixes and strong mod support. It is not abandoned, though major content updates are rare.
best_things: Fully simulated pixel physics: every pixel of sand, water, lava, acid, gas and fire reacts, so the world can be burned, flooded, melted or blown apart
Wand and spell crafting is hugely deep, with a very high skill ceiling; players describe building absurdly overpowered wands, black holes and infinite-heal setups
Enormous depth of secrets, alchemy, lore, puzzles and hidden content that the community is still uncovering years later (one reviewer with 1,000+ hours says mysteries remain)
Emergent, funny and spectacular deaths and moments; the chaos is often described as a large part of the fun
Huge replay value and the sense that you yourself improve since there is no persistent character power progression
Distinctive pixel art and particle effects that make the physics visually satisfying
Strong modding scene and Steam Workshop support extending the game
Rewarding 'breaking the game' fantasy: late runs let you become a near-unkillable god after struggling early
worst_things: Extremely punishing, often feels unfair: instant deaths from off-screen fast projectiles, single pixels of lava/acid/fire, polymorph, or accidentally hurting yourself with your own wand
Very little is explained; much of the knowledge needed to play well is hidden or requires a wiki, leading many to say it needs 50-500 hours before you feel any agency
High variance and randomness: several critics and reviewers say outcomes depend heavily on lucky early spells and wands rather than pure skill
Long, slow early game that you must repeat after every death, with enormous levels to crawl through for gold
Secrets and quests are cryptic (ARG/cryptography-style) and often require tedious trial and error or outside resources
Inventory is small relative to the number of spell options, making optimal experimentation feel like a walking and swapping chore
improvements: Better onboarding and in-game explanation of wand building, materials and core systems so players are not forced to use a wiki
A minimap or better navigation and possibly some fast-travel or shortcut to cut down on re-traversing huge levels
Less punishing instant-death sources or clearer telegraphing of off-screen and one-pixel hazards
Ways to skip or vary the early game and first-biome loop after repeated deaths
More inventory or quality-of-life for swapping wands and spells while experimenting
unique_things: Every pixel is an individual physically simulated material, unlike tile-based roguelikes
Wands are built from modular spells with modifiers, triggers and multicasts, closer to programming than picking items
A hidden alchemy system and layered secrets, including multiverse and 'new game plus' style content beyond the obvious ending
No persistent character upgrades; progression is entirely player knowledge plus what you find in a run
Made by veteran indie devs (Petri Purho of Crayon Physics Deluxe, Olli Harjola of The Swapper, Arvi Teikari/Hempuli of Baba Is You), and praised as a technical showcase (GDC Best Technology nominee)
Fully destructible world where digging, flooding and explosions are core strategies, not just scenery
tedious_or_disliked: Repeating the first mines area hundreds of times; several reviewers spent most of their time in it and found it dull after many runs
Crawling through huge levels clearing enemies for gold, with hours of tedious re-exploration after a cheap death
Secrets hunting and cryptic puzzles that feel like wasted time without a guide
The first boss ('tutorial boss') taking players dozens or even hundreds of runs, which some find off-putting
Walking back and forth to swap wand and spell loadouts because of the small inventory
Feeling underpowered even while dealing large damage, due to fragile health and one-shot hazards
divisive_points: Difficulty and opacity: fans call it resilience-building and rewarding, detractors call it vindictive and time-wasting ('the community has Stockholm Syndrome' is a representative complaint)
Luck versus skill: long-time players say skill and knowledge dominate and luck is minor, while critics and some players say early runs depend on random lucky drops
Hidden knowledge as a feature: many see the wiki and community-solved mysteries as part of the magic, others see it as a design failure
Critic reception: GameGrin gave 95 and Attack of the Fanboy 90, while GameCritics gave 45 and DarkZero 60, showing a wide critic split
community.reception_notes: Launched in early access in Sept 2019 and reached 1.0 on 15 Oct 2020, then got the Epilogue update (30 Mar 2021) and Epilogue 2 (8 Apr 2024). Accolades include 2019 IGF finalist in three categories, a 2020 GDC Awards Best Technology nomination, a 2020 Steam Awards Most Innovative Gameplay nomination, and Finnish Game Awards Game of the Year 2021. Critics landed at Metacritic 76 (20 reviews) while players sit around 95% positive on Steam, so players have been notably warmer than critics. Platform is Windows on Steam (also playable on Steam Deck per the wiki); no native Mac/Linux. Price is about $19.99. Some OpenCritic and Metacritic detail could not be retrieved directly, so the OpenCritic recommend rate is taken from Wikipedia and the top-critic average is unknown. The revenue and owner figures are third-party estimates, not audited.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Roguebook (2021) is a deck-building roguelike where you control two heroes at once while uncovering tiles of a giant book with ink and brushes. He loves it and calls it the template for a good deck builder, and says it would be an instant S tier. One flaw drops it a full tier: the animations are slow, cannot be sped up in the menu, and sometimes swallow fast card inputs. He lands it at an easy A, above Monster Train, and wishes for more updates and an animation fix that could push it higher.
praise: Blend of tactical two-character card combat with an explorable outside world (ink-and-brush tile uncovering)
Hero placement and switching adds interesting positioning gameplay
Exploration rewards: money, potions, more ink, cards and unique events that really transform the run
Five characters, any pair combo feels very different, so runs are varied almost every time
Great customization at run start, which he considers important for modern roguelikes
Phenomenal balance: almost every card is playable and strong builds feel earned through synergy hunting
Beautiful visuals and care put into animations
criticism: Animations are too slow and there is no menu option to speed them up
Must wait for each card animation to finish before acting; fast inputs sometimes don't register
Frustration with waiting is bad enough that he stopped coming back to it despite loving it
Wishes for more updates/content after the expansion, unsure it gets any
unique_points: Controlling two heroes at once with placement, combined with a tile-uncovering book map
Hero-pair combinations create entirely different decks from only five characters
Events that meaningfully transform the game
Design lesson: a speed-up option matters for veteran players; slow polished animations can hurt replayability
commentary.quote: this definitely is the template for how to make a good deck building game
design_criteria: Gameplay and exploration blend: card combat plus an outside-world map both engaging
Customization at run start: choosing two heroes with drastically different cards
Replayability/diversity: hero combinations make runs feel unique
Balance and synergies: nearly every card viable, power earned through strategy
Visuals/animation: beautiful but too slow, hurting pacing
Quality of life: no animation speed option, dropped inputs
Post-launch support: wants more updates beyond the expansion
Events: unique and run-transforming

community.one_liner: A roguelike deckbuilder from Abrakam (Faeria) with Richard Garfield's involvement, where you pair two heroes into one shared deck and spend ink and brushes to uncover a hex-tile map page by page.
community.consensus_summary: Roguebook is well regarded but not treated as a genre top-tier title. Steam sits at Very Positive (about 84% of roughly 4,600 reviews) and Metacritic critics give it 78 (Generally Favorable), with most praise going to the art, the two-hero swap system and the explorable map. Players who love it often put in 80-150 hours, but a large share of the positive reviews say it is best bought on sale, and the negatives are dominated by save-corrupting crashes and bugs, uneven balance, and a thin feel (few heroes, limited enemy variety). Developer and publisher (Nacon) support has effectively stopped according to recent Steam reviews, so the known bugs look permanent. It is a finished 1.0 release, not early access.
best_things: Art style, card art and animation are widely called gorgeous; much of it is reused and refreshed from Faeria
The two-hero system (front/back positions, block cards swapping who is in front, relics tied to one hero) is the most-cited standout mechanic
Ink and brush map exploration gives many more routing choices than the three-path Slay the Spire map, making runs feel different
Card pool is considered good and can feel breakable, with gems slotted into cards and upgrade options adding build depth
Runs take roughly an hour, a length players like, and there is a large meta-progression (pages/embellishments, 20 difficulty levels) that gives 80-100+ hours of content
Losing is cushioned by meta progression, so failed runs still unlock pages and perks
Extremely cheap on sale (frequently about $2.50-$9 with DLC), which many reviewers call one of the best value deals in the genre
Full controller support and Steam Cloud saves (per the Steam store page)
worst_things: Balance and pacing frustrate at higher ascension levels, with input lag on top; this is the single most-upvoted negative review (65 helpful votes)
Crashes can corrupt the save file and wipe all meta progress; this is the single most repeated complaint in negative reviews, including from players with 50+ hours
Other bugs: halved game speed, 3-5 second lag between playing a card and the animation, stuck UI notifications and glitched gem icons, high CPU use, and a DLC reported as buggy
Balance is lopsided: early enemies and bosses can burst for most of your HP while some hero/relic strategies trivialise everything, and the DLC hero is described as overpowered
Only four base heroes (a fifth is paid DLC), so runs become samey and the game feels small, with limited enemies, cards and only three acts
Developer support has stopped and the online/tournament features are reported as non-functional; support emails and Discord messages reportedly go unanswered
No real plot despite some hero banter, which reviewers feel was dropped or abandoned
Synergies are often shallow or depend on RNG, so some players feel little control over building a deck
improvements: Fix the save corruption and crash bugs and optimise performance/animation lag
Rebalance early-game damage versus block and healing, and relic pricing (legendaries and the Rose relic are called overpriced)
Add more heroes to the base game, and more enemies and cards, rather than selling a hero as DLC
Quality-of-life additions: skippable intro cutscene each run, larger card text option for accessibility, Steam Workshop or mod support, easier card removal or clearer accession system
Give the map exploration less randomness (for example guaranteed access to key upgrades) and trim the back-and-forth walking
Add a built-in way to retry or undo, since players currently rely on quitting to menu and continuing as a save-scum trick
unique_things: Open hex map uncovered with limited ink and brushes, instead of a branching node tree; it is a resource-management layer of its own
Two-hero team sharing one deck, with front/back positioning that changes which card effects apply and who takes damage
Gem-slot card upgrades and difficult card removal, so you improve cards rather than thin the deck (a larger deck is actually rewarded with passive bonuses)
Fog-of-war 'book pages' setting with seer tiles, lever events and tournaments that feed a persistent meta progression
Design pedigree: Faeria developers plus Magic: The Gathering creator Richard Garfield, funded on Kickstarter in 2019
tedious_or_disliked: Map exploration is slow and grindy: players feel forced to clear as many fights as they can for ink and gold, then walk back and forth across the map
Healing is scarce and hard to manage in the early game, so some runs become attrition grinds
Long-term meta progression drags; after roughly 8-20 hours players say they see the grind, and after about 100 hours the remaining unlocks mostly just raise difficulty
Losing a run to a bug or corrupted save after a long session
Needing to pay real money to unlock the fifth hero
Higher ascension levels feel like a balance and pacing slog rather than fair challenge, even to Slay the Spire veterans
divisive_points: Difficulty: some call it brutal early (a Dark Souls of deckbuilders, 'skill issue' replies), others say it is far too easy once you learn the genre or find strong combos
Map exploration is either the game's best idea or its slowest and most random system; several reviewers say both in the same review
Whether it beats Slay the Spire / Monster Train: a few players rank it higher, but many say it is a lesser alternative best bought cheap
community.reception_notes: Released on PC June 17, 2021 (Nacon publishing, Abrakam developing), then on PS4/PS5 and Xbox in February 2022 and on Switch in April 2022. Wikipedia notes positive aggregate reception on PC, PS5 and Xbox One and mixed reviews for the Switch version. Launch critics emphasised the look and map system but some flagged game-breaking bugs and too little content for more than a few hours. Years later, recent Steam reviews (up to 2026) say support has stopped, crashes still corrupt saves and online features do not work, and the Steam forum has threads asking whether any devs are still around. Commercial estimates: SteamSpy owners 200k-500k and steam-revenue-calculator.com estimates about $2.5M gross / $0.73M net on Steam, but these are order-of-magnitude estimates. Steam lists 5 DLC items (skin pack, art book, soundtrack, alternate art pack, Fugoro hero). OpenCritic could not be retrieved (its search and the guessed game ID did not resolve), so that score is null.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Skul: The Hero Slayer is a traditional 2D action roguelike where you play a small skeleton who swaps skulls, each with a distinct playstyle and abilities. He finds it fast, explosive and very satisfying, and he has kept playing since release, including a paid expansion DLC. His main complaints are a repetitive early game with the same starting skull, limited pre-run customization, and reused bosses across worlds. He places it firmly in A tier, above Have a Nice Death and roughly just under FTL.
praise: Swapping between skulls gives constantly new playstyles, and you can hold two at once
Combat is hack-and-slash with many enemies, big explosions and a strong sense of power
Large pool of items, each with unique abilities and randomized enchantments
Skulls can be upgraded multiple times, unlocking new abilities
The paid DLC added many features and a whole new world
Cute music, appealing art and a story he likes
criticism: Once all skulls are seen, the game gets somewhat repetitive
Pre-game customization is limited and every run starts with the same skull
The first world gets tiresome with the same weak starting skull and tiny abilities
Every world has the same bosses; he wants more variety
unique_points: Character-as-resource design: swappable skulls act as different characters within one run
Randomized item enchantments layered on top of unique item abilities add build variety
commentary.quote: I really like Skull, this is a really really good game
design_criteria: Character/ability diversity: skull swapping gives very different playstyles
Combat feel: powerful, satisfying hack and slash
Item variety: unique items with randomized enchantments
Replayability and repetition: same start skull and first world grow stale
Pre-run customization: limited
Boss variety: reused bosses across worlds
Charm and presentation: cute music, art and story
Content updates: paid DLC added a new world

community.one_liner: A 2D action roguelite platformer by SouthPAW Games (published by Neowiz) where you play a skeleton who swaps between dozens of skull 'classes', each with its own attacks and skills, to fight the human Imperial Army.
community.consensus_summary: Skul is received as a very good, Dead Cells-adjacent action roguelite: Steam shows Very Positive (about 93% positive across roughly 57,700 reviews in the local data; about 92% in the store's English/recent view) and Metacritic has a Metascore of 80 from 22 critics. Praise centers on the skull-swapping combat, build variety, pixel art and surprisingly good story. Criticism is that it is punishing with a steep difficulty curve, heavily RNG-driven, and repetitive once the novelty fades, with clunky keyboard controls and screen clutter. The Metacritic user score is noticeably lower (7.0, Mixed) than Steam, suggesting the harder-edged/grindy side bites some players. It is not abandoned: after 2020 early access and the Jan 2021 full release, it got console ports, a Mythology Pack DLC, mobile versions (2024), and Steam reviews still run 'Very Positive' recently; Wikipedia reports over 2 million copies sold by Dec 2023.
best_things: Skull-swapping is the core hook: you carry two skulls at once and swap mid-combat, and each skull (Grim Reaper, Davy Jones, Monkey King, etc.) plays very differently, so runs feel distinct.
Large variety of skulls, items and Quintessences that interact with each other, giving real theorycrafting and build depth; some players report hundreds of hours without feeling stale.
Pixel art and sprite work are repeatedly called beautiful and detailed, with distinct visual themes per zone and memorable bosses.
Story and tone surprised many reviewers for an action roguelite; several say it is emotional and has twists, with a serious-but-charming tone compared to Dead Cells' wackiness.
Bosses start out feeling impossible but become learnable pattern fights that players describe as rewarding.
Runs well on low-end PCs and on Steam Deck, even though it is not officially verified there; Steam reviewers report 40+ hours with excellent performance.
Post-launch content is well regarded: one reviewer says the Mythology Pack DLC added four new skulls plus a very strong legendary skull; the soundtrack is also singled out as fitting the theme.
worst_things: Difficulty is steep and unforgiving, with no easy mode; many negative reviews cite hitting a wall at bosses or around zone 4 and quitting.
Heavy RNG in items and skulls can make good builds hard to assemble and can doom a run outright.
Repetition: same enemies and layouts across runs, and meta-upgrades feel slow or small after the first hours, which produces 'fun for a few hours then a grind' reviews.
Keyboard controls are widely described as poor (remapping needed); controller is strongly preferred.
Screen clutter and over-animated skills/effects can cover much of the screen and make dodging hard; some call combat feel floaty or lacking weight.
Balance and pacing issues: some bosses take far too long (one reviewer spent 10 minutes in a single fight) and some players call the balancing and screen clutter among the worst they have seen.
Some item and system descriptions are overwhelmingly long or poorly explained, and build-enabling mechanics are not well signposted in-game.
improvements: Add an easier or assist difficulty, or a gentler on-ramp, for players who want the content without the punishment.
Better in-game explanation of systems (Quintessences, inscriptions, item synergies) with shorter, clearer descriptions so players do not need outside guides.
Reduce run-killing RNG through more reliable ways to shape builds and more useful low-tier items.
Improve default keyboard layout and controls, and lower screen clutter or add effect-reduction options.
Faster, more meaningful meta-progression so early failed runs feel less like a repetition loop.
More big content updates; one reviewer says the only issue is the lack of major updates.
unique_things: The playable character is a skeleton who swaps heads: each skull is effectively a class with its own moveset, and you hold two at once and switch mid-fight.
Skull rarity tiers plus a growing roster from bosses and story (including fan-favorite legendary skulls) create a collect-and-mix loop unlike most 2D roguelites.
Quintessences (active items) and item synergies sit on top of the skull system for a three-layer build structure.
Dark Quartz corruption adds a challenge layer for late-game and boss encounters.
A darker, more serious narrative with a villain-adjacent twist on the fantasy trope of heroes versus monsters, which reviewers say is more story-driven than typical roguelites.
tedious_or_disliked: Restarting from the very beginning after losing to a boss, fighting the same early enemies again, which several reviewers call exhausting.
Grinding for upgrades between runs; one player says multiple runs are needed per upgrade after about nine hours.
Long boss fights with heavy health pools (one reviewer describes a ten-minute fight).
Reading dense item and inscription text, and needing fan guides to understand builds.
Level layouts and enemy sets feeling repetitive across zones and runs.
divisive_points: Difficulty: fans love the challenge and mastery, while others want an easy mode and feel punished; many players drop off around zone 4.
Build restrictiveness and RNG: praised as replayable variety by some, called a love-it-or-hate-it restrictive build system by others.
Combat feel: some call it satisfying and simple-yet-deep, others say it is clunky, loose, floaty and lacks impact.
Comparison to Dead Cells: some say it is on par or more fun, while others say Dead Cells is clearly better.
community.reception_notes: Early access launched Feb 2020 and the 1.0 release followed in Jan 2021 on PC, with console versions in Oct 2021 and mobile in 2024 per Wikipedia. Wikipedia reports over 1 million copies by Jan 2022 and over 2 million by Dec 2023; the local SteamSpy-style estimate of 1-2 million Steam owners and a steam-revenue-calculator estimate of about $46.9M gross / about $13.8M net are rough Boxleiter-style figures, not audited. Wikipedia cites IGN comparing it to Dead Cells and Majora's Mask and Polygon liking the combat while noting translation issues. Mythology Pack DLC adds extra skulls; Steam lists it as a Player Favorite. Steam recent reviews remain Very Positive, so there is no review-bomb or abandonment signal, though some players wish for larger updates. Not officially Steam Deck verified, but players say it runs well. OpenCritic score could not be retrieved (web search budget was exhausted and a guessed OpenCritic URL returned the wrong game), so it is left null.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Streets of Rogue (2017) is a unique roguelike where you pick from many characters and are dropped into small village-like levels full of mini quests and missions needed to reach the next area. He says each character changes play so drastically that each feels like its own game. The levels themselves are fairly repetitive and not very dense, and he worries that once every character is mastered it may get old. With about 15 hours played, he enjoys it a lot and places it around a mid B (transcript reads 'mid eight', likely 'mid B').
praise: Very unique, interesting gameplay
Huge roster of characters
Each character drastically changes how you play, like a different game
Lots of random events and mini quests per level
High replayability across characters
criticism: Random levels are not very dense
Levels are fairly repetitive
May get tiresome after finishing the game repeatedly with every character
unique_points: Character variety carries the game and masks repetitive level design
Small village-style areas with side missions required to progress
commentary.quote: every character is its own game almost
design_criteria: Character diversity: drastically different playstyles per character
Level design: random but sparse and repetitive
Replayability: many characters keep it fresh until all are mastered
Mission/quest structure: mini quests and required missions per area

community.one_liner: A top-down, procedurally generated action roguelite/immersive-sim hybrid by Matt Dabrowski (published by tinyBuild) where you pick from 20+ wildly different character classes and complete city-block missions by fighting, sneaking, hacking, bribing or causing chaos.
community.consensus_summary: Streets of Rogue is a player-beloved cult hit: Steam shows 'Overwhelmingly Positive' at about 96% of roughly 23,100 reviews, with sandbox freedom, character variety and co-op chaos cited over and over. Critics were also favourable but the critic sample is small (Metacritic lists 82 on Xbox One from 5 reviews and 75 on Switch from 4; PC Gamer gave 84). The game spent roughly two years in Early Access from 2017 and reached 1.0 on 12 July 2019 on PC, then Switch, PS4 and Xbox One. Criticism clusters around clunky melee and gun aim, RNG and unfair late-floor modifiers, weak build synergy compared with deeper roguelites, and a solo experience that some find repetitive. A sequel, Streets of Rogue 2, is still listed as 'coming soon' on Steam with no release date, and much of the recent review traffic is fans waiting for it.
best_things: Huge sandbox freedom: every mission has many solutions (stealth, hacking, bribery, violence, distraction, using gang rivalries) and the game lets you pick your own approach

20+ character classes that change how the game plays (cop gets XP for arrests, zombie turns kills into zombies, shapeshifter possesses NPCs, gorilla, scientist, politician, etc.), driving replayability
Emergent chaos from interacting systems: rival gangs, scientists vs gorillas, explosions, fridges and generators as weapons, NPCs reacting to each other and to you
Excellent co-op (local and online up to 4 players); widely described as better with friends
Humour and tone: absurd gags and parody factions are frequently called out by reviewers and players
Strong long-term content: big quests, mutators, DLC characters, Steam Workshop support, sandbox/custom levels and characters (one reviewer logged thousands of hours)
Responsive developer and unlocks earned in play rather than paywalled (Steam and Metacritic user reviews)
Music praised as fitting, though some want more tracks
worst_things: Clunky combat: melee described as flailing, gun shots sometimes lock onto unintended targets, and knockback when shot from several directions can be deadly
RNG-driven deaths: bad trait offers, unlucky items or a random NPC fight can end multi-hour runs
Late-floor modifiers (falling bombs, spreading goo, everyone armed with rocket launchers) are seen by some as unfair rather than fun
Heavy menuing to interact with things, and stealth and combat feel stiff to some players
Limited build depth/synergy compared with Gungeon-style roguelites, per a co-op reviewer

Technical gripes: Switch version lag (Metacritic user), Steam Deck unplayable per top negative review (controller inputs not recognised, sub-20 fps docked), occasional save-data loss and online multiplayer breakage reported in negative Steam reviews

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Undermine is a top-down dungeon-crawling roguelike where you play a humble miner collecting gold and upgrades. It looks basic and has nothing structurally unique, and the early game deliberately feels underpowered. Once you get past the start, items synergize so well that you become absurdly overpowered and can break the game. He finds it packed with content and modes, and has returned to it many times. He calls it a really good game and places it in A tier.
praise: Huge number of items that synergize insanely well
Extremely easy and satisfying to break the game and feel overpowered
Packed with content: blessings, pets, customization, multiple game modes
Classic Roguelike mode is amazing and worth playing by itself
Looks basic but executes its fundamentals very well
Strong replayability; he has come back many times
criticism: Combat is pretty basic
Feels underpowered at the start, which is not a good feeling in roguelikes
Must grind the early game before unlocking the best content like the Classic Rogue mode
Game can crash or have duplication glitches when broken

Combat depth: basic fighting is a minor weakness

community.one_liner: A top-down, pixel-art action-adventure roguelite by two-person studio Thorium in which a peasant delves an ever-changing mine, blending Zelda-style combat and exploration with RPG-like gold, relic and permanent-upgrade progression.
community.consensus_summary: UnderMine is well received: Steam shows about 90% positive across roughly 9,900 reviews (Very Positive), and critics on Metacritic rate the PC version 79 and the Switch version 83, praising its polish, presentation and upgrade systems while noting it does little unexpected. Player opinion splits on its heavy meta-progression: fans call it a satisfying one-more-run loop with lots of secrets, while detractors find the early game weak, grindy and RNG/curse-driven. It left early access (Aug 2019) for a full 1.0 launch on Aug 6, 2020 with Xbox Game Pass inclusion, then came to Switch (Feb 2021) and PS4 (Mar 2021). The studio has since moved to UnderMine 2, which some recent reviewers read as a sign the original is mostly finished; the Steam store page shows a soft recent-review dip (small sample).
best_things: Polished, charming pixel-art presentation and fitting music, often highlighted even by players who dislike the gameplay loop
Strong sense of progression: failed runs still unlock upgrades, items, NPCs and permanent improvements, fueling a 'just one more run' feel
Huge amount of secrets, events, hidden rooms, recipes and achievements to discover, including after beating the main story
Rescuable helpers/NPCs with their own skills and permanent perks add RPG-style depth
Combat and relic/potion synergies can produce fun, sometimes absurd builds late in a run
Flexible pacing: you are not forced to rush or beat every boss each run, and post-game challenges and difficulty adjustments add replay value
Plays well on both gamepad and mouse-and-keyboard; easy to pick back up casually
Critics call it well-constructed, with clear mastery of controls, upgrade systems and overall design (Nintendo Life 90, Hey Poor Player 90)
worst_things: Grind is the top complaint: incremental meta upgrades make early runs feel intentionally weak and unfair
Many items and relics are seen as minor stat boosts that do not change how you play, so builds feel samey
Item pool and content variety are limited: the same items keep reappearing and only a few bosses repeat every run
Annoying or artificial difficulty: traps at room entrances, bomb-filled trapped chests, sliding off ledges, enemies swarming with little room to dodge
Curses and scarce healing can ruin an otherwise good run, which reviewers describe as anti-fun
Gold does not carry over between deaths, making it hard to save up for big purchases
Melee versus the ranged/boomerang option is seen as unbalanced, with the first boss hard to hit in melee
Some players report slightly delayed controls after actions, unclear item descriptions, and room mechanics with no explanation
improvements: More varied weapons or starting loadouts, since the base attack set never really changes
More impactful, build-defining relics rather than small numeric boosts
Greater variety in bosses and items, and post-game challenges that add new content instead of only self-imposed handicaps
Smoother early-game balance: faster gold, less RNG around healing and curses, less reliance on meta grind
Clearer in-game explanations of item effects and room interactions
Clearer in-game explanations of item effects and room interactions (already listed) and more polish on control responsiveness
Tighter control responsiveness; some reviewers note delayed actions when timing matters
unique_things: Gold-and-greed loop: you mine gold, spend it on upgrades and lose part of it on death, with a peasant-fodder dark-humor story
RPG-flavored stats, potions and shopping layered over Zelda/Isaac-style action, which some reviewers say suits RPG fans more than hardcore roguelike fans
Persistent NPC/helper rescue system and a huge web of hidden recipes and secret rooms
'Othermine' mode, praised as a purer start-from-zero roguelike experience once found
Mine that changes every run, with the freedom to descend at your own pace rather than speedrun
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding meta currency to get modest damage or stat boosts, which some call padding that stretches limited content
Repetitive loop of samey rooms and enemies after the first dozen hours
Having to survive many runs just to reach later bosses, especially for new players who die early
Low-impact relic drops and RNG-locked synergies that make good runs rare
Keys, bombs and healing feeling too scarce to open most of a floor
divisive_points: Meta-progression: some see satisfying RPG power growth, others see a grind that replaces good balance
Difficulty and RNG: curses, traps and heal scarcity read as fair challenge to some and as cheap to others

Originality: critics call it polished but unsurprising, and users compare it to Binding of Isaac, Enter the Gungeon, Moonlighter, Hammerwatch and early Zelda, sometimes favorably and sometimes as less complex or charming
Roguelite versus roguelike expectations: RPG fans like the progression, traditional roguelike fans are more likely to bounce
community.reception_notes: Early access began Aug 20, 2019; 1.0 released Aug 6, 2020 on Windows and Xbox One (Game Pass), Switch Feb 11, 2021, PS4 Mar 30, 2021; Wikipedia says about 600,000 downloads across Steam and Game Pass by Jan 2021, and SteamSpy-style estimates put Steam owners at 500k-1M. Third-party estimate (steam-revenue-calculator.com, Boxleiter method, treat as order-of-magnitude) is about $6.1M gross and $1.8M net on Steam. Critics were warm at launch; user reviews are split more sharply than critics, and Metacritic user score (7.0, 29 ratings) is mixed and listed on the Switch page. UnderMine 2 was announced Apr 2024 and is out, leading some reviewers to say the original is effectively finished. A live web search was not possible because the search budget was exhausted; Reddit and OpenCritic pages could not be fetched, so OpenCritic score is null. Steam store page also showed a recent-review dip (Mixed, small sample) that I could not verify further.

community.one_liner: A minimalist auto-attacking 'bullet heaven' roguelite by Poncle where you move around a screen while weapons fire themselves, collecting XP to build an absurdly overpowered loadout and survive 15-30 minutes against swarms of monsters.
community.consensus_summary: Near-universally praised as a cheap, endlessly moreish dopamine loop that essentially founded the 'bullet heaven' / survivors-like subgenre. Steam shows 98.3% positive (Overwhelmingly Positive, roughly 266k reviews) and Metacritic PC critics give it 86 with a 8.1 user score. It launched into Steam early access in Dec 2021, blew up via streamers/YouTube in early 2022, hit 1.0 in Oct 2022, and has since been ported to Xbox, mobile, Switch, PlayStation and Quest with a steady stream of free updates and paid collab DLC (Castlevania, Among Us, Contra, Balatro, etc.). It is actively supported, not abandoned. The small negative minority calls it shallow, mindless, too easy once powered up, and a time sink; some long-term fans are tired of the DLC cadence or breaking patches.
best_things: Extremely addictive 'one more run' loop: escalating power fantasy where a few minutes of play turns you into a screen-clearing god
Price and value: around $5 on Steam with hundreds of hours of content, frequently described as among the best-value games available
Huge roster of characters, weapons, evolutions, stages and secrets that reward experimentation and discovery
Low barrier to entry: one-stick control, auto-attacks, and runs simple enough to play with minimal attention yet deep enough for theorycrafting
Developer care: free wiki, cross-saves, online co-op and regular free content updates, earning a Steam 'Labor of Love' nomination per a reviewer
Performs well on low-end hardware, Steam Deck and phones; critics singled out Steam Deck suitability
Strong co-op appeal, including couch co-op on Switch and online co-op on PC
Nostalgic, Castlevania-style gothic pixel aesthetic and lots of fan service and references
worst_things: Gameplay is minimal: many players say you reach a point in each run where you no longer need to dodge and can effectively idle
Difficulty swings between trivial and overwhelming; some say it gets easier as it goes, with little real challenge once builds snowball
Screen fills with effects and clutter late in runs, making it hard to read what is happening
Many characters and items feel like stat-tweaked copies of each other; run variety is perceived as lower than the roster suggests
Progression and unlock conditions are opaque; reviewers complain they cannot tell which character or stage is needed next without a wiki
Stability complaints after some patches: crashes around the 10-minute mark and level-up soft-locks in multiplayer were reported in Steam reviews
Audio is repetitive, with complaints about a single looping track and one critic calling the soundtrack weak
Simple enemy and boss design: mostly slow melee mobs and bosses that feel like larger normal enemies
improvements: Clearer in-game guidance for unlock requirements so players do not need the wiki
Better difficulty scaling so late-run and endgame builds stay engaging instead of trivializing content
More enemy and boss variety, including ranged or pattern-based threats that force movement decisions
Quality-of-life options: skippable or disabled level-up animations, random-character select, less awkward level-up screens that drop you facing the wrong way
More balanced co-op, including restoring item slot counts that one player said were cut in a patch without notes
Fewer patch-introduced bugs and better communication of balance changes in patch notes
unique_things: Helped define the 'bullet heaven' genre: automatic combat where the only control is movement, inverting bullet hell
Runs are built around a soft 30-minute timer and a Reaper that eventually ends unwinnable runs
Weapon evolution recipes (specific weapon plus passive combos) create a discovery-driven build layer
Persistent meta-progression via gold-bought PowerUps plus a huge web of secret unlocks
Made by essentially one developer in Phaser, originally inspired by Magic Survival, and grew into a multi-platform franchise with licensed collabs, a spinoff (Vampire Crawlers)
Sold at a very low price point but sustained by paid DLC that adds large new content sets
tedious_or_disliked: 100%-ing is described as monotonous and grindy once you know all the mechanics; there is always something left to unlock
Runs are long (up to 30 minutes), so it is poorly suited to short sessions; chest and level-select pauses extend the timer and this must be toggled per run according to one reviewer
Some players say they just walk in circles collecting gems for 20 minutes
Unlock chasing can require playing specific characters or stages in opaque ways, which reviewers found frustrating
Players who feel it is 'slot machine' or clicker-like dislike the luck-driven level-up choices and passive play
Some long-time fans say the flood of DLC feels like it should be a sequel with fixes instead
divisive_points: Whether the low-input design is relaxing and hypnotic or boring, mindless and overrated; critics noted it either hooks you completely or not at all
Sheer quantity of unlockables and kitchen-sink content: seen as generous depth by some and bloat by others
Paid collab DLC: praised as substantial and optional by many, criticised by a few as a sign the base game should have been iterated on or sequelised
Randomness and power-curve: some love the snowballing build chaos, others find it unsatisfying with little agency
community.reception_notes: Early access launched on Steam in Dec 2021 and exploded in early 2022 (30k concurrent Steam players by late Jan, 70k+ the next month) through streamers and YouTube; version 1.0 shipped Oct 20, 2022 on Windows/macOS. Ports followed: Xbox (Nov 2022), free ad-supported mobile (Dec 2022), Switch with 4-player local co-op (Aug 2023), PlayStation (Aug 2024), Meta Quest (Nov 2025). It moved from Phaser to Unity starting around v1.6. Awards per Wikipedia include a Golden Joystick Breakthrough Award (2022), D.I.C.E. Action Game of the Year (2023), two BAFTA Games Awards in 2023 (Best Game, Game Design) and a BAFTA Evolving Game award (2025). Console launch bugs were noted by Game Informer. Steam shows a recent version around 1.16.x with pinned patch-note and save-recovery threads. A few recent negative reviews complain about a patch that crashed the game and a co-op item slot cut made without patch-note mention. A reported mid-2026 rename of the game was not independently verified and should not be relied on. Steam lists a Mac build but no Linux. OpenCritic could not be retrieved, so that score is recorded as null (unverified).

community.one_liner: A colorful twin-stick action roguelite by Swedish studio semiwork, focused on hunting bosses through corrupted levels with hundreds of weapons and power-ups, a jump/backflip and stomp mechanic, and local co-op.
community.consensus_summary: Players love it: Steam shows Overwhelmingly Positive (about 96.5% of roughly 4,900 reviews), with many calling it an underrated hidden gem comparable to Nuclear Throne, Enter the Gungeon and The Binding of Isaac. Praise centers on weapon/item variety, snappy animation, music and goofy personality. It entered Early Access in Feb 2021 and had its 1.0 release on Jun 8, 2023. Critic coverage is thin: Metacritic lists only two critic reviews (both 90/100, no Metascore yet) and OpenCritic had no entry found. Attention picked up after semiwork's later hit R.E.P.O., with fans asking for online multiplayer or a sequel; the price has dropped to $4.99 (from about $20 per reviewers). Note: web search quota was exhausted during this research, so community detail relies mainly on Steam reviews, the Steam discussions page and store page.
best_things: Huge pool of weapons and power-ups (reviewers cite hundreds) that stays reasonably balanced and gives strong replayability
Fluid, snappy pixel animation, bouncy combat feel and satisfying gameplay loop
Backflip/jump plus stomp combos give movement a distinct identity versus a standard dash or roll
Level design built around finding and cleansing corrupted beacons makes most enemy encounters optional rather than lock-in arena rooms
Strong music, sound effects, character design and humor; collected items are visibly represented on the character
Multiple difficulty levels and a quick, useful tutorial; early runs feel fair rather than impossible
Extremely cheap at $4.99 with local co-op and Steam Deck / full controller support
Boss-focused structure with varied enemies and bosses that flee mid-fight
Widely called a criminally underrated hidden gem and outstanding value, the most repeated theme in top reviews
worst_things: Screen clutter and visual chaos, especially late-game with lots of particles and projectiles
Some weapons and starting items feel weak or useless, with melee weapons most often called out
Final boss and ending disappoint some players: the last boss resembles a regular run boss and post-credits reward is mostly a harder difficulty
Technical complaints: 60 FPS cap, stuttering reported by some, limited graphics settings and slowdown on laptops
Art style and pixel look does not land for everyone; a couple of reviewers mention motion sickness or find it too busy
Feels derivative to some, described as a mix of existing twin-stick roguelikes without much that is new
Content can feel thin after a number of runs
improvements: Online multiplayer (co-op is local/split-screen only) is the most repeated request
More graphics and performance options plus an uncapped frame rate
Deeper item synergies and character-specific mechanics to make builds feel more distinct
Rebalance weak starter items, perks and melee weapons
More post-game content or a stronger ending, plus more content overall
A sequel or new content from semiwork, asked for frequently since R.E.P.O.'s success
unique_things: Jump/backflip mover with stomp attacks used in combos, unlike dash-based twin-stick shooters
Beacon-cleansing objective structure that makes enemy rooms optional and lets players rush the boss
Wacky improvised weapons (for example wielding Mjolnir or martial-arts staff builds) and items that visibly show on the character
Bosses that flee mid-battle, forcing chase and positioning decisions
Split-screen local co-op and Remote Play Together in a genre often single-player only
tedious_or_disliked: Stomp mechanic is seen as forced by some, with parts of the game depending on it
Late-game chaos can reduce play to spamming dodges rather than deliberate movement
Hunting for weapons or perks that feel good can be unrewarding early on
Unlocking everything (for example the last character essence) is confusingly unclear for completionists
Repetition after several runs reported by lower-hour reviewers
divisive_points: Art style and visual busyness: loved as stylish and full of personality by many, called cluttered and off-putting by others
Stomp and movement system: praised as distinctive, criticised as shoved onto the player
Ending and final boss: some call the game a near-perfect S-tier but find the finale a letdown
Originality: some see a refreshing take on the sub-genre, others see just another pixel-art twin-stick roguelike
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched Feb 25, 2021 and 1.0 shipped Jun 8, 2023 (Steam lists the game as 2023; the task labeled it 2021 after the EA date). Reviewers describe it as criminally underrated and under-marketed at launch, with a spike of new players after R.E.P.O. became a hit; the price has been cut to $4.99 from a reported $20. Windows only (no Mac/Linux); Steam Deck reportedly works well. Metacritic has two critic reviews (both 90) and seven user ratings averaging 8.0, too few for a Metascore. No OpenCritic entry could be confirmed (search page returned no data). Revenue and owner figures are third-party estimates, not audited.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Wizard of Legend is a flashy top-down hack-and-slash roguelite where you pick spells and feel extremely powerful. praise: Core gameplay of unique spells and items makes repetitive content fun
Makes you feel super powerful
Very flashy and fun to play
Huge variety of builds
Strong personal attachment; he played it a ton over years
Each past update made the game feel fresh and exciting

Repetitive: same layouts recur constantly
Fights the same enemies over and over while running between areas
No more updates; he wants a large DLC and more content
Gets a little boring after a very long time once everything is done

Design lesson: ongoing content updates keep a roguelite feeling fresh, and their absence limits replay

community.one_liner: A fast, spell-combo-driven top-down action roguelite by Contingent99 in which you fight through a dungeon of elemental trials to beat the Council of Magic, building a loadout of spells (Arcana) and relics.
community.consensus_summary: Wizard of Legend is well regarded by players (Steam 'Very Positive', about 90% positive across roughly 21k reviews in the local dataset) and generally favorably by critics (Metacritic PC 79, Switch 76). Praise centres on the huge spell and relic build space, the power-fantasy combo combat, and the couch co-op. The recurring complaints are dashes with no invincibility frames, pit deaths, stunlock from crowds, a slow unlock grind that gates viable builds, and thin environment and boss variety. It is a full release (2018, all major consoles, mobile in 2023) rather than early access, and it has kept receiving content updates. Many current Steam reviewers also compare it favourably to the 2025 sequel, which they say disappointed.
best_things: Enormous build variety: hundreds of spells and relics, and players report still finding new builds after 40+ hours
Spell combo combat gives a strong 'feel like a real wizard' power fantasy once a build clicks (Avatar-style elemental play is a frequent comparison)
Relics/Arcana have interesting effects rather than flat percentage stat bumps
Local couch co-op is frequently called out as a highlight, by reviewers and players alike
Polished pixel art, animated spell effects and music (Dale North soundtrack)
Lots of challenge and endgame content: Chaos Trials, challenge modes, a Boss Rush mode and powerful unlockable 'dark spells'
No microtransactions; Steam reviewers thank the dev for adding content rather than selling it as DLC
Good short-session runs: players use it for a quick 20-minute run to test a new build
worst_things: Dashes have no invincibility frames and any enemy can stagger you, so crowded fights feel like stunlock rather than skill
Easy to dash or get knocked into pits and void, described by several reviewers as a frustrating death source
Environments and bosses are limited (three dungeon themes in the original release), so runs feel repetitive over time
Combat can be cluttered by effects and cramped arenas, making telegraphs hard to read
Spells and items give little information before purchase, so it is easy to waste currency on gear that does not fit you
Early difficulty spikes; new players often stall on the second boss and some find the first waves brutal
Basic attacks dominate while strong spells sit on cooldown, which some find dull
Accessibility gaps, e.g. a colourblind player says ground markers are hard to see; Switch frame skips noted by Destructoid
improvements: Add dash invincibility frames or a more forgiving dodge
Add some form of light meta-progression (starting stat boosts or more starting spell/relic options) so unlocking feels rewarding
Show descriptions for cursed relics and spells in-game instead of forcing players to a wiki
More environment, enemy and boss variety to reduce repetition
Online co-op (the Destructoid review called out its absence)
Better colourblind options and clearer hazard/telegraph readability
unique_things: Spell-crafting around four base Arcana slots with combo timing and cooldown management, closer to a fighting-game or spell-cast rhythm than a hack-and-slash
Hard cap on how many unlocked spells you can start a run with, so it plays closer to a pure roguelike than most roguelites despite the unlock shop
Elemental magic theme with a large cosmetic and signature-spell layer (outfits, signature attacks)
Built-in local two-player co-op and Boss Rush / Chaos Trial modes
Relics with build-defining effects instead of generic stat boosts
tedious_or_disliked: Unlock grind: guides say to grind certain items first, so the 'steep learning curve' is really a prerequisite grind (a widely upvoted negative Steam review)
Buying and unlocking spells, relics and robes that many players never use feels pointless with no stat meta-progression
Many unlocked spells are felt to be weak or redundant compared with the starting set
Waiting out cooldowns while using basic attacks, and cornering/kiting enemies to pile them up
Story and boss dialogue beats are disliked by some and felt to undercut the ending
divisive_points: No dash i-frames and stunlockable player: some call it bad design, others say it is the core of the game's high-skill power fantasy and what makes success feel earned
Difficulty and unlock grind: long-time players love mastering it, newcomers and Hades fans often bounce off
Story and lore amount: one reviewer wants more, others find the narrative unsatisfying
Comparison to Hades: some find it a poorer fit for the Hades-style expectation, others enjoy it for being slower and more methodical
community.reception_notes: Kickstarted in June 2016 (about $72.7k raised vs a $50k goal), published by Humble Games, and launched on May 15, 2018 on PC, Mac, Linux, PS4, Switch and Xbox One; sold 300k copies in 16 days and passed 500k by end of July 2018 per Wikipedia. Steam revenue estimate is about $13.2M gross (about $3.9M net) per steam-revenue-calculator.com (Boxleiter-style estimate), with SteamSpy showing 500k-1M owners. Reception has held up since launch, with a recent Steam window still Very Positive (82% of 28 recent reviews when fetched). Mobile versions arrived Oct 2023. The sequel, Wizard of Legend 2 (Dead Mage), released in June 2025 and several 2025-26 Steam reviewers describe it as a letdown relative to the original. Note: I could not obtain an OpenCritic page (web search budget exhausted and the guessed page was for another game), and Metacritic user score is based on only about 114 ratings.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Alina of the Arena is a deck-building roguelike where cards are used to move and attack on a tactical board, blending Slay the Spire style deckbuilding with Into the Breach style positioning. He discovered it through a stream viewer's recommendation and fell in love with it after 10-15 hours. praise: A unique board-movement mechanic gives the game its own identity while keeping Slay the Spire familiarity
Cards are well designed and support many different builds
Each character starts with a unique deck and abilities, so runs feel different
Three floors that each look visually different give a sense of progression
Bosses have unique mechanics and encounter variety avoids repetition
A surprising story twist at the end and fun lore
Content looks easy to extend with new cards, characters and bosses
criticism: Balance is off: movement-related cards are extremely powerful and can carry a run
Fights can run long, especially with defensive builds
Fewer cards and builds than Slay the Spire; builds may converge over many hours
No unique card pools per character, only unique starting decks
unique_points: The board and movement mechanic is the gimmick that differentiates it from Slay the Spire clones
He argues modern deckbuilders need a unique mechanic or they feel like clones
Keeps near-identical cards and keywords to Slay the Spire while designing around the board
commentary.quote: I kind of fell in love with it
design_criteria: Unique mechanic/gimmick: must differentiate from Slay the Spire clones
Build diversity: many builds but fewer than Slay the Spire
Character variety: unique starting decks and abilities per character
Progression and level visuals: three visually distinct floors
Enemy/boss design: unique boss mechanics and varied encounters

community.one_liner: A hex-grid roguelike deckbuilder by PINIX where you play a gladiator and use cards, dual-wielded weapons, dodges and knockbacks in a Slay the Spire meets Into the Breach tactics system.
community.consensus_summary: Players like it a lot: Steam shows Very Positive (about 91.5 percent of roughly 3,970 reviews) and many call it their favourite Slay the Spire-style game because hex positioning adds real depth. Critics are warmer than lukewarm but thin on the ground: Metacritic lists 76 (about 11 critic reviews across platforms, 6 on Switch) and OpenCritic has a 75 top-critic average from 8 reviews, with only 50-57 percent recommending. It began in Early Access in January 2022 and went 1.0 on Steam in October 2022, then reached consoles in November 2023. Recurring complaints are limited content, samey classes, and a thin presentation. Some reviewers say the developer has stopped updating it, though it remains a well-priced, well-balanced tactics deckbuilder.
best_things: Hex movement is central: pushing enemies, dodging and positioning make fights feel like tactical puzzles, which reviewers say gives it more depth than Slay the Spire's simple block
Dual-wield equipment system (daggers, sword and shield, two-handed weapons) with card colours tied to each hand adds build identity
Soundtrack widely praised, with the Act 2 boss track singled out by a 100 percent completion reviewer
Pixel art, crunchy sound effects and animations feel polished and run smoothly, including on controller
Balanced and challenging but fair; difficulty can be set per run without losing unlock progress, and high difficulty and max-stage challenges extend play
Card synergies and cursed weapons enable satisfying combo turns and occasionally broken runs
Free demo, and a low price (often about 7 USD on sale) that reviewers call good value
Free-action tossing of rocks and dropped weapons from the ground is an appreciated small tactical layer
worst_things: Card and effect descriptions are vague (burn, focus, stacking wounds), so you cannot make informed decisions and regret picks
Limited content: small card pool, few bosses (about 7 major), and build-defining cards become obvious within a few runs
Classes are similar, sharing card pools with thin differences; starting class Strike/Defend cards are just renamed with the class name
Event encounters are text only, often just trade money for an item, with no illustrations or aftermath images
Almost no story or worldbuilding until the ending
Console reviewers cite awkward controls, weak UI and a small dim sprites problem on Switch; no touch support
Some players call the developer inactive and the game effectively abandoned; Steam Workshop is listed but content is thin
improvements: Write precise, numeric card and status text (for example deals 1 per stack per turn)
Add illustrated events with outcomes and a bit more narrative framing, such as intros or boss VS screens
Give each class distinct starting cards and names, and widen the card pool and viable builds
Add more content: bosses, enemy variety, arenas (there is only one board type) and more Workshop/mod content
Improve tutorial coverage and onboarding for the colour-switching and movement rules
Rebalance weapons (katana reported strong, ranged and heavy weapons weak) and make higher difficulties add mechanics, not just stat bumps
unique_things: Explicit fusion of deckbuilding with Into the Breach-style tactical grid movement, including knockbacks and dodges instead of simple attack/defend
Hand-coloured cards: equipment in left and right hands and colour switching shape what cards do
Classes styled like Dark Souls starting builds (Pyromancer, Deprived, Slave and others), encouraging themed builds
Dropping and throwing ground objects as a free action
Static arena with no map RNG, so all variation comes from cards, enemies and events
Per-run difficulty selection that keeps unlock progress
tedious_or_disliked: Long runs: normal runs reportedly take 1 to 1.5 hours and some up to 2 hours
Early game can be punishing because you start with few movement cards and depend on drawing them
Colour-switching and control schemes are confusing for newcomers, especially on a gamepad
Repeated fights and bosses feel repetitive after the first several runs
divisive_points: Build variety: some love the focused class identities; others find classes too limiting versus Slay the Spire
Difficulty: some call it brutal but rewarding, others call combat easy; also whether Veteran-level scaling is interesting
Value: praised as a bargain on sale but one reviewer rejected the roughly 12.49 EUR price as too short and repetitive
Whether the thin story and event presentation matters, given the fast gameplay loop
community.reception_notes: Early Access on PC/Mac began January 2022 with 1.0 on Steam October 13, 2022 at 14.99 USD. Consoles (PS4/PS5, Xbox, Switch) launched November 23, 2023; the Metacritic 76 shows on the page with Switch as the most-reviewed platform (6 of about 11 critic reviews); Metacritic user score is tbd. Steam reception has stayed Very Positive, with recent reviews in 2025-2026 still recommending it and mentioning it in the context of Slay the Spire 2's early access. Aggregator summaries and some reviews say the developer stopped updating it long ago. Third-party estimates (Steam revenue calculator, Boxleiter method, unaudited) put gross revenue around 1.85M USD and SteamSpy owners at 200k-500k. Steam lists no Metacritic score.

games.name: Astrea: Six-Sided Oracles
games.short_description: Astrea is a DICE-deck-building roguelike that flips the script on deckbuilders by using dice instead of cards and a unique dual “damage” system: Purification vs Corruption.
