commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Astrea is a dice-based deck-building roguelike with six playable characters. He admires how it solves the usual strategy-versus-randomness problem of dice games: every die face has a usable effect, and the game is built around deliberately swinging your health up and down. It is very complex, with long fights and heavy keyword load, so he recommends it mainly to experienced deck-builder fans. Audiovisuals are excellent, and he places it in A tier.
praise: Dice design keeps strategy meaningful: every face (including self-damage) can be exploited, so no roll is wasted
Health-bar mechanic where low/high health thresholds unlock abilities, encouraging a constant take-damage/heal loop
Six characters, each with roughly ten unique, complicated keywords
Great music, amazing art and strong visual effects
Secret final boss unlocked by beating the game with all six characters gives long-term progression motivation
Unique events and companion 'friends' with their own mechanics add depth
criticism: Extremely complicated, possibly one of the most complex deck builders he has played
Keywords are numerous and dice show only small icons, making it hard to remember what each does (harder to read than cards)
Fights are very long (only about three fights per floor); final boss took him about an hour
Both worlds look too similar (mostly blue), so it is hard to tell which world you are in and it is less immersive
The default starting character is the least interesting one
unique_points: Designed around wanting to take damage, turning randomness into something you can always benefit from
Health thresholds act as the activation system for abilities, creating a low-high-low-high health rhythm
Solves the common dice deck-builder issue of diluted strategy without removing the RNG
commentary.quote: this is going to be a solid a tier uh for Astria
design_criteria: Strategy vs randomness: dice with drastically different faces that are all usable keeps planning meaningful
Complexity/readability: many keywords and icon-only dice hurt accessibility
Run/fight length: long, strategic fights with few encounters per floor
Character diversity: six characters with unique keyword sets
Meta-progression: secret boss gated behind winning with all characters
Audio/visuals: great music, art and effects, but repetitive world colors
Difficulty: challenging, aimed at veterans of the genre

commentary.label: Top 10 of 2024 (#5)
commentary.summary: Astrea is a turn-based roguelike deckbuilder that uses dice instead of cards, with a Slay the Spire-style map of shops, events and elites. He calls it one of the most complicated deckbuilders he has played. Its core is a dual purification/corruption system where dice can heal or damage either side, and a virtue bar that only unlocks when your health is low. He finds it very rewarding when everything clicks, but would not recommend it to casual players. He ranks it fifth of the year.
praise: Multi-purpose dice effects and self-damage make every roll usable, which reduces the luck factor
Each character plays very differently, with roughly 30 unique mechanics apiece
Turns and fights are puzzle-like, and winning with efficient use of technical mechanics feels very satisfying
Sentinels, dice editing/destroying/duplicating and blessings (passives) add depth to builds
Beautiful visuals and a fantastic soundtrack
Meta-progression via unlocking characters and a teased mystery locked door
criticism: Very complex and not suited to casual players, and hard for newcomers
Dice symbols are small and harder to remember than card text
Luck still matters, and he wants more rerolling options to cut its impact
The first available character is probably his least favorite
One misplay can cost all your health given the low max-health cap of seven
unique_points: Corruption self-damage feeds the virtue bar, then purification heals you back in a cycle
Dice serve dual purposes, used on self or enemy, which turns RNG into decisions
Complex mechanics paired with complex strategy, the opposite of his usual preference for simple mechanics with deep strategy
commentary.quote: it's nice to find a more complex deck building game done well
design_criteria: Mechanic complexity vs strategic depth: usually prefers simple mechanics, but here the complexity works
Luck/RNG mitigation: multi-purpose dice reduce reliance on rolls
Character diversity: each character has many unique mechanics
Risk vs reward: self-damage to fuel virtues versus dying to a misplay
Meta-progression: character unlocks and a mystery door
Audio/visuals: beautiful art and fantastic soundtrack
Accessibility/readability: small dice symbols are hard to remember

community.one_liner: A Slay the Spire-style roguelike deckbuilder by Little Leo Games where you build a pool of six-sided dice instead of cards, with a dual Purification/Corruption damage-and-healing system.
community.consensus_summary: Astrea is well regarded: Steam shows about 4,561 reviews at roughly 92% positive (Very Positive), Metacritic critic score is 85 and OpenCritic top-critic average is 87 (all critic reviews recommend it). Critics and players praise the fresh dice-building spin, the Purification/Corruption health-as-resource idea, six distinct Oracles and the striking art. Complaints cluster around heavy RNG, information overload and unclear iconography, weak damage previews, and (from some) runs that are either too easy or too samey. It is a finished game, not early access: PC launched Sep 2023, consoles Sep 2024, mobile Jul 2025, with post-release balance passes and content still appearing on Steam into 2026. Metacritic user score (6.9 on only 14 ratings) is far lower than Steam and is too small a sample to trust.
best_things: Purification vs Corruption turns your health bar into a resource: players deliberately take damage to unlock health-tied Virtues, and the risk/reward balancing is called addictive
Safe / Balanced / Risky dice tiers let you choose your own volatility, and die faces can be rerolled, inverted, forged or permanently converted, giving real control over the randomness
Six Oracles with very different playstyles, each with several viable archetypes; critics say all feel viable
Huge content pool for replay: 350-750+ dice (store-page vs GameGrin counts differ), 170+ Blessings, Sentinel companions and ascension-style Anomaly difficulty levels
Distinctive art direction with crystalline character designs and a blue/red palette; soundtrack also praised by some critics
Three regenerating lives forgive mathematical mistakes and encourage greedy builds
Fresh feel in a crowded Slay the Spire-like genre; many reviewers call it one of the better recent deckbuilder variants
worst_things: Iconography and UX overload: each Oracle has its own keywords and symbols, and every die has six faces to read, so evaluating choices is mentally exhausting
RNG is heavy and not fully seeded (random targets, values, crits and the rolls themselves), so losses can feel undeserved and first turns differ even with identical choices
No damage or outcome preview, and some corruption values are hidden, so players resort to pen and paper to avoid being blindsided
Runs can feel samey: fewer random encounter types and less enemy variety than Slay the Spire, with the first act reportedly identical in demo and full game
Balance: some critics and players say it is too easy or breakable once you find each character's best approach, while others hit brutal bosses and luck spikes at high Anomaly levels
Safe dice and some Blessings are called too weak or too keyword-dependent, pushing builds toward Risky dice
Later Oracles are very micro-heavy and slow to play, and some reviewers say too many systems make turns play themselves
Short runs and price: several top negative reviews say a roughly 1-hour run feels shallow for $24.99 (would be fine at a discount); Steam listing is Windows only
improvements: Add a damage/effect preview (e.g. like Monster Train) and clearer surfacing of hidden corruption and damage sources
Simplify or clarify iconography and die-face readability; some players shelved the game waiting for a UX fix or mod
Fully seeded or more deterministic RNG and more consistent balance across Oracles and Anomaly levels
More event and encounter variety plus more enemy variety to reduce repetition between runs
Rebalance Safe dice and underpowered Blessings, and tighten keyword clutter across characters
Reviewers and players wished for a richer story (the narrative is short and generic) and better Japanese/Korean localization
unique_things: Dice instead of cards: each die has six faces with different effects and you can edit those faces over the run
Dual-direction Purification/Corruption damage: purification damages enemies or heals you, corruption the reverse, so the same effect can help or hurt depending on target
Health-linked Virtues: repeatable passive abilities unlocked by your current health level reward playing near the edge
Black Hole Blessings (powerful with notable downsides) and Star Blessings (smaller, no downside), plus Sentinels as companions
Risk-tiered dice (Safe/Balanced/Risky/Epic) as the core build axis, with self-inflicted corruption dice you must play or swap
tedious_or_disliked: Reading six faces on each of several dice every turn and every reward screen
Micro-management on later characters that makes early turns painfully slow until a build forms
Saving-scumming or restarts felt necessary at high Anomaly levels because of dice variance
Short runs (often about 1 to 1.5 hours) that some find shallow, while others say they get repetitive quickly
Each character starting from the same difficulty with separate progression, which some found grindy
Performance and UI issues reported on handheld devices (freezes, long autosaves)
divisive_points: Difficulty: a few players won on their first run in under an hour and called it too easy, while others find high Anomaly levels unpredictable and luck-driven
RNG: praised as controllable thanks to reroll, convert and invert tools by many, yet a core reason for negative reviews from others
Dice vs cards: some feel dice add novel tension; others say face-editing is less interesting than unique cards and the dual-damage system is partly marketing
Visuals: widely praised, but a few players find the blue/red palette and stylized icons bland or confusing
community.reception_notes: Launched on Steam Sep 21, 2023 at $24.99 from Little Leo Games, published by Akupara Games; released on PS4/PS5, Switch and Xbox Sep 26, 2024 and on iOS/Android Jul 17, 2025. Critics were consistently positive (OpenCritic 10 reviews, 100% recommend; Metacritic only 6 critic reviews, all positive). The Steam score is high in aggregate (about 92%), though the vaporlens aggregator shows 72% positive, implying lower sentiment in some recent or platform-specific reviews; recent Steam reviews from 2025-2026 are still mostly positive and mention updates. Post-launch the devs did balancing passes per Oracle. Steam Spy style estimates put owners around 100k-200k, and steam-revenue-calculator estimates about $2.6M gross and about $766k net (Boxleiter-style estimate, not audited). Platform notes: Steam is Windows only; handheld reports mention freezes and long autosaves.

games.name: Atomicrops
games.short_description: A twin-stick, bullet-hell, roguelite where you must cultivate and defend the last farm in a post-apocalyptic wasteland. Farm mutated crops, upgrade your weapons, marry townsfolk, and kill every mutant creature that tries to invade your homestead! Yee-haw!

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Atomicrops is a top-down bullet-hell shooter fused with a farming sim, where you plant and harvest crops while fighting at the same time. He had not played it before this video and found it surprisingly deep, with a large pool of unique passives and builds. His main complaints are the poor tutorial, the overwhelming simultaneous farming and fighting, and the lack of any pause or time-stop for planting and choosing pickups. He considers it a really solid game that he would not recommend broadly, and places it in A tier.

Surprising variety of unique passive abilities and builds (pig, chicken, bee) that change how you farm and fight
Many weapons and marriageable NPCs that grant unique bonuses, giving run choices
Late game is super cool, with a variety of bosses and many ways to approach each run
Huge content volume keeps long runs from feeling the same

design_criteria: Onboarding/tutorial: judged poor and overwhelming
Build diversity: many unique passives and weapons across runs
Mechanical complexity: straightforward shooting is seen as appropriate for an action game
Pacing and pressure: real-time farming plus combat with a sundown timer is stressful
Replayability: lots of content and approaches per run
Run length: long runs make roguelite unlocks slow
Difficulty: eight difficulty levels ramp up very quickly
Accessibility/player agency: lack of pause or time-stop hurts approachability
Boss and late-game content: variety and payoff praised

community.one_liner: A twin-stick bullet-hell roguelite by Bird Bath Games (published by Raw Fury) where you farm mutated crops by day and defend the farm from mutants and bandits by night, across a 12-day year with bosses every third night.
community.consensus_summary: Atomicrops is well loved by the players who stick with it (Steam: Very Positive, about 92% of roughly 6,350 reviews) and received a solid-but-not-glowing critic reception (Metacritic 78 from 9 reviews, OpenCritic top-critic average 75 with 69% recommending). Critics and players agree the farming-plus-bullet-hell juggling act is original and addictive, with great pixel art and music. The recurring caveats are a brutal, poorly explained first few hours, visual clutter, thin meta-progression, and a fixed map that repeats. It left early access on Epic and launched on consoles in May 2020 (Steam release listed Sep 2020), got a free crop-system update and the Halloween Deerly Beloved DLC in 2022, and several 2025-26 Steam reviews say the game has gone roughly two years without a patch while fans ask for a sequel or co-op.
best_things: The core hook: juggling planting, watering, harvesting and shooting at the same time works as a tower-defense/bullet-hell/farming hybrid, which many reviewers say should not work but does
Very addictive one-more-run loop; Steam reviewers report hundreds of hours and repeat returns years later
Pixel art by Toby Dixon and the quirky, catchy soundtrack are widely praised (though music is a minority complaint)
Build variety and item synergies, such as weed-cutting, slow-bullet and farm-animal combinations that turn a bullet hell into bullet time
Distinct playable characters (Robusta and the DLC characters are named favorites) that change pace and difficulty
Humor, marriage/polygamy mechanic and memorable bosses give the wasteland a lot of personality
Lots to unlock and high replayability with late challenges like deeper years and cat/kitty modifiers
Tight controls in the Binding of Isaac / Enter the Gungeon mold, with a plant-defense feel compared to Plants vs Zombies
worst_things: Poor onboarding: the tutorial and item descriptions explain very little, so early runs feel confusing and unfair
Visual clutter and low readability in later years, making it hard to tell friend from foe or what hit you
Weak or slow meta-progression; critics and players call the unlock tree (ant colony) close to pointless or just a list you eventually exhaust
Economy and shop balance: weapon shop prices and weapon upgrade costs feel punishing, and runs can hinge on affordability luck
Fixed repeating map layout (the same handful of fields) with little randomness, which some feel is not level design
Difficulty spikes in late years (around year 9) with off-screen charges and poorly telegraphed attacks
Performance and framerate problems reported at console launch, and some scrolling judder complaints on PC
Permadeath clashes somewhat with the theme of growing things, per one critic
improvements: A proper tutorial and clearer in-game explanation of items, economy and farming rules
Better visual clarity and enemy/projectile readability, especially late in a run
More meaningful meta-progression and more weapon and shop variety
Rebalancing of characters, weapon pricing and upgrade cost scaling
More map or level variety (or randomization) plus an endless mode, which some users request
Co-op multiplayer and a sequel or further DLC, frequently asked for in recent Steam reviews; ongoing patch support
unique_things: Farming sim time management fused with nightly tower-defense bullet-hell waves, all in one loop
A seasonal calendar structure: a 12-day year across four seasons, bosses every third night, and runs continuing through successive years
Crops double as currency and health economy, so farming decisions directly affect survival and upgrades
Marrying townsfolk (including multiple spouses) gives run-altering perks
Farm animals, cats and other allies, plus tool and turret placement, change how you defend the farm
Health is scarce and hard to replenish, pushing a risk-management style unlike typical twin-stick roguelites
tedious_or_disliked: Constant multitasking under a timer feels stressful or chore-like to some players, who expected a chill Stardew-style farming game
Accidentally uprooting turrets or using the wrong tool in hectic combat, and losing items when airlifted away
Grinding for unlocks across the same five fields and same music tracks; a few players say full unlock takes very long
Repeated early restarts while learning the game, since little carries over between runs early on
Sameness of runs for some, with two dominant build styles and shops that restrict purchases
Some dislike the music, art style or camera scrolling and feel the game is too chaotic visually
divisive_points: Difficulty and learning curve: many call it addictive and rewarding once it clicks, others refund or quit within hours
Fixed map: praised by fans as working well for mastery, criticized by others as repetitive with no level design
Farming versus combat balance: Rock Paper Shotgun-style takes felt farming was weaker than the shooting, while fans see the multitasking as the whole charm
Meta-progression: some see useful carry-over like the time capsule, others see it as negligible
community.reception_notes: Metacritic's 78 rests on only 9 critic reviews and 27 user ratings, so treat the user 7.1 as low-sample. OpenCritic lists 30 critic reviews (top-critic average 75, 69% recommend) across PC, Xbox, PlayStation and Switch; Eurogamer recommended it after the launch build improved health management, IGN called it less relaxing than farming sims but recommended it to fans of both genres, and PlayStation Universe flagged framerate issues. Early access ran on the Epic Store before the May 28 2020 full launch on consoles and PC (Steam page lists Sep 17 2020, Windows only). Post-launch support included a free Steam update with a revamped crop progression system and the $4.99 Halloween DLC Deerly Beloved (Oct 2022) plus other DLC packs; a mid-2026 Steam reviewer says there has been no patch in about two years, and fans keep asking for co-op and a sequel. Third-party estimates (steam-revenue-calculator.com) put Steam gross revenue near $2.6M and net about $765k with SteamSpy owners 200k-500k, which are order-of-magnitude guesses.

games.name: BlazBlue Entropy Effect
games.short_description: Enjoy action-packed flashy combat with incredibly satisfying combos and responsive controls! Numerous characters, each with completely unique playstyles and loads of unlockable moves & upgrades! This action roguelike sets the bar for fluid fast-paced action.

other_scores.source: OpenCritic for BlazBlue Entropy Effect X (console edition)

placements.verbal_evidence: blaze blue entropy effect is going to be an a tier for me um probably here

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: BlazBlue Entropy Effect is a 2D action roguelite with hack-and-slash combat that leans toward fighting-game feel. The developers sent him the game for review. He finds it impressive, visually stunning and very satisfying to play, though not especially unique in mechanics. Its bosses and story are the highlights, while repetition in rooms and builds plus visual clutter hold it back. He places it in A tier.
praise: Fighting-game-like action: each character has a drastically different move set with input-timed combos
Roughly 20+ bosses, each designed uniquely with different mechanics; bosses are where the game shines
Strong story focus with many cutscenes and NPCs, giving an RPG-like feel
Stunning visuals, great VFX and sound effects, character voice lines
Epic anime-style final boss
Many characters, each with two to three viable builds, giving a good amount of runs
criticism: Repetitive once you have played each character a couple of times; not much new per run
Elemental/proc abilities are always the same and not very interesting
Flashy visuals make attacks hard to read, including the final boss, and he lost runs to it
Inconsistent telegraph colors, e.g. the lone enemy firing yellow projectiles that always hits him
Few unique events or levels, and rooms of fighting enemies take a while
Voice lines have no cooldown so jump-spamming makes characters shout repeatedly
unique_points: Pushes roguelite action toward a fighting-game style with per-character move sets and combos
Story progression gated behind talking to particular NPCs, RPG-style
Design lesson: elaborate visuals can undermine readability compared to simple pixel art telegraphs
commentary.quote: blaze blue entropy effect is going to be an a tier for me
design_criteria: Character/move set diversity: drastically different characters with combos drive variety
Boss design: 20+ unique bosses weighed heavily
Visual clarity: flashy visuals hurt readability of telegraphs
Repetition: similar rooms, few events and levels, builds run dry
Story and presentation: heavy narrative, VFX, audio, voice lines
Build variety: 2-3 viable builds per character, but elemental upgrades bland
Uniqueness: not highly unique but well executed

community.one_liner: A 2D action roguelite by 91Act (published with Astrolabe Games) that turns BlazBlue fighting-game characters and moves into a fast combo-driven run-based brawler, with solo and co-op play.
community.consensus_summary: Players and critics agree the combat is the draw: fluid, combo-heavy, fighting-game-flavoured action with a large roster and many build paths. Steam sits at Very Positive (94.3% of about 36.7k reviews), Metacritic has 83 from 6 critics and OpenCritic 84 from 15 reviews. Weak spots are a thin, generic story and setting, repetitive rooms and enemies, a cluttered neon look, mediocre music and a BlazBlue brand that feels tacked on. The game passed through early access and has been updated often (new characters, a Dead Cells collab with The Prisoner, the larger 'X' story content that also shipped on consoles). Recent Steam reviews are noticeably worse than lifetime ones because of post-update stuttering, crashes and co-op desyncs, and the later release revamps split early-access fans.
best_things: Combat feels fast, snappy and deep, with ground combos, launches, air follow-ups and cancels that reward fighting-game-style execution
Large roster of characters with distinct playstyles, adapted from their BlazBlue fighting-game moves (including guest characters such as The Prisoner from Dead Cells)
Strong build variety: tactics (elemental and status upgrades), legacies and unlockable move branches let a run change how a character plays mid-run
Approachable for people who are bad at fighting games, yet with a high skill ceiling for mastering characters
Scalable difficulty via the Entropy/Extreme settings, where harder modes also let you get stronger and bosses change behaviour
Solo, local co-op and online co-op are all supported
Developers keep supporting it with content and updates; many reviewers call it great value, and the standard roster is considered enough without paid characters
Bosses and set-piece fights are often cited as a highlight
worst_things: Story and setting are generic sci-fi and hard to follow; many reviewers say it feels disconnected from the BlazBlue universe
Stages and rooms repeat a lot, with the same bosses and stage layouts run after run, so variety wears thin after the early hours
Enemy designs and animations are plain compared with the detailed playable characters; heavy neon glow and screen clutter hurt visual clarity
Soundtrack is called only okay and repetitive, not matching BlazBlue's reputation for music
Performance and netcode complaints: stuttering, crashes and multiplayer desyncs, worse after recent updates; one review also blames the dev-authoritative netcode for input delay with distant partners
Quick boss kills or very high damage in co-op can cause desyncs or softlocks that wipe a run
Mixed comments on the hub: slow to navigate and heavy on dialogue/quests for a fast game
Systems and skill descriptions are dense and not well explained, so players turn to guides
Some players find the combat and content too simple or limited: it is fun but wears thin after a few hours, with little reason to continue once the story is beaten
improvements: Fix performance, stuttering, crashes and co-op desync/softlock bugs introduced or exposed by recent patches
Add more BlazBlue-specific content, story integration and lore so the license feels like more than a skin
Open up the new X story content earlier on PC instead of locking it behind finishing the original story
Improve enemy variety and level design, and reduce room and boss repetition across runs
Better explain progression, evolutions and legacies in-game and improve visual clarity of effects and boss attacks
Shorten or vary the start of each run and streamline the hub
unique_things: Fighting-game move lists translated into a roguelite, so characters unlock and expand their own movesets during a run rather than only stacking stat upgrades
Combo-count and cancel-based play that feels closer to character-action or a 2D brawler than a typical dodge-and-shoot roguelike
Entropy system that lets you raise difficulty in exchange for stronger buffs, with bosses changing behaviour at higher levels
Characters from other franchises (for example The Prisoner from Dead Cells) implemented as fully playable roguelite characters
Support for local and online co-op in a fighting-game-derived action roguelite
Layered build system of elemental tactics, move-expanding potentials/legacies and evolutions, supporting dozens of distinct builds
tedious_or_disliked: Early progression leans on grinding and unlocking; some players dislike having characters stripped of their signature fighting-game moves until they get them by RNG within a run, with nothing carrying over
Runs feel long and similar at the start, and some find them easy until a late boss spikes the difficulty
Astral Finish (a boss instant-kill type move that bypasses revives unless perfectly dodged) is called unfun by at least one 300-hour player
Dialogue, quest and hub overhead between runs can interrupt players who just want to keep running
New story (X) content locked behind finishing the original story, which can take new players 20+ hours
Waiting for online co-op partners in your region can take a long time, according to one heavy player
divisive_points: Difficulty: some find it too easy because recovery frames were added and enemies are not threatening, while others praise Extreme 100 with max mutations and complain about a few unbalanced late bosses

The 1.0 and X revamps: early-access fans say removing or reworking systems (corruption, mind upgrades, arena, a story subplot) made combat feel slower and more RNG-driven, while newer players praise the clearer new story
BlazBlue link: fans of the franchise split on whether it is a great action roguelite with BlazBlue paint or a missed chance at a real BlazBlue experience
Complexity: some love the depth of systems and skill trees, others feel overwhelmed by the number of attacks and mechanics
community.reception_notes: Steam lists release as Feb 14, 2024 at $11.99 (Windows and Mac) with paid character packs (Hazama, Rachel, Bullet, Naoto). Launch reviews were strong, with critics praising combat and docking story and BlazBlue integration. The game saw an early-access-to-1.0 overhaul and later the Entropy Effect X expansion with new story content; an early-access thread complains that reworks made combat feel clunkier and more RNG-heavy. The Dead Cells collab added The Prisoner, praised for design but blamed by some recent reviewers for bugs and stuttering. A review-summary site rates recent sentiment around 66% positive, well under the 94% lifetime, driven by performance, crashes and co-op desync after updates. Third-party revenue estimates (Steam Revenue Calculator, Boxleiter method, not audited) say roughly $18.9M gross and $5.6M net; SteamSpy-style owner range is 500k to 1M. A console port (X) is also on OpenCritic with about 83. The Nintendo Life review page and Steam discussion 6363076374193246966 could not be read (403 or not fetched).

games.name: Ember Knights

Wield weapons & skills, build synergies with game-changing relics and free the universe of Praxis’ corruption.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Ember Knights is a basic, traditional top-down action roguelike dungeon crawler that does not try any unique mechanic but executes the fundamentals very well. He loves its visuals, distinct worlds, bosses with difficulty-scaled forms, and long meta-progression. His main gripes are disconnected spells and overpowered crit builds at high difficulty. He sees it as a very solid Hades-like and places it in A tier.
praise: Great visuals and art style, with each world looking completely different, giving a strong sense of adventure
Cool bosses; higher difficulties give bosses entirely new move sets and forms (e.g. the first-world spider has three forms)
Meta-progression is substantial, requiring many roguelite elements to reach the first boss and ten more levels of difficulty to reach the true final boss
Weapons have unlockable forms and play fairly differently from each other
Satisfying, fun fights and gameplay without needing gimmicks
Probably fun in multiplayer
criticism: Spells feel disconnected from the rest of the game and are not impactful
Crit builds are overpowered and practically required at the highest difficulties, a balance issue
He could be nearly invincible against the final boss on top difficulty because the game is easy to break
Can get chaotic on higher difficulties with fast enemy move sets bundled together
unique_points: Deliberately does nothing unique mechanically; shows action roguelikes can succeed on satisfying fights alone
Boss difficulty scaling swaps in different move sets and forms rather than just raising stats
Each world has a very distinct visual identity, which he says many top games struggle with
commentary.quote: if you liked Hades odds are you will like Ember Knights
design_criteria: Visual identity: distinct worlds and art style aid immersion
Boss design: difficulty-scaled move sets and forms
Meta-progression: long gated path to true final boss
Weapon diversity: multiple forms with differing playstyles
Build balance: spells weak versus overpowered crit builds
Combat feel: satisfying fights over unique mechanics
Difficulty: hard, with chaos at higher levels

community.one_liner: A Hades-inspired top-down action roguelite by Doom Turtle (published by Twin Sails Interactive) built around 1-4 player local/online co-op, relics, weapon mods and skills, fighting the sorcerer Praxis across planets.
community.consensus_summary: Ember Knights is well liked by players: Steam shows Very Positive overall (about 94% of roughly 7,000 reviews positive in the local snapshot), and is most often recommended as a polished, snappy co-op roguelite with lots of build variety and an endless supply of relic synergies. Critical coverage is thin: Metacritic has only one critic review (God is a Geek, 85) so no Metascore exists yet, and the user score is 7.5 from a handful of ratings. The recurring caveat is value and depth: several reviewers call it solid but not standout, more a discount or co-op pick than a Hades replacement, and some say it gets repetitive or grindy. It left Early Access (April 2022) in July 2023, later got free modes (Daily Dungeon, Boss Rush, Chaos Run, pets) and a paid DLC, Wrath of the Architect. Note: the web search budget was exhausted during this research, so community detail leans on Steam reviews, Steam forum thread titles, Metacritic pages and the store page rather than Reddit.
best_things: Co-op is the headline: 1-4 players, local split-screen and online, described as easy to access and not drastically raising difficulty
Fluid, responsive controls and snappy combat; a large build space (7 weapons, 9 mods per weapon, dozens of skills, 100+ relics per the store page) with synergies that can get gloriously broken
Cohesive, cute pixel-art visuals and charming touches (pet companions, dialogue, secrets, weapon skins from trials)
Good performance and polish for most players; described as optimized with no crashes or slowdowns
Plenty of post-clear content: Endless mode, Boss Rush, Daily Dungeon, Chaos Run, trials and the DLC, which adds biomes, weapons and relics
Reads as Hades-like without being a clone; often recommended to Hades fans and for playing with kids or family as a gentle intro to build-crafting
Meaningful two-currency meta-progression (ability/weapon upgrades plus permanent health and damage buffs)
worst_things: Multiplayer loot flow: rewards are picked one player at a time and stat gems drop in a shared pile, which some find a slow, excruciating time waster and poor design
Unskippable cutscenes and boss intros/outros, plus invulnerable boss phases that force waiting, are repeatedly called out as killing the pace
Enemy design: many enemies have ranged or dash attacks from across the screen, which makes ranged weapons much stronger than melee and makes charge attacks impractical
Balance and depth complaints: weapons unbalanced, build diversity felt lacking by some, and the DLC final boss described as easy or a joke
Technical problems for some: freezing or stuttering, high CPU use in menus, launch hangs, and it fails to run under Proton for at least one reviewer
Online lobby friction: hard to rejoin after a crash, no Steam direct join, no visible lobby ID, plus multiplayer lag and lobby-start failures discussed in the Steam forum
Value: multiple reviewers say it should cost about $10 rather than $19.99, and that the DLC feels like a reskin of the main campaign
improvements: Let co-op players pick rewards simultaneously and offer personal loot or a shared-out option instead of a shared pile
Add quality-of-life options: skippable or shorter cutscenes, pause or stop the speedrun timer out of combat, and show the time goal for the time-limit capsule
Add more skills (one reviewer suggests about 45 versus the roughly 32 they counted) and more build variety or balance between weapons
Improve online connectivity tools: direct Steam join, visible lobby ID, reliable rejoin after a crash
Consider checkpoints or shorter runs, since replaying the same worlds is boring for some

Make unlocks require using items or skills in runs (Binding of Isaac style) rather than unlocking nearly everything in about 10 hours; clearer indicators for attack-recharged abilities near the character
unique_things: First-class 1-4 player co-op, including couch split-screen, in a genre that is mostly solo
Abilities recharge by landing attacks rather than on pure cooldowns
Weapon modification system (9 mods per weapon) layered on top of relics and skills
Hades-style structure combined with a planet-hopping sci-fantasy setting and cute pixel look
Game modes beyond the main run: Daily Dungeon, Boss Rush, Endless and Chaos Run, plus pet companions you can pet
Time-limit challenges per planet and tiered trials that unlock cosmetic weapon skins
tedious_or_disliked: Long, unskippable cutscenes and boss invulnerability phases in every run
Solo players report a grind-heavy progression; the Daily Dungeon pays far more resources per room than regular runs, pushing players to repeat it
Repeating the same worlds with no checkpoints makes runs feel samey after a while; several reviewers say it wears out its welcome or gets boring quickly
Taking turns at the end-of-stage loot pick in co-op, and loot piling up on top of each other or under the HUD
Screen clutter from enemies and effects makes combat hard to read; you can usually only land a light attack or two before needing to dodge
divisive_points: Multiplayer: praised by most as the best reason to play, yet a vocal minority calls it one of the worst co-op roguelites because of loot handling
Solo play: some say it is amazing alone, others say it is not built for single player and is grindy
Hades comparison: a strength for fans who want more, a turn-off for others who say just buy Hades
Price and value: many call it a great deal or worth it with DLC, others say it is only worth it on sale
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched April 20, 2022 and 1.0 released July 18, 2023 on Steam ($19.99); it is also on Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X (Windows only on Steam, no Mac or Linux). Free updates later added Daily Dungeon, Boss Rush, Chaos Run and pets; the paid DLC Wrath of the Architect (2024-25) adds biomes, weapons, relics and a new final boss, which some players found too easy. An older store snapshot showed Overwhelmingly Positive (95% of about 3,900 reviews); the local snapshot shows 93.8% of 7,056 reviews, and recent reviews are still mostly positive with a steady stream of complaints about multiplayer and performance. Steam forum threads include pinned multiplayer-issues and controller-issues threads. Metacritic had only 1 critic review and 13 user ratings at fetch time. OpenCritic page could not be located (no search access) so that value is null.

games.name: Nordic Ashes: Survivors of Ragnarok
games.short_description: Nordic Ashes: Survivors of Ragnarok, is a challenging Norse inspired roguelite-survivor game, where you’ll have to survive hordes of creatures that come your way.

placements.verbal_evidence: it's probably going to be like a low a tier but it's very very solid

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Nordic Ashes is a horde-survivor style roguelike with a single-level-per-world structure, where you play many different characters and level them through a skill tree instead of finding unique abilities. He was impressed by how much content it has: roughly nine or ten worlds with their own enemies, mini bosses and bosses, plus lots of unlockable characters. He calls it one of the better games of the genre and a very solid take, placing it in low A tier. He enjoys it regularly because unlocks come fast and every run feels rewarding.
praise: Skill tree is surprisingly deep, with many build options despite being the same tree each run
Only a few skills can be fully upgraded, forcing choices about which attack becomes the main one
Each character plays very differently and has a unique skill tree
Nine or ten worlds, each with unique enemies, mini bosses and bosses, giving a real sense of exploration and adventure
Large amount of content and many characters to unlock
Fast, rewarding unlock cadence that keeps him excited for the next thing
criticism: Passive abilities found during runs are the least impactful part of the game
Could have used a bit more variety in the abilities found in runs
Skill-tree-based progression might seem less surprising since you always know what to expect
unique_points: Leveling via a shared skill tree instead of unique per-run abilities, yet still produces varied runs
Multi-world structure gives the horde genre an adventure feel rather than a single repeated arena
Forced specialization, since only a handful of skills can be maxed, drives run variety
commentary.quote: it's probably going to be like a low a tier but it's very very solid
design_criteria: Build variety: skill tree choices and limited max-level slots create distinct runs
Content volume: many worlds, enemies, bosses and characters
Level/world design: nine or ten distinct worlds with unique enemies and bosses
Character diversity: each character plays drastically differently with own tree
Meta-progression: fast, frequent unlocks that feel rewarding
Ability diversity: in-run passives are low impact and somewhat limited

community.one_liner: A cartoony Norse-mythology survivors-like (bullet heaven) where you fight through nine realms in short runs, buying gear at checkpoints and chasing a large meta-progression of characters, constellation skill trees and relics.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate it Very Positive (about 88% positive; roughly 6,300 reviews in the local dataset, about 1,950 shown on the store page's main view), with a softer recent score (75% of 20 recent reviews at the time of the store fetch). Fans call it one of the better survivors-likes: charming art, a strong soundtrack, a large varied roster, cheap price and frequent developer updates. Critics are few and lukewarm-to-positive, scoring it around 78-80. The recurring complaints are a very grindy meta-progression, builds that converge on the same optimal setup, balance problems across characters and difficulties, and two grievances with the developer: a repeated bug that pushes the Yggdrasil leaf balance negative after updates, and a first DLC many players dislike. It entered Early Access on Dec 15, 2022, launched 1.0 on Apr 26, 2024 and is still actively updated, with a DLC (Twilight of Yggdrasil) released in 2026.
best_things: Charming hand-drawn cartoon art and a strong Norse theme; several reviewers single out the soundtrack as a highlight
Large roster (about a dozen base characters, more with DLC) that plays differently thanks to per-character constellation skill trees shaped like their theme
Huge amount to unlock: realms, weapons, relics (150+), skins and 150+ achievements give a constant carrot to chase
Short runs that are easy to jump in and out of; good for quick sessions
Runs great on Steam Deck (Deck verified, 60 fps at low wattage per one reviewer); full controller support
Cheap price (about $9.99) and steady content updates; daily challenges with global leaderboards and a Tower mode add replay value
Item synergies and upgrades, plus a checkpoint shop and ultimate abilities, add decisions beyond plain auto-fire
worst_things: Meta-progression (Yggdrasil leaves, skill points with steeply rising costs) is slow and described as a chore or 'grindy hell', especially for completionists who must play every character on every realm

Balance: some characters are weak or unviable on harder realms and difficulties (e.g. Niflheim on Expert), and several reviewers find end bosses trivial while earlier trash enemies or specific mechanics feel unfair
Builds feel samey: players quickly settle on a meta build and randomly offered stats or altar picks replace real build-crafting; one critic (The Games Machine) flagged limited build variety
Slow feel for some: movement, time-to-kill and early progression are called sluggish compared with Vampire Survivors-style rivals
Clunky controls and annoyances: mouse-movement mode locks out keyboard, long death cam, confusion effect that scrambles controls, enemies stuck outside the golden circle trapping the player
Repeated updates push Yggdrasil leaf totals negative (devs say a bug gave free leaves), forcing hours of re-grinding and angering some players
Nightmare mode freezes and weak optimisation reported on Steam Deck and other handhelds by some players
Some felt it gets less fun over time rather than more, with little identity compared to other survivors-likes
Skill trees are described as linear and dull, with few meaningful decisions compared with Vampire Survivors
improvements: Speed up or flatten the meta-progression cost curve and leaf drops so unlocks do not require repeating the same early levels
Give players real build choice (evolutions, fewer random stat picks) so runs differ more
Rebalance characters, bosses and the Expert tier so every hero is viable on all realms and end bosses are not trivial
Fix the recurring negative-leaf bug and communicate update side effects more respectfully, or compensate affected players
Improve quality-of-life: skippable death screen, keyboard/mouse switching, handheld optimisation, better leaderboard criteria (kills rather than shop time)
Add co-op, which several players say they miss compared to Vampire Survivors
unique_things: Checkpoint shop between waves: each realm has three waves with bosses, and gold is spent on items, unlike pure pick-one-upgrade survivors-likes
Per-character constellation skill trees that are laid out in shapes matching each character (for example a bow for the hunter)
Nine Norse realms from Midgard to Asgard, each unlocking the next realm and a higher difficulty tier
Hidden meta characters such as KAOS that play very differently from the regular roster
Distinct DLC modes: Remnants of Corruption is effectively a separate game mode with its own rules and progression
Twitch chat integration for streamers, daily challenges with global leaderboards, and a Tower mode
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding leaves and achievements for unlocks, with costs rising steeply (one reviewer says a single upgrade cost about three full runs around 200 leaves)
Replaying the same realms and enemies with every character to chase completion
Randomly generated daily quests described as unfun when they force a fragile hero with a weak weapon
DLC content that keeps a separate grind, and some achievements locked behind paid DLC
Hunting the last enemy or the last leaves to finish a wave or collection
Early hours are very slow before the roster and meta tree open up
divisive_points: Grind: many players call it a satisfying long-term loop (hundreds of hours, 96% achievements), others call it the worst grind in the genre
DLC: the first DLC (Remnants of Corruption) is seen as a rough failure by some and, after patches, as a solid extra mode by others; Twilight of Yggdrasil is better received by fans
Difficulty and balance: some find it fair and satisfyingly powerful once maxed, others find it too easy after shopping or unfair on harder realms
Art and music: praised by most, but one reviewer finds the art childish and the audio effects cartoonish
community.reception_notes: Early Access began Dec 15, 2022; 1.0 released Apr 26, 2024 on PC, later on consoles (PlayStation, Switch as 'The Complete Saga', Xbox) and GOG per the studio site. Five DLC packs exist (Twilight of Yggdrasil, Remnants of Corruption, Dark Knights, soundtrack, artbook). Metacritic has only two critic reviews (no Metascore yet) and five user ratings averaging 6.0, so it is not a meaningful signal. OpenCritic could not be confirmed (no entry found). The main controversy is that patches repeatedly pushed players' Yggdrasil leaf balances negative; the developer said a bug let some upgrades skip their leaf cost, and players with negative balances are excluded from leaderboards until fixed. Steam Spy style estimates put owners at 200k-500k and estimated gross revenue near $1.4M (Boxleiter method, not audited). Note that this session's WebSearch budget was exhausted, so community detail comes from Steam reviews (local file and store pages), a Steam Community thread and Metacritic, not Reddit (Reddit fetch was blocked).

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Nuclear Throne is a chaotic, fast-paced top-down bullet-hell shooter that he sees as a key game in the modern roguelike revival. He loved it at release and still finds it very enjoyable, with distinct characters and quick runs you can finish or drop easily. He says it would have been S tier years ago, but he rates it on what he recommends to people today. It lands in a 'high' tier without a stated letter, and he would play it over Neon Abyss.
praise: Super chaotic, explosive, fast-paced gameplay
Characters each have pretty unique abilities
Short runs are easy to finish or drop and return to later
Gameplay is fun enough that repeated weapons don't matter
Many secrets, unique events, unlockables and secret bosses
Looping the game gives unique, very different bosses rather than just harder enemies
Real effort put into late-game content
criticism: Weapon pool is small; you keep finding the same weapons after a few runs
Would have roughly three times more weapons if made today
Starting to show its age by roguelike standards

Old-school hidden secrets and events reward exploration
Late-game content is given unusual design attention

Character diversity: unique abilities per character
Weapon variety: limited pool is a drawback but offset by gameplay feel

Aging/recommendability today: judged by current recommendation, not historical impact

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Nuclear Throne is an older, chaotic action shooter roguelite. It is one of the re-reviews from his previous tier list, where he had it in B. After replaying it following viewer comments, he reversed his earlier complaint that it needed more content. He found it a blast, full of secrets, and with a looping endgame that adds unique bosses. He bumps it up to A tier and recommends it as an entry point for people new to roguelikes.
praise: Chaotic nature of the gameplay is super fun and enjoyable
Full of secrets that can still be discovered hours into playing
Looping after the final boss adds unique bosses only found by looping
Holds up well over time despite its age
Easy to understand even though it is hard, making it a good roguelike entry point
criticism: Previously felt it was an older game that needed more content (he now backs off this)
Looping is really hard
unique_points: Loop mechanic after the final boss with bosses exclusive to loops
Secrets that keep surfacing deep into playtime
Has served as a gateway roguelike for many newcomers
commentary.quote: I had an absolute blast and the chaotic nature of the game is super super fun
design_criteria: Chaos/feel: frantic shooter action is a major source of fun
Secrets and discovery: hidden content rewards long-term play
Replayability/endgame: looping with unique bosses extends the game
Content amount: earlier concern about too little content was dropped
Accessibility: easy to grasp despite difficulty, good for newcomers
Longevity: aged well as an older game

community.one_liner: Vlambeer's fast, brutal top-down roguelike shooter where a cast of mutants fights through irradiated wastelands toward the Nuclear Throne.
community.consensus_summary: Nuclear Throne is widely treated as a genre landmark of arcade-style action roguelikes: Metacritic 89 from 15 critics, Steam Overwhelmingly Positive (about 96% of roughly 19.8k reviews), and the last-30-day snapshot on the store page still Very Positive (92%). Players and critics praise its gunplay, game feel, sound and soundtrack, and run-to-run variety, and many reviewers describe it as addictive. The recurring complaint is difficulty that feels cheap to some players: near-instant deaths, no invincibility frames after a hit, and luck-heavy spawns. It spent over two years in Early Access (launched fully Dec 2015), went quiet for years, then got a surprise 10th-anniversary Update 100 in Dec 2025 (13th character, four-player co-op, widescreen, higher frame rate), which brought a wave of warm Steam reviews. The Metacritic user score (7.7 from 294 ratings) is noticeably lower than the critic score.
best_things: Gunplay and game feel: weapons feel punchy, with screen shake, audio feedback and fast movement (Steam reviews repeatedly mention 'juice' and crisp sound effects)
Jukio Kallio's soundtrack and sound design, frequently singled out as a major reason the game resonates (an IGF audio honorable mention in 2015)
Distinct cast of mutant characters, each with a special ability that changes playstyle, giving strong replay value
Short, pick-up-and-play runs with an arcade score-chasing feel, plus daily challenges and loops past the final area for long-term play
Clear readable action, bright pixel art and strong presentation; reviewers call it stylish and chaotic in a good way
Weapon variety and mutation choices that add variety rather than making success mandatory, per several positive reviewers
Modding community (e.g. Nuclear Throne Ultra mods mentioned by players) extends life of the game
Developer goodwill: players highlight the studio reuniting years after disbanding to ship the anniversary update
worst_things: Perceived cheap deaths: many enemies and explosions can kill very fast, and the lack of post-hit invincibility frames is the most repeated Steam complaint
Heavy reliance on RNG: spawn positions next to enemies or explosive objects, bad starting weapons, and chest-gated secrets can doom a run outside the player's control
Final area difficulty, including a final boss that some players say can kill them before the fight properly starts
Difficulty spike between mid areas (3-1 to 4-1 cited) and a progression where upgrades feel underwhelming compared to broken-build roguelikes
Input feel issues: one reviewer says it cannot decide between controller and keyboard/mouse, each favoring shooting or dodging
Technical roughness: complaints of clunky legacy engine quirks (melee through walls, fire passing diagonal tiles), Steam Deck/Proton startup trouble, and Remote Play Together co-op issues
Limited depth compared to knowledge-heavy roguelikes; one fan review concedes it lacks the depth of other roguelikes and leans arcade
improvements: Add post-hit invincibility or a more forgiving damage model, or at least clearer telegraphing for enemy attacks and explosive hazards
Reduce RNG cheapness: safer level-entry spawns, and less luck-gated secret and route access
Better information presentation and level transitions, and more meaningful or powerful perks and passives
Quality-of-life fixes and bug cleanup (Steam community has a huge bug report subforum); Steam Deck/Linux stability
Steam Workshop support for mods (repeatedly requested in Steam discussions)
More content updates; fans treated Update 100 as a rare positive exception and want more
unique_things: Extremely lean, bullet-hose arcade design where aggression and reading chaos matter more than build theory or item synergy
Each character has a signature mechanic (e.g. Melting, Robot eating weapons, Fish rolling), making character choice a core part of identity
Mutation pick per level-up as the primary build system, with weapons found in the run rather than meta-progression power
Loop mode after beating the game, escalating enemies into harder cycles, offers a second layer of endgame
Created from a 2013 48-hour charity game jam and developed with live 'performative development' on Twitch, which helped build its audience
Stylized post-apocalyptic mood paired with a western-tinged guitar soundtrack
tedious_or_disliked: Death feels sudden and often uninformative, so players say they must die repeatedly just to learn what kills them
Restarting to chase specific secret areas or required items when a chest roll misses
Hazards placed next to objectives (e.g. explosive car beside a portal) that punish piercing weapons or allies
Keyboard versus controller trade-offs and some clunky legacy behaviors
Reflex-driven gameplay with limited learnable strategy frustrates players who prefer planning (comparisons to Noita and Enter the Gungeon appear in negative reviews)
Too much damage too quickly: players say 6-10 'HP' is effectively 1-2 hits, so levels feel unfair for casual players
divisive_points: Whether the difficulty is fair and skill-based or cheap and RNG-driven; the same no-i-frames design is praised by fans as arcade purity and condemned by critics of the game
Whether the lack of build depth is a feature (lean arcade) or a weakness compared to modern roguelikes
Whether the game has aged: some call it still unmatched a decade later, others say later roguelikes took its best ideas and it would need an overhaul
community.reception_notes: Launched fully Dec 5, 2015 after 2+ years in Early Access (over 100k units and $1M+ in Early Access). Critics were strongly positive (Metacritic 89); Eurogamer rated it Essential per Wikipedia. Later released on Switch (2019) and Xbox One (2021). After roughly eight years without updates and a 2020 studio disbanding, Update 100 arrived for the 10th anniversary in Dec 2025 with a 13th character, four-player online co-op (Nuclear Throne Together), widescreen support and 60+ fps; Steam reviews from that period are heavily positive and appreciative, though post-update issues like Remote Play Together problems and Steam Deck launch trouble show up in negative reviews. Revenue estimate from steam-revenue-calculator is about $8.1M gross and $2.4M net on Steam (Boxleiter-style estimate, order of magnitude only); SteamSpy lists 500k-1M owners. Note: OpenCritic was not retrievable in this run (the URL guess returned a different game and web search budget was exhausted), so opencritic is null; Reddit and Eurogamer/PC Gamer pages were also not fetchable, so community signal comes mainly from Steam reviews and discussion forum plus Wikipedia and Metacritic.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Risk of Rain Returns is the 2023 remake of the original 2D action roguelike Risk of Rain. PepperHead played 80+ hours of the original and sees this as simply the better version: same core game and art style, cleaner, with more content, characters and items. He places it in a very high A tier, saying it is only below S because he personally prefers two other games, and that it could be an easy S for many people.
praise: Faithful remake that keeps the core of the original while improving nearly everything
Same art style, just cleaner
More content: characters, items, and unique challenges
Great diversity between characters, with fun core gameplay mechanics as the focus
Constant item pickups keep runs rewarding and pacing fast
Removed the need to clear the whole map after the boss (toggleable in options for fans of the old way)
New challenges offer an easier alternative way to unlock alternate skill sets
criticism: Items and abilities do not change how you play a run, usually a weak sign, though it works here
Some may find the unlock challenges make alternate skills too easy to get, though he disagrees
Placed below S mainly due to personal preference for other games rather than flaws
unique_points: Original was among the first action-based roguelikes, so a modern remake benefits from years of genre learning
Options let players choose original or faster post-boss pacing, so both old and new fans are served
Low-impact items still work because the core gameplay is the fun and loot flow is constant
commentary.quote: it's just the better risk of rain one
design_criteria: Core gameplay feel: the fun comes mostly from the core mechanics
Character diversity: great variety between characters
Item/ability impact: items do not change run style, yet it works
Pacing: fast, constant item rewards, no forced map clearing
Content quantity: more characters and items than the original
Unlock systems: challenges make alternate skills easier to unlock
Visuals: same art style as the original, cleaner
Accessibility/options: options cater to both old and new fans
commentary.rerank_note: Remake of Risk of Rain 1, which he reviewed on his original tier list; this game was not out then. He notes the slow post-boss pacing issue he raised there is now fixed.

community.one_liner: A ground-up 2D remake of the 2013 co-op action roguelike Risk of Rain: pick a survivor, loot stacking items across timed stages while difficulty climbs with the clock, and fight your way to the final boss, rebuilt with new survivors, items, artifacts, and overhauled multiplayer.
community.consensus_summary: Critics and players largely see it as a model remake: Metacritic sits at 84 from 13 critics and Steam at about 90% positive across roughly 28.7k reviews (Very Positive). Reviewers highlight the extra survivors and items, polished pixel art, music, and much better multiplayer, while noting it stays conservative and still feels dated next to modern roguelites and to Risk of Rain 2. It is not early access and is a finished game with no DLC beyond the soundtrack. Steam reviewers wish for more post-launch updates, and a vocal minority find the core loop, hit feedback and Providence Trial unlock gating frustrating.
best_things: Faithful but much more polished remake: sharper pixel art that keeps the original's look, plus quality-of-life options that can mostly be toggled individually.
Soundtrack and atmosphere repeatedly called out by critics and Metacritic users as a highlight.

Large new content layer: new survivors (for example the Drifter, a scrap-gathering brawler), extra items and Risk of Rain 2 fan-favorite content alongside the classic roster (about 15 survivors on the store page).
Item-stacking power fantasy: players like growing from weak to screen-clearing god and learning which items and survivors combine best.
Overhauled multiplayer with up to four players online and local split-screen, which critics (GameSkinny, for one) single out as the best way to play.
Short-ish, replayable runs and no-DLC completeness, which Steam reviewers appreciate compared with the sequel.
Accessible to some newcomers and a clear upgrade for returning fans: several reviewers call it the right way to do a remake, while others say the original felt too hard or dated to them.
Feels distinct from RoR2 in a positive way: a 2D, more arcade-like cousin that some players prefer for its aesthetics and pacing.
Co-op is the emotional hook in the most-upvoted reviews: couples and parents play it with partners and kids, and the chaotic item-grabbing and frequent deaths are treated as part of the fun.
worst_things: Combat readability: late-game hordes overlap, enemy attacks have little telegraphing, and players say it is hard to tell when they have been hit.
Flying enemies and magma worms are widely described as oppressive, since 2D aiming and movement limit how you answer them.
Core loop feels repetitive to some: walk away from the crowd and spam skills, little positioning depth or macro play compared with RoR2.
Providence Trials are required for some unlocks, and reviewers call the challenge design punishing rather than teaching.
Technical rough edges in reviews: crashes, freezes when the screen fills up, sticky controller input, and controller deadzone or menu issues.
Multiplayer connection problems reported (disconnected from host errors) and local co-op camera or scale issues on TVs.
No mid-run save, which The Games Machine flagged, and some players lose a run after force closing.
improvements: More post-launch updates and content; 'lack of updates' is a repeated complaint even among positive reviews.
Better feedback and telegraphing of enemy attacks and hits, and clearer screen readability in late-game chaos.
Mid-run saving and more robust stability and performance when many objects are on screen.
Fix multiplayer connection reliability and improve split-screen camera behavior for local co-op.
Rework unlock gating so that Providence Trials are not needed for core item and ability unlocks, and improve controller handling and remapping.
unique_things: Difficulty scales with elapsed time rather than stage count, forcing a tradeoff between looting thoroughly and moving on.
Huge roster of stackable items whose interactions are unpredictable, producing build variety that players call esoteric and satisfying.
Survivors with very distinct kits plus alternate skill unlocks, and Artifacts that mutate a run.
Providence Trials, a set of skill challenges that double as unlock content.
A 2D side-scrolling co-op format with online and local play, unusual next to the 3D Risk of Rain 2.
Reviewers frame it as remake-plus-superset: it keeps the original's feel while folding in RoR2 content.
tedious_or_disliked: Very short, sparse item availability per map makes scavenging feel slow while enemies outscale you, per a critical review.
Randomness of drops (especially the active item) means many runs feel alike to some players, and progression for new survivors can feel slow.
Providence Trial unlocks and some achievement hunts are described as gatekeeping and sadistic.
Runs can drag at around an hour, and long late-game hordes get repetitive for some.
Heavy difficulty for newcomers: several reviewers bounced off even after hours.
divisive_points: Returns vs Risk of Rain 2: many prefer the remake's look and feel, while others say it lacks RoR2's movement and skill expression and is overshadowed by it.
Difficulty: fans see earned power growth, critics call it unfair, sponge-like enemies and scaling.
Art update: most love the added detail, some prefer the simpler original pixel art.
Conservative remake: some say it changes too little, others call it the right way to do a remaster.
community.reception_notes: Launched Nov 8, 2023 on PC (Steam) and Nintendo Switch, developed by Hopoo Games and published by Gearbox/2K at $14.99. Critic reception was strongly positive (Metacritic 84 from 13 reviews; 80-90 range for most outlets). Steam has held Very Positive with about 90% of roughly 28.7k reviews. OpenCritic could not be retrieved (web search budget was exhausted and guessed OpenCritic URLs resolved to unrelated games), so the score is null. Steam forum threads and negative reviews show continued bug reports around controller input, achievements and multiplayer connections, plus mild disappointment threads; positive reviewers wish for further updates. Steam lists a Windows-only build; the only add-on is the soundtrack.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Roboquest is a first-person shooter roguelike that he calls one of the two big FPS roguelikes alongside Gunfire Reborn. He says it was a notable omission from his original list. He thinks it is a very solid game that does everything well, and shines most as a campaign-like adventure in its first ~15 hours. He would put Gunfire Reborn just barely above it, but says he will rank Roboquest very highly too, without naming a tier letter.
praise: Strong core mechanics: dash, jump, projector, jetpack and varied abilities from the start
Character upgrades and mobility make the moment-to-moment FPS gameplay fun even before unlocks
Lots of unique worlds, secrets, characters and bosses to unlock, giving a campaign feel
Builds still differ between runs and the roguelike elements are good
Both the shooting and mobility are done very well for first-person shooter fans
criticism: Runs feel more repetitive than Gunfire Reborn, with weaker replayability
Abilities found during a run are less impactful than in Gunfire Reborn
Much of the mobility must be unlocked and takes a while
So much exploration content that the ending is somewhat disappointing (spoiler, not elaborated)
unique_points: Campaign-like structure: scattered unlockables and a required quest before reaching the final boss
Emphasizes core movement and character kit over run-found abilities, the opposite of Gunfire Reborn
Gives a unique adventure rather than endless run variety
commentary.quote: I think this is a really really really solid first person roguelike
design_criteria: Core gameplay feel: movement, dash, jetpack and gun feel carry the game
Replayability: runs feel repetitive compared to Gunfire Reborn
Build diversity: present but less dramatic than Gunfire Reborn
Unlockables and meta-progression: many characters, bosses, secrets and mobility unlocks
Campaign structure and exploration: worlds and quest gating give an adventure feel
Ending payoff: exploration content makes the conclusion a letdown
commentary.rerank_note: Not covered in his original list; newly added in this video. He says Gunfire Reborn would sit just above it.

community.one_liner: A fast, colourful co-op-capable first-person shooter roguelite from French studio RyseUp Studios, where a rebooted Guardian robot blasts through branching, procedurally arranged levels of hostile bots.
community.consensus_summary: Roboquest is received very warmly: Steam shows Overwhelmingly Positive (about 95% of roughly 24k reviews, 97% of the most recent 30-day sample), and its small Metacritic critic set (5 reviews) averages 85 with a 8.5 user score. Players praise its movement, gunplay and soundtrack and often call it the best or fastest FPS roguelite. Criticism concentrates on unreliable peer-to-peer co-op with no rejoin after a disconnect, bullet-sponge enemies and unclear projectiles, and some weapons and build archetypes being far weaker than hitscan. It was in Steam Early Access from August 2020 and hit 1.0 on 7 Nov 2023; the developers announced in May 2025 that they would stop producing content updates, so it is effectively finished rather than abandoned mid-way. It later reached PS4/PS5 (May 2025) and has a separate VR spin-off.
best_things: Movement and gunplay feel: the most repeated praise, with reviewers calling it a fast, flow-state shooter with smooth mobility and satisfying weapon animation and feedback
Synthwave soundtrack (critic: Carpenter Brut-inspired) is singled out by critics and many players as a standout
Buildcrafting and variety: many characters/classes, weapons, abilities and upgrades so that most builds can win, and runs do not hinge on finding one perfect seed
Branching level paths, secrets and multiple difficulty levels give replay value; easier modes do not lock you out of content
Colourful comic-book art style praised; one top reviewer says it does the look better than Borderlands
Meta-progression that feels meaningful, with gadgets and unlocks that change how you move
Co-op with friends is considered very fun when it works, and it runs well on modest PCs
Good value and feature-complete: players call it an 'ol reliable' they keep installed since 2020, with years of post-launch content (weapons, a class, Endless mode, Dead Cells crossover)
worst_things: Co-op stability: a very large share of negative reviews cite disconnects or crashes mid-run with no way to rejoin, which wipes 30-45 minutes of progress
Enemies are described as bullet sponges, and ranged enemy projectiles of different speeds overlap and hide fast attacks, so hits feel unavoidable
Status effects (hacks, stuns, blinding orbs) that come from off-screen interrupt the movement flow and feel unfair in a twitch game
Weapon balance: hitscan weapons are consistently the reliable choice; melee, projectile and close-range options fall off in later stages
Some enemy types (hidden turrets, teleporting one-shot enemies, no-cover arenas) punish aggressive movement and push players into camping or sniping
Difficulty curve is uneven, with easy modes described as a cakewalk and the jump to standard/hard described as steep
Repetitive enemies, levels and music after long sessions, and a limited weapon/upgrade pool cited by veteran roguelike players
improvements: Fix co-op networking and add rejoin/reconnect so a dropped player does not end the run for everyone
Make projectile, melee and close-range weapons more viable against late-game enemies, and rebalance hitscan dominance
Add a dodge/dash or proper strafing option, since some players find base movement sluggish
Improve readability of enemy projectiles and status-effect sources; reduce visual clutter
Smooth difficulty scaling between easy, standard and hard, and revisit the final boss being effectively gated behind full meta-progression
Offer shorter runs or a way to save or pause a long run (runs can exceed 30-45 minutes)
unique_things: Arguably the fastest-paced FPS roguelite, combining mobility gadgets (grapple, rocket jumping) with boomer-shooter-style arena combat
Hero-shooter-style classes (Guardian and others) with their own upgrade trees inside a roguelite structure
Branching level route choice between stages, Star Fox-like, with secrets and side paths
Meta-progression delivered as gadgets and crystals that unlock movement and abilities rather than pure stat boosts
Cross-platform co-op and a cheerful comic-book robot world with a light story, backed by a synthwave soundtrack
Crossover content such as the Dead Cells collaboration and an Endless mode
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding meta-progression (gadgets, crystals, upgrades) before the final boss becomes beatable, reported by one reviewer as roughly 20 hours
Time-based level grading that pushes speed over exploration, disliked by players who want to poke around
Long runs with no way to resume after a disconnect, making co-op feel risky
Hunting for hidden gadgets and collectibles that are key to movement, which some say requires guides
Eye strain reported by at least one player from fast motion and saturated colours
Repetitive enemy attack patterns (lobs, missiles, zaps) that reduce play to cover-peek cycles
divisive_points: Difficulty and fairness: some find it fair and well balanced, others find normal and above spiky, with deaths from unseen projectiles or status effects
Movement: many call it top-tier and smooth, while others find it sluggish and want a dodge mechanic
Replayability: long-time players log hundreds of hours, but others find the weapon and upgrade pools thin and the game quickly repetitive
Weapon feel: praised as lovingly animated by many, but a few call the weapons bland or unimpactful
Story, characters and music: liked by many, but some players dismiss the characters and story as weak (music is also called repetitive by a minority)
community.reception_notes: Launched in Early Access in August 2020 and was well liked well before 1.0 (Nov 7, 2023, on Steam, Epic, Xbox One and Series X/S). Post-launch updates included the Arsenal update (April 2024), a Super Update with a new class, weapon and level (June 2024), a Dead Cells crossover (August 2024) and Endless mode (November 2024), with PS4/PS5 versions on May 27, 2025. In May 2025 the developers said they could not keep supplying content to players with over 1,000 hours and ended content updates, stating it was never meant as a games-as-a-service title; recent Steam reviews largely accept this while noting it feels complete. The biggest persistent controversy is co-op disconnects without rejoin, which players say has lasted for years and was not fixed by an attempted patch. Windows-only on Steam; consoles via Xbox and PlayStation. Sales estimate from steam-revenue-calculator.com (Boxleiter-style, order of magnitude only): about 13.2M USD gross and 3.9M net, with SteamSpy-style owner range of 500k to 1M. Limitation of this research run: the session's WebSearch budget was exhausted, so no additional press reviews or Reddit threads were read and OpenCritic's numeric score could not be confirmed.

Many classes and a lot to uncover
Extensive tutorial and rewarding once mechanics are learned
One of the games he would pick if stuck with only one or two for months
