community.one_liner: A free, open-source (with paid Steam/GOG builds) tactical turn-based fantasy roguelike RPG by Netcore Games (Nicolas 'DarkGod' Casalini) with a huge roster of races and classes, cooldown-based talent trees and optional permadeath.
community.consensus_summary: Players regard it as one of the deepest and most replayable roguelikes available: Steam sits at Very Positive (about 94% of roughly 7,500 reviews) and GOG at 4.5/5, and Wikipedia reports the wider community rating it very highly. Metacritic is thinner and cooler: the critic score is not yet formed (only 2 reviews, 100 from USgamer and 80 from GameGrin) and user score is 7.3 from 71 ratings, with about 21% negative. Critics and fans alike praise class design, build variety and the forgiving life/difficulty options, while detractors cite a steep learning curve, UI-heavy play, balance spikes, long runs and instability on some setups. It is not early access; core content is complete (three expansions through 2018, version 1.7.6, seasonal events such as Pikataclysm in 2025), but Steam reviewers describe balance and bugs as untouched for years and some keep asking for the long-promised Lost Land content. A late-2025 YouTube video sparked a wave of new and returning players.
best_things: Class and race design: dozens of classes (10 races, 27 classes per GOG listing) with distinct mechanics, e.g. time-controlling archers, psionics dual-wielding with mind and hands, slime mages, and well-liked necromancers
Enormous build variety and synergy space, so two runs rarely play the same; many reviewers have 500 to 1,500 hours in it
Tactical cooldown-and-resource combat that sits between slow classic roguelike and action RPG, and enemies use the same classes and rules as the player
Loot with unique effects plus a meta-progression of unlockable classes, races, arena and endless dungeon modes
Flexible difficulty and lives: multiple difficulty levels, roguelike permadeath, or extra lives/unlimited save options, so both casual and hardcore players are served
Passion-project feel: free official version, strong QoL features like auto-explore, autotravel and item transmogrification, modding via Lua addons, and an active community
Surprisingly good lore and writing for the genre, plus about 1,800 achievements that reward unconventional play
Cheap: Steam price around $3.49 and a free official download, making it very high value
worst_things: Dated, minimal graphics and animation; some tilesets are confusing on dense vegetation maps, and music and sound are described as repetitive
Steep learning curve and a cluttered, unintuitive UI; the tutorial covers only the basics, so new players struggle with item and talent knowledge
Balance is uneven: players describe easy cruise-control through trash mobs, then sudden deaths to a unique or boss with a nasty CC or percentage-damage ability they cannot see coming
Stability issues reported on Steam: crashes on zone load, freezes at loading bars, and corrupted or lost saves (only one save slot is kept)
macOS build reported as problematic, with screen-setting and cursor-lock issues
Steam vault (item sharing between characters) is locked if you run non-whitelisted addons, which some see as unnecessary always-online restriction for a single-player game
UI scaling bugs: increasing font size can make interface elements overlap
Runs can be very long (reports of 20 to 30 hours per full campaign), which makes failing late very costly
improvements: Better onboarding: a deeper tutorial and clearer in-game explanations of talents, status effects and why a monster is dangerous
Clearer feedback on enemy threats and deaths, such as easier inspection of abilities and readable danger indicators
Enemy and boss balancing pass, including fewer hard-counter or percent-damage spikes and more consistent threat throughout a run
Reduce junk loot and the sorting burden, and add shorter run options or mid-run pacing improvements
Stability and save safety fixes (multiple save slots or automatic backups), plus better macOS and UI scaling support
More content and new updates: fans keep hoping for the long-awaited Lost Land expansion or at least a dev update, and want more animation and visual polish
unique_things: Hybrid of classic roguelike depth with RPG-style skill trees, cooldowns and resource management rather than pure tile-based bump combat
Lineage from Angband/Zangband/PernAngband/ToME 2 and 3, rewritten in 2009-2012 as an original high-fantasy setting, using its own T-Engine (C plus Lua) with shaders and particle effects
Lives system and difficulty options that let you choose permadeath or a gentler mode, with an achievement-based life economy
Enemies that play by the same class rules as the player, making their talents readable and sometimes exploitable
Free official download with donation-unlocked online features (character vault, chat, stats), alongside paid Steam and DRM-free GOG editions with Workshop and addon support
Won the ASCII Dreams Roguelike of the Year award three years running (2010-2012)
tedious_or_disliked: Auto-explore-and-one-shot loop: many players say most fights require no thought, with real tactics only mattering at bosses or dangerous uniques
Sorting through large amounts of mediocre loot, and optional escort quests that players call frustrating
Very long runs and heavy knowledge requirements, so dying late or to a counter-build feels punishing
Losing progress to one-shot deaths from enemies you cannot see or understand, and a perception that luck plays a large part
Achievements that do not register lower-difficulty versions once a higher-difficulty one is earned, which annoys completionists
Fighting the interface and absorbing huge amounts of ability detail, described by some as the main enemy of the game
divisive_points: Depth versus illusion of depth: fans see one of the most intricate tactical systems ever, while critics say the complexity hides an autopilot loop with many weak skills
Randomness and luck: some call the outcomes a slot machine where unique enemies or boss counters decide runs, others say knowledge and preparation beat luck
Visuals and audio: many say to look past the graphics, others find them and the music a real barrier
Difficulty: the roguelike mode is praised as tense, but others call it masochistic, and player-facing options (extra lives, saves) are viewed as either accessible or as diluting the stakes
community.reception_notes: Launched on Steam on Dec 12, 2013 via Greenlight after years as a free download (ToME 4 released 2012). Early reception was strong: USgamer called it the pinnacle of the fantasy roguelike in 2013, and it won ASCII Dreams Roguelike of the Year for three consecutive years. Expansions followed: Ashes of Urh'Rok (2014), Embers of Rage (2016) and Forbidden Cults (2018). Steam ownership was estimated at over 150,000 by 2016 (Wikipedia via SteamSpy), although a current SteamSpy range shows 50,000 to 100,000 owners, and a third-party revenue calculator estimates about $1.47M gross and $433K net revenue; these are rough estimates only. Metacritic has no formed critic score because only two reviews exist. OpenCritic has no entry. Current Steam reviews show a surge of new players in autumn 2025 after a popular YouTube video and recurring hopes for the Lost Land expansion; some reviewers complain that balance and bugs have not been touched for nearly a decade. Steam has a handful of mixed/negative reviews about crashes, a macOS build that behaves badly, and the addon-whitelisted vault restriction. Platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux; Steam version supports Workshop and trading cards, GOG is DRM-free. WebSearch budget was exhausted during this research, so Reddit and Steam community threads could not be fetched directly; community themes come mainly from the Steam review file, GOG, te4.org, Wikipedia, RogueBasin and Metacritic.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Tiny Rogues is a simple top-down dungeon crawler roguelike that he previously rated in an earlier tier list. A huge content update transformed it, adding a large amount of weapons, builds, characters, secrets, bosses and a full meta-progression layer. He loves the expanded game but notes it is now less approachable because items and keywords carry much more text and stats. He still recommends it, including to newcomers to the genre, and moves it up from B to A, placing it above Atomic Crops.

Core mechanics remain simple and easy to pick up
Still very approachable and recommended for people new to roguelikes

Item text and keywords are secondary to gameplay; players pick them up over time

design_criteria: Content volume: weapons, builds, characters, secrets and bosses add replay value

Simplicity and approachability: core mechanics stay simple but item text raises the barrier

community.one_liner: A solo-developed (RubyDev) pixel-art action rogue-lite with bullet-hell combat, RPG-style stats and an enormous pool of weapons, equipment and traits, played in roughly 30-minute runs down 20+ floors.
community.consensus_summary: Players love it: Steam shows Overwhelmingly Positive (about 96 percent of roughly 10,800 reviews), and many reviewers call it one of their favourite roguelites, praising build depth and value at $9.99. Metacritic has a page but no critic or user reviews, and no OpenCritic entry was found, so critic coverage is essentially absent and reception is almost entirely community-driven. The game is still in Early Access after launching in September 2022. The last big content update was around late 2023, which produced a steady stream of 'is it abandoned?' complaints, though the developer posts monthly devblogs through 2026 and is doing a near-total rewrite (new hub, dual wielding, consumable rework, mid-run saving, localization promised). The most repeated practical complaints are no mid-run save, late-floor screen clarity, and occasional freezes.
best_things: Extreme build variety: hundreds of weapons, 500+ equipment items and 100+ traits combine into 'fireworks' synergies, and many reviewers say learning them is the core joy
Snappy, smooth combat and dodging with a strong 'one more run' loop; a run takes about 30 minutes, which busy players like
Price-to-content ratio: repeatedly described as underpriced ('price of a fast food meal') for the amount of content
Large roster of unlockable classes (34 per the store page) that change playstyle, with unlocks that keep coming without watering down the game
Responsive, passionate solo developer with human, transparent devblogs; several reviewers cite this as a reason to recommend
Easy to learn controls with deep, complex systems underneath; compared favourably to Binding of Isaac, Hades, Enter the Gungeon and Nuclear Throne
Optional difficulty scaling (Cinder system) and optional progression, so the game stays fun without forced grinding
Pixel-art charm, a catchy soundtrack and memorable boss personalities that reviewers say give the game heart despite simple graphics
worst_things: No mid-run save or pause-and-resume: runs can last 1-1.5 hours and players with jobs or kids find this a dealbreaker; it is the single most repeated complaint
Long stagnation in Early Access: reviewers say no meaningful content update since late 2023, leading to 'abandoned' and 'dead game' talk (a 44-comment Steam thread) despite ongoing devblogs
Screen clarity on later floors: bullet-hell density and effects make it hard to see what is happening, leading to 'spray and pray' play
Stability: several reviewers report hard freezes mid-boss or at floor transitions 30+ minutes into a run, plus a controller-detection bug with Wooting keyboards
Weak onboarding: most content is unlocked by default with little explanation, and the Alignment mechanic required to progress past floors 10-11 is not explained
Some classes feel too similar (ranged DPS with small gimmicks), undercutting the headline class count
No official Chinese (or other) localization despite being requested for years; promised for the rewrite
Some boss fights are very short (seconds) or, conversely, specific bosses like the Jousting Champion are called un-fun
improvements: Add a mid-run save/suspend function (promised in the 2026 rewrite announcement)
Ship the long-delayed big update with real new content and endgame progression, and give a clearer release timeline
Improve visual clarity on late floors (readability of projectiles and effects)
Add endgame or post-unlock progression: one reviewer was stuck after unlocking the first 16 characters, and there are requests for an endless mode
Better tutorialisation of mechanics such as Alignment, keywords and trait interactions
Make classes and early-unlock characters more mechanically distinct; fix freezes and input bugs; add localization
unique_things: Generates a new 'character' each run by combining class, weapons, armor, traits and consumables, closer to an RPG loadout than a fixed character
Bullet-hell dodging mixed with stat-driven, dungeon-crawler build-crafting; tagged as a blend of Isaac-style item synergy with Nuclear Throne-like speed
Extremely fast rooms and bosses when the build works: several reviewers say encounters are a 'test' of whether you understood the systems
Sheer content scale for a solo dev: 40+ bosses, 400+ weapons, 20+ themed floors, random events and NPCs
Planned rewrite introduces a Rogue Hideout hub for informed floor selection, dual wielding instead of weapon swap, and PoE-style crafting orbs and scrolls
tedious_or_disliked: Early floors (first ten) are too easy for experienced players, so they go on autopilot for about 40 minutes before real difficulty starts
Floor 10 onward is a sharp difficulty spike with bullet-heavy chaos that some players cannot get past, blocking character unlocks
Long, unskippable animations (for example the loot sequence after floor bosses)
Trait and loot selection RNG and the need to reroll around starter items; choices tend to repeat across runs
Grind to unlock later characters feels samey for some, and playstyles run out of steam
Keyword and effect overload makes builds feel hard to parse
divisive_points: Complexity: praised as deep build-crafting by fans, but called both 'too simple and too complex' and keyword soup by critics
Difficulty curve: some find it too easy early and brutal late, others say it is never unfair
Passive versus active feel: a few reviewers feel build effects are passive (enemies burn) so the game feels closer to an autobattler than Noita or Roboquest, while fans praise the combos
The upcoming rewrite: fans are excited, while some worry that adding pillars and pitfalls could break the rhythmic looping movement feel they currently love
community.reception_notes: Launched in Early Access on Sep 23, 2022 at $9.99 (Windows only, no Mac/Linux) and built its audience through word of mouth; the developer stated the game would get pricier with each major expansion. The original plan was to leave Early Access around December 2024 or later, which has slipped. Content updates slowed after late 2023, the community's main frustration. In Feb 2026 the developer announced a full rewrite with a 67-page design doc, promising localization, mid-run saving, performance gains and modding support; devblogs from March to September 2026 show the rewrite largely done and content production in progress, with a new programmer and artist joining and a delay from the developer's gallbladder surgery in June 2026. No date for the big update was found. Note: web search was unavailable (budget exhausted), so no professional press reviews were found; Metacritic's page exists but has zero reviews, and OpenCritic could not be confirmed.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Vault of the Void is a deck-building roguelike with an unusual stress-meter mechanic, where managing stress matters as much as health and higher stress brings more enemies. PepperHead says plainly that he did not like it, even though it has very positive reviews and he has played a lot of deckbuilders. He found the gameplay boring and the art and environments unappealing, and felt the game did not feel alive during card fights. He played about 10 hours and concedes that more time with different card combinations might have changed his view. He places it in high D tier and stresses that D tier means not for him rather than a bad game.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Vault of the Void is a fairly standard deck-building roguelike that he re-evaluated after playing it longer. He originally tried it for a few hours, disliked it and placed it in C tier, but viewer comments and his own deck-building design video research pushed him to revisit it. He now finds it really solid, with a lot of content and replayability. He moves it up to A tier (described as low A), admitting he was wrong before.
praise: Very solid, well-executed core deck-building loop
Lots of small mechanical details that make moment-to-moment play interesting
Large amount of content: many cards and artifacts
High replayability
Has its own vibe despite similarity to Slay the Spire
One of the few deck builders without unique gimmicks that still succeeds just by doing the basics well
criticism: Lacks really unique mechanics, which is normally risky for deck builders due to Slay the Spire comparisons
Fairly similar to Slay the Spire in some aspects
His first impression was poor, suggesting it may not hook players quickly (he partly blames his own mood and short playtime)
unique_points: Succeeds through execution and content volume rather than a novel hook
Design lesson: a game does not always need long playtime to be good, but some games reward giving them more time, and timing/mood affects judgment
commentary.quote: I was wrong I think this game is really really solid and deserves to be an a tier
design_criteria: Mechanical depth: many small interacting mechanics make it interesting
Content volume: lots of cards and artifacts
Replayability: a ton of variety across runs
Originality: lack of unique mechanics is a risk versus Slay the Spire, but execution compensates
Polish/execution: doing the standard formula well counts heavily

community.one_liner: A roguelike deckbuilder from Spider Nest Games built around planning and player agency: fixed 20-card decks, full map vision, deck swaps between fights, and Void Stone card upgrades.
community.consensus_summary: Players rate it Very Positive on Steam (about 92% of roughly 3,000 reviews locally, 93% on the store page), and a loud minority of genre veterans call it their favourite deckbuilder, often ahead of Slay the Spire and Monster Train. Praise centres on control over RNG, build variety and depth. Critics have barely covered it: Metacritic holds one listed review (God is a Geek, 70/100) and no aggregate score. The main complaint is front-loaded complexity, a weak tutorial and a busy UI, so it is seen as a deep cut for experienced players rather than an entry point. It left Early Access (Nov 2020) for 1.0 on Oct 4 2022, then added a new class and kept updating: a Nightmare update, a Halloween update mentioned by reviewers, and The Weaver DLC on Oct 30 2025 (87% positive, 62 reviews). Mobile ports (iOS, Android) and a Switch listing exist. Steam-revenue-calculator estimates about $1.5M gross and $444k net (Boxleiter-style, not audited).
best_things: High agency over randomness: full map visibility, intent shown before enemies act, and control over draw order and card rewards
Swapping cards in and out of your deck between fights, so builds can be tuned and rethought constantly
Four classes plus a DLC class, each with three distinct starting decks and spells, so runs feel different from the first fight
Retain and purge/energy systems that reward sequencing and turn-order planning
Large content pool: 440+ cards, 320+ artifacts, Void Stone upgrades, and 50 challenge coins with modifier-based and goofy empowered runs
Scalable difficulty, including a customisable Impossible mode, which fans of hard Slay the Spire ascensions enjoy
Cross-save between platforms, singled out by players as underrated
Reviewers say it is polished and more fleshed out than a Slay the Spire clone; one calls it a quiet technical pleasure with lots of depth
Repeatedly called an underrated hidden gem that gets buried on Steam and rarely appears on best-of-genre lists
worst_things: Steep learning curve: around 20 mechanics arrive at once and the tutorial explains them poorly (discard vs purge vs exhaust is a common confusion)
Busy UI with heavy mental arithmetic, which some find hurts readability
Mechanics feel more complicated than necessary just to be different from Slay the Spire (negative reviewers' view)
Mandatory 20-card deck and near-mandatory starter cards prevent thin-deck strategies and make starter cards hard to drop
Killed enemies still deal their damage until the whole fight ends, which players find counter-intuitive
Theme, plot and art are described as generic or bog-standard, with only serviceable visuals
Steam Deck and controller bugs reported, including missing map art, invisible portraits and audio dropouts
Some translation, typo and crash or save-recovery threads on the Steam forum
Several reviewers, including players past Impossible 20+, find it solid but unexciting or lacking variety, and prefer Slay the Spire or Monster Train
improvements: A better tutorial that introduces keywords gradually and explains the core mechanics in depth
A cleaner, less cluttered UI with clearer numbers and names
Fixes for Steam Deck and controller compatibility bugs
More language support and localisation fixes (forum requests)
Clearer item and ability descriptions (forum reports on Zeal tree confusion and an equipment misrepresentation bug)
Some fans single out the Bare Bones challenge coin as unfun, suggesting balance tuning
unique_things: Fixed 20-card deck that you can restructure between every fight, instead of an ever-growing deck
Retained cards can be deleted for energy or mana on later turns
Full map vision plus enemy previews before battle, reducing hidden-information gambles
Void Stones and runes inserted into cards as a customisation layer, alongside potions, relics and spells
Reset-fight option to brute-force a puzzle or undo a mistake
The Weaver DLC class commands a team of 25+ pets across five slots with Weave and Unravel mechanics
tedious_or_disliked: Learning the dense keyword system in the first runs, which some bounced off (several recommend the free demo first)
Constant deck micromanagement between fights, which some players find unappealing
Mental maths and planning overhead on every turn
Starter-card dependence makes deck-building feel less free than in Slay the Spire
Bare Bones challenge coin called out as the one unfun piece even by a 200-hour fan
divisive_points: Complexity: fans call it depth and a rewarding puzzle, detractors call it needless and unintuitive
Deck-swapping and heavy agency: praised as fixing RNG frustrations, disliked as removing tension and adding micromanagement
Art and theme: some rate the art style good to great while others call the presentation generic
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched Nov 20 2020; 1.0 released Oct 4 2022 on Steam (Windows, Mac) and listed on iOS, Android and Switch. Steam user reception stayed Very Positive throughout and was 90% positive over the last 30 days (only 10 reviews, so low current volume; about 28 concurrent players in local data). Critic coverage is thin: Metacritic has one review (70/100) and no aggregate, and I found no OpenCritic page (search returned 404). The developer kept supporting it: a Nightmare update, a Halloween update players were awaiting, and The Weaver DLC (Oct 30 2025, 90+ cards, 50+ artifacts, 3 challenge coins). Note: the web search budget ran out during this task, so community detail comes from Steam reviews, the Steam forum and Steam store pages, and I could not read Reddit (fetch blocked) or the God is a Geek review text (403).

games.name: Wildfrost
games.short_description: Take on the elements in Wildfrost, a tactical roguelike deckbuilder! Journey across a frozen tundra, collecting cards strong enough to banish the eternal winter…

other_scores.score: approx $5.6M gross, approx $1.66M net; SteamSpy owners 500k-1M

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Wildfrost is a board-focused deck-building roguelike where you play one card per turn and units act on countdown timers. He adores its visuals, music and approachable-yet-strategic gameplay, and has played it heavily, near 100%. His main complaint is the complete lack of card rarities, which makes finds feel random and flat, and he wants a larger card and unit pool. He still calls it a phenomenal game and lands it in A tier.
praise: Immersive, beautiful visuals that made him want to play immediately
Phenomenal soundtrack; several tier-list music tracks come from it
Simple concept (one card per turn) that is approachable but still strategic
Countdown numbers under units create interesting pacing
Gameplay itself is almost not random; only the draw is, so everything can be figured out strategically
Final boss becomes your next run's deck, upgraded, which works well as progression
Very hard true final boss on top difficulty is satisfying to beat
criticism: No rarities at all, so all cards and units feel equal in power and finds are less exciting
Card offers are often three weak or off-build options, making runs inconsistent and less satisfying
Too few cards and units; he thinks it could use double
Lack of rarity plus small pool creates a weird limbo of randomness
unique_points: Only deck-builder he knows with no card rarities
One card played per turn while enemy and friendly units tick on countdowns
Beaten final boss becomes your deck in the next run, upgraded, as a fight
One of the least RNG-focused deck builders in terms of in-combat play
commentary.quote: I love the game myself it is a nice eight tier
design_criteria: Visuals/charm: immersive art is a major draw
Audio: standout music
Simplicity vs strategy: approachable one-card-per-turn design
Randomness: combat deterministic, deck acquisition random
Rarity system: absence hurts excitement and consistency
Content diversity: too few cards and units
Meta-progression: final boss becoming your next deck
Difficulty: very hard true final boss
Build variety: many builds possible but inconsistent to reach

community.one_liner: A tactical roguelike deckbuilder from Deadpan Games and Gaziter (published by Chucklefish) where you lead a tribe leader and companions through a frozen tundra in cooldown-based card battles on a two-lane, six-slot board.
community.consensus_summary: Wildfrost is well received by both players and critics: Metacritic PC sits at 80 (17 critic reviews) with a user score of 8.0, and Steam shows Very Positive (about 83% across roughly 8,860 reviews in our local snapshot; the store page itself showed a higher figure, so treat exact percentages loosely). It is praised as a distinctive, hard, synergy-rich alternative to Slay the Spire with standout art and music. The main friction is difficulty and perceived RNG unfairness, a grind-heavy unlock structure, and a divisive post-win 'previous champion becomes the final boss' mechanic. It is a finished, released game (Switch/PC April 2023, mobile April 2024, Xbox December 2024) with Steam Workshop support, daily runs and difficulty customisation via Storm Bells; one reviewer notes balance patches fixed early turn-0 infinites and overpowered final bosses. Players still ask for more content.
best_things: Distinctive cooldown-counter combat where every card played ticks down both your units and enemies, making turn order and positioning the core puzzle
Charms (up to 3 per card) allow deep, creative unit customisation and exponential combo builds, often compared favourably to Inscryption-style run modification
Huge variety of companions, cards and keywords across three tribes (Snowdwellers, Shademancers, Clunkmasters) gives many viable strategies
Strong, charming cartoon art style and animation; critics and players both single out the visual polish
Well-liked music and atmosphere; one reviewer discovered the game via its soundtrack
Satisfying skill-testing difficulty: failures usually traceable to misjudged turn order or overlooked enemy effects, and wins feel earned
Accessible to learn but deep; some families play it together, and reviewers say it stays as dynamic on the twentieth run as the first
Meta-progression through Snowdwell town building, daily runs, challenges and Storm Bell difficulty scaling adds replay value
worst_things: Unfairness and RNG: random starting leader stats, bad character/enemy rolls, and enemy groups that feel like they counter-pick your strategy
Turn outcomes are hard to predict because of many interacting mechanics and poorly explained order of operations; players lose turns they thought were perfect
Uneven build viability: a few keywords and archetypes per tribe dominate, and many unlocked companions or cards are conditional or worse than starter options
Early pacing is tough because placing a single unit costs a whole turn while multiple enemies already race ahead
Steep learning curve and a high barrier to entry for genre newcomers (Twinfinite cautioned this); IGN France cited very high difficulty and inconsistent card balance
Post-victory 'posse' final-boss design can lock players out of repeating a win if their winning run was very strong
Windows-only on Steam (no Mac/Linux); a top-voted negative Steam review is purely about publisher Chucklefish's alleged treatment of unpaid interns, not gameplay
Limited content depth for some players who finish unlocks and want more

The leader doubles as your lose condition, and the abundance of area attacks, counter-attacks and reflects can make the leader's own attack kill it in retaliation (tactics-minded players find this infuriating)
improvements: Add a preview or simulation mechanic for a turn so players can confirm the outcome before committing, given the many interacting effects
Offer an alternate or less punishing boss mechanic after the first win so a strong champion does not soft-lock replayability
Reduce or smooth randomness in starting leaders (for example, reroll or choose stats) so bad draws do not force restarting runs
Rebalance weaker cards, companions and keywords so more archetypes are viable, and make unlock rewards less conditional
Explain unusual mechanics and interactions better in-game
Release more content (cards, tribes, modes), which reviewers explicitly request
unique_things: Cooldown-counter (tick-down) combat on a six-slot, two-lane board instead of energy/mana-based hands
Losing your leader ends the run instantly, while allies can be rescued in later attempts
Charms applied to cards for extreme per-unit customisation, with some players saying it does this better than Slay the Spire 2's augmentations
The previous run's winning champion returns as the next final boss, scaling difficulty with your own success
Secret true boss unlocked at maximum Storm Bell difficulty
tedious_or_disliked: Unlock grinding that reveals conditional or weak content, frustrating players who put tens of hours in
Restarting runs or cancelling them from the town just to reroll better starting leaders
Hour-long runs ending in a loss to a boss built from your previous best run
Having to mentally simulate many stacked effects each turn and losing runs to misunderstood ordering
Feeling forced into a small number of dominant keywords per tribe on higher difficulties
No quick-restart option, and manually calculating every stacked effect each turn because the game shows no damage predictions
divisive_points: The winner-becomes-the-final-boss loop: some call it inventive and self-scaling, others call it unsustainable bad design
Difficulty: fans call it rewarding and among the hardest deckbuilders, detractors call it unfair and luck-driven rather than skill-driven
Randomness and unlock structure: part of the roguelike appeal for some, a time-waster for others
Comparison to Slay the Spire: some place it among the genre's best, others feel mechanically something is missing despite the polish
community.reception_notes: Launched on Switch and Windows on April 12, 2023 to strong reviews, later ported to Android and iOS (April 11, 2024) and Xbox (December 10, 2024). Early balance problems (turn-0 infinite combos, overpowered final bosses) were reportedly patched. The game is not abandoned but players still ask for new content. Steam recent reviews were still Very Positive (about 85%) at fetch time, with low review volume in the last 30 days. PC is Windows-only. Note: OpenCritic could not be retrieved (web search budget was exhausted and OpenCritic/Reddit/RPS/PC Gamer fetches failed), so opencritic is null, and community detail draws mainly on Steam reviews and Metacritic user reviews rather than Reddit.

games.name: Archons
games.short_description: Archons is a Roguelite/Survivor game where you control two characters, the Archons- simultaneously! Customize your build and abilities to fit your own unique playstyle and blast your way through enemy parasites and bosses!

placements.verbal_evidence: I think Arkin deserves a solid A spot.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Arkins is a horde-like (vampire survivors / bullet heaven) game where you control two characters at once, which he says he has never seen done before. He treats the single-player two-character setup as the more interesting way to play and calls it a pleasantly amazing surprise. The music-synced sound design and slow, forgiving onboarding win him over. The main complaints are the short length (three levels, repeated bosses) and that many abilities do nothing in single-boss fights. He places it in A tier.
praise: Two-character control is a unique twist on the horde-like genre and feels great once it clicks
Abilities tie into the two-character movement, so each run feels different
Everything is synced to the electronic music beat, and this can be used strategically (e.g. timed grenades)
Gentle progression: starts simple, introduces more, slow early gameplay lets players adjust to the controls
Good damage feedback and readability, so he usually knows why he took damage even with characters far apart
Solid meta progression and enemy design; attractive look and feel
criticism: Game is short: only three levels, each ending in a boss
Bosses are identical every run and the difficulty meter adds little new
Wants more content and enemy variation in levels
On-death and bounce-type abilities are useless against lone bosses with no adds, discouraging those boons
The two-character control may not click for everyone
unique_points: Controlling two characters at once in a horde-like is a novel mechanic combined with a fitting genre
Beat-synced damage ticks and ability triggers merge music and sound design, and enable rhythm-based strategy
Design lesson: give boss fights small adds so on-kill and bounce effects still trigger
commentary.quote: Arkin deserves a solid A spot.
design_criteria: Novelty/unique twist: two-character control is the core hook
Audio/music integration: beat-synced effects and sound design
Meta-progression: substantial unlocks that suit the learning curve
Onboarding and difficulty curve: slow, forgiving start that builds comfort
Readability/feedback: clear cause of damage
Content volume: only three levels and repeated bosses
Boss design and build synergy: lone bosses invalidate some ability types
Enemy design: liked, but wants more variety
Replayability: abilities plus movement make runs feel different

community.one_liner: A short roguelite/survivor bullet-hell from BulletHell Studios in which one player controls two characters at once, one per hand/stick, with weapons that fire in time to the music.
community.consensus_summary: Archons is a small, cheap indie (Steam, Windows only, Dec 6 2024) that sits at Very Positive on Steam (about 92-94% of roughly 430 reviews). Players love the two-character control hook, the tight positioning-focused combat and the music that syncs with weapon attacks. The recurring complaints are that it is short (around 3 hours for the main story, 3 bosses/levels), that content and enemy variety are thin, and that solo play is very mentally taxing while the game is clearly tuned for a controller or local co-op. It has no Metacritic or OpenCritic entry, so there is no critic consensus; reception is entirely player-driven. A few reviewers feel it is under-supported, and one said it seems abandoned, but I found no public patch notes confirming or refuting that. It is frequently discounted to about $1 (90% off the $9.99 base).
best_things: The dual-character mechanic is fresh: controlling two Archons at once is hectic but 'just works' and creates a flow state
Weapons and attack animations are synced to the soundtrack, praised as a standout (composer Oliver Orand is named in a review)
Movement and positioning matter more than spamming abilities; you cannot stand still or circle-strafe and win
Polished and respects your time: a short run-based experience, with endless mode and a hard mode for replay
Spectacular boss fights and satisfying build combos when rolls line up
Great value at its frequent steep discounts; StarCraft references delight some players
Full controller support and local split-screen co-op
worst_things: Very short: main story is only 3 stages/bosses, and reviewers call it short or a bit short
Limited enemy variety; reviewers say many enemies use the same attack pattern and there are few maps
Maps are too dark and hard to read; some players had to raise brightness
No camera control and a rotating camera that adds to the stress
Mouse and keyboard play is poor or problematic; a controller is strongly recommended
Weak ability synergies and lackluster ability evolutions; the Archon ultimate is a static barrage
Polish and optimization issues reported, plus poor translation and UI complaints in one negative review
Ultimate is hard-coded to F even after rebinding (one reviewer)
improvements: Add a real single-character or AI-companion mode so solo players are not forced to control two characters
More content: more bosses/stages, maps and enemy types with distinct attacks
Give abilities real synergies with the Archon ultimate and stronger ability evolutions
Improve map brightness/visibility and add camera options
Fix mouse and keyboard support, rebinding bugs (ultimate on F) and UI/translation rough spots
Add online co-op (requested in Steam discussions) and New Game+ / quality-of-life features
Differentiate the two characters visually (color suggestion in discussions)
unique_things: You control two characters simultaneously, one per hand, as a survivor-style bullet hell, compared by one reviewer to It Takes Two meets Furi
Attacks and weapons are rhythm-synced to the music
Bloodrunes let you sacrifice health for power, and there are multiple currencies to spend
Local split-screen co-op where each player pilots one Archon, versus solo where one player pilots both
Positioning-first design rather than screen-filling particle chaos or auto-fire snowballing
tedious_or_disliked: Solo play demands a lot of mental juice and is described as stressful; one reviewer called it the most stressful roguelike they had tried
Some unlocks/research feel grindy ('after a few grind sessions') and one reviewer said difficulty collapsed once a certain research was unlocked
Healing pickups are time-limited and released by breaking containers, so they get wasted when damage breaks them at random
Dark maps and lack of camera control are frustrating
Reported bugs: freezing after reroll, an ice-ground mechanic problem in Endless Hard mode, and an achievement (Heartache) not unlocking
divisive_points: Solo vs co-op: some say the game is meant to be played solo (that is the challenge), others say it is made for co-op and solo is too hectic
Price and length: some call it great only on discount while others say even full price is fair for the polish
Difficulty: challenging until the two-character skill clicks, then some find builds too easy or some weapons unviable on hard mode
community.reception_notes: Launched Dec 6 2024 on Steam for Windows only (no Mac/Linux listed, no console release found). Steam reviews have stayed Very Positive, with about 410-430 total and a recent-review score of 92%; it still gets positive reviews in 2026, including several by players who say they slept on it. Base price is $9.99 and it is heavily discounted to about $1 at times. Steam Community threads in early 2026 show the dev-facing asks (online co-op, mouse support, single-character mode) and some bug reports; one negative reviewer felt it was abandoned and lacked an Early Access tag, though I could not verify the update cadence from public patch notes. No professional critic reviews, Metacritic or OpenCritic pages were found; Deku Deals lists Metacritic as not yet available. Revenue and owner figures are third-party estimates (Boxleiter method), so treat them as order of magnitude only.

commentary.summary: Cobalt Core is a space-themed, turn-based deck-building roguelike where cards move your ship and fire its cannon, with each crew combination bringing its own mechanics. Easy-to-grasp but strategic core mechanics: cards move the ship and shoot depending on where the cannon is
Characters have distinct mechanics (overheat cards, auto-firing turrets), giving strong replayability via ship and crew choice
Encounters each tell a story; events and relics are fantastic roguelike elements
Every enemy fight feels unique, with its own mechanics and strategies to adapt to
Memories unlocked from beating runs add emotional lore; very homey, immersive vibe
Large amount of content that takes a long time to exhaust
criticism: Not intuitive at first; trickier to comprehend unless you are used to deck-builders and turn-based games
Some characters are more complicated or less fun than others

commentary.quote: it's probably a low S tier uh high A
design_criteria: Audio/music: a major reason for his love, hits him as a musician
Core mechanics: simple to understand but strategically deep, with a learning curve
Character diversity and replayability: varied ships and crew, though some are weaker
Roguelike elements: relics, events and encounters that tell stories
Enemy design: each fight is unique and requires adaptation
Vibe/story/charm: emotional, homey, immersive with lore memories

community.one_liner: A sci-fi roguelike deckbuilder by Rocket Rat Games in which you pilot a spaceship with a three-character crew through a time loop, dodging enemy fire by moving left and right to line up cannons.
community.consensus_summary: Cobalt Core is very well received by both critics and players: 96% positive on Steam (Overwhelmingly Positive, about 4,400 reviews), Metacritic 94 and an OpenCritic top critic average of 89 with 100% of critics recommending. Reviewers present it as a compact, tactical take on the Slay the Spire formula, with the lateral-movement mechanic, crew-mixing and charming writing as the standouts. The recurring caveats are content volume and difficulty: several players and critics say it is easy even on top difficulty, runs repeat the same events and bosses, and the unlock arc is short. It is not early access, and it got free updates after launch (1.1 added enemies and alternate bosses, 1.2 in Jan 2025), a Mac port in July 2025 and Linux support reported in Aug 2025. It was nominated for Strategy/Simulation Game of the Year at the 27th D.I.C.E. Awards.
best_things: Movement is the core hook: dodging incoming missiles while lining up your own cannons adds a tactical puzzle layer absent from other deckbuilders (FTL / Into the Breach flavour).
Crew mixing: picking three of the characters to form your starting card pool gives a lot of combinations and distinct archetypes (drones, heat, corrosion, shields, infinites).
Characters and writing: crew members banter reactively based on cards played, damage taken and who is paired together; widely called charming, funny and endearing.
Enemies telegraph their next shots, so outcomes feel driven by player choices and planning rather than pure luck.
Snappy, polished feel: UI, sound design and animation make runs fast and satisfying.
Time-loop story told through unlockable memories ties neatly into the roguelike structure and pays off; some reviewers say the story is better than typical for the genre.
Multiple ships with their own rules and playstyles, none strictly better than the starter, plus daily challenges and a codex that encourages completionism.
Minimal meta-progression: no grinding for power, you win by getting better; a small team (three people) delivered an unusually polished game.
worst_things: Limited content: the same events, enemies and bosses recur every run, card and artifact pools are smaller than Slay the Spire's, and players report seeing everything in roughly 10-20 hours.
Too easy: multiple reviewers beat hard and harder difficulties within a few runs and say they must self-handicap with weaker crews or ships to be challenged.
Same-y builds: all of a character's cards unlock immediately, so the best cards become obvious and runs converge.
Map traversal and pathing are considered uninteresting compared with other genre entries.
Shield feels underpowered relative to movement/dodging, narrowing viable defensive strategies.
Critics noted boss fights lack randomness and the total unlock arc is short compared with peers.
Some players find the core loop of shifting left or right with hit-or-miss draws unengaging and feel cards/effects are underwhelming.
improvements: Add much more content: players ask for roughly double or triple the cards, enemies, events, bosses and gimmicks (events and ship count were singled out in reviews).
Offer harder difficulty tiers or modifiers so experienced players are challenged without self-handicapping.
Add randomness or variation to boss encounters and more alternate bosses per zone.
Make map traversal more meaningful (more interesting route decisions).
Add an undo option and show card upgrade outcomes without having to click into every card.
Rebalance shield versus movement and further distinguish the crew so fewer cards are obvious picks.
unique_things: Single-axis tactical combat: you slide left or right to dodge and line up shots, rather than just playing cards against a health bar.
Your deck is built from the three crew members you choose, making crew selection a pre-run strategic layer.
Dynamic crew dialogue that reacts to specific game state, inspired by Star Trek and Reigns.
Time-loop framing with story memories unlocked through runs, inspired in part by Inscryption's meta-awareness.
Ships change the ruleset of the run (different meta rules), and the game is compact rather than sprawling.
Distinct cobalt-blue pixel-art look with a light-hearted tone and serious undercurrents.
tedious_or_disliked: Repetition: seeing the same events and enemies every run becomes tedious after the first dozen runs.
Feeling underpowered in fights and chipping away at enemies, with no Balatro/Monster Train-style moment of unlocking an overpowered build (one 16-hour reviewer).
No undo for misclicks and having to inspect each card to see upgrade results.
Some find the unlocks spaced both too far apart and too thin, and the story not compelling enough to motivate unlocking.
RNG-driven draws can leave you without the movement or range card you need, which some reviewers find frustrating.
Short playtime-to-content ratio: several negative reviewers (8-10 hours) beat hard or harder difficulty within a few runs and call it thin for the price, wanting a steep sale.
divisive_points: Difficulty: some celebrate that skill reliably wins, others find even the hardest mode too easy and then feel there is little left to do.
Movement mechanic: loved as fresh and tactical by most, but a minority finds moving left/right and hoping for the right card dull or RNG-heavy.
Value: fans put hundreds of hours in (one reviewer 520 hours, another calls it their favorite roguelike), while others call it thin for about $20 and recommend waiting for a sale.
Versus Slay the Spire: some see it as a mini StS clone, others rank it above StS.
community.reception_notes: Launched Nov 8, 2023 on Windows and Switch after an October 2023 Steam Next Fest demo, and was praised at launch as a standout from a tiny three-person team. Metacritic critic score is based on only 5 reviews and the user score (7.7) on only 23 ratings, so treat them as thin samples; Steam (96%, 4.4k reviews) is the more robust signal. Post-launch: update 1.1 added six new enemies and alternate bosses, update 1.2 arrived Jan 2025, macOS port July 2025, and Linux support reported Aug 2025; the game is not early access and is not abandoned, though no major expansion was found. Steam-side estimates suggest roughly 100-200k owners and about $1.65M gross revenue (third-party Boxleiter-style estimate, order-of-magnitude only). Recent (2025-2026) Steam reviews still praise it heavily while repeating the same complaints about content depth and low difficulty; some players mention modding as a way to extend it. Nominated for Strategy/Simulation Game of the Year at the 27th D.I.C.E. Awards.

community.one_liner: A gothic, Lovecraft-flavoured turn-based party RPG by Red Hook Studios where you run a roster of flawed heroes through procedurally assembled dungeons, managing both health and mental stress, with permanent death and a hamlet hub that carries progress between expeditions.
community.consensus_summary: Darkest Dungeon is widely regarded as a modern classic of the genre: about 91.7% of roughly 163k Steam reviews are positive (Very Positive), Metacritic sits at 84 and OpenCritic at 84 with about 93% of critics recommending it. Critics and players praise the art, narrator, stress system and tense, consequential party tactics. The recurring complaint is that the late game turns into a grind, compounded by swingy RNG (back-to-back crits, surprise ambushes) that can wipe out heroes you spent hours levelling. It was in Steam Early Access from Jan 2015 and launched fully on 19 Jan 2016, and it is still being updated: a new DLC, The Fire's Edge, appears in current Steam data. Sequel Darkest Dungeon II (Steam appid 1940340) is a different, more run-based roguelite structure.
best_things: Distinctive gothic storybook art direction and Lovecraftian atmosphere that critics and players call hauntingly beautiful
Wayne June's narrator performance and the audio/music, repeatedly singled out as elevating every expedition
The stress/affliction system: mental health as a second resource that creates emergent story moments and meaningful risk
Tactical turn-based combat built around rank positioning, with deep hero class variety, quirks, and team synergies
High stakes and permadeath make every decision, victory, and loss feel weighty; 'easy to learn, hard to master' as one long-time player puts it
Hamlet hub progression gives persistence even when heroes die, so failure still moves the meta forward
Rewarding loot and trinket hunting, lots of bosses and dungeon variety, plus a large modding scene
Strong content additions over time (The Crimson Court, The Color of Madness, The Butcher's Circus PvP arena)
worst_things: Late-game grind: players feel they must repeatedly farm low-level dungeons to replace fallen heroes before attempting the Darkest Dungeon itself
RNG swinginess: chains of enemy crits, missed high-accuracy attacks, and turn-order variance can undo 20 hours of progress
Hero level restrictions that bar a stronger hero from easier quests, which forces awkward roster juggling and farming
Quests are slow (20 to 60 minutes) with slow animations and back-and-forth map movement, so the game can feel like it does not respect player time
Knowledge-check design: you often learn a boss or curio mechanic only by dying to it, so many players lean on wikis and guides

Heavy economy drain from stress relief, disease cures, quirk removal, provisions and expensive final gear upgrades (for example thousands of gold per top-tier weapon, 100+ deeds mentioned by one forum poster)
Some reviewers found the stress acting-out and Crimson Curse systems annoying, and a critic cited rough mouse controls and a thin tutorial
Game does not respect player time: reviewers note most players never field a full roster of max-level heroes, and losing a few heroes means regrinding many low-level dungeons
improvements: Give end-game experience a better path, such as resolve-level XP or easier ways to level heroes, so replacing losses is less of a grind
Relax or remove the hero-too-strong-for-quest restriction so players can farm efficiently
Tune the three-tier structure to feel less padded (one forum suggestion: two tiers plus a max-level run at the Darkest Dungeon)
Reduce the randomness of ambushes, camping attacks, and crit streaks, or offer more counterplay and information beforehand
Better onboarding and in-game information so boss and curio mechanics are not pure trial-and-error; smoother mouse controls
Speed options and less tedious quest pacing (animation speed, map traversal) for respect of player time
unique_things: Psychological stress as a core mechanic alongside hit points, with heroes developing afflictions or virtues that can help or sabotage the party
Rank-based positioning combat in which skills work only from certain slots and move enemies and allies around
Permanent death in a persistent hamlet hub: a roguelite meta-loop of rosters and town upgrades rather than fresh runs
Torchlight and provisions management that raises tension and alters loot and enemy strength
Narrator-driven tone that comments on your successes and failures with a dark sense of humour
Hero quirks and diseases that make each recruit feel like a character rather than a disposable unit
tedious_or_disliked: Repeating near-identical low-level missions to level replacement heroes before high-tier content
Expensive upkeep for stress relief, curing diseases, and removing bad traits that drains gold after every trip
Slow animations and traversal that stretch each quest to 20 minutes or more
Ambushes while camping and unavoidable hallway encounters that can kill high-level heroes
Emotional toll of losing favourite heroes; some players say sessions leave them stressed rather than entertained, and the Butcher's Circus arena was not liked by at least one long-time player
divisive_points: Whether the difficulty is fair: many fans say knowledge and preparation remove most RNG, while detractors say it is about 50% luck
Whether the grind is a satisfying meta-loop or a waste of time; fans defend the economy as part of the tension, critics call it padding
Stress system: loved as innovative storytelling by most, but some find the random acting-out and afflictions infuriating
Loss tolerance: fans see permadeath as the point of the game, others bounce off after losing a high-level hero
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched Jan 2015 after a Kickstarter that raised over $313k; the early period drew complaints that it was too difficult, too random, and unfair, and streamer feedback shaped balance before the Jan 19, 2016 release. Sales reportedly hit 650k in the first week, 1M by Nov 2016 and 2M by Dec 2017 (Wikipedia); estimators put Steam owners at 2 to 5 million and gross revenue around $23.9M (Steam-revenue-calculator estimate, not audited). Ports followed for PS4/Vita, Switch, Xbox One, iOS and Linux; Metacritic platform scores range 80 to 85. DLC: The Crimson Court (2017), The Color of Madness (2018), The Butcher's Circus (2020), and The Fire's Edge (newly listed in Steam data). Some critics felt the ending stumbled by lengthening the game with tougher endgame limits, and the Radiant difficulty and mods are common recommendations to ease the grind.

More lore per character, with quests that unlock abilities via little puzzle minigames
A relationship system between characters adds depth
Large amount of meta progression to unlock

Character-specific story quests with small puzzle minigames that permanently unlock abilities

Meta progression: lots to unlock, but a single shared currency creates tension with power upgrades
Animation and visuals: standout smooth animation and distinct art style
Audio: music remains fantastic
Content and variety: many events, characters and differing runs

Characters and lore: more story per character but less attachment

community.one_liner: A turn-based gothic-horror roguelike from Red Hook Studios in which a party of flawed heroes rides a stagecoach across a ruined land in long, permadeath-driven expeditions to stop a cosmic apocalypse.
community.consensus_summary: Critics received it well (Metacritic 81, OpenCritic 81, 'Strong' tier), praising the combat puzzle, art and atmosphere, while players are more split (Steam 'Mostly Positive', about 75% of roughly 27k reviews; Metacritic user score 6.3/10). Much of the player backlash comes from the shift from the first game's hamlet-and-roster management to a roguelike with long expeditions and meta-progression, which many series fans did not want. It launched in Early Access on Epic in October 2021, hit 1.0 on Steam in May 2023, and has since received major updates, including the free Kingdoms mode and the Inhuman Bondage DLC in January 2025, plus console releases. Some recent Steam reviews (Dec 2025) still argue it feels unpolished, with classes and systems still being reworked.
best_things: Combat plays like a tactical puzzle: party composition, positioning and the token system reward planning and cut some of the first game's pure RNG
Gothic/Lovecraftian art direction, improved 3D-style animation and atmosphere are praised as top tier
Narrator (Wayne June) and atmosphere carry the dread and tone, though some players find the soundtrack and narration less memorable than the first game
Hero backstories and the affinity/relationship system between party members add personality and strategic complexity
Varied regions and hazards make each expedition feel distinct and tense
Runs are more compartmentalised and experimental than the first game's endless roster grind, so some find it less of a slog
High-stakes, white-knuckle difficulty feels cathartic and rewarding once it clicks
Post-launch support has been substantial: new heroes, Kingdoms mode, balance reworks and console ports
Fresh take on the DD formula: some players prefer it to a near-copy of DD1 and like its more synergy-focused party building and avoidance of DD1's snowballing party-wipe problem
worst_things: Too different from Darkest Dungeon 1 for many fans: no hamlet, no persistent loot, and characters reset after each run
Poor onboarding: mechanics are opaque, tutorials thin, and success can depend on wiki knowledge
Early runs lean heavily on RNG, with long 2-3 hour Confessions expeditions that can be lost to bad luck or a single mistake
Meta-progression unlocks (stagecoach upgrades, candles for items, trinkets and inn items) are slow and feel like a prerequisite grind
Some boss gimmicks feel like instant-fail encounters without prior knowledge, for example the Confession 5 mirror mechanic when the copy is stuck in an unreachable position
Stuns need two hits, healing is conditional and on cooldown, and reliable damage/stress mitigation was removed, so incoming damage feels overwhelming and difficulty feels 'fake' or RNG-driven
Random quirk replacement and the lack of a separate fixed character for re-specs annoy players
Combat math and buffs feel inconsistent (e.g. a 50% damage-reduction buff cutting far less than half), undermining trust in planning
improvements: Better tutorials and in-game explanation of systems so the wiki is not required
More shortcuts, checkpoints or ways to soften the loss of a failed 2-3 hour run
Faster, less grindy meta-progression and unlock pacing
Replace quirks in a predictable order (oldest first) rather than randomly
Fix frustrating boss gimmicks, especially Confession 5 mirroring and unreachable copies
Further polish and balance of classes and mechanics that are still being reworked
unique_things: Sequel that turns a dungeon-crawl roster game into a roguelike road trip with a stagecoach as a mobile base
Mental-health stress/meltdown system where heroes can crack and turn on the party
Affinity and relationship system between heroes that affects combat and story
Two modes: long Confessions expeditions and the free Kingdoms campaign-style mode
Token-based combat and positioning puzzle layered over the original's turn-based formula
Lovecraftian tone with a narrator voice as a signature feature
tedious_or_disliked: Unlock grind: reviewers report roughly 20 hours to gather stagecoach upgrades, then many more hours for other unlocks, before later bosses feel viable
Long runs of 2-3 hours with no checkpoints make failures costly
Grinding candles and stagecoach upgrades to reach a viable power level for later bosses
Slow stagecoach travel and repetitive battles, though the developers reduced battle counts from Early Access
Constant reliance on outside guides because of unclear mechanics
divisive_points: Whether it should be judged as a sequel to DD1 or as its own roguelike; reviewers who do the latter tend to rate it higher
Paid DLC heroes are seen as greedy by some and as fair value by others
Difficulty and RNG: hardcore roguelike fans find it rewarding, while DD1 loyalists find it unfun and punishing
Roguelike structure itself: some see it as hiding a lack of content behind a linear grind, others prefer it to DD1's roster grind
community.reception_notes: Early Access began in October 2021 on the Epic Games Store; 1.0 launched on Steam on May 8, 2023 with strong critic scores but a notably mixed player response driven by comparisons to the first game and accusations of review bombing versus real design disappointment. Since then: the Binding Blade DLC, then in January 2025 the free Kingdoms mode (with the Hunger of the Beast Clan module) and the Inhuman Bondage DLC with The Abomination hero, which reached PS5 and other consoles later in 2025. Available on PC, Mac, Switch, PS4/PS5 and Xbox. Third-party estimates (steam-revenue-calculator, Boxleiter method, not audited) put Steam gross revenue near $41M, with SteamSpy owners at 1-2 million. Steam price $39.99.

community.one_liner: A hand-drawn roguelike deckbuilder from Ultra Piggy Studio where you can replace almost any number on screen (enemy HP, energy, card values, gold, relic charges) with a dice roll, built around a five-colour mana system.
community.consensus_summary: DICEOMANCER is an Overwhelmingly Positive Steam hit (about 96% of roughly 5,600 reviews, released Oct 9-10 2024 at $14.99). It reportedly sold 50,000 copies in two weeks, and estimates put lifetime ownership at 100k-200k. Players love the change-any-number gimmick, the class variety and the storybook art, and often pitch it to Slay the Spire and Balatro fans. The recurring complaints are that it is too easy and gets padded by a per-character ascension grind, that run variety and enemy design are thin, and that the developers have gone quiet with little or no post-launch content (several 2025-2026 reviews call it abandoned). Critic coverage is minimal: Metacritic has no Metascore yet (1 of 4 needed critic reviews) and OpenCritic has no findable entry, so reception is almost entirely player-driven.
best_things: The change-any-number dice mechanic is seen as genuinely novel, and players enjoy gradually discovering how many numbers it can touch (enemy health, energy, gold, shop prices, event checks, relic charges)
It lets you break the game in creative ways, for example a burn-everything deck or turning shop items into near-free purchases, which players say produces memorable stories
Distinct classes with their own gimmicks and playstyles, and a large pool of cards (about 500) with unusual keywords like Load, Summon, Construct, Phantom and Flow
The five-colour mana system, where you discard, exhaust and manipulate cards to pay for powerful ones, adds a Magic-like layer of decisions
Hand-drawn storybook art with 8fps animation, a humorous tone (the goal is simply to go fishing) and a well-liked soundtrack
Corruption/purple mist on the map pressures you to limit dice use while allowing backtracking, which is unusual for the genre
Strong value for players who like Slay the Spire, with some reviewers saying it surpasses it in places; 20-30 hours of fun is a common estimate, and some players log 70-200+ hours
worst_things: Too easy: overtuned cards, easy energy and draw, and stockpilable dice charges let experienced players delete bosses, sometimes on turn 1
Balance is uneven between classes (Builder and Berserker are named as strong; red classes can feel samey), and every class tends to have a run-breaking card or two
Limited enemy variety; outside a handful of bosses, enemies barely matter and you can ignore their intents
Little or no post-launch support; multiple reviews from 2025-2026 say the developers disappeared and did not expand a great concept
Content can feel thin for the price; one reviewer beat it in about 6 hours, and another said to wait for a sale
Complexity and keyword overload make the early hours confusing for some, with the demo cited as confusing
Some players say the dice gimmick is over-hyped in trailers because in most cases you only use it for things like cutting huge boss HP to a small number
A few reviewers find early enemies scaling too harshly or off-colour mana generation frustrating, which is the opposite complaint to the too-easy camp
improvements: Add new content (enemies, cards, events, upgrades); veteran players with 130+ hours specifically ask for new enemies
Add harder late-game difficulty: a fourth act, harsher ascension scaling and more meaningful modifiers
Share ascension progress across characters instead of making players climb 20 ascension levels separately for each of the six classes
Give a reason to linger in corruption or explore the map, such as rewards or new cards for taking risks
Put some limit or cost on stockpiling dice charges and on altering non-card numbers so the core mechanic stays tense
Improve enemy variety and make enemy intents matter more, and tune class balance
unique_things: You can swap almost any on-screen number for a die roll, including meta-genre numbers like cards per turn, reward choices and exhaust, which reviewers describe as commentary on deckbuilder tropes
Origin as the GMTK 2022 game jam entry Dice is the Way, which placed in the top 20 of more than 6,000 entries
Five-colour mana with a purple dice/chaos colour and cards that double as resources
Enemies with multiple health bars and a spreading purple fog that punishes dice use, balancing the power of the mechanic
Backtracking on the map, which most roguelike deckbuilders do not allow
Whimsical fishing-trip premise in a world with swords, magic and guns, plus a fully hand-drawn art style
tedious_or_disliked: The 20-level ascension ladder has to be repeated for each character, which reviewers call artificial padding when runs are all similarly easy
Runs can feel samey for classes that want a tiny deck, because you skip most card rewards
Enemies repeat often and feel largely irrelevant outside a few bosses, so runs play out as executing the combo you built

Some players dislike the dice mechanic as too game-defining or feel it trivialises the game, and a minority complain that dice feel rigged or rolls look seeded after restarting (an anecdotal claim in one review)
Keyword overload and complex cards make the early hours hard to parse (even the demo is cited as confusing)
divisive_points: Difficulty: a large group finds it far too easy, while newcomers and a few reviewers find it hard or scaling harshly
Dice mechanic: hailed as the most creative deckbuilder idea in years by many, but a few call it a cheat button or a gimmick that wears off after a few runs
Complexity: some find the mana and keyword system clever depth, others find it muddled and hard to understand
Value: players with 20-200 hours call it a bargain, while a few say it is too dry on content for $15
community.reception_notes: Launched Oct 9-10 2024 on Steam (Windows only, $14.99) and quickly earned Overwhelmingly Positive, with 50k sales reported within two weeks and a peak of about 2,300 concurrent players in launch coverage. Reception has stayed around 96% positive through 2026, with recent reviews increasingly mentioning the lack of dev updates and requests for new enemies and upgrades. No Mac or Linux build. Metacritic shows a pending Metascore (1 of the 4 critic reviews needed) and a 9.6 user score from only 5 ratings, so that user figure is not meaningful. I found no OpenCritic entry. I could not find a specific patch list or roadmap in the sources searched.

games.name: Halls of Torment
games.short_description: Slay hordes of terrifying monsters in this horde survival roguelite. Descend into the Halls of Torment where the Lords of the underworld await you. Treasures, magical trinkets, and a growing cast of heroes will grant you the power to vanquish these horrors from beyond. How long can you survive?

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Halls of Torment is a horde-survivor roguelike with a dark, old-school Diablo look. It keeps core gameplay simple and instead leans on exploration, a huge amount of unlockables, and a strong sense of progression. He compares the early hours to first playing Vampire Survivors. Drawbacks are poor UI and stat explanations, limited replayability once everything is seen, and too little content per level. His main complaint is simply wanting more, and he places it in A tier.
praise: Visuals evoke classic Diablo and have a unique charm
Massive amount of unlockables, with achievement boards per character and general boards
First few hours of progression feel amazing, like early Vampire Survivors
Each new level looks different with new enemies, bosses, characters and abilities
Hidden quests in levels (find a tome, follow a blood trail) reward exploration, e.g. boss damage and unlocks
Abilities are cool and some unique; upgrading then evolving them feels great
Infinite borderless level layouts encourage exploring

Less replayable than other horde-likes once all levels, bosses and abilities are seen
Only one unique quest per level, which disappointed him once he knew

In-run quests narrated by a voice tie exploration to boss damage and unlocks
Unlock-driven structure where progress is constant, with thousands of things to unlock

Visuals/charm: Diablo-inspired look is a major draw
Enemy/boss variety: new enemies and bosses per level are a highlight

commentary.label: Top 10 of 2024 (#10)
commentary.summary: Halls of Torment is a top-down bullet heaven (which he calls a 'horde-like') with simple controls: move and occasionally aim abilities. He calls it one of the best horde-likes of the year even though it is less unique than other games on his list. Its Diablo 1 style look and hack-and-slash feel are a highlight. His verdict is a solid pick for anyone wanting a simple take that recaptures some of the Vampire Survivors thrill.

Plenty of unlockable characters
Unique equipment that opens up many possible builds

Early-game discovery loop of maps, secrets and characters keeps runs feeling rewarding

Aesthetics: Diablo 1 inspired look and feel
Build variety: unique equipment enabling many builds

community.one_liner: A Diablo 1/2-styled horde-survival (Vampire Survivors-like) action roguelite with pre-rendered retro art, from Chasing Carrots (Stuttgart), where you pick a hero, auto-fire abilities into huge mobs and fight a timed ~30-minute run to a boss.
community.consensus_summary: Halls of Torment is rated Overwhelmingly Positive on Steam (about 95% of roughly 31.9k reviews) and scores 88 on Metacritic from 8 critics (user score 7.6). Critics and players alike treat it as one of the best Vampire Survivors-likes, mostly on the strength of its Diablo-era atmosphere, build variety and deep meta-progression, though several note it does not reinvent the genre. It was in Early Access from May 2023 (70k+ sales in week one) and had its 1.0 release on Sep 24, 2024; it is still being updated (Boglands DLC Nov 2025, a free Archives preview-update series running through Sep 2026). Recent reviews are a bit cooler (about 83% positive over the last 30 days in one snapshot), driven by stability complaints on high Agony difficulties and by fatigue with fixed-length runs.
best_things: Diablo 1/2 pre-rendered pixel aesthetic, gothic atmosphere and music nail late-90s ARPG nostalgia; PC Gamer and many Steam reviewers single this out
Large hero roster with distinct playstyles plus a huge pool of traits, abilities and items (reviewers cite 1,000+ traits, 60 items, hundreds of rare variants) gives real build variety
Deep meta-progression and unlocks (maps, heroes, quests, Agony difficulty tiers) keep the 'one more run' loop going for hundreds of hours
Excellent value: usually under $10, and several players report 100-300+ hours
Satisfying power fantasy as builds snowball and the screen fills with effects; ARPG-style itemisation and loot feel instead of only passive upgrades
Polished quest/achievement tracker (500 achievements) that gives clear goals; one reviewer calls it the best tracker they have seen
Actively supported developer: years of free updates, paid but well-received DLC, plus mobile (Oct 2024) and PS5/Xbox (Oct 2025) ports
worst_things: Fixed ~25-30 minute runs: the first ~10 minutes are busy, then long stretches of low-decision autopilot waiting for the boss timer; many negative reviews cite boredom here

Crashes and performance problems in late-game/high Agony content with massive hordes, especially certain abilities (for example Avalanche) and the Boglands map; also reported on Steam Deck and Linux despite 'Verified' status
Buildcraft and map design can feel samey: some players say unlocking all maps/heroes changes little, and Ars Technica (per Wikipedia) noted levels lack distinct identity
Does not innovate beyond the Vampire Survivors formula; several critics and positive reviewers say so
Some achievements depend on rare RNG spawns/events that may not appear, turning completion into waiting
Missing quality-of-life options: no game-speed or run-length toggle, no save-and-resume mid run, no mute when unfocused (per one reviewer)
Sparse 'dopamine drip' feel: one reviewer said it made them hyper-aware of time spent and they walked away
Some reviewers find the game slow and primitive early on: few skills, several heroes feel alike, and some characters are noticeably weaker than others
improvements: Add run-length options, a speed-up/turbo toggle, or save-and-return so the 30-minute loop is less of a commitment
Fix stability and memory issues at Agony 3+ and in the Bog before shipping more content (a recurring 'fix crashes first' request on Steam)
Make achievements less RNG-dependent so quests/spawns reliably appear
Increase decision density mid-run (more mid-run choices, events, more differentiated maps) to cut the autopilot stretch
Add audio option to mute when the window is not in focus and general QoL settings
Make buildcraft more exciting / make hero and map unlocks change gameplay more meaningfully
unique_things: Fully Diablo-flavoured presentation: pre-rendered sprites, ARPG loot vocabulary, dark fantasy underworld framing and 'Lords' as bosses
Creative director's pitch: Diablo as a three-course meal, this as the candy bar; it plays like a compressed ARPG instead of an arcade score-chaser
Very deep trait/item/rare-variant system and a 500-quest progression layer on top of the usual survivors loop
Timed structure with a mid-run boss spawn and a 30-minute main boss, closer to a Diablo act structure than endless survival
Built in the open-source Godot engine after the team moved away from Unity; five-person studio and a cheap ($6.66) price point
tedious_or_disliked: Long stretches of standing and auto-attacking after the map is cleared, waiting for the 30-minute boss
Grinding the 500 achievements, especially those tied to rare enemies or events that refuse to spawn
Crash-induced loss of progress and the need to avoid certain abilities or maps to stay stable at high difficulty
Unlock treadmill where heroes/maps unlocked late do not noticeably change how runs play
Level-up and item pause screens stretch the nominal 30-minute run to roughly 40 real minutes, with no suspend option
divisive_points: Run length: some love 30 minutes as a satisfying build-up to a boss, others find it far too long for this genre
Depth vs sameness: fans say it has enormous depth if you dig down, critics of it say builds and maps blur together
Innovation: 'best in genre execution' versus 'nothing new beyond Vampire Survivors'
Value of the Boglands DLC and the post-launch updates: praised by many, but one reviewer reported game-breaking bugs two weeks after the DLC launch
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched May 24, 2023 with 70k+ units in week one; 1.0 launched Sep 24, 2024 with peak concurrents since Aug 2023, and 1M+ Steam sales by Oct 2024. Steam Revenue Calculator estimates about $7.0M gross and about $2.1M net (Boxleiter-based, order-of-magnitude only). Nominated for Mobile Game of the Year at the 28th D.I.C.E. Awards. Mobile ports Oct 2024 (Erabit Studios) and PS5/Xbox Oct 2025. Boglands DLC arrived with the Nov 2025 Bog update, and a free 'Archives' preview update series ran from Mar 2026 through Sep 28, 2026; fix patches for crashes and resource leaks shipped Nov 2025 and Apr 2026, though some recent reviews still report crashes at Agony 3+ and Steam Deck issues. The Steam forum keeps a pinned known-issues thread and the crash/technical topics dominate player discussion. Windows and Linux on Steam, no Mac.

games.name: Magicraft
games.short_description: "Magicraft" is a Roguelike game that uses a variety of spells to match unimaginable spell effects, and the construction of ultra-high degrees of freedom cannot even be exhausted by developers.

other_scores.score: Approx $8.18M gross, approx $2.41M net to developer; SteamSpy owners 500k to 1M

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to give this a uh pretty solid uh ranking of of A.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Magicraft is an action roguelike built around crafting wands instead of using fixed weapons, heavily inspired by Noita but with a conventional Hades-like run structure of biomes, rooms and bosses. He finds it chaotic, fun and very approachable compared to Noita, since it is far less punishing outside the wand system. He enjoys building broken wand combos, though runs get somewhat repetitive late, the vibe and music disappoint him, and the roguelike layer (relics, events, bosses) could be deeper. It was in his 2024 top 10, and he lands it in A tier.

Much more approachable and less punishing than Noita, a gentle intro to the wand-crafting idea
Mid-game is the sweet spot where you discover cool wand combinations
Expanded wand types, including wands that cast spells on their own
Broken builds are achievable fairly quickly, not after very long play
Roguelike elements outside wands (relics, potions, characters) are pretty good
Very satisfying and something he would return to

Difficulty/accessibility: far less punishing than Noita

Replayability/variety: late-run repetition, wants more events and bosses
Roguelike content depth: relics, potions, characters are decent but could be richer
