commentary.rerank_note: Not a re-rank; he notes it was in his top 10 of 2024 and covers it only briefly here, having discussed Noita in his first tier list.

commentary.label: Top 10 of 2024 (#9)
commentary.summary: Magicraft is a top-down action roguelite in the Hades vein where spells and weapons are craftable wands, heavily inspired by Noita's wand system. It dials back Noita's difficulty and complexity in favour of chaotic, satisfying gameplay. He finds the spell fusing and synergy system, starting characters, meta progression and biome pacing strong. Drawbacks are repetitive gameplay once the screen fills with spells, limited elite and boss variety, and a goofy fantasy tone that didn't work for him. Overall he calls it a very fun, satisfying game and ranks it ninth of the year.
praise: Wand crafting with a huge number of ridiculous spell combinations
Fusing and upgrading spells adds diversity without needing a huge spell pool
Spells synergize with each other well
Choice of starting characters and meta progression keep it exciting
Good pacing; each biome feels like a new world
Decent enemy variation and a reward at the end of every room keeps runs fulfilling
criticism: Gameplay gets repetitive since it is easy to fill the whole screen with spells
Wants more elites and boss variety
Relics are not very interesting compared to spells and wands
Story and tone (goofy mixed with fantasy) did not connect with him

Spell fusion/upgrade as a simple way to add diversity without many spells
commentary.quote: a very fun and satisfying game with great in-depth wand mechanics
design_criteria: Synergies: spells and wands combine in chaotic ways
Diversity: fusion/upgrades extend spell variety
Difficulty: easier and more accessible than Noita
Meta-progression and starting characters: keep runs exciting
Pacing and biome variety: each biome feels new
Enemy/elite/boss design: decent enemies, wants more elites and bosses
Rewards: room-end rewards keep runs fulfilling
Tone/story: goofy fantasy mix did not land

community.one_liner: A top-down action roguelite from Wave Games (published by bilibili) where you build wands by slotting spells and modifiers into ordered sequences, blending Noita-style wand crafting with Binding of Isaac room-based dungeon crawling and a Hades-like hub.
community.consensus_summary: Players receive Magicraft very warmly: Steam shows Very Positive at about 92.8% across roughly 16.9k reviews, with many reviewers describing it as Noita meets Binding of Isaac in a friendlier package. The spell-and-wand tinkering, build variety and screen-filling power fantasy are the main draws, and long-playtime reviewers (100 to 700 hours) are common. Criticism centres on RNG-dependence, balance (poison and multicast dominance), long runs with repetitive multi-wave rooms, visual clutter late game, and on some machines crashes, hangs and localization problems. Critic coverage is essentially absent: Metacritic has no critic reviews, and OpenCritic has no findable listing. It left Early Access (launched Nov 2023) with 1.0 on Nov 1 2024 and has kept receiving free updates, costume DLC and crossovers, but a few reviewers worry about an unfinished feel or later-patch stability.
best_things: Wand crafting: slotting spells, modifiers and staff perks into ordered sequences lets players build absurd, emergent synergies, and many reviewers say it is easy to lose hours in theorycrafting
Friendlier take on the Noita/Isaac formula: forgiving enough that dying feels less punishing, while still escalating to chaos late game
Breaking the game is encouraged: overpowered builds are a feature and the game then escalates challenge to meet them
Large content pool: about 100 staffs and 80 relics, multiple character sets, puzzle side rooms, and a practice area for testing already-found spells
Humor and charm in the art, town and writing, plus good animation and enemy/level design noted by several reviewers
Accessible hardware demands: reviewers note it runs on an older non-gaming laptop, and there are options to tone down spell-effect visibility
Generous free updates, free DLC packs (e.g. Dave the Diver content) and crossover content; reviewers describe the game as feeling complete
Strong value: priced around $12 with many hundreds of hours reported by the most engaged players
worst_things: Heavy RNG dependence: good runs hinge on getting the right spells and relics, and several reviewers feel skill and judgment count for too little

Balance: a reviewer with a DPS breakdown claims poison stacking is the dominant meta for beating the final boss; others say a lucky early spell can carry the entire run while some spells are nearly useless
Endgame visual mess: multicast and nova-style builds cover the screen so you cannot see enemies or your own character
Runs get long: multiple high-HP waves per room, shops, upgrade rooms and puzzle rooms add up and some reviewers find it grindy
Technical problems reported by some players: hangs and freezes (one reviewer blames a 2024 patch), crashes after recent updates, and bad input under Linux Proton
Localization issues: some English wording is unclear and German UI text overflows and swaps languages, with complaints that the developer is unresponsive on this
Controller support is weak for wand/inventory management and certain spell mechanics; keyboard and mouse are recommended by experienced players
Some reviewers call it an inferior, dumbed-down blend of Noita, Isaac and Hades that gets boring fast
improvements: Streamline run length: fewer repeated waves per room and quicker shops and upgrade rooms, without just raising enemy HP
Fix balance outliers, including poison and multicast dominance, weak spells, and spells that do not interact as their descriptions suggest
Reduce randomness or give players more control over getting needed spells and relics, and remove anti-build design choices (e.g. more rooms between bosses, key and chest luck)
More variety in common enemies, bosses, wands, relics and spells, since some reviewers feel the pool runs thin after many hours
Better spell targeting or aim assistance for range-limited spells, and improved controller handling
Polish localization and translation, and improve stability after patches; also update in-game and wiki info for relics and spells, which reviewers say is outdated
unique_things: Noita-like wand logic (cast delay, recharge, ordering, modifiers) inside a room-by-room Isaac-style structure with keys, chests and a max-HP-for-perks room
Staff types that impart their own perks, and wand modifiers with odd effects such as reversed casting direction or random colors that apply rider effects
Hades-style town hub with humor and meta-upgrades plus unlockable character sets and difficulty tiers
Combat requires dodging bullet-hell patterns while spell builds escalate into screen-filling spectacle
A side path granting Epic relics for no-physical-damage play, paid for with max HP (a tip shared by a reviewer, not official documentation)
Crossovers and collaboration content such as Dave the Diver and Lost Castle 2
tedious_or_disliked: Late-game clutter: so many projectiles and effects that tactical play gives way to mashing the cast button
Long multi-wave rooms with high-HP enemies, plus slow shops and puzzle rooms
Meta-progression depends on unlocks and money; one 280-hour player says there is little to spend currency on after buying every upgrade, while another calls low-unlock runs a gacha-like feel
Losing a large share of runs on harder difficulties to bullet-hell bosses, with difficulty spikes from some stages (the third area is called out as annoying by some)
Inventory and wand juggling is tedious on controller
Crashes, hangs or freezes on certain setups
divisive_points: Difficulty and forgiveness: fans call it a gentle Noita/Isaac while critics complain about luck-driven spikes and a bullet-hell dodge requirement
Balance: some love that it lets you break the game, others feel it makes spell choice shallow or punishes experimentation
Depth versus derivative: some call it a perfect blend of inspirations, others an inferior version of Noita, Isaac and Hades
Run length and content: replayability is praised by hundreds-of-hours players but called short or repetitive by a few
community.reception_notes: Early Access began Nov 1 2023 and 1.0 shipped Nov 1 2024. Steam reception has remained very positive through and after EA, with reviewers who followed it from alpha calling it complete and praising free updates. Recent Steam announcements (September) describe patches v1.2.42 and v1.2.43, a Lost Castle 2 crossover with a new Rune Mage set, 4 crossover spells, 2 bosses and 6 relics, a global leaderboard restored for Nightmare 3, a 25 percent base-game discount, and fixes for freezes with specific relic combos. The Steam forum shows crash and save-loss reports following recent updates, and some users say a 2024 patch triggered chronic hangs. The Metacritic user score of 6.1 rests on only 11 ratings and contradicts Steam's sentiment, so treat it as noise. PC (Windows) only on Steam; Steam Deck reportedly works well; no console ports announced; Linux via Proton has reported input problems.

games.name: Mortal Sin
games.short_description: Mortal Sin is a chaotic, blood-soaked roguelike where skill is power, and overconfidence is death. Carve through procedurally generated nightmares with brutal melee and flashy, satisfying combos.

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put Moral Sin as a low eight tier (ASR for 'low B tier')

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Mortal Sin is a first-person, bloody action-combat roguelike dungeon crawler where you hack through hordes with melee weapons and dismantle enemies limb by limb. It is combo-centric, with many classes each having unlockable combo chains, and a run is split into three biome runs with a hub in between. He calls it a really solid and very unique game with deeply satisfying core combat, though visually and enemy-wise repetitive and light on hub content. He places it in low B tier.
praise: Core first-person combat is very satisfying; dismembering enemies changes how they behave
Combo system with many class-specific combos adds depth beyond simple swinging
Auto-combo feature makes the game beginner friendly and suits the fast pace, with a slight penalty
Weapon durability forces constant weapon and equipment switching, keeping combat fresh
Very unique visuals with adjustable filters so players can tone down the intensity
Many classes and hidden content, plus signs of a true ending, encourage replay
Three-stage run structure with hub upgrades gives a sense of building a character
criticism: Hub has too little to do given you return to it between biomes
Enemies and environments are visually repetitive
Classes feel different but not dramatically so; mostly combos and killing next to you, little ranged play
Roguelike elements found in runs are enjoyable but not game-changing
Default visuals can be overwhelming, and dark levels make it hard to see what is going on
Has been in early access for 4+ years; full run is long at roughly an hour and a half

Auto-combo option that shuffles combos automatically, while manual play avoids unwanted effects like the mage freeze
Three separate runs per character with a hub in between, like a very long run with soft permadeath
Limb-loss enemy behavior and weapon durability drive the moment-to-moment variety
commentary.quote: Moral Sin really, really solid game. A very unique as well.
design_criteria: Combat feel: core first-person combat is the main draw and very satisfying
Combo design: class-specific combos with small extra effects, scored for chaining
Accessibility: auto-combo lowers the barrier in a fast-paced multi-class game
Class diversity: many classes but only moderately different in play
Run structure and meta-progression: three biome runs with hub upgrades, long total run length
Visual identity and options: unique, dark, adjustable filters, but repetitive enemies
Item/weapon systems: durability forces weapon switching
Replayability: hidden content and a likely true ending

community.one_liner: A solo-developed, first-person, dark-fantasy action roguelite about chaining class-specific melee (and gun/magic) combos through procedurally generated dungeons full of gore and dismemberment.
community.consensus_summary: Mortal Sin is received very positively by players (about 94% positive on Steam across roughly 5,900 reviews, Very Positive) and modestly by critics (PC Gamer 81, Movies Games and Tech 70, 3DJuegos recommended). It left Early Access on Aug 29, 2025 after a long run that began March 2023, and the solo dev is widely praised for frequent updates and for acting on community feedback. The love is for the fast, bloody, stylish combo combat and the comic-book art; the complaints cluster around a rhythm-like combo system that is both opaque and mandatory, chaotic hordes that feel samey, and low-impact run upgrades. Recent reviews are more mixed than the lifetime score, with some long-time players upset that later combat reworks changed the feel.
best_things: Fast, visceral first-person melee with combo chains, kicks, dodges and heavy dismemberment that many reviewers call addictive and 'crack-like' once the systems click
Distinctive comic-book / manga-like art direction in red, black and white tones with dark-fantasy iconography, praised by 3DJuegos and Steam users
Large roster of classes (16 per one review, including Berserker, mage, pirate, gun users) each with their own combos and unlockables that drive replay
Very responsive solo developer: adjustable graphics/eye-strain settings were added within about a week of a forum post; Berserker was made the starting class after feedback
Steady stream of free content and reworks through Early Access and after 1.0 (new languages, unique items, the Blitz Ascension mode with daily challenges)
Good pick-up-and-play feel for short adrenaline sessions, and many players with hundreds of hours say it holds value for the price
Helpful onboarding tools once you find them: combo list on Esc that can be pinned on screen, a practice dummy in the hub, and an auto-combo option for newcomers
worst_things: The combo system is a core mechanic that some describe as DDR/Guitar Hero-style input; players who dislike it say the game cannot be enjoyed without it, since unused combos leave you underpowered
Combat can feel weightless, mashy and chaotic: enemies spawn behind you, floor effects kill with little warning, and hits lack impact according to several negative reviews
Enemy variety looks large but enemies feel alike, and fights become 'build a setup and spam your best combo' with few situational decisions
Run upgrades and randomized loot are often described as not impactful enough, making later runs feel samey
Opaque systems and confusing UI: multiple mana bars, inventory/RPG screens and unexplained mechanics force players to watch videos or read a wiki
Some traps and the secret platforming portals are disliked, especially the forest branches/hands
Limited content per critics: one review counted only six areas with three gated behind story progression, and the first three zones repeat over 15 levels
Reports of bugs or performance regressions after updates, such as a mouse cursor locking and FPS drops on camera movement
improvements: Better in-game explanation of combos, stats, mana bars and inventory so new players do not need outside guides
More impactful and build-defining run upgrades and loot so runs diverge more
Slower, more readable encounters with more distinct enemy behaviours that require different approaches (a common wish from players who want parry/pattern-learning depth)
Stronger hit feedback and weight in melee combat, and tighter integration of block/parry with the combo and power-up systems
Rebalancing of classes (a monk is called underpowered in one review; a Steam thread calls Gladiator broken) and more varied levels
Options to reduce combo dependence, e.g. richer auto-combo, and quality-of-life options such as turning off the leaderboard or fixing cursor issues
unique_things: First-person melee roguelite with a per-class combo-input system rather than simple attack spam, combined with a Doom-like pace
Comic-book, sketch-like dark-fantasy look with PS2-style textures, volumetric fog and gory dismemberment that changes how enemies behave
Over a dozen classes spanning greatswords, guns, claws and magic, each with distinct combos
Hundreds of hand-crafted rooms stitched into procedural maps, plus randomized quests and secret platforming zones
Blitz Ascension mode with time pressure and daily challenges, plus a true ending in the 1.0 release
tedious_or_disliked: Memorizing and executing combo inputs while hordes surround you; some feel they spend all their attention on controls
Repetition: several reviewers say runs get repetitive or exhausting after a couple of hours because enemies and upgrades feel alike
The final boss, called tedious and unbalanced by some players: long health pool and one-shot moves
Unreadable deaths and ambush spawns or floor hazards that kill without clear warning
Platforming portal sections and certain environmental traps
Cluttered HUD and inventory UI that some never get used to
divisive_points: The combo system: praised by many as the crux of the game's depth, and called the thing that ruins it for others

The combat reworks (class-specific combos replacing universal ones, faster weapons): some long-time Early Access players feel the game got monotonous and worse, while many consider the patched version better
Price at $24.99: some call it great value, others say it is overpriced or fine only on sale
Chaos vs readability: the frantic Doom-like pace is a selling point for some and a mess for others
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched March 2023 and the game reached 1.0 on Aug 29, 2025. Steam lists 94% positive overall, but the recent-30-day snapshot seen on the store page was only 64% positive from a small sample, and the newest negative reviews (Aug-Sep 2026) are from veteran players unhappy about combat system changes, so sentiment has softened among long-time fans. Metacritic currently tallies only 2 critic reviews (PC Gamer 81, Movies Games and Tech 70) and shows no Metascore yet (needs 4), plus 6 user ratings averaging 8.5. Developer news on Steam references a 300,000-copies milestone, a Blitz Ascension mode, and new localizations. Third-party estimates put owners at 200k-500k and gross revenue around 2.0M USD (about 584k net) on the Boxleiter method, which are order-of-magnitude figures. Windows only. Streamer/YouTuber exposure drove some purchases, and a few buyers say they bought without realizing how central combos are. One review mentions community frustration over a separate dev controversy (not verified). OpenCritic listing could not be found; the Web search tool budget was exhausted so Reddit threads could not be read directly.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Picayune Dreams is a horde-survivor with very simple mechanics (movement plus auto-triggering abilities and a black-hole-style effect) wrapped around a dark, mysterious, fourth-wall-breaking story. He found the story gripping enough to play for about four hours straight on a flight. The gameplay alone he rates above average for the genre, but the narrative makes it stand out. praise: Story is mysterious, dark and disturbing, and hooked him deeply
Gameplay feels great, with clear hitboxes and hurtboxes and an evasion focus
Bosses are well designed and play like bullet hell experiences
Large meta-progression upgrade tree outside runs, and you don't need to finish it to beat the game
Has a committed community and a rare, story-driven hook for the genre
Simple gameplay deliberately serves the story, similar to Undertale
criticism: Gameplay is the weakest part and has few mechanics
Low replayability in terms of gameplay since abilities all do similar things
He sometimes wished he could skip to the next story beat without the gameplay
Endless mode is just chaos where you barely move
Story is a one-time experience

Story breaks the fourth wall and is built around repetition and mystery
Rare for a horde-like to make him unable to put it down for the narrative
commentary.quote: I'm going to put a Piking Dreams as a solid A tier.
design_criteria: Story and narrative: main driver of the game's value and memorability
Gameplay feel: clear hitboxes, evasion-focused and satisfying despite simplicity
Boss design: bullet hell style fights praised
Meta-progression: large upgrade tree outside runs, optional to complete
Replayability: limited since abilities are similar; hard and endless modes help somewhat
Mechanical depth: minimal mechanics, auto-triggered abilities

community.one_liner: A psychedelic, webcore-styled bullet heaven / bullet hell roguelike by Stepford, Andyland and milkypossum (published by 2 Left Thumbs) in which a space cyborg fights endless horrors while a surreal, Yume Nikki-inspired story unfolds.
community.consensus_summary: Picayune Dreams is a cult-favourite indie with an Overwhelmingly Positive Steam rating (about 98.9% of roughly 4,665 reviews) at a $4.99 price. Players praise the breakcore soundtrack, loud visual identity, the bullet-hell dodging layered on top of survivor-style auto-fire, and a strange but emotionally effective story. Critic coverage is thin: Metacritic has no critic score and only a handful of user ratings, and I found no OpenCritic entry. The small negative camp says runs feel samey, upgrades are hard to read, meta-progression is confusing or grindy, and endgame difficulty is lacking. It is a full release (not early access) and still gets sporadic content updates, which players say are large when they land.
best_things: Breakcore/hardbass soundtrack is repeatedly called top tier; some players say they found the game through the OST
Cohesive psychedelic webcore / early-internet aesthetic, with weapons, upgrades and death screens presented as code and damage numbers doubling as XP pickups
Blend of bullet hell dodging with Vampire Survivors-style build knowledge, so skill matters more than a pure knowledge check
Screen-filling, dopamine-heavy chaos where your bullets outnumber the enemies
Story with heavy Yume Nikki / Evangelion-style dreamlike feel that some players say made them care about the characters
Bosses with bullet hell patterns that are approachable for newcomers but still challenging
Game speed options (including 2x) and other quality-of-life features that let players tune the pace
Very low price and a free demo; many reviewers call it badly underpriced, and the major post-launch update was described as huge
Absurd, funny, meme-heavy tone (throwing dynamite at Geocities fish gifs, getting attacked by burgers in space) that reviewers clearly enjoy
worst_things: Runs feel structurally identical to some players: same bosses, map layout and backdrops each run, little difference between weapons
Upgrades and powerups are poorly explained, and many permanent upgrades feel minor
Difficulty falls off once you have a decent build; one 80-hour reviewer says it becomes trivially easy and that higher overdrive levels only add FPS drops rather than challenge
Performance problems at high difficulty and a known FPS-drop issue during the final boss
Limited roster (one playable character and a handful of weapons) compared with Vampire Survivors or Halls of Torment
Some players feel underpowered early on and never reach the screen-filling power fantasy shown in screenshots
Enemies and some weapons read as bland to a few reviewers; one disliked a specific boss (the biker) as boring
Flashing strobing visuals with no obvious photosensitivity/epilepsy option, per at least one reviewer
improvements: Add an epilepsy/photosensitivity setting to tone down flashing effects
Explain upgrades, weapons and meta-progression more clearly in-game
Give later difficulty tiers real challenge instead of just heavier load, and fix FPS drops at high overdrive and in the final boss fight
Vary runs more: more stages, backdrops, characters or build-defining choices
Rebalance weapons and some boss fights that players call questionable
Small UX requests from the community, such as making the four choosable paths clickable for faster selection, plus a Russian localization request
unique_things: Fuses Touhou-style bullet hell with Vampire Survivors-style auto-fire, with reviewers also citing Cruelty Squad and Yume Nikki as touchstones
Internet-nostalgia webcore presentation (Geocities-style gifs, hardbass, breakcore) rather than generic fantasy or sci-fi
Dream-memory story structure with lore-rich, surreal and transhumanism themes delivered through flashbacks between runs
Gameplay information presented as in-world code, and damage numbers that act as XP pickups
Daily and monthly challenge runs plus an overdrive difficulty ladder and a customizable skill tree
tedious_or_disliked: Meta-progression described by critics of the game as a grind of replaying to earn skill points rather than a meaningful loop
Repetitive runs with the same bosses and maps, and short runs that blur together
The edgy or tumblr-esque writing and rabbit emo character art put some players off, and they skip story scenes
Trial and error needed to understand builds because upgrade text is unclear
Dodging-dots focus leaves less room for the power-fantasy build crafting survivor fans expect
divisive_points: Story and tone: some find it moving and well written, others find it cringe, edgy or too internet-flavoured
Difficulty: newcomers find it hard at first, veterans report it gets easy once builds come together
Weapon balance and variety: praised as fun and chaotic by most, called samey or questionably balanced by a minority
Heavy flashing psychedelic visuals are a selling point for most but a health barrier for photosensitive players
community.reception_notes: Released Dec 4, 2023 on Windows only as a full release at $4.99, with a demo and a separate soundtrack. Reception has stayed extremely positive and it keeps appearing in recent reviews through 2026; a long-time reviewer says the first major post-launch update added about 50 hours for them, and updates since are described as sporadic. Steam community pins a FAQ, a Bug Reporting 2.0 thread and a known issue about FPS drops during the final boss. Metacritic shows only 11 user ratings (91% positive) and no critic reviews; OpenCritic could not be confirmed. Note: my web search budget was exhausted, so community and outlet coverage beyond Steam, Metacritic and the revenue calculator could not be checked (Reddit fetch was blocked).

games.name: RAM: Random Access Mayhem
games.short_description: The roguelike where you play as the enemies. Take control of your foes, turn them against each other in fast-paced combat, and leap to a new host before your current body breaks down.

other_scores.score: Audience Choice winner; Best Student Game finalist (per Steam page)

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put RAM in a solid eight tier in its current form (ASR of 'solid B tier')

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: RAM is a skill-heavy action roguelike where you have no body and instead possess enemy robots, constantly switching between them mid-fight. He finds it hard but fair, with tricky-to-master move sets and surprisingly strong roguelike upgrades. The vibe, music and hub are standouts, though levels and enemies get repetitive. It is early access, so he places it in B tier for now and expects it could rise.
praise: Body-swapping gimmick is fresh and the game pushes you to keep switching, rewarding fast swaps
Hard but feels fair; deaths are your own fault for not switching
Each robot has distinct, tricky mechanics with good tutorials
Level-up upgrades can radically change a robot (e.g. flamethrower becomes explosive fumes, shooter gains fire)
Fantastic visuals, electronic rock music and a beautiful living hub
Early access with unlockable content (new robot, final area) gives something to look forward to
criticism: Levels are beautiful but always the same, so runs feel repetitive
Wants more unique things to do during runs
Same enemies are encountered constantly, limited enemy variety
Not beginner friendly; every robot is difficult to get comfortable with
Fishing mini game in the hub is frustrating; meta progression is fairly small
unique_points: You only control enemies, so enemy variety is inherently capped by design
Fuel system ties switching and kills with different bodies to staying alive/invincible
Skill-heavy core gameplay paired with genuinely good roguelike upgrades is surprising
commentary.quote: I'm going to put RAM in a solid eight tier in its current form
design_criteria: Core gimmick/novelty: enemy possession and constant switching is the hook
Difficulty/fairness: very hard but feels fair
Skill ceiling: each robot needs mastery
Roguelike upgrades: build-altering changes to robots
Enemy variety: limited by premise
Level design: beautiful but repetitive, same layouts
Visuals/audio/vibe: standout music, hub and art
Meta progression: small, mostly skill-based
Run variety: focus on two robot types per run gives flexibility
commentary.rerank_note: Early access game sent to the channel; he notes it could move up as it develops.

community.one_liner: A top-down, fast-paced action roguelite by Xylem Studios where you play as a rogue AI that possesses enemy robots, swapping hosts before each one breaks down and turning foes against each other.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players are overwhelmingly positive (about 98 percent of roughly 670 reviews, 'Overwhelmingly Positive'), and the tone of the praise is unusually intense: reviewers compare it to ULTRAKILL and Hades and call it a GOTY-level hidden gem. The game left Early Access (live since Nov 2024) with its 1.0 launch on Sep 15, 2025 at $14.99, and it is still being discussed and patched in 2026 (reviews continue through mid-2026). It is a small-team, low-visibility title, with an estimated 20-50k owners and roughly $115k gross per third-party Boxleiter estimates, and many players wonder why it is not better known. No Metacritic or OpenCritic critic scores were found, so the reception picture is almost entirely player-driven. The main caveat is a steep learning curve and heavy information load that some players bounce off.
best_things: The core host-swapping loop: every enemy type is a playable body with its own moveset, and using them against each other feels creative and rewarding
High skill ceiling and emergent 'tech' (momentum, cancels, juggling, trick shots) that players compare to ULTRAKILL-style mastery design
Each bot feels weighty and distinct when it clicks, with real risk-reward in deciding when to swap
Two-layer progression: Hades-style meta-progression (Hyperparameters, Adversarial Learning) plus genuine player-skill growth, which reviewers find very addictive
Soundtrack is widely praised, and a separate OST exists on Steam
Funny writing, charming characters and surprisingly creative worldbuilding for a robot-apocalypse setting, delivered through a hub town
Per-bot tutorials/training regimens are described as essential and well made
Great value at $15, with daily challenge runs and modifiers adding replayability
worst_things: Very steep learning curve and high cognitive load: many bots, each with their own tech, all expected to be mastered because you keep swapping
Early hours before the game 'clicks' are rough; reviewers describe the start as punishing and a real time investment
Some bots control jankier or more awkwardly than others (Tachi and Epitaph are called intentionally unwieldy)
Swap/health rules (global health loss when a host dies, penalties for swapping back to the same robot, mite/aphid forms) are confusing and feel inconsistent to some players
Limited upgrade variety is mentioned even by fans, and certain upgrade paths (e.g. Deadlift) feel underpowered
Technical issues reported in a minority of reviews and on the Steam forum: crashes after a few minutes, performance problems (devs suggest running the OpenGL renderer), audio bugs, Linux-related bugs
improvements: Better in-game explanation of swap mechanics, the two juice/backup bars and death-to-mite rules, rather than relying on tutorials alone
Buff weak upgrade trees and add more upgrade variety
Add alternate areas or paths and more content beyond the current loop, which fans say they would love
Reduce friction between runs: one critic wants an instant-restart option instead of several screens
Give town quests more meaningful rewards, as they currently feel like a diversion
Fix crash and performance issues; a lower-pressure or easier-onboarding mode was implied by reviewers who found the pressure overwhelming
Trim some of the dialogue so the narrative flows more smoothly (raised by both a fan and a detractor)
unique_things: You have no player character of your own: you are a parasitic AI hopping between enemy robots, each of which is your moveset
Dying is part of the flow: the game pushes you to swap before a body breaks, and spare hosts are a resource
Style-based currency system inspired by Devil May Cry and ULTRAKILL rewards flashy play
Turning enemies against each other (friendly-fire exploitation) is the main tactic rather than a side gimmick
Hub-town narrative and dry comedic writing wrapped around a bullet-hell-adjacent action roguelite, made by a very small student-origin team (IGF 2024 Audience Choice winner)
tedious_or_disliked: Too much dialogue and humor for some: one reviewer found the writing self-satisfied and obstructive to gameplay
Several screens to click through before starting another run
Needing to relearn each bot's moveset, timing and combos after a break; the game punishes time away
Mandatory-feeling tutorials for each bot create an upfront time cost (one reviewer spent about an hour on tutorials)
Being forced into under-upgraded hosts because not every host type spawns in every room, so you must spread upgrades across all bots
divisive_points: Difficulty and 'no chill' pressure: fans see a fair, skill-based challenge where every death is your fault, while others find it overwhelming and stressful
Mandatory mastery of all bots: praised as depth and variety, criticised as a punishing, inconsistent rule set
Humor and narrative tone: charming and funny to most reviewers, insufferable to a few
community.reception_notes: Early Access began Nov 2024 after an IGF 2024 Audience Choice win; 1.0 released Sep 15, 2025 (Windows and macOS, no Linux build, though some forum users mention Linux issues). Reception has stayed overwhelmingly positive from launch to now, with reviews still arriving through mid-2026. Metacritic had a page with no critic or user reviews at the time of checking, and no OpenCritic entry could be confirmed (web search budget was exhausted, so outlet reviews and Reddit threads were not reached). Reviewers note the dev team creates YouTube content, which has driven some audience. Third-party estimates (Boxleiter method): about 20-50k owners, about $114.6k gross and about $33.8k net revenue. Steam community forum shows an active, modest-sized player base with devs pinning announcements and steering bug reports to Discord.

games.name: Returnal™
games.short_description: BREAK THE CYCLE Fight to survive as this award-winning third-person shooter brings Selene’s story to PC. Take on roguelike challenges. Engage enemies in bullet hell-fuelled clashes. Share your journey through Returnal™ with another player.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Returnal is a third-person shooter action roguelike, billed as the first AAA roguelike, where a big-budget studio adapted the indie-dominated subgenre. He loves the story, atmosphere, biomes, bosses and Metroidvania-style traversal unlocks, and he finished the whole game and enjoyed it. His main frustration is that the roguelike elements (relics, abilities) are dull and make runs feel too similar, which leaves replayability weak. He frames the game as one he likes and wants to be better, and places it on the board with only a vague location cue rather than a tier letter.
praise: Story and first-person segments are captivating
Big budget gives massive, immersive biomes and great visuals
Metroidvania feel: new traversal tools (e.g. sword) unlock across runs
Bosses feel cool
Core third-person gameplay is super enjoyable
Exploration and moving between worlds, especially the first time
criticism: Roguelike elements are disappointing; studio seems not to be a roguelike developer
Relics are boring (more health, more damage, simple triggers)
Runs do not feel different enough from one another
Replayability is weak once the story is finished
The more roguelike mode (the tower) is enjoyable but should be in the core game
unique_points: First AAA-budget roguelike, bringing narrative and world scale to the genre
Plays like a non-roguelike adventure with Metroidvania progression
Design lesson: relics and abilities should subtly change gameplay to differentiate runs without straying from core gameplay
commentary.quote: Even though I spent most of my time complaining about the game, it's just because I like it

commentary.label: Top 10 of 2024 (#8)
commentary.summary: Returnal is a third-person action shooter roguelite with metroidvania and horror elements, and one of the first big-budget non-indie roguelites. He thinks the core gameplay, presentation, story and bosses are excellent, but that the roguelite systems are disappointing. He has mixed feelings and regrets not being able to place it higher. It still lands at number 8 and remains one of his favorite roguelites he played this year.
praise: Looks great, with huge, detailed biomes and an immersive world
Grand-adventure campaign feel that indie games rarely match
Story full of mysteries and twists that holds attention
Genuinely creepy, compelling horror segments
Crisp, satisfying controls with great sound design and visual effects
Solid movement, including the grappling hook for high-speed mobility
Fantastic bosses
criticism: Most artifacts/parasites are simple number tweaks with no unique mechanical changes
Consumables are interesting but situational and not impactful enough to use over the weapon
Weapons drop constantly but with one weapon slot and no recycling they feel unnecessary

Huge maps can be slow to traverse and sometimes feel like a chore
Runs do not feel different enough from one another

Blends roguelite structure with metroidvania and horror elements
He thinks many consumable effects should have been artifacts instead
commentary.quote: it's sad that I can't put it higher on my list
comparisons: The best roguelites (as inspiration for a sequel)
design_criteria: Core gameplay feel: crisp controls, sound and visual effects
Movement and mobility: grappling hook and high speed
Boss design: rated fantastic
Story and atmosphere: mysteries, twists, creepy horror
Item/artifact design: number tweaks vs unique mechanical changes
Consumable impact: situational, not worth using over the weapon
Weapon system: one slot with no recycling makes drops unnecessary
Risk vs reward: malignant mechanic rarely worth it

community.one_liner: A third-person sci-fi bullet-hell shooter by Housemarque in which astronaut Selene relives death on the alien planet Atropos, with a roguelike run structure, Metroidvania-style traversal unlocks and a cosmic-horror time-loop story.
community.consensus_summary: Critics received Returnal very well: Metacritic is 86 on both PS5 (115 reviews) and PC (Climax Studios port, Feb 2023), and it won Best Game at the British Academy Games Awards. Players are more split: Metacritic user score is 7.4 (68% positive, 12% mixed, 20% negative), and Steam sits at Very Positive (about 81%, roughly 11,100 reviews). Nearly everyone loves the gunplay, movement, sound and atmosphere; the split comes from the brutal difficulty, long runs with thin meta-progression, and (on PC) technical problems. Sony has effectively finished updating it, so PC issues that appeared after the last patch are still open. The game is fully released, not early access.
best_things: Fluid, responsive third-person shooting and movement (dash, jump, melee, adrenaline mechanic) that feels arcade-tight and addictive
Bullet-hell enemy and boss design that is readable and rewards pattern mastery; players talk about getting noticeably better over time
Best-in-class sound design, music and lighting; the oppressive, eerie alien atmosphere (Giger/Beksinski-style visuals) is widely praised
Strong voice performance by Jane Perry and a mysterious psychological-sci-fi story that rewards digging into scout logs and secret endings
Weapon traits, parasites and artifacts create risk/reward decisions inside a run; Metroidvania-style tool unlocks open up traversal
Post-launch content: Ascension update added online co-op and the Tower of Sisyphus endless mode, praised by fans who want pure gameplay with no story
Runs acceptably on modest PCs and supports suspend-cycle saves since Update 2.0, making long runs less punishing
High feel of mastery: many Steam reviewers with 50-180+ hours call it a favourite game of the decade and a Hades alternative for action fans
worst_things: PC port stability: widely reported VRAM/memory leak and texture-streaming degradation after a late patch, forcing restarts every hour or two and never fixed
Crashes on launch or after the logos, black screens and poor frametimes for some players despite high fps
Unwanted Epic Online Services install and optional PlayStation account linking (with region-locked prompts) on Steam drew a wave of negative reviews
Co-op is buggy: lost runs after disconnect as guest, locked shops, reticle/ammo UI bugs, curses carrying over, loading-screen joins, and story progress only counting for the host
Very punishing difficulty with no accessibility or easier mode; a single early hit can cripple a run because healing only raises max health when already full
Environments are repetitive across biomes (same structures, palette swaps) and the loop feels samey after many runs
Sony effectively abandoned PC support; full price on PC years later is criticised, and the next Housemarque game (Saros) is not coming to PC
improvements: Add an easier or accessibility/narrative difficulty so story-focused players can progress
Stronger permanent meta-progression so failed runs feel like they move the needle
Fix the PC VRAM leak and crash bugs and keep patching the port
More build variety: larger pool of weapons, artifacts and non-stat-boost upgrades, plus more biome/environment variety
Shorter runs or more checkpoints beyond suspend-cycle for players with limited time
Fix co-op reliability (reconnect handling, shared story progress) and drop the forced extra launcher/online services
unique_things: Third-person bullet-hell shooter hybrid, rare in a genre dominated by top-down/2D roguelikes
Runs are long (often 1-3 hours) and open-ended with persistent tools and Metroidvania-style gating rather than short quick runs
Procedurally shuffled rooms paired with hand-built biome bosses and handcrafted story progression
Haptic/adaptive trigger and 3D audio design built around the DualSense, carried into a cosmic-horror time-loop narrative
Adrenaline, overload and malfunction systems (parasites, cursed items, weapon proficiency that persists) make every pickup a risk decision
Tower of Sisyphus endless mode and 2-player online co-op added after launch
tedious_or_disliked: Losing a long run to a single mistake, with minimal carry-over; runs feel like they do not respect player time
Having to replay early biomes repeatedly to reach where you died, seeing the same sequences dozens of times
Random trap rooms, laser-heavy rooms and spikes felt cheap or cause lag on some PCs
Incoming attacks are hard to track in chaotic fights, making hits feel unavoidable to some
Needing to restart the PC game every hour because of the memory leak
Unlocks and permanent progression feel too minor to help performance, so the grind feels unrewarding (a top-voted negative review)
divisive_points: Permadeath and no-checkpoint structure: fans see it as thematically perfect and the source of mastery, detractors call it exhausting and unfair
Story: some love the ambiguity and secret endings, others cannot follow it or find the heroine sparsely written
Roguelike credentials: judged as a roguelike, some say it lacks build variety and quick runs; others say it reinvents the genre
PC port: some report flawless performance on cheap hardware, others unplayable instability or VRAM leaks
community.reception_notes: PS5 launch (Apr 2021) was critically acclaimed, with debate over the no-save design; Update 2.0 (Oct 2021) added suspend cycle saves, and the free Ascension update (Mar 2022) added co-op and the Tower of Sisyphus. It sold about 866,000 copies by Feb 2022 and won Best Game at BAFTA. The PC version released Feb 15, 2023 (Climax Studios, PlayStation Publishing) with the same Metacritic 86; many current Steam negatives concern a VRAM leak introduced in a late patch, Epic Online Services and PSN linking, and co-op bugs. Steam data estimates 500k-1M owners and about $10.8M gross / $3.2M net on Steam (Boxleiter-style estimate, not audited). OpenCritic score could not be retrieved (web search budget exhausted, fetches failed), so left null. No first-hand Reddit or IGN pages were readable.

games.name: Slice & Dice
games.short_description: Tactical dice-rolling roguelike combat. Take control of 5 heroes, each with their own unique dice. Fight your way through 20 levels of monsters and try to take on the final boss. If you lose a single fight you have to start over so be careful (and lucky!).

placements.verbal_evidence: It's going to be a very high A tier. I'm putting it above Cobalt Core.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Slice & Dice is a turn-based dice roguelike where you control a party of five characters and move fight to fight, upgrading a character or giving out an item after each battle. Mechanically simple, it becomes very strategic through its huge pool of characters, items, upgrades and enemies. He already covered it in his top 10 of 2024, so he keeps this short. He calls it one of the better games he played last year and places it in high A tier, above Cobalt Core, and recommends it widely because it is so approachable.
praise: Enormous amount of content: many characters, game modes, and very distinct items
Simple rules that scale into deep strategy
Forgiving, casual structure: full regeneration between fights, nothing permanent lost within a run
Every run and every fight feels different; enemies have unique mechanics, like mini-games
Generous dice flexibility: keep or reroll any dice up to three times, softening RNG
Simple but fitting visuals and a chill, peaceful soundtrack with many tracks
Very approachable, easy to recommend to anyone who likes strategy games
criticism: Acknowledges a fair amount of RNG because of the dice, though mitigated by rerolls
Visuals are simple (said as a neutral/fitting trait rather than a real complaint)
unique_points: Turn-based dice combat with a five-character party rather than deck building
Each fight acts like a self-contained puzzle/mini-game thanks to enemy-specific mechanics
Low-punishment run design (about 20 fights, death just means half health next fight) makes bad starts irrelevant
commentary.quote: It's going to be a very high A tier. I'm putting it above Cobalt Core.
design_criteria: Content volume: characters, modes and items in huge quantity
Item/character diversity: each item is meaningfully unique
Strategic depth vs simplicity: easy rules, deep decisions
Risk vs punishment: low-punishment, casual run structure
RNG management: dice rerolls give player agency
Run variety: every run and fight feels different
Enemy design: unique mechanics per enemy
Visuals: simple but fitting
Audio: chill, plentiful music tracks
Accessibility: approachable for newcomers
commentary.rerank_note: Previously discussed in his top 10 of 2024 list; here placed in high A tier, above Cobalt Core.

commentary.label: Top 10 of 2024 (#6)
commentary.summary: Slice & Dice is a turn-based dungeon-crawling roguelike built around dice rolls, where you control five heroes, each with their own die, across 20 levels. Every monster brings a small mechanic that works like a fresh puzzle. He finds it easy to pick up but hard to master, and he values the huge amount of content and the optional bypass for locked content. It sits at number 6 on his 2024 list, and he describes it as a perfect game to return to now and then.
praise: Each monster has a small mechanic to adapt to, making every fight feel like a new puzzle
Two extra rerolls per die pick the desired result and reduce randomness compared with other dice games
Simple, easy-to-understand core gameplay that is easy to learn but hard to master
Large content volume: over 25 game modes, 128 heroes and 470 unique items
Option to bypass all achievement-locked content, good for a casual game
Surprising number of accessibility options
Trying new modes and characters gives a fresh experience each time, great to revisit
criticism: Dice-based roguelikes generally struggle to balance strategy with randomness (he says this about the genre, which Slice & Dice mitigates)
Much content is locked behind achievements, and some of those unlocks have more complicated mechanics that may not suit new players
unique_points: Rerolling each die twice makes dice randomness much more controllable than in comparable games
Per-monster mini-mechanics turn each fight into a puzzle
Option to bypass locked content alongside extensive accessibility options is notable for an indie game
commentary.quote: a perfect game for me to pick back up every now and then
comparisons: Other roguelikes that use dice as their core mechanic
design_criteria: Randomness vs strategy: dice rerolls tame variance
Enemy design: each monster has a puzzle-like mechanic
Content volume: modes, heroes and items keep it fresh
Accessibility: many options and bypass for locked content
Learning curve: simple to learn, hard to master
Replayability: new modes and builds give varied runs

community.one_liner: A tactical dice-rolling roguelike by solo developer Tann where you command a party of five heroes whose abilities live on their own dice, fighting through 20 levels to a final boss with permadeath on a single lost fight.
community.consensus_summary: Slice & Dice is received as a small-scale but unusually deep indie gem. Steam shows 'Overwhelmingly Positive' (about 97% of roughly 2,580 reviews) and itch.io shows 4.9/5 from about 766 ratings, with many reviewers saying they first bought it on mobile or itch and then bought it again on Steam. Only three critic reviews exist, all on the iOS version (TouchArcade 100, 148Apps 100, GAMES.CH 82), with no Metascore yet, and Metacritic users give 8.4 from only 7 ratings. It is not early access and appears actively maintained (itch build 3.2.13 in May 2025 added several translations), but sales sit in the low-to-mid hundreds of thousands of owners rather than hit territory. The negatives are narrow: RNG frustration, unknown late bosses, obtuse item text, uneven balance and awkward modding.
best_things: Every turn plays like a compact tactical puzzle because you choose which dice to reroll and how to assign results to heroes, so luck feels manageable rather than arbitrary
Class identity is built directly into each hero's die faces, which makes the 100+ heroes feel mechanically distinct
Enormous build and replay variety: hundreds of items, many monsters and modes, and randomly generated heroes, items and spells still producing new combos after hundreds of hours
Surprisingly strong balance and non-obvious decisions (junk tier-0 items having synergies, skipping level-ups, committing to one combo unit)
Undo/take-back lets you experiment with lines and treat fights as puzzles
Short runs suit both desktop and phone; many describe it as the ultimate time-killer on a bus or break
Modding via the built-in TextMod system and level editor is praised by some as the easiest custom-content sharing they have seen, extending replayability indefinitely
Distinct minimalist pixel art and music; good value at about $9 and a no-AI-assets, no-sales-or-bundles stance from the dev
worst_things: High RNG variance: a run lost to bad rolls, especially at the final boss, can feel demoralizing and some reviewers dismiss it as RNG slop
Unknown bosses and the final boss create a risk-management problem, since you cannot prepare for something you have not seen
Item and ability descriptions are described as poorly worded and obtuse, and a few items are reported as non-functional
Balance is uneven: some classes or heroes are called useless or a burden while others dominate
Permadeath after a single lost fight means a long run can end abruptly
Presentation is deliberately small, so players wanting big visuals, story or narrative adventure will find it thin
Some find the core loop simply not fun or hard to get into if they dislike adapting to imperfect rolls
improvements: Rewrite item and spell descriptions so effects are clear and accurate
Give players some way to know or preview the possible final boss and unknown bosses so they can plan
Rebalance weak classes/heroes and fix non-functional items
Make mod installation less convoluted; a negative reviewer objected to mods being gated behind progression and imported as pasted text
Offer a built-in unlock-everything option for players who do not want to grind unlocks (requested in a review)
unique_things: Heroes are literally dice: each class's kit is encoded in the faces of its die, with 3D dice physics and selective rerolls
Lose one fight and the run ends, yet every fight is solvable-feeling because of undo and careful dice assignment
Ultra-minimalist design (no XP system, small numbers) that reviewers compare to chance-operations art and to Balatro and Vampire Survivors in spirit
Native TextMod API and level editor let the community build total conversions, including a Slay the Spire-style mod
Huge content library from a single developer working about seven years: 128 hero classes, 73 monsters and 473 items per the Steam page, plus difficulty modifiers and Nightmare mode
Same game across Steam, itch.io, Android and iOS, with cross-platform fans buying it multiple times
tedious_or_disliked: Losing at the final boss after a long run, especially with no foreknowledge of what it will be
Unlock progression: players who want to try mods or all content have to progress through the game first
Decoding cryptic item text and learning which weird items actually work
Modding workflow based on copying and pasting text files, which one refunder called the worst modding experience they had seen
Dice-builders in general can feel unrewarding: a low-playtime reviewer simply could not see how the loop is meant to be fun
divisive_points: Randomness: fans see tense, skill-expressive dice management, while detractors see an RNG fest where risk management cannot save a run
Text-based modding: praised as intuitive and powerful by modders, but criticised as clunky and gated by a newcomer
Permadeath on a single loss: adds tension for some and demoralises others, especially at the end of a run
Minimal presentation: charming and focused to most, too small for players who want spectacle or story
community.reception_notes: Launched on Steam on March 20, 2024 at $8.99, after years on itch.io and Android where it already had a devoted following (reviewers report hundreds of hours on those versions). Steam reviews have stayed near 97% positive, and the Steam page reported 100% positive in the last 30 days at the time of fetch. Metacritic shows no Metascore yet (needs 4 critic reviews; only 3 iOS reviews exist) and only 7 user ratings, so treat it as thin. No OpenCritic entry was found. Third-party estimates (SteamSpy) put Steam owners at 200k-500k and steam-revenue-calculator.com estimates about $608k gross and $179k net, both rough Boxleiter-style figures. Desktop builds exist for Windows, Mac and Linux, plus Android and iOS. The dev pledges no AI use and no sales or bundles. Itch version 3.2 added French, Italian, Russian, Spanish and Portuguese in May 2025, with 3.2.13 following later that month. Research limits: the session web search budget was exhausted, Reddit and search-engine pages were unreachable, so community detail comes mainly from Steam reviews, itch.io and Metacritic.

games.name: Tower Factory
games.short_description: Tower Factory is a tower defense and automation game with roguelite elements. Optimize resource production using conveyor systems while defending against monster waves. Can you find and destroy the enemy tower before it's too late?

other_scores.score: 89.6% positive, Very Positive, 1,128 positive / 131 negative (~1,259 reviews)
~$228.7k gross, ~$67.5k net to dev, ~15,300 copies at $14.99 (order of magnitude only)

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put this as an eight tier here right on the RAM for now (ASR garble, most plausibly B tier)

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Tower Factory is an early-access tower defense roguelike that fuses Factorio-style resource chains with simple tower defense. You gather wood and rock, convert them through production chains, and expand a hidden map to find gems that win the run. He enjoys the satisfying visual flow and the genre fusion, and finds it solid for early access. He thinks it barely feels like a roguelike, the early game is repetitive, and the towers are too minimal. The tier is garbled by ASR ('eight tier'), most plausibly B.
praise: Fusing Factorio-style logistics with tower defense is a fresh concept for roguelikes
Cute, simple visuals that fit the game, with satisfying flow of resources along chains
Building things from gathered resources feels very satisfying
Long, slow-paced runs suit tower defense, since both genres build up gradually
Flexible tower target priority options
Win condition of exploring and expanding the map to find gems is a cool concept
Mid-game becomes really enjoyable with more flexibility

Runs feel long, roughly an hour or less
Building mechanics take a while to get used to, and it is early access so things may change

Winning by finding several gems through exploration rather than attacking an enemy base

commentary.quote: I think this game is really solid.
design_criteria: Genre fusion: combining factory building with tower defense is a fresh idea
Visuals and feel: cute, simple, satisfying resource flow
Run length: long runs but fitting for the genre
Replayability and variety: early game repetitive, towers never change
Roguelike elements: wants more map discoveries and unique tower upgrades

community.one_liner: A solo-developed tower defense and factory-automation hybrid with roguelite meta-progression, where you build conveyor-fed production lines to supply towers while uncovering fog of war to find crystals and the enemy castle.
community.consensus_summary: Players receive Tower Factory very well: about 89.6% positive across roughly 1,260 Steam reviews (Very Positive), with 14 recent reviews around 85% positive. Fans call it an addictive, satisfying blend of Factorio-style logistics and tower defense, and many report very long playtimes (100 to 250+ hours among top reviews). Complaints focus on difficulty and balance (enemies scale faster than production), luck in finding crystals under fog of war, grindy meta-progression and repetitive rebuilds, and missing quality-of-life features. It has been in Early Access since Nov 7, 2024, with a planned 1.0 in roughly 12-18 months (around 2027) per the store page; it is a solo dev project (Gius Caminiti) and the dev is praised by some for helping restore lost saves, while one reviewer says he resists suggestions. No professional critic coverage was found (Metacritic page exists but has no scores; nothing located on OpenCritic).
best_things: Fresh hybrid: Factorio-like conveyor logistics feeding tower defense, described as a cross between Factorio and Bloons-style TD
Satisfying optimization loop; players enjoy min-maxing production and feel rewarded when a new mechanic clicks
Exploration via beacons and fog of war that reveals resource chests, coin chests (meta progression) and crystals, making exploring part of the win condition
Varied towers that feel balanced and each matter against different enemy types
Clean, readable, charming art style
Good performance even with a lot on screen
Fast RTS-like feel with hotkeys and planning under pressure, yet relaxing once systems flow
Responsive solo developer; one reviewer had a 22-hour lost save restored, and others cite trust in the dev using his real name
worst_things: Balance: enemy waves, resource availability and belt throughput are seen as mismatched, especially on bosses and from level 3 onward, sometimes even on easy difficulty
Crystal and enemy-castle hunting is luck-dependent; a wrong direction or unlucky map can doom a run
Late game and higher tiers become tedious, hunting resources to reach tier 2/3 towers
Content is thin for the price: some finish the main content in about 6 hours, and endless mode is criticized by some as unsatisfying
Crashes and lost saves reported by a few reviewers (including a long-time player), plus a pinned Known Issues thread on the community hub
Limited in-game info about enemy weaknesses and stats
Tower feedback (visual and audio) is considered weak by at least one reviewer
Windows only; no Mac/Linux, and some ask for more languages (e.g. Arabic)
improvements: Fast-forward and a 'next round/skip wave' button
Bulk select/move for buildings and belts, blueprints and building upgrades
A clickable minimap marking points of interest and opened/unopened chests, plus castle-entry storage indicators
More information on enemy types and weaknesses
Rebalancing of difficulty curve, resource rates and level 3 tree yields, plus easier modes or more game modes
More content and replay value (more tiers/levels/modes) and endless-mode improvements
unique_things: Resources for towers come from a real automated factory rather than a simple gold currency
Fog of war exploration with beacons and fire towers doubles as both resource acquisition and win-condition discovery
Roguelite meta-progression through coin chests and 70+ permanent upgrades
Towers gain experience and upgrade choices trade off basic vs advanced towers
Offensive objective: find crystals and destroy the enemy tower, rather than only surviving waves
Multiple bosses and procedurally generated levels, with RTS-style time pressure
tedious_or_disliked: Repeatedly rebuilding similar factories each run combined with grinding meta upgrades before progress is possible
Constantly relocating harvesters and sawmills as resources deplete, without multi-select tools
With no fast-forward, long waiting stretches and click-a-rock busywork in the late game
Hunting for crystals or castle location that can stretch matches to 20+ minutes of frustration
Perceived punishing difficulty: enemies become relentless as soon as you extend vision to gather iron/coal
Grinding macro upgrades feels mandatory, with some saying only one strategy works
divisive_points: Whether mixing TD and factory pacing works: one fan review says the time pressure is incompatible yet still recommends it, while others call it the perfect blend
Difficulty: some find it gentle and cozy early and hard later, others call it a luck-driven grind; replays and rebuilds are either addictive or repetitive
Price: some say $14.99 is steep at full price (buy on sale), while many count the hours as great value
Developer responsiveness: praised for save restoration and fixes, but one reviewer claims he is reluctant to take suggestions
community.reception_notes: Released into Steam Early Access on Nov 7, 2024 by solo developer Gius Caminiti at $14.99 (Windows only). Reviews have stayed Very Positive since launch, with demo plays during Steam Tower Defense Fest converting buyers. Current content per the store page: six procedurally generated levels, six bosses, 13 towers plus upgrades, 20+ factory buildings and 70+ meta upgrades, with endless mode also discussed on the community hub. Active development continues (reviews dated into 2026 and a pinned Known Issues post), but a few users report save loss after updates. No professional critic reviews found; Metacritic shows 'tbd' and nothing located on OpenCritic. Web search budget was exhausted during research, so no outlet reviews or Reddit threads could be read; community detail comes primarily from Steam reviews and the Steam community hub. Note some descriptions of early-access content (levels count) may be dated.

games.name: Windblown
games.short_description: A lightning-fast 1–3 player co-op roguelite from the creators of Dead Cells. DASH, DIVE and DESTROY across a shattered world. Build wild loadouts, unleash devastating Alterattacks, and become the last stand against the Vortex.

placements.verbal_evidence: in current early access, I'm going to put it as a low A

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Windblown is a very fast-paced hack-and-slash roguelike from the Dead Cells developers, in early access at the time. He loves its visuals, music, sky-island world and dash-driven traversal, and finds the weapon-switch combat fun. His big complaint is the tiny gift (relic) slot limit, which he says knocks the game down a full tier. He places it at low A, hoping it rises with future updates.
praise: Fantastic visuals, audio and vibe, including an anime intro and an epic soundtrack
Beautiful, immersive sky-island hub and world
Very fast, satisfying gameplay with a spammable dash that resets between platforms, making long levels feel quick
Two weapons plus two active items, with a combo system rewarding weapon switching and granting i-frames
Weapon types feel great and different from each other
Gift/relic system is unique and impactful, enabling cool synergies
Enemies are cool, and he trusts the Dead Cells team to expand content
criticism: Gift slots are severely limited (capped around four, plus two bought in-run), so he is full by about 10 minutes in and cannot explore synergies
Strong individual gifts crowd out full synergy builds
Combo system seems abusable; optimal play is just attacking constantly to keep i-frames up
Some enemy attacks are instant or hard to read and hard to evade
Currently always fights the same bosses and content is limited in early access
unique_points: Very long levels made fast by a dash that resets on platform transitions, a deliberate choice for immersion and satisfaction
Combo trigger by switching weapons after enough hits, pushing players to use both weapons more than in Dead Cells
Gift effects built around marks, fire damage and dash explosions create synergy potential
commentary.quote: currently I would say that Windblown is a really really cool action game
design_criteria: Visuals and audio: charm, music and world-building weigh heavily
Movement and feel: fast dash traversal and satisfaction of speed
Level design: long levels made brisk by the dash mechanic
Combat depth: weapon-switch combo system, but abusable
Enemy design: cool enemies but some attacks too fast or unreadable
Synergies and build diversity: gifts are cool but slot limits block synergy play
Meta-progression: unlocks add slots but cap is too low
Content and variety: repeated bosses in early access
commentary.rerank_note: He mentions discussing the game in an earlier video; he says the gift-slot issue drops it a full tier, from high B or A range, and he places it at low A for current early access.

community.one_liner: A fast 1-3 player co-op action roguelite from Motion Twin (Dead Cells) with infinite dashing, dual weapons and weapon-specific Alterattack combo finishers, in early access on Steam since Oct 24, 2024.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate it Very Positive (about 88.7% of roughly 10,400 reviews, per local Steam data), with a steady stream of praise for fluid movement, combat feel, music and art. Critic coverage is thin: Metacritic lists no critic or user score yet and I found no OpenCritic listing. It is still early access after nearly two years, which is a recurring complaint. Sentiment swings with big updates: a late-2025 combat rework (Alterattack) angered some fans, while the March 2026 Break the Path map overhaul split players, and later patches (dash-canceling, hunting progression in June 2026, an Yua's Support damage-reduction assist) drew more positive comments. Recent negative reviews centre on map navigation, grindy meta-progression, repetitive runs and weak single-player balance.
best_things: Movement and combat feel: infinite dash, fluid, snappy controls and high-speed traversal are widely praised
Alterattack system (switching weapons to trigger combo finishers with i-frames) is the most cited unique hook and is satisfying once learned
Soundtrack (Evil Empire) is repeatedly called great, along with the colourful art style and intro
Multiplayer works surprisingly well for some reviewers (1-3 player co-op), though solo balance is a separate complaint
Active developer support and visible change during early access; many reviewers say recent updates improved the loop
Secrets, easter eggs and world/character charm; some reviewers find the affix/keyword build system easier to work with than Dead Cells
High skill ceiling and very satisfying combos once the game's punishing early learning curve is overcome
worst_things: Shallow, repetitive meta-progression: only a few weapons and 2-3 viable playstyles, similar levels and samey runs
Balance: solo play feels tuned for co-op and is very hard (one-hit kills at high difficulty), while 3-player co-op can be trivial
Some weapons and passives are much stronger than others; inconsistent animation cancelling and damage-output meta over defensive play
Visual clutter makes enemy attacks hard to read
Performance: frame drops when installed on an HDD, chugging in some biomes on Steam Deck, and a framerate hit in multiplayer
Still in early access after roughly 2 years, with some players expecting more progress and polish
Co-op quest progress does not sync between players (only one player progresses per run)
Recent big updates (late-2025 Alterattack/combat rework, March 2026 Break the Path) are blamed by some long-time players for killing the game's speed and flow
improvements: More biomes, weapons and build variety to keep long-term runs fresh
Sync quest progress in co-op and ease the multiplayer unlock/tutorial gating
Difficulty options or assist mode and better solo balancing (Yua's Support partly addresses this)
Improve map readability and add fast travel/teleporters to cut backtracking (announced for the next update)
Performance optimisation, especially Steam Deck, loading, culling and multiplayer framerate
Reduce visual clutter and make enemy telegraphs clearer; rebalance weapons and passives
Make currency and progression less grindy; allow skipping or streamlining dialogue
unique_things: Alterattack: each weapon has a combo finisher triggered by hits with the other weapon, granting i-frames and crowd control
Infinite dash with dual-weapon combat designed around speed and rhythm
Built-in 1-3 player co-op from the Dead Cells studio (Motion Twin), with Dead Cells-familiar weapons and skills
Skylanders-like stylised art and floating-island world under threat from the Vortex
Post-launch map system (larger open biomes, minimap, item rarity tiers up to Mythic) and a hunting-based progression loop added in 2026
tedious_or_disliked: Grindy meta-progression: one review cites about 200 Cogs per 20 min run versus 6000 needed for key upgrades, roughly 10-15 hours
Traveling between small enemy packs and exploration feels tedious or aimless to some; the map update adds frequent map checking
Collecting run-only currency by smashing pots, needed to refill the health potion, before bosses
Runs feel repetitive after about 8-10 hours, with the same few builds
Spammy dodge/attack mashing and button-mashing prompts tire some players
Repeating quests twice in co-op because progress does not sync
divisive_points: Break the Path (March 2026) map/exploration overhaul: some love open biomes and secrets, others say it killed the flow and pacing
The late-2025 combat/Alterattack rework: some felt it made combat bland and slow, others enjoy the optional-not-mandatory finishers
Co-op focus vs Dead Cells-like solo design, with comparisons to the Darkest Dungeon 2 shift
Whether it feels like Dead Cells in new clothes or a distinct game; also the charge of it being a cash grab and taking energy from Dead Cells support
community.reception_notes: Launched in early access Oct 24, 2024 (Windows only, $24.99) with very strong Steam reception; the store page fetch showed 92% positive at about 4.9k reviews in an earlier snapshot, now 88.7% of 10.4k, so sentiment has cooled. Steam store lists 7 biomes, 27 weapons, 17 trinkets, 20 hexes and 102 gifts at last fetch. Notable updates: Alterattack combat rework (late 2025, criticised), revenge mode replacing sudden death in co-op, Break the Path (Mar 25, 2026) map/rarity overhaul, dash-cancel and level-gen refinements in 0.9.2-0.9.4, Hunters Gonna Hunt (Jun 22, 2026) progression and accessibility, and an announced Sept 2026 roadmap for shop restructuring, transmuter, fast-return teleporters and optimisation. Full 1.0 is planned for 2026. Developer communication is criticised by some on the co-op quest sync issue. Caveat: my web search budget was exhausted, so I relied on Steam reviews, Steam announcements, the store page, Metacritic and Wikipedia; OpenCritic and Reddit/outlet reviews could not be retrieved.
