games.name: CloverPit
games.short_description: A rogue-lite slot machine nightmare. Gamble for your life in a never-ending debt simulator!

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put this game as a solid A tier.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Clover Pit is a first-person slot machine roguelike where you are locked in a room, gambling to earn enough money to get the key and escape. It blends Luck Be a Landlord's slot-machine idea with Balatro-style multiplicative scoring and Inscription's eerie, interactive-room vibe. He loves the gameplay and the run variety, and the escape motivation kept him playing. He holds it back from S tier because the eerie atmosphere promises a story and spooky events that never really arrive. He still highly recommends it and calls it very solid.
praise: Scoring stacks multiplicative bonuses on symbols and on their positions, which can then be duplicated, leading to trillions-scale numbers
Many different builds; runs felt different depending on relics and goals
Relics plus the phone's permanent passive upgrades (symbol odds, doubled values) combine well
Being locked in a room with an eerie vibe and a real incentive to escape is more motivating than Luck Be a Landlord's rent
Interactable room (toilet, door, telephone) adds charm and atmosphere
Getting the key and escaping was satisfying; there is also a true ending
criticism: Little content beyond the gameplay; the eerie setup promises a subplot that does not materialise
Wants random spooky events (power outage, alley sequence) even if purely cosmetic
Animations, like tickets and cards coming out, feel slow and tiring even when sped up
Many unlockable pre-run cards are uninteresting or too situational
Nothing crazy unique, in a crowded genre of Balatro-like games
unique_points: Uses a slot machine inside a first-person locked-room setting, unlike the 2D screen of Luck Be a Landlord
Stacks multipliers on both symbols and positions, each duplicable
Phone gives permanent passive bonuses alongside run-based relics
Icons matter less than in Luck Be a Landlord; the slot machine almost serves as the excuse for the game
commentary.quote: the game is very solid. It was a really good time
design_criteria: Synergies and multipliers: duplicating multiplications on symbols and positions creates huge number scaling
Build diversity: runs feel different based on relics and symbols found
Meta-progression: unlockable relics, pre-run cards and phone permanent passives
Atmosphere and narrative: eerie locked-room vibe, but underdelivered story and events
Motivation and stakes: escape goal is stronger than paying a landlord
Pacing and feel: slow animations become tiring over many runs
Originality: solid but not especially unique in the Balatro-like space

community.one_liner: A first-person, PSX-styled roguelite where you pull a demonic slot machine in a prison cell to pay escalating debt deadlines, buying Lucky Charms to bend the odds (Balatro meets Buckshot Roulette).
community.consensus_summary: CloverPit is received as a stylish, highly addictive slot-machine roguelite: Steam sits at Very Positive (about 90% of roughly 26k reviews), and critics are generally favorable (Metacritic 77, OpenCritic 81). Praise centers on the grimy atmosphere, sound and tactile feel, the number-go-up thrill and cheap price. The recurring complaint is that it has far less player agency than Balatro: it is luck-heavy, early deadlines can be lost on bad shop rolls, and the growing pool of niche charms dilutes good shops as you unlock more. Metacritic users are noticeably cooler (6.8, mixed) than Steam. After release the dev patched the game (1.2 nerfs, Hard Mode required for holographic memory cards, endless runs removed), which angered parts of the community; 1.3 softened some of this. A paid DLC (Unholy Fusion, April 2026) and console/mobile ports followed, and it reportedly passed 1 million copies by mid-November 2025.
best_things: Addictive loop: huge dopamine hits on jackpots and a 'one more run' pull, often described as Balatro plus Buckshot Roulette
Oppressive, grungy low-poly PSX visuals, humour and sound design create a distinctive tense tone (cramped cell, ticking deadline, intercom voice)
Satisfying number-go-up build-crafting once charm synergies (symbol value, patterns, luck, multipliers) come together, with values climbing into e-notation
Gambling thrill without real money; several reviewers even call it an anti-gambling statement
Very good value at $9.99, with a demo whose progress carries over to the full game
Phone/telephone permanent perks and memory cards add run-to-run variety; big unlock catalog (about 160 charms) gives long replay value for completionists
worst_things: Low player agency and skill expression compared with Balatro: you are essentially pressing a button, so outcomes often feel like pure luck
Charm pool bloat: as you unlock ~160 charms, many are niche or bad and pollute the shop, so progression can make runs worse
Many charms are considered never worth using (too specific triggers, non-functional effects, no supporting builds), leaving a narrow meta (e.g. interest farming)
Brutal early game: the first two deadlines are dominated by shop RNG and can fail on consecutive runs even with luck items
Drawer/charm swapping and camera turning is fiddly and time-consuming
Post-launch balance patches (1.2) were seen as mostly nerfs that removed fun builds and endless runs
Late-game and end-of-run flow: cannot just quit at run end, dialogue/animations hard to skip
Some critics and players find the game runs out of gas and gets repetitive after several runs

Players flag the in-game odds for the 666 jackpot as misleading (the top-voted Steam review says the displayed chance and the real chance look swapped, roughly 1.5% vs 1/4), which feels unfair in a luck-driven game
improvements: Rework or buff the large set of weak/niche charms and rebalance to reduce dead picks
Give players control over the shop pool (ban, favorite or remove charms) so unlocks do not dilute good options
Make memory cards easier to obtain and unlock, and allow reuse instead of single-use consumption; make holographic/Lord of the Pit achievable without forced Hard Mode
Improve the drawer/charm-swap UI so players do not constantly turn around and click back and forth
Add more player agency (e.g. freezing rows/columns or other ways to nudge the machine) and smoother early-game odds
More cosmetic unlockables and QoL: skip dialogue/animations, option to quit cleanly after a run, better accessibility (audio settings, flashing lights)
unique_things: Slot machine as the core roguelite engine, with charms modifying symbols, patterns, luck and payouts rather than a card deck
Survival-horror framing: escape-room cell, debt deadlines, trapdoor on failure, corpse parts and multiple endings
Telephone calls give permanent deadline-by-deadline abilities that combine with charms
Memory cards act as single-use run modifiers that can be upgraded (holographic/rainbow) for meta progression
Deliberate PSX low-poly look, tactile lever pulling and a first-person physical-space interface
Demo progress carries over to the full game
tedious_or_disliked: Constant charm shuffling in and out of drawers, with repeated camera turns, described as '90% prep, 10% play'
Grinding for specific memory cards and corpse parts/skull for the real ending, with no way to skip dialogue or animations
Losing early deadlines due to shop RNG and having to restart at Deadline 1
Rerolling the charm shop becomes an expensive second slot machine
Forced Hard Mode for holographic cards and 100% completion after the 1.2 update
Flashing lights and overstimulation (an option to tone these down was added in 1.3)
divisive_points: Luck versus strategy: some love the desperate, random feel and the thrill; others feel there is no real decision-making compared with Balatro
Dev nerfs and Hard Mode: many see them as needed anti-exploit balance, others as punishing players of a single-player game
Late-game balance: some say it is 'startlingly easy' once you optimize, while others say the early game is brutally unfair
Metacritic users (6.8, mixed) disagree with the much more positive Steam reception
community.reception_notes: Announced April 2025 with a demo at Steam Next Fest (over 680k downloads per Wikipedia), delayed to avoid Hollow Knight: Silksong, and launched on Windows Sept 26, 2025 at $9.99 (Panik Arcade, published by Future Friends Games). Reported 100k copies in one day and about 1M by mid-November 2025 (Wikipedia; third-party Steam revenue estimator returned $0 so no reliable revenue figure was obtained). Ports: Xbox/Game Pass Nov 2025, iOS/Android Dec 2025, PlayStation/Switch Aug 2026. Patch 1.2 nerfed many charms, removed endless runs and tied holographic memory cards to Hard Mode, drawing a wave of negative Steam reviews; 1.3 made Hard Mode fairer, reworked memory cards and added a reduced-flashing option but kept the holographic requirement. Unholy Fusion DLC (April 9, 2026) added a new ending and a charm-fusion Surgery Machine. Some users complained that Steam community discussion groups were locked. OpenCritic figures varied between fetches (81 rating, 27 to 30 reviews, 73-86% recommend). Not early access and actively supported.

games.name: Dome Keeper
games.short_description: Defend against waves of alien monsters in this unique roguelike action miner. Dig for resources, collect useful gadgets, and upgrade equipment to increase odds of survival – just hurry back before your dome is destroyed!

placements.verbal_evidence: I think I'm going to put this as a low A, high B. I'm think I'm going to put as a high high B for now.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Dome Keeper is a niche digging roguelike where each run you land on a planet, mine ore to buy upgrades, and periodically return to defend your dome from monster waves. He calls it a hidden gem that few people talk about and loves its chill-yet-stressful vibe and the way new gadgets and domes keep runs feeling different. The main drawbacks are slow, repetitive early game and runs that drag on when you cannot find the relic. He lands it at a high B for now, hedging toward low A, and says he may revisit it.
praise: Two distinct loops (digging and defending) that create tension when you must return from deep to defend
Huge variety from many gadgets, different domes (sword, turrets, guns, lasers) each with unique upgrade paths, and a new character with a different playstyle
Selective upgrading: you cannot max everything in a run, so choices depend on what you find and the challenge at hand
Unlocking new gadgets and starting gadgets drives replayability; every run feels like its own game
Minimalistic, peaceful audio with sparse music, plus satisfying visual effects and ore sounds that make the loop relaxing
Exciting discoveries underground, like unique interactables that reward figuring them out
criticism: Early game is slow and repetitive since you always start very weak
Digging can get repetitive and runs are long, especially when luck keeps the relic hidden (an hour and a half for some runs)
Excitement may fade once all gadgets have been seen
Permanent progression is not held onto as strongly as in other roguelikes
Personal gripe with the hard 1% health remaining achievement
unique_points: Challenge runs, not random runs, are the core and they unlock the permanent progression, which is rare for roguelikes
Defense is deliberately simple so the digging and discovery remain the focus
Hybrid of digging exploration and base defense with two very different paces
commentary.quote: I think this is kind of a hidden gem, honestly.
design_criteria: Replayability: new gadgets, domes and characters make each run feel different
Meta-progression: unlocks tied to challenge runs, light permanent progression
Build variety and choice: cannot max all upgrades, so selective upgrading matters
Pacing and run length: slow start and long runs when the relic is hard to find
Audio/visual feel: minimalistic music and satisfying effects support the chill vibe
Gameplay loop design: dig vs defend with intentionally simple defense
Discovery and exploration: unique finds underground are exciting
Risk vs tension: going deep while needing to return to defend
commentary.rerank_note: Provisional placement: he says 'for now' and that he will think about it later; he hedges between low A and high B.

community.one_liner: A 2D roguelite from Bippinbits (published by Raw Fury) where you dig underground for iron, water and cobalt between monster waves, then rush back to a dome to upgrade it and personally shoot down attackers.
community.consensus_summary: Players like it a lot: about 92% positive on Steam across roughly 22.5k reviews (Very Positive), with a long tail of players logging hundreds of hours. Critics were warmer than lukewarm but more reserved, landing at Metacritic 76 and OpenCritic 78, with a 71% critic-recommend rate and Eurogamer as the one outright no-recommend. The shared verdict is a tight, addictive short-session loop with great atmosphere that is repetitive and thin on content, particularly solo after roughly 10 hours. It is a finished 1.0 game that has kept receiving free updates: a Godot 4 migration with many new gadgets, later co-op multiplayer (local and online), a paid character/content DLC line (Engineer Gear Pack, The Lost Keepers), and an Xbox Series X/S release in December 2025.
best_things: Risk/reward tension of mining: every second underground is a second away from defending the dome, and players say that pull never goes away
Simple, readable, low-friction design that works for a quiet 30-minute run and is praised as a Steam Deck fit (clean UI, stable 60 FPS)
Atmosphere: pixel art, monster design and a sparse, crystalline sound design and soundtrack that reviewers and players both single out
Replayability from modes, relics, gadgets, multiple domes and keepers, map sizes and modifiers, plus meta-progression and challenges
Multiplayer/co-op added later is frequently described as a big upgrade and a great family or friends game
Approachable difficulty that scales, so newcomers and veterans can both find a setting; runs are short
Runs well on modest hardware and Steam Deck, with native Linux support
Ongoing developer support with free content updates
worst_things: Repetition: runs play out near-identically (dig, return, upgrade, fight), and the same optimal upgrade paths get picked each time (Shacknews, many Steam reviews)
Limited content at launch price: few unlocks, only two base keepers with more behind paid DLC, and some players report everything unlocked in 10 to 40 hours
Mining/defense split can feel like each half interrupts the other; Eurogamer said it struggles to make either a success in its own right
Late-game automation (drones, automated turrets) can make runs trivial, reducing the need to defend manually even on hard difficulties
Sparse tutorial; many mechanics and early challenges are opaque and players turn to the wiki
Technical complaints in Steam reviews: crashes on some setups, language-change bugs, a Steam Deck launch failure report, and frame-rate drops in Endless Prestige past about wave 35
Reports of RNG cave generation producing dense blocks with few resources, which can soft-lock a run or challenge
Some consider full price ($17.99) high for the content depth
improvements: Bigger late game: larger maps, more resource types, more weapons, base mods and artifacts (repeated by critics and testers)
A way to shorten or vary the opening, such as modifiers or unlocks that start you with basic upgrades or random early tech, since the opening is identical every run
More run variety and surprises from mining (more randomness, more enemy types) and some balance work on essential-upgrade builds
Better multiplayer progression: a shared token or upgrade pool and cheaper second gun so one player does not hog resources or babysit the tower
Free reroll on gadget choices and more forgiving resource generation to cut unlucky runs
Performance optimization for long Endless/late-wave runs and better onboarding for new players
unique_things: Reverses the tower defense formula: no building dozens of towers, you personally operate the dome's laser between digging trips
Comparisons to Motherload-style mining combined with wave survival and a roguelite meta layer
Three-resource economy (iron, water, cobalt) with transport by carrying, so logistics and depth decisions drive every run
Win conditions beyond survival, including relic hunts, scenario modes, guild challenges and endless modes
Multiple keepers, domes and worlds that each add a twist, plus up to 4 local or 8 online co-op players and cross-platform multiplayer
tedious_or_disliked: The early game of each run: slow hauling of resources, no meaningful upgrades yet, and a travel-heavy return trip for each wave, described as a chore
Having to go back to the dome constantly because waves come quickly, which some call more chores than stress
Progression gating: inter-run progress tied to guild challenges, some of them considered nearly impossible early and frustrating when a loss yields nothing
Searching blindly for the relic or specific ore; challenge runs like mazes or iron quotas can drag
Multiplayer tends to split into one tower babysitter and everyone else mining, with chores visible and little variation
divisive_points: Whether the dig/defend switch is the charm or the flaw: some love the tension, others find the fun part constantly interrupted by the boring part
Difficulty and depth: many praise scalable challenge, while others say as long as you keep busy you always win and automation trivialises later runs
Value: players who log hundreds of hours call it a bargain, while ones who finished in under 10 to 40 hours call it thin for the price
Repetition is seen by fans as a cozy loop with hidden depth and by critics as predictable
community.reception_notes: Released Sept 27, 2022 (Steam, Win/Mac/Linux) after an itch.io origin; launch reviews were favourable but not glowing, mostly praising the addictive simple loop and criticising content depth. The 2024 announcement of a major content update (new gadgets roughly doubling the set, Godot 3 to 4 migration) was followed by free multiplayer, which Steam reviewers credit with lifting the game from average to top-notch for groups. Additional paid content (Engineer Gear Pack, The Lost Keepers) exists, and some reviewers dislike characters sitting behind DLC. Xbox Series X/S version launched Dec 9, 2025 and mobile versions are listed as in development; Metacritic also lists an iOS entry. Estimated sales: SteamSpy owners 2-5 million, and steam-revenue-calculator estimates about $10.75M gross and about $3.17M net (Boxleiter-based, not audited). Steam reviews are recent and still coming, which indicates continued activity, with about 400 concurrent players in the local data.

games.name: Drop Duchy
games.short_description: Build your duchy piece by piece in this refreshing hybrid rogue-lite game. Use block-dropping mechanics to collect resources, recruit troops to fight against belligerent armies, and let every block shape your realm, leading your path to victory!

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put this as a high high B tier for now.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Drop Duchy is a Tetris-style land-building strategy roguelike where placed pieces generate resources, and you also position units and fight enemies and bosses. He already reviewed it in an earlier video and is re-evaluating it after the full release and a big update. Most of his original complaints were fixed, especially quality-of-life ones. He finds it unique, strategic and fun, but notes lingering gaps: no rewind button, only three bosses, and very long runs. He places it in high B for now.
praise: Very unique and interesting blend of Tetris-like placement with strategy and combat
Distinct factions (now a third via DLC) that play so differently they feel like new games
Multiple build paths such as river, mountain/military and religion/enemy-stealing
Bosses act as mini puzzle mechanics you must solve with your build
Map pathing requires real thought depending on your build, which he loves in deckbuilders
Simple rock-paper-scissors unit combat becomes surprisingly strategic and mathematical late game
Update added the constellation cooldown ability and many QoL fixes, like an option to stop pieces auto-falling
criticism: Still no rewind button, despite frequent small mistakes
Always the same three bosses; wants variety within them
Meta-progression mostly unlocks more options, which can clutter the reward pool
Wants more Slay the Spire-style narrative events with choices on the map
Runs are very long (hours), which is a caution even if pacing is good
Early on the game felt overwhelming, boring and repetitive until more was unlocked
unique_points: Tetris piece placement as the core of a strategy roguelike, with placement location changing building effects
Factions each change the game drastically, making the game feel new
Bosses designed as individual miniature puzzle mechanics
Rerolling map path choices tie terrain and unit presence to boss strength, creating a risk/strategy tradeoff
commentary.quote: I'm going to put this as a high high B tier for now.
design_criteria: Uniqueness: core Tetris-meets-strategy concept is what drew him in
Build diversity: factions and multiple build paths give variety
Boss design: puzzle-like bosses but lacking variety
Meta-progression: unlocks add options more than power, risking pool clutter
Quality of life: rewind and auto-fall options strongly affect his enjoyment
Strategic depth: map pathing and unit combat demand thought
Run length: very long runs are a caveat
Events: wants more choice-based events for immersion
commentary.rerank_note: Previously covered in an earlier video; this is a re-evaluation after the full release and update, where he says roughly 70% or more of his original issues were addressed.

community.one_liner: A Tetris-like block-dropping roguelite deckbuilder from Sleepy Mill Studio where terrain and building pieces build your realm, generate resources and troops, and feed turn-based battles against enemy armies and act bosses.
community.consensus_summary: Drop Duchy is well received by critics and most players: Steam shows Very Positive (about 89% of roughly 3,300 reviews in the local data), Metacritic critic score is 83 from 15 reviews, and OpenCritic has a 81 top critic average with 89% of critics recommending. Reviewers praise the fresh Tetris plus deckbuilding hybrid, the chill pace with forgiving undo, and deep faction-based meta progression. The recurring complaints are heavy RNG on piece draws, a progression tree that dilutes the draft pool as you unlock more, unclear combat math and UI, and uneven balance. It is actively supported: two paid faction DLCs (The Tribe, Aug 2025; The North, Dec 2025), a Game Pass Xbox release in Jan 2026, PS5 and Switch in Apr 2026, and a mobile port reported for late Sep 2026. It has not been abandoned. Metacritic user score is low (6.5 from only 23 ratings), contrasting with Steam.
best_things: Genuinely fresh twist on Tetris: terrain tiles (plains, forest, river) and building tiles interact, so placement matters more than clearing lines; completing a row triggers an 'exploration' that pays out resources by terrain
Satisfying synergy building: farms, lumberjacks and military buildings reshape nearby terrain and combo with each other; finding combos is repeatedly called rewarding
Rock-paper-scissors unit counters and enemy buildings that you are forced to place add a second layer of tactical thinking to block placement
Forgiving and relaxed: unlimited single-turn undo and quick reload of a battle, no time pressure on placement, good for short sessions and runs well on Steam Deck
Lots of content in the base game: 110+ cards, 100+ achievement-style challenges driving unlocks, multiple very different factions, branching paths and selectable boss order
Hooks grow over time: several players say it is gimmicky for the first hours and becomes addictive around 10 to 30 hours as depth appears
Polished, cute presentation with snappy actions and a pleasant evolving soundtrack; critics (Guardian, Vandal, Games Machine) singled out the clever design and clean interface
Good value at $14.99 with post-launch faction DLC and ascension/endless modes; Steam reviews at 89% positive across ~3,300 reviews
worst_things: Heavy RNG: with roughly 20 pieces per round, a few bad draws can ruin a run, and several reviewers say good play cannot always outskill a bad hand; GameCritics called it RNG-dominated
Unlock tree dilutes runs: as you unlock more tiles and passives the draft pool gets watered down, making later runs feel unfocused and harder to get the pieces you need

Combat math and information are opaque: players say enemy vs player buildings are hard to tell apart (poor contrast, small flags), and the UI lacks the info needed for informed placement; the dev reportedly acknowledged the explanation is confusing
Balance is uneven: some factions and cards feel far stronger than others, later-unlocked factions are more tile-order sensitive, and military buildings are often the obvious pick over resource ones
Some find it more of a deckbuilder with Tetris flavor than a real Tetris game; Tetris skill helps but the game offers no tutorial or training for newcomers
Boss and late-game design feel like mechanical checkpoints to some, and late-game reroll abundance makes builds samey
Minor technical issues reported: Steam Deck button dropouts, controls or keyboard layout resetting, resolution setting not applying, occasional stuck combat prep and visual flicker
improvements: Reduce RNG frustration with more draw control, better piece smoothing, or a fast retry that keeps the same seed
Rework the progression tree so unlocking more does not dilute the pool, and allow presets or loadouts for the progress tree (a requested Steam feature)
Clearer combat UI and tutorials: show unit math, make enemy buildings visually distinct, and add a Tetris primer or training mode
Rebalance factions and weak cards, and make peaceful/resource paths competitive with military
More varied bosses and a fresher late game (one reviewer asked for a different Act 4), plus more run-to-run variance
Fix reported platform bugs (Steam Deck input, controls resetting, French DLC translation error) and consider a GOG release that players have asked about
unique_things: Hybrid of falling-block puzzle, roguelite deckbuilder and light tactics; compared by players to Slay the Spire mixed with Tetris, or a single-player Catan
Line clears are 'explorations' that harvest resources from terrain rather than just clearing space, and you are sometimes better leaving gaps than clearing
Enemy buildings are shuffled into your deck and must be placed on your board, turning defense and counters into a placement puzzle
Faction design: Duchy, Republic and Order in the base game, plus Tribe (druid, constellation/combo mechanics, endless mode) and North (Viking, individual unit battles, ascension mode) DLC
Branching map with selectable order of the boss fights and a large achievement-driven unlock tree
Won Excellence in Game Design at the 2025 DevGAMM Awards and got D.I.C.E. and Pegases nominations; Todd Howard publicly praised it
tedious_or_disliked: Progression is grindy and opaque early on: other clans are gated behind crowns and tree unlocks, and one reviewer was 8 hours in before understanding how crowns are earned
Achievement-gated unlocks can stall progress (a reviewer stuck waiting on a rare card tied to a windmill achievement), and forcing you to play weaker starting cards for unlocks feels punishing
Choosing between a winning run on higher difficulty and an 'unlock run' is a disliked tension
Repetitive loop after roughly 20 hours: several positive reviews say they finished most achievements and hit the end of engagement
Combat often feels pointless or slow by the end of each round to some, and pace is too slow for those expecting fast Tetris
Late-game reroll and sell cycles feel like chore work when you can simply reroll until you get your build
divisive_points: RNG: fans see it as roguelite spice and part of adapting, while detractors say it removes the sense of skill and cleverness
Tetris identity: people who love Tetris techniques (T-spins, holding for key pieces) feel rewarded, others feel it is really a deckbuilder and Tetris newcomers feel lost
Depth vs overwhelm: some call the synergy depth addictive, others call the deck and combat systems overwhelming or over-complex
Longevity: 50 to 60 hour reviewers love the ongoing discovery while others feel done after 20 hours
community.reception_notes: Launched May 5, 2025 on Steam (Windows only) and was a critical and player success. Post-launch support has been steady: The Tribe DLC (Aug 18, 2025) added a druid faction and endless mode; The North DLC (Dec 5, 2025) added a Viking faction and ascension mode. The Complete Edition reached Xbox Series X/S via Game Pass on Jan 28, 2026, PS5 and Switch on Apr 21, 2026, and Wikipedia reports a mobile version on Sep 29, 2026. It was bundled in a Humble Bundle, which brought in some players who bounced off it. Recent Steam reviews remain Very Positive. Estimated Steam revenue (Boxleiter-style, unaudited): about $1.13M gross, roughly $334k net, and SteamSpy owners of 50k to 100k. Steam reports that the DLC (Tribe, North) are on sale separately. games.name: He is Coming

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: He is Coming is an early-access auto-battler roguelike where you walk a forest gathering items and events across a 3-day cycle, then fight a boss, repeating until a final boss. The moment-to-moment gameplay is deliberately simple, but the item pool is full of mechanics-changing pieces that enable many wild build paths. He also loves the asynchronous PvP mode, where you face other players' saved builds and chase king status. He calls it one of his favorite games of the genre and places it in an easy A tier, above Clover Pit.
praise: Simple, low-effort gameplay paired with deep, complex roguelike strategy
Huge variety of items that alter mechanics rather than giving flat stat bumps, enabling many build paths (bomb chains, acid/armor conversion)
Forest map is full of events, fusion, shopkeepers and unique weapons/pendants, so he still finds new things after long play
Speed options, skippable trivial fights and teleporting keep pacing fast and never boring
Bosses each have puzzle-like mechanics and you can adapt your build to the announced upcoming boss
Asynchronous PvP against other players' builds, with king progression, creates a meta and strong replayability
Clear, non-overwhelming pixel art and great classic eight-bit music
Low barrier to entry and selectable item bundles in PvP add flexibility; achievements unlock more items
criticism: Gameplay itself has almost nothing to do; the depth comes entirely from the roguelike elements
The second map is less simple and in his view weaker than the first map
Some build complexity gets very intricate, though he frames this as a positive
unique_points: Uses a very simple exploration/auto-battler loop and puts nearly all the depth into items and builds
PvP is asynchronous: your dead build becomes an opponent for others, with beat-five-to-become-king and unbeaten-king goals
Players can pick item bundles for PvP instead of having every item, shaping build diversity
commentary.quote: I love simple games with crazy strategies.
design_criteria: Build diversity and synergies: many mechanically distinct items enabling varied builds
Simplicity vs depth: simple gameplay is fine if roguelike elements are strong
Replayability and discovery: events and items in the forest keep surprising him

Multiplayer/meta: async PvP adds strategic layer and a meta

Progression: achievements unlock new items

commentary.summary: He is Coming is an early-access auto-battler roguelike in which you walk around a map collecting loot while fights resolve automatically. Simplicity vs depth: simple mechanics with deep strategy

community.one_liner: A pixel-art roguelite RPG auto-battler from Chronocle (published by Hooded Horse) where you explore a fog-and-daylight-limited map gathering and combining items, then face a new boss every three days, plus asynchronous PvP.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate it Very Positive (about 85% of roughly 4,200 reviews at time of research) and many call it an obsessive, build-crafting favourite with short runs and surprising depth. The single critic write-up found (Try Hard Guides, early access) is also positive, praising the streamlined loop and retro look while noting static combat and thin content. The loudest recurring complaint is that item synergies depend too heavily on RNG, and that unlocking more items dilutes the pool and makes good builds rarer. It has been in Early Access since 17 July 2025 with two biomes live and a third map and Demon King content still promised; the developer is praised for frequent patches, but some players say balance is being driven by PvP at the expense of single player. Note: web search budget was exhausted in this session, so community detail is drawn mainly from the Steam reviews file, Steam store page and forum overview, not Reddit.
best_things: Tight, addictive core loop with short runs (roughly 10-15 minutes), so a bad-RNG run costs little
Deep build theorycrafting: 350+ items, set bonuses, pairing items to merge them and save inventory slots; compared by players to MtG-style triggers and to Rummy
Second biome (swamp) brings new mechanics, status effects and items rather than a reskin
Kingmaker asynchronous PvP uses ghosts of other players' builds as bosses, and a daily hall of fame drives experimentation
Strong retro pixel art, sound design and catchy chiptune music with a nostalgic NES feel
Active developer: patches weekly or sometimes daily, listens to feedback
Large compendium with 100+ unlockable challenges and many achievements giving long-term goals; players report 100-300+ hours
Player agency in movement and item choices feels more direct than in Loop Hero, which some reviewers prefer
worst_things: Heavy RNG: synergies often require several specific pieces, and runs can be dead on day one if a key piece never appears
Unlocking items via the compendium dilutes the pool, so the game feels harder and less synergistic the more you unlock
Content is thin for some players: two biomes and a PvP mode, no final Demon King fight yet, two levels cleared in 3-4 hours by some
Auto-battle means you feel like a spectator; decisions mostly reduce to which item to take
Kingmaker PvP is accused of being meta-driven, sweaty and unfriendly to off-meta builds, with balance changes tilted toward PvP
Screen shake causes headaches for some players with no option to disable it (most-upvoted negative review)
Combat lacks animation, so fights look static and repetitive (critic and players)
Price ($19.99 / about 9.99 euro in some regions) judged too high by some for an Early Access title with limited content
Runs and campaigns feel short and easy: several reviewers say combos end before you get to enjoy them, and both maps can be cleared in about 3 hours
Game play feels shallow to some: mostly walking around picking up good items, with little strategy beyond matching items to the boss
improvements: Add more luck mitigation: rerolls, stronger banishing, more reliable ways to shape the item pool, and more useful transmutation
Add an undo or confirmation for accidentally swapping weapons, and let oils and edge upgrades carry over when changing weapon
Add more roguelite meta progression (permanent upgrades, better starts) to offset the item-dilution problem
Add an accessibility option to disable or reduce screen shake
Deliver the promised third map and Demon King final boss, and more single-player content so it is not dominated by PvP
Rework Gauntlet (real-time PvP) mode, whose path generation can be lopsided, and rebalance Kingmaker rewards and the crown system
Quality-of-life requests such as a paper-doll avatar showing equipment, who-killed-you info on the death screen, and a skippable intro
unique_things: Day-and-step limited exploration with darkness, watchtowers and campfires, so routing and scouting are a core skill
Boss every three days that you can challenge early to gain inventory slots, turning timing into a risk/reward decision
Items are the only progression (no levelling), with pair-merging to compress inventory
Asynchronous Kingmaker mode where bosses are other players' saved builds, plus a separate real-time duel (Gauntlet) mode
Hidden objectives in the compendium that unlock items, with biome-specific item sets
Often compared to Loop Hero, Backpack Battles and Slay the Spire, but mixes a map-exploration layer with auto-battle
tedious_or_disliked: Restarting repeatedly until RNG cooperates, especially on Hard and Very Hard difficulties
Opening chests and discarding them because you cannot store, craft or manipulate items between days
Filler fights against ordinary enemies that pose no challenge while you wait for a build to form
Grinding the compendium and achievements, after which motivation drops sharply for some
Keeping up with the PvP meta and heavy amount of item data to learn
Unskippable intro and overtuned bosses mentioned in community threads
divisive_points: RNG: some see it as the intended loop that you learn to work around, others call it slot-machine gameplay with too little control
Auto-battler format: a turn-off for some, the point for others who like pure build theorycrafting
Kingmaker PvP: praised as smart asynchronous multiplayer by some, called unfun, meta-bound and a drag on single-player balance by others
Value: worth $20 for 100+ hours to many, overpriced for an Early Access game with two maps to others
community.reception_notes: Launched in Early Access on 17 July 2025 at $19.99 (Windows only) and quickly built a strong Steam score. Metacritic has a page with one critic review and scores still marked TBD, so no critic or user score exists; OpenCritic listing could not be confirmed. Developer commitment is stated as additional bosses up to the Demon King, at least one new biome and more equipment with no price change at 1.0 and no exit date. Some reviews mention a third map being expected and a single-slot backpack being added; the last-30-day Steam sentiment (73%) is lower than overall, reflecting complaints about RNG dilution and PvP-focused balance. Steam revenue estimate sources returned $0 / no data, and SteamSpy owners showed 0-20,000 (unreliable), so sales figures are unknown; 3,852 Steam recommendations is the best hard number. Limitations: web search quota ran out and Reddit, OpenCritic, Steam announcements and Wikipedia pages could not be retrieved, so no Reddit or patch-note detail was read.

games.name: Megabonk
games.short_description: Smash your way through endless waves of enemies and grow absurdly powerful! Grab loot, level up, unlock characters and upgrade to create unique and crazy builds as you fend off hordes of creatures!

placements.verbal_evidence: for me, it's just going to be a very solid A tier; as it stands, it's a very solid A tier for me

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Megabonk is a 3D, third-person survivors-like inspired by Vampire Survivors and Risk of Rain 2, where you roam large maps full of shrines and chests. He thinks its hype comes more from its design than from the 3D novelty. He loves the build variety, movement skill and community, but does not place it alongside his S-tier picks such as Blueprints and Night Rain. His verdict is a very solid A tier, possibly limited by his personal taste.
praise: Layered upgrade system: tomes for stat paths, up to four weapons, chest items and shrines with minigames all feed builds
Weapon upgrades roll random attributes with rarities, so a rare or legendary roll that hits the stat you want feels great; the luck stat supports this
Movement is unusual for the genre and has real skill and tech (jumping, sliding for momentum), leading to late-game map-crossing flight
Maps are dense with shrines, chests and interactables, and climbing or falling enemies keep you moving; maps among the best in the genre
Characters scale with every level, and leveling stays frequent into the late game instead of tapering off
Items are mechanically distinct, and every unlocked item can be toggled on or off to avoid diluting the pool
Weekly-reset leaderboards with different metas, a strong community, great music and vibe, and engaging dev logs
criticism: Wants more unique events per run; the bush guy in the first level is a cool surprise but is the same every time
Very hard for a survivors-like; the tier-three bosses and some challenge runs are extremely tough, which he frames as both pro and con
Slightly less crazy late-game enemy hordes ('oozes') than he expected from the hype
Not S tier for him, partly due to personal taste
unique_points: 3D third-person survivors-like, rare in the genre, with movement as a real skill layer
Random attribute plus rarity on each weapon upgrade makes every upgrade feel distinct
Toggling unlocked items on and off solves the item-pool dilution problem common in roguelikes
Constant leveling through the whole run keeps progression rewarding
Community mystery around the anonymous developer and weekly competitive leaderboards boosted its attention
commentary.quote: it's just going to be a very solid A tier.
comparisons: Keeper (the previous game, upgrade system contrast)
design_criteria: Build variety and upgrade system: tomes, weapons, items and shrines give many upgrade routes
Luck and rarity: random rolls with rarities make rewarding moments
Movement and mobility: skill-based 3D movement tech
Level and map design: dense, interactive maps with things to hunt for
Character scaling: per-level gains keep leveling satisfying
Item pool management: toggling unlocked items on or off
Replayability and variety: wants more unique per-run events
Difficulty: very hard for the genre, with tough bosses
Meta and community: leaderboards, dev logs, community engagement
Audio and vibe: music and overall feel praised

commentary.label: Top 10 of 2025 (#5)
commentary.summary: Megabonk is a 3D survivors-like that asks what Risk of Rain 2 would look like as a survivor game. He praises its fast, physics-based movement, varied items, weapons and characters, and interactable-filled levels. The standout is the upgrade system, which combines randomised stat values with player choice and a mechanic for steering stats. He also loves the music, humour and a responsive, secretive developer. It ranks fifth of the year and has become one of his new favourite survivors-likes.
praise: Extensive 3D movement with physics that let skilled players traverse levels fast and precisely
Large pool of items, weapons and characters
Fun level design filled with interactables
Upgrade system: stat and weapon upgrades with randomised values and varying upgradeable stats each time
Tome mechanic lets players prioritise specific stats to curate runs while keeping controlled randomness
Fantastic music, fun vibe and humour
Active community and a developer who keeps updating and listens to feedback
Great balance of automation, strategy and skill in chaotic bullet-and-monster gameplay
criticism: No real criticisms stated in this segment; he only pre-empts the worry that the upgrade system adds too much randomness and says the tome mechanic addresses it
unique_points: Upgrade values and even which weapon stats can be upgraded vary per run, adding a layer of choice
Tome mechanic curates randomness so runs can be steered
Brings Risk of Rain 2 style items and 3D movement into the survivors-like format
commentary.quote: It's honestly genius design.
design_criteria: Movement: 3D physics allowing high-speed, precise traversal
Content variety: items, weapons and characters
Level design: fun levels filled with interactables
Upgrade/meta systems: randomised upgrades balanced by player control
Audio: fantastic music
Charm/humour: fun overall vibe
Community and developer support: constant updates, listens to feedback
Core genre fidelity: chaotic bullet-hell feel with balance of automation, strategy and skill

community.one_liner: A solo-developed 3D survivors-like roguelite that mixes Vampire Survivors-style auto-attacking and build stacking with Risk of Rain 2-style chests, shrines and platforming movement, wrapped in meme-heavy low-poly visuals.
community.consensus_summary: Megabonk launched on Steam on Sept 18, 2025 at roughly $10 and became a breakout indie hit: over a million copies in about two weeks and a peak of roughly 117k concurrent players. Steam currently shows 94.3% positive across about 106.5k reviews (Very Positive). The handful of critic reviews are strongly positive (Metacritic 88 from 4 outlets), praising the addictive loop and movement. Player sentiment has cooled among long-term players: the main complaints are a narrow meta, weak items and balance, grind for unlocks, and a slow update cadence. The game is treated by many as effectively complete or in maintenance mode, and Steam forum threads asking if it is abandoned are common. Even so, the dev did ship patches (1.0.7 through 1.0.12 pinned in the forum) and a Halloween-themed update, and newer reviews show a positive but more mixed tone.
best_things: Extremely addictive 'one more run' loop, the single most repeated praise in Steam reviews
3D movement with jumping, sliding, wall-climbing characters and physics quirks makes it feel distinct from 2D survivors-likes
Good blend of Vampire Survivors auto-combat with Risk of Rain 2-style chest, shrine and item systems
Very low price (about $10 per reviewers; Steam listing showed $5.99 at last check, frequent discounts) for dozens or hundreds of hours; many reviewers have 100-1000+ hours
Wacky busted builds and hilarious late-run physics moments when the screen fills with projectiles
Large unlock and quest list (about 20 characters, 70+ items, 240 quests) and daily leaderboards give goals to chase
Impressive polish for a one-person project; runs fine on Steam Deck and Linux
Humor and memes, dumb-fun presentation and soundtrack land well for many players (a few critics found the music wears thin)
worst_things: Balance: a small set of 'meta' items, tomes, weapons and characters are required to beat the hardest tiers while many others are seen as useless
Luck and XP tomes are close to mandatory, eating passive slots and limiting build variety
Difficulty and enemy HP scaling spike hard at tier 3 / final bosses; runs can feel decided by RNG and meta items within the first minutes
Little enemy variety (mostly walk-at-you damage checks) and only two zones with shared bosses, so runs feel samey
Thin depth for survivors-like veterans: 'mile wide, inch deep', decisions often reduce to stacking damage or projectiles with few real synergies
Some bugs and frustrations noted, such as a boss able to spawn on top of the player, crashes on high-difficulty runs, and a wonky camera/visual clutter late in runs
Humor and meme references are a turn-off for some (IGN called the humor shoddy); community described as toxic by some reviewers
Update cadence: many players feel it reads like an early-access build with a long gap between content updates
improvements: A full balance pass so more weapons, tomes and characters are viable, plus real synergies rather than plain stat bumps
Rework or remove luck/XP tome dependence, for example turning them into permanent shop upgrades, and soften tier 3 enemy HP scaling
More content: additional maps and biomes, distinct bosses per zone, more enemy types
Co-op multiplayer, one of the most requested features (repeated in top positive reviews)
Fix the unlock pool dilution: let players remove or ban unlocked items from the drop pool more effectively
Regular communication and updates from the dev, and less design focus on the optimized YouTuber/leaderboard meta
unique_things: Essentially a 3D Vampire Survivors / Risk of Rain 2 hybrid, where vertical movement, jumping, sliding and fall damage are core
Characters with distinct movement traits (for example a wall-climbing Monke, slow Amog, fast skeleton)
Silver-shop meta-progression gives only rigging tools (rerolls, bans, skips) and no permanent stat upgrades, so each run starts equal
Chest cost scales with each chest opened, Risk of Rain-style, alongside shrines that offer percentile boosts
Daily leaderboards with Steam friends and a physics engine that lets builds get absurd; meme-heavy 90s low-poly art style
Built by a solo dev (Vedinad, widely speculated to be DaniDev of Crab Game and Muck) which became part of its story
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding for unlocks and quests; some achievements need things like a 300k-kill run or beating the hardest boss with a slow character while RNG cooperates
Resetting runs repeatedly to hunt for meta items, which players call an 'RNG reset simulator' at higher tiers
Item pool dilution: each new unlock makes desired items drop less often
Late-game visual clutter and boss mechanics (for example orb pushback during pillar charging in the desert final boss)
Early-game levels feel slow at base movement speed, with some saying faster movement requires exploiting an engine quirk
Shallow modifiers (gold, silver, knockback) that feel meaningless
Having to fill 2 of 4 passive slots with XP/luck/difficulty boosters every run, which reviewers call lame and build-limiting
divisive_points: Whether the game is 'finished': defenders say a $10 game with no microtransactions owes nothing more, critics say it feels like early access and is abandoned
Meme humor and aesthetic: charming and funny to many, cringe to others
Difficulty and meta: some see hard tier 3 as an enjoyable challenge and a skill issue, others see it as forcing the same builds
Whether it is a derivative combination of Vampire Survivors and Risk of Rain 2, or a fresh and well-tuned blend of them
community.reception_notes: Launch was a viral success (1M+ copies in about two weeks, about 117k peak CCU, early Steam reviews around 95%+ positive). It was delayed two weeks from Sept 4 to Sept 18, 2025 to dodge Hollow Knight: Silksong. The dev withdrew the game from The Game Awards 2025 Best Debut Indie nomination because of prior work under other names, and the game was later nominated for a Steam Awards category. Critics (Destructoid, PC Gamer, Gamereactor, TheGamer, Rogueliker) were very positive; IGN was more mixed, citing limited map variety and humor. Post-launch, long-term players turned critical over balance and update gaps, with a first major (Halloween) update arriving around December and several patches later (1.0.12 pinned), plus community forum threads asking whether the game is abandoned. A newer Steam review (about a year after release) defends the dev for finishing a cheap game. Windows and Linux only per Steam (no Mac). Note: 'Megabonk Apocalypse' on Steam is an unrelated title by another publisher (TinyBig). Sales are the Wikipedia figure; SteamSpy and revenue-calculator data pulled locally were empty. OpenCritic page could not be located (search budget exhausted, guessed IDs returned other games).

games.name: Sephiria
games.short_description: Save Bunnyville from a doomed fate: a top-down action/RPG roguelite from the makers of Dungreed. Explore the depths of the tower, collect and upgrade artifacts, and defeat hordes of demons to keep your village safe.

other_scores.source: TheSixthAxis (9/10, also shown as 90 on Metacritic)

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put this as like a high high A tier and it could easily be an S tier. ... It's gained the highest of A tiers.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Sephiria is a top-down action roguelike dungeon crawler from the makers of Dungreed, currently in early access. Its hook is an inventory-placement system where artifacts and item positions power up your build rather than traditional leveling. He loves the adventure feel, story, weapon variety, pre-run customization and music. He calls it a hidden gem deserving more attention, placing it at the top of A tier with S potential if balance and content improve.
praise: Inventory management as the core progression: artifact placement buffs items, and level-6 items do drastically different things
Each weapon feels distinct, with special abilities, dash attacks, dashes and combos; gameplay more satisfying than Dungreed
Strong adventure, story and hub side-quest feel (even a creepy horror-tinged quest); each early-access update adds content
Lots of pre-run customization via multiple upgradeable 'mirrors' giving permanent stats, plus a newly added starting-item pool
Heat-style difficulty system that rewards permanent progression
Every run feels unique, with varied bosses and mini-bosses per biome; killer music
criticism: Elemental builds (fire, lightning) feel much stronger than anything else and are too easy to just collect into
Melee/stat builds require juggling many item types while elemental items all just work, so items need to be more flexible
Mana/spell system feels weak, unnecessary and not loved; spells not impactful
Same biomes and few secrets per run, and the true final boss is still missing in early access
Wants more secrets and alternate biomes like Dungreed had
unique_points: Inventory layout and artifact placement replace stat-based leveling as the way you get stronger
Many different mirror-style permanent upgrade tracks that you can keep switching between each run
Tablet imprint mechanic that embeds tablets without using an inventory slot; he wishes it could be a core, occasional option
Multiplayer support, which he has not tried
commentary.quote: This is another absolute hidden gem.
design_criteria: Build/inventory synergies: placement strategy and artifacts are the core, but elemental builds dominate
Combat feel: weapon diversity and satisfying moveset
Meta-progression: many mirrors, hub unlocks, starting-item pool
Replayability/run variety: unique runs despite repeated biomes
Difficulty: heat-style system with permanent rewards
Story/adventure and immersion: hub quests and ongoing content updates
Balance: elemental versus non-elemental and mana/spells
Audio: praised music
Content/boss variety: two boss and mini-boss variants per biome, missing final boss

community.one_liner: A top-down pixel-art action roguelite from Team Horay (makers of Dungreed) where you play a bunny defending Bunnyville, building power by fitting artifacts and tablets into a Tetris-like inventory grid, with up to 4-player online co-op.
community.consensus_summary: Sephiria is received as one of the best recent action roguelites: the local Steam snapshot shows about 12,970 reviews at 94.5% positive (Very Positive), and the Steam store page showed an Overwhelmingly Positive rating earlier (97% of roughly 2.9k reviews), so sentiment has cooled slightly as the audience widened at 1.0. Players and critics praise the inventory-puzzle build system, big weapon/costume variety, pixel art and co-op. The two Metacritic critic reviews are 90 (TheSixthAxis) and 83 (This Is Game). Complaints cluster around netcode and disconnect-loses-the-run in multiplayer, artificial pacing gates, boss design that pushes evasion builds, and repetitiveness after many hours. It left Early Access (April 2025) for a full release on July 31, 2026, and some fans felt little was added between the last EA build and 1.0.
best_things: The inventory-management build system (placing artifacts/relics around tablets and talismans in a grid) is called unique and addictive; several reviewers describe optimizing the grid as the core puzzle of the game
Large variety of weapons (6 main weapon types, each with 50+ upgrades that change how it plays), costumes with unique stats and set bonuses, and artifacts gives many viable, distinct builds
Snappy, responsive combat with a wide range of archetypes (tank, greatsword, bomber, frost, lightning, meteor mage)
Clean, expressive pixel art and cute character designs; boss music and chill soundtrack are singled out
Smooth progression curve: weapons, artifacts and unlocks are introduced gradually, with very wide meta-progression and plenty of secrets to unlock
Co-op for up to 4 is seen as well balanced and a standout feature for playing with a partner or friends; you can leave a co-op run and return to your own village
Strong quality-of-life features such as loadout preferences and control over favored item spawn rates, plus multiple difficulty levels
Large amount of content and polish with a charming story and lots of care from a small studio; players report hundreds of hours
worst_things: Multiplayer netcode: delay-based and server-priority hit registration makes dodging unreliable for clients, especially at 100+ ping; many negative reviews are purely about this
A disconnect or host drop ends the run for everyone with no rejoin and no mid-run save, which can waste an hour or more; it also happens on LAN for some players
Progress can be lost on game crashes, reported by some players including on Linux
Boss design: large unavoidable-feeling attacks, unclear telegraphs, long invulnerable phases, and one boss with a screen-wide tentacle barrage that some find annoying or unfair
No epilepsy or photosensitivity warning and no flashing-reduction toggle despite a newer chapter 3 boss with map-wide flashing attacks; raised repeatedly by affected players and their friends
Some reviewers find combat shallow or hollow (one-button combos) and enemy rooms either too easy early or visual damage-soup late
Story is called over-the-top or cliche by some, and cutscenes/dialogue get skipped; boss cutscenes are repetitive when retrying
Localization quality issues (for example a Russian reviewer rates the current translation about 4/10)
improvements: Add rejoin/reconnect and a mid-run save or checkpoint for multiplayer and crashes; several reviewers suggest a save point after the first boss
Move to client-side hit detection or rollback-style netcode so non-hosts are not penalised
Add an epilepsy warning and a flashing-effects toggle, plus other accessibility options such as OLED-friendly text colors and a way to disable hold-to-continue prompts
Rebalance evasion/defense builds and healing scarcity so tanking and offensive builds are viable; tune boss telegraphs and invulnerability phases
Reduce the artificial progression gates (some chapters require extra runs for small lore rewards) and speed up meta-progression and rewards for winning runs
Improve translations and add more post-1.0 content (players noted little changed between Early Access and release); a voting system for which floor to take in co-op was also suggested
unique_things: The Tetris-like inventory grid where artifact placement next to tablets and talismans is the main source of power, comparable by one reviewer to a Materia or Attache Case system
Deep roguelite meta-loop with a village (Bunnyville) and story chapters gated behind repeated runs
Weapon upgrade system where anvil upgrades make the same weapon play like a different one
Costumes that act as class-like set bonuses (evasive cat, big-inventory fox, fast white wolf, scholar lizard) with trade-offs
Co-op where main story progression belongs to the session host while you can still return to your own village
Dungreed-style synergy ideas expanded into the central build mechanic, presented in cute bunny-themed pixel art
tedious_or_disliked: Runs get long (an hour or more for some) and the constant inventory shuffling plus fast-travel backtracking through non-continuous map paths pads the time
Repetition after roughly 20+ hours: players settle into one build and have little reason to vary it because the game is easy once core synergies click
Padding in progression: extra runs demanded per chapter and slow meta unlocks feel like a grind
Late-game boss fights described as bosses spamming hard-to-avoid attacks; the final boss can kill in one attack and delete an hour or two of progress
Evasion is widely seen as mandatory, which flattens build diversity at the top end
divisive_points: Difficulty: some call it very difficult and hectic, others say it becomes trivial after a few talents and that evasion is overpowered
Inventory management: praised as the best feature by most, but described as 50% of the game and a time sink by a few (even a joking positive review calls it a puzzle game)
Build variety: praised as huge by many, but others feel builds are a checklist and that costume set bonuses lock you into specific routes
Story: sweet and charming for some, cliche and skippable for others
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched April 3, 2025 and 1.0 released July 31, 2026 on Windows and Mac (no Linux build, though some players report running it on Linux). Launch at 1.0 brought a larger audience and a dip from about 97% to about 94.5% positive, driven by multiplayer netcode, disconnect handling, pacing/padding, and the lack of epilepsy warning after a new chapter 3 alternate boss. Metacritic has no Metascore yet (only 2 of 4 required critic reviews) and the user score rests on just 6 ratings; OpenCritic could not be found. Revenue estimate from the local data (Boxleiter-style, unaudited) is about $1.4M gross and $415k net, with estimated owners of 100k-200k and a price of $17.99; treat as order of magnitude. Peak concurrency in the local snapshot was about 2,268. A WebSearch budget cap prevented additional searches, and Reddit could not be fetched, so community detail comes mainly from Steam reviews and discussion topics.

games.name: Shape Shifter: Formations
games.short_description: Shape Shifter: Formations is an action twin-stick shooter with rogue-lite elements, where you must destroy hordes of geometric enemies alone or with a friend. Select your ship and combine a large variety of weapons, abilities and infinitely stacking upgrades to craft your own unique build.

other_scores.score: about $55.8k gross, $16.4k net (Boxleiter estimate; no copies figure given)

placements.verbal_evidence: this might be an S tier game for me. Maybe the highest A tiers.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: A neon-styled survivor-like where you pilot a small ship with a single aimed weapon, a dash and a ship-specific ultimate. It was sent in by a viewer and he says he has sunk huge hours into it. He is blown away by the amount of content, build variety and level-up choice depth, calling it one of his favorite survivor-likes and a hidden gem. Main gripes are slow unlocking of build potential and uneven boss design. He hedges between S and top of A.
praise: Absurd amount of content: roughly 20 ships, about 15 weapons, many unlocks via achievements
Level-up screens offer four choices that can be banished, skipped, rerolled, duplicated, plus a glitch system that can double an upgrade
Upgrades are mostly mechanical rather than number tweaks, with builds that synergize across corrosion, lightning, fire and more
Multiple layered progression trees (skill tree, paragon, ultimate tree) plus rare legendary upgrades with big impact
Shop fills with new mechanics as you unlock, giving lots of player choice
Chaotic, satisfying neon visuals and tight control with close dodges feeling great
Has co-op/multiplayer and strong solo play
criticism: Takes a while to get going since you must unlock a lot to have real build potential
Number-adjustment trees (skill tree/paragon) unlock late; he wishes they came earlier
No luck stat, which he feels the game could benefit from
Some bosses are far harder than others
Some bosses have no adds, which undercuts on-kill and bounce synergies
Some balance issues here and there
unique_points: Single-weapon, dash and ultimate core loop differs from typical multi-weapon survivor-likes
Level-up manipulation tools (banish, reroll, duplicate, tag prioritizing/removal) are something he has not seen elsewhere
Legendary artifact unlocks found roughly once every few runs that alter on-kill/on-hit behavior
commentary.quote: this might be an S tier game for me. Maybe the highest A tiers.
design_criteria: Synergies: builds intertwine across damage types and mechanics
Build diversity: many ships, weapons and upgrade paths
Player choice: heavy level-up and shop options with manipulation tools
Meta-progression: multiple skill trees, achievements, unlocks, though slow start
Visuals/charm: neon art style and chaotic spectacle
Boss/enemy design: uneven difficulty and bosses lacking adds
Balance: some tuning issues
Game feel: control and dodging satisfaction

commentary.label: Top 10 of 2025 (#9)
commentary.summary: Shape Shifter Formations is a neon twin-stick survivor-like where you pick a ship and weapon and fight hordes of geometric shapes. He calls it an absolute hidden gem and says it surprised him after more than 50 survivor-likes this year. He stresses the diverse, interesting upgrades and the level-up manipulation tools, plus smooth gameplay and satisfying effects. He strongly recommends it to survivor-like fans and notes it has gotten little recognition. It lands at number 9 on his 2025 list.
praise: In-game upgrades are very interesting and allow a huge amount of build diversity
Once meta progression is unlocked, players can roll, banish, lock, transmutate or dual-select upgrades, making level-ups strategic
Upgrade choices stay exciting throughout the whole late game
Gameplay is very smooth for the genre
Visual effects are amazingly satisfying
Large content: 20 ships, 20 weapons, 193 unique upgrades
criticism: Unlocking the important meta progression can admittedly take a while
Has received very little recognition (a discoverability issue rather than a design flaw)
unique_points: Upgrade manipulation tools (roll, banish, lock, transmutate, dual select) add real decision-making to level-ups in a genre often lacking it
Makes upgrade selection exciting even in the late game, which he rarely sees in survivor-likes
commentary.quote: I cannot remember the last time I had a survivor-like game get me this excited about choosing upgrades
design_criteria: Upgrade diversity: how many distinct build options the upgrades allow
Level-up decision-making: tools to shape which upgrades you get
Meta progression: unlocks that gate key features, somewhat slow
Game feel: smoothness of gameplay
Visual effects: how satisfying they are
Content volume: ships, weapons and upgrade counts

community.one_liner: A Geometry Wars-style neon twin-stick shooter / bullet-heaven roguelite by Castec Studios with 20 ships, 20 weapons, a huge skill-tree meta layer and infinitely stacking in-run upgrades, playable solo or in local co-op.
community.consensus_summary: Players receive it very warmly: about 91% of roughly 276 Steam reviews are positive (Very Positive), with many reviewers logging 50 to 270 hours. It left Early Access (entered Sept 2023) with a 1.0 release on May 27, 2025, followed by a run of hotfixes through 1.0.4 in late June 2025, so it is a finished game that has been actively patched. Commercially it is a small niche title: a third-party Boxleiter-style estimate puts it near $56k gross (about $16k net); no copies-sold figure was published by the source (SteamSpy range 0-20,000 owners), and one reviewer says it deserved far more success. No professional critic coverage or Metacritic/OpenCritic scores were found; Metacritic has a page but shows no critic or user score yet. Complaints cluster around opaque unlock and upgrade information, occasional performance drops at high threat levels, and a lack of online co-op.
best_things: Deep build variety: 20 ships, 20 weapons, about 800 skills in skill trees, and 200+ infinitely stacking upgrades make runs feel different

Level-up choice tools (reroll, banish, lock, transmute, dual pick, plus a tag system to promote or blacklist upgrade tags) give real control over builds, which reviewers say keeps late-run picks exciting
Strong Geometry Wars feel with clean, readable neon visuals; reviewers say they rarely got lost even in hectic moments
Satisfying meta-progression and unlock loop that gives a 'one more run' hook and starts paying off once you unlock more of the skill tree
Difficulty is seen as fair, with scaling threat levels and deaths that usually feel like build or skill problems rather than pure RNG
Good local co-op and ongoing developer support (1.0 added a final boss arena, three save profiles, and several balance/bug patches)
Flexible settings: optional auto-aim, toggle auto-fire added in 1.0.1 for accessibility, and a granular difficulty-modifier system
Runs are around 30 minutes with an endless mode, so they are easy to fit into short sessions
worst_things: Many unlocks do not say how to get them; a reviewer could not work out how to unlock the Swarm ship because locked items do not name what unlocks them
No wiki or official Discord was noted by one negative reviewer at 1.0, which makes the opaque unlock system worse

Performance: a Steam Deck reviewer measured FPS dropping to 1-2 for seconds at threat level 25 and occasional full freezes; another positive reviewer had to change video settings to get normal performance
Save-data loss reported by at least one reviewer (51 hours lost), and the Steam forum has a pinned 1.0 saves notice and a bug about restarts forgetting tags and bans
Startup problems reported on the forum: hangs on first launch and prompts to install the .NET Framework
Some upgrade text is unclear or misleading (for example, how overkill works, and '100% reduction' not reducing a duration to zero)
Balance gaps: the stealth ship is called overpowered and long-range/auto-target weapons much easier than others; one forum thread calls Ability Duration Up bad
improvements: Add online co-op; reviewers note the game only has local co-op and the forum has a complaint about needing a controller in multiplayer
Explain unlock conditions and upgrade mechanics better in-game (name the item an unlock requires, tooltips for overkill, dual pick and percentage stacking), or provide a wiki
Fix performance spikes at high threat levels and Steam Deck stutters
Rebalance ships and weapons so non-stealth ships and manual-aim weapons compete, and buff weak upgrades like Ability Duration Up
Improve save reliability and preserve tags and bans when restarting a run
Add more content after 1.0 (reviewers explicitly hope for more)
unique_things: Tag system that lets you promote or blacklist upgrade categories in the level-up pool, which one reviewer credits with dramatically improving the roguelike element versus similar games
Unusual level-up options: reroll, banish, lock, transmute and dual select in the same run
Geometry Wars twin-stick action fused with a survivor-like/bullet-heaven upgrade structure and infinite stacking upgrades
Ship-specific and weapon-specific skill trees with around 800 skills, giving much deeper pre-run customization than typical bullet-heavens
Threat-level (heat/NG+) scaling and endless looping with rising enemy counts
Community-made UEVR mod lets you play it in VR, which a reviewer raves about
tedious_or_disliked: Slow start: one reviewer says it takes a while to get going and feels weak until you unlock skill-tree nodes
Unlock grind: a player at 12 hours had unlocked only about 25% of content and found the hidden unlock conditions annoying
Chaotic late-game screens for players using non-auto-target weapons, where dodging and max damage dominate
Performance stalls mid-run that cannot be played around because the ship is immobile or the run ends
divisive_points: Grind: one reviewer calls it one of the best 'mindless grind' roguelikes while another finds the unlock system frustratingly opaque
Balance of ease versus challenge: some reviewers say difficulty is well tuned with a good threat spike, while others find non-stealth and manual-aim ships much harder than auto-target builds
Local-only co-op is praised as great co-op by some and a dealbreaker limitation by others
community.reception_notes: Early Access began Sept 29, 2023; 1.0 launched May 27, 2025 at $14.99 (Windows only) and was followed by hotfixes 1.0.1 and 1.0.2 (May 30), 1.0.3 (June 6, balance and boss fixes) and 1.0.4 (June 25, bug fixes). Steam reviews continued through 2026 with some of the most enthusiastic from players with hundreds of hours, and a review from a YouTube bullet-heaven reviewer recommended it highly. Negative reviews are a small minority (24 of 276) and mainly cite saves, performance and opaque unlocks. The game was not found on any critic aggregator with scores. Research limitation: the session web-search budget was exhausted, so no outlet reviews, Reddit threads or OpenCritic data were retrievable; findings rest on Steam reviews, the Steam store, news feed and forum, Metacritic page status and the revenue estimate.
