games.name: SWORN
games.short_description: SWORN is a 1-4 player co-op action rogue-like. Explore and reclaim a fallen Camelot from the reign of a corrupted Arthur and his Knights of the Round Table.

other_scores.score: Very Positive, about 80% positive of roughly 5,185 reviews (store page showed 82% of 2,696 at a different time)

placements.verbal_evidence: So, this is going to be a solid A tier.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Sworn is a multiplayer-focused Hades-like that openly mimics Hades in music, animation style, gods and boss structure. He finds it a well-made near-spin-off, with heavy roguelite progression and lots of pre-run customization. He was a bit disappointed that the full release added little over early access, and he notes lingering bugs. Despite being not very unique, he respects the effort required to make a Hades-like and places it in a solid A tier.
praise: Huge pre-run customization: four characters, four weapons each, four spells each, with flippable variations
Distinct meta-progression with multiple skill trees (support, god, defense, offense), some flippable into two versions
Weapons, spells and boons feel good and support many different build paths
Final boss and true final boss are really well designed
Art style is fairly different from Hades and the music is good
Executes the Hades formula very well, feeling like a spin-off; added voice acting at full release
criticism: Full release added little over early access, leaving him a bit disappointed
Bosses are always the same; he hoped for variations
Heavy meta-progression: weapons can be terrible without upgrade-branch investment, which he wished was toned down
Still has bugs, including boons whose numbers do not change and a stuck on-screen text visual bug
Story and characters engage him less than Hades; not very unique overall
unique_points: Multiplayer-focused Hades-like, which Hades itself lacks (he only played solo)
Loadout diversity is intended so players in multiplayer do not all share the same setup
Doing a good Hades-like is much harder than a survivor-like, which earns it respect despite heavy copying
commentary.quote: It's just Hades. It doesn't even try to hide it.
design_criteria: Customization/variety: character, weapon and spell combinations before a run
Meta-progression: multiple skill trees, but weapon-upgrade gating is too heavy
Boss design: strong final bosses but repetitive regular bosses
Game feel: weapons, spells and boons feel good
Build diversity: many paths to different builds
Originality: heavy derivation from Hades limits uniqueness
Polish: remaining bugs and non-working boons
Art and audio: distinct art style, good music
Story: added voice acting but less engaging than Hades
commentary.rerank_note: Was covered in early access previously; after full release his thoughts have not changed much and he places it in A tier.

commentary.label: Top 10 of 2025 (#10)
commentary.summary: Sworn is an action roguelike that borrows very heavily from Hades. He says a good Hades-like needs a lot of content, build variety, meta progression, customizable starts, distinct biomes, varied monsters and strong bosses, and that Sworn delivers on all of it. It lands at number 10 on his 2025 list mainly because it does little to stand apart from Hades. Even so, he counts it among his favorite action roguelike experiences of the year.
praise: Gameplay feels great
Boons have cool designs that make runs differ from one another
Lots of pre-run customization
16 weapons and 16 spells give top-notch replayability
Plenty of content, meta progression, distinct biomes, varied monsters and cool bosses
Emphasis on co-op, which Hades lacks
criticism: Very little makes it stand out compared to Hades
Lack of uniqueness is what keeps it from ranking higher
unique_points: Its co-op focus is the main differentiator from Hades
Shows what a solid Hades-like requires: content volume, build variety, meta progression, customizable starts, distinct biomes
commentary.quote: There isn't much that makes this game stand out compared to Hades.
design_criteria: Content volume: needs lots of content to sustain a Hades-like
Build variety: boons with distinct designs that make runs unique
Meta progression: tons of it expected and present
Customizable starts: pre-run customization boosts variety
Biome and enemy design: distinguishable biomes, wide monster variety, cool bosses
Replayability: 16 weapons and 16 spells
Originality: lack of uniqueness caps its ranking
Game feel: gameplay feels great
Co-op: a differentiating feature

community.one_liner: A 1-4 player co-op, Hades-style isometric action roguelite by Windwalk Games (published by Team17) in which you play a Soulforged champion retaking a corrupted Camelot from Arthur and the Knights of the Round Table.
community.consensus_summary: SWORN is received as a competent, fun but heavily derivative 'Hades with co-op': Steam sits at Very Positive (about 80% of roughly 5,200 reviews) while Metacritic's three critic reviews land between 73 and 85 and its user score is a Mixed 7.2. Players most often say it is worth buying on sale, mainly with friends, and that solo it feels like a slower, less polished, less charming clone. The biggest recurring sore spot is multiplayer stability: disconnects are common and there is no way to rejoin or save a run, which drives most of the negative Steam reviews. It left Early Access (started Feb 2025) with a 1.0 launch on Sep 23, 2025; recent Steam reviews were noticeably worse than all-time at one point (Mixed, about 64%), with some players fearing slowed support and missing content, though later reviews mention new content updates.
best_things: Four-player co-op is the main selling point; many reviewers say it is the best part and the reason to pick this over Hades itself
Build variety from four characters, each with four weapons and four spells, plus 200+ blessings from eight fae lords, yielding very different builds
Solid, responsive moment-to-moment combat with both controller and keyboard and mouse
Boss fights are frequently singled out as a highlight (King Arthur especially), with alternative bosses per act and a boss rush mode
Strong Mignola-inspired hand-drawn art style and Arthurian setting
Good progression feel: every run earns resources and there are many things to unlock, giving a lot of hours of play (many reviewers at 40-100+ hours)
Challenge events and optional modifiers break up the room-clearing loop, and higher difficulties offer more variety
worst_things: Multiplayer disconnects are frequent and a dropped player (or host) cannot rejoin, so the whole run is lost; this is the single most common complaint in negative Steam reviews
No mid-run save and quit, so runs of 15-45+ minutes cannot be paused, and a crash loses everything
Seen as a near 1:1 Hades copy (room layouts, boon structure, duo boons, pets, hub) that lacks Hades' writing, voice acting, music and personality
Regular enemies and levels feel repetitive and copy-pasted, with few biomes and limited enemy variety
Slower, slightly clunky combat pacing (dodge cooldown, attack recovery, floaty movement) that stops players reaching a flow state; hits can feel cheap
Balance problems: some blessings and weapons are far stronger than others (Gogmagog repeatedly cited), while melee versus ranged balance and some weapons feel underwhelming
Story is thin and social/narrative content is sparse
Rough UX details: awkward controller menu navigation, small interaction ranges at the blacksmith, player collision in the hub, barebones options menu, hard-to-see cursor
Crashes and forced restarts during co-op sessions (some players report the game taking down their PC), adding to the lost-run frustration
improvements: Add rejoin-after-disconnect and more stable netcode/servers for co-op, and possibly host migration
Add save-and-quit mid-run for solo play
Unlock boss rush from the start and add a skip option for boss intro sequences
More content: additional biomes, bosses, routes, weapons, abilities and regular enemy types, plus clearer roadmap communication
Rebalance blessings, weapons and higher-difficulty enemy health so builds beyond the top few are viable and fights are not damage-sponge slogs
More impactful upgrades and meta-progression (many are flat percentage bonuses) and better late-game rewards once currencies are capped
Crossplay, better in-game communication in co-op (only emotes and a few phrases), and more UI and controller polish
unique_things: Four-player online co-op in a Hades-like structure, which the original Hades lacks
Arthurian legend setting with a corrupted Camelot, Merlin's Soulforged champions, and fae lords as the blessing-givers
Class system: four distinct characters each with their own weapons and spells, rather than one protagonist with a weapon roster
Hand-drawn isometric art inspired by Mike Mignola
Boss rush mode and alternative bosses per act, plus a secret late area built around a curse mechanic
tedious_or_disliked: Higher difficulties: enemies become damage sponges and you must grind meta-progression before you can realistically progress
Early-game upgrades feel negligible until stacked, and weapon upgrade materials such as Holy Grail Water are scarce
Meta upgrades are described as boring flat bonuses and some players run out of meaningful currency sinks around the 15 hour mark
Boss rush is buried behind much of the game (roughly 15-30 minutes of a run to reach) and boss intro cutscenes cannot be skipped
The secret final area and the penultimate chapter were called unfun or pointless by some players because of the curse mechanic and wave-style combat
Losing long co-op runs to disconnects makes hour-long hard-difficulty runs feel risky
divisive_points: Hades comparison: some love having more Hades-style gameplay with co-op and call it a great clone, others dislike the derivative feel and lack of its own identity
Combat feel: some call it responsive, snappy and deep, others find it slower and clunky than Hades
Solo worth: several reviewers say it is only good with friends, while others with 50-100+ hours played it mostly solo and recommend it
Multiplayer reliability: some report 20+ hours of co-op with almost no issues and call the netcode robust after Early Access fixes, while many others report disconnects in most runs
community.reception_notes: Entered Steam Early Access on Feb 6, 2025 and launched 1.0 on Sep 23, 2025 (Windwalk Games, Team17). Some reviewers say the game felt better in Early Access than at release and that co-op was troubled during that time, while others say the multiplayer now feels solid; the no-rejoin and no-save complaints persist into 2026 reviews. Steam recent reviews were Mixed (about 64% of 65) when the store page was fetched, versus about 80% all-time, with players asking about roadmap communication and worrying support had slowed, though a few later reviews mention new content updates. Metacritic lists PS5, Xbox Series X, PC and Switch, while the Steam page only mentions Windows PC; no Metascore is assigned because only 3 critic reviews exist. Revenue estimate (third-party Boxleiter-style calculator, not audited): about $1.2M gross and $353K net; SteamSpy owners estimate 20,000-50,000. OpenCritic score could not be retrieved (search budget exhausted and page id unknown).

games.name: White Knuckle
games.short_description: White Knuckle is a first-person roguelite speed-climbing game. Ascend through the guts of SUB-STRUCTURE 17 using precision movement mechanics. Sharp reflexes and resource management will bring you out from under ten thousand meters of concrete and decay.

other_scores.score: 98% positive, Overwhelmingly Positive, 14,963 reviews (per local data)

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put this as a really solid A because of just how unique and enjoyable the gameplay is.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: White Knuckle is a first-person horror climbing roguelike in early access, where you grab surfaces with left and right mouse buttons and climb out of a hellish place while a rising ooze chases you. He finds it very unique, intense and immersive, with a very high skill ceiling and a stressful, punishing feel. His main complaints are that it takes too long to reach its best content and that it lacks meta progression. He recommends it for players who want a hardcore experience and places it in A tier.
praise: Highly unique combination of climbing, horror and a Portal-like comedic radio voice
Minimalistic controls that are hard to master, giving a very high skill ceiling
Many varied biomes and hidden late-game areas he calls awesome
Immersive, spooky and intensely stressful atmosphere
Lots of secrets and a strong community (debug world, terminal secret area), reminiscent of Inscryption
Stamina and grip mechanics that reward experimentation
Extra roguelike game mode with more replayability
criticism: Very punishing: a big fall can end a long run, and runs take a long time
Most players never see the later biomes because of difficulty; it takes too long to get there
Little meta progression; the shortcut system is so cruel it is not worth using
Consumables with hidden effects are unhelpful and mean in such a punishing game
Few passives, some much weaker than others; room layouts become repetitive once seen
unique_points: Fuses first-person climbing with horror and a Portal-like comedic radio narrator
Campaign is a fixed biome order with randomness only from picking room layouts from a library
Hidden debug-world secret reachable via terminal commands found by the community
commentary.quote: I'm going to put this as a really solid A
design_criteria: Uniqueness: rare genre combination of climbing and horror
Difficulty: extremely punishing, high skill ceiling, hurts accessibility
Meta-progression: minimal, shortcuts not worth using
Run length: very long runs make failure costly
Level design: fixed biomes with randomized room layouts from a library
Atmosphere/immersion: spooky and stressful with comedic radio narration
Item design: hidden consumables that are opaque and frustrating
Replayability: extra roguelike mode adds more, campaign is one-and-done
Secrets/community: lots of secrets and discovery

commentary.label: Top 10 of 2025 (#8)
commentary.summary: White Knuckle is a first-person climbing horror roguelike where an unfortunate character tries to escape horrors by going ever upward. He calls it possibly the most unique game on his list, blending 3D platforming with horror. The mechanics are easy to grasp but have a very high skill ceiling, and the story mode is an excellent adventure. He admits it is the hardest to recommend because it is punishing and very stressful, but still suggests trying this stressful gem, especially in early access.
praise: Most unique game on the list, mixing 3D platforming and horror, two uncommon roguelike subgenres
Simple to understand but with an extremely high skill ceiling
Dedicated community showing insane climbing speed is fun to watch
Main story mode is an incredible adventure
Each biome is unique, with its own disturbing and fun obstacles
criticism: Very punishing and possibly the most stressful roguelike he has played, which can be a pro or con
Early section is constantly on the clock, leaving beginners little room to experiment and risking missing later highlights
Early section differs wildly from the rest of the game
Roguelike elements are not the focal point
Community speed feats can be discouraging; content still thin in early access (wants more biomes, layouts, secrets, consumables, passives)
unique_points: Combines 3D platforming and horror in a roguelike, a rare pairing
Climbing upward as the escape loop, with a high skill-ceiling movement core
commentary.quote: this stressful gem
design_criteria: Uniqueness: rare genre blend of 3D platforming and horror
Skill ceiling: simple mechanics but very high mastery potential
Level/biome design: each biome has distinct obstacles
Difficulty/accessibility: punishing and stressful, harsh for beginners
Roguelike depth: elements are secondary, wants more consumables and passives
Content/replayability: wants more biomes, layouts and secrets in early access

community.one_liner: A first-person roguelite speed-climbing horror game where you grab ledges with left and right mouse buttons and ascend the vast SUB-STRUCTURE 17 while monsters, hazards and permadeath push you along.
community.consensus_summary: Players love it: Steam lists it as Overwhelmingly Positive at about 98% of roughly 15,000 reviews (14,662 positive, 301 negative), and the review sample shows very high playtimes (many 60 to 400+ hours), which signals unusual stickiness. The tactile two-hand climbing, the horror atmosphere and a very high skill ceiling that feeds a speedrun community are the headline praise. It launched in Early Access on 17 April 2025 from Dark Machine Games and publisher DreadXP, and reviews from late 2025 into 2026 describe regular large content drops (new regions such as the Nest, an Endless mode, an elevator for skipping climbs). Formal critic coverage is thin: Metacritic shows only two early critic reviews without a score, and I could not find an OpenCritic page. The small negative camp mostly likes the core climbing but dislikes permadeath, lack of mid-run saves, RNG perks and harsh late-game enemies.
best_things: Climbing feel: holding ledges with separate left and right mouse buttons feels tactile and physical, and players compare the immersion to Shadow of the Colossus-style grabbing
Very high skill ceiling; a first campaign clear can take an hour or more while top players finish in under 10 to 20 minutes, which drives heavy speedrun/competitive engagement
Sweaty-palm tension: horror atmosphere, sound design and the constant risk of falling combine into genuine anxiety, with no easy respawn or checkpoint
Environments become more colorful and varied as you ascend, and a full-scale structure with no loading screens gives a strong sense of place
Depth layered under a simple premise: secret rooms, item caches, facility upgrades, artifacts, and lore people keep uncovering after the first clear
Frequent substantial content updates during Early Access (new regions, Endless mode, new perks/artifacts) keep long-time players returning

Distinctive dark humor and community in-jokes (roach currency at vending machines, a joke-review culture around the elevator), plus controller support although keyboard and mouse is widely considered best
Critics who covered early builds noted it was nearly bug-free for Early Access and had a motivating faster-and-longer loop
Streamer-driven word of mouth: several top reviews say they bought it after watching Jerma struggle with it, and many joke-reviews celebrate the clenching tension
worst_things: Permadeath sends you back to the start of a long run; many negative reviewers say progress loss is soul-crushing and time-wasting, especially for new players
No cheap mid-run save: saving and quitting is costly (bugs currency) or awkward, and floppy-disk backups only respawn you at the computer where you inserted them
Late-game areas (the Abyss, Hanging Gardens, later regions) are called brutally hard, with enemies like the flying head and harpoon barnacles criticised as frustrating or unfair on precarious terrain
Heavy trial-and-error: several reviewers describe the campaign as a series of knowledge checks, and deaths can feel like they come from RNG or ragdoll/enemy randomness rather than player error
Physically demanding for long sessions; one older reviewer found the continuous intense mouse-and-keyboard input exhausting
Grab detection is seen by some as finicky (crosshair must sit on a hold for a moment), making recoveries inconsistent
Recent regions (the Nest) were criticised by a few high-hour players as repetitive, visually hard to read and thin on tile variety
Roguelike layer feels thin to some: perks are rarely offered and lackluster, so there is little power-growth excitement compared with other roguelikes
improvements: Add a casual/campaign mode with checkpoints or persistent progress so players can reach new areas without replaying old ones
Make saving and quitting mid-run cheaper and more accessible, or let floppy-disk backups be banked or transferred between computers
Rebalance late-game enemies (Abyss and Hanging Gardens threats, harpoon barnacles) and reconsider the gun-driven last section
Clean up or merge the perk pool so weak perks do not dilute runs, and make perk offers feel more impactful
Improve transparency of mechanics such as inventory weight and its effect on movement speed, and add clearer on-screen tutorials
Commonly requested extras: a relaxed zen/no-enemy mode, a level editor or workshop, and more cosmetic/collectible content
unique_things: A first-person climbing roguelite where your two hands are literally the core input, which almost no other game matches
Runs are a vertical ascent through a single continuous megastructure (SUB-STRUCTURE 17) rather than generic room-to-room levels
Horror that comes from physical exertion and fear of falling, not jump scares; chasing threats like the Mass force you to keep moving fast
Speedrun-first design: a built-in timer, a competitive mode that trims the perk pool, and a community that clears the campaign in minutes
Endless mode with an Abyss section where players compete for altitude (one reviewer reports steady runs around 5000 m)
Roach/bug currency, vending machines, floppy-disk lives and computer respawn points as a quirky meta-layer
tedious_or_disliked: Replaying the same early regions every run because there are no real checkpoints is the most repeated complaint
Long time per run before reaching the next section, which punishes players with limited play time
Low-value or rarely offered perks can make early runs feel empty when RNG gives nothing useful
Rage-inducing hazards in the Abyss and Hanging Gardens where enemies block or harpoon you mid-traverse
Repeated tile reuse in newer regions makes Endless mode feel like a slog to some veterans
divisive_points: Roguelite structure: fans see permadeath and randomness as the tension that makes it special, while several reviewers call it a great climbing game held back by being a roguelike
Difficulty of late-game and new content updates: hardcore players welcome the challenge, but some high-hour players say recent regions are overtuned or less fun than earlier builds
Input method and stress: some call it relaxing, others find it physically and mentally exhausting, and there is debate whether permanent progression and perks smooth or distort the skill challenge
community.reception_notes: Launched into Early Access on 17 April 2025 (Steam, Windows only, about $16.99 in local data) with a demo available, and the original roadmap cited about a year in Early Access with seven regions and extra modes. By 2026 Steam reviews mention multiple large content drops including the Nest region and Endless mode changes; the store listing in local data still shows the Early Access genre tag. Streamer exposure (for example Jerma and Spiff are named in Steam reviews) appears to have driven discovery. Steam-revenue-calculator.com estimates roughly $2.8M gross and $833K net revenue, but it appears to use an old review count (5,230), so this likely underestimates; SteamSpy in local data lists 100,000 to 200,000 owners. Metacritic shows only two early critic reviews (Try Hard Guides and Loot Level Chill) and no Metascore or user score. No OpenCritic page was found. I was unable to run web searches (session search budget exhausted) and could not read Reddit, so community detail relies on Steam reviews plus fetched pages; I could not verify exact patch names or dates.

games.name: Absolum
games.short_description: Fight as the outcast heroes of Talamh in a fierce battle to retake magic from Sun King Azra’s grasp in Absolum, an original roguelite beat ‘em up by Dotemu.

other_scores.source: Try Hard Guides / The Outerhaven / Eurogamer Germany

placements.verbal_evidence: this is going to be our first uh a tier of today

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Absolum is a 2D beat-em-up roguelike where you fight through a large adventure to beat the Sun King. He is pleasantly surprised that it pairs a very strong combat core with rich roguelike elements, which he normally sees as a trade-off. He finds it skill-heavy, rewarding, full of content and great to look and listen to. Flaws are minor: stun-lock, drop RNG, unclear hitboxes and thin tutorials. He places it as the first A tier of the video and highly recommends it.
praise: Combat is extremely satisfying, with flashy combos and clash slow-motion moments
Multiple characters with unique move sets and combos
Boons enhance attacks, specials and throws and can add new moves, so the same character plays differently each run
Varied boon effects (roses, fire, wind, bubbles) without feeling overwhelming
Skill-heavy and rewarding as mastery lets you trivialize bosses that once crushed you
Strong sense of adventure: story, quests, exploration and a world that feels new each run, plus good meta progression
Great replayability, enjoyable-looking co-op, fantastic music, sound and visuals
criticism: Easy to get stun-locked, especially early on
Some enemies can take half your health in one combo with little recourse
Drop RNG from barrels (money, health or nothing) can be punishing early
Some hitboxes are unclear
Wants more tutorials on combos and tips, especially in the mid game
unique_points: Fuses beat-em-up gameplay with roguelike elements, a rare genre combination
Has both a strong core gameplay and deep roguelike systems, which he usually sees as mutually limiting
Exploration and questing make each return from a run feel like visiting a new world
commentary.quote: an absolutely great game
design_criteria: Core gameplay feel: combat must be satisfying on its own
Roguelike elements/synergy: boons that alter attacks and add combos
Build diversity: same character plays differently per run
Difficulty/skill: skill-heavy and rewarding mastery
Content and meta progression: quests, story, exploration
Audio and visuals: music, sound effects, clash slow-motion
Randomness fairness: drop RNG and enemy variety
Clarity and onboarding: hitboxes and tutorials

commentary.label: Top 10 of 2025 (#6)
commentary.summary: Absolum is an adventure beat-em-up roguelike where outcast heroes try to take magic back from the sun king. He notes that good beat-em-ups are rare these days, and rarer still as roguelikes. He says it balances strong core combat with real roguelike components better than most. The world is large, with many levels, biomes, unlocks and side quests, and the pacing is strong. He calls it one of his favorite action-adventure roguelikes in recent years, and he keeps checking for updates while waiting for the full release.
praise: Very enjoyable core beat-em-up gameplay with satisfying combos and varied ways to approach fights
Unusually good balance of strong combat and strong roguelike components
Roguelike elements make each run feel unique
Massive world with many levels and biomes that immerses the player
Constant unlocks of new zones and side quests, with lots of content to discover
Great pacing with plenty of meta progression and things to do after every run
criticism: No real criticism given; he notes only that it is still in early access awaiting full release
Implicit genre caveat: games with strong core gameplay usually have much weaker roguelike elements, which Absolum avoids
unique_points: Beat-em-up roguelike is a rare combination
Manages both a great combat system and a strong roguelike layer, which is uncommon
Over 20 hours in, he still had runs with no fixed goal, showing how much persistent content there is
commentary.quote: Definitely one of my favorite action adventure rogikes in the last few years
design_criteria: Core combat: satisfying combos and multiple approaches to fights
Roguelike integration: run variety must stay strong alongside the combat
World and level design: large world with many levels and biomes
Content breadth: new zones, side quests and unlocks
Pacing: steady sense of progress after each run
Meta progression: plenty of persistent progression and post-run activities

community.one_liner: A hand-drawn, Hades-style roguelite side-scrolling beat 'em up with four playable heroes and two-player co-op, made by Guard Crush Games (Streets of Rage 4) and Supamonks and published by Dotemu.
community.consensus_summary: Absolum is very well received by both critics and players: Metacritic sits at 87 on PC (52 critic reviews) and PS5 (22 reviews), 89 on Switch (11 reviews) with only one mixed and none negative, and Steam shows about 92% positive across roughly 10,800 reviews (Very Positive). Praise centres on tight, satisfying combat, gorgeous animation and art, a strong soundtrack, and build variety. The main critic dissent is IGN's 70, which argued the roguelite structure does not serve the beat 'em up well. Players who dislike it mostly cite enemy-stacking and elite-enemy design in late game, hitbox and verticality problems, and online co-op instability. It is not early access: it launched in 1.0 on 9 Oct 2025, got the 1.1 'Threads of Fate' update in Feb 2026, full cross-platform multiplayer in May 2026 and another fix/tweak patch in Aug 2026. It has been nominated for The Game Awards 2025 Best Independent Game and won two Pegases awards.
best_things: Fluid, punchy combat with light/heavy chains, arcana specials and three defensive tools (dodge, deflect, clash) that reward timing; often compared favourably to Streets of Rage 4
Hand-drawn art and animation (Supamonks) widely called among the best 2D visuals of the year, with a soundtrack praised as memorable
Four heroes (Karl, Galandra, Cider, Brome) with distinct movesets and six arcanas each, so runs feel different and builds can get absurd and overpowered
Boon-like Ritual system with real synergies (water/tornado combos, thrown coins, thorn daggers, summons) that encourages experimentation
Excellent two-player couch co-op, repeatedly described as the best way to play, including parents playing with kids
Branching routes, secret areas, side quests and NPC stories give exploration and narrative texture beyond a plain arcade brawler
Boss fights described as deliberate and not just damage sponges; assist and difficulty options make it accessible to older or casual players
Good value at $24.99 for most reviewers, and runs well on Steam Deck
worst_things: Online co-op reliability: many negative Steam reviews cite disconnects, crashes mid-run and broken matchmaking, some saying it got worse after the crossplay update; no rejoin once dropped

Late-game and Corrupted Biome encounters flood the screen with enemies, teleporting-in attackers and projectiles hidden behind big enemies, plus bloated enemy HP pools in co-op, which many find unfair rather than hard
Hitbox and verticality complaints: enemy and boss attacks seem to reach past their animations or hit across the whole depth plane while the player must align precisely
Elite and super-armored enemies and shield enemies are seen as unengaging and punish defensive play; dodge is widely called weak compared with deflect and clash
Visual clutter and unclear telegraphs, plus a few reports of poor PC performance and softlock/stuck bugs
Some quests make the game harder with little or no reward (for example extra enemies or boss changes added permanently)
Co-op UI quirks: both players' inputs can hit the same NPC dialogue and trigger unwanted map changes; co-op lacks the solo difficulty sliders
improvements: Fix online co-op stability, allow reconnecting to a run, and only spend revive perks once both players are down
Balance rituals so weak or junky options and dominant elements (water, chaos) are more even and fewer boons feel like filler
Make dodge and defensive options more reliable against wide AoE, super-armor and shield enemies, and tidy hitboxes and telegraphs
Offer difficulty adjustment in multiplayer and reduce stacked late-game enemy spawns

More content and variety: levels feel repetitive across runs to some, the game is short for completionists (under 10 hours to clear everything for one reviewer), and fans ask for DLC, sequels and maybe four-player co-op
Stronger narrative integration; some critics found the story thin compared to the worldbuilding
unique_things: One of the few roguelites built on a true arcade beat 'em up foundation, from the Streets of Rage 4 co-developer, with fixed level layouts but randomised rituals and branching paths
Mounted combat: riding and taming creatures adds a different combat mode and is upgraded with elite mounts in 1.1
Clash mechanic (strong attack just before being hit) alongside dodge and deflect gives a parry-flavoured defence layer uncommon in brawlers
Persistent world with quests, NPC side stories and secret routes across runs, tied to a soul-tree meta progression and a harder true ending
Mystic Ordeals (custom run modifiers with shareable codes), Boss Rush and Horde modes added post-launch
Character-locked quirks: each hero's arcana and pickups (for example thrown objects as grenades, air-dash builds) can reshape how they play
tedious_or_disliked: Meta-progression grind and repeated runs through the same stages and bosses, especially for people who would prefer a one-shot arcade mode
Getting the true ending takes many runs and was called stretched out by some reviewers
Linear, mandatory stat upgrades in the meta tree rather than new options
Corrupted Biomes and elite enemies turning late runs into cheese-build checks
Having to wait for startup frames to clash or dodge instead of freely cancelling out of combos

Some players say the roguelite layer is weak: in-run upgrades mostly gate moves and meta upgrades are flat stat bumps (the most-upvoted negative reviews call it a great beat 'em up but a poor roguelike)
divisive_points: Roguelite structure itself: praised as what keeps it fresh and deep, but IGN and some players say it dilutes the beat 'em up and leans on numbers over skill
Combat depth: some call it simple but fun, others find the defensive system clunky or the combo limiter and spacing shallow
Art style and character design: near-universal praise, though a minority of Metacritic user reviews dislike the character designs
Difficulty: older or casual players love the assist options, while veterans complain about balance in corrupted late-game content
community.reception_notes: Launched 9 Oct 2025 on PC, PS4/PS5 and Switch; sold over 200,000 copies in week one and passed 500,000 by end of January 2026 (per Wikipedia). Xbox Series X/S (Game Pass) followed 25 Mar 2026; Switch 2 and mobile versions are listed for later in 2026. Patch history: a 23 Oct 2025 hotfix fixed softlocks; 1.1 'Threads of Fate' (Feb 2026) added Mystic Ordeals, Corrupted Biomes (replacing Rifts), new skins/emotes and upgraded elite mounts; full cross-platform multiplayer launched 12 May 2026; an Aug 2026 patch made Corrupted Biomes and Boss Rush available earlier, added quick restart, companion respawn, more dash cancels and many crash fixes. Steam negative reviews still heavily feature online co-op disconnects, with several saying it worsened after crossplay; some say late-game balance worsened after 1.1. Awards: The Game Awards 2025 nomination (Best Independent Game), D.I.C.E. Awards 2026 nomination (Action Game of the Year), two Pegases wins. OpenCritic score could not be retrieved (web search budget exhausted and the OpenCritic page was not fetchable), so it is null. Steam revenue estimate site returned $0 (no data), so no revenue figure is given. IGN, Reddit and Rock Paper Shotgun pages could not be fetched; their views come via Metacritic/Wikipedia summaries.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Brutal Orchestra is a turn-based, positioning-focused tragedy game where a dead protagonist travels through a weird in-between realm with a party of misfits. He loves its disturbing, distinct vibe, art, music and highly unique colored-pigment combat, and he played through to the true final boss. His main complaints are that the roguelike layer is minor, abilities and items barely change between runs, and unlocks come too slowly. He places it in low A tier.
praise: Extremely distinct art style, music and disturbing overall vibe
Very unique gameplay built on colored pigment mana and overflow damage
Strong emphasis on positioning for both attacks and evading, with depth despite simple abilities
Great character variety, with characters that play drastically differently
New enemies, biomes and bosses with fresh mechanics keep appearing and are a blast
Dark, insulting story and plenty of content
criticism: Roguelike elements are quite minor, so runs get repetitive
Character abilities are fixed per run and can be upgraded but not changed; items are limited (about one per character) and often uninteresting
Protagonist must always be on the team, limiting team freedom
Unlocks of new characters and side quests come too late; meta-progression pacing is slow
Random enemy attack directions feel out of place in a planning-heavy game
Few rewards beyond limited money; full party conflicts with keeping open space to evade

Tension between a full team and open tiles for dodging forces a meaningful choice
Enemy attacks telegraph direction so encounters can be planned like a puzzle
commentary.quote: I'll put this in the low A.
design_criteria: Gameplay uniqueness: novel pigment and positioning mechanics weighed heavily
Visuals and audio/vibe: distinct art, music and atmosphere are a major plus
Roguelike depth: minimal run-to-run variation in abilities and items counts against it
Character variety: very different characters, but the team is largely fixed once chosen
Meta-progression pacing: slow unlock of characters and content is a flaw
RNG: random enemy moves undermine the strategic planning
Content amount: boss, biome and enemy variety supports its rating
Risk vs reward in team composition: full team versus evasion space

community.one_liner: A turn-based tactical roguelike set in a Hieronymus Bosch-inspired Purgatory, where you recruit a party of grotesque 'fools' and fight using a colour-coded pigment resource, made by Talia bob Mair and Nicolas Delgado and published by Hellbent Games.
community.consensus_summary: Brutal Orchestra is a cult favourite with an Overwhelmingly Positive Steam rating (about 97.6% of roughly 2,100 reviews) and very long playtimes among its fans, some in the hundreds of hours. Players praise its distinctive art, music, dark humour, story and a pigment-based combat system that rewards planning. Critic coverage is thin: Metacritic has a page with no critic score yet and only a handful of user ratings (9.1 from 7), and OpenCritic shows nothing I could find. It is a full 1.0 release (Dec 2021), not early access, and Steam reviews say the developers were still adding free content years later, with an active Workshop mod scene. The main complaints are heavy RNG, pigment lockouts, weak-feeling items and characters, and a steep, unclear learning curve. Web search was unavailable for this run, so coverage of outlet reviews and Reddit is limited to Steam reviews, Metacritic and wiki pages.
best_things: Striking, grotesque art direction drawn from Hieronymus Bosch, with unusual enemy and companion designs
Music and atmosphere: reviewers repeatedly call the soundtrack and per-enemy battle themes a highlight
Pigment system: damaging enemies yields pigment matching their health-bar colour, which you spend on abilities, creating a dynamic puzzle of who to hit and in what order
Positioning and enemy mechanics give turn-based fights a tactical, puzzle-like feel; many say each enemy and boss has its own mechanics
Dark, bittersweet humour and a personal-feeling story; several reviewers call the narrative moving
The full game opens up after the first winning run, with extra enemies, bosses, companions, difficulty and story that pull players to keep playing
Large unlock pool (items, fools, achievements) that encourages replay without feeling like a chore, according to some reviewers
Active Steam Workshop modding scene (40+ mods catalogued on the community wiki, including character, enemy and item packs) extends playtime for veterans
worst_things: Heavy RNG: random starting party members, coin-flip movement shifts on hit or attack, a roughly 40% chance for extra pigment, and random instant-kill moves on some enemies
Pigment lockouts: if enemies do not supply the colour your party needs, you can be stuck with bad or forced abilities, or overflow pigment and take damage
Characters have very few moves (two or three, sometimes randomly assigned) and one item slot, so builds feel limited and upgrades feel small
Many items, especially before unlocks, are described as weak or useless, and some party members as nearly dead weight
Only three zones and a limited enemy pool, so the same content repeats quickly (a Metacritic user notes seeing every enemy and boss by about the fifth run)
Many enemy abilities and status effects are hard to keep track of; some players resort to guides or other players to learn the rules
Some find the UX poor, and one Steam reviewer notes the tutorial could not be saved mid-way and lacks Steam Cloud saves
improvements: Reduce or give players more control over RNG (party selection, random skill assignment, coin-flip movement)
Give characters more moves and more meaningful equipment or build customization so pigment restrictions feel less punishing
More zones, routes and variety, with some fans explicitly asking for a larger sequel with more than three routes
Add Steam Cloud saves (the store page lists none) and let the tutorial be saved or resumed mid-way
Make normal fights less trivial on hard mode and strengthen meta-progression, since some players feel their team does not grow across runs
Clearer onboarding and in-game explanation of statuses and enemy abilities, since many reviewers say it is confusing until it clicks
unique_things: Pigment economy where hits generate colour you then spend on abilities, tying positioning, targeting and ability choice together
Bosch-inspired Purgatory setting with grotesque, humorous characters and a story that unlocks more fully after the first winning run
Party of oddball companions ('fools') with very few but distinctive abilities, instead of a large skill tree
Boss and enemy fights with bespoke mechanics and theme songs, described as puzzle-like
Strong mod support through Steam Workshop and a dedicated modding API and wiki
tedious_or_disliked: Combat can be slow and methodical because losing HP is costly, so players feel they must be careful in every encounter
Being 'pigment-screwed' (missing or overflowing colours) is compared by reviewers to mana screw in Magic, which makes some fights feel low-agency
Hard-mode bosses are criticized as unforgiving, with healing transformations, repeated spawns and one-shot moves that can drag fights out (one review cites about 25 minutes on a single boss)
Needing to read and memorise many enemy abilities and passives before each fight overwhelms impatient players
Repeated runs through the same three zones feel repetitive to some, with less novelty after the first clear
divisive_points: RNG: critics call it excessive and unfair while other reviewers argue the complaint is overstated and that knowledge and planning dominate outcomes
Pigment mechanic: loved by many as the heart of the game, called annoying or agency-removing by others
Whether it is truly a roguelike: one reviewer argues it is not a roguelike at all, and another says it should not have been one, while many others name it a favourite of the genre
Story after the first win: praised by some, but one reviewer felt it fades after the first successful run on each difficulty
community.reception_notes: Released on Steam on Dec 17, 2021 (Windows and Linux, no Mac or console versions listed) at $19.99, and it has remained at Overwhelmingly Positive. Metacritic lists only 7 user ratings and no critic reviews, so critic coverage is essentially absent and the game's profile is built by word of mouth and Steam reviews. Steam reviewers say the developers were still adding free content about five years after release, and the Workshop mod scene (with a legacy-version beta branch for older mods) is a major reason veterans keep playing. Some players say it is popular with deep-playtime fans but a love-or-hate game, pointing to a low achievement-completion rate for the tutorial. Note: web search was unavailable (session budget exhausted), so no outlet reviews or Reddit threads were read.

games.name: Caves of Qud
games.short_description: Inhabit a deeply-simulated science fantasy world and chisel through layers of thousand-year-old civilizations. Build a character from over a hundred mutations and cybernetics. The award-winning sandbox roguelike & RPG full of robots, deep lore, and sentient plants.

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put this as a low A myself because I've only starting to discover the true genius of this game.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Caves of Qud is a turn-based traditional roguelike with a huge, freeform RPG campaign and deep lore, often compared to D&D and Dwarf Fortress. He says it demands patience and commitment, the text-style visuals will repel some players, and it is hard, with the advice to use the non-permadeath storyteller mode. He has only put in a small fraction of the hours fans recommend, so he finds it hard to judge. Many would put it in S, but he places it in low A for now, with a possible re-evaluation once he finishes the main quest.
praise: Massive, open-ended RPG adventure with many ways to approach everything
Very long main quest campaign
Strong replayability from drastically different classes and races
Deep lore and strong world-building focus
Rewards experimentation and mastering its mechanics; could be a 'one game for a year' pick
Considered by many one of the best traditional roguelikes
criticism: Visuals are limited and hard to grasp, and can put many players off
Needs lots of patience and commitment to learn
Tutorial is small relative to the game's depth and it does not hold your hand
Hard, with easy deaths from experimenting; default hardcore permadeath is punishing
Heavy reading and freedom can feel intimidating
unique_points: Extreme freedom: no single way to do anything, closer to tabletop D&D than most roguelikes
Storyteller mode lets players avoid permadeath while experimenting
Character classes and races differ drastically, driving replay value
Limited visuals lean on player imagination, which is part of the charm for fans
commentary.quote: I'm going to put this as a low A myself
design_criteria: Depth and freedom: many approaches to any problem, no hand-holding
Replayability: drastically different classes and races
Accessibility: limited visuals and steep learning curve count against it
World-building and lore: deep lore supports the setting
Difficulty: hard and punishing, mitigated by storyteller mode
Run/campaign length: very long main quest
Experimentation: rewards trying random things even at the cost of death
commentary.rerank_note: Provisional placement: he says many would put it in S and he may re-evaluate after beating the game; he is only about halfway through the main adventure.

community.one_liner: A deeply systemic, turn-based science-fantasy sandbox roguelike/RPG from Freehold Games (published by Kitfox), set in a strange post-apocalyptic world with mutations, cybernetics, factions and a handcrafted main quest inside a procedurally generated map.
community.consensus_summary: Caves of Qud is received as a landmark of the genre: Steam shows Overwhelmingly Positive (about 95% of roughly 12.7k reviews), Metacritic is 91 from 8 critics, and OpenCritic has a top critic average of 90 with 90% recommending. It left early access on 5 Dec 2024 (Kitfox became publisher in 2023) after roughly nine years of weekly updates, and adds a new graphical UI, the final stretch of the main quest, and later a Switch port (Feb 2026). It won the 2025 IGF Excellence in Narrative award and the 2025 Hugo for Best Game or Interactive Work. Praise centres on writing, worldbuilding and freedom of build and play; the recurring complaints are a steep learning curve, unclear interface and information, unfair-feeling deaths and debuffs, and the claim that its 'depth' is more build variety than true simulation. Players who bounce off it tend to bounce hard.
best_things: Worldbuilding and prose: item, place and creature descriptions are poetic and strange, with heavy Gene Wolfe (Book of the New Sun) flavour, and make the world feel ancient and mysterious
Huge build variety: over a hundred mutations and cybernetics, true-kin vs mutant castes, and many playstyles (psychic, tinker, sniper, multi-armed brawler, etc.)
Emergent, absurd stories: befriending or recruiting hostile creatures, turning into odd things, making a serial killer a companion, all through interacting systems
Everything can be talked to and belongs to a faction, so reputation and relationships feel consequential and the world feels inhabited
Handcrafted main quest and lore woven into a procedurally generated map, plus nearly a million explorable maps
Distinctive pixel-art and eerie soundtrack identity; the 1.0 graphical UI and controller support (runs well on Steam Deck) improved accessibility
Tons of content and replay value, with players logging hundreds of hours; classic vs roleplay (save-friendly) modes and Steam Workshop mods
Critics call it a genre-defining achievement in roleplaying freedom and flexibility
worst_things: Steep, vertical learning curve: barebones tutorial, many systems and keys to learn, and players often need the wiki to progress
UI/UX legibility problems: low-contrast tiles, hard to tell actors from items, message-log spam, fluid splatter obscuring the map, clunky keybind and settings menus and a weak mouse interface
Deaths can feel unfair or opaque: one-shots from off-screen enemies, unreliable threat information, rest not interrupting when attacked, autoexplore walking into harm
Crippling permanent and temporary debuffs (diseases, fungal infections, limb loss) that the game explains poorly, often pushing players to reload saves
Procedural generation sometimes yields incoherent or blocked spaces, enclosed rooms, teleport-plant traps, and a 'getting lost' overland mechanic some find punishing
Faction reputation rules can produce arbitrary-feeling penalties, such as killing a hostile legendary creature angering a friendly town
Some critics of the 'depth' hype say NPCs are flavour-text cardboard cutouts and the simulation is shallower than Dwarf Fortress-style comparisons suggest
Prose can turn word-salad or over-pretentious to some readers and hinder clarity of ability descriptions
improvements: Better onboarding: fuller tutorial, in-game explanations of debuffs, diseases and how to cure them, and labelled controls
Improve visual clarity: contrast, distinguishing items and merchants, reducing message spam and fluid clutter, more accurate ability descriptions and damage numbers
Better keybinding and settings UX and more capable mouse support (comparison made to Tales of Maj'Eyal)
Improve map generation validation so interiors connect and the player is not trapped, and reduce movement- and sight-blocking clutter
Rebalance character options: tinker and some mutations or classes seen as weak, psychic powers as strong, true-kin vs mutant imbalance and the ease of breaking the game late
Make the faction reputation system and legendary-creature rules more coherent and less grind-dependent, and add more variety to the main quest across runs
unique_things: A science-fantasy post-apocalypse setting with a literary, Wolfe-inspired voice rather than generic fantasy or dungeon-crawl tropes
Deep simulation sandbox rules: nearly any object or creature can be interacted with, recruited, dismantled, or converted (memed 'you can become a chair')
Mutations plus cybernetics character creation with true-kin and mutant paths, unmatched in breadth among traditional roguelikes
Procedurally generated world history and sultan legends that feed into a fixed main story
Faction and reputation system that governs who is hostile or friendly across the entire map
Classic (permadeath) and roleplay (saveable) modes letting one game serve both hardcore and story-focused players
tedious_or_disliked: Reputation grinding and hunting random legendaries or villages to befriend or slay is described as un-fun but effectively required for endgame survivability
Cloning shopkeepers and scouring for loot is called boring intended cheese in one long-time player's review
Autoexplore and bumping weak enemies early, then slogging across big empty overland regions, feels repetitive to some
Dealing with diseases and permanent injuries by reloading or consulting the wiki
Combat that some say becomes shallow or boring after the first 10-15 hours, plus an extremely long time investment before the game clicks
divisive_points: Whether 'depth' means systemic simulation (critics say it is mostly build variety and scripted weirdness) or rich, interconnected worldbuilding (fans say it is unmatched)
Difficulty and permadeath: loved as consequential and funny by fans, called opaque and hostile by detractors, with many preferring the roleplay mode
Writing style: hailed as the best prose in games by some, labelled pretentious or word-salad by others
Graphics and UI: the minimalist pixel look is praised as distinctive, but readability complaints are common even among positive reviewers
community.reception_notes: Development began in 2007, a public beta came in 2010, and Steam early access in 2015 with consistent weekly updates for about nine years. Early access reviewers praised depth but found the interface confusing; Kitfox Games became publisher in July 2023 and the 1.0 release on 5 Dec 2024 added a new fully graphical UI and the last leg of the main quest, then drew universal acclaim (Metacritic 91). A Nintendo Switch port followed on 16 Feb 2026 (Nintendo Life 8/10). Awards: 2025 IGF Excellence in Narrative, 2025 Hugo for Best Game or Interactive Work; nominated for 2025 Golden Joysticks Best Indie Game and a D.I.C.E. Strategy/Simulation nomination. Platforms: Windows, macOS, Linux (Steam, GOG), Switch; Steam price $29.99 with Workshop mod support (GOG reviewers note mod restrictions vs Steam). Steam recent reviews (~94% positive over 30 days) remain strong as of late Sep 2026. Steam-side estimates (SteamSpy owners 200k-500k; steam-revenue-calculator gross about $12.1M, net to developer about $3.6M) are rough Boxleiter-style estimates, not audited. Note: the WebSearch budget was exhausted in this session, so no Reddit threads were read directly (Reddit and Eurogamer fetches were blocked); community detail comes from 18 negative and top positive Steam reviews plus Metacritic, OpenCritic, Wikipedia, GOG and Steam pages.

games.name: Decktamer
games.short_description: Deck-building meets monster catching in this turn-based roguelike. Recruit enemy cards to your party as you dive into the depths of the abyss. Will you kill them or will you tame them?

other_scores.source: Softpedia (via Metacritic, only critic review listed)

other_scores.score: 86% positive, Very Positive, about 2,409 reviews (local data snapshot)

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put this one as a really solid A tier.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Deck Tamer is a board-centric deck-building roguelike where you fight beasts, capture them into your team, and extract their actives and passives to move onto other monsters. Combat is simple: place beasts, pick an ability each, and they attack automatically left to right. He finds it a deeply strategic, under-the-radar game that more people should know about. He beat it, calls it challenging, and places it in a really solid A tier, describing it as one of the best deck builders of recent years.
praise: Very simple core gameplay (place beast, choose ability) that produces extensive, domino-effect strategy
Fair encounters: you always fight things you could field yourself, so nothing feels unfair
Capture-and-extract system (syringes, even mid-combat) creates unique self-made synergies and varied runs
Pokemon-like tension of weakening enemies to capture them rather than kill them
Every monster stays relevant, even weak starters, since they can absorb blows; constant deck churn
Undo/redo mechanic that scales down with difficulty, good for teaching then committing
Strong audio-visuals with attack art popping out; not AI generated; single final boss makes no-capture feel justified
criticism: Animation/zoom is a bit claustrophobic; he wishes it could zoom out to appreciate visuals
Only two path choices before each battle; he wants a third
Capture chance RNG (e.g. 80%) can abruptly end a deep run, which feels bad at high levels
Losing monsters permanently feels rough at first and takes getting comfortable with
Challenging; requires wrapping your head around many possibilities
unique_points: Monster-collecting plus extracting abilities/passives between monsters for self-made synergies
Forced use and disposal of monsters and consumables teaches you not to hoard
Limited redos as a core, difficulty-scaled mechanic
Starter monsters always retain value
commentary.quote: one of the best deck building games I've played in the last few years
design_criteria: Simplicity vs depth: simple inputs yielding extensive strategy
Synergy/build variety: ability extraction and capture create diverse runs
Risk vs reward: capture chances and sacrificing monsters
Fairness: enemies are always fieldable by the player
Difficulty/teaching: redos scale down with difficulty
Art and audio: strong visuals, immersive attack art, biome feel
Meta-choices/pathing: wants more than two path options
RNG: capture failure can ruin runs

community.one_liner: A turn-based roguelike deckbuilder where you tame enemy creatures into your deck, sacrifice or evolve them, and transfer mutated abilities between monsters while descending a Lovecraftian abyss.
community.consensus_summary: Decktamer launched on Steam on Oct 27, 2025 (Horizon Edge, published by Assemble Entertainment) and sits at Very Positive, about 86% of roughly 2,400 Steam reviews. Players love the hand-drawn creature art, the taming-and-mutation hook and the tactical combat. The recurring complaint is a steep, sometimes punishing difficulty curve with attrition and RNG. Even many positive reviews carry caveats about balance, and several negative reviews call it a good game that is not yet tuned. It is a full release, not early access, and the dev appears active: players mention a published roadmap, community creature-submission events and difficulty rework. Critic coverage is thin: Metacritic shows one critic review (Softpedia 85), too few for a Metascore, and OpenCritic could not be confirmed.
best_things: Striking, surreal, Lovecraftian hand-drawn creature and card art (reportedly by essentially one artist/dev), cited in nearly every positive review
Taming mechanic adds real tension: monsters you tame are permanent-until-dead, so you weigh healing vs taming a stronger unit vs sacrificing
Mutation/syringe system lets you move abilities between creatures, enabling inventive and sometimes broken synergies (e.g. speed-buff stacking snowballs)
Deep tactical, puzzle-like combat; reviewers describe it as highly deterministic and min-max friendly
Moody soundtrack and atmosphere, plus well-written bestiary and explorer diary lore entries that reward collecting new creatures
Good value at $15.99 with many modes, bosses, secret bosses and high replayability for players who click with it
Responsive developer who engages the community, runs creature-submission events and published a roadmap to address complaints
worst_things: Difficulty is widely called overtuned, even on the lowest settings; one reviewer cited under 41% of owners beating the medium difficulty
Attrition problem: your creatures do not heal between fights while enemies do, so regen/lifesteal tanks dominate and glass-cannon or gimmick builds become liabilities
Healing items and taming items are the same resource, forcing painful tradeoffs that feel punishing rather than fun to some
RNG dependence at higher difficulties: missed tames, weak event rolls or no synergistic creatures late in a run can make it unwinnable
Performance and optimization complaints: high GPU use, card shine effects with many syringes, older PCs struggling
Some UI clunkiness and unclear unlocks/rewards (scrolling through abilities, battle reward clarity)
Windows only on Steam (no Mac/Linux) and only partial controller support
Limited long-term depth: some reviewers feel they have seen most of what the game offers after a few runs, citing too few ascension-style modifiers
improvements: Retune the difficulty curve and give better guidance for learning higher difficulties, where reviewers say there is no reference for what works
Add more between-battle activity and events, such as a Slay-the-Spire-style run map; events are few and their order is random
Offer a toggle to turn off or speed up effect explanations and animations, especially for Endless mode where battles drag on
Make the undo/redo on easier modes more useful; it only returns to before combat and does not refund items or placements
Add more content and meta-progression: more ascension-style modifiers, since extra modes are seen as only added harshness, plus more bosses and events
Broaden viable builds so that not only high-HP regen units work, and add optimization options
Additional language support (Russian requested repeatedly) and platform support
unique_things: Creature-catching as the deck-building engine: enemy cards are recruited into your deck rather than picked from reward pools
Nuzlocke-like permanence: units that die are gone, and low-tier tames are treated as disposable fodder to trade up
Ability extraction and mutation system (syringes) that moves abilities between monsters, which affects how creatures evolve
Enemies have non-static moves and abilities, so the same monster species can appear stronger or weaker in later stages
Lore delivered through a bestiary and explorer diary tied to the monsters you tame
Turn-based battles closer to tactical puzzles or XCOM-style positioning than typical card-draw combat
tedious_or_disliked: Runs feel draining: roughly 8 encounters per depth, each needing heavy thinking with little breathing room between them
Very long turns and runs (turns of several minutes; Very Hard runs around 1.5-2 hours; Endless waves taking about 15 min each due to effect text)
No sense of attachment or build identity: every creature eventually gets scrapped, so some players feel nothing builds on itself like in Slay the Spire
Counterpoint complaint that levels are too short to assemble a deck, leaving finished levels feeling unsatisfying
Losing runs teaches little, because the next run's creatures and events differ so much
divisive_points: Difficulty: some say it is fair and rewarding once you adopt the sacrifice mindset, others say it is brutal or unbalanced even on easy
RNG vs determinism: some praise it as deterministic and min-maxable, others find late-game RNG and unreliable tames decisive
Run length and pacing: slow deliberate turns are a feature for some and draining for others
Disposable units: seen as fresh tension by some and as a lack of long-term attachment by others
community.reception_notes: Metacritic needs 4 critic reviews for a Metascore and currently has 1 (Softpedia 85); user score 8.3 from only 8 ratings. Steam: Very Positive, with the scraped page showing 89% and a recent-30-day 88% positive; the local dataset shows 86.2% of 2,409. Early negative reviews focused on difficulty and balance, and several reviewers reference a difficulty rework, a published roadmap and developer assurances to rebalance, so reception has been partly shaped by ongoing patches. Commercial data is unavailable: steam-revenue-calculator shows $0 and SteamSpy shows 0-20k owners, so no reliable sales figure. Limitation: web search was unavailable (session budget exhausted), so this is based on Steam reviews, the Steam store and forum, and Metacritic; OpenCritic, Reddit and outlet reviews could not be read, and Steam patch notes were not retrievable.

games.name: Haste
games.short_description: Run fast, soar through the air, and master your landings as you speed through procedural worlds to outrun the end of the universe, by yourself and with friends!

placements.verbal_evidence: "I prefer it more than cave... I'm even going to put it here." No tier letter spoken.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Haste is a fast-paced 3D running roguelite where you race from the start to a portal while a void chases you, chaining dives and perfect landings to keep energy up for your active ability. He finds it skill-intensive but deeply satisfying once it clicks, with excellent visuals and standout music. The roguelite layer is light but impactful, deliberately so as not to disturb the core movement. Updates since his earlier review fixed many of his complaints. He enjoyed it enough to keep playing well past what the tier list required and places it high on the board, though the exact tier letter is not spoken.
praise: Core movement and dive/perfect-landing system feels great and rewards mastery
Excellent visuals and a large, high-quality soundtrack he listens to outside the game
Roguelite elements (passives, actives, gems) blend well without straying from the core running
Active abilities (board, wings, jump) enable distinct playstyles
Post-launch additions: per-level modifiers, harder modes, better keyword and item explanations
Extremely satisfying and fun; he kept playing beyond what he needed for the ranking
criticism: Losing all health costs a life and restarts the same level layout or boss, which feels tiring
Active abilities are too expensive, discouraging experimentation with builds
Loop mode gives few items, making an endless mode less appealing
Bosses can be frustrating and are hard to make work in a running game
Hub area could use more secrets and things to do; runs do not differ drastically from each other
unique_points: Momentum-and-angle based movement with perfect landings feeding an energy system
Roguelite layer kept intentionally minor to protect the core mechanic
Four biomes repeated at higher intensity with randomized levels
commentary.quote: What you see is what you get.
comparisons: Cave (Cave of Qud-style pick unclear; he says he prefers Haste)
design_criteria: Core gameplay feel: movement and skill ceiling dominate the evaluation
Roguelite integration: elements should support, not disrupt, the core mechanic
Visuals and audio: art and music are major strengths
Meta-progression: stats and unlocks acceptable but active abilities overpriced
Run variety: modest differences between runs, deemed acceptable
Failure/retry design: restarting the level on life loss is tedious
Boss design: uneven, constrained by the running genre
Hub and endgame modes: hub lacks content, loop mode lacks items
Clarity of information: improved keyword and item descriptions
commentary.rerank_note: He reviewed the game previously in a standalone video; since then it has been updated and many earlier issues were fixed, so this is a re-evaluation.

community.one_liner: A third-person, momentum-based 3D parkour/runner roguelite from Landfall in which you play Zoe, sprinting and gliding across procedurally generated levels and chaining perfect landings to outrun a collapsing universe, solo or in online co-op.
community.consensus_summary: Haste is received very positively overall: Steam sits around 92% positive across roughly 14,000 reviews (Very Positive) and Metacritic shows an 81 Metascore from 6 critics with a 7.5 user score from 49 ratings. Nearly everyone, including the people who downvote it, agrees the movement and sense of speed are outstanding, and the soundtrack and art get frequent praise. The recurring complaint is that everything wrapped around the movement (procedural levels, pick-3 item roguelite layer, only three bosses, wordy story) is thin and repetitive, with novelty fading around shard 3-4. It launched on PC on April 1 2025 (a full release, not early access); console versions with crossplay followed later, and a late patch note says the last planned content update has shipped, so future work is ports and bug fixes rather than new content.
best_things: Movement and sense of speed: chaining perfect landings, reading terrain and weaving obstacles feels fluid, tactile and arcade-like; repeatedly compared to what a good 3D Sonic or Tiny Wings in 3D would feel like
Soundtrack: drum-and-bass style tracks with smooth blending between levels are called out by players and by critics (e.g. But Why Tho) as a highlight
Art style and character design are widely described as charming and gorgeous
Skill expression: no jump button, high skill ceiling, and S-rank chasing gives mastery payoff; flow state when it clicks
Late-game and endless-mode item snowballing (RoR2-style) lets runs go absurdly fast, which fans find hilarious and satisfying
Runs great, including 60fps on Steam Deck, and DualSense haptics are praised
Good value and broad appeal: cheap-ish at $19.99, Sonic-fan catharsis, works as a chill or background game
Critics (But Why Tho 9/10, Vandal 82, The Games Machine 80) call it a refined arcade experience
worst_things: Levels are procedurally generated and, per many negative reviews, blur together with mostly palette and obstacle changes across the 10 shards
Only three (some say four) bosses, recycled and made tougher in later shards; the final boss is called underwhelming by some
Roguelite layer is shallow: many items are small stat or condition bonuses, few change how you play, and runs feel similar
Story and dialogue are frequently criticised as wordy, flat or badly paced for a game about going fast; many players skip it
Procedural generation can produce bad terrain or no-win stretches, with obstacle clusters forcing hits and some boss setups depending on luck
Bugs and performance issues reported by some: crashes, freezes, black screen after Continue, stuttering, lag in extreme endless runs
Multiplayer is thin: players share a world but barely interact beyond gifting lives and items, so buying extra copies disappoints some
Repetition after the early shards (novelty wears off around shard 3-4) leads several reviewers to a thumbs-down despite loving the core
improvements: Hand-crafted or curated levels (Clustertruck, Neon White and Cyber Hook are cited as better comparisons), possibly with time-trial and leaderboard support
Items that change playstyle or act as permanent mechanics rather than small stat boosts; more build variety
More bosses and more distinct biomes and level variety per shard
Stronger, better-paced story or an option to skip or trim dialogue; UI readability (speed indicator is easy to miss)
Fixes for procedural-generation edge cases (no-win landings, luck-dependent bosses) plus accessibility options such as a screen shake toggle and the ability to decline challenge rewards
More content or DLC and mod support; players were disappointed the devs said no more content updates are planned
unique_things: Sonic-like speed and momentum fantasy in a roguelite with no jump button; speed is built by timing landings on downslopes
Landing-quality mechanic (perfect, good, bad landings) that drives both speed and score
Sparks economy and item snowballing that can let endless mode reach absurd speeds
Ten-shard campaign with a node map, characters and story wrapped around a runner, plus an endless mode and later time trials
Drop-in online co-op with crossplay on consoles, and a Workshop mod scene (e.g. character swaps)
Built by Landfall (Totally Accurate Battle Simulator, Clustertruck) with a playful tone and Steam Deck-friendly performance
tedious_or_disliked: Shards can run around 20 minutes and feel long and samey once novelty fades
Forced dialogue and story beats between levels; many skip them
Grindy achievements: one reviewer cites the 5000 km achievement as requiring a long endless slog, and shard 10 achievements as annoying
Permanent upgrades (anti-spark and similar) feel like plain stat bumps, and some players need repeated runs for them
Collision or terrain trapping in ditches, unavoidable obstacle clusters, and luck-driven level layouts that can ruin a no-hit attempt
Challenge nodes and the map feel tacked on, and several reviewers say items and map choices can be ignored while still getting S ranks
divisive_points: Whether the roguelite structure belongs: many negative reviewers say a hand-crafted level game would be better, while positive ones say procedural runs and item snowballing drive replayability
Story and characters: some find Zoe and the cast cute and delightful, others find the writing boring and overlong
Difficulty: some call it too easy (items and speed trivialise it) while others hit boss and level-generation spikes they find unfair
Multiplayer: fine as a casual drop-in for some, disappointing as true co-op for others
community.reception_notes: Launched April 1 2025 on PC (Windows, Mac, Linux) and became a strong word-of-mouth hit, boosted by short-form video clips; Steam-based revenue trackers estimate roughly $5.0M gross and 100-200k owners (estimates, not audited). Landfall kept patching for about a year: 1.8 added inventory reordering and Wraith story content (Nov 2025), 1.9 a UI overhaul and cooldown item rebalance (Dec 2025), 1.10 Time Trials (Feb 2026), 1.11 crossplay and console launches on PS5, Xbox and Switch 2 (Apr 2026), then 1.11.b and 1.11.C stability and endless-mode save fixes. The devs said the last planned content update has shipped, and some reviewers are sad about that. Current Steam community threads show scattered bug reports (stuttering, black screen after Continue) and accessibility requests. Steam also lists a demo. Note the Steam listing title is just Haste, and the store page's own copy says ten Shards and 90+ items. OpenCritic score could not be retrieved; web search budget was exhausted so Reddit and OpenCritic were not reached.
