games.name: Moonlighter 2: The Endless Vault
games.short_description: Experience an action-RPG with roguelike elements where you live the double life of an adventurer and a merchant. Dive into vibrant dimensions to fight enemies, gather loot, and manage your backpack. Rebuild your shop and turn profits into gear for the next adventure!

placements.verbal_evidence: Moonliner 2 is going to be a uh solid A tier and can only go up from here.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Moonlighter 2 is the early-access sequel to Moonlighter, pairing a Hades-style room-by-room action run with a shopkeeping and inventory-fusion loop. He has played a lot of it and is really enjoying it, calling the amount of content and the out-and-back loop standout. Combat feels decent but clunky, and the boon system and run pacing need polish. He places it in a solid A tier for now and expects it to rise as the game is fleshed out.
praise: Run-to-shop loop makes you want both to finish a run and start a new one
Hades-like daily selling boons (e.g. legendary sales give more gold but leave a stain to sweep) make selling interesting
Item curses and fusing effects to raise item quality is a fun inventory mini-game with big payoffs
Huge meta-progression breadth: weapons, shop, pets, guns, badges, potions, stickers, and more
Vault money goal gives visible progress and permanent big upgrades
Music, visuals and story are excellent; the hub is pleasant to just sit in
Runs are quick with lots to do (chests, hidden events, secrets) and boss fights are impressive
criticism: Combat feels clunky: input buffering, slow animations amid fast surroundings, hard-to-read action
Some weapons (e.g. spearheads needing positioning) feel weak; gun aiming can be slow
Buffed basic attacks make specials pointless, leading to repetitive play
Some boons are too situational, relying on environmental triggers absent in boss fights
Enemies that run away while you are slow; up to five rooms can pass with no build change
Only three biomes (day and night each), and bosses can drag; inventory management may feel tedious to some
unique_points: Combines two very different loops (dungeon and shop) and the sequel handles that hard problem better than the original
Selling-day boons borrow the Hades boon structure for the shop side
Cursed items are not purely negative; their effects are combined to raise item quality and price
Trade-off between taking boons versus chests for loot to sell and progress meta
commentary.quote: Moonliner 2 is going to be a uh solid A tier and can only go up from here.
design_criteria: Two-loop integration: how well the dungeon and shop halves complement each other
Combat feel: input buffers, animation speed and readability
Boon/build system: situational boons and synergy usefulness in boss fights
Meta-progression: breadth of shops and upgrades driving replay
Run length and pacing: quick runs, but stretches with no build change
Content quantity: only three biomes in early access
Audio and visual charm: music and art praised heavily
Risk vs reward: boons versus chests for loot
Boss design: big impressive fights that can run long
commentary.rerank_note: Early-access evaluation; he has discussed it on the channel before and notes it can only go up as it develops.

community.one_liner: A 3D action-roguelite from Digital Sun (published by 11 bit studios) where you fight through procedurally generated island runs by night and price and sell the loot in your shop by day, with a Tetris-style backpack puzzle linking the two.
community.consensus_summary: Generally favorable but more polarized among fans than among critics. Steam sits at about 81% positive overall (Very Positive; roughly 4,100 reviews in the local data), while a separate live Steam page fetch showed recent reviews dipping to about 70% positive. Metacritic PC is 80 from 8 critics, and Wikipedia cites OpenCritic at 83% of critics recommending from 46 reviews. Critics praise the deeper, interlocking run-and-shop loop and the 3D presentation. The loudest complaints come from Moonlighter 1 fans who see it as a Hades-style reinvention rather than a true sequel, plus grind, bugs and Steam Deck performance. It launched in Early Access on 19 Nov 2025 and reached 1.0 on 2 Sep 2026 on PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2.
best_things: Addictive 'one more run' loop: expeditions, shop pricing and progression all feed each other (The Big Lead called the two loops much deeper than in the first game).
Backpack inventory puzzle is praised as improved. Players enjoy stockpiling item categories and building chain-reaction synergies that multiply item value.
Combat is cleaner and more responsive than ML1, with four weapon classes and unlockable weapons that change playstyle noticeably.
Cute, cohesive 3D art and cozy-yet-adventurous atmosphere; several reviewers defend the move away from pixel art.
Risk/reward push-your-luck decisions inside runs (take one more level or risk losing part of the haul's value) plus plenty of meta progression.
Relic/perk system with many relics and build variety, and traps/turrets that reward creative play.
Developer responsiveness on performance: stuttering was reportedly fixed in Nov 2025 patches and some Steam Deck reviewers flipped to recommended.
worst_things: Not a true continuation of ML1 for many fans: dungeon crawling replaced by a node-based island map, reducing exploration and the layered crafting/loot gameplay.
Loot comes mostly from chests rather than monster drops, and items do not stack, which makes gathering feel like a chore.
Perk/boon interactions are shallow compared to Hades, so builds feel less varied and runs become samey.
Boss and miniboss design criticized: long invulnerable phases on bosses, overly predictable miniboss patterns, and damage sponginess on high difficulty.
Combat clarity issues: camera loses enemies behind objects, ranged enemies fire from offscreen without tells, charged shots cannot be interrupted, and input priority feels inconsistent.
Stability and polish: crashes when continuing a run, soft-locks, infinite-fall animations, NPC dialogue getting stuck, audio distortion in tech areas.
Weapon balance: many weapons (for example fists and gun variants) seen as weak, and upgraded weapons can carry negative traits, so players keep the starter gear.
Some see the shop layer as simplified versus ML1 (armor, elemental weapon effects and crafting reduced) and the story as average.
improvements: Stagger or interrupt options for charging ranged enemies, telegraphs for projectiles, and better camera behavior.
Rebalance weapons and the late-game economy so upgrade costs do not balloon and spending choices feel meaningful.
More depth in perk synergies and more run variety, such as Hades-style optional difficulty modifiers.
Shop customization: layout freedom and customer-flow mechanics, since the shop reads as static to some.
Steam Deck/handheld optimization and shorter load times.
Save system that lets players resume mid-day instead of having quitting skip ahead in the day/night cycle.
unique_things: Fuses a shopkeeper sim (price-setting, customer reactions) directly with an action-roguelite, in the tradition of Recettear but in 3D.
Backpack-management puzzle whose item placement produces synergies and affects profit, blending Backpack Battles-style inventory play with roguelite relics.
Push-your-luck extraction mechanic where the value of hauled loot is at stake when deciding whether to continue a run.
Move from 2D pixel art to a stylized 3D look with Hades/Wind Waker-like influences, per Wikipedia's development section.
tedious_or_disliked: Late-game grind: upgrade and shop costs scale steeply, with one 150-hour reviewer describing repeated boss farming for upgrade resources.
Non-stacking, chest-sourced loot makes collection feel like busywork.
Dungeons and runs start feeling samey and repetitive over a long playtime.
Too many competing money sinks (weapons, health, shop, town, relics) make progress feel slow.
Bosses with long invulnerability windows make fights a waiting game.
Quitting mid-run skips forward in the day cycle, punishing short play sessions.
divisive_points: Hades-like influence: some call it a watered-down or poorly done Hades hybrid, while others say it stands as its own game and that the Hades complaints are unfair.
The 3D art style: one camp misses the pixel art and charm, while another finds the new style cute and cohesive.
Shop management: some find it deeper and more rewarding, others find it repetitive or simplified compared with ML1.
Difficulty and combat feel: fluid and fun for some, annoying or unfair on higher difficulties for others.
community.reception_notes: Early Access began 19 Nov 2025 (delayed from 23 Oct) with 3 biomes, 120 relics and 4 weapons. EA feedback was split: fans of the demo and first game were wary, with Steam Deck stuttering and crashes the main early complaints, which the developer patched in Nov 2025. 1.0 arrived 2 Sep 2026, adding PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2 versions. Steam lists Windows only, no Mac or Linux. A community-management controversy (a Steam reviewer alleges staff mocked a negative review in Discord) is mentioned in one negative Steam review and is unverified. Checkpoint Gaming said the roguelite eventually runs out of steam. The Steam review counts in the local data (about 4,100) differ from the live page fetch (about 1,700 shown), so figures are approximate. Sales and revenue figures: no reliable data found (steam-revenue-calculator shows $0 and SteamSpy owners 0-20k, both unreliable for this new release).

games.name: Sculplings
games.short_description: A creature-collecting roguelike where every monster is sculpted in real clay and brought to life! Collect and battle a random assortment of hand-sculpted monsters in order to become the #1 Sculpling Champion!

placements.verbal_evidence: I am putting this as an A tier because it's just so unique

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Sculplings is a turn-based, Pokemon-style roguelike where you field a team of four creatures, each with four attacks and a passive, and counter elemental types. Its hook is that every asset is physically hand-sculpted by a single developer. He stresses that the gimmick alone would not be enough, but the game underneath is solid and truly adapted to a run-based format. He finds it very funny and content-rich, though he tires of Pokemon-style gameplay himself. He places it in A tier for its uniqueness and the sheer amount of work behind it.
praise: Hand-sculpted-in-real-life art by one person is unique and impressive
Pokemon formula reworked for roguelike: faster progression, quick evolutions, many abilities and items
Surprising amount of content; each Elite Four is fought one at a time across a run, plus a fifth final boss
Humor, NPC writing, attack and creature names are some of the funniest he has seen in a roguelike
Meta-progression is unlocks and cosmetics rather than raw power, and handmade cosmetics are motivating
Joy of discovering creatures, items, moves, jokes and evolutions
criticism: Pokemon-style gameplay gets repetitive and tiring for him, so he has not finished it
Runs are pretty hard and require understanding the systems
Discovery value fades once you have seen all the sculplings, leaving just gameplay and humor
Type system is a bit all over the place (food, spooky, etc.)
unique_points: Every creature and cosmetic is actually sculpted by hand in real life by a solo developer
Turns the Pokemon Elite Four structure into repeated roguelike run goals
Discovery of handmade creatures is itself a core reward loop
commentary.quote: I am putting this as an A tier because it's just so unique
design_criteria: Uniqueness/originality: hand-sculpted art is the standout hook
Genre adaptation: Pokemon formula reshaped for roguelike pacing
Content volume: lots to discover and unlock
Humor and vibe: writing and naming are a major strength
Meta-progression: cosmetics and unlocks rather than power
Difficulty: runs are hard and need system knowledge
Replay/discovery: value drops once everything is seen
Team building: four creatures with four attacks and a passive, elemental counters
commentary.rerank_note: Previously featured in his video on five little-known interesting games; this is a re-feature, not a tier move.

community.one_liner: A turn-based creature-collecting roguelike where every monster, item and environment is a real clay sculpture that was scanned into the game; you catch a team each run and beat the Top 5 ranked trainers to become champion.
community.consensus_summary: Sculplings is a small, solo-dev-plus-one indie (Conor Garity and Liam Kerrigan) that left Early Access (launched March 4, 2025) for a 1.0 on March 17, 2026. It holds Very Positive on Steam, about 191 positive vs 1 negative of 192 reviews (99.5%) at the time of the data pull, and players call it a charming, funny Pokemon-meets-Slay-the-Spire hybrid with no grind. The few reservations are polish, bugs, balance spikes and a shortish content pool. There is no Metacritic or OpenCritic critic coverage yet (the Metacritic page exists but has zero critic and zero user reviews), so reception is entirely player-driven. The developer is active, shipped a run of 1.0.x fixes and a 1.1.0 content patch on April 28, then said updates will stay small because of burnout; an unknown number of reviewers also mention being friends or community members of the dev, so read the near-perfect score with some salt.
best_things: Hand-sculpted clay art is the headline: creatures and even scenery with faces are real sculptures, giving the game a distinct identity that players say avoids the Temu-Pokemon look
Humor and writing land well: silly creature names, on-the-nose jokes, a few swears, an edgy rival and cliche trainers played for laughs
No grinding: each run you pick 1 of 3 starters, catch up to 4 creatures, collect items/pins and adapt, which players say removes the usual monster-tamer XP grind
Roguelite structure gives real build variety and strong 'one more run' pull; some players report ways to break the game wide open with scaling attacks, though these are not mandatory
Buffs and debuffs persisting through switches, plus a solid type chart and clean UI, make the simple turn-based combat feel more strategic than expected
Meta-progression is mostly new options (pin slots, unlocked items, cosmetics, upgraded boss passives) rather than raw power
Cheap at $10.99, runs well on Steam Deck in reviewers' reports, and the dev engages with the community
Handmade, no-AI-art production is a recurring selling point for reviewers
worst_things: Lack of polish for a post-Early-Access release: settings not persisting, visual oddities, typos, ghost inventory slots, and boss/miniboss AI sometimes wasting a turn
Bugs on the Steam forum: the Tank achievement and Pudduo passive misfiring, pins not working, a swap bug, revive behavior, Stoompy issues, and cloud backup/save problems
Boss mechanics are not telegraphed, so you can lose a run learning a gimmick the hard way
Occasional balance spikes such as an enemy move that instantly kills a creature and can be used repeatedly
Content is on the short side with a limited creature and item pool compared to established monster-tamers
Windows only (no Mac or Linux build); saves live in an obscure LocalLow folder and cloud sync has had problems
Not deep by the standards of the genre, per some otherwise positive reviewers
improvements: Proper controller support (the top recurring request; the dev said it is nearly complete)
Game speed or faster animation/text options, since battle animations and XP gain feel slow on long sessions
Item bloat management: chests have no reroll and finding wanted items gets harder as unlocks accumulate (enemy-drop rerolls for coins were since added)
More content: new creatures (a frog with a tongue is requested), legendaries, and paid DLC that some fans say they would buy
Better save and quit feedback, persistent settings, working cloud saves, and an unlock-requirement menu for pins and emblems
Ultrawide and GeForce Now compatibility were raised on the forum
unique_things: Every monster, item and environment was physically sculpted in clay (300+ sculptures per the official site) and scanned into the game
Roguelike run structure applied to Pokemon-style catching: a fresh team each run, pick 1 of 3 starters, randomized paths through 5 environments
100+ creatures, 30+ passive Pins and 15+ bosses, with Top 5 rank trainers each having unique mechanics
Stat buffs and debuffs persist across switches, which is unusual for the genre
Shiny variants and evolution guessing game, plus cosmetic collectibles, in a roguelite wrapper with a cheeky adult-ish humor tone
tedious_or_disliked: Default-speed animations, text boxes and post-fight XP gain linger too long, which would wear over many runs
Learning boss gimmicks by dying to them with no foreshadowing
Hunting for the item you want among a bloated unlock pool with no chest reroll
Minor jank and bugs interrupting flow, plus some mis-tracking achievements
Repeating runs is required to see the story, so the run count needed to finish can feel long to some, even though there is no traditional grind
The game reportedly pushes players to leave a Steam review (the sole negative review says it 'kinda forces you to make a review'), which feels naggy and may also inflate the near-perfect score
divisive_points: Depth: some praise 'decent depth and many viable builds', others say it is not the deepest game and feels like a vibe-out experience
Humor: many love the on-the-nose silly writing, while one reviewer notes the swearing and adult themes make it unsuitable for young kids despite the cute visuals
Balance: infinite-scaling attacks are called the strongest option by some, though others say the roguelike balance is well tuned
Polish: several reviewers call the bugs forgivable at the price, others say they would suggest waiting
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched March 4, 2025 and 1.0 shipped March 17, 2026, with reviews from Early Access playtests still on the page (some reviewers logged it months before 1.0). Post-launch patches 1.0.1 to 1.0.4 fixed softlocks, achievements, an infinite reroll exploit with the rabbit foot pin, music sliders and broken moves like Bloom and Hive Mind; 1.1.0 (April 28) added the capturable plant-type Stoompy, fixed a swap bug and rebalanced XP and evolution stats. The dev later announced lighter updates due to burnout, focusing on small additions and bug fixes and not big features like legendaries, with controller support nearly done. Steam-based ownership trackers show owners of 0 to 20,000 and a revenue calculator page reported $0 (an unreliable placeholder); with 192 reviews a rough Boxleiter-style guess would be single-digit thousands of copies, not a sourced figure. Windows only, priced $10.99.

games.name: Sol Cesto
games.short_description: Sol Cesto is a tactical and frantic roguelite where mastering your luck is key. Choose a hero, upgrade them using cursed teeth and magical items, and descend to the bottom of an ever-changing dungeon. In this dark world, every action has consequences…

other_scores.score: 89% all-time (2,278 reviews) / 91% recent (136 in last 30 days)
about $794,649 gross / about $234,422 net developer revenue; order-of-magnitude only

placements.verbal_evidence: none; only says it would be a 'high B' if visuals were basic, then places it 'under Scoplings' without a letter

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Sol Cesto is a turn-based, luck-driven roguelite where each turn you pick one of four lanes, each with a chance of enemies, treasure or traps, and you bend the odds with items, consumables and stats. He is drawn in mostly by its strikingly unique, dark-yet-bright hand-animated art, which reminds him of the artist Felix Colgrave. He finds the meta progression well balanced against in-run spending, and likes the hidden secrets, but the early game and run-to-run variety feel repetitive and RNG heavy. Verdict: really solid and enjoyable, elevated well above a plain B by its visuals, and placed just below Scoplings on the board.
praise: Some of the most unique art and animation he has seen in a roguelike, with a striking dark/bright blend
Every enemy has a different animation depending on whether you can kill it without taking damage
Meta progression vs in-run spending of gold is balanced well and makes sense
Lots of secrets, including fourth-wall-breaking puzzles and a true ending gated by collecting gems
More strategy than expected: removing one spot changes the probabilities on the whole floor
Different biomes bring new enemies and traps that keep discovery exciting
criticism: Early game is repetitive and runs feel similar and luck based until you unlock interesting characters, builds and passives
Some meta unlocks cost a lot for unknown content and some upgrades feel less satisfying than others
Still RNG heavy, especially early, with 'just unlucky' outcomes
Runs lack variation and he keeps hitting the same biomes, so he saw everything quickly relative to remaining secrets
Gameplay itself could be more interesting
unique_points: Core loop of picking one of four lanes with visible odds, where eliminating spots shifts probabilities
Art style and per-enemy animation states that react to whether you avoid damage
Secret-heavy design with fourth-wall-breaking puzzles and codes
commentary.quote: Even though I think that the game play could be even more interesting.
design_criteria: Visuals and animation: the major draw, carries the game above a plain B
Meta progression: balance between spending on meta vs the run, some unlocks frustrating
Run-to-run variety: too similar, same biomes repeated
Luck vs strategy: RNG-heavy core but with real probability-manipulation strategy
Secrets and endgame: true ending via gems, hidden fourth-wall puzzles
Enemy and biome design: varied enemies and traps per biome, animated states

community.one_liner: A French-made tactical roguelite where you pick one of four tile rows per floor and percentage odds decide which monster, treasure, trap or strawberry you land on, with cursed teeth used to rig those odds as you descend a dungeon to find a lost sun.
community.consensus_summary: Sol Cesto is well received by players (Steam Very Positive, about 91% of roughly 5,200 reviews in the local data; the store page showed 89% all-time and 91% recent) and is praised above all for its strange, hand-drawn tarot-and-medieval-marginalia art, animation and music. The odds-manipulation loop is seen as original and addictive for the first 10 to 20 hours. Criticism is consistent: heavy RNG, a brutally swingy opening area versus a trivial late game, thin run-to-run variety, and a grindy meta-progression that competes with in-run shopping. It entered Steam Early Access on May 27, 2025 and hit 1.0 on Apr 10, 2026 (Windows; priced $13.99). The 1.0 launch drew complaints about bugs and a controversial UI restyle, with some fixes reported within a week. Professional coverage is thin: Metacritic has only 3 critic reviews (no Metascore yet) and no OpenCritic page was found.
best_things: Distinctive art direction: tarot-card and medieval drollery style, grotesque-whimsical, with hidden interactables in the art; many reviewers buy or recommend it for the visuals alone
Animations, sound effects and music are repeatedly called spectacular, with one reviewer happy to listen to the soundtrack for hours
Core loop of nudging percentages with teeth and items is described as a genuinely novel, addictive take on risk and odds management ('a gambling game where you can change the odds')
Quick-run, pick-up-and-play feel that suits short sessions; scratches a Slay the Spire-like itch for some
Secrets, hidden interactions and a mysterious tone reward curiosity (beggar stories, final-level unlock puzzles)
Forgiving of small mishaps once you learn how to manage uncertainty, so risk-taking is viable rather than pure luck
Tooth and shop item combos allow different builds for strength versus magic characters
Runs well on Steam Deck according to reviewers; good value around $10-14, with advice to buy on sale
worst_things: RNG dominates: rooms can be statistically near-unwinnable, even on the very first floors, and reviewers report restarting the first screen repeatedly until a survivable layout appears

Difficulty curve is inverted: the first area is the hardest part of a run, then the game becomes easy once meta-progression and a good start are in place; early bosses are called easier than the first room
Low variety between runs and across characters; many teeth and items are weak while a few are obvious must-picks, so players converge on the same strategy within a few hours
Character balance: starting characters with 2 total power are seen as worse than the 3-power Knight/Peasant, so most players stick to one hero
Meta-progression is gated behind saving in-run gold, forcing a choice between mid-run shops and permanent upgrades, which many call a padded grind
Unskippable animations (camera zoom per row, floor clear, boss intros) that must be watched hundreds of times

Bugs and technical rough edges: boss-exit soft locks, animation errors covering the exit, phantom windows on Alt+Tab, a click-registration issue on the Sun power, reports of progress deletion; built in Construct 3 which a reviewer tied to hangups
Content ends quickly for completionists: roughly 20-30 hours to unlock everything and beat every character, versus hundreds of hours for genre benchmarks

Shallow moment-to-moment play: the top-upvoted negative reviews say strategy collapses into clicking the row with the best percentage, so every run and character feels the same after the first hours despite the striking art
improvements: Revert or rework the 1.0 UI: new star text borders and overall restyle are called harder to read and less fitting than the Early Access look (two highly upvoted positive reviews lead with this)
Smooth the opening difficulty, for example a low-health healing option, character-aware odds adjustment, or an earlier blacksmith, so early floors are not decided by an unwinnable layout
Add animation skip or speed-up options and a fuller options menu; avoid forcing four manual row picks on floors already safe to clear
Rebalance characters, teeth, flute spells and weak items, and make more of them viable; let flute spells recharge between areas instead of once per run
Add run-saving/resume (quit and return later) and controller support, which appear in user requests

Loosen the artificial gating to the final level and give reasons to experiment with different characters (character-specific secrets), plus more enemy and shop variety and better late-game money sinks
unique_things: Row-selection combat where you pick a row but probability, not you, picks the tile; the game is about editing those percentages
Stone and metal 'teeth' as a cursed, body-horror-flavoured upgrade system that modifies encounter odds and triggers combos
Slot-machine / gambling-meets-dungeon-crawler hybrid with a tarot-inspired dark-fantasy presentation
Quest for a lost sun through roughly 120 rooms across five biomes, with many hidden secrets and a mysterious, light-on-lore story
Meta-progression funded by depositing run gold back home, rather than a separate currency
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding the opening floors repeatedly for a decent roll, then gold and runs for unlocks (about 10 hours of mostly grind to get key unlocks, per a 100% completionist)
Unskippable, repeated animations and cutscenes and manual clicking through floors that are already won
Having to skip shops to bank gold for meta upgrades, which many see as a punishing tradeoff rather than an interesting decision
Late-game repetition: after the sun is reached, unlocking achievements and story with each character feels like repeating near-identical runs
Random shop rolls blocking specific item combos (e.g. hunting for a candle for hours)
Unclear mechanics and tutorial gaps about how certain upgrades or unlocks are obtained
divisive_points: Randomness: some players find managing uncertainty the whole appeal, others call it a slot machine with no real agency and get angry at unavoidable deaths
Depth versus longevity: fans accept roughly 20 hours of delightful play as enough, while others say it runs out of variety and compare it poorly to Slay the Spire
The 1.0 UI and art-border overhaul, loved by the devs' direction but disliked by several reviewers who preferred the Early Access look
Audio/visual quality: overwhelmingly praised on Steam, though a Metacritic user called graphics and sound poor
community.reception_notes: Early Access began May 27, 2025 at 11.99 EUR; early reviews already praised art and flagged repetitive runs. commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Sulfur is a first-person extraction-shooter roguelike with 3D environments and 2D sprites, where gear is lost permanently if you die. He thinks it is probably the best game of its sub-genre, praising satisfying gunplay, deep gun customization and a large amount of content. Main complaints are a slow start, messy inventory management, repetitive corridor-to-room dungeons and a lack of stealth or special events. He places it in low A tier.

Discovery-based cooking system where you combine random items to unlock recipes

community.one_liner: A single-player first-person shooter from Swedish studio Perfect Random that blends a looter-shooter with a PvE extraction-style roguelite: you dive through biomes, loot, cook, craft and enchant guns, and lose everything you carry if you die before getting home.
community.consensus_summary: SULFUR is received as a strong, distinctive Early Access hit: Steam shows Very Positive at roughly 87.6% of about 10,500 reviews, with the launch-period score around 90%. Players praise snappy, satisfying gunplay, the deep weapon modification and crafting systems, the lo-fi 3D-plus-2D-sprite art and soundtrack, and the tense lose-it-all risk/reward loop. The most vocal criticism in recent reviews is about balance philosophy: several big patches (oil and scroll rebalance, ammo caps, durability costs, removal of picture-in-picture scopes) nerfed popular builds and pushed the game toward a slower, more hardcore economy, which many see as a betrayal of the power fantasy. Critic coverage is very thin (Metacritic lists only two early-access critic reviews, so no Metascore), so reception is driven almost entirely by players. The game is still tagged Early Access on Steam with ongoing updates (Dungeons & Magic in Jan 2025, later Qiosk's Plenty and Scholar's updates, ghosts, endless mode) and console versions are advertised on the official site.
best_things: Gunplay feels snappy and punchy, with distinct weapon handling, strong sound design and satisfying gore and enemy hit reactions
Deep weapon-building: oils, scrolls, enchantments and attachments let you make oddball guns (homing magnum, near-instant LMG reloads, infinite-ammo style builds)
High-stakes risk/reward: dying loses your whole loadout, and deciding when to use the recharge-limited teleport amulet creates constant push-your-luck tension
Distinctive art style mixing 3D environments with 2D vector-style sprite enemies that have layered damage and vital areas
Strong soundtrack, dry humour and a quirky lore without a heavy story burden
Stash, storage and area unlocks give a sense of steady progression, and the hoarding/cooking/crafting side loops are addictive for many
Flexible pacing: can be played as a slow, careful explorer or a fast bullet frenzy; an easy mode removes the death penalties
Runs well, is good value around $25, and ships frequent updates (though some reviewers question the developers' balance direction)
worst_things: Major balance patches nerfed the most-used oils, scrolls and attachments (including rebalancing 100+ oils and adding an ammo cap), making many builds unviable, and changes apply retroactively to already-built guns
Weapon durability drain per shot makes multi-projectile and heavily modded guns break quickly, forcing repair kits and discouraging experimentation
Many scrolls and attachments are seen as strictly worse than an empty slot or are outclassed by a few best-in-slot picks, so build variety is narrower than it looks
Repetitive level and enemy structure: several levels per biome feel alike and many enemies are faction reskins, with large rooms that trigger everything at once
Enemy AI is considered easy to exploit and player power can outscale threats, while a handful of fast or cheesy enemies and bosses spike difficulty
Endless mode scaling is criticised as unbalanced (enemy HP, size and damage scale while the player mostly scales HP), and reaching stage 20 takes hours for an achievement
Some players feel it lacks a clear identity, doing neither roguelite meta-progression (stamps feel like minor QoL) nor extraction shooting as deeply as dedicated games
Bugs and corruption worries have been reported, including save file issues, controller and Steam Deck quirks, and dialogue pacing bugs
improvements: Buff weak oils, scrolls and attachments instead of nerfing strong ones, so more builds are viable
Add inventory sorting and the ability to suspend or save a run mid-dungeon (quick-sort was later added in the Dungeons & Magic update, suspend remained a request in reviews)
Add character progression or more meta-progression beyond gear, since some players say only storage and items progress
More biomes and late-game content, since players who beat the desert area reported running out of levels
Tune endless mode scaling and remove the multi-hour achievement requirement
Improve enemy AI and variety, and reduce the grind needed to re-gear after dying in later areas
Restore picture-in-picture scopes or fix the underlying optimisation so scopes feel good again
unique_things: Combines a looter-shooter and a PvE extraction loop in a single-player roguelite, with no classic meta-progression beyond what you stash and what you learn
Hand-held teleport amulet you must charge at mid-run or pay for, and which you trigger manually, so you choose when to bail out
Cooking, enchanting and oil-based gun modding form a crafting-heavy economy that players describe as an extraction cooking game with guns
Weapon level-up by using the gun, with upgrade slots and powers that cost durability
Insurance attachment that protects a single item, a rare and expensive hedge against the lose-everything rule
Visual identity of flat, stylised 3D worlds with 2D sprite enemies, plus gory limb and organ looting
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding weapon ranks before you can fully mod a gun, made more costly by patches that stopped melee kills from awarding gun XP unless the gun hit the enemy first
Re-running earlier areas to rebuild gear after dying in a late area, because all loot is lost on death
Inventory hoarding and Tetris-style stash management, and the lack of an easy sort in earlier versions
Ghosts added in a later update that can drain health, ammo and healing once they catch you, which some say wrecked atmosphere and difficulty curve
Repeated same-feeling levels and the same few weapons used through an entire act, which drags out runs
Annoying named threats called out repeatedly, such as forest birds, the castle boss that blinds and ignites you, and ambush dog packs
Endless mode's stage-20 achievement takes roughly 4-8 hours in one session, which reviewers call a pointless time sink
divisive_points: Hardcore direction vs power fantasy: some welcome tradeoffs and scarcity, others feel developers are repeating the Helldivers-style pattern of nerfing what players enjoyed
Death penalty: loses-everything is the loved tension for many, but others find it punishing enough to cause rage-quitting (an easy mode softens it)
Difficulty and learning curve: first hours are confusing and hard, but once it clicks many say the game becomes easy and trivial versus the AI
Whether it is a real roguelite or an extraction shooter in disguise, and whether that mix is a strength or a lack of identity
community.reception_notes: Launched into Steam Early Access on Oct 28, 2024 at $24.99 (the page warned the price would rise at 1.0) and was well received from the start, with a free demo helping discovery and frequent discount sales. Post-launch patches were frequent (for example 0.19.x patches and the Dungeons & Magic update in Jan 2025, which added a dungeon overhaul, melee knockback, 16 new oils and quick-sort). Later in 2025 and 2026, reviews show mood splitting over big balance updates (Qiosk's Plenty, which replaced picture-in-picture scopes, and the Scholar's Update that rebalanced 100+ oils and capped ammo), alongside a later ghost mechanic and an endless mode. Despite the negative patch-day reviews, overall Steam score stayed Very Positive and long-time players report very high playtime, and several 2026 reviews call it a possible GOTY. Windows only on PC; the official site lists PlayStation, Xbox and Switch versions as planned. Metacritic has only two early-access critic reviews and no Metascore; I could not find an OpenCritic page (web search budget was exhausted so OpenCritic and Reddit could not be checked). Revenue figures are algorithmic estimates, not audited.

community.one_liner: A Lovecraftian twin-stick survival roguelite by solo dev flanne where you actively aim and shoot hordes for twenty minutes, stacking runes/upgrades into wild builds (a Vampire Survivors-like with manual aiming).
community.consensus_summary: Players like it a lot: Steam sits at roughly 90% positive (about 29k reviews, Very Positive) at a $4.99 price, and it is widely described as great value and a fun, snappy, build-driven survivor-like for short sessions. Critics are thin but positive (OpenCritic 77 from 6 reviews, scores 7.5-8/10 from most, one 5/10), praising weapon/upgrade variety and complaining about limited content. Steam early access began June 2022, 1.0 landed June 2023, and a Switch port followed in Dec 2023. The dominant modern sentiment is frustration rather than hatred of the game itself: the PC version appears abandoned (promised updates and a beta build never shipped) while the mobile versions keep receiving content, and many negative Steam reviews are about that rather than gameplay.
best_things: Active manual aiming and shooting makes positioning and accuracy matter, unlike auto-attack survivor-likes
Rune/upgrade system with no cap on picks allows wild, sometimes broken synergies; called a sandbox for build crafting
Large roster of characters each with distinct abilities, plus weapons that evolve mid-run and change how they play
Darkness difficulty levels add different modifiers (faster/tankier enemies etc.) and give a reason to keep winning
Dark, minimalist pixel art with a Lovecraftian mood; cute character designs
Very good value at about $3-5, often on sale; many players report 10-60+ hours
Short, snappy runs suit quick sessions and the game runs smoothly for most players
Nothing important is locked behind achievements; unlocks are bought with gems so experimentation is free
worst_things: Only three maps, which are barren with few gimmicks; same muted palette throughout
Limited enemy variety and repeating bosses make runs feel samey after roughly 10 hours
Balance problems: summons and elemental builds are overtuned at top difficulty while pure gun-ability builds and some characters/weapons (e.g. Hastur) are weak or unviable
Endless mode becomes easy and repetitive quickly and is not sustained by enough content
Performance: builds that trigger many procs can cause lag or stutter late in runs
Single repeating music loop and weak soundtrack per several reviewers
Difficulty spike past about 15 minutes that is not well telegraphed, and RNG can produce unwinnable runs
PC version abandoned; promised updates and reworks never arrived
improvements: Add XP magnet/vacuum effect so collecting gems across the map is less tedious
More maps, enemy types and bosses, plus a rebuilt Endless mode (previously promised)
Rebalance builds so summons do not dominate and more characters/weapons are viable at high darkness levels
Ship the long-promised update (Emberpath/beta content) and communicate with the community
Accessibility: colorblind options and better visual clarity during dense fights
Achievements that reward creative play rather than repetitive high-difficulty clears
Surface more stat/info detail in-game; a reviewer who 100%ed the game says it hides too much information about how stats work
unique_things: Survivor-like with twin-stick manual aiming and reloading rather than auto-attacks
Fixed 20-minute standard run (plus 10-minute Quickplay and Endless with adjustable difficulty up to 15 levels)
Each character has a unique ability and weapons evolve into stronger forms mid-run
Runs are built from unlimited rune/upgrade picks, enabling very broken combinations
Near-monochrome Lovecraftian pixel aesthetic
Solo-developer, very cheap, with parallel PC, Switch and freemium mobile versions
tedious_or_disliked: Gem collection without a magnet and long unlock grind for characters, weapons and runes
Achievement hunting (reported ~60h) requires repetitive runs at highest difficulty with many characters
A full 20-minute run plus rising darkness levels that mostly just inflate enemy HP/speed feels like numbers rather than new challenge
Repeated bosses and three maps make later runs feel rote; some call the clicking monotonous
Dying repeatedly while testing builds is slow because every choice starts to funnel into the same few picks
divisive_points: Abandonment: many reviewers refuse to recommend it on PC; others say a cheap solo-dev game is fine 'as is' and expect no endless updates
Depth vs repetition: fans call it a build sandbox with huge replay value; others say it runs its course in about 10 hours
Art and palette: praised as moody and stylish by many, criticised for eye strain and low visual clarity by some
Difficulty: some find it easy and unbalanced, others hit a hard wall late in runs
community.reception_notes: Early access launched June 8, 2022 and reportedly earned over half a million dollars in its first week; mobile versions (a free ad-supported one and a premium one) arrived Sept 2022, Steam 1.0 on June 8, 2023, Switch Dec 21, 2023. Initial reception was very enthusiastic, including a critic naming it a favourite of 2022. Since roughly 2024 the Steam build has had no content updates despite a posted promise of big reworks and new characters/weapons, with a beta build available for a long time; mobile keeps getting updates and events, leading to a steady stream of 'abandoned' negative reviews (top negative reviews are nearly all about this). Overall Steam score remains about 90% positive. Metacritic has no page/score; OpenCritic has 6 reviews (77 top critic average, 50% of critics recommend). Mac and Windows only on Steam, no Linux.

community.one_liner: A gothic pixel-art auto-battler survivors-like where you play a necromancer who raises and merges undead minions that do the fighting while you dodge and collect bones.
community.consensus_summary: Steam reception is Overwhelmingly Positive (about 96% of roughly 5,400 reviews) for a $4.99 game from solo-ish studio caiysware, with praise centred on sheer content volume, minion-centric build variety, chiptune music and dark humour. Critics coverage is sparse: Metacritic lists the game with no Metascore yet (awaiting 4 critic reviews) and a 7.1 user score from only 12 ratings, and no OpenCritic entry turned up. Indie blogs (GamingOnLinux, a Substack review) were warm, with GamingOnLinux calling it a favourite and Steam Deck Verified. Negative reviews are a small minority but are highly consistent: the visuals are cluttered and hard on the eyes, and mechanics/tooltips are poorly explained. The game left early access and has kept receiving content updates well past 1.0, per player reviews.
best_things: Huge amount of content for the price: many classes, minion types, relics, spells and bosses; one player reports around 85 hours to 100 percent it
Minion-centric gameplay feels distinct from Vampire Survivors: your army does the fighting, and combining/mutating minions is rarely seen elsewhere
Deep, layered meta progression with a deliberate drip-feed of unlocks that keeps runs feeling novel
Chiptune soundtrack widely singled out as excellent
Gothic pixel art and crude, innuendo-heavy dark humour give it a strong identity
Secret extra modes such as a strategy card game (Clashful Cards), Castle Conquest, Architect Mode, endless and daily challenges
Developer is passionate and keeps shipping updates after 1.0; Steam Deck Verified and runs well on Linux/Proton
Very low price and few bugs reported even after 90 hours
worst_things: Visual clutter: enemies, minions, projectiles, weather and pickups blur together, making it hard to track your own character late in a run
Color scheme/saturation causes eye strain or headaches for some players; a few compare it to seizure-warning territory
Poor affordance design: no tooltips for spells, unclear meaning of gems and telegraphs, no way to re-check a class's strengths after a run starts
Text descriptions for minions and upgrades are written for flavour rather than clarity, forcing players to read multiple sentences or use external guides
Minions can look like enemies and XP can look like enemy projectiles, per critical reviewers (an early comment said outlines were later added to help)
Sparse audio feedback for much of the on-screen action, according to one reviewer
Limited control over minions, which only loosely follow you
improvements: Clearer readability: stronger player/minion/enemy/pickup differentiation and options to reduce effects and saturation
Better tutorial and in-run info: tooltips for spells, a class summary screen, clearer minion upgrade/merge rules
Plainer, more concise upgrade text instead of roleplay-style descriptions
More build variety and bosses to sustain interest after the first wins
Rebalanced difficulty curve, since meta progression makes the game far easier as you unlock everything
More distinct character classes (a recurring complaint in sentiment summaries)
unique_things: Inverted fantasy: you are the necromancer under attack by heroes, and minions rather than the player deal the damage
Bones from slain heroes are the resource used to raise the army
Minion combining/mutating upgrade system
Hidden upgrade effects revealed only after acquisition, encouraging discovery
Bundled side modes including a card game and map-hopping Castle Conquest, plus a tongue-in-cheek unlockable plumber character
Shares a universe/tone with the developer's other game Spirits Abyss
tedious_or_disliked: Reading dense upgrade text and puzzling out systems every level-up
Everything can be unlocked within a few hours for some players, after which runs feel like free wins
Repetitive loop once build variety is exhausted; some say if you have played one survivors-like you have played them all
Slow, small-feeling start and a few runs needed before options open up
Completionist tasks such as the achievements monument are off-putting to some
divisive_points: Art style: praised as charming retro pixel art by many, dismissed as ugly and unreadable by others
Difficulty: some find it too easy after meta progression, others find early runs unfair or unplayable
Info density: some enjoy the discovery and depth, others find the mechanics opaque and exhausting
community.reception_notes: Launched in early access in 2022 (GamingOnLinux wrote it up in Aug 2022 when it was about $1.99) and hit 1.0 on Mar 9, 2023 at $4.99; it was included in a Humble survivors-like bundle around then. Positive sentiment has held and steady content updates continue (Steam reviews dated into 2026 mention ongoing additions). Windows only on Steam; Steam Deck Verified and runs on Linux via Proton. A separate soundtrack DLC exists. Metacritic page exists with a 'tbd' Metascore and a 7.1 user score from 12 ratings. Players with under 2 hours are far more negative (about 10 percent positive per VaporLens), suggesting the opening and readability are the main barrier.

community.one_liner: A story-driven pixel-art action RPG roguelite by Dead Mage (published by 11 bit studios) in which you rotate through the members of the Bergson family, each with a distinct playstyle, through procedurally generated dungeons on Mount Morta, with optional local or online co-op.
community.consensus_summary: Children of Morta is received as a polished, warm, well-presented indie: Steam is Very Positive (about 88% of roughly 23,000 reviews), Metacritic sits at 82 from critics with a 7.9 user score, and OpenCritic at 83 with about 90% of critics recommending it. Praise centres on the family narrative, the narrator, the pixel art and music, and the variety from multiple playable characters. Complaints are about repetitive dungeons and enemies, a grindy meta-progression, kiting-heavy combat, pacing and difficulty inconsistencies, and buggy or unstable co-op. The game is finished and released on PC, consoles and mobile, with DLC (Ancient Spirits, Paws and Claws, Family Fireside Fables), so it is not early access or abandoned. Many players say it plays best in co-op and is weaker solo.
best_things: The Bergson family story and the narrator: the narration gives warmth and emotional weight to runs and cutscenes, and the family theme is repeatedly called the heart of the game
Pixel art and animation are widely called gorgeous, with atmospheric music and audio design also praised
Each of the playable family members feels different (archer Linda, melee, caster and others), which encourages rotating characters and lets players find a favourite
Fast, snappy action combat that critics describe as satisfying, with a steady stream of buffs and powers stacking up over a run
Co-op, local and online, is described by many players as the best way to play and a joy with friends
Dying does not lose gold or XP (you are sent back to the family home), and story events fire between runs, so the loop rarely feels purely punitive
Approachable difficulty for newcomers to the genre; reviewers call it a good entry-level roguelite and several players report it plays well on Steam Deck
worst_things: Combat often collapses into hit-and-run kiting; several negative Steam reviewers say fights lack depth beyond attack, retreat, repeat
Repetitive environments and limited enemy and location variety, with the mid-game described as tedious in the Game Critics review and elsewhere
Grinding for permanent upgrades and for levelling all characters is a frequent complaint, and the early dungeons can feel punishing until you have upgrades

Uneven difficulty and pacing: the Corruption fatigue system is seen by some as artificial padding; some characters (tanky melee, Lucy's rooted casting) feel weaker or clunkier than ranged ones like Linda
Late-game escort and timed missions were singled out by a critic as ill-advised
Bugs, co-op instability and controller issues are noted by reviewers and players; long load times also appear in critic complaints
Story progression is tied to deaths and run ends, so skilled players who rarely die can skip or scramble dialogue and quests, per a highly upvoted negative Steam review
Gameplay loop goes stale late in the campaign, and several positive reviewers say the story and replayability are not strong enough to keep them coming back
improvements: More variety in enemies, biomes and dungeon layouts so later runs differ more from earlier ones
Deeper combat with more reasons to stand and fight rather than kite, including better balance across family members
Less grindy, more meaningful meta-progression, and more run-to-run build variety so power-ups change how you play
Progression and story pacing that adapts to players who advance faster than the designed skill curve, plus an option to go back and power up before hard boss fights
Better co-op stability and sync, clearer UI, and more reliable controller support
Clearer enemy attack telegraphs and more forgiving dodge and ability queuing, raised by struggling new players
unique_things: A family-drama narrative wrapper with a narrator, unusual for a roguelite, where the cast develops across runs
A rotating roster where the whole family gets bonus traits from levelling every member, pushing you to play them all rather than main one class
Death returns you to the family home with no loss of gold or XP, so the home hub and between-run story events drive the pacing
Story told boss by boss with scripted beats between procedurally generated dungeon runs
Hand-crafted pixel art presentation and cinematic cutscenes that stand out among action roguelites
Native local and online co-op built into an ARPG roguelite structure
tedious_or_disliked: Replaying the same early dungeons to buy upgrades before you can progress
Constant kiting against damage-sponge enemies and elites that resist stagger and crowd control
Corruption fatigue system, which limits playing one character and forces rotation
Escort and timed missions in the late game
Narrator commentary becoming tiresome for some players, and a clunky UI for some
Long load times and buggy co-op sessions
divisive_points: Solo versus co-op: fans say it shines in co-op, while many negative reviews say it is mediocre or grindy when played alone
Difficulty: some find it gentle and ideal for beginners, others hit early difficulty spikes or sudden hard bosses
Forced character rotation: praised for variety by some, resented as grind and padding by others
Replay value: several positive reviewers finished the campaign and felt no urge to replay, while others sink 30 to 50 hours into it
community.reception_notes: Launched September 3, 2019 on PC to strong critical reception (Metacritic 82, OpenCritic 83) and later came to PS4, Xbox One, Switch, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and mobile. Steam shows roughly 1 to 2 million owners by SteamSpy estimates and estimated gross revenue of about 2.76 million dollars (net about 0.81 million) on a Boxleiter-method calculator, which is order-of-magnitude only and covers Steam only. DLC includes Ancient Spirits, Paws and Claws and Family Fireside Fables. Developer is Dead Mage, an Iran-based studio. Recent Steam reviews mostly repeat the same co-op, kiting and narrator themes, and some mention Steam Deck as a good fit. No major controversies found.

games.short_description: Crypt of the NecroDancer is an award winning hardcore roguelike rhythm game. Move to the music and deliver beatdowns to the beat! Groove to the epic Danny Baranowsky soundtrack, or select songs from your own MP3 collection!

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Crypt of the NecroDancer is a top-down dungeon crawler roguelike where every action must be made on the beat of the music. PepperHead, a drummer himself, was excited to play it but admits he is bad at it after three separate attempts over the years. He respects the design and is glad a rhythm roguelike became so successful, but it is too demanding and skill-based for him personally. He lands it at low B, explicitly refusing to drop it to C.
praise: Rhythm-driven core concept is well designed and he respects it
Phenomenal soundtrack that carries the experience
Good variety of playable characters
Great that a rhythm-based roguelike became so popular and successful
Rewards mastery: knowing enemy patterns lets you act precisely to the music
criticism: Very hard for a random person to pick up; fast-paced with many things to track at once
New areas bring new enemies with new patterns that must be memorised or progress is hard
Not a huge number of items, and runs rarely produce crazy builds
Never feels overpowered; purely skill-based mastery rather than build power
unique_points: All actions tied to the music beat, making it a rhythm game fused with roguelike dungeon crawling
Progression comes from player skill and pattern knowledge more than from builds or synergies
commentary.quote: I can't put it as a c tier I'm gonna put it as a low B
design_criteria: Difficulty/accessibility: too hard and fast for a casual pick-up
Enemy design: per-area patterns must be learned by heart
Audio/music: phenomenal soundtrack central to the game
Build variety/synergies: few items, no crazy builds
Character diversity: many characters
Skill vs power: mastery-based, never overpowered
Core concept originality: rhythm mechanic

community.one_liner: A hardcore roguelike dungeon crawler where every move and attack must be made on the beat of the music, by Brace Yourself Games with a soundtrack by Danny Baranowsky.
community.consensus_summary: Critics and players both treat it as an inventive genre fusion and a modern indie classic: 87 on Metacritic and OpenCritic, and 95.5% positive across about 26.5k Steam reviews (Overwhelmingly Positive). The soundtrack, tight beat-based movement and the amount of unlockable characters and items get near-universal praise. Reception is tempered by a steep learning curve, a brutal late game (only about 8% of Steam players finish the final zone) and complaints about a long tail of paid DLC. It left Early Access in April 2015 and has been supported since with the Amplified expansion (2017) and the Synchrony DLC (online multiplayer and modding), so it is not abandoned.
best_things: Soundtrack by Danny Baranowsky is called one of the best in games; reviewers say there is no weak track, and you can also play to your own MP3s
The rhythm-plus-roguelike fusion is seen as genuinely innovative, turning turn-based dungeon crawling into something frantic and tactile
Enemy movement patterns are learnable, giving a Souls-like mastery loop: players say it is deeply satisfying once it clicks into a flow state
Large roster of characters with different rules (Aria, Bolt, Dove, Coda and others) and many modes gives huge replay value
Good value at $14.99 for a game with a huge roster of characters and modes; the Amplified expansion is described by fans as adding a lot of content
Clever, inventive bosses and enemy design; clean, readable pixel art
Good for short sessions and quick runs; some players with ADHD say it suits brief bursts
No Beat Mode and broad accessibility options give an on-ramp for people unsure about rhythm play
worst_things: Very steep difficulty spike: early enemies and mini-bosses can kill in one or two hits, and Zone 4 and All Zones are a wall for many players
The beat system is rigid and leaves little room for flexibility, so one mistake can cascade into death
Some reviewers find the roguelike layer repetitive: the loop wears thin and enemy variety is low (many reskinned skeleton variants)
Bosses are sometimes called gimmicky rather than threatening
Heavy 100% completion demands: a few achievements and harder characters are described as near-impossible
Some players report desync between visuals, audio and input that makes timing feel off on certain setups
Item and inventory UI can be unclear: items are hard to identify by name and weapon damage is not shown
Damage feels inconsistent and unforgiving: a perfect run can collapse to a single ranged hit that removes half your health
improvements: Better explanation of items, scrolls and weapon stats in the UI and a gentler onboarding for non-rhythm players
More enemy variety and less reliance on palette-swapped skeleton and shield enemies
More meaningful hub/shop unlocks beyond mostly new loot in chests
Rebalance the hardest characters and the late-game zones, which many players call a wall
Make online multiplayer and mod support part of the base game instead of paywalling them in Synchrony
Smaller, cheaper DLC bundling; reviewers dislike the number of separate paid add-ons
unique_things: Everything moves on the beat: enemies, traps and the player are all locked to the soundtrack, with a beating-heart UI
Score multiplier system tied to staying on beat, with coins rewarding rhythm consistency
Bring your own music: custom MP3s generate beats for levels
No Beat Mode and several characters that change the rules (for example single-heart or bard-style restrictions), so it is effectively many games in one
Composed by the Super Meat Boy and Binding of Isaac composer, making music the core mechanic rather than decoration
Spawned crossovers and spinoffs (Cadence of Hyrule, Rift of the NecroDancer) and a large modding scene
tedious_or_disliked: Dying repeatedly in the first zone for new players before the timing becomes instinctive
Repeating zones 1-3 just to get a fresh attempt at Zone 4, then relearning them at 3 hearts in All Zones mode
Completionist grind: a handful of very hard achievements, and 100% is described as a huge time sink
Constant DLC upsells: some longtime owners are annoyed by repeated DLC promotion and the count of paid add-ons
Music can wear on some players, and a few find the rhythm requirement stressful or ill-suited to ADHD or weak rhythm
Frequent in-game popups and prompts pushing tips and DLC, which some players find annoying
divisive_points: Rhythm mechanic itself: some call it the best part of the game while others find it only neat for ten minutes or feel it is more a roguelike than a rhythm game
Difficulty: fans see it as rewarding mastery; others call it exclusionary and poor design in late zones
Synchrony DLC value: praised for rollback online multiplayer and modding, but criticised as thin content for its price and with a low online population
community.reception_notes: Launched from Early Access around 23-24 April 2015 to very strong reviews (early Steam score around 99% positive per community comments). Metacritic: 87 from 45 critic reviews (Generally Favorable) with a user score of 7.8 from about 310 ratings; OpenCritic: 87 top critic average, 96% of critics recommend, 47 reviews, 98th percentile. Steam owner estimates are 1-2 million, and steam-revenue-calculator estimates about 16.8M USD gross and about 5.0M net (Boxleiter-method estimate, not audited; no exact copies figure found). Amplified (2017) was well received as a content doubling; Synchrony (online co-op, modding) drew mixed feelings over price and paywalled features. Available on PC, PS4, PS5, Switch, Xbox One, Vita and iOS.

commentary.summary: Cult of the Lamb is a management sim fused with an action roguelite: you tend a cult village between short dungeon runs. community.one_liner: A cute-but-macabre action roguelite from Massive Monster (published by Devolver Digital, 2022) where you play a sacrificed lamb who founds a cult, alternating between dungeon runs and managing a village of followers.
community.consensus_summary: Cult of the Lamb is received as a highly successful, charming genre blend: critics sit at Metacritic 82 (88 reviews) and OpenCritic 84 (143 reviews, 88% recommend), and Steam players rate it Overwhelmingly Positive (about 96% of 130k reviews). Praise centres on art, music, tone and the addictive loop between combat and cult management; criticism centres on thin combat depth, limited run variety and management that can turn into micromanagement. It has been supported for years with free updates and paid DLC (Sinful Pack, Pilgrim Pack, and the large Woolhaven expansion in January 2026), and is not early access or abandoned. A minority of players find both halves shallow or repetitive, and Woolhaven launch brought some save-corruption and bug complaints.
best_things: Distinctive cute-meets-dark art style, humour and tone; very widely praised
Catchy, memorable soundtrack that players mention repeatedly
Combat is responsive, fast and easy to pick up, with short, satisfying dungeon runs
The loop of running dungeons to feed cult management, then returning to build, is called addictive and cozy
Emotional attachment to followers (naming, marrying, reviving them, grieving deaths) creates stories players love
Strong accessibility and difficulty options let players with disabilities or different skill levels enjoy it
Generous free post-launch content and later DLC; co-op on the Steam version
Rich lore, hidden quests and steady new unlocks keep progression engaging for fans (though some find the ending and final boss underwhelming)
worst_things: Combat is shallow compared with Hades or Binding of Isaac: few real builds, limited weapon/curse variety and little run-to-run difference
Dungeons start to feel samey once you have cleared several; repetition sets in over time
The two halves do not fully integrate and some critics call it two genres each done competently but not deeply
Vague or unexplained mechanics and building descriptions, which the game then punishes you for missing
Bugs and technical issues: performance on some platforms, menu pause not stopping the village simulation, and save corruption reports around DLC
Enemy bullets and clutter can be hard to read, and healing items are rare, so early damage can ruin a run
Endgame does not go as far as other roguelites for players wanting huge replayability
improvements: Add more combat depth: parry mechanics, more build-defining weapon and curse synergies and more run variety
Explain systems, quests and building effects better in-game
Split-screen or independent village play in co-op so the second player is not tethered and idle during management
Fix save corruption and pause behavior; clearer timers that do not punish absences
More variety between dungeon layouts and more endgame replay incentives
Clearer readability of enemies and projectiles
unique_things: Fuses an action roguelite with a cult-running colony sim (Animal Crossing/Stardew style) in one loop
Adorable woodland-animal aesthetic used to tell a dark, sacrificial cult story with black humour
Followers have traits, loyalty and lives; you can indoctrinate, marry, sacrifice or revive them
Choose moral direction of your cult through doctrines, rituals and sermons, with real tradeoffs
Side activities like fishing, farming, gambling and decorating plus a large cosmetic/customisation set
Woolhaven adds winter, animal husbandry and new enemies as a second campaign-scale layer
tedious_or_disliked: Constant follower needs (feeding, cleaning waste, curing illness, sermons, quests) can feel like chores or laundry rather than fun
Day/night pressure and timed follower quests add stress and a sense of maintenance over achievement
Unlock pace slows sharply after the first ~6 hours, with long unlock animations and grindy costs, so progress feels slower over time
Losing part of your haul on death and rare healing feels punishing to players who came for base building
Grinding resources and travelling between activities (for example fishing just to support base management) feels like busywork to some
In co-op, the village management phase leaves one player bored or left out
Followers age and die quickly, and naming or bonding with them makes deaths and forced sacrifices feel bad for some players
divisive_points: Difficulty and roguelike elements: developers said they are core, while some players want them softened; others find Normal just right and praise the difficulty options
Whether the management half is relaxing and cozy or stressful micromanagement
Whether the game-of-two-halves structure is a strength or means neither half is excellent
Whether the game is a masterpiece or merely a charming, repetitive game carried by style
community.reception_notes: Launched Aug 11 2022 on PC, consoles and later iOS to strong critic scores and big sales (Steam Revenue Calculator estimates roughly $116M gross, about $34M net to the developer; SteamSpy owners 2-5M; estimates only, not audited). Steam price $24.99 and it is often discounted. The game kept receiving free updates and paid content; Woolhaven (Jan 22 2026) reportedly sold over 60,000 copies on Steam at launch and outsold earlier add-ons, though some players reported save corruption and bugs, especially when adding or removing DLC. Steam and OpenCritic user scores are high, while Metacritic user score (7.9, 70% positive) is notably lower than Steam, suggesting more mixed sentiment there. Available on Windows and macOS on Steam, not Linux.

community.one_liner: Klei Entertainment's hand-drawn, Tim Burton-flavoured wilderness survival game with permadeath, procedurally generated worlds, and no tutorial.
community.consensus_summary: Don't Starve is regarded as a modern survival classic: Steam shows 'Overwhelmingly Positive' at about 96.5% across roughly 113k reviews, and critics landed in the high 70s (Metacritic 79 on PC, Generally Favorable). Praise centres on the gothic art style, the discovery-driven learning loop and the tension of permadeath. Both players and critics flag the lack of guidance and punishing early hours as the main barrier, and several say the loop turns tedious once survival is mastered. The original single-player game is effectively in maintenance mode, since Klei's content updates moved to the multiplayer Don't Starve Together. Many recent Steam reviewers, even positive ones, tell newcomers to buy DST instead, even for solo play. It is not early access; it released in full in April 2013 after an alpha/beta period.
best_things: Distinctive hand-drawn, Burton-esque gothic art with fluid animation, plus a gramophone-style soundtrack and strong atmosphere
Permadeath loop where every death teaches something specific (bees, darkness, hunger), making learning itself the reward
Survival systems that interlock: hunger, sanity, health, seasons, day/night cycle and creature behaviour create emergent stories
No hand-holding; players respect that Klei kept a cohesive identity instead of chasing mainstream accessibility
Huge replayability from randomly generated worlds, many unlockable characters with different perks, and adjustable world settings
Everything has multiple uses (monsters can be turned against each other, even death can be exploited), which rewards experimentation
Strong value, often very cheap on sale; expansions like Reign of Giants, Shipwrecked and Hamlet are described as near full games
worst_things: Almost no tutorial or in-game explanation; many mechanics (bird cage for food, bunnymen hostility to meat carriers, final Adventure level in darkness) are only learnable via the wiki or trial and error
Early hours are brutal and feel unfair because death often comes from not knowing rules rather than player error
Losing a long run to a hidden mechanic feels especially demoralising after dozens of hours
Adventure mode is seen as poorly designed: fetch-quest errands across levels, then a surprise difficulty spike
Once you can survive indefinitely the game loses purpose and becomes chores; a common critique is weak long-term goals
Clunky real-time combat, especially clicking on moving targets with mouse and keyboard
Some reports of crashes (e.g. loading worlds with caves via DST) and a black-screen lockup bug in recent negative Steam reviews
Some players feel abandoned: the single-player game receives no new content while DST keeps being updated
Base game feels dated next to Don't Starve Together (e.g. weaker crafting menu and quality of life), per reviewers who played both
improvements: Better in-game teaching or hinting (food values, creature behaviour) so players do not need a wiki or mods like craft pot and minimap
Clearer feedback on why a run ended so failure teaches specific lessons instead of feeling like repetition
New content and updates for the original game instead of leaving it behind DST
More mid and late-game goals beyond surviving longer, and a redesigned Adventure mode
Quality-of-life features built into the base game that players currently get via mods (geometric placement, minimap, displayed food values)
Stability fixes for crashes and the black-screen bug
unique_things: Survival-crafting game with roguelike permadeath and procedural worlds but no levelling meta-progression; the only thing you carry over is knowledge
Sanity as a third resource alongside health and hunger, with hallucinated monsters and shifting behaviour
Darkness is lethal: night without light means death, which defines the pacing of every day
Seasonal cycle (autumn, winter, spring, summer) each with its own threats, forcing long-term planning
Art direction of a storybook with gothic undertones, with a cast of oddly distinct playable characters
Emergent, systemic monster ecosystem where hostile creatures can be baited to fight each other
tedious_or_disliked: Constant resource gathering and base upkeep (chopping, mining, food, fuel) that becomes chores once mastered
Learning by dying repeatedly with little carried over between runs, which some find repetitive rather than empowering
Needing a second monitor with a wiki open to progress efficiently
Adventure mode fetch-quest grind across multiple levels
Solo play can feel repetitive and unstructured; several reviewers say the game works better in multiplayer
divisive_points: Deliberate obtuseness: fans call it rewarding discovery, detractors call it artificial difficulty (even a 7/10 PopMatters-style review called the learning process laborious)
Original vs Don't Starve Together: some prefer the simpler, less bloated original, while many recommend DST even for solo play because of more content and ongoing updates
Whether it is really a roguelike: permadeath and procedural worlds say yes, but the open-ended sandbox survival structure says otherwise
Punishing permadeath: thrilling for some, demoralising for others as runs get longer
community.reception_notes: Launched to Generally Favorable reviews (Metacritic high 70s), with critics praising the art and addictive loop and criticising the steep, poorly explained learning curve. Klei focused later development on Don't Starve Together and released the Reign of Giants, Shipwrecked and Hamlet expansions for the original, but the base game now gets little or no new content, which feeds recent negative reviews complaining of abandonment. It is on PC, Mac, Linux, consoles, Switch and iOS. The Metacritic figures conflict between sources: Steam lists 79 for PC, while the fetched Metacritic page showed 78 and user 7.1, apparently for the PS4 edition; a PC user score could not be verified and is left null. the base-game OpenCritic figure could not be verified and is left null; the OpenCritic page fetched was for the Switch edition (80).
