community.one_liner: A 2D pixel-art action roguelite dungeon crawler by Lamina Studios (Dec 2016) that mixes Nuclear Throne-style shooting/melee, Risk of Rain-style item stacking and snowballing power, with 10 classes and local co-op.
community.consensus_summary: Dungeon Souls is received as a decent but derivative budget roguelite. Steam players rate it Mostly Positive (about 74% of ~2,200 reviews by the local data; the store page shows 77% of 1,310), and Metacritic sits at a Mixed 67 from 8 critic reviews with a 6.0 user score. Critics called it a fun, casual tribute to older dungeon crawlers that borrows heavily from its inspirations and is quickly forgotten. Long-time players say it gets addictive once the between-run upgrades start compounding. It is a finished 2016 release (not early access); the Steam forum has threads asking whether the game is dead, and recent negative reviews cite unresolved controller and crash problems on modern systems. Web searches were unavailable for this run (search budget exhausted), so community color is drawn from Steam reviews, Steam forum titles, and the Destructoid and Metacritic pages.
best_things: Ten distinct hero classes with different abilities (e.g. Barbarian with health and area attacks, Cleric with bouncing projectiles and a shield) that change how a run plays
Items and passives (50+) provide a snowballing, overpowered-build feeling in the Risk of Rain mould; one 40-hour reviewer says runs start short but become an avalanche once meta upgrades kick in
Addictive, replayable loop with lots of RNG and unlocks; one reviewer calls it among the most addictive dungeon crawlers they have played in a while
Bite-sized, turn-your-brain-off action that suits short sessions; Hardcore Gamer said practice and learning the characters eventually pays off
Pleasant pixel-art presentation and simple fitting audio, plus local split-screen co-op
Nostalgic old-school dungeon crawler feel; one reviewer feels it set a standard later games improved on
worst_things: Heavily derivative of Nuclear Throne, Risk of Rain and Spelunky without its own identity (Destructoid, LEVEL, High-Def Digest: forgettable)
Bland, repetitive procedurally generated environments with poor visibility; traps blend into the dark
Melee characters are poorly balanced in a bullet-heavy game with no dodge mechanic; enemies feel like bullet sponges
Unfair hazards: floor traps in narrow corridors, ritual-marker rooms, and enemies that spawn directly on the player
Confusing interface and item placement (chests look like shop items, accidental warps to secret levels)

Technical issues: stated Xbox controller support reportedly does not register input (negative reviewers say unresolved since at least 2018), mouse is not captured on multi-monitor setups, black screen and crash reports on newer Windows
Low-sophistication story and visuals; the plot is described as merely present
improvements: Fix controller detection and make the advertised Xbox controller support actually work
Capture the mouse cursor and fix window/taskbar handling for multi-monitor play
Add a dodge or mobility option and rebalance melee classes against projectile-heavy enemies
Make traps, chests and shop items readable against dark backgrounds; clarify interface and warp triggers
Stabilise the game on modern Windows 11 to stop crashes and black screens
Clearer explanation of how to unlock characters (Brawler, Redeemer) and find crafting recipes such as Nimby's Grace
unique_things: Cross-breed of Nuclear Throne action, Risk of Rain item scaling and Overture-style dungeon crawling, according to its own store description
Activating marks/altars on a level to open the escape portal rather than simply reaching an exit
Crafting system with recipes that players must discover, plus permanent meta upgrades between runs
Ten hero classes with unlockable characters such as the Brawler and Redeemer
Shared/split-screen local co-op and Remote Play Together support in a pixel-art roguelite at a low price
tedious_or_disliked: Early runs feel short with little progress until meta upgrades accumulate; one reviewer calls the meta progression 'dark' and monotonous
Slow walking speed makes fleeing traps and enemies hard
Random monster spawns punish stopping to level up, so the pace forces constant movement
Crafting reportedly disables gameplay while it is active (one negative review)
Losing a run's progress by exiting to the main menu (Steam forum PSA) and unclear save behaviour
Limited variety between characters according to a negative reviewer, with monotonous gameplay over time
divisive_points: Simplicity: some enjoy mindless, easy-to-pick-up action; others find it monotonous and shallow
Difficulty and balance: Hardcore Gamer says mastery pays off, while Destructoid found melee classes badly outmatched by bullets
Derivativeness: some see a loving tribute to the genre's greats, others an unoriginal copy
Class variety: praised by critics and many players, but one negative reviewer says characters offer little gameplay variety
community.reception_notes: Launched Dec 2, 2016 to mixed-positive reviews (Metacritic 67, 8 critics ranging 60 to 80). The Steam page lists a Digital World Game Expo Best Game award. Steam forum has a v1.1 bugs thread, a 'Dungeon Souls 2?' thread and an 'Is the game dead?' thread, suggesting development has stopped. Recent (2025-2026) Steam reviews are still mostly positive from nostalgic players, but negative ones report crashes on Windows 11, non-working controller support and mouse capture issues. Available on Windows, Mac and Linux. OpenCritic has no matching entry that could be confirmed (the page fetched belonged to a different game), so opencritic is null. Revenue and owner figures are third-party estimates, not audited.

community.one_liner: A fast 2D run-and-gun roguelite platformer set inside a living comic book, where each room is a comic panel and ink is the upgrade currency; playable solo or in local/online co-op.
community.consensus_summary: Fury Unleashed is well liked but rarely treated as a genre heavyweight. Steam shows about 87% positive across roughly 2,900 reviews (Very Positive), and Metacritic critic scores sit in the high 70s (79 on PC, 76 across platforms), with user reviews and critic reviews both calling it polished, tight and cheap fun. Reviewers compare it to Contra/Metal Slug crossed with Dead Cells and Rogue Legacy, and lean on its combo system and control feel. Criticism centres on repetitive content (few level themes, samey bosses), modest meta-progression, and spongy enemies on the default Hard setting. The other recurring complaint in recent years is flaky online co-op. It is a released, non-early-access game (Steam release listed as May 8, 2020); the developer keeps an active Steam community presence (bug-report threads, Discord), but recent reviews show online co-op and platform issues (Steam Deck, Linux audio, crashes) are still open pain points. No OpenCritic page was located.
best_things: Tight, responsive controls: dash, double jump, stomp, shoot and melee feel smooth and precise, which reviewers call the game's strongest asset
Combo/heat system rewards aggressive, damage-free play with escalating rewards such as health and shield drops, and is described as the freshest mechanic
Comic-book framing: chapters are individual comics and stages are laid out as comic panels, which players find creative and cohesive
Big arsenal and many power-ups with trade-offs, giving varied runs; cited as a source of replayability, plus about 40 bosses
Very customisable: adjustable difficulty sliders, full button remapping and character/face customisation
Couch and online co-op make it far more fun with a friend, and two controllers even work in single-player for a silly shared-character mode
Great value: often heavily discounted, with many reviewers saying it is worth more than they paid
Strong soundtrack and a fast, chaotic, adrenaline-heavy feel that several players call an underrated gem
worst_things: Online co-op is unreliable: players report failing to connect over half the time, desyncs, and in 2026 reviews it is described as hard to get working
Co-op design gripes: in online lobbies only the host can customise a character while the guest waits
Repetition: only four level themes, rooms, weapons and bosses can feel alike over long sessions
Enemies are spongy on Hard, slowing the pace; some find enemies spawning underneath them cheap
Progression is seen as minor and mostly stat upgrades (health, etc.) rather than changing how you play; some upgrades are barely noticeable, like the blink invulnerability
Weapon drops are random, and some runs go long stretches with nothing good
Stability issues reported by some: a top-upvoted negative review reports consistent crashes shortly after launch; Steam forum topics mention black-screen crashes, Steam Deck and Linux audio problems
Some reviewers find it short and, for solo play, outclassed by better action roguelites
improvements: Fix and modernise online co-op connectivity and sync, and let guests customise their own characters
Add more level themes, enemy types and boss variety to reduce sameness
Deeper meta-progression: unlocks that change playstyle rather than small stat bumps
Rebalance enemy health on the default Hard difficulty to keep pacing brisk
Smoother Switch performance (Nintendo Life cited framerate issues) and better Steam Deck/Linux support
More reliable weapon availability per run so a run is not dead for long stretches
unique_things: Every stage is a page of a comic book, with rooms as panels and chapters as issues, tied into a story about a creator who has lost faith in his hero
Ink is both the currency dropped by enemies and the thing you spend on upgrades
Combo meter tied to survival: a whole run on one continuous combo is a stated challenge, and heat increases damage and healing drops
Full customisation: players can change every difficulty setting, remap every button and design their character's look
Hard is the default, with Easy mode locking leaderboards and achievements, plus harder modes and a secret final level unlocked later
Roguelite with light grinding until the late secret final level, blended with old-school Contra-style run-and-gun
tedious_or_disliked: Hard-mode enemy sponginess and tiptoeing around damage makes some runs feel slow and tedious
Early-game low-level runs feel very hard before upgrades make it easy (one reviewer likens it to Destiny: the game starts at full level)
Upgrade grinding is called a grind by some, and the secret final level surprised and frustrated a reviewer
Repetitive bosses, which one reviewer summarises as jumping around and shooting
Connecting to online co-op is a hassle, sometimes harder than playing the game
Basic for genre veterans: one top negative review says anyone who plays a lot of roguelikes will get bored of it
divisive_points: Difficulty: Hard default is praised as challenging-but-fair by some and as spongy, tedious and unfair by others

Art style: some enjoy the personality of the paper cut-out comic look; Gameblog.fr called the art direction insipid, and one reviewer admits he dislikes games that look like flash games (though he ended up recommending it)
Value: many call it a steal on sale, while a couple of reviewers say it is not worth full price and is better with a friend than solo
Progression depth: some find upgrades motivating and enough to keep playing; others find them too minor to matter
community.reception_notes: Metacritic lists PC, PS4, Xbox One, Switch and iOS versions. PC Metascore is 79 from 9 reviews (90% positive, 10% mixed, 0% negative) and the all-platform page shows 76 from 10, with user score 7.5 from 31 ratings. Steam sample: 87% positive of about 2,900 reviews, with a SteamSpy owner estimate of 20k-50k and a steam-revenue-calculator estimate near $125k gross (order-of-magnitude only, Boxleiter method). Steam lists release May 8, 2020, no early-access history was found on the store page, and the developer describes five years of polish. Price is $19.99 but heavily discounted often. Recent (2025-2026) Steam reviews still praise it as a cheap, fun game but increasingly flag broken or hard-to-use online co-op. The Steam forum has an active bug-report thread, Discord, and topics about Steam Deck, Linux audio and crashes. community.one_liner: A satirical action roguelite from Aggro Crab (published by Team17) where an unpaid intern fights through dungeons built from failed tech startups, using office junk as breakable weapons.
community.consensus_summary: Players rate it Very Positive on Steam (about 90% of roughly 4,175 reviews) and critics were mostly favourable (Metacritic PC 78 from 11 reviews). Almost everyone agrees the art direction, writing and corporate-satire theming are the main draw. The action roguelite gameplay is the weak point: many reviews call the combat sluggish, shallow or janky, and the content thin. Commercially it underperformed: Wikipedia says Aggro Crab cancelled a planned extra dungeon because of poor base game sales. It is a complete, 2020-released game with a post-launch 'Working from Home' update, it is frequently discounted to around $2, and a recommend-on-sale verdict is common even among lukewarm reviewers.
best_things: Sharp, funny satire of startup and gig-economy culture; several reviewers say it has aged well and will trigger flashbacks for anyone who worked at a startup
Distinctive art direction that turns corporate clip-art/Memphis-style design into something charming rather than soulless, plus a solid soundtrack
Charming, archetypal cast and witty dialogue; talking to coworkers between runs is a highlight
Everything-is-a-weapon system: you pick up desks, office supplies and more to swing, throw or shoot, with a varied weapon pool
Generous accessibility and difficulty options: an Assist mode and difficulty changes at any time without disabling achievements
Choose-your-starting-item mechanic avoids runs ruined by a bad first pickup
Good length that does not overstay its welcome (roughly 10 hours for a casual clear) and runs well, including on Steam Deck
Boss fights and enemy/dungeon theming (three themed dungeons) praised as creative
worst_things: Combat described as floaty, sluggish and clunky: commitment to attack animations, slow dodges, imprecise hits, and enemies able to stun-lock you
Cluttered, cramped rooms and exploding traps can make damage feel unfair rather than hard, with off-screen enemies hard to spot
Thin content: only three dungeons, and the second half replays them in a hard mode, so many feel they saw everything in the first section
Weapon durability means weapons break every few fights, which some find tedious rather than fun, and shields on many enemies make this worse late game
Humour leans on dated memes and references for some reviewers, and characters lack depth
Final boss and late game spikes are called out as frustrating or unfair
Keyboard support is poor: controls cannot be rebound, and the weapon-switch keys are awkward; it plays best on controller
Progression and unlocks feel unimpactful; runs feel samey and skill descriptions are unclear
Sluggish, poorly optimized menus; one top negative review also says known bugs were never patched
improvements: Add rebindable controls and better keyboard/mouse defaults, including an option to stop auto-pickup on dodge
Speed up the post-run flow: multiple menus and loads before you can restart a run are a frequent complaint
Tune combat: more responsive attacks and dodges, clearer enemy telegraphs, less unavoidable off-screen damage
More content and variety: a fourth or fifth dungeon (the cancelled extra dungeon is the obvious gap) and less copy-paste in the hard-mode half
Clearer perk and skill descriptions and more meaningful unlocks
Camera improvements, or a locked isometric-style view, so furniture and walls do not hide threats
unique_things: Dungeons are the ruins of failed tech startups, each themed on a parody of a startup archetype
Breakable office-supply and furniture weapons you can also throw, instead of a fixed weapon loadout
Mentor and coworker bonding system that unlocks abilities, tied into the narrative
Corporate clip-art aesthetic with a mix of 2D and 3D art and gibberish-style voice work
Narrative-first roguelite where the satire drives the structure, and the ending is widely praised by fans
Assist and difficulty toggles that can be changed mid-game without penalty
tedious_or_disliked: Long menu and loading sequence between death and the next run
Constant weapon breakage and needing to spend scarce cash on food and healing in shops
Repetition: hard mode repeats the same three dungeons, and runs feel similar
Grinding for unlocks, with many skills described as pointless or unclear, which some players only finish by beating the game before unlocking everything
Dodge and stun-lock frustration when crowds of enemies or explosions pile on in tight rooms
Slow animations combined with imprecise weapons make fights feel like work
divisive_points: The humour and writing: many find it the best part, a minority find it dated, meme-heavy or unfunny
Combat feel and difficulty: some call it light and accessible, others call it janky or unfair, with Assist mode the usual recommended fix
Whether the game is a worthwhile roguelite or mostly a narrative/satire experience: several positive reviewers say it is for people who want the theme, not the mechanics
Art style: praised as distinctive, but a few find it fuzzy or hard to read
community.reception_notes: Launched September 24, 2020 on PC, Switch, PS4 and Xbox One, with physical editions for Switch and PS4 from Limited Run Games. Critics were mostly favourable, with platform Metacritic scores ranging 73 to 81, praising the satire and weapon variety, while a minority such as TheGamer (2.5/5) found the combat repetitive versus Dead Cells or Hades. Post-launch the 'Working from Home' update added weapons and a hard mode, but a planned additional dungeon was cancelled because of weak base sales. Steam lists it at about $2.49 at time of data collection, with estimated 200k to 500k owners and roughly $1.8M gross (Boxleiter-style estimate, order of magnitude only). Recent Steam reviews in 2025 to 2026 remain positive, with some players finding it via Game Pass or sales. Steam is Windows only. OpenCritic score could not be retrieved because the web search budget was exhausted and direct page fetches failed.

community.one_liner: A third-person action RPG wrapped in a roguelite deck-builder, where a mysterious Dealer lays out a card-built board-game dungeon and you fight real-time combat whenever the cards demand it.
community.consensus_summary: Critics and players largely agree it is a clear, more ambitious step up from the 2015 original, with a Metacritic score of 80 and Steam 'Very Positive' (about 84% of roughly 5.8k reviews in the local data). The atmosphere, writing, narrator and the unusual card-as-dungeon loop are the main draws. The persistent complaints are combat that is serviceable but shallow and repetitive, randomness that can ruin a run, and bloat or grind in longer play. The developer Defiant stopped making new games in 2019 and only maintains the title, so the game is effectively in maintenance mode (not early access). The Steam store page showed recent reviews as only Mixed (66% of 15) against Very Positive overall, which suggests a small, aging player base with some lingering technical complaints.
best_things: Atmosphere and presentation: art, music, sound design and the Dealer narrator's personality are repeatedly called out as the standout feature
A genuinely unusual gameplay loop: you build a hand of encounter and equipment cards, then navigate a board-game map that unfolds like a choose-your-own-adventure
Strong writing and story-driven scenarios (20+ campaign quests plus endless mode) with varied outcomes built from the cards you unlock
New mini-game-style challenges (dice, pendulum, wheel) add skill-based variety beyond the original's card-shuffle challenge
Companions with their own questlines and abilities improve both exploration and combat compared with the first game
Unlockable gear that levels up and token challenges give a steady reason to keep unlocking cards and equipment
Combat grows more satisfying in later acts once riposte and block-breaking mechanics open up (Arkham-style comparison appears in several Steam reviews)
Character customization and more diverse cast were noted as improvements
worst_things: Combat is the weakest pillar: Arkham-lite, one-enemy-at-a-time feel, repetitive and often just spam-attack once you out-gear encounters (echoed by PC Gamer and Game Informer per Wikipedia summary)
Randomness and luck-based challenges can be run-killing or feel unfair in later campaigns; GameSpot noted some quests lean too heavily on luck
Late-game bloat: decks of 20+ cards with no search or filter make pre-run deck building a chore
Technical rough edges in some Steam reviews: long loading screens before each fight, enemy AI breaking (reported fix: turn vsync on), bugged dice rerolls, an unlocked sword not appearing in equipment
Sluggish-feeling hero evade and chaotic, hard-to-read fights in crowded encounters according to negative reviewers
Progression and grind: Wccftech scored it 60 citing unsatisfying progression, punishing randomness and clunky combat; some Steam reviewers call it overpriced at $30 and repetitive
Later campaigns spike in difficulty and feel unfair to some players, leading to frustration (and grinding for gold-token gear) before progress is possible
improvements: Deeper, more varied combat: more enemy variety and more tactical options beyond attack, counter and block
Deck-management quality of life: a search or filter for the growing card collection and a faster way to build hands
Shorter or skippable loading screens and intro animations when restarting encounters
Better balance for Endless mode, where item degradation makes daggers nearly useless
Less punishing RNG or more mitigation tools so one bad draw does not sink a long run
Bug fixes, since the studio is in maintenance mode and some bugs reported in 2025 remain
unique_things: The dungeon is literally a tabletop built from cards that the Dealer lays out, and the cards you choose determine encounters, loot and events
A sitting-in-the-Dealer's-wagon framing with a charismatic narrator who comments on your successes and failures
Hybrid of deckbuilding and real-time third-person action combat, often compared to Arkham-style fighting with a card-game shell
Tarot-flavoured theming and choose-your-own-adventure storytelling rather than a pure arena roguelike
Hand-built campaign scenarios with persistent unlocks, rather than fully random runs, plus a separate Endless mode
Steam tags label it a roguelike deckbuilder, but most players describe it as closer to a narrative adventure with roguelite unlock progression
tedious_or_disliked: Repeating the same lock-on combat over many encounters; some players mash attack to get through it
Scrolling a large card collection to build a deck before each run
Long loading and intro sequences each time you retry a level
Luck-heavy mini-games that must be passed for story progress and can be frustrating
Grinding the campaign to unlock the cards and gear needed for later, harder scenarios
Endless mode's item degradation making some weapon types feel pointless
divisive_points: Combat: some find it fun and increasingly rewarding, others find it the weakest, clunkiest part of the game
Difficulty and RNG: some enjoy the tension and sense of accomplishment, others see late campaigns as unfair and want to uninstall
Value: recommended by many at full price as a unique experience, but some say wait for a sale at $15 or less
Roguelike label: players split on whether it satisfies roguelike cravings or plays more like a campaign-based adventure
community.reception_notes: Launched November 2017 on PC, PS4 and Xbox One to generally favourable reviews (Metacritic 80 from 27 critics; user score 7.0 from about 99 ratings). It won an AGDA Game of the Year award and was listed among Kotaku's top 10 games of 2017 per the Steam page. Defiant reported Hand of Fate 2 earned about 40% more revenue than the original in its first six months. Three story DLC packs followed (Outlands and Outsiders, The Servant and the Beast, A Cold Hearth). Defiant stopped making new games in July 2019 and moved to a caretaker mode, so the game gets no active development; in 2025 it only began publishing the spin-off Hordes of Fate. Steam's recent reviews were Mixed on the store page, driven by technical complaints like load times and bugs. Third-party estimates (Steam revenue calculator) put gross revenue around $1.67M and SteamSpy owners at 200k to 500k, but these are Boxleiter-style estimates and exclude console sales. No OpenCritic score was confirmed, so it is left null. Metacritic 80 (27 critics) and user 7.0 (99 ratings) were re-verified on the Metacritic page; individual outlet scores in 'other' were not independently re-checked and the AGDA/Kotaku award claims are unverified.

community.one_liner: A pixel-art, top-down action roguelite from Crackshell (published by Team17) where you push through procedurally generated dungeon floors solo or in 4-player online co-op, sending gold and ore back to a persistent town to upgrade seven (nine with DLC) heroes.
community.consensus_summary: Players rate it Very Positive on Steam (about 87-88% positive, roughly 9.5k reviews in the local data; the store page shows about 4.7k English reviews, with the last 30 days sitting at Mostly Positive, 75% of 20 reviews). Metacritic has no critic reviews, and its 14 user ratings average 7.2, which is less enthusiastic than Steam. The core combat, class variety and co-op are widely liked, but the most common complaint is that the meta-progression is slow and padded, which Steam reviewers describe as grindy well beyond the norm for a roguelite. It is a finished, content-rich game with three DLC expansions (Witch Hunter, Pyramid of Prophecy, Moon Temple) and a Workshop/level editor. Reviewers still report old bugs as of late 2025, including a character-overwrite save bug and black-screen issues, so polish is uneven. Its successor Heroes of Hammerwatch II now exists, so this entry is in maintenance territory. I could not retrieve critic reviews from major outlets, so critic sentiment is essentially absent.
best_things: Moment-to-moment top-down hack-and-slash/shoot combat is praised as good fun, even by reviewers who quit over grind
Persistent town with shopkeepers and upgrades gives a satisfying early progression loop; town unlocks carry across all heroes
Strong co-op: up to 4 players online, and several reviewers say it is far better with friends than solo
Seven distinct classes (nine with DLC) with different skill sets, plus item sets that scale builds as you collect pieces
Simple item model: no equipment management, pickups apply instantly, which keeps runs quick and easy to jump into
Risk/reward gold banking: you must send gold to town (with a random tax rate) or lose it if you die, which creates tension
Huge content volume: lots of floors, secrets, traps, bosses, New Game+ tiers and three expansions
Steam Workshop and a built-in level editor extend the game; mods are popular for speeding up or unlocking content
worst_things: Grind is the dominant complaint: maxing one character reportedly takes hundreds of thousands of gold while a run earns about 10-20k before tax
The gold tax mechanic (more gold held means a worse rate) is called pointless padding that slows progression
Upgrades and town purchases are per-character in many cases, so each new hero means re-buying expensive upgrades
Most traps and some enemy attacks have no invincibility frames, so players can be chain-hit and killed instantly
Chest/key system feels random: players report holding keys with no chests, or finding locked chests with no keys, and needing 40+ of a material that does not drop
Build diversity is shallow; many items are flat damage or speed boosts, and late runs feel like stacking bigger numbers
Reused assets and enemies from the first Hammerwatch make it feel less fresh to returning fans

Long-standing bugs: a reported save bug that deletes a character and replaces it with a copy of the last played one, random crashes, black screens on exit or at the final boss, and lobby disconnects in co-op
improvements: Share more upgrades (potions, blessings, stat upgrades) across all heroes instead of per character
Reduce or remove the gold tax, and lower prices of items like pets (one reviewer says 25k for a pet is too much)
Fix the character-deletion save bug and black-screen/crash issues that players say have persisted for years
Give more build variety and less flat-number item design so New Game+ runs feel different
Raise or remove shopkeeper purchase limits in dungeons and make key/chest and material drops less random
Add crossplay and improve multiplayer stability and desync handling; also better controller and Steam Deck support
unique_things: Town-building meta progression shared across a roster of heroes, rather than a single run-based unlock tree
Gold banking with random tax: send money home to keep it, or carry it at risk of losing everything on death
Item-set system with instant-apply pickups and no inventory or gear slots
Shortcut/skip mechanics and alternate paths through tiers, plus a huge New Game+ ladder (achievement hunters cite NG+7/NG+8 requirements)
Built-in level editor and Steam Workshop support, with popular mods adding classes and unlocks
Roguelite evolution of the original Hammerwatch's lose-it-all roguelike formula, set in the same universe
tedious_or_disliked: Repeating the same floors to farm the same two materials (gold and ore), with progress that feels slower the further you get
Needing to beat every boss with every character because those clears give permanent bonuses to all heroes, even classes you dislike
Progression slows after roughly NG+2 as runs become numbers-only scaling, per a 112-hour solo player who stopped at NG+4
Small corridors and heavy ranged enemy spam make individual fights annoying for some, especially solo
Death resets feel punishing because runs that die before banking resources yield nothing, which one Metacritic user called a hamster-wheel design
divisive_points: Co-op vs solo: reviewers repeatedly say it shines with friends but the grind is hard to justify alone
Grind tolerance: some players love the long town-and-character progression while others call it worse than mobile gacha games
Difficulty and build freedom: some find it easy and relaxed, others feel underpowered without gold spent on upgrades and find traps unfair
Workshop mods: several players say the game is only fun with progression-speed mods, which others see as a fix for design flaws
community.reception_notes: Released March 1, 2018 (Steam, Windows/Linux, no Mac) at $14.99, developed by Crackshell and published by Team17. The local Steam data shows a Very Positive all-time rating, and the recent window is slightly lower at Mostly Positive. Three paid expansions exist: Witch Hunter, Pyramid of Prophecy and Moon Temple. A sequel, Heroes of Hammerwatch II, exists and has its own DLC. Metacritic lists no critic reviews and only 14 user ratings (7.2), and I could not find an OpenCritic listing. I could not retrieve Reddit, news patch notes or outlet reviews because of tool limits, so launch-era critic reception and recent patch history are not verified here. The original Hammerwatch (2013) has a Metascore of 72 per Wikipedia, which is a different game. Late-2025/2026 Steam reviews still mention save-deletion, black-screen and disconnect bugs, suggesting low ongoing patch activity.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Loop Hero is an auto-battling strategy roguelike where the player places terrain tiles like mountains, lakes and roads around a looping path, and those tiles spawn the scenarios the hero automatically fights through. praise: Very unique concept: tile placement as the 'deck-building' layer that shapes the loop
Got a lot of praise and did well commercially/critically

community.one_liner: A retro pixel-art idle/auto-battler roguelite from Four Quarters (published by Devolver Digital) in which the hero walks a looping path automatically and the player places terrain, building and enemy-spawning cards around it, then retreats to camp to rebuild the ruined world.
community.consensus_summary: Loop Hero launched in March 2021 to strong critic and player reception (Metacritic 82 on PC, 84 on Switch; Steam Very Positive at about 92.7% from roughly 36.5k reviews) for its novel tile-placement-meets-autobattler hook, art, soundtrack and dark story setup. The steady criticism, from both critics and players, is that it becomes repetitive and grindy: camp-resource progression is slow and runs start to feel samey after roughly 5-30 hours. Many players feel the game is effectively complete-but-abandoned, since there have been no significant content updates in years, some item slots remain unobtainable, and fans keep asking for DLC or a sequel. It has since shipped on Switch (Dec 2021), Xbox (Apr 2023) and mobile (Apr 2024), and it is frequently recommended as a cheap, discount-friendly 30-40 hour experience. Steam Mac reviewers report crashes.
best_things: Distinctive core idea: you do not control the hero, you shape the world around them by placing cards, which players describe as deep and surprisingly addictive
Hidden tile synergies and combos (for example 3x3 grids of rocks and stones turning into mountains, farms turning into raided farms next to a battlefield) reward experimentation
Risk-reward tension of tuning enemy density and scaling against gear, then deciding when to retreat with loot versus push for the boss
Pixel art in a dark 80s/90s fantasy style and a memorable eerie soundtrack, which some Steam reviewers call the best art and music direction in a decade
Dark, intriguing story premise (the Lich and the looping void) with witty dialogue that keeps some players going to see the ending
Low-attention, relaxing play that works well on a second monitor; good value at a low price, especially on sale
Three classes, several acts and bosses give a solid roughly 30-40 hour campaign for many players
worst_things: Progression is widely described as grindy: camp buildings and unlocks need large amounts of slow-to-collect resources
Runs become samey; many players find the same tile layouts work every time once a build is found
The game can feel brain-dead or passive, since much of it plays itself and the important decisions are made before or early in a run
Heavy RNG, including runs lost to swingy loops or to monsters stealing gear unnoticed, which can feel unfair rather than skill-based
Weak onboarding: stat interactions and tile combos are obscure, so many players need a wiki or guide to see most of the combinations
Content feels unfinished: some equipment slots (belt and gloves were mentioned) cannot be obtained, and the game has not been meaningfully updated in years
Some reviewers report that the Mac version crashes despite being listed as supported
improvements: Add new content through updates or paid DLC (more classes, cards, buildings, endgame or New Game+), which several long-time players say they would happily buy
Implement or remove the unused item slots so the gear system feels complete
Speed up meta-progression and camp unlocks, or reduce the amount of resource grinding required for each new building
Explain tile interactions and stats better in-game so players do not need external guides
Add more tile combinations and deeper synergies; some players say most are only 0-2 layers deep
Fix Mac compatibility on Steam
unique_things: Indirect control: the player is essentially a dungeon-master style planner placing terrain, buildings and spawners around a fixed circular path
Fuses idle/autobattler, deckbuilding-style card drops, roguelite retreat-or-die risk and base building into one loop
Adjacency-based tile combinations that transform tiles into new ones, many never explicitly documented by the game
Retreat-with-loot mechanic where the expedition's resource payout depends on whether you leave before dying
Story told through conversations with characters, including monsters, unusual for an idle-adjacent roguelite
Retro-computing/dark-fantasy pixel aesthetic with distinctive music that carries much of the identity
tedious_or_disliked: Slow camp-resource farming: reviewers describe needing dozens of short loops to afford a single building
Repeating the same safe loop strategy (go around a few times, retreat) because pushing your luck is punished
Constant gear micromanagement during runs even though the game is nominally hands-off
Runs that feel identical after the first several hours, leading some to drop it around the 5-10 hour mark
Unexplained mechanics that force a guide lookup to understand which tiles actually work
divisive_points: Grind: some players, including 100% completionists, love the slow relaxing progression, while others call it unbearable
Passive gameplay: praised as a chill, second-monitor-friendly autobattler by some, dismissed as too hands-off or brain-dead by others
Depth of the tile system: fans call it deeper than it looks, while critics say combinations are shallow or obscure and players just stack everything in one place
Punishing death and retreat rules: seen as good tension by some and a disincentive to be brave by others
community.reception_notes: Launch reception was strongly positive: Metacritic lists 58 critic reviews, about 90% positive and 10% mixed. Wikipedia notes critics such as Polygon praised the experimentation the loop allowed, Ars Technica liked its take on idle games, and PC Gamer felt the lack of new cards hurt the late game. It was nominated for Best Independent Game at The Game Awards 2021 and multiple D.I.C.E. categories. Platform timeline: PC March 4, 2021; Switch December 9, 2021; Xbox April 4, 2023; mobile April 30, 2024. Recent Steam reviews (2025-2026) are still mostly positive but repeatedly mention no updates in over 3 years, demands for a sequel, and Mac crashes. Steam lists about 348 concurrent players per the local data and price $14.99 (frequently discounted). OpenCritic could not be verified (search budget exhausted), so opencritic is null, not confirmed absent.

commentary.summary: Luck Be a Landlord is a minimalist gambling roguelike where you spin a slot machine to earn money to pay your landlord, adding tokens each spin. community.one_liner: A pixel-art roguelike deckbuilder by solo dev Dan DiIorio (TrampolineTales) in which you fill a slot machine with symbols and items to earn enough coins to pay ever-rising rent.
community.consensus_summary: Very well received by players: Steam sits at roughly 93% positive (about 11,500 reviews, Very Positive). It is widely described as a short, addictive engine-building game and is best known as the game LocalThunk has called the largest influence on Balatro. Critics who covered it (mostly on the mobile ports) were favourable, with a few saying the design is rigid. Complaints concentrate on a bare-bones UI, heavy luck, thin long-term progression, and the 777-wins achievement. It left early access in Jan 2023 after starting in Jan 2021, and later shipped on mobile and consoles. Steam reviews in the local data show it still gets content updates, and some players say those updates caused symbol bloat.
best_things: The core loop of spinning, adding symbols and relics, and building adjacency synergies to outrun rent is called simple, quick and addictive
Runs are short and easy to start; reviewers call it a fun 10-20 hour game (one finished in ~13 hours) and say a single run is quick
Multiple viable builds: players describe broken engine runs (for example suns plus flowers) alongside disastrous bricks, which keeps runs surprising
Symbol picking works like deckbuilding, so players feel they have more agency than in a pure slot machine, and some rate it above Cloverpit for that reason
Charming retro pixel art, music and humor, including anti-capitalist theming and quirky symbol interactions
Low price and no real-money gambling or microtransactions, which suits people who like gambling mechanics without the predatory side
Steam lists Linux and Mac builds, Workshop support, full controller support and accessibility options (adjustable text size, colour alternatives, contrast controls)
Historical significance as the main inspiration for Balatro, which makes many players curious enough to try it
worst_things: UI and menus are described as messy: tooltips can be walls of text, the library view is ugly, and there is little at-a-glance information about what you already own while drafting
Very high RNG: a number of reviewers feel the outcome depends more on luck than on skill and that upgrades matter little
Shallow replayability with no meta-progression: new and veteran players have identical starting content, and a run gives you knowledge only
Weak or non-synergising draws can sink a run; some reviewers say upgrades barely matter and they only get past rent 4 in about 1 of 4 runs
Some players call it passive, because much of a run is watching the reels spin
Price complaints from a minority, who say $10 is steep for a game with one core mode and that free browser games do similar things
Some reviews report crashes (for example around the 4th rent payment), although these are isolated
improvements: A clearer, more readable UI with better item and symbol tooltips and a nicer library view
More information or control while drafting, such as seeing a summary of your current symbols and synergies
Some form of meta-progression or additional modes and variance after the first win, since players want more content beyond one level
More reliable drafting: fewer dead draws and more ways to steer toward a build, so runs depend less on luck
Curbing symbol bloat from updates, which some long-time players say makes early rent payments fail due to weak, non-synergising draws
A less grindy achievement set, with the 777-wins and RNG-dependent achievements repeatedly named as unnecessary
unique_things: The slot machine is the board: symbols occupy a 5x4 grid and adjacent symbols trigger each other, which makes it feel like a spatial deckbuilder
The win condition is paying escalating rent to a landlord, a satirical anti-capitalist framing rather than fighting enemies
Explicit design goal of a gambling-style game without real-money gambling or microtransactions
Acknowledged direct influence on Balatro, endorsed by its creator, plus a positive nod from Magic: The Gathering designer Richard Garfield
Built and updated by a single developer, who started in early access in Jan 2021
Symbols have cross-interactions (ghosts, dwarves, pinatas etc.) that produce absurd emergent stories
tedious_or_disliked: The win 777 games achievement is widely called insanely grindy, especially since a win takes 30+ minutes and cannot be guaranteed
Luck-based achievements can require hundreds of resets, according to one reviewer with 300+ resets on one
Symbol bloat and sheer number of symbols can make getting the synergies you want a matter of luck
Dense, cluttered UI and menus (one reviewer calls the drafting UI a mess and the graphics indecipherable)
Repeating the same loop with limited variance after the first tens of hours
divisive_points: Skill versus luck: fans say you steer builds through drafting, detractors say it is mostly RNG
Whether later additions enriched the game or caused symbol bloat that hurts run consistency
Value: many call it a bargain 10-20 hour game, others feel it is too thin at full price
Comparison with Balatro and Cloverpit: some say it is the charming raw original, others say it is less polished and less deep than newer games it inspired
Presentation: some love the barebones retro graphics and UI as charming, others find them hard to read

community.one_liner: A top-down action RPG with rogue-lite dungeons where you loot randomized-layout dungeons by night and run your own shop in the town of Rynoka by day (Digital Sun / 11 bit studios, 2018).
community.consensus_summary: Moonlighter is broadly liked: Steam shows Very Positive (about 81% of roughly 24.6k reviews) and Metacritic critic scores sit in the mid-70s to low-80s depending on platform (PC 74, PS4 81, Switch 83). Players and critics love the pixel art, soundtrack and the addictive loot-sell-upgrade loop, but a recurring verdict is that both halves (combat and shopkeeping) are shallow, the loop gets repetitive after several hours, and the novelty fades. The game is fully released (not early access) and has had post-launch content (a New Game+ mode, companions, extra room layouts, and the Between Dimensions DLC, July 2019), and is now often free or deeply discounted on Steam. Its sequel Moonlighter 2: The Endless Vault went into early access in November 2025, which has revived attention. Persistent complaints on Steam are controller-first design with poor keyboard and mouse support and a few long-standing bugs.
best_things: Pixel art and animation are widely called gorgeous and charming, and the soundtrack is praised as cozy and atmospheric
The core loop of dungeon looting, selling in your own shop, then upgrading gear and the shop is described as addictive and 'one more run' compelling
The day/night split gives a satisfying rhythm: shop management is a relaxing break from dungeon crawling
Smart inventory risk/reward: loot has curses and takes up limited backpack space, forcing choices about what to carry out
Steady, readable power curve; upgraded armor and weapons make you feel stronger, with five weapon types offering different playstyles
Dungeon bosses are well designed and memorable; several players say combat reaches a good feel once you have a favorite weapon and armor set
Good value and accessible: family friendly, runs well on Steam Deck, roughly 15-25 hours to finish and 40+ for completionists, often on deep sale or given away free
worst_things: Combat is frequently called clunky and stiff: slow weapon animations with animation lock, awkward dodge roll, and unreliable hitboxes
Shopkeeping is seen as undercooked: pricing boils down to trial-and-error micro-tuning with little strategic depth or consequence
Dungeon design is shallow: rooms are enclosed arenas where you clear every enemy, and with only a handful of dungeons the layouts and encounters repeat
PC port problems: built for gamepad, no mouse support even in menus, some keybinds cannot be rebound, and menu keys are not explained in game
Long-standing bugs reported years after launch, such as the interact button also switching weapons and a sporadic bug where the day cannot be ended after opening the shop
Late game sputters: the final dungeon and final boss are called anticlimactic by some, or a sudden difficulty spike by others
Inventory management becomes a chore because loot is so plentiful and bags fill quickly
No colorblind mode; red-green colorblind players report being unable to see slimes
improvements: Proper keyboard and mouse support and fully rebindable controls, including menu navigation, plus a colorblind mode
Deeper shop simulation: more meaningful customer behavior, pricing gambles or risk, and stronger links between shop choices and dungeon play
More dungeon variety and stronger randomization (more rooms, enemy mixes and mechanics) so runs stop feeling memorized
More responsive, varied combat: better hitboxes, more fluid dodge and attacks, more weapon depth
A more satisfying endgame and final dungeon, and meaningful persistent progression (Game Informer felt the persistent elements had too little impact)
Fix old bugs and skippable cutscenes and quality-of-life items such as better inventory handling
unique_things: The hybrid of dungeon crawler and shop sim: the loot you risk your life for is literally the stock you price and sell, which also funds town growth and gear
You price items yourself and watch customer reactions (from overjoyed to overpriced) to learn each item's value
Retail-style upgrades to the shop (chests, display stands, hired staff like a cashier, and a town of shops to expand) tie into the dungeon-diving economy
Cursed items and a backpack-as-puzzle inventory where item placement and curses matter during a run
Fixed hand-built dungeon rooms shuffled per run rather than fully procedural rooms; comparisons often cite Zelda and Binding of Isaac for dungeons and Recettear and Stardew Valley for the town loop
Gear is crafted and enchanted using dungeon loot, and dungeon gates act as story-driven progression
tedious_or_disliked: Price-tuning every item in the shop becomes repetitive, and some players call the shop a gimmick that stops being interesting after a couple of hours
Looting, selling and upgrading turns into a monotonous grind to afford the next gear tier before you can push the next dungeon
Re-clearing the same rooms and enemies with identical patterns; some players say they saw everything within an hour or two
Managing a cluttered inventory and dealing with cursed items during runs
Unskippable, lengthy cutscenes and thin story
Fighting menus and control schemes on keyboard; some spent around 20 minutes remapping
divisive_points: Whether the shop is a charming relaxing counterbalance or a shallow gimmick
Combat feel: praised as fair and satisfying with the right weapon versus clunky and sluggish
Difficulty: some find dungeons sufficiently challenging and bosses fair, others find the final boss a spike or the early game grindy and punishing
Replay value: some enjoy 40+ hours and New Game+, others feel the game peaks early and gets worse the longer they play
community.reception_notes: Launched May 2018 on PC, PS4 and Xbox One to generally favorable critic reviews, with the PC version scoring lower on Metacritic (74) than consoles (81-84), consistent with player complaints about the keyboard and mouse port. Switch followed Nov 2018, iOS Nov 2020, Android 2021/2022 (via Netflix Games). The Between Dimensions DLC arrived July 2019. Steam user sentiment has drifted slightly lower over time (81% all-time, 79% recent), helped along by reviews from people who got the game free or cheap, and by recurring complaints of unfixed control and bug issues dating to 2018. Wikipedia lists SXSW Gaming and Gamers' Choice nominations. The sequel Moonlighter 2: The Endless Vault entered early access Nov 19, 2025 (PC Metacritic 80, OpenCritic 83% recommend) with 1.0 planned for Sept 2, 2026. Sales data is not officially published; third-party Steam estimates (2-5M owners, ~$1.6M gross Steam-only via SteamSpy and steam-revenue-calculator) are rough and likely undercount cross-platform revenue and overcount free-giveaway copies. Note: WebSearch budget was exhausted, so community discussion was drawn from Steam review samples and Metacritic user reviews rather than Reddit (Reddit fetch blocked); the OpenCritic numeric score was not retrievable.

community.one_liner: A fast run-and-gun 2D action-platformer roguelite from Veewo Games (published by Team17) where you descend a neon-soaked Greek-myth-meets-cyberpunk dungeon collecting hundreds of items, hatching pets and stacking synergies.
community.consensus_summary: Neon Abyss is Very Positive on Steam (about 86% of roughly 23.6k reviews) and Mixed-to-Average with critics (Metacritic PC 74 from 12 reviews, user score 6.6). Players and critics agree it is a fun, colourful, chaotic Binding of Isaac / Enter the Gungeon-style shooter with a huge item pool and a great soundtrack, and that it is cheap and often on deep sale. The recurring complaints are visual clutter (enemy bullets hard to tell from yours), items that are mostly shallow 'chance to do X when Y' effects, clunky controls with no dodge, and long-standing bugs including some reports of lost saves. Support has effectively stopped: DLC landed in 2021 (Alter Ego) plus later cosmetic/character packs, Veewo moved on to Neon Abyss 2 (Early Access from July 2025), and recent Steam reviews (last 30 days) are Mixed at about 68%, with reviewers noting bugs are years old and the game has not been updated for a very long time.
best_things: Fast, fluid run-and-gun gameplay that is immediately fun and works well in short sessions (one reviewer calls it a go-to when they have 30 minutes)
Huge pool of weapons, items and abilities (500-600+) that gives runs a different feel, with some strong build-defining combos that make you feel invincible
Striking neon/cyberpunk pixel art and a high-energy soundtrack that many reviewers single out
Pet hatching and evolution system and the quirky mini-games/shops add personality and extra ways to power up
Varied bosses and dungeon evolution system (choices change the ruleset of later runs), plus a progression/unlock tree that keeps you coming back
Distinct playable characters, including DLC characters like the katana-wielding Saya whose melee playstyle is well liked
Very good value: frequently discounted to about 5-7 USD and players report 20-80+ hours
worst_things: Hard to distinguish your own bullets from enemy projectiles; enemy bullets are layered under the player's, so late-game screens become unreadable
Many items are shallow 'chance to do X when you do Y' effects or simple damage/key/coin conversions, with few creative interactions despite the advertised unlimited synergies
Item descriptions are hidden unless you use a specific character or find a specific item, so you pick among 500+ items by name and icon alone
Long-standing bugs (some reported as 6+ years old): falling through platforms stops working, broken menu/controller input, collection or progression blocked
Reports of save data being wiped or progression lost, including after cloud/Epic versions
Clunky controls and aiming: no dedicated dodge button, awkward default controller layout, inconsistent hitboxes, movement described as slow by some
Uneven economy: rooms give few coins while keys cost about 30, so a poor early luck stretch leaves you weak for the rest of the run
Procedural generation is repetitive with limited room and environment variety, and the English translation is described as weak by some
improvements: Add a dodge/dash button and more precise aiming and hitbox behaviour
Render enemy projectiles over player bullets or make them visually distinct to fix readability
Show item descriptions to all players by default (or via an in-game codex) instead of gating them behind a character or item
Make items interact more meaningfully and cut filler 'chance to' effects; make different characters matter more
Fix the old platform-drop, menu-input and save-loss bugs and optimize performance (lag spikes reported)
Rebalance the coin/key economy and improve achievement design; players also asked for mod support and the ability to save and resume runs
unique_things: Dungeon evolution system in which choices alter the ruleset of the dungeon in later runs, plus the hub bar that modifies runs
Pet egg hatching and evolution as a core power-up loop alongside guns and items
Greek-mythology gods reimagined with a neon cyberpunk aesthetic
Wisdom/violence mechanic tied to certain characters, where taking damage converts charge and can ruin builds
Casino-style slot and mini-game gates for chests and doors, plus a card/gacha-style cheat system
A 'thriving, not surviving' design ethos praised by PC Invasion: a platformer-shooter blend of Isaac-style items with run-and-gun movement
tedious_or_disliked: Runs grow long (around an hour, more with mini-games) as deeper levels unlock, and reviewers find the repeated levels and bosses repetitive after a while
Mini-games and challenge rooms that sometimes break or bar access to loot feel like small inconveniences stacked on the run
All enemies spawning at once on room entry overwhelms players, and screens fill with effects
Achievements such as die 99 times or enter a room 999 times are called grindy and poorly designed; the upgrade accumulation was called a long slog in early press
No way to save and resume mid-run (raised in the top-voted Steam review) makes hour-long runs awkward for players with limited time
divisive_points: Synergies: fans say builds get wild, critics and many negative reviewers say most items are dull and rarely combine
Difficulty: some find it about the right challenge, others find it easy once patterns are learned, while item RNG swings runs between overpowered and hopeless
Controls and feel: described as tight by some and clunky or slow by others
Comparison to Enter the Gungeon / Binding of Isaac: a fresh platformer take to some, a weaker imitation to others
community.reception_notes: Note the data file lists 2022 but the game launched July 14, 2020 on PC, Switch, PS4 and Xbox One (Windows only on Steam). Launch press was broadly positive (Metacritic PC 74, top scores 85 CD-Action, 81 Hooked Gamers, 80 from Hardcore Gamer, The Indie Game Website and The Games Machine; lows 70 PC Games and Multiplayer.it, and a 40 from Screen Rant). Critics praised item variety and presentation while noting repetitive procedural levels, visual chaos, PS4 performance issues and lack of a dodge button. Steam revenue estimates (steam-revenue-calculator, Boxleiter method) are about 4.7M gross / 1.4M net, and SteamSpy estimates 2-5 million owners; treat as order-of-magnitude. Post-launch: the Alter Ego pack (2021) and further DLC (Lovable Rogues Pack, Chrono Trap) were added, but recent reviewers say no meaningful update in a very long time and some bugs persist; it was also given away on Epic Games Store at one point, which reviewers mention. Neon Abyss 2 entered Early Access on July 17, 2025 and a reviewer said it is not recommended; the Steam forum shows 677 problem-report threads covering controller mapping, PS5 controller, resolution and platform-drop bugs.

community.one_liner: A real-time, grid-based action roguelite by Thomas Moon Kang where you build a spell deck and dodge enemy attacks on a 4x4 battlefield, openly inspired by Mega Man Battle Network and Slay the Spire.
community.consensus_summary: Both players and critics rate it well. Steam lists it as Very Positive (about 93% of roughly 7,700 reviews), PC Metacritic is 82 from 9 critic reviews, and the user score is 7.8 from only 41 ratings. The praise goes to the deck-and-dodge hybrid, the build variety, the pixel art and the soundtrack. The complaints are the brutal early difficulty, screen clutter and thin explanations. It left Steam early access on March 26, 2020, and has since come to PS4, Xbox/Game Pass and Switch. Its spiritual follow-up Duelists of Eden came out in 2024, and the Steam reviews show people still playing with mods in 2026. The Switch version scored noticeably lower (74, mixed) than PC.
best_things: Fast, dynamic mix of deckbuilding and dodge-based action. Reviewers and players call it easy to learn and hard to master.
High replayability: 9 heroes with distinct playstyles, 200+ spells, 100+ artifacts, alternate kits to unlock, and 'god seed' sharing of exact runs.
Skill matters more than luck. Screen Rant called the roguelike structure a highlight, and players say knowledge of cards and enemy patterns is rewarded.
Focus and type-preference systems let you steer which spell categories you are offered, which softens deck RNG.
Pixel art, character design and animation are widely praised.
The soundtrack is repeatedly called outstanding; some reviewers say it sits in their playlists for months.

Deep difficulty and modifier ladder (Hell passes up to Hel Mode 14), multiple endings (pacifist, genocide, a secret one) and the shopkeeper challenge give very long-term goals; several reviewers have 100-500+ hours.
Strong nostalgia pull for Mega Man Battle Network fans, plus Steam Workshop mods, local co-op and PvP.
worst_things: Extremely fast pace with poor readability in busy fights. Enemy and hazard sprites blend into the background and into each other, and many low-hour negative reviews cite this.
Steep, punishing opening hours. Critics say the first hour is disheartening, and even the lowest difficulty is too hard for some players.
Weak tutorial and explanation: many keywords and status effects are only learned by trial and error (PC Invasion and Screen Rant both flag this).
Enemies feel unfairly strong compared to the player: large AoE attacks, locking you to a tile, limited telegraphing.
Some characters lock you into one archetype (for example a frost hero only makes sense with frost), so the deckbuilding feels narrow.
Slow unlock progression for new abilities and characters (GameMAG, TheGamer).
Multiplayer modes were criticised as poorly designed in the Wikipedia reception summary.
Too many keywords and status effects with too little in-game explanation; the top negative Steam reviews call for an intricate UI rework.
improvements: Clearer UI and keyword tooltips, plus a more thorough tutorial.
A better difficulty curve or gentler onboarding between casual play and bullet-hell difficulty.
Better visual clarity and animation so enemies and projectiles are easier to tell apart, for example spawning enemies in one at a time before a fight starts.
Some kind of pacing or rhythm indicator (a 'metronome' UI was suggested) to help read action flow.
Faster, more rewarding unlock progression.
More spells and content to bridge the casual and expert difficulty tiers, and better balance for trap or useless spells.
unique_things: A genuine real-time action take on the Mega Man Battle Network chip-and-grid formula, not turn-based deckbuilding.
Cards (spells) are cast continuously from a cycling deck while you dodge, so your deck is also your moveset.
Defeated bosses become playable characters, and every hero has its own mechanics and alternate loadouts.
The Shopkeeper 'pacts', the pacifist / genocide / secret ending structure, and the Hell pass difficulty ladder.
Seed-based runs you can repeat exactly, plus Steam Workshop mods, local co-op and PvP.
tedious_or_disliked: Hunting the remaining unlocks, endings and Hell Mode levels can feel like a grind, and unlock pacing was called slow.
Layered RNG (spell offers, artifact offers, focus picks) can ruin a run even when you play well.
Memorising enemy and boss patterns is the main route to improvement, which some players find wearing.
Many spells are niche or weak, so filling out a coherent deck can feel like sifting through clutter.
Runs start the next battle immediately, with no beat to read the new enemy lineup.
Some players say the speed and screen clutter make it feel like luck rather than skill, and that the real-time format loses the deck-perfecting of Battle Network.
divisive_points: Mega Man Battle Network fans are split. Some see it as the best spiritual successor, others feel it lacks the deck-perfecting of the original.
Difficulty: fans call it balanced and mastery-rewarding; others call it unfair or inaccessible.
Whether it is truly a 'deckbuilder' or an action game with card flavour. Some players want deeper deck control, others are happy with focus-steered randomness.
community.reception_notes: It was funded by a January 2019 Kickstarter that reached its $15,000 goal in two days and paid for extra features such as pets and Switch support. It launched on PC and Switch on March 26, 2020, then PS4 (June 2020), a physical Switch release in Japan (Feb 2021) and Xbox One / Game Pass (Nov 2021). Critics were favorable on PC, with scores ranging from 60 to 100 and most in the 80-90 band, and the main knocks were difficulty and thin explanation. Steam sentiment has stayed Very Positive, with Steam reviews from 2025-2026 still recommending it and praising mods. Third-party estimates put it at 200k-500k owners and about $4.3M gross / $1.26M net revenue on Steam (Boxleiter-style, unaudited). No official sales figures were found. I could not verify a separate OpenCritic score, and no controversies were found beyond the recurring difficulty and readability complaints.

New dungeons feel much the same after about 10 hours; travel between locations is repetitive with tile types
Sidekick character has an annoying voice (but it does not affect rating)
unique_points: Taming monsters as a core roguelike mechanic, each with its own abilities
Campaign-style world expansion layered on runs
commentary.quote: probably gonna be like a low B tier

Uniqueness: taming gimmick and world exploration stand out
Charm/visuals: cute, distinctive art style
Complexity/readability: four abilities per monster overwhelms

community.one_liner: A cute hand-drawn twin-stick bullet-hell roguelite/metroidvania where you lasso and ride 50+ monsters through a huge jungle labyrinth called Patchlantis, collecting pins, plants and pets.
community.consensus_summary: Patch Quest is well liked by players (Steam 'Very Positive', about 93.5% of roughly 2,800 reviews per the local data; the Steam store page itself showed a higher, Overwhelmingly Positive figure on a smaller review count) and by the handful of critics who reviewed it (Metacritic 80 from 5 scored reviews, ranging 60 to 90). Praise centres on the charm, the variety of rideable monsters, tight controls and a real sense of exploration and progression. The recurring complaint is that the loop becomes repetitive and the very large, non-random map turns into a long trek, with enemy damage ramping up so runs must be restarted. Released in early access in May 2021 and in 1.0 on March 2, 2023; it is a finished game with a soundtrack DLC, is Windows-only on Steam (Metacritic also lists iOS), and is frequently discounted to a few dollars. Recent patch history could not be confirmed.
best_things: Lasso-and-ride mechanic: taming any monster and using it as a mount with its own attacks and traversal ability (leap, glide, surf, tunnel, websling) is the signature hook and widely loved
Charming hand-drawn art, goofy monsters and pun-heavy writing; several players said the art put them off at first, then became part of the charm
Very smooth, responsive twin-stick controls; one reviewer called them among the smoothest they have played
Deep customisation: ammo fruits and charge shots, badges/perks, pets, mounts, biomes and a customisable home base give lots of build variety
Metroidvania-style exploration with pins, shortcuts and gadgets gives persistent progression on top of the roguelite runs; players report a shift from 'fooling around' to strategising runs
Local co-op is praised by one reviewer who 100%'d it with a partner as one of the best co-op games out there (local only; others wanted online co-op)
Low-commitment 'one more run' loop with lots of content: reviewers describe getting sucked in for hours and a real sense of progression
worst_things: Repetition: several negative reviewers say they had seen nearly everything after roughly 5-7 hours; enemies and bosses behave similarly across the map
The map is huge and fixed (not randomly generated), so crossing it repeatedly is slow; one reviewer estimated about 20 minutes just to reach a far goal
Enemy damage ramps up over time, forcing restarts roughly an hour into a run and making players re-tread the same ground
Enemies are very tanky so encounters drag, and some players feel rewards (treasure perks, unlocks) are underwhelming relative to the effort
Fast travel only works on tiles visited in the current run
Mounts and bullet types feel too similar to some players, and the gun itself never changes, only its effects
Co-op is local only; a few players wanted online co-op and did not find a way to play remotely (Remote Play Together is the only listed workaround)
A minority report technical problems: startup crashes, frame drops, sticky movement (Steam community thread titles and one negative review)
improvements: Shrink or restructure the map, or make shortcuts and fast travel much stronger so backtracking is less of a slog
Add variety to enemy behaviour and boss patterns so monsters across regions feel different
Rebalance enemy health and damage scaling so runs are not forced to reset and fights are quicker
Let players bring more than 3 pets per run and carry spare pins/decorations between runs, to reduce completionist grind
Add real online co-op (players asked for it, and local-only is repeatedly called out)
Improve the late-game reward quality and story payoff; one player found the story fine but unsatisfying
unique_things: Monster-taming in a bullet hell: every enemy you can capture becomes a playable mount with its own moveset, rather than picking from a fixed character roster
Fusion of genres: twin-stick shooter, Pokemon-style creature collecting, roguelite runs and metroidvania map progression in one package
Ammo crafting by blending fruits/plants into different bullet effects, with charge shots per ammo type
A large hand-made (not procedurally generated) labyrinth map with shortcuts that persist between runs
A home-base island with pets, decorations and customisation, plus a post-game challenge mode on hardest difficulty
tedious_or_disliked: Long, interrupted walks across a very large map, especially after dying or after the damage scaling forces a restart
Completionist chasing: missed pins and decorations are hard to track down, decorations require clearing 4 tiles each, and some do not spawn in a given run
Only 3 pets can be brought back per run, which a reviewer computed as about 20 runs to collect them all
Needing both sticks constantly; players on keyboard and mouse find it awkward and it has a learning curve
Bosses and some enemies create very dense bullet patterns; a few reviewers describe being killed in 5-6 hits even with maxed stats
divisive_points: Difficulty: some call it surprisingly hard and brutal, others say the casual mode, bullet cancelling and assist options make it friendly to casuals as well as hardcore players
Length and map size: seen as content-rich and engrossing by many, but as bloated and padded by the negative reviewers
Repetitiveness: critics and players split on whether the creature variety carries the loop or whether 'once you learn one monster you know them all'
Value: several positive reviewers bought it on deep sale ($3) and say it would be worth full price, while one negative reviewer felt it was not worth $15
community.reception_notes: Early access launch May 7, 2021 (devlog series helped build a following; several reviewers say they followed it from those devlogs), 1.0 on March 2, 2023 from Lychee Game Labs and publisher Curve Games at $14.99. Metacritic critic coverage is thin (5 scored reviews; Polygon's review is listed as praising how it juggles genres, score tbd; TheGamer is the outlier at 60, calling it repetitive with limited progression impact). Metacritic user score is 7.2 on only 10 ratings, so not meaningful. OpenCritic could not be retrieved (no data found, reported as null). Steam: Windows only, no Mac/Linux; a soundtrack and a guide add-on exist. Steam review counts differed between sources (local data 2,792 reviews at 93.5%; the store page fetch showed 95% of 1,057), likely reflecting language/time filters. Note: the WebSearch budget for the session was exhausted, so no Reddit or broad web discussion could be retrieved, Reddit and Polygon fetches were blocked, and I could not confirm any recent patch notes or console ports; community themes come from Steam reviews, Steam forum topic titles and the fetched critic pages. OpenCritic left null.

community.one_liner: A turn-based roguelike card crawler where enemies, loot and shrines sit as cards arranged in a ring around you and you choose what to act on each turn.
community.consensus_summary: Ring of Pain is well liked by players (about 91% positive across roughly 5,100 Steam reviews, Very Positive) but only middling with critics and Metacritic users (Metascore 74, user score 7.1). Everyone agrees the ring layout, dark art and cryptic rhyming writing are distinctive and the core loop is easy to pick up. The dominant complaint in both critic and player reviews is that runs are decided more by RNG and item luck than by skill, with swingy balance and a hard late-game spike. It is a finished, complete game (released Oct 2020, later ported to Switch and Xbox One), not early access or abandoned; current Steam concurrency is tiny (about 30) and recent reviews are still positive. Several players say it is overpriced at $19.99 and lacks endless or modding options.
best_things: The ring layout is a fresh twist on card crawling: you decide which card around you to hit, loot or skip, and each step is a risk/reward choice
Dark, creepy art direction, audio and atmosphere are consistently praised; the rhyming dialogue and mysterious Owl character add personality
Simple to learn in minutes yet with real depth in how stats interact with turn order and survivability
Large unlock pool (Steam lists 300+ items) with real build variety, including combos like petrify, gem and spellbook builds
Short runs suit quick sessions, and some players use it as a relaxed, low-thought game to play while listening to something
Daily Dungeon mode with modifiers and multiple difficulty levels and endings add replay value
Players who love the genre call it a creepier, harder cousin of Slay the Spire with its own identity
worst_things: Heavy RNG: the most common complaint, with reviewers calling it a glorified slot machine where a great build can die to one unlucky encounter
Item balance is uneven: a few common items can reportedly auto-win a run while many legendaries need several other items to work
Hard difficulty feels too hard while medium feels too easy, so the difficulty curve is awkward
Late-game and final boss difficulty spike (TheSixthAxis describes a 500 HP final boss against a 29 HP player)
Runs can be lost to misreading enemy info or a misclick, and some enemies in the back of the ring are hard to see
Some players find the lore confusing and the ring format not adding enough beyond stats and items
Some feel it lacks variety and depth once you know the dominant strategies, and compare it unfavourably to Slay the Spire or Balatro
improvements: Add an endless or post-game mode, since players who hit both endings say there is little reason to continue
Rebalance items and enemy scaling so fewer runs are won or lost on item luck
Smooth the medium-to-hard difficulty jump and the late-game spike
Let players unequip items without needing a replacement, and give shrines clearer information about outcomes
Better information UI, for example a way to tab out and inspect the board while choosing stat upgrades or items
Workshop or modding support, which a long-time player said would have helped the game a lot
Lower the base price (a reviewer argued it is priced too high to convince friends to try)
unique_things: Encounters are arranged in a ring around the player, so the core decision is which card to interact with rather than which card to play from a hand
Gear, loot, enemies and shrines are all cards in the same ring, and standing still or sneaking past are real options
Inventory is a limited slot set where swapping equipment and sacrificing health to shrines carry risk
Horror-tinged dungeon crawl tone with an Owl narrator, a shadow figure and rhyming speech
Two main endings (light and dark path) plus candle difficulty modes and a Daily Dungeon
tedious_or_disliked: Some achievements require replaying the start of a run over and over for hours, and unlocks can be grindy or extremely nasty
One player reports 802 runs started with 519 abandoned, largely because bad RNG made them give up early
Final fights with some builds, such as petrify, can take around 30 minutes, which discourages trying hard mode
Once you find a cheap winning strategy, the game feels samey and repetitive
Gated difficulty and 'die 250 times' style achievements feel like padding
The Owl mascot and overly stylised tone grated on at least one reviewer
divisive_points: RNG: some players love the high-variance chaos and 'win when it works' feeling, others say skill barely matters
Price: praised as cheaper than a movie ticket by some, called too expensive at $19.99 by others
Depth: some see substantial build variety, others find it shallow compared to Slay the Spire and similar deckbuilders
Difficulty: some enjoy the brutal challenge as fitting the name, others find it unfair rather than hard
community.reception_notes: Launched Oct 15, 2020 on PC (Windows and Mac) by Simon Boxer / Twice Different and publisher Balor Games, then came to Nintendo Switch and Xbox One. Critics were mostly mixed-to-good (9 Metacritic reviews from 55 to 85), with 'enjoyable but luck-dependent' as the recurring theme; no critic scored it negatively. Steam players are warmer (Very Positive all-time) though the most helpful negative reviews focus on RNG and balance. Steam lists a Daily Dungeon mode and 300+ unlockable items. No major controversy found; the Mac build is listed as not officially supporting M1 chips. OpenCritic score could not be retrieved in this run (web search budget was exhausted and the OpenCritic page could not be located), so it is recorded as null rather than guessed.

commentary.summary: The original 2D side-scrolling action roguelike where each survivor has fixed abilities and runs are shaped by the items you collect. He finds it flashy, satisfying and still fun today, especially for fans of Risk of Rain 2, though builds feel samey. He lands it at high B and is excited about the announced remake.

Characters each have unique abilities that stay constant across runs
Items found during runs are what change the gameplay
You can get really overpowered with the right item combinations
Still holds up today; an oldie but a goodie
