community.one_liner: A 2D pixel-art action platformer roguelite from Hopoo Games where up to four players fight through escalating, time-scaled waves on a hostile planet while stacking passive items.
community.consensus_summary: Risk of Rain is regarded as a genre classic: Steam shows Very Positive (about 93% of roughly 29.8k reviews) and Metacritic has a 77 critic score (PC) with an 8.0 user score. Critics called it addictive and worth the struggle, while noting dated presentation and rough controls. Today many players recommend it as an important, still fun game but point newcomers to the 2023 remake Risk of Rain Returns, which fixes many of the original's rough edges. Recent Steam sentiment has been dented by a 2025-2026 EULA change (forced arbitration and a class action waiver under Take-Two/2K ownership), plus reports of crashes and poor controller support. It is a finished game, not early access.
best_things: Difficulty-equals-time design creates constant risk/reward tension between looting for items and rushing the teleporter
Item stacking: dozens of passive pickups combine until a run turns from barely surviving to screen-clearing chaos
Distinct survivors with different abilities, unlocked through challenges, that change how each run plays
Chris Christodoulou's soundtrack and lonely sci-fi atmosphere are near-universally praised
Gritty pixel art that is readable once you adjust to the visual noise
Fun online/local co-op for up to 4 players
Good value: very cheap, frequently on sale, and with a strong modding community
Runs escalate into a satisfying power fantasy by the late stages
worst_things: Dated presentation: PC Gamer (via Metacritic summary) criticised awful maximum resolution and tiny sprites
Poor controller support, especially in menus and on Steam Deck; many keyboard-rebinding complaints, including awkward diagonal jumping
Crashes and stutter reported by recent reviewers, including crashes during the final boss
Combat feels repetitive: for many survivors it is run away, fire abilities, run again, which gets old in 2D and makes melee survivors and the sniper feel weak
Difficulty can feel artificially inflated by the timer, with enemies that take ages to kill once you linger
Enemies can spawn very close to the player, and some elites (e.g. Overloading Magma Worm) kill suddenly
Opaque item effects and little onboarding make the first hours unintuitive
Recent review bombing over the EULA/arbitration terms and distrust of Take-Two
improvements: Proper controller support and menu navigation, including Steam Deck
Higher-resolution graphics and UI scaling (addressed by Returns)
Better netcode and co-op stability (Returns reworked networking)
Stability fixes for crashes and periodic freezes on the Steam version
Clearer tutorialisation and item descriptions for newcomers
Reversal of the forced-arbitration EULA that players have to accept to keep playing
unique_things: Difficulty scales with elapsed time rather than stage count, so the player controls pacing and risk
Enemy spawning uses a director point system that also creates elite variants when the player gets strong
Near-total reliance on stackable passive items over permanent upgrades, so each run is about emergent builds
Roguelite platformer blending 2D movement/platforming with bullet-hell chaos and boss-rush teleporter events
Born as a two-student University of Washington project that raised over $30,000 on Kickstarter (goal $7,000) and won the 2014 IGF Student Prize
Launched the franchise that became Risk of Rain 2 and the 2023 remake Returns
tedious_or_disliked: Repetitive levels and a grindy unlock structure, cited by some as getting boring after a while
Kiting-based play that some find unengaging (run, shoot, repeat) especially with melee survivors
Lack of permanent upgrades is a dealbreaker for some players who want meta progression
Stressful, steep difficulty for casual players, one negative reviewer compared it to The Binding of Isaac and did not enjoy it
Late-run slowdowns and frame rate drops on weak hardware as the screen fills
Having to accept a new EULA to keep launching a game already owned
divisive_points: Original versus remake: many say Returns is strictly better, others say the original has more enemies and items, better exploits/cheese and a rawer indie charm
Original versus Risk of Rain 2: some call the sequel superior in nearly every way, while others prefer the 2D game's levels and feel that it has less punishing RNG
Difficulty: celebrated as fair and learnable by some, called unfair and artificially inflated by others
Simple mechanics: loved as tight and approachable by some, dismissed as shallow by others
community.reception_notes: Launched on Windows in Nov 2013 after a 2013 Kickstarter; Mac/Linux followed in Oct 2014, PlayStation in 2016, Switch in Sep 2018 and Xbox One in Aug 2019; it passed 3 million copies sold by 2019 (Wikipedia). Steam-revenue-calculator estimates about $2.0M gross for the Steam PC version alone (Boxleiter-style estimate), and SteamSpy lists 500k-1M owners. Gearbox acquired the franchise in 2022 and released the Returns remake in Nov 2023, after which the original became the cheaper, rougher option. The 2025-2026 EULA/arbitration change and the Take-Two/2K ownership have triggered a wave of negative Steam reviews from otherwise fond players. OpenCritic's numeric average could not be retrieved; only the 73% recommend figure from Wikipedia was found. Note: web search quota was exhausted, so community detail relies mainly on Steam reviews plus fetched Metacritic/Wikipedia pages; Reddit and Polygon fetches were blocked.

community.one_liner: A 2D action-platformer roguelite from Cellar Door Games where each death passes the torch to a new heir with random traits and class, and gold spent at a persistent castle provides permanent upgrades.
community.consensus_summary: Rogue Legacy 2 is very well received: Metacritic critic score is 88 (PC, 34 reviews) with 97% positive critic reviews, and Steam sits at Very Positive (about 90.8% of roughly 15,150 reviews). Critics and fans praise its fluid combat, the big pool of classes and weapons, the trait system and the addictive always-earning progression loop. The main complaints are the grindy stat upgrades, bullet-heavy late bosses and off-screen attackers, the large character hitbox that makes platforming feel clumsy, and some controller aiming quirks. It began in Early Access in 2020, hit 1.0 on April 28, 2022, reached Switch in November 2022 and PlayStation in June 2023, and was still getting content updates afterward (a pinned Steam post references the v1.2.0 Swan Song update). Metacritic user score (7.3) is noticeably lower than the critic score.
best_things: Fluid, tight movement and combat; reviewers describe it as much smoother than the original
Large variety of classes (around 15) and weapons (around 30), each with a different attack style, encouraging experimentation instead of locking into one build
Heir trait system (up to two traits per character, from cosmetic quirks to drastic gameplay changes) keeps every run feeling different; negative traits grant extra gold
Addictive 'you are always earning' progression: even failed runs add to the castle, so critics and players say it avoids wasted runs
Heirloom system praised as a better design than the first game's rune system
House Rules and accessibility options let players tailor difficulty, which critics consider a big plus
Charming art and small NPC side stories/lore that do not overstay their welcome (one reviewer still prefers the first game's art style)
Strong replayability: a true ending, New Game Plus tiers (some players report NG+100) and secrets; native Linux build
Developer support during Early Access was praised for timely updates, detailed patch notes and listening to feedback
worst_things: Meta progression is grindy: large gold costs for small percentage upgrades to health/damage, compared by some reviewers to an idle game
Difficulty scaling is seen as outpacing the power the player gains, with hard spikes at specific bosses or challenge rooms
Bosses and enemies spam projectiles and overlapping AOE attacks; off-screen and through-wall projectiles draw frequent complaints
Large character hitbox and floaty feel make platforming and hazard-dodging clumsy for some players (no i-frame dodge was also cited)
The two newer biomes are called very linear and wear out their welcome quickly by one negative reviewer
Controller aiming bug: turning the stick quickly can make the character backslide or face the wrong way, which was reportedly also present in the first game
Certain mechanics such as the boogie board scar/ability are disliked for awkward controls
Slow or rough opening hours: several reviewers say the early game is the weakest part and some bounce off before the loop clicks
The generational premise is undercut by an unchanging castle hub: NPCs and blacksmith treat every heir as the same person, which one reviewer says breaks immersion
improvements: Fix controller aiming/turn-around behavior
Rebalance late-game bosses and the new harder modes so they rely less on projectile spam and unavoidable overlap
Make meta upgrades more interesting and less frontloaded; one reviewer says all class and facility unlocks come within about an hour, leaving only small stat bumps to save for
Reduce grind or make upgrade scaling less incremental
Return players to the last cleared room instead of the last teleporter after leaving a run (one reviewer's wish)
Improve the early-game learning experience, since some players bounce off before their first clear
unique_things: Generational heir premise: each run is a new descendant with a random class and traits (colour blindness, pacifist, vertigo, tiny view radius and so on)
Persistent, upgradeable castle hub where gold is reinvested between every run, even fruitless ones
Traits that can drastically change how the game plays, with more rewarding negative traits
Semi-open, hand-crafted-then-shuffled Metroidvania-style world with biomes and bosses instead of pure procedural levels
House Rules that let you scale difficulty and assist options without a separate easy mode
Class mastery/leveling bonuses and heirlooms that reward playing many styles
tedious_or_disliked: Farming gold for tiny stat increases, especially when progress stalls before a boss wall
Having to grind to make the mid/late biomes survivable; some players turned on House Rules just to finish
Repeating bosses and biomes for the first clear before the game opens up
Enemy projectile density and off-screen attacks described as constant barrage
Meta upgrades after the first hour are mostly small stat bumps (+armor, +health), leaving little interesting to save for
divisive_points: Grind and incremental upgrades: some love the 'numbers go up' loop and playing in short bursts, others call it cookie-clicker padding
Difficulty: fans praise the challenge and mastery; detractors call late bosses and hazards unfair or punishing
Character size and movement: praised as fluid and tight by many, called floaty or brick-like by others
Whether it beats the original and other genre leaders such as Dead Cells: several reviewers call it far better than the first, others find it the same or worse
community.reception_notes: Early Access began in 2020 and the game reached 1.0 on April 28, 2022 on Windows and Xbox, then Switch on November 9, 2022 and PlayStation on June 20, 2023 (per Wikipedia). Critics scored it in the high 80s to 90s; IGN called it a transformative sequel that rebuilds the influential original as a modern roguelite, and Destructoid stressed that you are always earning. Steam reviews remain Very Positive years later, with recent long-playtime reviewers (hundreds of hours, NG+100) calling it a favourite game, and a minority of negative reviews focusing on grind, projectile-heavy bosses and hitbox size. One negative review complains that the developers responded to feedback on a harder new mode by suggesting players enable House Rules. The Steam community pinned thread references the v1.2.0 Swan Song update, so the game has been supported well beyond launch. Sales figures are third-party estimates only (1M-2M owners on Steam per SteamSpy; revenue figures are Boxleiter-method estimates, not audited). community.one_liner: A minimalist, isometric roguelite tower defense from Die of Death Games in which the enemy path keeps expanding and splitting as you level up, and you build from randomly drawn tower and upgrade cards unlocked through meta progression.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate it Very Positive (about 83% of roughly 5,900 reviews; the store page shows a lower 71% for recent reviews). Fans call it an addictive, deep, chill-but-tricky TD with huge replay value, and many logged hundreds of hours. Detractors focus on RNG-heavy card draws, late-game balance spikes, and a bare-bones feature set: no mid-run save, no speed-up, poor UI scaling and few settings. Critic coverage is almost nonexistent; Metacritic lists one critic review (PLAY! Zine, 90) and a Mixed 6.5 user score from only 17 ratings. The developer appears inactive, and the game is effectively finished as-is; the modding community on Thunderstore fills many QoL gaps.
best_things: Expanding, branching enemy path (extra lanes unlocked as a difficulty ramp) gives the game its hook and forces you to spread defenses out
Real depth under a simple look: elevation range/attack bonuses, mana, three enemy health types, and several ways to earn gold
Card-draw build variety: 400+ cards and upgrades mean runs differ, and you adapt to what you roll rather than following one solved strategy
Slow unlock tree for towers means the game does not overwhelm newcomers, and progression feels carefully tuned
Relaxed pace makes it a favorite 'play while on a call, podcast or TV' game; several players say it is addictive even if they dislike TD or roguelikes
Humorous boss/enemy names and themes, and no time wasted on lore
Lots of content for the price: around 140 achievements, very hard ones for completionists
Strong value at $14.99 for many fans: several reviewers call it their favorite or one of the best TD games they have played, though the fan praise often leans on mods for QoL
worst_things: No mid-run save or save-and-quit, which is repeatedly called a deal breaker since runs can run a long time
No pause or game speed controls in vanilla; waiting on a few slow stragglers wastes round time and it takes about 20 minutes to know whether a build works
UI/UX widely criticised: tiny or unreadable text, UI scale option insufficient on some displays, clicks passing through buttons, a persistent WASD graphic, few settings (resolution/window mode)
Heavy RNG: card draws can make or break a run, so skilled planning sometimes matters less than luck
Late-game balance: enemy scaling ramps hard (robots from wave ~26, bosses that one-shot unprepared builds, walls around wave 37-55), and enemy stats are not visible in a run
Tower variety is questioned: at least one popular review says nearly everything besides the ballistae is flashy but impractical (a single-reviewer claim, not a consensus)
Developer is described as inactive and unresponsive; some find the fan base dismissive with 'skill issue' replies
Plain visuals and forgettable music; Unity-default look
Thin permanent progression: the most-upvoted negative review says it lacks more permanent upgrades and loses replayability after roughly 15-20 hours
improvements: Add mid-run saving and a proper pause menu with quick restart
Add speed controls (2x/3x) and fast-forward
Fix UI scaling, add resolution/display settings, and allow map rotation so tiles are not hidden
Add card reroll or banish options and a way to refund accidental upgrades, plus a reset-XP option
Show enemy stats and unit info, and add a tower stats view that does not block the map
Rebalance late game and underused towers; more permanent upgrades and variation or legendary upgrades per tower to extend replayability
unique_things: The path itself expands and splits during a run, rather than a fixed map with fixed lanes
Roguelite card draft for towers and upgrades layered on TD, with an unlock tree meta-progression
Height/elevation matters for tower range and damage
Mana system and three enemy health types add layers most TD games lack
Enemy faction type is picked from a set of three per wave, each with distinct gimmicks, revealed only on encounter
A sizable community mod scene (BepInEx/Thunderstore: BanishCards, DarkMode, BetterPauseMenu, UpgradesMenu, and even a multiplayer mod)
tedious_or_disliked: Slow, long runs without speed-up, making early game feel repetitive
Grinding for unlocks, with players noting that some menu upgrades only add items to the random pool rather than being permanent
Achievement hunting is very luck-dependent, and some achievements were reportedly made impossible by balance nerfs
Cannot plan a strategy when the cards you need may never appear
Some players say the game runs out of content after around 15-20 hours
divisive_points: RNG: some find it makes each run exciting and addictive, others call it 'non-interesting' randomness with no sense of progress
Difficulty and balance: fans accept losing as part of the roguelite loop; critics see unfair spikes and a difficulty level that outscales upgrades
Minimalist look and simple gameplay: charming and focused to some, cheap-looking and clunky to others
Replayability: hundreds of hours for some, done after 15-20 hours for others
community.reception_notes: Released Jan 28, 2022 on Steam (Windows only) at $14.99. It kept Very Positive status over time, though the recent-review window has dipped to Mostly Positive. Metacritic has only 17 user ratings and one critic review, so its 6.5 is weakly grounded, and no OpenCritic entry was found. The Steam forum shows 287 topics, with threads about tiny UI, crashes after updates, requests to rebalance difficulty and reset XP, and few official replies; reviews from 2025-2026 describe the dev as gone. A sequel is hinted at by a reviewer but nothing confirmed was found. Reddit, Google and DuckDuckGo could not be fetched and the web search budget was exhausted, so community coverage relies on Steam reviews, the Steam forum, Metacritic and Thunderstore.

community.one_liner: A 2D pixel-art action RPG roguelite by Sean Young (SmashGames) where a squad of Galactic Cadets, solo or in co-op, hops between procedurally generated planets to fight bosses, loot, and craft gear with permadeath softened by carry-over progression.
community.consensus_summary: Roguelands is rated Very Positive on Steam (about 80% of roughly 3,700 reviews positive, 2,984 up vs 739 down) and is remembered fondly as a distinctive, deep, addictive crafting-and-loot roguelite, especially in co-op. The dominant caveat is that the developer stopped updating it after 2017 (last substantial patches were 1.5 and 1.5.1 in Feb 2017) while the game still feels unfinished, so even positive reviews are hedged with warnings about abandonment, missing content and bugs. Critics barely covered it: Metacritic has no critic score and only a handful of user ratings, and no OpenCritic entry was found. Its price ($9.99) and abandonment make many recent reviewers suggest it is best bought on sale, and a modding community plus fan wiki carry a lot of its longevity.
best_things: Distinctive blend of Terraria-style 2D action, loot grinding and roguelike permadeath that reviewers say they have not found elsewhere
Deep crafting and build-making: Droids harvest resources, Emblems craft gear, and there are 80+ weapons, augments and Combat Chips for varied builds
Slow, rewarding progression where items and some progress carry over between characters, softening permadeath
Co-op is described as insanely fun when it works; solo play is also considered enjoyable
Music gets praise in reviews, and the pixel art and planet variety are part of the game's pitch (store page and tags), though review praise for them is sparse
Plenty of content for the price: reviewers report 60-190+ hour playtimes and say you get a finished game's worth despite being 'unfinished'
Story and lore via rescued NPCs and the Destroyer plot, including the Gray Enigma storyline added in v1.4
Active modding community and an in-depth fan wiki add content and fixes (mods are said to make the game feel far more complete)
Fans appreciate that an abandoned game can no longer be nerfed or changed under them (a recurring tongue-in-cheek positive in reviews)
worst_things: Developer abandonment: no meaningful updates since early 2017, promised content never arrived, and many negative reviews are about this rather than gameplay
Feels unfinished: no proper final boss or ending for some storylines, tier 4+ items reportedly not craftable, half-implemented features such as drones
Multiplayer needs port-forwarding or tools like Hamachi rather than Steam integration, which is a serious barrier to the co-op that fans love most
No Steam achievements or stat tracking and no controller support (a 276-comment Steam thread asks for it), which stands out against modern roguelites
Bugs and rough UI polish: fans list issues such as quest UI, overlapping UI layers, dialogue glitches and potions unusable at full HP
Level layouts described as repetitive copy-pasted square loops joined by tunnels, with limited layout variety
improvements: Steam-integrated multiplayer (lobbies/invites) instead of port-forwarding or Hamachi
Achievements, stat tracking and controller support, the most repeated feature asks on the Steam forums
Longer, more varied level layouts and better map generation
Quality-of-life fixes: quick-stack to chests, deposit chest for shops, health bars on enemies and bosses, item rarity colors, a proper quest UI
A tutorial or better onboarding, since the early game is described as confusing
Finish the missing content: ending/final boss, uncraftable tier 4+ gear, recipes marked with question marks, and unfinished drone features; also replace 'die to unlock' unlock conditions
unique_things: Mixes roguelike permadeath with RPG character levels, loot and a Terraria-like crafting loop in a 2D side-on planet-hopping format
Droid-based resource gathering and Emblem crafting system is unusual among roguelites
Legacy-style carry-over: you can bring some items/progress from dead characters into new runs
Sci-fi setting of Galactic Cadets chasing the Destroyer, which eats planetary Aether cores, rather than generic fantasy dungeons
Playable races and classes unlocked over time, plus Ultra Bosses and a Forbidden Arena added post-launch
Shares a creator and spirit with Magicite, and some reviewers frame it as a spiritual sequel or evolution
tedious_or_disliked: Late-game and item hunting become very grindy, with repetitive farming of the same levels
Harsh permadeath frustrates some players, especially 'die to unlock' unlocks that force sacrificing a long-term character
Early game is confusing with little guidance
Setting up multiplayer (port-forwarding, Hamachi) is seen as a chore
Repetitive, samey level layouts make long sessions feel monotonous
Bugs and UI quirks that will now never be patched
divisive_points: Is it complete? Some reviewers say it is story complete and worth it, others say it is clearly unfinished and abandonware
Price value: some say $9.99 is fine for 100+ hours, others say it is only worth it at about $5
Permadeath and grind: some enjoy the slow progression and difficulty, others find it tedious
Whether it lives up to Magicite or its original premise, with mixed opinions from Magicite fans
community.reception_notes: Roguelands launched on Steam in 2015-2016 (a fetched store page gave Nov 6, 2015 while the local Steam data lists Jun 13, 2016, likely Early Access versus 1.0, not confirmed) and got major content updates through v1.4 (Oct 2016, Gray Enigma storyline, new races, Forbidden Arena boss) and v1.5/1.5.1 (Feb 2017, eight Ultra Bosses, new gear sets, droid stat mechanics, balance fixes). The last developer news post is from Feb 2019, when Sean Young announced Wraithslayer (another SmashGames title programmed by Devin Cole) and said he hoped to hire programmers by end of 2019 to revamp Roguelands; that revamp never appeared and recent reviews (2025-2026) treat the game as abandoned. Recent review volume is still active, with several reviews asking for it to return. Available on Windows, Mac and Linux. The Steam forum has long pinned Bug Reports (2,500+ comments) and Suggestions (1,400+ comments) threads and a small demand for a Roguelands 2. Web search budget was exhausted during this task, so Reddit, OpenCritic and editorial reviews could not be checked; the lack of critic coverage is based on Metacritic showing none and OpenCritic search returning nothing.

community.one_liner: A vertical, digging-focused action roguelite spin-off of Shovel Knight, made by Nitrome with Yacht Club Games, where you dig down a collapsing well chased by an ever-rising buzzsaw.
community.consensus_summary: Critics received it warmly (Metacritic PC 81 from 26 reviews, Switch reportedly 85) for tight Shovel Knight platforming, charm and Jake Kaufman's music, while Steam players are more mixed (75% of ~909 reviews, Mostly Positive) and Metacritic users land at 6.5 from only 31 ratings. The recurring split is between people who love the core movement and digging feel and people who find the roguelite layer shallow, repetitive and punishing. It is a finished, supported game rather than early access: two free DLC updates (Fate and Fortune in 2023, Wicked Wishes in 2025) plus PS5/Xbox Series ports in May 2025. Third-party estimates put Steam sales in the 20-50k owner range, which is modest, and the $24.99 price draws recurring complaints.
best_things: Tight, responsive Shovel Knight controls; digging downward at speed feels satisfying
Procedurally generated wells still deliver handcrafted-feeling platforming challenges with hidden side rooms and Cog collectibles
Jake Kaufman's chiptune soundtrack is widely praised, as are the art style and charm of the world and characters
Fast, bite-sized runs that make 'one more run' easy; some players report 100+ hours
Variety of terrain and hazards across well regions, plus Knightmare difficulty modes and armors extend replay value
Free DLC (Fate and Fortune, Wicked Wishes) added content and quality-of-life improvements
Critics and fans call it a worthy, polished entry that adapts the series' moveset to a new structure
worst_things: Tiny relic/item pool and weak synergies; runs feel very similar, and you can hold only one relic
Item usefulness varies hugely; some relics are situational to a single enemy or region
Enemies constantly spawn and respawn from awkward angles, with low health and rare health upgrades, so deaths can feel cheap
Permanent progression is thin: armors carry downsides, so you rarely feel meaningfully stronger between runs
Bosses are described by some as simplified compared to the original and beatable by spamming the shovel
No mouse-button binding, and menu controls tied to gameplay rebinding, were called out as poor PC options
Price ($24.99) seen as steep for the content; several reviewers recommend buying on sale
Some reports of softlocks and unresponsive characters on Steam forums; one user reported gem-banking problems
improvements: Much larger item and modifier pool with real build synergies
Let players equip newly unlocked upgrades for the next run instead of requiring a lucky drop
Better permanent power progression so repeated runs feel cumulative
Options to disable relic auto-swap, difficulty settings and more accessibility options
Bindable mouse buttons and separate menu vs gameplay control rebinding on PC
Clearer or less convoluted true-ending quest and less busywork in hub quests
unique_things: Vertical digging roguelite where downward movement is the core verb, inspired by Downwell, Spelunky and Dig Dug
An unstoppable buzzsaw above forces constant downward momentum instead of letting you explore slowly
Retains Shovel Knight's shovel drop and platforming toolkit adapted to randomized wells
Hub camp with friendly characters, quests and unlockable areas, plus a prequel-style story set with Drill Knight and the Hexcavators
Knightmare mode and hidden fountains/secrets add optional challenge layers
tedious_or_disliked: Repeating the same set of actions and early sections after every death feels like insane tedium to critics of the loop
Hub-world quests and minigames seen as busywork for replayability; the multi-step true-ending quest is considered convoluted
Unlock conditions for certain achievements and unlocks described as ridiculous
The rising buzzsaw pressure forces rushing, which some find stressful rather than fun
Falling past items with no chance to backtrack, or into unseen hazards, frustrates players
Very high Knightmare difficulty (Knightmare 5 and up) is called out as infuriating by some long-time players, e.g. dying to unseen enemies right after a secret fountain
divisive_points: Whether the roguelite structure suits Shovel Knight: fans of the original's curated levels say it loses the magic, others say it is the best spin on the formula
Difficulty and pace: pressure and cheap-feeling enemy placement read as tense to some and unfair to others
Depth: some see a simple, fun, short-session game, others an under-built roguelike with an item pool too small
Value: worth it for Shovel Knight devotees, overpriced for everyone else
community.reception_notes: Launched Sept 23, 2022 on Windows, Switch, and iOS/tvOS (Apple Arcade); Yacht Club Games partnered with mobile studio Nitrome after franchise fatigue, four years of development. Free DLC Fate and Fortune (Mar 2023) added Knightmare mode and QoL; Wicked Wishes (May 2025) added more content alongside PS5 and Xbox Series X/S ports. PC is Windows only on Steam. Steam estimates: 20-50k owners (SteamSpy), about $367k gross / $108k net (Boxleiter-style estimate, order of magnitude only). Could not retrieve OpenCritic, Reddit, IGN or PCMag pages (blocked or unavailable) and the web search budget was exhausted, so community detail leans on Steam reviews and Metacritic user reviews.

community.consensus_summary: Solitairica is received as a clever, addictive mobile-born hybrid that critics scored well (Metacritic 82 from six mostly iOS reviews, 70 to 100) and Steam players rate Mostly Positive (about 76-78%, roughly 574 reviews). Fans love the twist on solitaire and the class/deck variety; detractors, who dominate the most-upvoted negative reviews, say the RNG feels unfair, unlock grinding is slow, and animations drag. It is a small-scale niche title (Boxleiter-style estimates put it at 100k-200k owners and low six-figure gross), not abandoned: the Steam forum has pinned threads for an 'Anniversary Update' and a '2025 FAQ' with activity through December 2025, and reviewers mention an update after years of silence. The mobile version originally launched in 2016 and PC came later.
best_things: Fresh hook: solitaire card-clearing drives RPG combat, described as 'solitaire where you can actually lose and cast spells'
Four-resource system (Attack, Defense, Agility, Willpower) fuels spells, and synergy between spells, relics and enemy modifiers is praised as satisfying to figure out
Many classes/decks to unlock, each with different starting resource generation and spell sets, giving variety between runs
Relaxing, flow-state play that suits short bursts, podcasts or background TV; works well on Steam Deck
Strong 'one more try' pull and high replay value for solitaire fans and returning mobile players; one reviewer calls the replay value 'insane'
Accessible and easy to pick up; one reviewer plays it with their son, and the difficulty curve is described as easy to understand
Critics called it a good fit for touch platforms and praised its addictive loop (AppAdvice 100, TouchArcade 90)
Developer returned with an anniversary update years later, which some long-time players say improved the game
worst_things: RNG is the dominant complaint: stuns, poison, fire and card-altering effects are perceived as stacking unfairly, and the last needed card often fails to appear
Late-game and final boss damage or card-flooding can exceed what a run can handle; some runs feel unwinnable regardless of build
Progression grind: upgrades and decks cost 40-60 crystals while a failed run yields roughly 6-18, so unlocking everything takes many runs
Animations and card flips feel slow even with the speed-up setting on
Runs can feel samey: enemies are roughly the same each playthrough with only shuffled order and modifiers
Little player agency over draws (no real tools to control card selection), which undercuts the 'strategy' tag for some
Launch-era critic note that depth is limited and players repeat favourite spells after unlocking classes (Gamezebo 70)
No cross-save or cross-play with the mobile version; PC release is Windows only
improvements: Add a middle difficulty option or softer RNG/difficulty curve (requested by several negative reviewers)
Speed up animations further or allow skipping them
Reduce the crystal grind or make early upgrade costs cheaper relative to run payouts
Give players more tools to mitigate bad draws (mulligans, wildcard/joker-style effects) and review RNG bias, a topic raised on the Steam forum
Controller support is a recurring forum request
Cross-platform progress sync with the mobile version, and Mac/Linux builds
unique_things: Solitaire movement rule where you can play a card one rank above or below the exposed card, used as the core turn action
Clearing specific card types charges resources that power spells, and boss/enemy attack timers force you to clear cards quickly
Class-specific decks (warrior, rogue, wizard, bard and others) that each change how resources accrue
Comically stuck-in-solitaire fantasy theme with Emperor Stuck as final boss, plus Aces/Kings/Queens as unlockable powerful deck cards
Bridges mobile casual solitaire and roguelike deckbuilding, with Steam tags spanning Roguelike Deckbuilder, Relaxing and Addictive
tedious_or_disliked: Repeating the same early levels to farm crystals for each upgrade on each deck
Slow card-flip and enemy-turn animations, cited as a reason to quit within minutes
Turns spent passing while enemies add cards, poison, stun or drain abilities
Achievement hunting: beating the final boss with every deck and a near-pure-RNG 'go from 1 health to full' achievement
Bugs reported on the forum around the Bard class (spell purchasing, crashes on repeated Inspiration) and stacking effects
divisive_points: RNG: fans see it as the source of variety and say good builds smooth it out; others call it rigged and unfair
Grind versus progression: some enjoy slowly unlocking slots and decks, while many call it painfully slow
Mood: seen as a relaxing time-killer by some and as frustrating or boringly slow by others, with comparisons to Balatro as the more 'mature' alternative
community.reception_notes: Metacritic's 82 is based on six critic reviews (AppAdvice 100, TouchArcade 90, Apple'N'Apps 80, Multiplayer.it 80, Pocket Tactics 80, Gamezebo 70) that mostly reviewed the 2016 iOS version; Metacritic lists PC and iOS. The user score of 7.0 rests on only about six ratings, so it is not meaningful. No OpenCritic page was found (the search URL 404ed, and web search budget was exhausted, so absence is unconfirmed). Steam PC release was May 31, 2016 at $9.99, Windows only; it won an Unreal Developer Grant in March 2016. The game resurfaced on Steam with an Anniversary Update around 2025, praised by returning players, and the forum lists known issues (Bard bugs, RNG bias debate, save transfer, controller support requests). Note: Reddit, Wikipedia, and several outlet pages were not fetchable, so community detail leans on Steam reviews and forum.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Soulstone Survivors is a hack-and-slash chaos simulator played on a single-level layout where you upgrade spells and kill ever more enemies. He finds it chaotic, hectic, casual and fun to watch, but says it gets old very quickly. Once you have found your spells, later upgrades are mostly number tweaks, so the gameplay stops changing. Despite his many problems with it, he still considers it a fun game and places it in low B.
praise: Wildly chaotic, visually pleasing spectacle that goes well beyond what the trailer shows
Very amusing and entertaining to watch; hectic but casual and fun
Super satisfying to play without thinking, just to see things explode
Spells are found during the run and can be shared across characters, adding some variety
criticism: Gets old very quickly
Little customization at the start beyond character choice
After you find your spells, upgrades are just number adjustments (area, defense, speed) that feel boring
Gameplay barely changes as chaos increases; you just run in circles
Single level layout with no variety in setting
unique_points: Spells are offered during the run and can come from other characters, so character choice matters less
Chaos scales far beyond what marketing shows
Design lesson: spells could be more tame but have branching upgrade paths (e.g. lightning zap that chains, or leaves an energy cloud) for real build identity
commentary.quote: it is super satisfying to just play randomly if you just want to have a blast
comparisons: Other single-level survivors-like games he has covered
design_criteria: Upgrade depth: later upgrades are flat number boosts, which he finds boring
Build customization: wants branching spell upgrade paths rather than chaos
Level design: a single level layout limits variety
Replayability/run pacing: fun at first but repetitive quickly
Visual spectacle: chaotic, pleasing visuals are a plus
Moment-to-moment feel: satisfying, casual, hectic gameplay
commentary.rerank_note: He says he discussed this game at length in an earlier video of his, but this is not a re-ranking.

community.one_liner: A 3D-styled single-player action roguelite / survivors-like from Game Smithing Limited where you pick one of ~22 characters, stack 350+ skills, runes and weapons, and kill Void Lords and Titans across kill-based stages and endless modes.
community.consensus_summary: Soulstone Survivors is well liked: Steam shows Very Positive at about 91% across roughly 26,900 reviews, and the six critic reviews aggregated on Metacritic (all from the PS5 version) average 82. Players and critics praise the sheer amount of content, the power-fantasy escalation, the colourful visuals and the steady free updates. The recurring complaint from players is that builds, characters and maps feel too similar once you understand the tag/debuff stacking, and that the grind for meta materials and achievements is heavy. It spent about 2.5 years in Early Access (Nov 7, 2022 to full 1.0 on Jun 17, 2025), launched on PS5 and Xbox Series X around the 1.0 date, and is still receiving updates. Many reviewers give a positive vote with caveats, describing it as very solid but shallow in practice.
best_things: Huge amount of content: about 22 characters with 4-5 weapons each, 350+ skills, 100+ craftable weapons, a large passive/meta tree and nearly 500 achievements
Fast, satisfying power escalation: players say you reach absurd damage quickly, which is what they play the genre for
Kill-count based stage completion instead of a fixed timer, so strong builds can finish and leave early, with optional endless continuation
Colourful, eye-catching 3D cartoon visuals and very good music; critics liken the look to a World of Warcraft-style aesthetic
Meta-progression with the option to toggle parts of it off, plus difficulty and curse modifiers that raise rewards
Ongoing free content updates after 1.0 (new characters, weapons, maps), praised even by negative reviewers
Accessible and easy to pick up, with real full controller support; several reviewers call it a more fleshed-out step up from Brotato or Vampire Survivors
Story framing with cutscenes and a Void King final goal, unusual for the genre, noted in the PlayStation Universe review
worst_things: Builds, characters, weapons and runes feel fundamentally the same: one review says you just stack debuffs on a target, with a dominant Doom-style damage tag available to everyone
Gameplay at higher difficulty reduces to dashing in circles around bosses while dodging red zones and projectiles
Little variety between stages and modes: maps have few gimmicks, and critics note arenas are small, walled areas
Content feels inflated by reuse; one long review says character mechanics are the same system repackaged with different visuals and stats
Late-game screen clutter and power creep make the screen an unreadable mess, and the combat feels floaty or like hitting damage sponges to some players
Crashes on long runs (an hour-long run lost to a crash with no mid-run save) and performance dips on PS5 when the screen fills up
Loud, constant XP-pickup audio and GPU-heavy effects are mentioned as annoyances
Balance is uneven: some characters' skills, artifacts and ascension passives are much stronger, so players fall back to a few proven builds
improvements: Add a pause-and-resume or save between waves/rounds for long runs, so a crash does not waste up to an hour
Make builds, characters and stages mechanically distinct (real stage hazards, character-specific mechanics) so choices matter
Add co-op, including local co-op: several positive reviewers explicitly wish for it
Reduce the material grind and rebalance dominant tags like Doom so more build archetypes are viable
Improve performance and visual clarity when the screen is full, and offer more audio tuning (players ask for XP pickup sound options)
A roadmap and Workshop/mod support are recurring community requests on the Steam forum
unique_things: Stage completion is based on kills rather than surviving a timer, which changes pacing versus Vampire Survivors-style games
Skill tags and debuff stacking systems with runes, plus the ability to swap attacks/abilities during a run
Real 3D fantasy-ARPG presentation with ~90 enemy types, Titan bosses and cutscenes, rather than pixel art
Very large persistent progression: character levelling, passive grids, craftable weapons, ascension and optional meta toggles
Multiple modes (clear-and-boss, arenas, endless) with curse/difficulty modifiers that scale reward
Steam listing includes Mac and Linux builds as well as Windows, plus PS5 and Xbox Series X versions
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding crafting materials and meta currencies; one positive reviewer calls the material grind borderline excessive
Maxing every character and chasing achievements becomes a grind after roughly 38 to 40 hours of genuine progression
Very long endless runs, where low-DPS builds need minutes to kill bosses and some players burn out not knowing when to stop
Repetitive bosses and basic environments (a point raised in the Critical Hits review) and lack of map variety
Some players feel they see everything within a few hours, with the rest of the unlocks not changing decisions in a run
Matches feel long and brainless once the build is settled; negative reviewers say unlocks and achievements never change the actual gameplay (top negative-review theme, 100+ helpful votes)
divisive_points: Depth versus illusion of choice: fans see deep build theorycrafting, while many negative reviews say every build plays the same
Difficulty and feel: GameSpew found it forgiving and easy, while others find late-game chaos and dodging demanding or unreadable
Value: commonly recommended at a discount (one reviewer says under 10 euros), with many calling it good value even while criticising the design
Endless modes and long runs are either a feature (power fantasy, optional) or a burnout trap
community.reception_notes: Early Access began Nov 7, 2022 and 1.0 shipped Jun 17, 2025 (Steam lists release date as Jun 17, 2025 with price $14.99). The critic scores on Metacritic all relate to the PS5 release, six reviews from mid-June to late July 2025; the Metacritic user score of 7.9 rests on only about 23 ratings, so is not robust. OpenCritic did not load (404), so no OpenCritic score was found. Steam reception has remained Very Positive (about 91%) and the game has a supporter pack and soundtrack DLC. Negative Steam reviews mostly come from long-time players, sometimes with hundreds of hours, who acknowledge the free content additions but say the core loop was never addressed. Note: the web search budget ran out, so community detail leans heavily on Steam reviews and the Steam forum page, and no Reddit threads could be fetched (Reddit blocked). Verification: Metacritic page re-fetched; PS5 Metascore 82 from 6 critics and user 7.9 from 23 ratings confirmed; Xbox Series X shows 88 from 4 critics; PC has 3 critic reviews without a score.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Spelunky 2 is the 2020 sequel to the classic Spelunky, a brutal, secret-filled platformer roguelike. PepperHead admits it is not his preferred play style and he has only about five hours in it, so he treats this as a partial review. He found it more fun and more readable than the original, with great art and VFX, but still very punishing later on. He places it in B tier with the note that he may bump it up once he plays more.
praise: Traps and overall readability feel easier and clearer than the first game
Even more secrets and things to find than the original
Early game feels friendlier
Art direction is very good
VFX are especially great
He respects the amount of work put in and understands why many would rank it S tier
criticism: Still super brutal; later in a run things explode and you die quickly
Not his kind of play style, limiting how much he enjoys it
He has limited playtime, so his verdict is provisional
unique_points: A huge number of secrets to discover, many found online
Sequel improves visual clarity of what is happening on screen
Strong VFX that contribute to feel
commentary.quote: I'm gonna put it as a solid beat here that I might bump up

design_criteria: Difficulty: brutal, with late-run spikes that kill quickly
Readability: clearer visuals make traps and hazards easier to parse
Secrets/content depth: lots to discover
Art and VFX: praised as excellent
Personal play-style fit: affects his enjoyment
Early vs late run pacing: gentle early, explosive late
commentary.rerank_note: He explicitly says the B placement is provisional and he might bump it up in the future after more playtime.

community.one_liner: Derek Yu's 2D procedurally generated platformer-roguelike sequel in which Ana Spelunky, daughter of the original hero, descends through a much larger, more interconnected set of caves on the Moon, with one-life runs, physics-driven chaos and optional 4-player co-op or arena play.
community.consensus_summary: Spelunky 2 is received as a superb, more-of-the-same-but-bigger sequel: critics gave it near-universal acclaim (PC Metacritic 91, IGN 10/10) and Steam players rate it Very Positive (about 93% of roughly 22k reviews). Praise centres on its deep systems, secrets, mounts, branching paths and hilarious emergent deaths. The recurring caveats are brutal difficulty with hidden one-hit-kill hazards, a no-save/no-checkpoint structure that turns the true ending (Cosmic Ocean) into a multi-hour endurance test, and, in recent Steam reviews, long-running online multiplayer/crossplay bugs. Some long-time fans feel it is slightly less tightly balanced than Spelunky HD. It is a finished, shipped game (PC/PS4 2020, Switch 2021, Xbox 2022, PS5 2025) rather than early access, though developer updates appear to have been sparse after the initial patches.
best_things: Systems-driven chaos: liquids, fire, explosives, thrown items and enemy interactions create funny, memorable emergent stories (players describe deaths as punchlines)
Huge, dense secret and unlock content with branching paths (Jungle/Volcana, Tide Pool/Temple), alternate routes, and shortcuts that reward exploration
Mounts (turkeys, rock dogs, axolotls, qilins) and new environments add real tactical variety while keeping the classic feel
Strong mastery loop: reviewers and players describe progress as learning to read threats, with winning a run being unusually satisfying
Polished art, animation and soundtrack, more expressive visuals than the original, plus a coherent world with NPCs and a family-themed story
Excellent couch and online co-op for up to four players, plus a customizable arena/deathmatch mode with 40 maps and bots, daily challenges and seeded runs
Enormous replay value; many Steam reviewers have 100 to 1000+ hours and call it a near-perfect or desert-island game
Quality-of-life improvements over the first game (e.g. more consistent shopkeeper balance, expanded exploration) that some players think make it more approachable
Best with friends: reviewers repeatedly say the chaos and deaths are funniest in co-op, and a few call it a calming, even cozy, game once you learn its rules
worst_things: Many instant-death or combo-death situations, including hidden hazards such as bear traps concealed by terrain, which critics (e.g. Destructoid) called frustrating and players call cheap or trolling

Online multiplayer problems widely reported on Steam: stuck on the loading screen, inability to join, crossplay-related breakage, and a bug requiring workaround input to load the next area; some reviewers say it has been broken for months or over a year
Perceived lack of developer communication/support after launch; Steam complaints mention no word from the developers for a long stretch
The Dwelling, Jungle and Volcana are called disproportionately hard for early worlds by some veterans, and certain levels feel specially designed to ruin a run
Some dedicated players feel the added mechanics (and the 'Sunken City'/Cosmic Ocean path requirements) dilute the tight risk-reward balance of Spelunky HD
Movement/controls friction: no dedicated pickup/drop/throw/climb buttons, leading to accidental climbs or item handling mistakes that kill the run
Short-range whip and thrown-item ricochet feel punishing to newcomers, who complain about taking damage just to hit a stationary enemy
Gameplay randomness (seed quality, needing specific items to spawn for shortcut unlocks) is cited as unfair by players who wrote negative reviews
improvements: Fix online co-op stability and crossplay bugs, and communicate about fixes on the Steam forums

Offer optional accessibility or difficulty options (e.g. extra health, easier modes, checkpoints/continues); one reviewer called their absence sadistic, though the developers deliberately preserve the no-continue design
Reduce reliance on concealed or unreadable hazards so deaths feel more telegraphed and learnable
Add dedicated buttons or rebind options for pick up/drop/throw/climb to reduce accidental actions
Smooth the early-game difficulty ramp (Dwelling and Jungle in particular) and make unlock requirements less dependent on random spawns
More post-launch communication and updates; reviewers complain of over a year of silence while plush merchandise was announced
unique_things: Every level is a hand-tuned procedural layout built from templates, so runs feel random but readable and fair at a systems level; the series is the reference for this style
Permadeath with literally no meta-progression in power: only shortcuts, unlocks and knowledge carry over, so skill is the main upgrade
Shared physics and item interactions where almost anything can kill you, including your own thrown items, enabling speedrun and trick strategies
Branching world structure with hidden areas, alternate paths and a secret true ending (Cosmic Ocean) requiring a long perfect run
Integrated multiplayer modes: 4-player couch and online co-op over the same campaign, and a full arena deathmatch mode with map variety
Distinct personalities for shopkeepers, NPC family members and the ghost mechanic that punishes slow play
tedious_or_disliked: Cosmic Ocean: a many-hour endurance sequence with no saves that many call the main grind; Steam reviewers joke about not being able to spare four hours and about few reaching it
Starting over from 1-1 after a sudden death, which newcomers and some critics (Gameblog.fr at 60/100) find unpedagogical and demoralizing
Repeated tedious retries to unlock shortcuts and characters, with rewards like a victory screen and a new character considered underwhelming by some
Status effects such as poison and curse described as run-ending annoyances
Fighting the interface and inputs (accidentally climbing or not being able to drop items) rather than the game
Bug-related restarts in online mode, such as getting stuck on the 'walls are shifting' screen
divisive_points: Difficulty and fairness: fans call it a masterclass, others call it a troll game; critics at Destructoid and GameSpot (8/10) noted excess one-hit-kill traps while IGN scored it 10/10
Versus Spelunky HD: some find 2 the better, more expansive game, while others think HD's risk-reward balance was tighter and that 2 is merely 'more Spelunky' with added complexity
Randomness vs skill: some players love the unpredictability, others argue too many deaths come from unfair spawns rather than player error
No-continue philosophy: praised as the source of the game's tension and reward, criticised as disrespectful of player time and a barrier that steers casuals away
community.reception_notes: Launched on PS4 (Sept 15, 2020) and PC (Sept 29, 2020) to universal acclaim and a Best Indie nomination at The Game Awards 2020; later ports came to Switch (Aug 2021), Xbox One/Series (Jan 2022) and PS5 (Mar 2025). Launch reception was about difficulty and refinement; the current Steam conversation (recent negatives) is dominated by online co-op and crossplay breakage, with reviewers saying a crossplay update made friend sessions unreliable and that developer communication is scarce. Gameblog.fr (60/100) was the notable critical outlier on pedagogy and progression. Revenue figures are third-party estimates only; no official sales numbers were found. OpenCritic score could not be retrieved: the web search budget was exhausted and the guessed OpenCritic URLs returned other games, so it is left null. Metacritic critic score depends on platform (PC 91, main page 87 (41 reviews), Switch 92); PC is used here to match the Steam listing, and the 8.0 user score came from the main (PS4) page.

games.short_description: Sundered is a chaotic hand­-drawn metroidvania where you resist or embrace ancient eldritch powers, a challenging and unique take on a classic genre from the creators of Jotun, now with local co-op!

placements.verbal_evidence: it's going to be a low B tier

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Sundered is a Metroidvania with roguelike elements bolted on. He thinks the visuals, world and story make a great Metroidvania, but the roguelike layer feels like a last-second addition that hurts it. Build randomization is stripped out, leaving only randomized map portions and enemies. He would recommend it to some people for the visuals, but says it would be much better if it were not a roguelike. He places it in low B.
praise: Visuals and art direction look amazing
Strong world and story as a Metroidvania
Unique genre mix of Metroidvania and roguelike
He enjoyed playing and streaming it for the look
criticism: Roguelike elements feel tacked on and make no sense for the game
No random build aspect, only randomized map pieces and enemies
Randomized platforming within maps is clunky and frustrating
Enemies pop up randomly in levels not designed for them
Randomness hurts what would otherwise be a great game
unique_points: Metroidvania-roguelike hybrid where the world is fixed but rooms' platforming and enemy spawns are randomized
Design lesson: randomization must fit level design, or it undermines it
commentary.quote: this game has no right being a roguelike
design_criteria: Randomization and level design: random platforming and enemy spawns clash with planned levels
Build variety: lacks random build elements, weakening roguelike identity
Visuals and charm: a major strength
Genre fit: roguelike elements feel forced onto a Metroidvania
Story and world: praised

community.one_liner: A hand-drawn Lovecraftian Metroidvania from Thunder Lotus (Jotun) with procedurally assembled maps, endless enemy horde rooms, and a corruption-based power system.
community.consensus_summary: Sundered is well liked overall: Steam shows Very Positive (about 82%, roughly 5,200 reviews), and Metacritic sits at a Mixed-or-Average 74 from 39 critics, with user score 7.1. Nearly everyone praises the hand-drawn art, animation, atmosphere, boss designs and the fluid movement and abilities. The split is over the core design: the endless horde spawns, semi-procedural maps and stat-driven progression delight some players and feel repetitive and tedious to others. It is a finished 2017 release (Eldritch Edition added the free Magnate of the Gong update with new areas and local co-op); it is not early access. Some recent Steam reviewers mention a dip in recent ratings, and the top positive reviews push back on it.
best_things: Gorgeous hand-drawn art and fluid animation, the most universally praised element (Thunder Lotus signature, compared with Jotun and Spiritfarer)
Large, memorable boss fights that reward learning patterns
Movement and traversal feel great, and new abilities (especially corrupted versions via eldritch shards) make you feel powerful
Atmospheric Lovecraftian world, soundtrack and sparse, evocative lore with a narrator voice and multiple endings
Sprawling central skill tree and build variety give a real sense of progression after each death
Procedural layout keeps exploration fresh and makes a blend of Metroidvania and roguelite that some call the most meaningful one they have played
Non-linear exploration and currency collection, plus difficulty options and easy 100% achievements for completionists
worst_things: Endless horde rooms and waves of weak, repeated enemy types (palette swaps) feel overwhelming, spammy and screen-covering
Combat is described as button mashing or dodging, with little depth outside bosses
Long stretches of empty or samey rooms; the map is not very helpful and the start is confusing with little explanation
Some boss fights are considered poorly designed (either trivial with the right build or slow and tanky)
Local co-op is widely called a letdown: the second player cannot die, collect items or meaningfully interact
Keyboard play suffers, notably the grappling hook section (works far better on a gamepad)
Story is told obliquely and is easy to miss or forget; it is also short (roughly 10 to 20 hours)
improvements: Clearer onboarding and tutorials, including explaining shard destruction and corruption mechanics
More enemy variety and less reliance on palette-swapped stronger variants
Better map and navigation clarity in a procedurally assembled world
A meaningful co-op design where player two has health and can interact with the world
More flexible save slots, since players say the three slots limit getting all endings without replaying
Clearer storytelling and more content or length
unique_things: Resist or Embrace system: corrupt abilities with eldritch shards for power at the cost of humanity, leading to different endings
Procedurally assembled Metroidvania map with handcrafted elements rather than a fixed hand-built world
Horde-based combat where huge numbers of enemies spawn continuously in some rooms
Roguelite-style permanent upgrades via a central skill tree that let you come back stronger after death
Lovecraftian setting in an abandoned underground military base with huge boss sprites
tedious_or_disliked: Endless enemy respawns that force you to stop and fight while chipping away at your health, then chase you back through rooms
Grinding perks and shards; guides reportedly recommend AFK or boss farming for money, which players read as a flawed progression loop
Three endings requiring separate playthroughs, repeating the same path and looting
Running through many empty rooms to get from A to B
Overly complex skill tree with few exciting unlocks for some players
Early game frustration before upgrades arrive
divisive_points: Procedural generation: some love the replayability, others say it undercuts what makes a Metroidvania (authored level design)
Horde mechanic: seen as fitting chaotic eldritch atmosphere by fans and as an annoying pacing killer by detractors
Difficulty and feel of combat: empowering and smooth once upgraded vs. shallow and sloppy
Value and length: worth it at the price for many, bare-bones and only decent on sale for others
community.reception_notes: Launched July 2017 to generally strong reviews from outlets such as GameSpot (8), Eurogamer and Rock, Paper, Shotgun per the Steam page, while the Metacritic aggregate is a more modest 74 because of mid-range scores tied to repetition. The Eldritch Edition added the free Magnate of the Gong update (new areas, quest chains, a boss, local co-op). Platforms: Windows, Mac and Linux on Steam; Steam Deck and controller support noted in reviews (keyboard play is weaker). Estimated 200k to 500k Steam owners and about $2.9M gross revenue (third-party Boxleiter-style estimate, not audited). Several long-time players say recent Steam ratings have dipped to Mixed and call it undeserved; negatives cite the horde design and co-op.

Enormous depth of systems and content

community.one_liner: A 16-bit-styled, turn-based traditional roguelike/dungeon crawler by Impact Gameworks with a job system, pet taming and a town hub, with an optional no-permadeath Adventure Mode.
community.consensus_summary: Tangledeep is well regarded: Steam shows Very Positive (about 82% of ~1,490 reviews positive), Metacritic critics average 79 from 7 Switch reviews, and GOG lists about 78 on OpenCritic with 100% critic recommend. Players and critics praise the pixel art, Andrew Aversa soundtrack, mix-and-match job system and flexible difficulty, and often call it a hidden gem and a friendly entry to traditional roguelikes. Detractors find it shallow, easy or a grind for veterans, and find the controls, tutorial and run length rough. Metacritic user score is a middling 7.4 on only 25 ratings. It is a full release (Feb 2018) with paid expansions (Legend of Shara, Dawn of Dragons) and Steam reviews are still arriving in 2026, so it still has an audience; I did not find evidence of it being abandoned, but did not verify current patch cadence.
best_things: Polished SNES-era pixel art and an acclaimed soundtrack (composer Andrew Aversa with guest composers) that reviewers repeatedly call captivating
Job/class system with about 12 base jobs where you can mix and match abilities and passives via multiclassing, giving lots of build freedom
Very customizable difficulty: four difficulty tiers including a no-permadeath Adventure Mode plus 10+ optional modifiers; praised by GameCritics as something more games should copy
Approachable for roguelike newcomers while still offering depth; several players call it a cozy, chill traditional roguelike
Large amount of content: side areas, quests, item dreams (mini-dungeons to upgrade gear), a town hub, farming, pet taming and breeding; one player logged 192 hours without seeing everything
Good controller support plus fully rebindable keyboard controls; players say it plays well on gamepad and the Switch version gets long playtime
worst_things: Top-voted negative review (12 votes): beautiful art and good music but 'a whole lot of unmemorable stuff in between'; never reaches its potential
Combat and build depth felt shallow to veterans: few enemy types, skills maxed out early so tactics stop changing, equipment rarely changes how you play
Generally too easy for experienced roguelike players, who say a no-death clear in one attempt is plausible (while Nintendo Life cautioned difficulty spikes for newcomers)
Clunky interface and controls per several players: unhelpful default keymapping, menus described as convoluted, and movement described as clunky
Tutorial is thin and mostly leaves players to figure mechanics out
Late-game gear selection becomes a slog, with strategies dictated by RNG loot and lots of unusable drops for your class
Some feel it does nothing better than its genre predecessors and lacks the creativity and humor of games like Dungeons of Dredmor
Music cannot be turned off until after character creation, cited as a UX annoyance
No character customization beyond class choice (4 votes)
improvements: A better, more informative tutorial and clearer default control/keymap labelling (controller Start/Select confusion, WASD vs arrow keys mismatch reported)
More enemy variety and skills/equipment that change tactics rather than giving flat passive boosts
Cleaner menus and inventory UI; Steam reviewers called the interface clunky despite an unlimited text inventory
Fewer rough edges for ranged/melee play such as automatic weapon switching back to melee (one reviewer complaint)
Mitigations for run length and RNG punishment, since full runs are reported at 6-14 hours and a late death is demoralizing
More build-defining synergies so the multiclass system feels necessary rather than optional
unique_things: Capture-and-breed pet system: catch monsters, keep one fighting beside you and breed them in a Monster Corral
Job system with free class switching (for a fee or free) and cross-class ability mixing, reminiscent of JRPGs
Item Dreams: random mini-dungeons you enter inside an item to strengthen it, a Disgaea-like idea
SNES/JRPG-flavored presentation with town hub, farming, banking and shared progression between characters, blending roguelike with Mystery Dungeon and classic RPG feel
Adventure Mode without permadeath alongside a hardcore mode, plus a heavy modifier menu and challenge leaderboards
tedious_or_disliked: Full runs are very long (one player reported 6-7 hours at best, up to 9-14 hours), so a late death feels painful
Catching pets is called a drag (GameCritics) and pets feel almost necessary for some players
Grinding for gear upgrades and sifting through lots of junk loot late in the game
Some players say winning favors patient defensive play rather than tactical skill, making long runs feel repetitive
Turn-based movement and menu navigation felt slow or unintuitive to some new players
divisive_points: Difficulty: newcomers and some critics report spikes, while veterans find it easy and never close to dying
Depth: fans see great build freedom via multiclassing, detractors say abilities are basic and multiclassing is unnecessary
JRPG-adjacent style and pet/farming features read as charming to some and as distraction from a pure roguelike to others
Permadeath pacing: long hardcore runs are praised for stakes by some and called unfulfilling by others
community.reception_notes: Launched on Steam Feb 1, 2018 at $14.99 (PC/Mac/Linux) and later reached Switch, where Metacritic's 7 critic reviews range from 70 to 90. Steam holds at Very Positive (82%); Metacritic user score is lower (7.4, 25 ratings) but the sample is tiny. The OpenCritic figure (78, 100% recommend) comes from the GOG store page, and I could not load the OpenCritic page itself. Expansions Legend of Shara and Dawn of Dragons add classes and content; the Steam store also sells two soundtrack packages. Reddit and Nintendo Life pages were blocked, and my web search quota was exhausted, so community themes rely on Steam reviews, the Steam community forum, GOG and critic pages. The Steam forum shows typical support threads (job trials, New Game+ bug, requests for GOG updates, Russian localization). Estimated copies: Steam owner range 20k-50k per SteamSpy data in the local file; the revenue calculator gave no copies figure.

community.one_liner: A match-3 puzzle deckbuilding roguelite, cardboard-craft prequel to The Binding of Isaac, by Edmund McMillen, James Interactive and Ridiculon.
community.consensus_summary: Players rate it Very Positive on Steam (about 81% of roughly 5.9k reviews in our data), while Metacritic sits at a Mixed 73 critic / 6.4 user. The core loop of matching tiles to cast spells and building a loadout is widely called addictive and charming, but it is held back by heavy RNG, thin explanation, a grindy unlock system and lots of bugs. Development was rocky: the original programmer left, and the last official patches came around 2021 before a later community-linked 'Windfall' update was announced. Many negative Steam reviews read like 'fun game, but unfinished and buggy', so the score is dragged down by polish rather than by the core idea.
best_things: The match-tiles-to-cast-spells loop is satisfying and addictive, with big combo turns feeling great when a board lines up
Cardboard cut-out art style and child-like Isaac-prequel atmosphere are charming
Deckbuilder-style decisions (skills, items, trinkets) pay off when you plan around the board
100+ items, 80+ trinkets, several playable characters and 10 bosses give a decent item pool
Isaac-style humor and lore expansion appeal strongly to Binding of Isaac fans
Ridiculon soundtrack is praised (Steam tags include Great Soundtrack)
worst_things: Very buggy: softlocks (especially from clicking too fast), run resets, broken puzzle boards and visual glitches
Achievements and unlocks often fail to trigger or duplicate; players resort to third-party fixes
Steam achievements are so unreliable that players say a third-party fix (the Windfall mod) is practically required; the last official patch was around March 2021
Save data can be lost, and saves are local rather than properly cloud-synced
Heavy luck dependence: a bad board or a room with 5-6 enemies can end a run before you act
Little is explained, so boss and enemy mechanics become knowledge checks
Limited content at launch (four dungeons) and the game feels unfinished or abandoned to many
Critics called the UI feedback (tooltips, tile highlighting) unpolished and mobile-like
improvements: Fix the long list of bugs, achievement issues and save problems
Reduce run-ending RNG from board draws and enemy stacking, and tighten balance
Explain enemy and boss mechanics in-game instead of relying on trial and error
Rework the slot-machine-style item unlock system so progress is not so grindy
Add more content and more creative synergy/deckbuilding options, since many builds feel samey
Improve UI feedback such as tooltips and tile highlighting
unique_things: Mixes a match-3 board game with roguelite deckbuilding and Isaac-style items
Handmade cardboard look and tone, as a literal toy-theatre prequel to Isaac
Spells are fueled by matching colored tile types, so board reading and spell planning interlock
Gross-out Isaac humor applied to puzzle combat (for example flinging excrement at enemies)
Edmund McMillen's biggest project by his own account, after a roughly four-year development
tedious_or_disliked: Unlocking new items is gated behind a chance-based system that only rolls after winning long runs, so the grind is painful
Some later areas and progress are gated behind playing specific characters
Limited coins per floor make stat upgrades and shops feel too scarce
Enemies that resist everything or multi-hit counters can make turns feel unfair
Repetitive play over extended sessions, per critics
divisive_points: Price: some call $15 too steep for the content and state; others find it worth it
Difficulty and RNG: some see it as tense roguelite variance, others as unfair and unwinnable runs
Whether it is a real roguelike with synergies or an easy game that lacks roguelike depth without them
community.reception_notes: Launched on Steam in Nov 2019 with softlock issues; programmer James Interactive could not continue, so McMillen brought in Isaac: Rebirth programmers in late 2020. Ports followed: Android (Dec 2020), Epic/GOG (Feb 2022), Switch/PS5/Xbox (June 2022). Steam reviews note the last official update was around March 2021 and that a third-party mod called Windfall is treated as near-required for achievements and fixes. A Steam community thread titled Windfall Update 1.5 was posted in May (year unclear, I could not read its contents), so it is unclear whether this is now official. OpenCritic score could not be verified: web search budget was exhausted and the guessed OpenCritic URL returned a different game, so the value is null. Steam revenue estimates from local data: ~$2.97M gross, ~$876k net, owners 1-2M (estimate from Boxleiter-style sources, order of magnitude only). Reddit could not be fetched, so community detail relies on Steam reviews and discussion pages.

games.name: Vagante
games.short_description: Vagante is an action-packed platformer that features permanent death and procedurally generated levels. Play cooperatively with friends both locally and online, or adventure solo in this challenging roguelike-inspired game.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Vagante is a classic fantasy 2D dungeon crawler that he describes as a Spelunky wannabe, but with swords, bosses and far more character upgrading. He says it has little roguelite meta-progression but plenty of in-run growth, class choice and inventory management. It is brutal, with traps that can one-shot you, yet he had more fun with it than with Spelunky because of its stronger roguelike feel. He admits most people would rank Spelunky far higher and that this is just his opinion. No tier letter is stated in this segment.

Each run feels fairly different from the last
Lots to do within each individual run, including inventory management
Multiple completely different classes with different spells
Great customization and in-run character building (e.g. axe skill, defensive focus)
Co-op multiplayer looks fun

Little roguelite meta-progression, mostly upgrading within runs
Is not a huge fan of this style of brutal Spelunky-like game generally
