Class variety with distinct spells and playstyles changes how each run is played
commentary.quote: it's just my own opinion
design_criteria: Run variety: each run feels different due to equipment and class
Character build depth: skills, spells and classes change playstyle
Inventory management: adds decisions within a run
Difficulty: brutal with one-shot traps
Meta-progression: minimal roguelite unlocks
Roguelike feel: personal preference for growing a character across a run
Co-op: looks fun but not weighted in his judgment

community.one_liner: A dark-fantasy 2D pixel-art platformer roguelike from Nuke Nine with permadeath, procedurally generated caves, RPG classes and up-to-4-player local/online co-op.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate it Very Positive (about 89% of roughly 5,000 reviews), and the reviews that praise it describe a punishing but rewarding Spelunky-meets-RPG loop with strong class variety and excellent co-op. Critics are lukewarm: Metacritic shows a 69 Metascore (Switch, 7 reviews; PC has too few) with PS4 at 79 and Xbox One at 75, and a 7.0 user score from very few votes (9 ratings). Reviews split into strong 80s from outlets like TouchArcade and Hobby Consolas and a 40 from Nintendo Life, which called it incomplete. Steam lists the full release as Feb 21, 2018, the price is $14.99, and a Steam Community thread asks whether the game still gets updates, so it reads as a finished, largely dormant title kept alive by co-op fans, the Workshop and a Vagante Remastered mod. Note: live web search was unavailable (session search budget exhausted), so this draws on Steam data, Metacritic pages and Steam Community.
best_things: Steep but rewarding learning curve: players say runs feel fairer and more controllable as they learn items, spells and boss patterns
Class and build variety: each class plays differently, any class can use any item (a mage can wield a knife), and most weapons and stats are described as viable
Co-op with up to 4 players locally or online is repeatedly called the best way to play, producing chaotic, funny moments (reviews mention reviving friends, shared trap deaths)
Tight, responsive movement and combat; one reviewer notes they rarely felt a death was out of their control, and jeuxvideo.com praised 'millimeter-tuned' gameplay
Atmospheric pixel art, oppressive dungeon mood (catacombs named) and a well-liked soundtrack
Depth from item identification, shrines/offerings, magic versus burning books for healing, and gambling on unidentified potions
Replayability and completionist content: Book of Secrets unlocks, hard achievements, Steam Workshop and custom levels, plus a community Discord
Reminds players of Spelunky and UnEpic (Steam reviewers), with RPG-style classes layered on a platformer
worst_things: Controls draw repeated complaints on keyboard/mouse and especially controller; some players report needing Steam Input settings or a restart to get a pad recognized
Trap deaths (spikes, arrow traps, boulders) and instant kills feel cheap to some players, who say traps rather than enemies dominate the difficulty
Combat is called simple or repetitive by some (Hobby Consolas, and a Steam reviewer who says the RPG layer is a facade over platforming)
Weak onboarding: Nintendo Life and Metacritic users cite minimal tutorials and unexplained mechanics
Hard-to-see hazards, including traps that blend into the environment, make some deaths feel unfair
Online multiplayer is reported as a bit buggy, with sparse public servers per Metacritic users
Limited content scope for some critics: jeuxvideo.com wanted more biomes and Nintendo Life found the adventure short with no story
Dev support appears to have ended, with Steam forum users asking if the game still receives updates
improvements: Better, rebindable and more reliable controller support and general control feel
Real tutorials or in-game explanation of hazards, items and systems
Difficulty or accessibility options, for example ways to tone down traps, since one reviewer found the devs offered none and modding them out is hard
More biomes and content variety, plus some narrative or goals beyond the dungeon crawl (critic feedback)
More varied and complex enemy mechanics so combat carries more of the challenge than traps
More stable online co-op and matchmaking, and continued post-launch updates or a sequel (Steam forum users want one)
unique_things: RPG-style classes, skins and backgrounds with free item mixing inside a Spelunky-like platformer
Item identification, curses, shrines and offerings that make item use a risk-reward gamble, close to classic ASCII roguelike design
Up to 4-player local and online co-op built into a hardcore permadeath platformer
Steam Workshop custom levels plus the Vagante Remastered community mod
Hard mode and Rift bosses give high-end endgame challenges for veterans
tedious_or_disliked: Repeated early deaths, sometimes within seconds of starting a run, from traps or bad RNG
Item roulette: unidentified items and randomized loot can make or break a run
Losing long runs (an hour or more) to a single spike or boulder
Learning mechanics by dying because the game explains little
Achievement hunting is described as extremely difficult though fair, with 100% completion taking 180+ hours for one reviewer
divisive_points: Difficulty: Steam reviewers call it brutal yet fair and rewarding, while Metacritic users and some Steam negatives call it punishing for its own sake
Combat: praised as good on every class by some players, but called simple and repetitive by some critics and a co-op reviewer
Trap-heavy design: a feature that demands awareness to fans, a cheap source of deaths to detractors
Critic scores vary widely by outlet, from 80 (TouchArcade, Hobby Consolas, jeuxvideo.com) to 40 (Nintendo Life), with Pure Nintendo and Gamezebo at 70 and Nintenderos at 60
community.reception_notes: Steam lists the full release as Feb 21, 2018 (developer Nuke Nine, price $14.99 after a reported permanent drop from $25 per a user review), though the game predates that in a 2014 alpha/early-access era. Console ports on Switch, PS4 and Xbox One drew mixed-to-good reviews (Metacritic Switch 69, PS4 79, Xbox One 75) with Eurogamer's Switch score shown as TBD on Metacritic. PC players rate it far higher than Metacritic's small user sample (7.0 from 9 ratings) and recent Steam reviews remain about 91% positive. Steam data estimates 200K to 500K owners, and revenue tools put gross at roughly $2.2M (net about $640K), which is a rough estimate only. Steam forum chatter suggests updates have stopped, and the community now carries it via Workshop levels, the Vagante Remastered mod and a Discord. No OpenCritic entry could be confirmed, and the session's search budget was exhausted so no Reddit threads were read.

games.name: 暖雪 Warm Snow

commentary.summary: Warm Snow is a Chinese hack-and-slash roguelike that plays its serious tone straight and pulls it off. Everything in it is wildly overpowered, both the player and the enemies, which makes it visually crazy and very fun. He admits the balance is only okay, but he has played it a lot and keeps enjoying it. The lack of boss variety holds it back from S, so he places it at the top of A and recommends it to fans of action-heavy hack and slash.

community.one_liner: A Chinese-mythology dark-fantasy action roguelite by BadMudStudio (published by bilibili) in which swordsman Bi-an fights the Five Great Clans using melee weapons plus recallable flying swords, with a deep relic/sect build system.
community.consensus_summary: Warm Snow is a well-liked, somewhat under-the-radar action roguelite: Steam shows about 39k reviews at roughly 93% positive (Very Positive), with the Steam store page showing a dip in recent reviews (about 79% on a small 30-day sample). Players praise build variety, the flying-sword combat and the ink-painting art style; they criticise slow meta-progression, unclear or badly translated text, a linear fixed map and fodder enemies once a build comes together. Formal critic coverage is thin: Metacritic has only two critic reviews (90 and 80), so no Metascore yet, and no OpenCritic entry was found. It is a full release (Jan 2022), not early access, with a paid DLC (The End Of Karma), a free DLC (Shao Meng / 烬梦) and console ports (Oct 2023). Commonly compared to Hades, usually as solid but a step below it in presentation and story.
best_things: Large build variety: sects, relics, weapons and deities combine into many synergies, and players report late-game runs feel very flexible
Distinctive gear system: the same relic or piece of gear has a different effect depending on which slot it is placed in, and can be re-slotted at any time
Fast, fluid combat built around melee plus flying swords that can be launched and recalled
Striking art direction inspired by ancient silk/ink painting, with Chinese mythology theme and a well-liked soundtrack
Scalable difficulty and challenge options give high replay value; reviewers cite 30-40+ hours to unlock everything and multiple stories/endings
Good boss fights and decent enemy variety according to several positive reviewers
Lots of content for the price (around $18), including a free DLC and a paid expansion
worst_things: Translation problems: English text overflows UI boxes, some keywords and item effects are mistranslated or unclear, and some end-of-boss text is untranslated
Meta-progression is described as very slow to upgrade, which a top-voted negative review calls the game's major flaw
Fixed, linear level layouts and repeated bosses make runs feel repetitive compared with procedurally generated roguelites
Many item and relic effects reduce to 'do more damage when X', so playstyle changes less than the item count implies
Enemies become fodder with a decent build but feel like HP sponges in early runs or on weak builds
Dash and movement are called clunky or slow by several reviewers; game feels dated to some
Story and characters are seen as weak or forgettable compared with Hades, with average presentation of the narrative
Some players report stuttering and performance problems on PC
Weapons lean on specific relics to reach full power, and many weapons reuse the same swing animation so they feel like stat swaps
improvements: Clearer UI, status and keyword explanations and a proper retranslation of the English text
Faster or less grindy meta-progression and unlock pacing
More varied or procedural level layouts and more enemy types
Better balance so that some relics/weapons are not dependent on specific relic pairings and some builds are not broken
Stronger narrative delivery and more developed characters
Tighter dash and movement feel
unique_things: Slot-dependent relic effects: the same item behaves differently in each of the four slots and can be rearranged freely
Floating flying-sword projectiles alongside melee, with a recall mechanic
Sect and deity choices at run start that shape the build, inside a Chinese mythology / dark wuxia setting
Multiple stories (about three) with a hidden true ending that requires collecting fragments across many runs
Extremely nuanced status-effect and condition-trigger item system (poison, bleed, burn, frost) with deep stacking rules
tedious_or_disliked: Slow meta-progression and farming enemies for fragments to unlock all stories and the true ending
Early runs feel repetitive before enough content is unlocked
Nothing is explained well; players often have to play to learn what a keyword does
Fixed maps and repeated bosses get samey over a long playthrough
Completion is a long grind: unlocking everything means farming fragments across many runs, and some reviewers regret the hours sunk into 'unlock it all'
divisive_points: Hades comparison: some praise it as a top-tier roguelite, others say Hades and its sequel exist so just play those
Build depth: many praise huge variety, while critics say effects mostly boil down to more damage and do not change playstyle
Difficulty and balance: some find it hard, others find bosses and enemies trivial with a good build
Chinese voice acting and translation: some see it as flavourful, others as a barrier for English speakers
community.reception_notes: Released on Steam Jan 18, 2022 (Windows only, priced $17.99) by BadMudStudio / bilibili and never in early access. It had a strong Chinese launch and later gained an English audience; console versions (Xbox, PS, Switch) followed around Oct 2023. Post-launch content includes the free 'Shao Meng / 烬梦' DLC and the paid 'The End Of Karma' DLC. Steam-wide all-time rating stays around 93% positive, but a recent-reviews dip (about 79% on a small sample per the store page) suggests newer players are more lukewarm, mainly over translation and meta-progression. Third-party estimates (steam-revenue-calculator, Boxleiter-based, order of magnitude only) put Steam gross revenue near $30M and owners at 1-2M. Limitations of this research: the web search budget was exhausted, so no Reddit threads or major outlet reviews could be read; OpenCritic has no confirmed entry and Metacritic has only two critic reviews (no Metascore).

games.name: Wildermyth
games.short_description: Wildermyth follows heroes over their whole careers, from their pitchfork days to their powerful primes, and on into old age and memory. It’s a party-based procedural storytelling RPG where tactical combat and story decisions will alter your world and reshape your cast of characters.

commentary.summary: Wildermyth is a turn-based tactics game on a board, with Fire Emblem-style play and a heavy emphasis on story, characters and relationships. praise: Strong focus on narrative, decisions and branching scenarios
Characters you meet have relationships with your party, and you can choose whether a new character becomes a partner or best friend
Fire Emblem-like turn-based tactics on a board
Board-game-like look of 2D sprites on a 3D environment, which he finds all right

community.one_liner: A party-based tactical RPG from Worldwalker Games that procedurally stitches handcrafted story events into the lifelong tales of your heroes, who age, bond, get maimed and can return as legacy characters across campaigns.
community.consensus_summary: Wildermyth is received as a critical and player darling: Metacritic 86 from critics, Steam 'Very Positive' at about 94.6% of roughly 18k reviews, and a cluster of 90 scores from PC Gamer, IGN, Edge and Metro GameCentral (Guardian 100, Game Informer 88). It is better known as a story generator with light tactics than as a classic roguelike; Steam tags include Rogue-lite but the structure is campaign chapters plus a legacy system. Its main weakness is repetition: once a player has seen the finite pool of events and narration, the magic fades, and a minority find the prose purple or the combat shallow. Active development ended in May 2024 with the Omenroad expansion (which adds a node-map roguelike challenge mode); console ports followed in October 2024. Some long-time fans wish it were still getting content.
best_things: Heroes have real lifespans: they age, fall in love, form rivalries, get injured or transformed (lost limbs replaced by wooden or stone parts, wolf or ghost forms), retire or die, producing memorable personal stories
Handcrafted events are assembled procedurally around each character's traits and relationships, so the same scene plays differently for different casts
The legacy system lets favorite heroes return in later campaigns and build a personal pantheon
Papercraft / storybook art style and atmospheric soundtrack are widely called charming and cozy
Tactical combat is approachable but has depth: class and ability stacking, and an environment-based mystic magic system that players single out as clever
Excellent co-op (online and LAN); groups voice their characters and treat it like a tabletop RPG session
Flexible difficulty and campaign length (a run can be finished in a couple of sittings), plus an easy pick-up-and-put-down rhythm
Steam Workshop modding and a level editor; Omenroad gets praise from longtime fans for its lore-rich campaign
Top Steam reviews repeatedly call it a favorite-of-all-time for readers: the writing and quiet emotional story beats land hard (e.g. lines about never daring to write one's own stories)
worst_things: Event and narration pool is finite, so duplicates appear quickly and replay value erodes after roughly 15-20 hours for some players
Prose can feel over-flourished, metaphor-heavy and clunky; several reviewers say every character ends up sounding like the same poetic voice
Procedural events often have little lasting consequence, so choices can feel cosmetic
Combat is simple and repetitive for some, and late-chapter enemy spikes can feel unfair
Escape-the-map objectives with endless enemy spawns can be punishing depending on where the party stands when they trigger
Random dialogue between fights can feel like spam when you just want to play
Omenroad DLC sits at only 'Mostly Positive' (72% of ~170 reviews) on Steam, versus 'Very Positive' for the base game
improvements: Add many more events, dialogue variants and campaigns so repeat playthroughs stay fresh (a common wish given that active development ended in 2024)
Option to skip or reduce narration and cutscene text, or tone the prose down
Warn or confirm before clicking an empty tile or mis-targeting an attack (a mis-click complaint from a reviewer; there is also a user report that the hide-enemy-popup hides range info)
Make story choices carry more visible campaign consequences
More language support: Italian and French are repeatedly requested in Steam forum threads
Rework the campaign pressure systems, such as escalating danger and legacy points, which some players dislike
unique_things: Treats the party's entire lifespan as the core loop: youth, prime, old age, memory, then legacy, unlike most roguelikes that focus on one run
Procedural storytelling assembled from authored fragments driven by character traits and relationships
No item inventory: gear picked up stays with the hero until replaced, which speeds pacing
Environmental magic where the mystic class manipulates terrain, plants and light in battle
Story-first, low-stress roguelite structure that is closer to a tabletop RPG than an XCOM-style permadeath grind, with LAN and online co-op
Omenroad adds a node-map roguelike gauntlet mode on top of the story campaigns
tedious_or_disliked: Clicking through a large volume of dialogue and narration (one reviewer put it at around 60% of the game)
The slow campaign map where you watch time tick while tasks complete
Seeing the same events again and again after many hours
Procedurally recombined story that some players feel is an RNG remix rather than a human-written yarn, making events feel pointless
Endless-spawn escape objectives late in chapters (top negative Steam review theme)
divisive_points: Writing quality: critics and many fans call it witty and moving, while other players find it clunky and over-written
Procedural vs authored story: some find the emergent character tales magical, others feel RNG makes everything pointless
Combat depth: praised as approachable and clever, but criticised as shallow or repetitive
Replayability: hundreds of hours for some (players above 750 and 1,400 hours), a 'play for a week then leave' game for others
community.reception_notes: Early Access began Nov 14, 2019; full 1.0 release Jun 15, 2021 on Windows, macOS and Linux (Steam, GOG, Epic, itch). It drew Golden Joystick nominations (Ultimate Game of the Year, Best Indie Game, Best Storytelling) and a D.I.C.E. nomination. Metacritic lists the critic score as 86 (Steam store page also shows 86) from 23-26 critics with no negative reviews; user score of 7.5 from 117 ratings is lower than Steam sentiment, with more complaints about shallow combat and repetition. Steam's own estimate put owners at roughly 1-2 million; steam-revenue-calculator.com estimates about $19.4M gross and $5.7M net, a Boxleiter-style order-of-magnitude figure, not audited. Active development concluded May 24, 2024 with the Omenroad expansion; PlayStation, Xbox and Switch versions launched Oct 22, 2024. Price $24.99. Recent Steam reviews remain Very Positive (about 88% in a 30-day sample on the store page I read). OpenCritic score could not be retrieved: web search quota was exhausted and guessed OpenCritic IDs returned other games, so it is reported as null.

commentary.summary: Barony is a first-person, classic dungeon-crawler roguelike with many drastically different classes and a huge amount of content. He finds it deep and potentially great, especially in multiplayer, but very punishing, slow, repetitive early on and confusing for newcomers. Emergent, somewhat Dwarf Fortress-like creativity that produces surprising wins

community.one_liner: A first-person, voxel-style dungeon-crawling roguelike from Turning Wheel with 1-4 player co-op, inspired by NetHack, Ultima Underworld and Hexen-era RPGs.
community.consensus_summary: Barony is well loved by players: Steam shows Very Positive (about 90.7% of roughly 18,200 reviews) and many long-time players with hundreds of hours call it a genre standout, especially in co-op. Critic coverage is thin; OpenCritic lists only two mid-tier critic reviews (7/10 and 7.1/10, averaging 7.05, both for the Switch port) and Metacritic has no Metascore, only a small user score of 7.5 from 45 ratings. The game is still being developed a decade after launch (new DLC and a large systems overhaul), and the most recent wave of negative Steam reviews is largely about that overhaul, not the original design. Common complaints are steep, sometimes unfair difficulty (especially solo), long runs with no meta-progression, and races and classes sold as paid DLC.
best_things: Co-op is the main draw: up to 4 players (online, LAN, split screen), and the party dynamic and class mix is what the game is balanced around
Deep, interlocking NetHack-style systems (item identification, cursed gear, alchemy, skills, magic, traps) that reward accumulated knowledge across runs
High replayability from many classes, races, gear and spells, plus Steam Workshop mods and adjustable difficulty/assist options
Charming retro voxel look, humor (cream pies, chat callouts, RPG-Maker-style sound effects) and a nostalgic Hexen/Heretic feel
Runs on modest hardware, has good controller support and remapping, is DRM-free/open source and runs on Linux
Responsive developers: one reviewer says a dev personally helped fix a startup problem, and content updates have continued for about a decade
Frequent sales make it cheap; many call the base price a good value
worst_things: Brutal early game: instakill boulder traps, swarms of rats and other deaths before players understand what hit them; a steep learning curve and tutorial issues
Best enjoyed in co-op; several reviewers say solo play is very hard and some classes seem designed only for parties
Base game feels stripped: one playable race and about 13 classes, while 13 races and 8 more classes cost extra in DLC (roughly $60 total in one reviewer's math)
Runs are long (multi-hour) and a late death wastes it; no pausing to take a break in multiplayer and hunger keeps ticking
Melee combat is described by some as flat/clunky and loot as underwhelming in early floors, with repetitive locales
Multiplayer desync/lag and crashes at startup or on Steam Deck/Windows are reported by some players
The 2025-26 systems overhaul is heavily criticised by veteran players as slower and less rewarding (see reception_notes)
improvements: Add meta-progression or unlocks so long runs leave something behind; several reviewers call it an arcade score-chaser with no rewards for dying late
Make classes/races unlockable in-game or reduce DLC gating of core content; players also dislike having to beat the game with each race to mix DLC races with classes
Smooth the early game and tutorial, and telegraph hidden traps and instakill threats more fairly
Give players options to keep the pre-overhaul mechanics (lore/identify, swimming, magic progression) rather than telling them to roll back versions
Deepen and polish melee combat and skill variety; some say classes differ only by starting kit
Improve multiplayer stability and add official language support (e.g. Spanish, Russian, Portuguese)
unique_things: One of very few true first-person 3D roguelikes, and with cooperative play without forced PvP; the developer themselves said they rarely see similar games
Combines NetHack-like cryptic item knowledge and permadeath with real-time first-person Ultima Underworld-style dungeon crawling
Proximity-style chat/voice and callouts, enemy chatter and combat music act as gameplay information cues
Open source, DRM free, Linux support, with Steam Workshop mods such as hardcore overhauls
Race and class combinations (including DLC races like salamander or scion with new magic schools) change the playstyle significantly
tedious_or_disliked: Constant defensive play: peeking corners, listening for music and chatter, watching the ceiling for boulder traps
Item identification: the newer Lore skill makes players wait (reportedly minutes) to identify items, and players still have to pick everything up
Being pressured by the Minotaur timer to move faster than a careful style would like
Long, unpausable multiplayer sessions where one mistake can erase hours of progress
Grindy magic progression in the new three-school system, with reaching max in all schools called nearly impossible
Feeling of needing to min-max everything just to survive, and deaths from things you cannot know without prior knowledge
divisive_points: Difficulty: fans say every death teaches you something and it is fair, while others call it punishing in a not-fun way; 'git gud' replies are a recurring complaint from critics
The big systems overhaul and its DLC: some like parts of it, but many long-term players with hundreds of hours gave negative reviews in protest
Price and DLC value: some say it is a steal at sale price, others feel it is a lite base game needing about $60 of content
Whether it is worth playing solo at all versus strictly as a co-op game
community.reception_notes: Released June 2015 on PC (Steam, Mac, Linux; also GOG, Epic and a Switch port) by the small team Turning Wheel. It has stayed a steady seller with a loyal community; Steam Spy estimates 500k-1M owners and a revenue calculator estimates about $3.1M gross (estimates only, not audited). The game has three paid DLCs (Myths & Outcasts, Legends & Pariahs, Deserters & Disciples). Recent Steam reviews show a clear split: a large recent update reworked long-untouched systems (Lore identification, swimming removed, magic split into three schools with level-100 rewards removed, many nerfs) and veteran players wrote protest reviews, some complaining that the developers told them to roll back to an older version rather than add options. Despite this, the overall score remains Very Positive. Because the recent-review sections are based only on a handful of top helpful Steam reviews, the extent of the backlash is not fully measured. No Metascore exists; OpenCritic has only two Switch-era reviews and no aggregate number was found.

games.name: Death Must Die
games.short_description: Descend the nether in search of Death himself! Choose from God-given powers to slay his hordes of minions. Unlock new heroes, collect powerful items and create game-breaking synergies in this roguelite hack and slash survivors game.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Death Must Die is a top-down horde-survivor (Vampire Survivors-style) game that openly borrows Hades' structure, with gods offering boons and duo combinations. He considers it one of the better entries in a flood of low-quality clones. He likes the boon synergies, the explorable map and the readable art. He is let down by bloated, boring stat-stick loot, near-identical characters, and runs that repeat the same enemies and bosses. He places it in high B tier.
praise: Hades-style gods offering boons with keywords that combine, including duo boons, are unique and change how you play
Combining gods for different effects is enjoyable
Effectively infinite map with random events and upgrades rewards exploring instead of only killing for XP
Art style is simple but fits the theme, and screen clutter stays readable (e.g. big red Nova attacks are clearly visible)
Good humor and personality in character dialogue
Loot/equipment layer persisting between runs is a cool roguelite element
criticism: Most equipment is boring stat bonuses; 20+ items per run and a stash of 60 makes sorting annoying
Characters feel nearly identical (swipe vs stab vs swirl), with only one minor unique attribute each; Mage is the exception
Runs are repetitive: same enemies, waves and bosses at the same times in a roughly 20-minute run
Exploration events are hard to find and not unique enough
unique_points: Hades-like boon system grafted onto the horde-survivor formula
Exploration of a huge open level yields character upgrades, an alternative to pure grinding for XP
Loot layer with per-character equipment persisting between runs
commentary.quote: it is literally just Hades but Vampire Survivors, which is fine
design_criteria: Synergies: boon keywords and duo boons combining across gods
Level design: large explorable map with events versus minimalistic single levels
Character diversity: characters too similar mechanically
Loot/meta-progression: too much boring stat equipment
Run variety: identical enemies, waves and bosses each run
Visual readability/art: clear, fitting style amid chaos
Humor/charm: character personality and dialogue
Genre context: quality relative to many low-effort clones

community.one_liner: A pixel-art roguelite action RPG 'bullet heaven' from Realm Archive that mixes Vampire Survivors-style horde survival with Hades-style god blessings and a Diablo-style loot and talent system, in Steam Early Access since November 2023.
community.consensus_summary: Players rate it highly overall: Steam shows about 90% positive (roughly 21.8k reviews, Very Positive) at a low price (about $7), and the art, combat feel and build crafting get consistent praise. Recent sentiment is noticeably worse, because the last substantial content update (Act 3, April 2025) is more than a year old, developer communication is sparse, and the team announced a large rebuild of core systems. Many negative reviews come from players with many hours who say they enjoyed it but cannot recommend it until updates resume, while positive reviewers keep defending it as not abandoned. Professional coverage is mostly promotional or news-style (Act 3 and roadmap pieces), and no Metacritic or OpenCritic scores exist.
best_things: Polished, detailed pixel art and strong sound design, praised as remarkable for a very small team
Smooth, responsive combat ('smooth as butter'); reviewers also report it running well on low-end PCs and on Linux
Hades-style god blessings let runs snowball into distinct synergy builds (lightning storms, crit executions, etc.)
Diablo-like gear with affixes plus per-character talent trees gives a satisfying loot and build-crafting loop
Heroes play differently (Druid shapeshifting, summoner-style options), giving replay value across characters
Short, intense runs that deliver an empowered 'high-level ARPG character' feeling quickly, good for limited play time
Strong value: many reviewers report 50-150+ hours for about $7
Hub with unlockable characters, vendor and skill trees gives a sense of long-term progression
worst_things: Content drought: last big update (Act 3, The Darkmoor) came in April 2025, and content is limited to three acts/maps with repeating enemy variety
Poor and infrequent developer communication; many reviews cite six months or more of silence and abandonment fears
Missed original release window; Early Access has run since 2023 with updates taking a year or more each
Heavily RNG-dependent loot and god-blessing rolls, so runs can feel luck-gated
Balance issues: between patches dominant god combos emerge while other gods are nearly useless, and the game gets too easy after the early stages
Terrain and map problems, with reports of getting stuck on terrain while taking attacks that are hard to avoid
Some players say the game does neither survivors nor ARPG well and lacks a clear creative direction
Loss of identity: several reviewers say recent updates made it feel like 'yet another survivors-like' and forgettable, and object to the announced rebuild/about-face of the gameplay
improvements: Regular progress updates and roadmap communication (devs have said they dislike weekly posts, but fans want more than silence)
More maps, acts, enemies and unique items to reduce repetition
A talent tree preview or calculator so players can plan without paying the reset cost each time
Better in-game tutorials and clearer progression explanations, since many players rely on wikis
Loot and progression tweaks such as reroll or more deterministic options to reduce RNG frustration; balance pass on overpowered gods and builds
unique_things: Hybrid of Vampire Survivors-style auto-fire horde survival, Hades-style gods and Diablo-style gear and talent trees
Persistent hub that upgrades over time with new characters, vendor trading and skill trees
Item affix and loadout system deeper than typical survivors-likes, letting gear define the build
Olympian-style pantheon with personality-filled gods and a light, optional lore layer
Planned five-act structure, with Act 4 announced alongside a rework of core systems such as terrain generation and sprites
tedious_or_disliked: Loot-hunting for affixes can mean collecting lots of useless items, and reviewers call the RNG loot system bloated
Repetition sets in once the three acts are cleared (about 10 hours to beat the final act per one reviewer), because enemy variety does not change with difficulty
Paying a reset cost to re-spec talents after a misplaced point
Some players find a few gods' voice lines cringey
Getting stuck on terrain while being hit by attacks that are hard to avoid (one of the most upvoted negative reviews)
divisive_points: Whether the game is abandoned or just slow: positive reviewers point to blog posts and a rebuild in progress, negatives say the last year showed almost nothing
The planned rebuild toward more handmade, less procedural content: some see ambition and a fix for staleness, others see scrapping the game's identity mid Early Access
Whether it succeeds as a blend of survivors-like and ARPG, or is unfocused

community.one_liner: A top-down action roguelite by Arrowfist Games in which you play a bioengineered 'Bioshell' inside a microscopic viral world and turn enemy projectiles (and your own) back on enemies by deflecting them.
community.consensus_summary: Deflector is well liked but niche: Steam shows 87% positive (Very Positive) from roughly 355 reviews, and the few critics who covered it were positive (Keengamer 8/10, Nine Over Ten 9/10, NaviGames 9/10, GameGrin 90). Praise centres on the deflect mechanic, build variety, the soundtrack and the Hades-like visual polish. The recurring complaints are a thin story, a fairly conventional roguelite loop and a lot of systems to track. It launched in Early Access on Jan 27, 2022 and hit 1.0 on Mar 24, 2023, with Switch and Xbox ports from Sept 2023 (PS4 listed on Metacritic). Its audience is small (estimated 20k-50k owners, about $113k gross), so there is little large-scale community discussion beyond Steam.
best_things: The deflect mechanic turns bullet-hell defence into offence: bouncing projectiles back at enemies, sometimes for huge damage, feels satisfying and skill-based
Real build variety from a free-form upgrade/mutation system where skills combine (for example clones, duplicated deflected shots, ground rupture)
Multiple Bioshell characters with different weapons and deflect behaviour, from the starting boomerang-wielding Eradicator to ranged and melee options
Strong soundtrack, praised by reviewers and Steam players
Polished stylised visuals, compared favourably to Hades in early coverage
Fast runs and non-linear path choices (combat, shops, rest areas) keep the pace brisk
Runs well, including on Steam Deck, with full controller support and plenty of achievements
worst_things: Story is barebones: a cool premise in the intro with little elaboration afterwards
Core roguelite structure is seen as conventional; critics say it does not reinvent the genre beyond deflection and setting
Some players call it a clunky Hades-like without enough of its own hook
Too many systems and modifiers to keep track of for some newcomers
Environment variety was criticised in early access and choosing locations had little gameplay impact
Only the starting character is available at first, so the early hours limit playstyle choice
Metacritic user reviewers (only 7 ratings) cite repetitiveness and limited enemy variety
improvements: Flesh out the narrative and world beyond the opening (raised by early access and 1.0 reviewers and Steam players)
Make location choices matter more to gameplay, not only to level progression
Add more visual and environmental variety across worlds
Give clearer objectives and clearer explanation of the many systems and modifiers
Unlock additional Bioshells faster or more clearly so early runs have more variety
unique_things: Deflection as the core verb: you can reflect enemy projectiles and your own weapon shots back for damage
Microscopic viral setting where you play as a prototype cure, with 'Apex Virus' bosses ending each world
Pitched by the developer as Diablo meets bullet hell, blending ARPG build crafting with bullet-hell patterns
Free-form skill combination system in which upgrades stack into unexpected effects
Hub with research modules and DNA/mutation progression that persists between runs
tedious_or_disliked: Gradual unlock of Bioshells and mutations requires repeated runs before the game opens up
Keeping track of numerous upgrades, modifiers and interactions is tiring for some players
Story and objectives give little incentive to push on for players not hooked by the combat
Runs can feel repetitive with limited enemy variety (Metacritic user ratings, small sample)
divisive_points: Originality: some critics and players call it a fresh take on bullet-hell roguelites, others say it does nothing special beyond deflection
Complexity: many enjoy the deep build-crafting, while others feel overloaded by what they must track
Value: a Metacritic user complaint mentions a steep price drop shortly after launch, which soured some buyers
community.reception_notes: Metacritic has no Metascore yet (needs 4 critic reviews; GameGrin 90 and KeenGamer 80 are listed) and its user score of 4.1/10 rests on only 7 ratings, so it is not meaningful. OpenCritic lists 4 reviews but no aggregate average on the page (scored ones average about 7.6/10). Early Access coverage from But Why Tho and Rock Paper Shotgun was unscored and positive about the mechanic and visuals. 1.0 launched Mar 24, 2023 on Steam ($19.99, Windows only), followed by Switch and Xbox in Sept 2023. Steam review volume is low and recent reviews are still positive; SteamSpy-style estimates put owners at 20k-50k and gross revenue at about $113k (Boxleiter-based estimate, order of magnitude only). community.one_liner: A pixel-art roguelite auto-battler by Konfa Games (tinyBuild) where you recruit and equip an army of up to 49 puny humans, march through procedural dungeons managing food and shops, then test your build against other players' teams asynchronously.
community.consensus_summary: Players rate it Very Positive on Steam (about 84% of roughly 3,360 reviews), and critics are lukewarm-positive (Metacritic 73 from only 4 reviews, OpenCritic 73 with 55% recommending). The core loop of drafting weird synergies, min-maxing and watching tiny units fight is widely called addictive and charming. The recurring complaint is that it is shallow and short: once you have won a run there is little reason to continue beyond PvP leaderboards and mutation grinding. Many reviewers say it is worth buying only on sale. It launched in Early Access in 2021 and went to 1.0 on Sept 29, 2022 on PC and consoles; it still receives player discussion and some seasonal content as of late 2026, but this is a finished game, not abandoned.
best_things: Gorgeous, detailed pixel art and weapon animations, plus a well-liked soundtrack
Addictive core loop: drafting classes and weapon synergies and trying a different build after each failed run
Asynchronous PvP (fighting ghosts of other players' builds, leaderboards, King of the Hill/Brawl modes) is the most-loved part for many
Dark, cheerful-cruelty humor and pop-culture references in the writing and unit designs
Accessible and streamlined: easy to pick up, hands-off battles are quick to read, runs are short
Progression unlocks give new options rather than raw power, so you can still lose to your own bad decisions
Food-meter mechanic stops aimless wandering and limits army size in an interesting way
Good value when bought on sale; several reviewers say they got their money's worth (e.g. 41 hours in)
worst_things: Little replayability after the first victory; many players feel the game ends too early and call it a long demo
Shallow strategic depth and one-note items/classes; PvE gets boring quickly
PvP is dominated by a few meta builds and RNG rolls, and PvP balance concerns spill into PvE
Levels and biomes feel samey; minimap icons and some rules (magic damage) are confusing
Heavy RNG and sudden difficulty spikes in later floors, including shop availability that can leave you unable to refill ranks
Mutation/achievement completion becomes a grind
Bugs reported in places (loading-circle bug in Brawl runs, mantrap enemies seen as unfairly tanky)
Many reviewers will not recommend it at the $19.99 full price: 'wait for a sale', and one calls it a very long demo
improvements: More content and variety in biomes, enemies, classes and items to extend replay value after the first win
Better PvP balance and anti-meta measures so non-meta builds can compete
Fairer, more reliable shop/market access so runs are less RNG-gated
Clearer tutorialisation and UI (mutation reminders, minimap icons, magic damage explanation)
Make it more of a true roguelite with lasting meta-progression rather than a one-win-then-PvP structure
Bigger, more explosive death feedback so losses register (early reviewer suggestion)
unique_things: Roguelike dungeon crawl combined with auto-battler army building at up to 49 units, rather than a small party
Food meter as a run-length and army-size constraint
Asynchronous PvP where your winning run becomes a ghost team for others, with a leaderboard
Class synergy by equipping a number of unique items from the same class, unlocking powerful abilities
Part of the Despot universe (Despotism 3k, Slime 3K) with a shared puny-humans pixel-art style and dystopian dark comedy
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding all mutations and achievements (one 79-hour reviewer enjoyed the first 20-30 hours, then found it a slog)
Replaying runs until RNG hands you the meta build for PvP
Early PvE repeated across runs feels brain-dead or easy once solved
Hands-off combat leaves some players feeling it is fun to watch rather than play
Late-floor traps/bosses such as mantraps and repeated first-biome bosses that can wipe high-XP units
divisive_points: Value: many call it great on sale and a ripoff at full price
Hands-off auto-battle: some love the streamlined fights, others want more control or interaction
PvP emphasis: loved as the endgame by some, called pointless (bragging rights only) or meta-driven by others
Roguelike vs roguelite identity: some wish it were more of a roguelite with persistent progression
community.reception_notes: Launched in Early Access in 2021 (reviewers then already found it essentially complete) and released 1.0 on Sept 29, 2022 on PC, PS4/5, Xbox and Switch. Critics praised art, writing and gameplay loop but noted difficulty pacing and randomness; Switch controls were called lackluster versus PC. Metacritic has very few reviews (4 critics, 13 users), so scores are low-confidence. Steam rating stays Very Positive years later. One angry reviewer wants developer attention on Slime 3K instead of seasonal updates (single review, not a trend). OpenCritic lists 11 critic reviews. tinyBuild acquired Konfa during development. community.one_liner: A dice-driven roguelike deckbuilder by Terry Cavanagh in which you play a living die in Lady Luck's game show, fighting through dungeons with equipment you slot dice into.
community.consensus_summary: Critics received it warmly (Metacritic 80, OpenCritic about 82 with roughly 88% recommending), and Steam sits at Very Positive (about 89% of 11.9k reviews). The praise centres on the six characters that each rewrite the rules, the puzzle-like turns, the art and Chipzel's soundtrack. The recurring complaint is luck: players on harder episodes feel the dice decide the outcome and that the enemy gets the exact rolls it needs. The Metacritic user score is only 7.3 (Mixed, 106 ratings), and the many negative Steam reviews cite short runs and little meta-progression or build variety. It is a finished, fully released game with free DLC (Halloween Special, then Reunion in July 2022) and ports to consoles and mobile.
best_things: Each of the six characters (Warrior, Thief, Robot, Inventor, Witch, Jester) has its own rule set, so every character feels like a different game rather than a stat reskin
Every turn works like a small puzzle: you assign rolled dice to gear, and critics say losses usually felt traceable to your own choices (Destructoid's reviewer)
Charming art, funny game-show framing with Lady Luck, and a bouncy soundtrack
Chipzel's chiptune soundtrack is praised in critic and Steam reviews
Short runs suit play in bursts, and the game is easy to learn but hard to master
Large amount of content: per-character episodes with stacking handicap modes, plus the free Halloween Special and Reunion episodes
Difficulty options and a relaxed pace make it approachable; Steam reviewers report 100+ hours and replaying after finishing
No grindy meta-progression: some players count this as a strength, since skill and decisions are what improve
worst_things: RNG dominates at higher difficulty; many reviewers feel enemies roll exactly what they need while they fall one point short
Some characters and episodes (Robot, Thief, Witch episodes are named on Steam forums) are seen as near-impossible without a long lucky streak
Enemy statuses such as freeze, curse, blind and lock can wipe out a whole turn, and several reviews call freeze too strong
Armor is weak because it expires after your turn, and healing cards are said to be poor value
Low build variance: reviewers say most characters' runs feel alike, with few items that reshape a strategy
Gimmick rules of some episodes are not explained up front and have to be discovered by losing
Critics such as USgamer felt the game does not expand enough on its early hours, and some said runs get short and repetitive
Some find the $14.99 price high for what they consider a shallow roguelike
Top-upvoted negative review (42 votes) says lack of meta-progression makes the game feel hollow over time
improvements: Add meta-progression or longer-term structure, which is the top complaint from veteran deckbuilder players
Add more build options, events or relics, since upgrades are limited to learning a skill and upgrading it once
Give players more ways to mitigate RNG so bad rolls can still be turned around
Rebalance freeze, healing and armor, and episodes with punishing handicaps
Explain each character's special mechanic in-game instead of leaving it to trial and error
Community mods that cut enemy HP by about 25% and buff defences are cited as a fix for balance
unique_things: Dice are the core resource: you slot rolled dice into equipment with conditions (for example 'needs 4 or under' or 'needs an even number')
Each character is effectively its own rule set, for example the Witch's four slots with six spells and the Robot's cap on total dice value
Stealing enemy equipment is possible as the Thief
A rigged-game-show premise makes the unfair dice a deliberate theme
Structured as episodes per character with handicap-stacked replays rather than one open-ended run
Made by Terry Cavanagh of VVVVVV and Super Hexagon, with a soundtrack by Chipzel
tedious_or_disliked: Dying repeatedly to bad rolls on the same episode, with reports of ten losses in a row as Witch
Replays after the base difficulty force you to play under debuffs that feel like random punishment
Repetitive enemy attacks and sticking to the same strategy once you have seen all characters
Top-reviewed negative theme: after the first few characters runs feel repetitive, with the same enemy attacks and the same strategy (several upvoted reviews)
The 'Loud Bird' complaint: players feel the enemy's dice streaks are unfair, with enemies hitting 70%+ odds over and over
divisive_points: Skill versus luck: fans say you can manipulate dice and plan around variance, detractors say the game is about waiting to get lucky
Lack of meta-progression is praised by some and is the main reason others quit
Unfairness is thematic (a rigged game show) for some critics but feels cheap to some players
Whether the game suits veterans: some call it a great on-ramp for newcomers to roguelikes, others find it too simple
community.reception_notes: Released Aug 13, 2019 on PC (Steam, itch), then Switch and Xbox, with iOS/Android arriving alongside the free Reunion DLC on July 7, 2022. Launch reviews were strong, with OpenCritic placing it in roughly the 89th percentile. Halloween Special and Reunion added substantial free episodes, and Reunion reworked the identity of each character. Steam estimates: 200k-500k owners (SteamSpy) and about $5.4M gross / $1.6M net revenue (steam-revenue-calculator, an order-of-magnitude Boxleiter estimate, not audited). Recent Steam reviews show the same split as at launch: praise for content and charm, negatives about luck and lack of meta-progression. No major controversies or abandonment.

community.one_liner: A Hades-style isometric action roguelite from Afterburner Studios in which you play Cassidy, alternating between building relationships in the waking city of Redhaven and fighting nightmares in procedurally generated dream dungeons, with a story centred on anxiety, isolation, grief and loss.
community.consensus_summary: Dreamscaper is well liked by both critics and players, with a Metacritic critic score in the low 80s (80 listed on Steam for PC, 82 on the Switch Metacritic page, 12 reviews, 92% positive) and a Steam rating of Very Positive (about 88% of roughly 3,200 reviews). The praise clusters around the acrobatic dodge-heavy combat, the build variety, the painterly dream visuals, the soundtrack, and an emotionally sincere mental-health story. The recurring reservations are the daytime overworld (dialogue, crafting and gifting felt like padding to many), combat balance and clarity, and a rough start for new players. Metacritic user score is noticeably lower (6.8 from only 28 ratings), which reflects a small, more divided sample. The game went through Early Access before its 1.0 release on 5 Aug 2021 and players mention later patches (such as 1.1) that nerfed overpowered leech effects; there is no sign it was abandoned. Steam lists it as Windows-only, with console versions covered by the Switch critic reviews.
best_things: Fluid, dodge-centred melee combat with weighty acrobatic moves; critics called it fun and rewarding
Large amount of build variety from weapons, dodges, shields, elemental affinities and artifacts, so runs feel different (players mention fire/lightning/water combos such as extinguish crits)
Emotionally sincere story about anxiety, grief and loss; several reviewers (including But Why Tho) called the mental-health focus well done and powerful
Striking painterly, surreal dream-world art and atmosphere
Soundtrack widely praised as atmospheric and non-repetitive over long sessions
The day/night structure ties narrative to mechanics, with relationships unlocking permanent upgrades (critics cited the synergy of story and roguelike loop)
Good pick-up-and-play pacing: players like being able to do a floor and save after bosses, and a difficulty ramp that can be raised after the first clears
Calmer, cosier alternative to Hades for people who want a lower-pressure action roguelite
worst_things: The waking overworld is the most criticised part: NPC dialogue felt slow, cringey or skippable to many players, and some called the dialogue the weakest element
Combat balance: life-leech / heal-on-hit effects are regarded as far stronger than other stats even after a nerf, and some weapons and moves feel clearly worse than others
Some players find movement and combat clunky or slow, with attacks lacking punch compared with Hades
Visual clarity problems: busy effects and sparkles make it hard to tell important items or telegraphs from decoration
Enemy variety wears thin over long playtimes (one 60+ hour reviewer called enemies samey)
Story and characters outside the core emotional themes were called simple or forgettable by some players
Confusing onboarding: several negative reviews say the tutorial bombards you with controls and mechanics and leaves you without direction
improvements: Better onboarding and tutorial: negative reviewers describe being overloaded with controls and mechanics early and not being told about dodge and mana
Clearer in-game guidance or map for the overworld, since some players report getting stuck with no direction
Rebalance leech and other dominant stats and underperforming weapons and moves to make more builds viable
Improve combat feedback and readability (punchier hits, clearer audio and visual telegraphs)
Make the overworld relationship and crafting systems less padded or more optional/skippable, and tighten the writing
Smooth the early difficulty curve
unique_things: Day/night loop: daytime social exploration of Redhaven and nighttime dream dungeons feed each other, with relationships giving permanent power
Direct, personal treatment of mental health (anxiety, isolation, grief) that is rare in action roguelites
Bosses are embodiments of emotions such as Isolation, Fear and Loss
Lucid powers that let you manipulate the environment and surreal artifacts in the dream levels
Nintendo Life summed it up as lacking originality in genre terms but making up for it in heart
tedious_or_disliked: Overworld conversations and gifting/relationship chores that many players skip without feeling guilt
Crafting described as pointless by a 100%-completion reviewer
Grinding weapons up and hunting for completion, which some enjoy but others find repetitive (the same player enjoyed the weapon grind but not the rest)
Dungeon layouts and encounters repeating immediately after a failed run, cited by a new player as frustrating
Early difficulty spikes and being thrown out after a scripted first boss loss for unprepared newcomers
Sluggish movement and slower pacing compared with Hades-style peers
The grind: a positive reviewer calls it insane, and a negative one dislikes that run unlocks and purchases vanish when a run ends
divisive_points: Story and mental-health themes: some players say it pulled them through hard times and is among their favourites, while others find it depressing, shallow or heavy-handed
Combat feel: praised as smooth and weighty by critics, called clunky or slow by some Steam reviewers
Comparison with Hades: some call it a relaxing Hades-like, others say it is not like Hades at all and does not hold up to it
Controls: at least one PC reviewer felt it was designed for controller and played poorly with mouse and keyboard (Steam lists full controller support)
community.reception_notes: Launched into Early Access before the full 1.0 release on 5 Aug 2021 on Steam (price $24.99, developer Afterburner Studios, publishers indie.io and Maple Whispering Limited). A long-time Steam reviewer who followed Early Access mentions that patch 1.1 prompted them to restart, and another notes a recent nerf to leech effects, so post-release balance support is visible. Critics scoring the Switch version were 92% positive with no negative reviews; Nintendo Life's take was that it deserves more attention than it received, hinting at a modest commercial profile. The Metacritic PC score (80) and Switch page (82) differ slightly; the critic sample is small (12). I could not retrieve an OpenCritic score, and revenue and owner figures are third-party estimates, not audited numbers. Steam is Windows-only with Steam Cloud and full controller support. Note that Steam shows a 2020 to 2021 span because of the Early Access period.

games.name: God Of Weapons
games.short_description: Embark on a thrilling journey in God of Weapons, an action roguelike where you must ascend the tower of Zhor to reclaim the last light for the world. To survive the monster onslaught on each tower's level, you'll need to obtain and carefully organize weapons and accessories in your inventory.

placements.verbal_evidence: "this is one of the better ones so I'm going to put it probably right under Death Must Die" (implied A; no letter stated in this segment)

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: God of Weapons is a single-level horde/bullet-heaven game that adds a shop and inventory-management layer between rounds, where item placement changes what items do. He likes how well the inventory system fits the bullet-heaven gameplay and the variety of builds. His main complaint is that a huge amount of content is locked behind slow meta-progression that competes with character power upgrades. Once things are unlocked he finds it very replayable and satisfying. He ranks it among the better games of its kind, placing it just under Death Must Die.
praise: Combines bullet-heaven with inventory-management, a pairing that fits well
Item placement in the inventory changes what items do, which is fun
Many different builds are possible
Great replayability once enough characters and items are unlocked
Full of content, with hundreds of unlockable items
Very satisfying when unlocks come quickly
criticism: Massive amount of content locked behind meta-progression
First few runs feel repetitive because the same items show up every time
Unlocking items takes too long
Unlock currency is the same one needed to upgrade the character, forcing a choice between being stronger and unlocking variety
Takes a long time before the game gets interesting
unique_points: Merges vampire-survivors-style bullet heaven with backpack-style inventory management in the shop between rounds
Item positioning in the inventory affects item behavior, giving build depth
Design lesson: separate character power upgrades from content unlocks, possibly with a second currency despite his usual dislike of multiple currencies
commentary.quote: this is one of the better ones so I'm going to put it probably right under Death Must Die
design_criteria: Uniqueness within the crowded horde-survivor genre: needs a hook to stand apart
Inventory-management synergy: placement-based item effects fit the gameplay
Build diversity: many different builds available
Meta-progression: content locked behind too much grind and shared currency with power upgrades
Replayability: great once content is unlocked
Early-run variety: repetitive items in the first runs hurt first impressions
Pacing of unlocks: takes too long to become interesting

community.one_liner: An isometric bullet-heaven / survivors-like action roguelite by Imagine Games where weapons auto-attack and you build by fitting shaped weapons and accessories into a limited grid backpack between waves while climbing the tower of Zhor.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate it Very Positive (about 84 percent positive across roughly 5,250 reviews in the local Steam data), and the common verdict is a cheap, addictive Brotato-meets-Backpack-Battles hybrid whose inventory puzzle carries it. Critics are fewer and more split: Metacritic shows a 74 Metascore from just 4 Xbox Series X reviews (ranging 60 to 90) and a 5.1 user score from 7 ratings. The praise is for the inventory twist, class variety and value; the complaints are repetitive arenas, weak balance, poor readability and clunky UI and controller support. It is not abandoned: a large free update plus the Eternal Nightmare DLC shipped in May 2025, Xbox arrived in June 2025 (PS5 announced), and 1.5.x patches continued through mid 2025, with recent Steam reviews still positive.
best_things: The grid-inventory puzzle (rotate and place weapons, gems and accessories, adjacency bonuses) is the standout hook and is often described as more important than the combat itself
Low price and high value: many reviewers say it is easily worth around 6 dollars, and several 100-plus-hour players say it has held up
Wide roster: around 8-10 classes with 3 subclasses each, and 250-plus items, giving build variety and lots of unlocks/achievements to chase
Dodge/dash movement gives more skill expression than Vampire Survivors-style games, and it is easy to learn and addictive in 30-60 minute sessions
Being able to swap gear mid-run softens bad RNG compared with other survivors-likes
Satisfying audio/visual feedback once a synergistic build comes online; reviewers also praise character designs and the soundtrack
Post-launch support: auto-save/resume, Endless Mode, Favour/Banish system, training dummy, extra enemies, bosses and weapons were added in free updates
worst_things: Maps and runs feel monotonous: small, samey arenas with little to do beyond core combat, and uninteresting bosses
Readability is poor: dark, muddy brown/grey palette, enemies and projectiles blend into the map, and screens get cluttered with swarms; some players report getting stuck on unseen obstacles

Balance is uneven: a few dominant builds (lifesteal, lightning staff, stand-still reroll strategies) trivialise the game while most items, classes and melee weapons feel ignorable; difficulty tiers barely change the experience for some
UI and inventory handling is clunky: sell/use/combine buttons sit close together with no undo, combining cost is revealed late, limited put-aside slots, dragging restrictions, and lingering screens
Controller support is widely reported as incomplete or broken despite the store claiming full support (fixed dash/aim bindings, cannot preview shop items with a pad)
Bugs: crashes, UI freezes when using upgrade items, bugged achievements that some players say were unfixed for years
Thin meta-progression and little story or world-building, so there is not much reason to stay invested outside of runs
Hitbox and camera angle complaints: weapons (especially melee) miss, and enemies are hard to judge positionally
Pre-run character select / walk-around hub and general menus are called clunky and poorly designed by several negative reviewers
improvements: Fundamental rebalancing of items, classes and weapons rather than more content, so more than a handful of builds are viable
Better onboarding: tutorials and explanations for inventory rules, weapon placement restrictions and currencies (Tech-Gaming scored accessibility lowest for this)
Improve visual clarity with a brighter palette, stronger enemy/projectile contrast and a bigger roll-ready indicator
Inventory QoL: undo for accidental sells, drag-and-drop over items, more stash slots, combine-cost preview, clearer selection state
Proper controller support with rebinding and full shop/inventory navigation
More varied stage layouts and more distinct classes; deeper, more imaginative item interactions than simple adjacency bonuses; stackable/upgradable duplicates were also asked for
unique_things: Combines a survivors-like/bullet heaven loop with a Resident Evil or Backpack Battles style tetromino grid inventory where placement drives stats
Isometric action roguelike with an active dodge/dash rather than purely static movement
Run-specific risk/reward modifiers: e.g. more XP but tougher enemies, or extra inventory slots at the cost of elite spawns
Subclass system (ten classes, three variants each) plus gems, anvil upgrades, weapon combining and, in the DLC, summon item types and an Infinity Mode
A large item pool (250-plus) with a Favour/Banish system to steer drops
tedious_or_disliked: Spending long stretches optimising the grid for marginal gains, then dying quickly; reviewers joke the game is 95 percent shop menu
RNG-heavy item offers with few banishes (5 per run) and a currency for tweaking odds that is only reliably farmed on the top difficulties
Long runs and repetitive single-room arenas; several players felt they had seen everything in around 2 hours
Late-game degenerates into an idle loop of standing still and rerolling the shop for known strong items
Achievement completion needs the paid DLC and some achievements are bugged, which frustrates completionists
Multiple clicks and fiddly menu steps to move, sell or upgrade items, plus easy misclicks
divisive_points: Inventory management is either the best part or the most tiresome part; engagement with it decides whether people like the game
Class distinctiveness: some find each class plays in its own enjoyable way, others say classes and gameplay blend together
Difficulty: some runs are frustratingly hard at first and then game-breakingly easy, while high difficulty tiers are praised by a few as the real challenge
The DLC is seen by some as adding good value and new systems, by others as unneeded complexity
community.reception_notes: Launched on PC Sep 12, 2023 at a low price (about 5.99 USD currently) and built a steady audience; SteamSpy-style data estimates 200k-500k owners and a peak around 300 concurrent players at the time of capture. Steam lists no Metacritic score; the Metacritic page exists only for the Xbox Series X version (4 critic reviews, 7 user ratings, so very low sample size). No OpenCritic entry was found. The free May 11, 2025 update added auto-save, Favour/Banish, Endless Mode, a training dummy, and status-effect redesign, and the paid Eternal Nightmare DLC (new character, mechanics, weapons, Infinity Mode) released the same day. Xbox release came Jun 12, 2025 with PS5 announced. Patches 1.5.62 to 1.5.65 (May-Jun 2025) fixed controller dashing, FPS cap, freezing, Steam Deck and ultrawide issues and added quick-sell. Steam thread lists still show controller, inventory-lock and achievement bugs, and a locked God of Weapons 2 discussion. Note: my web search budget was exhausted, so community coverage relies on the Steam review file, Steam community pages and critic reviews rather than Reddit (Reddit fetch is blocked).

games.name: Goobies
games.short_description: Battle thousands of blobs in this roguelike auto-shooter. Travel from island to island, defeat bosses, collect and upgrade items to become more powerful and discover lag-inducing combos in an endless blobbath.

other_scores.score: Very Positive, about 90.9% positive of 1,962 reviews
About $190.5k gross, about $56.2k net developer revenue

placements.verbal_evidence: none

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Goobies is a top-down, single-level horde roguelite that embraces chaos and does not care about balance or taking itself seriously. He finds it satisfying to become absurdly overpowered and break the game, and he was briefly addicted while pushing it. The appeal fades after a few runs once you know how to break it. He first considered C tier but, having had a blast, moved it higher and calls it a guilty pleasure that is cheap and worth grabbing if you like breaking games. He never states the final tier letter aloud.
praise: Satisfying power fantasy of becoming completely overpowered and broken
Chaotic, fun, explosion-filled gameplay that does not take itself seriously
Level-up stat wheel gives wildly random boosts (5% vs 50% crit damage)
Different game modes and several characters that play a little differently
Hub world meta-progression points that let you max stats once you learn to break it
Cute, charismatic main character and very cheap price
criticism: Deliberately unbalanced, with no real care for balance
Abilities are fun but somewhat forgettable
Once you learn to break it, it is easy and you are done after a few runs
Visual mess, such as the screen filling with a single colour from massive explosions
Not very minimalistic or deep; a basic game overall
unique_points: Embraces being broken as a core design choice, focusing on player power fantasy over balance
Random stat wheel with huge variance between outcomes
Breaking the game quickly unlocks full meta-upgrade maxing in about three or four runs
commentary.quote: It's kind of like a guilty pleasure
design_criteria: Balance: intentionally ignored in favour of fun
Power fantasy: the joy of becoming overpowered
Randomness: stat wheel with extreme variance
Replayability: fun fades after a few runs once broken
Meta-progression: hub points that are quickly maxed
Charm: cute, charismatic characters
Variety: several game modes and characters
Value: very cheap price
commentary.rerank_note: Considered placing it in C tier, then decided to put it higher after enjoying it; placed as a guilty pleasure. Letter not stated.

community.one_liner: A cheap 3D-rendered, top-down roguelike auto-shooter (bullet-heaven/survivor-like) where you kite thousands of goofy blobs across islands, beat bosses and stack item and weapon synergies, from solo Swedish studio Hoganas Spel.
community.consensus_summary: Goobies is Very Positive on Steam (about 91% of roughly 1,960 reviews, 1,868 counted on the store page) and sells for about $6, so most players treat it as a charming, cheap, easy-to-pick-up survivor-like. The praise centres on the bubbly art style, build combos and quick runs. The criticism is slow progression, repetitive enemies and maps, balance that breaks once everything is unlocked, severe late-game lag and clutter, and cloud/save problems. It has no Metacritic critic coverage and no confirmed OpenCritic coverage, so reception is almost entirely player-driven. The developer shipped patches from 1.0.6 (Aug 2023) to 1.1.3 (Jan 2024), plus a small artifact tweak in Oct 2025, then announced development was on hold to focus on the sequel. Recent negative reviews complain of no content updates, and Goobies 2 (third-person co-op, demo out, 2026 release) is the successor.
best_things: Cute, goofy, bubbly blob visuals and humorous character names give it a distinctive charm; even negative reviewers call the look its strongest part
Simple to start and easy to begin or abandon a run, which suits short sessions and casual players
Item and weapon synergies, including 'lag-inducing' combos, and weapon upgrades that evolve into stronger versions with added traits rather than plain stat boosts
Satisfying power fantasy of mowing through swarms of thousands of blobs; described as addictive and mindless in a good way
Five champions with different passives, 30+ items and 20 artifacts give a fair amount of build variety for the price
Developer was praised in Steam reviews for quickly implementing player suggestions (leaderboards, rerolls, boss mutations)
Low price (about $6) and low barrier; one reviewer suggests it is a gentle, non-violent way to introduce kids to the genre
worst_things: Severe late-game performance problems: FPS drops, lag that can crash the engine, and lag from large numbers of XP pickups
Visual clutter in mid and late game makes threats hard to read ('I can't see anything')
Repetitive content: basic maps, low enemy and boss variety, and runs feel same-y after a few hours
Balance issues: with everything unlocked from the start and no real stacking limits, builds converge and runs feel too easy or dull; some also call RNG harsh
Cloud save handling is a recurring complaint; some players report save resets or wiped progress after touching save settings
Bugs: Queen units spawning inside terrain and becoming invincible, a controller menu selection bug, and swarm spawns landing on the player
Development has been paused, with no major content updates in a long time
improvements: Fix late-game optimization and lag from pickups and enemy counts
Add more content: enemy and boss variety, maps, and a real objective or ending for runs, since runs are endless
Rework balance and add limits or unlock gating so builds stay varied and challenge holds up
Improve readability: transparent projectiles, fewer cluttering effects, and options to reduce screen shake or protagonist motion
Make cloud saves work reliably and expose clear save management
Quality-of-life and feature requests from reviews: multiplayer, better mouse and dual-monitor handling, and better keyboard control for some characters
unique_things: Soft, inky, non-violent blob aesthetic in 3D with a bouncy momentum-based player character, unlike gritty Vampire Survivors clones
Island-to-island structure with discrete levels and a boss at each island, instead of one continuous timer
Weapons evolve into stronger variants with added traits rather than just stat upgrades
Boss mutations that accumulate over time, a daily leaderboard and a 'Mega Crit' mechanic (added in patches)
Item and roulette rerolls (one per island) plus artifacts that change core mechanics
Sequel Goobies 2 adds third-person camera, co-op, genetic mutations and Omens, showing the series moving beyond top-down
tedious_or_disliked: Slow levelling: around level 40 players report roughly one level-up per world or boss
Steep meta-progression grind that feels unrewarding for the hours invested
Kiting blobs in circles and dodging AOEs against a limited roster of enemies feels repetitive
Endless runs with no satisfying conclusion; the only real goal is Steam achievements
Late-game lag and screen clutter turn the endgame into a chore
Motion sickness from the bouncing or wobbling protagonist movement around screen centre, reported by at least one reviewer
divisive_points: Simplicity: praised as approachable and kid-friendly, but others find the strategy too shallow and boring
Difficulty and balance: some love the broken combos, others say everything unlocked from the start makes runs trivial and samey
Momentum-based player movement feels charming to some and awkward or nauseating to others
Value: at about $6 many call it a bargain, while some say it does not respect your time and recommend other genre entries
community.reception_notes: Released July 14, 2023 on Windows only (no Mac/Linux) at about $5.99. Early patches added cloud saves (1.0.6, Aug 2023), daily leaderboard and Mega Crit (1.0.7), boss mutations and rerolls (1.1.0), Queen nerfs (1.1.1, 1.1.2), and Chinese/Russian localization, autosave cycling and save-loss fixes (1.1.3, Jan 2024). An Oct 2025 tweak made the Abnormal Autopsy artifact easier to unlock. A pinned developer post says development is on hold, and players ask whether the game is dead. Despite that, recent negative reviews in 2025 to 2026 still complain about cloud saves and lost progress, so those issues persisted or recurred. Metacritic has a page with no critic score and only 3 user ratings (below the 4-rating threshold, so no user score shown), and OpenCritic coverage could not be confirmed. My WebSearch budget was exhausted, so no press reviews or Reddit threads were read; the picture rests on Steam data, store and community pages, and sampled Steam reviews. The top helpful positive review sample was empty in the local file, so praise comes from the Steam community top-rated page summary and the store page.
