games.name: Necrosmith
games.short_description: A necromancer simulator. Assemble the dead using different body parts while upgrading your tower, combine the abilities of the different fantastic races to fight your way through the hordes of enemies and overrun the ’chosen ones’. To tell the truth, the dead are pretty, uhm, dumb.

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put this as a a mid beat Tier this was a pretty enjoyable game all things considered

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Necrosmith is a base-builder where you assemble undead monsters from collected parts and send them out to fight and gather more parts. The world expands as your monsters grow stronger, unlocking new biomes and base additions. He found it immersive and fun to explore, almost a guilty pleasure. The AI is poor, it gets repetitive, and it plays more like a campaign than a roguelite. He places it in a middling tier, which he calls mid B.
praise: Immersive look and feel
World seems to expand endlessly as monsters get stronger, unlocking new biomes
Satisfying to build monsters from parts and see their different abilities
Strong sense of adventure and exploration
Permanent upgrades between runs let you expand faster and go further
criticism: Monster AI is miserable and follows few commands well
Units wander into enemy armies and die with no explanation or way to track them
Very little control over what happens
Gets repetitive and boring after a while
Once all biomes and monsters are seen there is little left; feels like a campaign rather than a roguelite with new builds
unique_points: Genre-blending: base-building with a monster-crafting army, loosely like a very basic Starcraft
Roguelite meta-progression is framed as exploration and world expansion rather than build variety
commentary.quote: it almost feels like a guilty pleasure where I really did love exploring the world
design_criteria: Immersion and world feel: expanding world and look made it engaging
Meta-progression: permanent abilities and hub upgrades let runs go further
AI and player control: poor unit AI and limited commands hurt it
Repetition and replayability: repetitive, campaign-like, limited build variety
Exploration and discovery: new biomes, monsters and parts drive motivation

community.one_liner: A pixel-art necromancer tower-defense/action roguelite by Alawar where you stitch together undead minions from body parts, send them out to destroy enemy lairs, and upgrade your tower to escape.
community.consensus_summary: Necrosmith is a cheap (about $3) cult-ish indie that Steam players rate Very Positive (about 86% of roughly 5.4k reviews in the local Steam data), with the body-part monster-crafting hook as the near-universal draw. The main complaint is that once you build your army you have very little control: minion AI is weak, you can only directly steer one unit at a time, and the game leans on grind and difficulty spikes. Critics barely covered it: Metacritic has no critic score and only a 7.5 user score from 4 ratings, and no OpenCritic entry could be found. The Steam store page shows recent reviews slipping to Mostly Positive (about 76% on a small sample), and some recent negatives say it has not been updated in years, while a sequel, Necrosmith 2, exists and several reviewers say it fixes the first game's control problems. It is a full release (not early access).
best_things: The body-part assembly system: mixing limbs, cores and weapons into odd creatures (skeleton chickens with lasers, vampires, robots, dragons) is called addictive and funny
Recipe discovery: valid combos are saved to a book, get cheaper in mana and gain bonus stats, and can be summoned with one click
Sense of progression and learning across runs; the game speeds up and gets fun after some early upgrades
Pixel-art style, dark humor and personality; compared by reviewers to Vampire Survivors and old Flash games
Very cheap; reviewers say it is worth a few dollars, with roughly 10-30+ hours of play reported
Large variety of unit types to build, which reviewers applaud
Good for casual, low-stress 'throw parts together and see what happens' sessions
worst_things: Minion AI is poor: units wander out of the base area, into dangerous biomes, and fail to defend the tower
Direct control is limited: only one creature at a time via WASD, and the control spell reportedly lasts only a few seconds before the camera snaps back with very sensitive scrolling
Late-game balance: enemy lairs spawn swarms far stronger than your units, and the 15-minion cap makes that hard to overcome
Boss/timer pressure combined with meta progression that is weak early and then near-mandatory (e.g. daily starting parts upgrade), so runs can feel walled
Permanent upgrades can make completing the game harder according to one reviewer, and one says it takes at least 3 runs for a single upgrade
Limited replayability and depth: short, no story, strategy reduces to picking which units to keep and casting spells
Some players report launch crashes or black screens on old installs, and the map is not very interactive
improvements: Better AI and stronger tactical commands (defend area, ranged units keep distance, hold position without being defenseless)
Make the 'control minion' effect last until cancelled, or allow finer control of more than one unit
Auto-craft specific units when parts are available and auto-sell surplus parts for mana
Rebalance late-game enemy lair spawns and the 15-unit cap, and smooth the jump in meta-upgrade value
More interactivity and variety in the map and more content/replay value
Clearer guidance on recipe discovery (a Steam thread asks how to intuit recipes)
unique_things: Necromancer workshop fantasy: you build the army from harvested body parts rather than picking premade units
Hybrid of tower defense, action roguelite, light strategy and factory/automation management
Tower upgrades (assembly line, cat house, blueprints) are gathered by destroying enemy lairs, with the goal of building an escape from the world
Recipe book that unlocks cheaper, stronger versions of discovered combos
tedious_or_disliked: Slow, grindy start before upgrades make the game 'even out'
Micromanaging minions or spamming the control spell because the AI cannot be trusted
Heavy RNG on parts and repetitive late-game loops
Needing several runs per meta upgrade
Some players say they do not understand how to win, and a few threads ask whether micromanagement is required
divisive_points: Short length and low replayability: some call it fine value for $3, others call it too thin
Meta progression: some find it a satisfying ramp, others say it swings from tangible to mandatory and can wreck a save
Unit AI and autonomy: some enjoy the hands-off chaos, many consider it the main flaw
Versus Necrosmith 2: several reviewers say the sequel is strictly better, while a few say the first is more forgiving than later entries
community.reception_notes: Released July 13, 2022 on Windows only by Alawar (developer and publisher), priced at $2.99 with frequent deep discounts; it is a full release, not early access. games.name: Nova Drift

commentary.summary: Nova Drift is a space shooter where you pilot a ship, move and shoot, and constantly pick up upgrades. The basic controls are simple but feel very satisfying. Abilities and upgrades arrive constantly, with frequent level-ups offering many options
Choosing weapon and core mechanics at the start acts like picking a different character each run

Visually appealing and enjoyable to replay every now and then

Replayability: good for returning occasionally
Visuals: appealing

community.one_liner: An Asteroids-style arcade space shooter with momentum-based movement, rebuilt as an action-RPG roguelite where you chain 200+ modular upgrades into absurd ship builds over roughly 120-wave runs.
community.consensus_summary: Nova Drift is received very warmly by players: Steam shows about 14,000 positive vs 650 negative reviews (95.6%, Overwhelmingly Positive), with a recent-30-day slice slightly lower (Very Positive, 89% on a small sample). It spent years in Early Access (March 27, 2019) before its 1.0 launch on August 12, 2024 (price $17.99, Windows and Mac). Critic coverage is thin: Metacritic has no Metascore yet (only 2 critic reviews posted, Hardcore Gamer 80 and a Polygon entry without a number), and Game Informer is quoted on the store page as praising the unlocks and customization. Praise centres on build variety, feel and sound; criticism centres on the unorthodox tank-style controls, a gentle early difficulty curve, and repetitive enemy/arena variety.
best_things: Enormous build variety: 200+ mods across weapons, shields, bodies and 'super' upgrades that chain into wild synergies (homing fragmenting missiles, shield thrown as a blade drone, bullet-ship builds)
Satisfying audio and visual feedback: reviewers call out the SFX, soundtrack, clean neon look and screen-filling explosions
Inertia-based drifting movement feels distinctive and rewarding once it clicks, reminiscent of classic Asteroids
Plenty of replay hooks: endless mode, draft mode, boss rush, daily challenges and stackable mode modifiers that act as custom difficulty
Runs are short and decision-dense (about 30-40 minutes, around 30 upgrades), good for 'one more run' sessions
Meta-progression unlocks steadily add new mods and super mods, so the game keeps changing as you learn it
Good value and accessibility: cheap for the content, runs well on old hardware, controller support praised by some despite a 'Mostly Playable' label
Scales from chill score-chasing to punishing high difficulty, with hard achievements for veterans
worst_things: Movement/steering (rotate and thrust, no twin-stick aiming, no move-backwards) is the most common reason players bounce off or refund; several negative reviews cite controls alone
Enemy and arena variety is seen as thin: same empty space, recycled wave formations, and few genuinely threatening enemies
Early difficulty levels are too easy, so some players feel they have 'beaten' it within a couple of runs before mutators unlock the real challenge
Balance is lopsided in places: a few reviewers say missiles (or a handful of builds) are the only viable route for very deep runs, and many perks are narrowly specialised
Some deaths feel cheap, e.g. being one-shot by enemies with extreme modifiers
Controller polish gaps: no sensitivity setting, limited control customisation
Occasional technical complaints: performance troubles on some machines, launch issues with certain capture hardware, Linux support dependent on Proton
improvements: Add controller sensitivity options and broader control remapping, plus alternative control schemes (twin-stick or a reverse/brake input)
More bosses and more enemy/arena variety so later runs feel less repetitive
Better onboarding: the practice run is progression-locked and gives little reward, and the UI shows upgrades that are not yet unlocked without explaining why
Tune difficulty so early tiers are more engaging and weaker weapon families are competitive in deep endless runs
Smooth out the time-to-unlock for the strongest super mods, which one reviewer says takes a while
Add a multi-point/bulk upgrade option and more customisation, which players request on the Steam forums
unique_things: Fuses ARPG-style build theorycrafting with Asteroids-style arcade physics, an unusual mix in the roguelite shooter space
Ship is assembled from interchangeable weapon, shield and body parts with deep interaction rules rather than generic stat boosts
Score-attack/leaderboard framing rather than a story-driven goal, with mode modifiers letting players author their own difficulty
Momentum and collision physics matter: you can ram, use shields as weapons, or turn yourself into the projectile
Small-studio project (Chimeric, published by Pixeljam) with a long Early Access road and active community feedback loop
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding through meta-unlocks before the best mods and harder mutators appear, which some call slow and others accept as pacing
Runs can feel samey because arenas are empty space and wave types repeat, leading some players to drop off after 5-10 runs
Endless mode after the final boss feels like the same bosses plus more enemies, with little new content
Score-chasing focus does not suit players who want a final goal or narrative progression
Steering learning curve: newcomers often describe the first runs as awkward until drifting becomes second nature
Some find heavy projectile and effect spam visually noisy
divisive_points: Movement: many call the inertia-based controls the heart of the game; others find them unintuitive or worse than twin-stick and leave
Difficulty: some say it is too easy even with modifiers enabled, while others call late tiers and endless very hard

Post-1.0 direction: at least one negative reviewer blamed the 1.0 planning and the developer's Discord community for decisions they disliked, though this is a single player's view and most reviewers are positive
Depth vs repetition: fans see near-limitless builds, sceptics see the same handful of strong builds repeated
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched March 27, 2019 and the game built a loyal following over roughly five years; 1.0 shipped August 12, 2024. Steam community review sentiment stays overwhelmingly positive; the negative reviews are mostly about controls, repetition and controller options, plus one review criticising the developer community around the 1.0 design process. Metacritic lists no Metascore (needs more critic reviews) and OpenCritic could not be confirmed, so critic consensus is light. The steam-revenue-calculator.com estimate (Boxleiter-style, unaudited) puts gross revenue near $11.2M and net near $3.3M, and SteamSpy-style data suggests 200k-500k owners, both order-of-magnitude figures. Steam lists Windows and Mac; the Steam forums mention Proton support being restored for Linux. Note: the web-search tool budget was exhausted during research, so Reddit and several outlet pages could not be read directly and community detail leans on the Steam review file and Steam forum/store pages.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Ravenswatch is an Early Access action roguelike that he describes as essentially Diablo in roguelike form, with selectable heroes, big explorable maps, mini quests and random events. As a big Diablo fan he was excited, but he finds the gameplay clunky and the difficulty scaling poor. He thinks many issues are easy fixes and looks forward to the full release. For now he places it in mid B tier.

community.one_liner: A MOBA-flavoured action roguelike from Passtech Games (Curse of the Dead Gods) where fairy-tale and legend heroes such as Beowulf, Scarlet and Geppetto fight a corrupting Nightmare across three timed chapters, solo or in up to 4-player online co-op.
community.consensus_summary: Players land at Mostly Positive on Steam (about 80% of roughly 22.8k reviews) and critics are warmer (Metacritic 84 from 11 reviews, Metacritic user score 7.0 from 110 ratings). Almost everyone agrees the art, the distinct hero kits and the co-op are excellent, and the people who click with it log hundreds of hours. The common complaint is thin content: the same three maps and bosses forever, with new post-launch content mostly arriving as heroes, skins and events. Netcode problems, in particular no way to rejoin after a disconnect, and a steep and poorly explained learning curve sour many negative reviews. It left Early Access on 26 Sep 2024 (1.0) and has kept getting updates, though some players call the pace slow and dislike paid hero DLC.
best_things: Heroes play like MOBA champions (passive, abilities, ultimate unlocked at level 5) and feel genuinely different from each other
Fairy-tale and literary roster; the art style, animation polish and music are praised even in negative reviews
Co-op is the highlight: no meta-progression gaps between friends, so anyone can jump in on equal footing, and some heroes (Romeo and Juliet) reward playing off each other's moves
The countdown to the boss creates risk/reward routing: rush the boss for bigger rewards, or clear the map for power at the cost of a harder boss
Day/night cycle and map points of interest affect which enemies and objectives are worth doing, rewarding map knowledge
Skill and game knowledge matter more than grinding; several long-time players say every hero has multiple strong builds and the game becomes addictive once it clicks
Highly replayable for enthusiasts: multiple reviewers report 300 to 1000+ hours, and free updates added events, enemies and quests
Critics call it an accessible, polished, stylish roguelike (Metacritic scores 78 to 100)
worst_things: Only three maps, three chapter bosses and a limited set of enemies, so runs feel samey after the first ~20 hours

No rejoin after a crash or disconnect, and if the host drops the whole run is lost; players report this persisting for years along with lobby bugs, random disconnects and multiplayer that fails to start for some
Steep learning curve with little in-game explanation of items, map objectives and build synergies; newcomers often die a lot and bounce off
Combat and difficulty scaling: enemies feel spongy, and higher difficulties mostly add HP, damage and XP penalties rather than new mechanics
Shallow meta-progression and few reasons to continue after clearing the top difficulty; build variety within a hero is described as narrow by some
Hero balance is uneven and some heroes (for example Scarlet and Geppetto) are called poor starting choices
Steam Deck complaint of a locked 720p image with black bars
Sound and music become repetitive over long play
improvements: New maps, bosses and enemy factions, not just new heroes and skins; this is the most repeated request
Reconnect and host-migration support plus more stable netcode and lobbies
An endless or sandbox-style mode for power-fantasy play after the highest difficulty, plus more meaningful reasons to attempt higher difficulties
Better onboarding and tutorials for items, map objectives and heroes
Deeper build choice and wider use of the co-op combo mechanic from Romeo and Juliet across the cast
Accessibility and platform fixes (colour-blind modes, Steam Deck resolution)
unique_things: A PvE MOBA-style roguelike: hero kits with passives and ultimates in an ARPG-roguelike loop, compared by reviewers to Battlerite and Risk of Rain
A visible timer to the boss that scales the boss up if you are late, and offers bigger rewards if you go early
No traditional meta-progression: unlocks are horizontal additions to the item and talent pool, so power comes from knowledge, not hours
Day/night system that changes enemy behaviour and what you should fight and when
A roster built on folk-tale and literary figures
tedious_or_disliked: Repeating the same three chapters, about 18 minutes each, many times to beat each difficulty; top difficulties feel slow and grindy
Reduced XP on high difficulty means you barely level or find loot, leaving some players quitting after the first stage
Losing long runs to disconnects or crashes, since there is no rejoin
Scale-or-perish pacing: the timer forces fast snowballing, which some find stressful and punishing, especially when missing telegraphs under visual clutter
Paid hero DLC on top of the base game irritates some players
divisive_points: The boss timer: seen as excellent pressure and routing by some and as unwelcome stress by others
Difficulty: fans say it is fair and rewarding once learned, while others find it punishing and not rewarding like Elden Ring-type games
Build variety: some players find strong builds for every hero, others say the best build is obvious
Content roadmap: some see steady free updates (events, Songs of Thieves) while others call the updates hollow and object to paid DLC heroes
Patches: a co-op group reported each update made runs harder and diluted the reward pool, while others enjoy the added events
community.reception_notes: Launched in Early Access in 2023 and reached 1.0 on 26 Sep 2024 on PC, with PS5, Xbox, Switch versions and a Switch 2 release listed on Metacritic. Post-1.0 support includes the Nightmares Unleashed update (Jan 2025), the paid Merlin hero DLC (Jan 2026), the free Songs of Thieves update (27 May 2026, new Thieves faction, boss Stingy Jack, multiplayer pause) and a Kintaro hero DLC that Steam news lists for Oct 2026. Steam lists the price at $24.99. Patch notes through 1.4 and 1.5 mainly target network stability, reconnect pop-ups and bugs. Steam-side figures from third-party estimators (not audited): SteamSpy owners 200k to 500k, and steam-revenue-calculator estimates about $7.9M gross and $2.3M net revenue. OpenCritic score could not be located. Some recent negative Steam reviews accuse the developer of locking the discussion board and of slow content pace, while veteran players are fairly positive about the game today.

community.one_liner: A 2D hand-drawn roguelite platformer by Blobfish (the studio behind Brotato) in which quirky potato-like prisoners fight through procedurally assembled gladiatorial arenas on the alien prison planet Tartarus.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate it Very Positive (about 90% of roughly 480 reviews), and the people who stick with it praise the tight movement, the variety of characters and the tough, customisable difficulty. It is widely described as an overlooked hidden gem that never found a big audience: the SteamSpy estimate is only 20-50k owners and revenue calculators put it near $118k gross. Critic coverage is very thin. Metacritic has one critic review (But Why Tho, 70/100) and only 4 user ratings averaging 7.8, and I found no OpenCritic entry. It launched in Early Access in October 2019 and hit 1.0 on 10 March 2021, with console and mobile versions following (the Metacritic page lists a May 2023 release on PS4, Xbox One and Switch). Recent Steam reviews from 2025-26 mostly compare it to Brotato, and several ask the developer to revisit and rebalance it, mainly because of slow progression. Note: the web-search quota ran out mid-task, so this is built from Steam data, Steam store and community pages, Metacritic and a revenue estimator rather than a wide sweep of outlets and Reddit.
best_things: Buttery-smooth movement and controls; you start with a dash that has i-frames plus a double jump, which players say makes platforming combat feel great
Each of the playable characters (eight per the store page) plays noticeably differently, with easy and hard characters
Large item pool (300+ weapons, pets and trinkets per the store page) with risk/reward unlocks
Difficulty is customisable and deep; a reviewer with dozens of hours had only cleared the second of five difficulties for most characters
Goofy, charming space-potato humour and hand-drawn art that contrast with grimdark roguelites
Strong replayability and achievement hunting (100+ achievements; some players have 70-190 hours)
Varied levels built from hundreds of hand-crafted rooms, with 50+ enemies and 10 bosses
Short-session charm: many reviewers with 70-190 hours call it a favourite and a hidden gem, with a few rating it as high as 9/10
worst_things: Progression is slow: you level up and collect items so gradually that runs can feel like a slog before any build comes together
Items feel sparse early in a run, so the game leans heavily on the core combat being fun, which some players find merely okay
Some players found the movement and combat unsatisfying or unhappy-making (short negative reviews)
Steam community describes it as light on content overall
Reported technical problems in the forums: the game not launching for some and progress not saving on exit
The mobile version reportedly does not feel good to play compared with PC or console
improvements: Rebalance or speed up levelling and item acquisition so runs reach their payoff sooner (most commonly requested in recent reviews)
A developer revisit or content update; several recent reviewers explicitly ask Blobfish to update the game
Mod support to extend content, requested in the Steam community
More content depth, since some players say it runs out of things to do
Clearer explanation of how to unlock higher difficulty (danger) modes
Fix launch and save-progress bugs reported in discussions
unique_things: Plays as a potato-style prisoner gladiator in a space prison, with deliberately absurd cast and tone
Mix of arena-style combat and platforming with dash i-frames and double jump, closer to Nuclear Throne or Hollow Knight than top-down arena shooters
Risk/reward item unlocks and a five-tier difficulty system with extra difficulty customisation
Comes from the same studio as Brotato, so players frequently frame it as the less famous sibling with a very different (platformer) format
Room-based levels built procedurally from many hand-crafted rooms, plus treasure rooms and merchants
tedious_or_disliked: Slow levelling that makes the mid-run feel grindy and not worth the time, even for players who enjoy the game
Long runs before item impact is felt, described as boring by a Brotato fan who stopped after minutes
Hard characters and upper difficulty tiers can be punishing, even on the easy characters according to one reviewer
Unlock grind for items and achievements is a long haul, though some like it
Save and launch issues mentioned by community posters
divisive_points: Pace of runs: fans call it addictive and balanced, while others find it a slow slog
Comparison with Brotato: some see it as underrated, others say it is only decent next to that hit
Difficulty: praised as deep and challenging by veterans, but a barrier for players who want faster payoff
Core combat feel: described as smooth and satisfying by most, unsatisfying by a few
community.reception_notes: Early Access in October 2019, full 1.0 on Steam on 10 March 2021 at $14.99. Steam reviews are consistently positive and the game has a small but loyal following; the critic record is almost empty. Metacritic lists a 2023 release on PS4, Xbox One and Switch where But Why Tho scored it 70/100, calling it simple yet satisfying, easy to start and hard to master. The developer Blobfish later became far better known for Brotato, and recent (2025-26) Steam reviews often reference that game and request a rebalance or update. Forum complaints mention launch and save issues and light content. I could not verify a recent patch history, and the Metacritic page may mainly reflect the console release.

Audio and music: strongly positive
Exploration and adventure pacing: positive, bosses build excitement
Core gameplay depth: basic move, roll, shoot
Genre fit: adventure more than roguelike, judged as single player

community.one_liner: An isometric, Don't Starve-styled survival-roguelite shooter from Galvanic Games (published by Devolver Digital) in which you craft guns, elemental bullets and a wizard-tower base, then drop into procedurally generated worlds that collapse on a five-minute Chaos timer, solo or in 1-4 player co-op.
community.consensus_summary: Players rate it Very Positive on Steam (about 80 percent of roughly 4,000 reviews) and it carries a Mixed Metacritic critic score of 72 from 25 reviews, with Metacritic user score at 5.5 on a tiny sample. Nearly everyone loves the art, music and the gun-plus-bullet-plus-powder crafting system, and co-op is the best way to play. The recurring complaints are a core loop that runs out of surprises, grindy material gathering, clunky controls, weak solo balance and a thin or anticlimactic endgame. It is effectively finished: the Better Together update (May 2024) added four-player co-op and custom difficulty, and Galvanic Games closed in June 2024, so the game is not getting the extra content it hinted at.
best_things: Art direction, Don't Starve-like look and soundtrack are praised by both positive and negative reviewers
The gun, bullet and powder crafting system is the standout: many bullet types, elements and gun classes (rifle, shotgun, Uzi, minigun, mortar, bounty weapons) that combine in fun ways
Co-op with friends (up to four players after the May 2024 update) is where most people say it shines
The five-minute end-times timer, extendable by killing Chaos enemies, keeps hub-to-expedition pacing tense
Base building and gradually unlocking crafting stations and benches gives a satisfying sense of progression
Engaging lore and a clear cliffhanger-style setup, plus biome and boss variety with distinct mechanics
Good value on sale; PC Gamer called it a lean roguelite that does not waste your time
worst_things: Core loop becomes repetitive after a handful of runs; several reviewers say they had seen everything in 7 to 15 hours
Controls and aiming feel loose or clunky on both mouse and gamepad; the camera angle makes judging distance awkward
Combat and difficulty feel balanced for co-op, leaving solo play weaker (no self-revive) and some enemy abilities stun-lock you into losing your whole inventory
Enemies and bosses are considered bland and unthreatening; the final boss and ending are called anticlimactic (IGN)
Limited inventory space and having to run between 20+ chests in the base make crafting and resource logistics tedious
Sparse endgame content; gameplay feels like a mobile or tablet game to some, with Unity-related rough edges and occasional connection or performance problems
Multiplayer progression is host-centric: some achievements and progress only count for the host, with no cross-progression for guests
improvements: Better solo balance and a revive or escape option for solo players
Clearer teaching of the crafting system and of niche mechanics (the summon-object tree, force bullets, powder combinations) which many players never use
A better way to organize and pull materials for crafting, such as shared storage, since players resort to mods to avoid chest-running
More powder and synergy variety plus properly tuned harder difficulties
Tighter aiming, camera and control feel, including weapon-slot switching when out of ammo
More endgame content and a stronger final boss and ending; content the devs seemed to have planned (DLC, more zones) never arrived
unique_things: Reimagines a wizard fantasy as a gunsmith game: customizable guns fed with crafted elemental bullets and powders rather than spell lists
Mixes Don't Starve-style crafting and base building with extraction-style loot risk: die and you lose what you carry, so you must run home
Five-minute end-of-the-world timer that progressively destroys the map and can be extended by killing Chaos beings
Bullet effects interact with the world, for example burning trees for charcoal or filling the ground to build traps
Open procedural worlds that you enter through a time portal, tied to rebuilding a time machine and assembling a band of wizards
tedious_or_disliked: Heavy material grinding for building and upgrades, felt most strongly late in the game
Inventory management and chest-hopping in the hub
Early game time pressure feels rushed in a game that otherwise wants you to slow down and craft, especially on high difficulty
Overwhelming crafting systems dumped on the player at the start
Stun-lock enemy auras and lost-inventory deaths feel unfair, particularly solo
divisive_points: Difficulty: some call it easy and chill, others find the early timer and stun-lock deaths punishing
Crafting depth: lauded as the best part by many, but others say many bullet and spell combos are gimmicky or go unused
Solo versus co-op: praised as a fun co-op game, but criticized as poorly balanced for solo play
Genre fit: some call it a survival game, others say it is really a roguelite or extraction shooter and the survival label misleads
community.reception_notes: Launched October 17, 2023 on PC, PS5 and Xbox Series (Switch port never dated) to Mixed critic reception (PC Metascore 72 from 25 critics, user score 5.5 from only 22 ratings), with wide critic spread from 95 to 40. Steam players are friendlier than critics. The Better Together update on May 13, 2024 added four-player co-op and customizable difficulty, and Galvanic Games (Seattle) shut down in June 2024 because, per a Steam review, profits were too low to continue; recent positive reviewers stress the game was not abandoned half-done though it clearly points to unbuilt content. Steam price is $24.99 with frequent deep sales; owner estimates are 100k to 200k, and third-party Boxleiter-style estimates put gross revenue near $2.3M and net near $0.68M (order-of-magnitude only). OpenCritic score could not be retrieved (web search budget exhausted; a guessed OpenCritic page fetch returned a different game), so it is left null.

games.name: A Robot Named Fight!
games.short_description: A Robot Named Fight is a Metroidvania roguelike focused on exploration and item collection. Explore a different, procedurally-generated labyrinth each time you play and discover randomized power-ups to traverse obstacles, find secrets and explode meat beasts.

placements.verbal_evidence: this is a pretty solid Btier game here

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: A Robot Named Fight is a Metroidvania roguelike that openly imitates classic Metroid, with randomized levels, enemies and bosses each run. He considers it the best attempt at fusing the two genres, since they conflict by nature. He enjoyed it and finds it unique, but it is slow to get going each run and works better as a Metroidvania than a roguelike. He places it as a solid B tier.
praise: Unusual, faithful blend of Metroidvania and roguelike; best of its kind in his view
Randomized levels, enemies and bosses vary by run
Great enemy variety and plenty of items and bosses to find
Pixel art and music fit well and evoke nostalgia
First-time exploration feels strong, like a real Metroid game
Simple, straightforward lore and strong vibe
criticism: Genres conflict: replayability suffers and each run restarts from a weak, minimalist start
Gameplay is simple and awkward, with old Metroid controls (hold button to aim diagonally)
Early biomes have limited enemy pools, so runs start feeling the same
Levels can be long; backtracking and enemies respawning every room feel tedious
Unexplained items and shrines make risky purchases punishing since death is permanent
Wishes he could skip to the midgame more often
unique_points: One of very few true Metroidvania roguelikes; he does not count Dead Cells as one
Bosses differ by seed, giving new encounters each run
Metroid-style opacity clashes with roguelike permadeath, making unknown gambles feel harsher
commentary.quote: I can't think of a better game out there that does it.
design_criteria: Genre fusion: how well Metroidvania exploration meshes with roguelike runs
Replayability: runs restart weak and slow to reach the interesting midgame
Level design: long levels with tedious backtracking and respawns
Enemy design: good variety but limited pools in early biomes
Controls: intentionally awkward old-school Metroid aiming
Risk vs reward: unknown shrines/items punish gambles under permadeath
Charm/visuals/audio: pixel art and music fit and feel nostalgic
Randomization: levels, enemies and bosses generated per run

community.one_liner: A Super Metroid-inspired metroidvania roguelite by solo dev Matt Bitner (Morningstar Game Studio) in which you explore a freshly generated labyrinth each run, collect randomized weapons and items, and blow up fleshy Megabeast monsters.
community.consensus_summary: Players rate it Very Positive on Steam (about 88% of 897 reviews), and its core appeal is a faithful Super Metroid feel combined with a run-based item-synergy loop. Critics were warmer than lukewarm but less enthusiastic than fans: Metacritic 71 on Switch from 9 critic reviews (user 7.5 from 33 ratings), OpenCritic 73 Top Critic Average from 18 reviews, with scores ranging from 6/10 to 9/10. The recurring caveats are a bland presentation, inconsistent procedural level design, and a roguelike reset that clashes with metroidvania exploration. Launched on Steam in Sept 2017 and on Switch in April 2018 (published by Hitcents); the dev is solo and has been inactive on new content for years, yet recent 2025-26 Steam reviews still call it an underrated gem and ask for a sequel.
best_things: Movement and shooting feel very close to Super Metroid, which Metroid fans treat as the main draw
Huge pool of randomized weapons, items and synergies makes each run and build feel different
Strong 'one more run' loop once the slow opening minutes of a run are past; some players report hundreds of hours
Procedural maps are still gated by ability checks, so it keeps a sense of metroidvania exploration and secret hunting
Lots of secrets, multiple endings and final bosses, plus unlocks that keep replays fresh
Local co-op and full controller support
Chunky, gross enemy and boss designs are called out as a highlight even by lukewarm critics
worst_things: Presentation is seen as generic or bland, lacking the moody atmosphere of the game it imitates
Procedural level design is inconsistent; generator can occasionally produce awkward or dead-end layouts
Some runs do not give enough upgrades to handle later bosses, making RNG swingy
Breakable secret walls are unmarked, so players feel they must shoot every surface; walls and enemies respawn and undo opened passages
Difficulty is uneven: early bosses are considered too easy for a roguelite while later ones require long runs to reach
Reviewers flagged very long item-pickup fanfare and some platforming precision issues on tight gaps
Story is minimal and voice acting is heavily processed and hard to understand
A few bugs and annoyances remain and the game is no longer actively updated
Some later enemy groups with lock-on projectiles can cause cheap, instant-feeling deaths (Metacritic user complaints)
improvements: Allow rebinding movement abilities such as slide, which is tied to a two-key combo on keyboard and easy to misfire
Give some form of persistence or run-saving so death does not always mean restarting from the very beginning
Make breakable walls telegraphed and stop them from respawning instantly
More consistent boss counts per region, and fewer reused bosses; give the final region an alternate variant and treat the hard mode as a proper mode with achievements
Larger, more intricate environments and more enemy, boss and biome variety (a sequel is frequently requested)
Explain the cryptic shrine and offering system in-game instead of requiring outside guides
unique_things: Grafts a roguelike run structure directly onto a Super Metroid skeleton, rather than following the Dead Cells or Rogue Legacy action model
Slower, more old-school pace than typical action roguelites, emphasising verticality and wall-jumping
Procedurally generated maps still use gated upgrades, so runs feel like miniature metroidvanias
Machine-god shrines with number-based offerings add a cryptic meta layer
Multiple endings, final bosses and a lore-heavy hard mode behind repeated completions
Couch co-op on a Metroid-style game, which is rare in the subgenre
tedious_or_disliked: Early minutes of every run feel slow while you only have weak starting weapons and limited movement
Restarting after every death becomes repetitive, especially for players who want metroidvania-style persistent progress
Constantly shooting walls to find secret passages, then re-breaking walls that respawn
Reaching the harder late bosses can take an hour or more, so failed attempts are costly
Learning what items do requires many runs and some outside research
Co-op camera system is a turn-off for some players
divisive_points: Whether roguelike structure and procedural generation belong in a metroidvania at all; 2018 commenters argued permadeath and randomness are opposite to hand-crafted exploration, while fans say it works surprisingly well
Difficulty: some find it too lenient and easy to break, others find bad RNG runs and late bosses punishing
Originality: praised as a loving homage to Super Metroid by some critics and dismissed as close to a fangame by others
Player skill fit: fans of Super Metroid find it comfortable, while players unfamiliar with that movement hit an extra learning hump
community.reception_notes: Steam launch was Sept 7, 2017, and the Switch version followed Apr 26, 2018 from publisher Hitcents, with critic coverage clustering around the Switch release. Outlet scores ranged widely (53/100 to 90/100), with OpenCritic showing a 73 average but only 59% of critics recommending it. Steam sentiment has stayed strongly positive and recent reviews (2025-26) keep calling it an overlooked gem. Reviewers note the dev has been away from programming for a while, so no new content is expected. Steam sales estimates from third-party sites: about 50k-100k owners (SteamSpy range) and roughly $200k estimated gross (Boxleiter-based, order-of-magnitude only). Also available on PS4, Xbox/Microsoft Store, Mac and Linux.

games.name: Ballionaire
games.short_description: BALLIONAIRE is a fast-paced, kinetic roguelike where strategy meets physics to create outrageous wealth! Find and exploit game-breaking synergies as you theorycraft your way to victory. Welcome to the autobonker genre!

other_scores.source: Steam user reviews (Very Positive, about 84% of 2,705 per local data)
Steam-revenue-calculator estimate (gross revenue, about 842.7k dollars; Steam owners est. 100k-200k)

placements.verbal_evidence: I think I'm going to put this game as a B because all things considered

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Ballionaire is a real-time ball-drop roguelike where you place items on a board, press a button, and watch chaotic chain reactions escalate into huge numbers. He credits it as unique, fun and well done, with good music and goofy art, but says he was more disappointed than most people because he expected more given the hype. He found it hard to follow why numbers go up, easy to break early, and bloated with overly specific synergies. He places it in B, stressing that it is not a bad game and that he might come back to it.
praise: Unique concept that turns a simple real-life ball-drop mechanic into an infinitely scaling roguelike
Satisfying and fun, especially the first time a board goes off
Some definite cool synergies to discover
Different maps each have their own twists
Music is pretty good
Well done at its core and fun to play
criticism: Less visually satisfying than Balatro; chaos makes it hard to tell why numbers are rising
Too easy to get a broken board, even on his third attempt with little unlocked, so the win felt unearned
Unlocks bloat the item pool with highly specific synergies, making early runs with fewer items feel easier
Many items are useless unless you have one exact other item, and there are too few broad items usable across builds
Maps matter little since any board goes boom once a few pieces are placed
Real-time, no-input drops feel less satisfying than the turn-by-turn payoffs of Luck Be a Landlord
unique_points: Takes a familiar real-life ball-drop toy and makes it a scoring-engine roguelike that can go infinite
You only press a button and watch the fireworks; ball direction is automatic
Closest comparison in his view is Luck Be a Landlord rather than Balatro
commentary.quote: I think I'm going to put this game as a B
design_criteria: Power fantasy / breaking the game: he loves feeling overpowered, but here it felt too easy and unearned
Feedback clarity: hard to follow why numbers go up compared with Balatro
Synergies: too specific and narrow, bloating the pool as unlocks grow
Difficulty: broken boards arrive easily, making losses rare once one appears
Level/map variety: maps have twists but barely affect play
Content: wants more content, but worries more items would worsen synergy bloat
Visuals/art: goofy, charming enough
Audio: music is pretty good
Uniqueness: strong, distinctive concept

community.one_liner: A pachinko-style roguelike 'autobonker' by newobject (published by Raw Fury) where you place pegs and triggers on a board, drop a ball, and watch it chain combos to hit escalating money goals.
community.consensus_summary: Ballionaire is received as a fun, addictive, charming number-go-up roguelite that is well liked on Steam (Very Positive, about 84% of roughly 2,700 reviews, per local data) and generally favorable among critics (Metacritic 76, OpenCritic 74). Praise centers on satisfying combo chains, build variety and its cartoony presentation. The recurring complaints are heavy RNG with little control once the ball drops, poor balance (a few dominant builds, easy once learned), unclear item descriptions and limited long-term content with no endless mode. It launched in Early Access in December 2024 at about $12; recent negative reviews say the game has not had a meaningful update in over a year and feels abandoned, although Raw Fury reportedly had an item ban/unban feature on an experimental branch and mod support exists. Typical playtime to see everything is about 15-20 hours.
best_things: Addictive 'big number go up' loop with strong audio and visual feedback when a multi-minute combo goes off
Large variety of pegs, triggers, boons and boards that enable game-breaking synergies and theorycrafting
Colorful, irreverent cartoon presentation; screen is readable despite chaos (art improved during Early Access)
Fast, chill, pick-up-and-play sessions that suit Steam Deck and short bursts
Multiple difficulties, boards and starting builds; Lab and Custom modes for sandbox play; Steam Workshop/mod support
Good value when on sale (often under 5 dollars) for roughly 15-20 hours of fun
worst_things: Heavy RNG: after the ball drops you have almost no agency, so runs can fail 'through no fault of your own'
Balance problems: a handful of builds (players often cite Dam and roughly five playstyles) dominate, making the game trivially easy once learned, even on higher difficulties
Perceived abandonment: several top-voted negative reviews say there has been no meaningful update or balance patch in over a year
Many top-voted negatives say the game feels bland or gimmicky and that most choices do not matter, so players get bored within the first hours
Many items do not synergize with each other, which dilutes the pool and makes building a specific strategy unreliable
Runs start to feel samey and repetitive; limited replay depth once everything is seen
Some item and peg descriptions are unclear, with a steep reading burden to understand triggers
Top difficulty (Ballionaire++) is seen by some as cheap and punishing rather than challenging
Visual chaos makes it hard to appreciate a well-built machine, and some find the dancing 3D stick-figure mascot annoying or out of place
Reports of placeholder text and of freezing/black screens in recent reviews
improvements: Add an endless mode and higher difficulty tiers beyond Ballionaire++
Add item ban/unban to fight pool dilution after everything is unlocked (Raw Fury said this existed on an experimental branch)
Rebalance dominant builds and overpowered items, and make underused synergies viable
Redesign 'anti-fun' Tribulations (for example 500 damage dealt or heavy immutable object placement) that force constant restarts
Better in-game explanations of pegs, triggers and how they interact
Quality-of-life: prompt or auto-skip when the goal is already met, and more agency beyond boons and triggers (for example better flipper/pinball board)
unique_things: Self-described 'autobonker' genre: you build the pachinko board and strategy, then RNG physics plays out the drop
Pachinko board-building where pegs, triggers and food-themed combos (like pizza) chain into huge scores
Comparisons to Peglin, Peggle, Luck Be a Landlord and Balatro, but with a more chaotic kinetic physics feel
Tribulations and rule-bending boons that alter the rules of a run
Lab Mode and Custom Mode sandboxes plus Workshop mod support
Distinctly goofy 2010s-cartoon humor and mascot
tedious_or_disliked: Watching 20-second ball drops repeat, with many players defaulting to 4x speed and finding it boring
Unlocking content is partly RNG-gated and some find the unlock grind (for example specific materials) annoying
Item pool dilution after unlocking everything, making targeted builds harder
Restart-scumming around bad Tribulations or a bad start
Needing to read or recall how every peg works to make good placement choices
Very long late-game drops when a runaway combo forces you to hunt for the 'end drop' button
divisive_points: RNG: some love the surprise and number-go-up dopamine, others find it too random compared with Balatro's player agency
Difficulty: some find it too easy once builds are figured out, others find Ballionaire++ and certain Tribulations unfairly punishing
Content and value: fine for 1-2 days of fun on sale for some, good for 15-20 hours for others, too thin for a full price for a few
Whether the large item pool adds diversity or is pointless bloat
community.reception_notes: Released Dec 10, 2024 on Steam (Windows only) at about $12.34 via Raw Fury, built in Godot; launched in Early Access per Rogueliker's review. Launch reception was strong, with the Steam rating around 86% in early 2025 and sliding to about 84% in later data. Critics were mostly favorable (Metacritic 76 from 9 reviews, OpenCritic 74 from 10), with GameGrin the notable dissenter ('Marmite' game). Some reviewers noted no endless mode. Later reviews complain of no update in over a year and abandonment, balance never patched; a Raw Fury rep said on the Steam forum that item ban/unban existed on an experimental branch, and Workshop mod support was added. Humble Bundle inclusion is mentioned in one review. Steam owners estimated 100k-200k with estimated gross revenue of about $843k (Boxleiter-style estimate, not audited); no official sales figures found.

games.name: Bing in Wonderland
games.short_description: A Roguelite monster killing satisfaction galore without any exploration elements. The game is filled to the brim with exotic enemies and stages with a collection of deep and robust boons, weapons, and items plus an abundance of pointless features and useless details. (CONTROLLER SUPPORTED)

placements.verbal_evidence: none

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Bing in Wonderland is a traditional 2D action roguelike with a watercolor look and a goofy, flash-game vibe. He enjoys the fast, fun combat and the hat-throw dash, but finds the roguelike layer (boons, build variety) minimal and replayability low. Runs are short, about 15-20 minutes, ending in a boss, across 15+ levels. He says he is placing it above Baloner, with no tier letter stated in this segment.
praise: Watercolor-style visuals and good-looking, varied biomes
Weapons (bow, axe, harp) play very differently from each other
Unique hat-throw dash that gives invincibility frames for the whole travel, longer if the hat is farther
Shield-break mechanic: stunned enemies can be jumped on for a big area-of-effect with a dramatic animation
Fast-paced, satisfying combat that feels powerful from the start of a run
Goofy charm (for example the food/pooping mechanic) and nostalgic flash-game feel
Bosses have enjoyable mechanics
criticism: Roguelike elements are minimal; boons only add to what you were already doing and do not change how you play
You do not feel very different from start to end of a run
Enemies can feel dull, similar to each other, and sometimes confusing; some bosses are just bigger enemies
Low replayability; the draw is finishing the levels rather than replaying runs
Some character unlocks are gated behind beating a specific boss with a specific weapon/item, which is easy to miss
unique_points: Hat-throw-then-dash as an invulnerable dash mechanic he has rarely seen elsewhere
Universal shield-break stun that feeds a jump-on AoE, central to the core loop
Meta-progression includes unlocking and fusing characters with minor effects
commentary.quote: I think I'm going to put Bing above Baloner.
design_criteria: Gameplay feel: fast, fun action with strong moment-to-moment combat
Weapon diversity: distinct weapon move sets
Roguelike depth: boons should meaningfully change play, and here they do not
Replayability: low, driven by completing levels
Run length: short 15-20 minute runs suit the flash-game style
Visuals/charm: watercolor style and goofy enemies
Enemy/boss design: similar enemies, bosses partly upscaled enemies
Meta-progression: simple stat unlocks and character fusion, with some annoying unlock conditions

community.one_liner: A fast-paced 2D ink-wash action-platformer roguelite by Wanba Studio where you fight wave-based stages with bows, spears, cannons, axes or harps, throw your hat, and use a signature butt slam.
community.consensus_summary: Bing in Wonderland has been received very warmly by players: Steam shows about 97% positive across roughly 2,160 reviews (Overwhelmingly Positive), and a long-running Steam Deck Verified status. Critics are fewer and more lukewarm: OpenCritic lists three reviews (GameGrin 8/10, Gaming Professors 8.5/10, Nindie Spotlight 6/10), and GameGrin's later Switch Power-Up Edition review gave 6.5/10, citing repetition. Metacritic has no Metascore or user score yet (only one critic review counted). The game is a small, content-limited indie that launched in Jan 2023 with a promise of updates, later received DLC skin packs and a Nintendo Switch Power-Up Edition (Feb 20, 2025). Recent Steam reviews (2025-26) still praise it but some players doubt more content is coming.
best_things: Simple, satisfying, addictive combat loop that is easy to pick up and hard to put down
The butt slam ('Big Sit') and hat-throw mechanics add a distinctive, fun, strategic layer
Wide variety of boons, weapons (bow, spear, cannon, axe, harp) and items enabling different builds
Charming ink-wash / hand-drawn art style and quirky, absurd enemy designs
Strong sense of humour, including funny achievements and deliberately wacky translation
Has a clear end goal rather than endless runs, with a rewarding progression loop
Fast stages (around 10 minutes each) and good controller and Steam Deck support
Very cheap price for the amount of playtime (low single-digit to ~$9)
worst_things: Content runs thin and gameplay becomes repetitive after several hours; levels and visuals (e.g. the desert stage) blur together
Sudden, sharp difficulty spikes in the mid-to-late game
The Big Sit mechanic becomes overpowered and can trivialize other weapons and options
Meta-progression feels long and grindy, with resources consumed quickly or poorly explained
Humour (toilet and fart jokes) and broken-English style text read as childish or hard to understand for some
Some indie jankiness in assets and overall polish
Short, looping menu/shop music noted as grating in the Switch review
Basic button-mashing combat feels shallow or plain to some; the most-upvoted negative reviews call it 'kinda boring' or just a thin action-platformer
improvements: More content: new weapons, stages, enemies and DLC beyond cosmetics
Higher difficulty modes or an infinite mode to extend late-game appeal
Clearer map and progression hints, and better explanation of upgrade resources
A more casual or less grindy play option / rebalanced permanent upgrades
Rebalance Big Sit so other builds stay competitive
More varied music and stage palettes
unique_things: The butt slam (Big Sit) stomp as a central combat and damage mechanic
Hat-throwing attack alongside charge shots and dashes
Spending 'wisdom points' as an alternative currency, which one reviewer had never seen before
Deliberately absurd Chinese-ink-painting world with surreal enemies (e.g. headbanging fish) and intentionally odd translation humour
Wave-based platform brawler structure with no exploration, unlike most roguelites
Self-aware 'pointless features and useless details' marketing tone
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding talent points and achievements between runs interrupts short-session roguelike play
Repetitive, monotonous battles after a few hours as variety plateaus
Looping shop/menu music during vendor stops
Permanent stat upgrades make it feel like grind-until-strong rather than a pure roguelite (one negative reviewer's complaint)
Difficulty spikes forcing reliance on grinding or a specific strategy like Big Sit
Plain button-mashing combat that feels boring or shallow to some players, especially fans of the developer's earlier, more inventive Wanba Warriors
divisive_points: Art style and humour: charming and quirky to many, childish or off-putting to others
Big Sit dominance: celebrated as the signature feature by some, criticised as a balance problem by others

games.name: BloodDome99
games.short_description: BloodDome99 is a game about nostalgia, capitalism, violence, and over-the-top absurdist fun. 80s arcade meets modern horde-survival roguelike. Create unique builds, master more than 40 weapons, and kill ever-growing hordes of contestants in the retro-futuristic gladiator gameshow BLOODDOME99

placements.verbal_evidence: I would say that Blood Dome 99 is a is a solid Btier.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Blood Dome 99 is a horde-like shooter sent to the channel by a viewer; he played it in early access and it is now fully released with three levels and an endless mode. You shoot from the center of the arena with a dash, and the twist is a money system: kills give XP and gold, gold buys upgrades, and the goal is to reach a gold target as fast as possible. He admires its unique visuals and mechanical upgrades but wants more depth in the money mechanic and end-of-run stats. Verdict: a solid B tier that stands out without reinventing the genre.
praise: Minimalist old-TV visual style with one color per element (player, bullets, blood, enemies), keeping the screen readable and cutting visual chaos
Accessibility options, including changing the colors
Money mechanic: spending gold on upgrades versus finishing the run quickly creates a real timing decision, since enemies scale and will eventually overwhelm you
Upgrades are mechanical changes rather than flat percentage boosts, with unique per-weapon upgrades (e.g. the bee gun)
Weapons offered every few minutes as a choice of three you must pay for, forcing spend-or-save choices
Meta unlocks do not feel bad because items do not depend on narrow synergies
Dash and movement feel great; music and the announcer narrator add charm
criticism: Run stats are lacking: only clear speed matters, not gold earned, and he wants big numbers at the end
No damage breakdown per weapon or item, which makes it hard to judge what is actually strong in a chaotic horde-like
Money and XP are effectively the same since both come from kills, so the fast-versus-level-up tension feels muted
The money concept was hard to grasp at the beginning
Wants more things to find during runs, such as events and mini bosses
unique_points: Gold as both currency and win-condition progress makes you choose between speed and power, a mechanic he rarely sees in horde-likes
Upgrades that change behavior per weapon instead of stat bumps
A game does not need to be wildly original; standing out visually and mechanically is enough
Suggests end-of-run damage stats should be a staple of horde-likes
commentary.quote: Blood Dome 99 is a solid B tier.
design_criteria: Visual clarity: one color per element avoids visual chaos and aids evasion
Risk vs reward: spend gold on upgrades or rush the run before enemies overwhelm you
Upgrade design: mechanical changes and per-weapon upgrades beat flat stat boosts
Meta-progression: unlocks add variety without bad synergy traps
Game feel: dash and movement are satisfying
Run information: stats and damage breakdowns help players learn
Audio and charm: music and narrator add personality
Content variety: wants more events and mini bosses in runs

community.one_liner: A retro 80s-arcade twin-stick horde-survival roguelite set in a satirical dystopian 1999 gladiator gameshow, where money earned is also money that keeps you from buying your freedom.
community.consensus_summary: BloodDome99 is a small, well-liked indie from Halftone Gaming that sits at Very Positive on Steam (about 94-96% of roughly 80-100 reviews). Players praise the pixel-art style, synth soundtrack and weapon/perk variety, and compare it to Vampire Survivors crossed with Smash TV. It has no Metacritic or OpenCritic critic scores; Metacritic has a page but shows critic and user scores as tbd. Coverage is limited to launch/update news (GamingOnLinux, CoGConnected) rather than formal reviews. It went into Early Access in December 2023 and hit 1.0 on 15 Nov 2024, is Steam Deck Verified, and is sold cheaply (about $4.99), with very low review volume and modest ownership estimates.
best_things: Retro pixel-art style and 80s dystopian/retrowave atmosphere, repeatedly called the best part
Soundtrack described as a banger by reviewers
Diverse arsenal of 40+ weapons (paper planes, flamethrowers, bee guns, snow blowers) and interesting perks enabling different builds
Addictive, well-made core loop that feels like a Vampire Survivors / Smash TV hybrid
Satirical premise where earning and spending money trades off against winning your freedom
Good achievement chase and challenge for completionists (one reviewer compares it to a polished version of mobile horde games)
Steam Deck Verified; one reviewer reports it runs fine on an M4 Mac mini
Reviewers say it is nothing groundbreaking for the genre but very well made, with real love and effort behind it
worst_things: Shallow for some: lack of variety and little progression according to a 5/10 reviewer
Key options like auto-aim/auto-fire are gated behind an unlock (the bouncer) instead of being a plain menu setting
Character moves very slowly while auto-firing and some upgrades slow movement further
Bosses have a huge health pool that some find infeasible early with few weapons
Enemy projectiles can be hard to read amid bullet hell (for example slow carriage projectiles easily missed)
Late-game EXP scaling is steep (asked to be easier)
Pace is noticeably slower than other horde survivors
Reported bug where the bouncer weapon can spawn dozens of looping bullets and cause lag
improvements: Make auto-aim/auto-fire plain menu options rather than progression unlocks
Remove or reduce the movement-speed penalty when firing
Improve projectile readability and color clarity in busy fights
Let players ban unwanted perks from the rotation, or start with better default perks so unlocks do not dilute the pool
Ease late-game EXP scaling and reduce boss health or give more early firepower
Balance autofire versus click-spamming so autofire is not slower (fire rate clamp or ramp)
unique_things: Economy twist: money buys power but pushes you further from the freedom goal
Satirical 'Running Man' style 1999 gameshow setting
Twin-stick arena shooter feel with manual aiming rather than pure auto-attack survivors gameplay
Meta-progression that unlocks weapons, perks, music, cosmetics and game modes
Started as a Juice Jam II entry with a free early version on itch.io
tedious_or_disliked: Grind to pay for access to the next arena even after beating the first one
Slow-paced progression and slow character movement compared with peers
Unlocking basic quality-of-life (auto-aim) through the bouncer gate is considered annoying
Long boss fights with few weapons
Late-game XP curve requiring long grinding
Unlockable perks that worsen your build diluting the rotation
divisive_points: Twin-stick manual shooter vs survivors-like auto-attack identity; some want it to pick one
Pace: called a slow burn by some and sluggish by others
Value: a 5/10 reviewer calls it exceptionally shallow for the price, while others call it a fantastic, challenging 100% chase

Steam Deck Verified. Reception has been consistently positive with small review counts; older negative reviews (early 2025 and before) focus on the unlock gating and slowness, while recent positives (late 2025 to mid 2026) suggest the game is still played and appreciated. Available on Windows and macOS (not Linux natively) on Steam; a free early jam version exists on itch.io. No aggregator critic scores; SteamSpy lists owners at 0-20k with low concurrent players and revenue estimates of essentially nil/unreliable.

games.name: Crown Trick
games.short_description: Enter a labyrinth that moves as you move, where mastering the elements is key to defeating enemies and uncovering the mysteries of this underground world. With a new experience awaiting every time you enter the dungeon, let the power bestowed by the crown guide you in this challenging adventure!

other_scores.score: 12 critic reviews (92% positive); user score 6.7 from 35 ratings

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm unfortunately going to have to put this as a low B, even though I can see a world where this could have been a high A

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Crown Trick is a turn-based, board-style roguelike where a sleeping princess explores a dream fantasy world, beats a realm boss, and returns for light meta progression. He loves its sense of grand adventure, with varied biomes, bosses and monsters that are hard to achieve in an indie game. The gameplay undercuts it: the free blink is so strong that most fights collapse into the same dodge-and-hit loop. Inconsistent enemy attack telegraphing led to deaths that felt unfair during long runs, and he never finished it. He places it at low B, saying it could have been a high A with some tweaks.
praise: Strong sense of a grand adventure from level, biome, monster and boss design
Clear run structure with an end goal that cannot be reached on the first attempt, with multiple realms and final bosses
Bosses with unique mechanics, such as the chess board boss where pieces move like chess pieces
Mini bosses convert into spirit buddies granting abilities, a concept he likes
Distinctive visuals and good story, characters and world building
Lots of content and enemy variety
criticism: Blink ability is so strong it distorts balance and makes most encounters a repetitive dodge-then-attack loop
Enemy attacks are telegraphed only some of the time, so instant unpredicted attacks cause cheap deaths (the Poseidon boss example)
Spirit buddies are unbalanced and there is little incentive to switch, so players stick with one build
Weapons feel similar to each other and meta progression is minimalistic
Runs are long (about an hour), which makes unfair deaths demotivating
unique_points: Turn-based movement combined with a free teleport blink that regenerates each room
Converting defeated mini bosses into spirit allies, two equipped at a time
Chess-themed boss that moves pieces by chess rules
commentary.quote: I'm unfortunately going to have to put this as a low B
design_criteria: Level and monster design: praised for creating a grand adventure feel
Meta progression: minimalistic and could be more interesting
Gameplay balance: blink is overpowered, causing repetitive encounters
Enemy telegraphing and fairness: inconsistent predictions cause unfair deaths
Build diversity: weapons similar, spirits not incentivised to swap
Run length: long runs raise the cost of unfair deaths
Boss design: unique mechanics are a highlight
Visuals and world/story: distinctive and charming

community.one_liner: A turn-based, Mystery Dungeon-style roguelite by NEXT Studios (published by Team17) in which the dungeon only moves when you do, with elemental magic, a limited teleport (Blink) and monster Familiars as the core toolkit.
community.consensus_summary: Crown Trick is received as a good-to-very-good tactical roguelite: Steam sits at Very Positive (about 85% of roughly 5,400 reviews), Metacritic PC is 83 and OpenCritic is 81 from 37 critic reviews. Critics and players praise the pace-flexible turn-based combat, cute pixel art and build variety, while the most common complaints are opaque UI and tooltips, uneven item and boss balance, punishing curses and repetitive dungeon layouts. The user Metacritic score is lower at 6.7 (only 35 ratings), and a few critics found it derivative. Several recent Steam reviewers say the developer has stopped updating the game, leaving long-standing readability and translation issues unfixed. It launched on Switch, PS4 and Xbox in 2020-2021 and reached Steam later; the Steam price is now about $4.99.
best_things: Turn-based combat where time only advances when you act lets you rush through trash rooms and slow down for bosses
Blink (teleport) and the Break/stun mechanic reward positioning and planning over reflexes
Elemental magic and debuff combos, plus a large pool of weapons, relics and spells, give lots of build variety
Mid-boss Familiars grant inheritable abilities, swappable between runs, which gives a satisfying sense of progression
Charming, colourful pixel art and funny enemies; the chessboard-style tile layout keeps the grid readable
Approachable for newcomers to roguelikes, with a gentle entry and plenty of unlockables (blueprints, soul shard upgrades)
Magic resources reset each room, which encourages actually using tools instead of hoarding them
worst_things: Poor information design: many keywords lack tooltips, there is no icon glossary, and elemental debuffs are explained only in wiki footnotes
Hard to tell which enemy is starting an AOE attack, since only the danger area on the floor is shown
Item balance is swingy: a few items carry a run while others ruin it, and level-up choices are sometimes all weak
Boss fights can demand specific builds, run long, and sometimes end a run with an instant-cast skill
Curses are effectively unavoidable and the downsides often outweigh the upside; one curse can destroy gems needed for permanent upgrades
Translation and skill wording are confusing (for example what 'shield absorption' means), and some relics read as nonsense
Enemy variety is limited, with stronger versions of the same foes, and dungeon layouts feel samey
Busy turns with many simultaneous triggered events make it hard to follow why you won or lost
Hard to read what is happening on your tile depending on camera angle, per a helpful negative review
improvements: Add tooltips for keywords, a proper icon glossary and real numeric values for items and skills
Show which enemy is causing each AOE telegraph
Let players decline or skip the intrusive tutorial pop-ups that cover half the screen
Rebalance items, curses and boss design so more build types are viable, and tame overpowered combos like the ice familiar stun
Make hub/meta upgrades and gold use more impactful and clearer about what gold is for
Fix Steam Deck/Windows launch problems, improve the translation, and vary audio and music more
unique_things: Mystery Dungeon/classic-roguelike style synchronized turns where every action, even attacking, is its own step
Blink teleport that does not cost a turn and recharges on room entry or after breaking enemies
Labyrinth that shifts as you move and a chessboard grid, described as a more accessible modern take on Brogue or Tangledeep-like design
Elemental system with debuffs and cross-element synergy as the main build axis
Mid-boss Familiars whose abilities you absorb and carry into later runs
Pace control: a turn-based game you can play fast or slow depending on the room
tedious_or_disliked: Intrusive tutorial prompts and the talking crown NPC interrupting play to explain things
Slow start and some grinding for soul shard/meta unlocks; 100% achievements need the free DLC and hard-mode boss clears
Controller inputs can be dropped while animations finish, causing accidental wrong-direction attacks that throw runs
Slot machines, cursed chests and curse deals widely seen as poor risk/reward, making chunks of each floor feel skippable
Long boss fights and repetitive room structure once you have seen what the game offers
Weak, generic story and dialogue per several critics
divisive_points: Replayability and depth: some call it a favourite that hooks them, others say meta progression feels thin and it is not something to return to after beating it
Difficulty: described as challenging without being too punishing by some, while others find bosses and curses unfair
Originality: praised as a fresh turn-based take on roguelikes, but one reviewer called it derivative and mobile-like
Audio and presentation: some love the art, others find the music and sound effects sleepy or limited
community.reception_notes: Launched on consoles first (Switch, PS4, Xbox One in autumn 2020 to 2021) and got generally positive critic scores (Metacritic 78-83 by platform). Steam reception is Very Positive. Estimated Steam gross revenue is about $3.16M (net to developer about $0.93M) and owners around 500k-1M per SteamSpy-style estimates; these are modelled figures, not audited. Steam is Windows-only; there were Steam Deck/Proton launch problems, with reviewers reporting that an older Proton version works. A recent Steam review says the developer stopped updating the game, and 100% achievements require the free Requiem of Elements DLC. Steam price is now about $4.99.
