games.name: Dicefolk
games.short_description: Wield magical dice and build a team of powerful Chimeras to stop a mysterious evil in this tactical roguelite adventure. As a Chimera Summoner, recruit and create your perfect team of mythical beasts and command them to victory using unique dice mechanics.

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to give this one a a uh a B tier.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Dicefolk is a turn-based deckbuilding-style roguelike where you run a team of three creatures (chimeras) and roll dice each turn to decide actions and positioning. He likes its cute-but-serious art style and its distinct gameplay, and finds the synergy-building satisfying. He finds it forgiving and fairly easy once the mechanics click. The main faults are a slow start with throwaway temporary creatures and a repetitive back half once a winning trio is locked in. Overall he calls it really solid and rates it B tier.
praise: Cute art style and vibe that still takes its story and characters fairly seriously
Unique dice-driven gameplay that feels different from the very start
Positioning of the three chimeras affects abilities, so switching and manipulating ally/enemy positions is strategic
Most dice faces give some benefit, so you rarely get screwed by a bad roll
Chimera abilities and item pairings allow very different builds; great feeling when a synergy comes together
Strong replayability because each run's creature lineup feels different
Plenty of content: events, berries, equipment, shops, new dice
criticism: Slow start: you begin with temporary creatures you do not care about until you find your first real chimera
Once you find your three-creature synergy (often by the second biome) there is no reason to change strategy, so the rest of the run is repetitive
Somewhat easy and forgiving once you understand the mechanics, with weak enemy dice
The enjoyable sweet spot in the middle feels too narrow; he wishes it were expanded
unique_points: Dice faces determine your available actions each turn, and you can choose which die to use, including the enemy's dice
Three-creature team with front-line positioning that interacts with abilities
Builds revolve around chimera synergies, such as movement-triggered buffs or damage-triggered effects
commentary.quote: it's just the game play being slow at the start and repetitive at the end
design_criteria: Visuals/charm: cute art and vibe weigh heavily in his appreciation
Gameplay uniqueness: dice-based turn system feels distinct from other deckbuilders
Synergies/build diversity: chimera and item combos create different strategies per run
Randomness/luck: dice luck is present but softened since most faces are useful
Difficulty: forgiving and easy once mastered
Pacing: slow opening and repetitive late game hurt it
Replayability: every run feels different due to varied chimeras
Content variety: events, shops, equipment, berries and new dice

community.one_liner: A tactical roguelite where you command a team of three Chimeras with dice-driven actions and, uniquely, also play out the enemy's dice each turn.
community.consensus_summary: Dicefolk is well received: Steam shows Very Positive (about 89% of roughly 1,130 reviews), critics land around 78-79 on OpenCritic/Metacritic (generally favourable), and the Switch version scores slightly higher on Metacritic. Praise centres on the clever 'you control both sides' dice combat, charming hand-drawn art and deep Chimera/equipment synergies. The recurring complaints are that runs feel samey, the game leans simplistic and RNG-heavy, and unlocking the large Chimera roster is slow. It is not early access; it released 27 Feb 2024 and kept receiving content (a paid Will Chimeras DLC and a large free update), and Steam reviews from 2026 show an active player base.
best_things: Signature combat twist: you roll and resolve the enemy's dice too, choosing order, targets and who rotates in, so fights feel like a puzzle where mistakes are your own fault
Synergy building between Chimeras, equipment and dice upgrades; 'busted' builds and one-turn boss kills feel great
Hand-drawn art, animations, clear UI with hover text and relaxed music get consistent praise
Large content pool: 100+ Chimeras (one review counts 129 with DLC), 100+ artifacts, 6 Tribes/classes, multiple challenge modes and difficulty tiers
Ascension-style difficulty adds buffs as well as challenge, so progression feels less punishing than Slay the Spire for some players
Less frustrating RNG than typical roguelikes: map always shows shops/upgrade nodes and the dice are manipulable
Good controller and Steam Deck support; accessible entry point for deckbuilder newcomers
Meta-goals like tracking which Chimeras you have won with and a compendium drive long play sessions (reviewers report 50-120 hours)
worst_things: Runs feel too similar; several reviewers quit after 3-10 runs because biomes, encounters and starting Chimeras vary little
Chimeras feel disposable: you keep swapping earlier ones for later finds and they do not grow in a meaningful way, which undercuts the creature-collector fantasy
Balance problems: some Chimeras and items are far stronger than others, and at high difficulty/modifiers some fights can become effectively unwinnable through bad random modifier combinations
Heavy RNG and thin decisions for some players: synergies are luck-dependent, and 'safe common synergies' become the default strategy
Battles can drag: long stretches of neutral actions and high Guard-dice uptime make many turns slow attrition
Narrative and world-building are thin; critics (Hardcore Gamer, Softpedia) note the lack of a compelling story
Some call it derivative or simplistic, with mediocre monster design compared with Pokemon or top deckbuilders
Price ($14.99) seen as steep by several negative and even positive reviewers (who suggest $7-9 or wait for sale)
improvements: Make runs more varied: more distinct biomes/encounter types and more differentiated starting teams
Let Chimeras grow or be invested in during a run (training/upgrading, or a catching mechanic) so attachment is not lost
Speed up the unlock curve for Chimeras so experimenting with only three per run is not so slow
Rebalance weak items/Chimeras and guard against unwinnable modifier rolls at higher difficulties
Shorten combat (cut neutral-action padding, tune Guard/healing stacking) and add a faster animation option
Fix map pathing annoyance (cannot change route once a destination is clicked), noted by MP1st, and add PC-specific options like rebindable controls (raised by one negative Steam review)
unique_things: You play both sides of each turn: the enemy's dice actions must all be used, so you choose how to minimize damage to yourself
Dice replace cards as the core resource; you upgrade and modify dice faces rather than build a deck
Three Chimeras rotate in a circular formation with leader position mattering
Creature-collector theming (shiny variants, shrines, compendium) fused with a Slay the Spire-style roguelite map
Items that carry downsides or curses, including one-time items that hurt now for permanent buffs, plus ascensions that grant buffs
Pokemon-adjacent cute aesthetic with non-pixel hand-drawn art
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding to unlock all Chimeras (one reviewer needed 10+ hours for the last compendium entry)
Long fights from repeated Guard/neutral actions and the amount of healing across artifacts
Repetition after the first handful of runs: same starting creatures and similar map flow
Losing earlier Chimeras as stronger ones replace them, making early-game picks feel meaningless
Randomly generated enemy modifiers and boss effects that can invalidate a build at high difficulty
Some players feel the core loop becomes number-crunching 'math micromanagement'
divisive_points: Controlling the enemy's turn: praised as a fresh tactical puzzle by most, but a few compare it to 'playing chess against yourself' and find it laborious
Difficulty: some find it forgiving and refreshing (winning early), others find it too easy to beat on the first try and less replayable
Replayability: 'endless' synergy experimentation and 100+ hour playtimes versus 'runs all feel the same'
Value: great at a sale or bundle price, too expensive at $14.99 for some
community.reception_notes: Released 27 Feb 2024 on PC (Steam, Windows only) and later on Switch; store listings also show iOS/Android. Critics were generally favourable at launch (OpenCritic 78, 80% recommend, ~24-25 reviews), with top scores from God is a Geek, Nintendo Life, TheSixthAxis and Gaming Nexus, and lower ones from Metro GameCentral and Pure Nintendo citing randomness and shortcomings. Metacritic user score is based on only 7 ratings (6.9), so it is not meaningful. The Will Chimeras Pack DLC (21 spellcasting Chimeras, 10 equipment) launched on Switch 24 Oct 2024 at $6.99 alongside a large free update (13-challenge special mode, 70+ equipment, four bosses, Fortune Talisman). Steam reviews through 2026 include 100+ hour players, and the store page shows ongoing art refreshes. Revenue estimates are rough (steam-revenue-calculator: about $237k gross, about $70k net; SteamSpy owners 50k-100k), not audited. A few negative Steam reviews call it a mobile port 'dumped' on PC and complain of missing PC settings.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Dungeon Clawer is a turn-based claw-machine roguelike in early access, where you fill a claw machine with items and grab them to drop onto enemies. He finds it very enjoyable and charming, and it does what it sets out to do well. His main gripes are that the base claw never improves, that missed grabs feel wasteful, and that the fixed final boss is too specific. He places it at a high B tier and is curious to see it after early access.
praise: Claw-machine premise is fun, with a clever pun title and a stop-motion trailer
Characters have unique abilities and suggest different item builds for the machine
Items added to the machine synergize with each other
Unique claws are very satisfying, if slightly overpowered
Sound design, especially the claw machine movement, is ASMR-like and satisfying
Music is good and relics/upgrades are pretty good
Works well on Steam Deck
criticism: A good grab feels great but a miss feels terrible and wastes a lot of time
Limited strategy in how to grab; items are loose and easily dropped
The normal claw is always identical with no way to upgrade it
Final boss is always the same with a specific mechanic, so it can be too punishing or too easy depending on build
Core gameplay could be more sophisticated
unique_points: A claw machine turned into a turn-based roguelike, with two claws per turn grabbing items to drop on enemies
Build around adding item types (e.g. metal) to the machine itself, varying by character
commentary.quote: this game does what it's trying to do very well
design_criteria: Core gameplay feel: satisfaction of grabbing with the claw, but misses are punishing on time
Synergies: machine items combine and differ per character
Character diversity: unique abilities encourage distinct builds
Meta-progression: unlocking new characters drove his enjoyment
Boss design: fixed final boss feels too specific and not broad
Audio: claw sound design and music are standout
Upgrade depth: base claw lacks upgrades while unique claws are strong
Charm/theme: novel claw machine concept and stop-motion trailer
Content: early access, more content expected
commentary.rerank_note: First early access game on the list; he reviews it in its current state and notes the rating may improve after full release.

community.one_liner: A roguelike deckbuilder where your 'deck' is a pile of weapons and items in a physics-based claw machine, and you grab them turn by turn to fight through a 20-floor dungeon.
community.consensus_summary: Players rate it Very Positive on Steam (about 89-91% positive across roughly 2.4k-4k reviews, depending on the snapshot), and the core idea of clawing your attack turn is widely called satisfying and surprisingly addictive. The 1.0 release came on April 30, 2026 after Early Access that began in November 2024, and the developer kept shipping new characters and items through and after launch. The long-running complaints are heavy RNG (where items land, which combos you draw), weak balance across a bloated item pool, a single repeating final boss, and runs that take 30-60 minutes. Critic coverage is thin: Metacritic lists only three Switch reviews (78-80 from two outlets, 60 from a third) and no final Metascore, and no OpenCritic page was confirmed. It is a niche, well-liked indie with a dedicated following rather than a critical darling.
best_things: The claw itself is fun and tactile: grabbing a cluster of items for a huge damage turn, or fumbling a grab, produces a constant dopamine-and-frustration loop
Strong 'one more run' pull, with some long-time roguelite fans comparing playtime to Balatro, Slay the Spire and Monster Train
Large cast of characters with distinct playstyles and many viable build archetypes (poison, frost, fire, melee and strength, gold/money builds)
Cute, charming art and animations (bunny protagonist, strong intro and ending animations) that give it a distinct identity
Easy to pick up; cheap price and a lot of hours for the money, with a cheap Steam price noted by several reviewers
Token system that lets you nudge the odds of getting certain item types
Frequent free updates adding new characters, items, pachinko/slot style minigames and difficulty changes during Early Access and after 1.0
Relaxing enough to play casually or while watching something; full controller support
worst_things: Heavy RNG in both item drops and physics: key items land in corners, get stuck out of reach, or get flung out of the machine, and a run can be lost before your build comes together

Balance is poor: many items are niche or never used, some characters are near-automatic wins while others need very specific pieces, and several builds (fire vs poison, water items with little water support) are seen as redundant or weak
Item pool bloat from each update's new characters makes builds more RNG-dependent; some players say it now feels like a slot machine rather than a claw machine
Only one final boss regardless of character or difficulty, and limited enemy and boss variety, so runs feel repetitive after the first few wins
Difficulty spikes: enemies that are trivial and then one-shot you, and a last boss that floods the machine with debuffs and counters some builds outright
Long runs (about 30-60 minutes even on the fastest speed) with mundane early fights; some say time-to-fun is poor
Shallow meta-progression: unlocks are mostly tied to winning runs with each character, and higher 'Debt' difficulties mostly raise enemy damage
Basic, unattractive map navigation screen
Losses often feel unearned: enemies that are easy until they suddenly one-shot you, so a run can end on a bad grab or bad item spawn rather than a decision (top-voted negative Steam review)
improvements: Add more bosses, enemies and act variety, especially alternate final bosses
Let unlocked claws/paws be used by other characters immediately instead of requiring a winning run with each character first
Add claw-machine-level modifiers or tools (extra grabs, bigger claws, a shake/jostle to reset a stuck board, swappable claws) to reduce dead runs from bad item placement
Rebalance the item pool and trim dead items; give materials/alchemy/transmutation and water-themed items real payoff
Stronger meta-progression and more customization, plus more music and layout variety

Respect player time with a faster-than-fastest speed setting, shorter run option, or skippable long minigames (slot machine minigame repeatedly called too slow); also requested: modding support, a short opt-in tutorial, and mobile cross-platform progression
unique_things: Combines a real physics claw machine with deckbuilder and roguelike structure, so your 'hand' is whatever the claw manages to hold
Items can be given different materials (for example floating or buffed ones) that change how they behave in the machine
Pachinko, slot and other gamble-style minigames and mystery locations mix into the dungeon route
Claw-specific 'paws' per character and escalating difficulty levels (reviewers mention 'anger' levels; the store/dev term may be 'Debt') that add handicaps
Rare genre mix: very few games make a claw machine the central mechanic, and it also exists on mobile/Switch/consoles
tedious_or_disliked: Stalemates where a scaling item is stuck in an unreachable corner, the enemy cannot kill you, and the battle drags on
Having to win a run with every character before unlocking their paws/items for others, which slows experimentation
Relearning the game after updates that add characters or rework the difficulty system, particularly for completionists chasing achievements
Slot machine minigame and long fights in early floors that get skipped or endured
Repetitive runs after the first win: once a combo is set around floors 7-9, the remaining floors play out identically
divisive_points: Luck versus skill: some reviewers say the later updates added real strategy and it is not luck based, while others say it is now pure lottery
Difficulty: some call it one of the hardest roguelites they have played, while others say experienced roguelite players can 'moonwalk' to victory or win on the first run
Content and value: fans with 100-200 hours call it a must-buy at its price, while others say the content runs out after 10 hours and is not worth $14.99
Frequent content updates are praised by most but seen by some as bloating the item pool and breaking balance
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched November 21, 2024 and 1.0 shipped April 30, 2026 on Windows, macOS and Linux, with ports to iOS, Switch, Xbox Series and PS5 listed on Metacritic (a mobile version also exists, and one reviewer mentions Play Pass on the app store). Reception during Early Access was already strongly positive; post-1.0 reviews split more, with criticism about balance, a bloated item pool and repetition, while recent reviews sit around 81% positive. Metacritic currently lists only three Switch critic reviews (avg about 73; 80, 78, 60) and shows both Metascore and user score as pending until 4 reviews/ratings; I could not confirm an OpenCritic listing. Revenue estimate from a Boxleiter-style tool: about $701k gross and $207k net on Steam, with SteamSpy owners at 200k-500k (order-of-magnitude only; actual copies not published). Price $14.99 at launch, with a Supporter Pack and Soundtrack DLC (one reviewer questioned the supporter pack). WebSearch budget was exhausted in this session, so no Reddit threads or outlet reviews beyond Metacritic's summaries could be read.

games.name: Emberward
games.short_description: Build twisting mazes with tetromino blocks and deploy unique towers in this strategic roguelite tower defense adventure!

other_scores.score: About $809k gross and $239k net estimated; SteamSpy owners 100k-200k

placements.verbal_evidence: none

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Emberward is an early-access roguelike that fuses tower defense with Tetris-style block placement: you lay blocks to build the enemy path into a maze, then place towers on it. He thinks the two-layer puzzle gameplay is very enjoyable and that the game improved notably during early access. His main complaints are pacing within the short six-wave levels, being flooded with blocks and money, and low difficulty. He places it on the board with no tier letter spoken, only that it could rise higher if the developers fix his issues.
praise: Combining tower defense with Tetris-block path building creates a fresh, puzzle-like maze-building hook
Relics synergize with specific tower types (e.g. electric towers triggering on poison) without being too restrictive to pursue
Early-access updates fixed his earlier complaints, including boring relics and too many take-damage relics
Level restrictions such as frozen zones and the drawing tool for planning enemy routes are great
Towers are unique and some have placement requirements; block tiles with element boosts reward matching towers
Boss fights, varied levels, unique starting characters and straightforward meta-progression add plenty of content
Visuals have a recognizable vibe for a tower defense game
criticism: Pacing problem inside levels: he is given so many blocks and towers so quickly that by wave five or six he places things randomly
Hand gets overloaded with blocks and chests give more blocks and money he has no time or space to use
Towers are shallow: place one and pick one of two upgrades, with no good way to spend the large surplus of money
Easy for tower defense veterans, winning even on the hardest difficulty while playing sloppily
Some giant creatures feel out of place visually
Restarting at wave one each level is inherently awkward for the genre hybrid and leaves the endgame of a level thin
unique_points: Building the enemy path with Tetris blocks turns level layout itself into a puzzle layered over tower defense
Runs are compressed to six waves with rapid resource gain as a deliberate fix for tower defense being slow for a roguelike, though it causes pacing tradeoffs
Genre hybrid is inherently hard: tower defense favors slow buildup while roguelikes favor fast iteration
commentary.quote: if you like tower defense games... I think this game is very enjoyable.
design_criteria: Genre fusion: whether combining tower defense with a roguelike works given pacing differences
Synergies: relic and tower combos that are meaningful but not restrictive
Relic design: dislikes 'if you take damage' relics in a game where damage is bad
Pacing: level length and resource flow, too much given too fast
Difficulty: too easy on top difficulty for genre players
Level design: restrictions and planning tools add interest
Meta-progression: basic stat upgrades, straightforward
Visuals: recognizable vibe, some oversized creatures
Content: bosses, levels, and characters
Run length: short six-wave levels keep runs from lasting hours
commentary.rerank_note: He had considered including it in an earlier tier list a few months ago but held off due to issues; it has since improved. Early access, and he says it could rise higher if the developers fix his issues.

community.one_liner: A roguelite tower defense game by Refic Games where you draw tetromino wall blocks from a deck to build a maze, then place towers, with heroes, flames (starting modifiers), runes and relics across short stages.
community.consensus_summary: Emberward is received as a very well-liked, polished maze-building tower defense game: Steam shows Overwhelmingly Positive (about 96.7% of roughly 4,300 reviews, with recent reviews slightly lower at roughly 94% Very Positive). Praise centres on the tetromino-as-cards mazing, tower variety and a responsive developer who shipped frequent updates through a long Early Access period before the 1.0 release in September 2026. Negative reviews are a minority but consistent: the game is too easy even on the top difficulty, runs and stages feel samey, relics and enemies have little strategic impact, and some felt 1.0 changes were a step sideways. Metacritic and OpenCritic had no critic or user scores at the time of checking, so reception is essentially Steam-player driven.
best_things: Mazing as a separate card-based resource from towers (tetromino wall cards drawn from a deck) gives freedom to shape enemy paths, praised as reviving Warcraft 3 custom-map TD nostalgia
Large variety of towers (single target, AoE, slow, elemental, and odd ones like towers you feed other towers into) plus relics/trinkets and artifacts that open different builds
Multiple heroes with distinct abilities, varied maps with terrain mechanics, and modes such as Endless, challenges, daily/weekly challenges and leaderboards that extend replay value
Polish: clean UI, smooth performance, good art/animation/sound on towers and enemies; runs well on Steam Deck and got controller support
Short-session friendliness: maps can be played in about 15 minutes, with mini-runs for limited time, and a 'just one more turn' pull
Very active, responsive developer with frequent updates, holiday content and QoL additions (damage-per-turn readouts, block texture cosmetics, talent grid reset)
Good value for price: reviewers report hundreds of hours, including 500+ hours across Early Access
worst_things: Too easy: multiple reviewers say even Heroic is trivial for TD veterans, with generous gold, blocks and rerolls letting you build a rough maze and spam towers; real challenge only comes from self-imposed modifiers, shards or Endless
Enemy design has little strategic influence; players say they never check what is coming or adjust towers to enemy types
Relics/perks and run RNG feel inconsequential or obvious picks, and relics and towers rarely interact in meaningful synergies
Stages and runs feel repetitive: every map starts from one turret and resets, and campaign maps repeat, so the roguelite variance feels shallow
Balance issues: some builds are far stronger (lightning, torch tower, a single element stacked wins), while the developer's nerfs of fun-feeling towers frustrate others
Interface/controls complaints from some: imprecise targeting of power-up cards without pausing, cluttered systems, no rebindable keybinds, mobile-like feel
Missing or sparse patch notes for frequent hotfixes, plus some unclear tooltips (buffs like poison show only a name)
Small effective tower/enemy pool: several reviewers say most towers are useless so they end up using only one or two, and the same enemies, towers and maps appear even after years of updates
improvements: Raise the difficulty ceiling and smooth the wave difficulty curve; early waves can need no input and then hit sudden HP spikes mid-level
Scarcer resources (fewer blocks, less gold, fewer enemies per wave) so placement decisions carry more weight, as one reviewer suggested
More enemy variety and special enemy mechanics that force different tower choices
Deeper relic/tower synergies and build-defining items so runs diverge
Better discoverability: publish hotfix patch notes, clearer buff/effect tooltips, rebindable keys and improved card-targeting UI

More content depth: more maps, different music (the soundtrack is called generic and repetitive), and meaningful reasons to continue past the victory screen rather than the optional 'more waves' button
unique_things: Tetris-style wall pieces are cards in a deck you draw each turn, decoupling maze construction from tower placement
Roguelite structure built from many short tower defense stages with shops, forges and events, rather than one long map
Flames/shards system to customise starting modifiers and scale difficulty, plus heroes with distinct abilities
Wide tower roster with oddities such as poison, drone and D20 luck-based towers, plus a tower you power up by feeding it others
Modes like Endless (80+ stages) and the fast-paced Enigma Sanctum, with daily/weekly challenges and leaderboards
Card enhancement with runes and mid-wave active options that keep attention on maze and towers
tedious_or_disliked: Rebuilding the maze from scratch every stage makes some players feel no attachment to their defences and find runs repetitive
Mid-to-late waves turn into chucking extra blocks to lengthen the path and placing towers absentmindedly because gold is abundant
Run length: some find stages too long to feel snappy yet too short to feel like a full experience, while others want shorter runs
Stale after around 10 to 30 hours for several reviewers who stop because they see the same towers, enemies, and maps
divisive_points: Difficulty: many praise accessible, relaxing play and the ability to self-tune challenge, while veterans find it a snooze and cite Defense Grid, Dungeon Warfare 3 or Variables 2 as more demanding
1.0 update direction: some say it improved (new stage, towers, QoL), while a 162-hour reviewer felt it less complete and misread Early Access feedback
Developer balance approach: frequent nerfs and daily hotfixes read as responsive to some and heavy-handed or undocumented to others
Roguelite structure fit for tower defense: some love the short-encounter variety, others want to invest in a single persistent map
community.reception_notes: Long Early Access period (reviews from late 2025 onward, some with 500+ EA hours) followed by 1.0 on Sep 17, 2026 at roughly $16.99 on Steam (Windows only; mac/linux not supported). Daily-ish hotfixes after launch drew requests for patch notes. Controller support and Steam Deck play were added and praised. Metacritic listed zero critic and zero user reviews at time of fetch, and OpenCritic returned nothing, so there are no professional scores. Web search quota was exhausted, so no outlet reviews or Reddit threads could be read; this summary relies on Steam reviews, the store and community pages, and the revenue estimate site. Figures across snapshots (review counts, price, developer name on the calculator) are inconsistent, suggesting cached pages.

games.name: Heroes of Hammerwatch II
games.short_description: A rogue-lite action-rpg that offers extensive persistent progression. Build your town, upgrade and equip your heroes, before taking on the ever-changing Dark Citadel - either solo or with a team of friends.

other_scores.source: TheSixthAxis (via Metacritic, only critic review, no Metascore yet)

placements.verbal_evidence: I think Heroes of Hammerrath 2 is going to be a very high B tier

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Heroes of Hammerwatch II is a top-down action-adventure roguelike sequel where you start in a village, push through fixed biomes (forest, cave, church, and so on) to a final boss, and rebuild the village between runs. He disliked the original somewhat but enjoyed this one enough to finish it twice. He loves the exploration, visuals, village-building meta progression and epic bosses, but finds the gameplay very simple and repetitive, with samey room-and-enemy levels. After beating the final boss he felt done. He places it at a very high B tier.
praise: Very nice, immersive visuals and environment that give a real sense of adventure
Village meta progression: new buildings and NPCs unlock new abilities after each death
Persistent character levelling with freedom to pick or switch classes at any time
Subclasses change playstyle drastically and make you much more powerful
Run-only abilities and items have cool effects and are enjoyable
Boss fights feel epic, killing huge monsters as a tiny character
Strong drive to upgrade and see the next area or boss; a solid sequel
criticism: Gameplay is extremely simple and gets repetitive, doing the same ability the same way
Levels are repetitive, mostly rooms of enemies despite good visuals
Characters and monsters are hard to see
Subclass unlocks arrive very late (about 70% through playtime)
Little reason to continue after the final boss; no hidden worlds or biomes like the first game's DLC
unique_points: Village-building meta progression gives an almost RuneScape-like feel of a persistent character
Fixed biome and boss order makes it about full exploration from village to deep final layer
Subclass system dramatically reshapes play, though gated late
commentary.quote: a very high B tier for a game that I really had an absolute blast
design_criteria: Meta-progression: village buildings, NPCs and persistent character praised as most satisfying part
Exploration/discovery: main enjoyment driver, but runs out after final boss
Visuals/atmosphere: immersive, though characters and monsters are hard to see
Gameplay depth: too simple and repetitive, same abilities used throughout
Level design: visually good but repetitive rooms of enemies
Boss design: epic feel despite simple combat
Class/subclass variety: subclass transformative but unlocked too late
Replayability/content: no hidden worlds, game feels finished after the final boss

community.one_liner: A pixel-art twin-stick action-RPG roguelite from Crackshell (published by Team17) where you build up a hub town, level seven classes and push through the Dark Citadel solo or in 4-player co-op, then grind endless New Game+ tiers.
community.consensus_summary: Players rate it Very Positive on Steam (about 82% of roughly 6,600 reviews, with the store page showing Mixed, about 69%, for the most recent 30 days), and it appears to have sold well (Boxleiter-style estimates of 1-2M owners, about $3.4M gross). The praise is for the snappy twin-stick combat, class variety, the account-wide meta-progression and co-op. The criticism is that it is light on roguelite variety (same zones in the same order), long-run balance collapses in New Game+, and content has been thin since the 1.0 launch in January 2025. Critic coverage is almost absent: Metacritic has one critic review (TheSixthAxis, 100) and no Metascore yet, and I could not find an OpenCritic page. It is fully released, not early access, and has received free updates (Epic Missions, Epic Weapons, hotfixes) plus the paid Celestial Ruins DLC with a new class. Some long-time fans now feel the developers are monetising a stagnant game.
best_things: Snappy, satisfying dual-stick combat with kiting; auto-fire skills and big lightning or piercing attacks that clear hallways of enemies feel great
Seven classes with three specialisations each; classes play distinctly and encourage experimenting
Account-wide buffs from levelling every class mean alternate characters make real progress, so you always keep something after a run
Town building and upgrades give a sticky long-term progression loop; the town is shared across characters and you keep most of your resources
Co-op for up to four players is a highlight, with easy drop-in and drop-out and the ability to leave and resume a run later; a Gauntlet-like slow-burn feel
Gorgeous pixel art, good lighting and effects, strong sound design; a solid sequel improvement over the first game's pacing
Runs are quittable and resumable at area boundaries, which suits short sessions and Steam Deck play
Responsive dev support on save problems and free post-launch updates that added missions, weapons and mode variety
worst_things: Roguelite elements are thin: the main run goes through the same zones in the same order with only tile and enemy shuffling, so runs feel alike
Late-game and New Game+ scaling breaks: enemy HP grows faster than gear and trinkets, some subclasses become too weak, and you eventually get one-shot with nothing to counter it
Content is limited after 1.0 (few bosses, maps, legendary gear); reviewers call it barebones or like an early-access game and feel 2025 roadmap promises were underdelivered
Character builds lack depth: no skill trees, upgrades are mostly flat stat increases, and loot is many tiny numerical bonuses with little identity
Save-file loss and character-deletion bugs reported by multiple players, including after updates, with some needing support tickets to restore backups
Balance issues: non-piercing weapons and single-hit defensive skills are weak at high difficulty, making some classes (e.g. Ranger) worse
Slow health and mana regeneration leaves you waiting between fights, and the screen can get cluttered by effects so you cannot read what is happening
Paid DLC (Celestial Ruins) drew anger from some players who say it should have been base-game content and that updates are scarce
improvements: More variety in tilesets, zone order, bosses and maps so runs differ more, which is the most common request
More build-defining depth: talent or skill trees, more abilities earlier, and loot with distinctive effects instead of small flat stats
Rebalance late-game and NG+ scaling so gear, trinkets and weak subclasses keep pace, and fix useless defensive skills and non-piercing weapons
Reliable cloud saves and save-loss fixes, plus an easy manual backup and copy option
Quality-of-life: faster out-of-combat regen, less visual clutter, local co-op, and more language translations (e.g. Spanish) requested on Steam forums
Deliver a larger post-launch roadmap with more maps, bosses and legendary gear
unique_things: Blends a Diablo-style ARPG with a roguelite meta-loop, built around a persistent town with NPCs and building upgrades
Account-wide class-level bonuses apply to every character, so alternate classes keep pushing your main roster forward
Dual-stick shooter-style combat with cooldown abilities, reminiscent of Gauntlet and Children of Morta
You can leave a run mid-dungeon at a level boundary and resume it later, including in multiplayer
Endless New Game+ tiers and one-time special maps unlocked through the town
Keep most resources on death (with a penalty of roughly 40% of carried gold and materials), so failure still yields progress
tedious_or_disliked: The early hours are a grind of the first zones; dozens of hours to build out the town and vendors in single-player
Re-fighting identical maps and enemies in the same positions and order across runs, including late game
Runs that turn into kiting huge mobs for long stretches once you are outscaled, with hundreds of enemies per floor on high difficulty
Waiting for health or mana to regenerate between encounters, sometimes alt-tabbing while you wait
Some permanent upgrades are per-character, so starting another class means regrinding
Control complexity for some: aiming, moving, dashing and managing several cooldowns at once (a reviewer refunded after 36 minutes)
divisive_points: Difficulty and pacing: some find it never unfair and even a bit easy, others call the early game a gear-check grind and the late game a slog
Whether it is really a roguelite: fans enjoy the slow-burn RPG progression, others say the roguelike mechanics barely matter
Value: many say it is worth the $20 and hundreds of hours, especially in co-op, while others say content runs out after 15-20 hours
Post-launch support and DLC: praised for free updates and dev responsiveness, but criticised as too sparse and monetised
community.reception_notes: Launched as a full 1.0 release on 14 Jan 2025 (Windows only, $19.99, Steam). Early reception was positive from players and TheSixthAxis gave a glowing review centred on NG+ replayability; Metacritic has only 1 critic review so no Metascore, and user score is 6.7 from 9 ratings. Steam ratings drifted: Very Positive overall but Mixed for the last 30 days as of the store page I fetched, with negative reviews in 2026 citing stagnant content, the paid Celestial Ruins DLC (new class, priced separately or in a Deluxe Edition) and lost saves after updates. The studio shipped free Epic Missions and Epic Weapons updates and hotfixes, and players mention a 2026 roadmap; some call that roadmap an undersell. Steam Deck works well per player reports, though sleep/resume can cause lag. Steam owner estimates are 1-2M and gross revenue estimates about $3.4M per steam-revenue-calculator (rough). Searches were unavailable (budget exhausted), so critic coverage beyond Metacritic could not be checked and OpenCritic was not located; Reddit was not fetchable.

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put this currently as uh you know like a probably like a lower B tier

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Let Him Cook is a food-themed horde-survival game in early access that uses waves and a between-wave shop rather than level-up upgrades. You carry two weapons and hire assistants who hold weapons and bring their own mechanics. He loves the jazzy music, comedic enemy designs, charm and exceptionally clear UI. He is bothered by balance problems, boss rules that nullify some builds, and a food-family mechanic that does not really change how he builds. He slots it currently in lower B with room to climb as it develops.
praise: Wave-and-shop structure with two weapon slots plus hired assistants that carry weapons and create synergies
Music is super jazzy, and parts of gameplay sync to the beat, such as the game slowing just before the beat drops

community.one_liner: A top-down, music-synced action survivor roguelite (Vampire Survivors / Brotato style) where you play a kitchen professional fighting food-pun enemies in a bullet-hell kitchen; solo dev Manny Feliciano (HF Studios), Steam Early Access since June 19, 2024.
community.consensus_summary: Coverage is extremely thin: there are only about 40 Steam reviews (39 positive, 1 negative, roughly 97% Positive), no Metacritic or OpenCritic scores, and no major outlet reviews or large Reddit threads that could be retrieved. Players who have played it praise the enemy and weapon variety, the challenging bosses and the store-page music-sync hook. The recurring worry is developer inactivity: one negative review says there had been no updates in over a year, a Steam forum thread asks whether the game is abandoned (March 2025), and a recent positive review (mid-2026) still hopes the dev will finish it. The Steam store page, however, states a planned full release between late 2026 and early 2027 with roughly four times the content. Treat it as a small, cheap, promising but uncertain Early Access title.
best_things: Enemy variety: one reviewer says enemies differ enough to keep each run fresh, unlike many survivor-likes
Weapons feel distinct, with many combinations possible (store page lists around 25 weapons)
Bosses feel like real bosses and are described as challenging
Music is a core mechanic (music-synced maps, per the store page and studio site)
Food-industry theme with live food puns and cartoony hand-drawn 2.5D art gives it personality
Class variety (store page says 10+ playable characters; the studio site lists Executive Chef, Sous Chef, Bartender, Butcher)
Cheap price ($6.99 USD, roughly $5 in regional pricing) and a free demo
Described by one player as a mix of Vampire Survivors and Brotato, with an endless mode and an achievement encyclopedia
worst_things: Seemingly stalled development: a negative Steam review cites no updates in over a year and calls it abandoned
A Steam forum thread titled 'Abandoned Game?' (March 2025) shows the same concern
Bug reports on the Steam forum: character unlock problems, a 'Chicken Fingers' character bug, controller menu navigation, trouble starting a run
Windows only (no Mac or Linux)
Very small player base, so little community content, guides or discussion
improvements: Ship the promised full release with the planned ~4x content (more bosses, characters, enemies, weapons)
Communicate a clear roadmap and update cadence (the studio site only points to Discord for news)
Fix unlock, character and controller menu bugs reported on the forum
Improve language and localization options
Address early-game balance and luck dependence raised in a forum thread ('Early Game Woes and Luck')
unique_things: Kitchen and restaurant theme: hero classes like Executive Chef, Sous Chef, Bartender and Butcher, with weapons such as chef's knife, peeler, salt rifle and cleaver
Hiring assistants as part of the run
Music-synced maps where the soundtrack drives the gameplay
Food-pun enemies and a humorous tone
Hand-drawn cartoony 2.5D presentation for a survivor-like
tedious_or_disliked: Waiting on updates: the stalled Early Access status is the main complaint
Early-game difficulty and dependence on luck, per a forum thread title (details not retrievable)
Unlocking characters is reportedly buggy, which makes progression frustrating for some
divisive_points: Whether the game is abandoned (forum and negative review) or still in active development (store page plans a late 2026 to early 2027 full release)
Whether it is 'better than most Vampire Survivors-likes' (one positive reviewer) or simply another entry in a crowded genre (no critic coverage to confirm either view)
community.reception_notes: Early Access launch June 19, 2024 at $6.99 USD with a free demo. Steam reviews are tiny in number but strongly positive. Developer activity appears to have slowed after 2024 to early 2025 (forum threads cluster July 2024 to January 2025; 'Abandoned Game?' thread March 2025; a Feb 2026 negative review says no updates in over a year). The store page nonetheless lists a full release window of late 2026 to early 2027 and says price will not change at full release. A June 2026 positive review still hopes the dev finishes the game. Metacritic has a page for the game but shows TBD for both critic and user scores. No OpenCritic entry found. Not on Mac or Linux. Revenue and copies-sold figures are unavailable or unreliable (SteamSpy range 0 to 20,000 owners). Note: a separate game 'Don't Let Him Cook' (appid 5043060) exists and should not be confused with it. Research limitation: WebSearch budget was exhausted, so no search-based outlet reviews or Reddit discussion were obtained and Reddit fetch was blocked; findings rest on Steam data, the Steam store page, the Steam forum summary, the studio site and Metacritic.

commentary.summary: Paper Planet is a cute, hand-drawn, paper-styled bullet-hell roguelike where you defend a small planet with a turret that slides left and right and teleports to the opposite side. Runs are extremely chaotic and usually end with the screen flooded with bullets. He enjoys the vibe, the simple core loop and the boss fights, but finds runs too samey, the meta progression weak, and the game too easily overpowered. He calls it a fun mess worth a few runs and places it in B tier for now.

Simple extra block mechanic for red bullets used sparingly

Power fantasy balance: being overpowered is satisfying but hurts reward when constant
Core gameplay: simple and enjoyable controls and mechanics
Item variety: cool items that create different chaos each run
Boss design: mechanic-driven bosses demanding attention
Run variety/content: same biomes and few bosses make runs repetitive

community.one_liner: A planet-defender arcade roguelike from Doodlegames (published by 2 Left Thumbs) where you fend off waves and bosses from a stationary circular planet with a hand-drawn, Flash-style look, using wildly synergistic items, in 1-4 player local co-op.
community.consensus_summary: Paper Planet is a small, niche Steam roguelite rated Very Positive (about 84% of roughly 530 reviews, per Steam data pulled locally; the store page shows 89% of 380 for one filter). Players like the doodle art, the chaotic item synergies and the couch co-op, and several say it is fun on sale. Complaints are about luck-dependent balance where you need a broken build or boss fights drag, a short content loop (one reviewer says they finished everything in about 2 hours), and achievements that have stayed broken for years. Critic coverage is essentially nonexistent: Metacritic has a page with no critic reviews and only one user rating, and no OpenCritic entry was found. Community threads include a 'Game abandoned?' topic, and a player review from 2026 says some achievements have been broken for over 2 years, so it reads as lightly supported since launch (Aug 2023). I could not retrieve patch notes, so update cadence is unconfirmed.
best_things: Hand-drawn, notebook-doodle, Flash-game art style that is coherent and charming
Item synergies are wacky and build-defining (bee-bullet swarms, electric walls, teleporting rocket bombs, bullet recycling)
1-4 player local couch co-op with Remote Play Together, good for chaotic party play
Lots of unlockable planets/characters, modes, modifiers and visuals tied to achievements
Option to skip the metaprogression grind and unlock everything immediately (praised by a 21-hour reviewer)
Fast, pick-up-and-play arcade runs with enough variety to be 'highly addictive' for a few hours
worst_things: Balance is lopsided: runs depend on getting a broken build, and without one boss fights become minutes of low-damage waiting
Most stats feel nearly meaningless; bullet count, fire rate and bullet recycling dominate while raw damage does little
At least 8 achievements reported broken for over 2 years, and '100% is bugged' is repeated in multiple reviews
Heavily luck-based, leaving little room for player skill according to some reviewers
Item upgrades lack descriptions, so players can't tell what they are picking (one review and a Steam discussion about item descriptions not showing)
Content runs out fast for some, with the loop feeling repetitive after an hour or two
Performance issues such as FPS drops in boss fights and lag from heavy bullet counts
Seen as too pricey for its content at $14.99 by at least one reviewer, even on discount
improvements: Fix the long-broken achievements so 100% completion is possible
Rebalance damage vs. fire rate/bullet count so that stats matter and weak runs are not a slog
Show clear item and upgrade descriptions in-game
Fix boss-fight FPS drops and raise the damage-counter integer cap (requested in Steam threads)
Add more content and variety to extend replay beyond a few hours
Visible developer communication and updates, since players ask whether the game is abandoned
unique_things: You defend a fixed circular planet that cannot move, described by one reviewer as Asteroids without movement
Blend of arcade bullet-hell shooter and tower-defense style planet defense
Flash/doodle aesthetic with a school-notebook vibe, cartoony and family friendly
Items combine freely with each other, leading to absurd overpowered runs
Local co-op for up to four players on one screen
A switch to unlock all metaprogression immediately, unusual for the genre
tedious_or_disliked: Boss fights that take minutes when your build is weak and you deal little damage
Waves of high-health enemies that become boring without good items
Achievement hunting blocked by bugs
Repetitive feeling after the first hour or two for some players
Chaotic screen with no item descriptions, making it hard to read what is happening
divisive_points: Randomness: some love wild, chaotic build luck; others find it too luck-driven with too little skill
Value: some call it a great casual game, others say it is too expensive and too short for the price
Chaos level: fun mayhem for some, unreadable for others who bounced in under an hour
community.reception_notes: Released Aug 21, 2023 on Windows only (no Mac/Linux), $14.99. Launch reception was positive among Steam players and it has stayed Very Positive, but it never drew critic coverage (Metacritic lists 0 critic reviews and a single 7/10 user rating from March 2024, with both scores 'tbd'). Steam discussions show user concern about abandonment, unlockable achievements that never worked, and FPS drops during bosses; a 2026 review says achievements have been broken for over 2 years, suggesting sparse post-launch support. I could not fetch patch notes or Reddit (Reddit blocked, WebSearch budget exhausted), so the update history is unverified. Revenue and owner figures are third-party estimates, not audited numbers.

games.name: Pogo Rogue

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Pogo Rogue is a free action roguelike where you ride a pogo stick up through levels, using your weapon's recoil to propel yourself. He first played it in early access, found the precise controls too hard and the game too thin, and expected to give it a C. After replaying the full release he found it much more forgiving, with more roguelike content and a big hub. He places it in B tier as a small, charming game with a unique twist, and praises the developers for making it approachable.

Full release is much more forgiving, with more room for mistakes (likely bigger levels and less annoying enemies)
Many weapons that feel very different because each gives different propulsion
Abilities (hat that shoots, jetpack, propeller) drastically change gameplay
Added hub world with lots to do
Free to play, which he finds remarkable for the quality

Early access version was too hard and not enthralling enough
Many players will try it for a few minutes and drop it due to inherent pogo difficulty

Meta-progression/hub: added hub world with content
Uniqueness of core gimmick: pogo mechanic is the hook
Scope: small game with limited content
commentary.rerank_note: Originally expected to give it C after early access; replaying the full release moved it up to B.

community.one_liner: A free, student-made 2D roguelite action-platformer where you ascend a factory by constantly bouncing on a pogo stick, using procedurally generated weapons, passives and active items.
community.consensus_summary: Pogo Rogue is a small, free Windows-only game from Bounce Back Games, made by University of Utah Division of Games students. It has a Very Positive Steam rating (196 positive of 213 reviews, about 92%). Players praise the tight, skill-based pogo movement, the addictive one-more-run loop and the fact that it costs nothing. The main friction is a steep learning curve for the movement and early difficulty, plus modest content length. It left Early Access in November 2024 with a final content drop, and the team said most members had moved on, so only occasional bug fixes were expected. Community discussion is sparse and there are no critic reviews, so the picture rests mostly on a few hundred Steam reviews and forum posts.
best_things: The pogo-stick movement system is distinctive and, once learned, feels natural and very satisfying (wall jumping and speedrunning get specific mention)
Addictive one-more-run loop; several reviewers say they lost hours unexpectedly
Variety of weapons, passive items, active items and synergy items keeps runs different thanks to procedural generation
Bosses are singled out as a highlight by long-time players (one reviewer with several hundred hours)
Free to play, and reviewers say the quality is well above what a free student game should be
Runs well on low-end hardware, Linux via Proton and Steam Deck; tiny install (around 100MB, i3 and 4GB RAM minimum)
worst_things: Steep, unforgiving early difficulty; one reviewer dropped after many deaths following only two boss kills
Movement takes a long time to learn before it clicks, and the tutorial does not fully explain it
Some players get stuck on level-navigation obstacles (for example a reviewer who could not work out how to get past a metal ceiling in the first area) and leave a negative review
Reports of bugs on the Steam forum: a solid-box hive item breaking, and the Constructus enemy leaving its arena
Occasional lag spikes reported on Steam Deck despite generally good performance
Windows only on Steam (no native Mac or Linux build)
improvements: Better onboarding and tutorials for the pogo movement and first-area obstacles
Control scheme options and more rebinding and controller-related settings were requested on the forum
Ability to swap active items, requested by players
More content: at least one reviewer calls it a little short
Balance fixes for exploits; a forum thread discusses a game-breaking strategy
Continued bug-fix support, since active development ended with the full release
unique_things: Entire movement is built around a constantly bouncing pogo stick, which makes it closer to a precision platformer than a typical combat-first roguelite
Skill-based difficulty: player execution matters more than build luck
Synergy items that combine active items, with free switching between a synergy item and its components
Hub area with NPCs such as Pogosmith and a Traveling Salesman, plus unlockable characters
Factory setting and a student-team pedigree from the University of Utah Division of Games
Free release with no monetization
tedious_or_disliked: Dying repeatedly while learning the movement before the game starts to feel fun
Hitting a difficulty wall at the boss stage after the early areas
Confusing early-level navigation without clear guidance
Early Access-era difficulty was high enough that the developers removed bats from area 1 and raised starting health in October 2024 patches
Bugs with certain item interactions
divisive_points: Difficulty: some find it a rewarding skill curve, others bounce off early
Content amount: praised for depth by high-hour players but called a little short by others
Steam Deck performance: several praise it, one recent review reports lag spikes
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched in April 2024, with major content updates on Oct 9, 12, 18 and 23, 2024 (new items, weapons, NPCs, characters, hub, balance changes and achievements). Full 1.0 release was on Nov 20, 2024, adding 8 passives, 4 weapons and 2 bosses. The developers stated the game is a free student project, most of the team had moved on, and future updates would be limited. The last visible forum post was June 2025, and Steam reviews continue to trickle in into 2026, so the game has a small, still-active audience. No critic coverage was found, Metacritic has a page with no critic score and too few user ratings, and there is no OpenCritic entry found. Sales data is not applicable because the game is free (SteamSpy estimates 0 to 20,000 owners). Research limitation: the web search budget was exhausted, so no Reddit or outlet reviews were found and Reddit could not be fetched; the picture relies on Steam store, reviews, forum and announcements.

community.one_liner: A fast, Hades-inspired action roguelike from Striking Distance Studios (The Callisto Protocol) where a low-ranking guard races rival survivors and infected inmates to the last escape pod out of Black Iron Prison.
community.consensus_summary: Critics and players land in the same place: a confident, stylish, punchy Hades-like with a distinctive twist (rival survivors and a run clock), held back by grind, repetition and some design friction. Metacritic shows a 77 Metascore from 11 critics (9 positive, 2 mixed, 0 negative) and a 7.9 user score; Steam sits at Very Positive (about 82% of ~360 reviews). It launched Oct 27, 2024 on PC (Steam and Epic), PS5 and Xbox Series X as a full release, not early access, and Steam reviews show the game still being played and patched into 2026. Commercially it looks modest: a third-party Steam estimate puts gross revenue at only about $142k, though that tool is an order-of-magnitude guess and ignores console and Epic sales. The YouTuber whose ranking prompted this research put it in a fairly high B tier.
best_things: Combat feels smooth and punchy, with a mix of melee, gun and kick/push, and environmental hazards and destructible areas to exploit
The Rivals system (competing survivors racing you to the escape pod, who you can sabotage via prison systems) is called a fresh take on the genre by several critics and players
Strong comic-book / cel-shaded art style and dark humor that gives the Callisto Protocol universe a punk, arcade tone
Fast-paced soundtrack (Mark Mothersbaugh is credited by a Steam reviewer) that matches the pace of the action
Wide variety of suits, weapons and experiments to build around; specific weapons (e.g. broken bottles, shankers) are fan favorites
Good level design and pacing once the game clicks; after the first win, many difficulty modifiers add replay value
Plays well on Steam Deck and with a controller, per Steam reviewers
Fighting your own corpse from previous runs and the do-or-die final run are memorable ideas
worst_things: Progression is very grindy: around six separate currencies, each unlocking one specific thing, and runs often yield only a handful of the one you need
The first roughly 8 hours are described as a slog because difficulty starts high and upgrades arrive slowly
Quick-time-event style button-combo minigames for attacking rivals get repetitive, often 10+ times per run (QTE can be turned off in settings)
Persistent bugs reported, including a long-standing screen-blocking bug that ruined a run late in the game, a locked-door exploit, and crashes entering a rare computer room
Difficulty scaling feels artificial to some, ramping as you play better rather than feeling earned
Very little synergy between upgrades: players say pure single-target damage is the only real strategy and status effects are not worth taking because key enemies are immune
Melee combat is considered weaker than the gun play by some critics, and level/room design gets repetitive
Epic Games version reportedly has support problems, e.g. achievement sync and a broken launcher screen
Constant choice between a temporary upgrade and currency for permanent unlocks: taking the currency leaves you underpowered and dying fast
improvements: Add in-game health bar / clearer health readout and a slot or list view of boons and which are mutually exclusive
Allow full controller button remapping (asked for on Steam discussions and in reviews)
Better explain the multiple currencies and accessibility options such as Guard Mode, and reduce the currency bottlenecks
Make the rival system less punishing early on; some players asked for an option to remove the rival entirely
Fix the recurring screen-blocking and softlock bugs, and improve Epic version support
Broaden build variety and synergies so non-damage upgrades matter; critics also wanted more variety in rooms and enemies
unique_things: Rival survivors race you to the single escape pod and you can attack them remotely through the prison's systems during the run
You fight the corpse of your previous self / fallen guards, tying death into the loop
Runs are on a clock, so speed matters more than in most Hades-style games; a top Steam review describes it as Hades on speed
Final-run gimmick: after clearing objectives, a high-stakes do-or-die run can wipe your unlock progression if you fail
Twin-stick shooter plus melee blend in the Callisto Protocol sci-fi prison setting with a punk graphic-novel look
tedious_or_disliked: Multi-currency grind and slow unlocks, especially early
Repeated button-combo minigames to hit or hinder rivals
The end-game reset: failing the final do-or-die run wipes unlocks, which several Steam reviewers call the worst design choice (others later came to like it)
Bosses and rooms that throw a lot of stuff at you and feel unfair or badly designed to some users
Keeping track of several rivals while fighting hordes under a time limit feels stressful and cluttered
divisive_points: Rivals system: praised as the standout idea by critics, but disliked by players who find it a hindrance and time pressure in the early game
Comparison to Hades: some say it borrows heavily but has its own personality, others call it a worse clone while a few say it beats Hades in places
The do-or-die reset: loved by some as real stakes, hated by others as deleting progress
Difficulty: rewarding once the rhythm clicks versus unforgiving from the start
community.reception_notes: Launched Oct 27, 2024 (PC, PS5, Xbox Series X) at $24.99 from KRAFTON and also released on Epic Games Store. Launch criticism on Steam forums targeted the marketing and trailers, and the Epic version has been called unsupported. Critic reception was solid and consistent (only GameSpot at 60 and GAMES.CH at 76 fell below 80), while Steam user sentiment is Very Positive but with a small sample. Steam reviews through 2026 show players with 100 to 700+ hours still playing, with bug complaints about a screen-blocking glitch persisting. SteamSpy lists 0-20k owners and very low concurrent users, and a Boxleiter-based estimate gives about $142k gross / $42k net on Steam alone, so treat the commercial picture as unverified and probably understated for multi-platform.

games.name: Ship of Fools
games.short_description: Ship of Fools is a seafaring cooperative roguelite. Set sail, man the cannons and battle sea monsters through the tempestuous seas of the Archipelago. Are you fool enough to stop the Aquapocalypse?

other_scores.source: Steam user reviews (82% positive, 6,287 reviews, Very Positive)

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm still going to give Ship of Fools a B uh a B tier; pretty good uh B tier

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Ship of Fools is an action roguelike where you defend a boat by manning cannons, refilling ammo and using a paddle to reflect projectiles, with a destroyed island as the hub. It is clearly designed around co-op, and he played both co-op with his brother and solo, finding co-op more fun. He loves the visuals, music, animation and early-game discovery, but finds the moment-to-moment gameplay thin and the item system too narrow and build-dependent. Post-clear rewards are weak, so overall he lands on B tier, admitting co-op may have lifted his opinion.
praise: Art style, environments, animation and music are top-notch and were what first drew him in
Hub island exploration, NPC discovery and world immersion make the first few hours very enjoyable
Trinkets/amulets give cool, fun benefits and were his favorite roguelike element
Each boss ends with a different reward (recycle an item, duplicate an item, big sell shop)
Areas look distinct and enemies feel varied; bosses look fantastic
Co-op is more fun than solo
Paddle reflect mechanic feels good when it lands
criticism: Gameplay on the boat is shallow and repetitive: refill cannon, shoot, occasionally paddle
Paddle charges slowly and is visually hard to read
Only about four ship slots, filled before the first world boss, so most new items are ignored
Items are highly build-dependent (harpoon, paddle, egg, dynamite), so off-build picks feel useless
Higher difficulties cost currency to unlock and give minimal rewards, so post-clear motivation is low
Bosses repeat with too little variation; auto-turret seems too strong not to use
unique_points: Ship-defense cannon/paddle loop feels like Overcooked-style co-op in a roguelike
Boss-end rewards differ each time rather than being a generic upgrade
Design lesson: build-specific items plus very limited slots leads to ignoring most of the content
commentary.quote: I'm still going to give Ship of Fools a B tier.
design_criteria: Visuals/charm: art style and environments are the standout strength
Audio: music described as great
Gameplay depth: boat mechanics too limited and repetitive
Synergies/build variety: item slots too restrictive and items too build-dependent
Meta-progression/replayability: paid, low-reward higher difficulties
Enemy/boss design: bosses look great but lack variety
Co-op: core focus of the design, more fun than solo
Exploration/world immersion: hub and discovery are a highlight

community.one_liner: A two-player (or solo) cooperative seafaring roguelite by Fika Productions (published by Team17) where you run a ship together, juggling cannons, repairs and steering against sea monsters to stop the Aquapocalypse.
community.consensus_summary: Ship of Fools is well liked, especially as a couch or online co-op game for exactly two people: Steam sits at Very Positive (about 82% of roughly 6,300 reviews) and Metacritic critics give it a 77 (PS5, 10 reviews) while Metacritic users are lukewarm at 7.0 from only 30 ratings. Critics and players praise the chaotic multitasking ship loop, charming art and strong soundtrack, but criticise thin content (only four bosses in fixed locations, a repetitive brightness-level grind), lack of build depth, and weak solo balance. Technical issues recur in reviews: second-controller detection failing in local co-op, co-op progression not syncing between players, save wipes, and Steam Deck breakage after an engine update. The game launched Nov 2022 on PC and consoles; Steam news shows patches through 1.5.3 (early 2026) and a console update in April 2026, but some recent reviewers feel it is abandoned and complain the developer now promotes its next game (Don't Kill Them All) in the menus.
best_things: Frantic, Overcooked-style co-op on a shared ship (steering, loading and firing cannons, patching leaks) that generates funny teamwork and arguments
Charming, cohesive art direction with distinct characters, enemies and bosses, plus a well-regarded soundtrack
Good couples/friend pairing game: challenging but not overwhelming, and partners can cover each other's weaknesses
Lots of item and talisman combinations, including memorably game-breaking synergies, without any single item being mandatory
Replayability through unlockable ships, characters, brightness (difficulty) levels and achievements; players report 30-130 hours
Excellent controller support and local couch co-op feel; also runs well on Linux for some
Low entry price ($9.99 on Steam) and frequent sales make it an easy buy for two players
worst_things: Hard 2-player cap: the single most upvoted review theme; players want 3-4 player support and say the game is a poor fit for groups of friends
Local co-op bug where the second controller is not recognised, reported since 2023 and still cited in recent reviews
Thin post-launch feel: several top reviews describe the game as abandoned and the developer advertising its other game and Discord inside the menu
Multiplayer progression is per-player and does not sync: one partner can reach 100% while the other is stuck, with developer support reportedly unable to fix it
Save/progress loss reported by several players, including Steam Cloud not recovering it and runs randomly kicking to the main menu
Post-update instability on Steam Deck (audio loss, lag) after the Unity engine update, and small/blurry text on TV for couch play
Little in-game information: no bestiary or codex, stats of guns and talismans not shown clearly, so players look things up externally
Thin content: only four bosses always in the same places, limited enemy variety, characters differ mostly by one passive
Network reliability in online co-op: trouble joining, staying on the ship or resuming runs even on good connections
Missing options: only resolution is adjustable in graphics, gamepad controls cannot be remapped, hardcoded menu binds
improvements: Support for more than two players (a commonly requested feature since the game is hard-capped at 2)
More bosses per area and more levels/enemy types so runs feel less identical
A bestiary/codex and clearer UI showing stats for guns, talismans and upgrades
Fix multiplayer progression syncing and multiple save slots; better solo mode and difficulty balance
Fuller settings: graphics options, gamepad rebinding, per-action binds, correct PS5 glyphs, readable text for TV play
Fix the local second-controller bug and engine-update regressions (Steam Deck, optimization)
unique_things: Co-op roguelite built around physically running around a ship and moving gear (guns, ammo, repair tools) rather than controlling one character
Tower-defense-meets-roguelite structure: you defend a moving ship in naval battles, compared by critics to a deck-defence game with Overcooked energy
Paddle-based ship steering with friendly fire, which blends party-game chaos with hardcore roguelite difficulty
Difficulty driven by unlocking successive brightness levels rather than purely random runs; Binding of Isaac-style item collecting but less punishing
Deliberately couch-first design for two players, with solo mode as a secondary option
tedious_or_disliked: Unlocking each brightness level means replaying the same few levels repeatedly; restarting runs can feel like a chore
Once you beat the four bosses, unlock-chasing and achievement grinding are what remains
Reloading guns and shuffling them around the ship becomes repetitive, with hectic moments that some find more stressful than fun
Sudden difficulty spikes (final boss, high brightness levels) and later-game balance that some call unfun, especially solo
Ads for the developer's other game and Discord in the menu
Short runs of content: several reviewers say they run out of new things to do after about 5 hours and are left grinding to 100%
divisive_points: Price: seen as a bargain at $9.99 by many, but a reviewer calls 22 EUR pricey for the amount of content
Difficulty: described as well measured by some co-op pairs, but too casual early and unbalanced late by others
Friendly fire and chaotic design: adds hilarious arguments for some couples and feels like a clash of tones for others
Solo play: some say it is very manageable, critics and other players say it is frustrating and clearly geared to co-op
community.reception_notes: Launched Nov 22 2022 on PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch to generally favorable reviews (Metacritic 77 on PS5). Critics liked the co-op chaos and unique roguelite take but flagged limited depth and a weaker solo experience. Steam user sentiment has stayed Very Positive (82%). Post-launch DLC adds characters and 'Duo' content packs (Deep Sea, Water Garden, Golden Bay), and patches ran through 1.5.1-1.5.3 in 2025-26. An Unity/engine 'Update Required' in Oct 2025 is linked by reviewers to Steam Deck and performance problems, and a console update shipped April 2026. A 2026 reviewer says the developer told players that supporting its next game is needed to keep updating Ship of Fools, and recent reviews describe the game as feeling abandoned with unfixed long-standing bugs. On PC it is Windows-only (no native Mac or Linux build), though some players run it on Linux. No OpenCritic score was found, so none is reported.
