games.name: SYNTHETIK: Legion Rising
games.short_description: SYNTHETIK is an unforgiving tactical shooter rogue-lite where freedom and experimentation is key. Fight in a world overrun by the Machine Legion and their Gods. Experience the next level in gun-play and dive into unparalleled build options and Android upgrades. Can you defeat the Heart of Armageddon?

other_scores.source: Metacritic critic reviews (3 individual, no Metascore)

placements.verbal_evidence: none

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Synthetik is a slow, top-down shooter roguelike that leans toward realism: stealth, deliberate aiming, weapon jams, reloads and scarce ammo. He admits it is the game on the list he played least, but respects how it breaks from the usual fast, spray-and-pray shooter formula. The guns, with their many modifiers and upgrades, carry most of the roguelike depth. Repetitive levels, overwhelming detail and a slow unlock system hold it back for him, though the gunplay feels great. He ends by placing it 'around here' on the board without naming a tier letter.
praise: Slow, deliberate shooter pacing that differs from typical fast-paced shooter roguelikes
Huge variety of unique guns with modifiers and upgrades, which is where most of the depth lies
Mechanics like jamming, reloading and limited ammo force awareness of build and gun behavior
Precise, satisfying gunplay; headshots feel great
Sound design and VFX are fantastic
Pre-run class choice with distinct mechanics and different starting weapons
criticism: Levels are repetitive and feel like one big room, reducing immersion
So much detail and complexity that bosses can kill him with no clear cause
Unlocking classes and starting weapons is slow, so runs begin with the same setup
Leveling is per class, so trying another class means starting from zero
Could be intimidating for newcomers
unique_points: Approaches the shooter genre realistically and slowly, rewarding stealth and careful aim instead of constant firing
Gun mechanics (jams, reloads, scarce bullets) are central to the roguelike build rather than a side detail
commentary.quote: it really is a very slow pace action rogike
design_criteria: Gameplay depth: complex gun mechanics and a slow pace are what make it distinct
Build variety: many unique guns with modifiers and upgrades drive the roguelike layer
Level design: repetitive, big-room feel counts against it
Readability: dense stats and details make boss deaths hard to understand
Meta-progression: class-locked leveling and slow unlocks limit starting variety
Audio/VFX: sound design and effects make shooting feel great
Accessibility: complexity may intimidate newcomers

community.one_liner: A top-down tactical shooter roguelite from Flow Fire Games where hands-on gun handling (active reload, jams, recoil, ammo types) meets randomized weapons, eight classes and a punishing five-floor run against the Machine Legion.
community.consensus_summary: Players love it: Steam shows Very Positive at roughly 94% of about 13,000 reviews, with many reviewers logging hundreds of hours and calling the gunplay among the best in the genre. Critics are few but favourable; Metacritic has only three critic reviews (84, 80, 70 per Wikipedia) and no Metascore yet, plus a user score of 8.1 from 32 ratings. It is a finished, fully released 2018 game (originally Synthetik, renamed Legion Rising after a free October 2018 expansion) with a free spin-off, Synthetik: Arena, and console ports on Xbox and Switch in 2020. A sequel, Synthetik 2, has been in Early Access since 2021. The core complaint is a steep, poorly explained learning curve plus heavy RNG, and some players report crashes and glitches in recent years.
best_things: Gunplay feel: active reload, magazine ejecting, jams/overheating and recoil make every gun feel physical and skill-dependent
Huge weapon pool (70+ guns with manufacturer variants and randomized stats) plus 140+ items (turrets, mines, mind control, orbital lasers) enabling very different builds
Eight classes/subclasses with long progression and prestige arcs, so new unlocks keep coming 30-40+ hours in
Very high replayability and skill ceiling; runs feel like mastery of a build rather than a fixed meta
Sound design and soundtrack are repeatedly called out as excellent
Modular difficulty (about 11 independent modifiers) lets players tune the challenge, including 220%+ for veterans
Two-player online co-op with shared loot is described as great fun by those who get it working
Cheap price for the depth, and a free Arena version works as a demo
worst_things: Poor onboarding: the game drops you into a run with a weak tutorial and items/weapons/mods whose effects are not explained, so reviewers say many mechanics must be discovered or looked up
Harsh RNG can starve a run of weapon crates or upgrade shops for several floors, and runs can end from a single small mistake
Crashes and game-ending bugs, including runs wiped by crashes and getting stuck on obstacles; co-op lobbies sometimes fail to connect
Unfinished or broken interactions (for example the Modular weapon mod is reported as unusable)
Display and UI problems: no real ultrawide or multi-monitor support, minimalistic UI that some find awkward, no item descriptions in shops
Late game spikes hard: floors 4-5, back-to-back gauntlet rooms and the final boss Armageddon are seen as a DPS check that only a handful of weapons can handle
Some features feel gated (a loadout tied to a friend referral code, locked DLC content) which irritated a few reviewers
improvements: A proper tutorial and in-game tooltips/item descriptions, including in shops
Stability fixes for crashes and run-ending bugs, and more reliable co-op lobby/connection
Better balance across the weapon pool so more than a small subset is viable into floors 4-5 and the final boss
Less punishing or more forgiving RNG for crate and upgrade-shop spawns
Display options: ultrawide/multi-monitor support, an earlier settings menu, and a way to disable screen flash
Finish or fix half-implemented content such as the Modular mod
unique_things: Hands-on gun mechanics in a roguelite: manual magazine eject, timed active reload, jams and overheating
Weapons generate with manufacturer-specific variants and randomized stats instead of fixed items
Eight specialist classes that change playstyle entirely, from sneaking assassin to turret engineer to heavy breacher
Engineer-style gambling dynamics (double or nothing with credits) and devil-offer red crates that trade health for power
Modular difficulty sliders and a prestige system rather than a single fixed difficulty
Free companion game Synthetik: Arena shares character and achievement unlocks with the main game
tedious_or_disliked: Long losing streaks while learning: only a small share of players beat the final encounter (one reviewer cites about 7% with the achievement)
Trial-and-error discovery of what items and weapons do, often costing a whole run
Late-floor gauntlets (three hard rooms in a row) and the final boss feel like a slog after a long run
Overwhelming enemy spam and explosive threats such as Doombots in solo play
Grinding class levels and unlocks, and repeating the long runs (8-hour sessions reported)
Screen flash on explosions with no option to turn it off
divisive_points: RNG: fans see it as brutal but fair chaos that creates stories; detractors call it unfair and run-deciding
Difficulty: some treat it as a mastery game and eventually love it, while others bounce within an hour or two
Solo vs co-op: co-op is praised but some find the game too complex or enemy-heavy for a casual co-op session
Synthetik 1 vs 2: at least one 870-hour reviewer says neither the Early Access sequel nor any other game grabbed them like the original
community.reception_notes: Launched March 2018 on Steam and became a large word-of-mouth hit, with multiple Steam reviewers crediting YouTuber Sseth's video for discovering it and one claiming it boosted sales dramatically. A free expansion in October 2018 renamed it Legion Rising. Synthetik: Arena (free, combat-focused) followed in January 2019, and Xbox and Switch versions in December 2020; console reviews noted control and interface issues. Synthetik 2 entered Early Access in 2021. Estimated revenue is about $1.78M gross and about $525k net (Boxleiter-style estimate from steam-revenue-calculator.com, order of magnitude only); SteamSpy-style owner estimate is 500k-1M. PC only on Steam (no Mac/Linux). Recent Steam reviews from 2025-2026 are still strongly positive, though a few report worsening crashes and glitches. Note: web search budget was exhausted in this session, so Reddit and OpenCritic could not be checked; OpenCritic score is unknown, not confirmed absent.

games.name: Vampire Hunters
games.short_description: To hunt vampires, you'll need guns. Lots of guns. Mow down hordes of undead creatures by stacking your guns into absurd, over-the-top builds. Unleash your firepower and survive the mayhem in this Roguelite Survivors FPS.

other_scores.source: PlayStation Country (single critic review on Metacritic, no aggregate)

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put it as a low B tier, right around here.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Vampire Hunters is a first-person horde-survivor game where you collect and upgrade many weapons while dodging and shooting through swarms in 3D levels. He finds it chaotic and unique for its first-person view, and the first few hours were fun. He felt it was unfinished, with poor balance, repetitive gameplay and a broken final boss. He places it in low B.
praise: First-person perspective is rare for a horde-like and feels unique
More mechanical variety than typical horde-likes: jumping, dashing, character-specific abilities, an ultimate
Characters feel different from one another
Meta progression is enjoyable
Different environments and visually cool bosses
The chaotic, messy weapon-collecting is fun in the first few hours
criticism: Serious balance problems: some weapons are roughly ten times stronger than others and some feel terrible
Some items feel unimpactful and there are few character upgrade options
Runs are repetitive: the same move-to-edge, kite a train of enemies loop regardless of character, weapon or map
Unlocks require playing one particular character a lot, and he saw all weapons and items quickly
Bosses stop mattering once meta progression makes you strong, and the final boss Dracula seems broken
Feels dropped before finished; the party-like music does not fit the game
unique_points: A first-person horde-like is rare and a fresh take on the subgenre
Uses 3D space with jumping and dashing instead of top-down 2D movement
Weapon upgrades are fixed but you choose which weapons to prioritise
commentary.quote: It really does feel like the game was dropped in development before it was finished.
design_criteria: Balance: weapon power gaps and weak items hurt the game
Variety/repetition: runs, characters and maps play too similarly
Meta progression: enjoyable but unlock gating is grindy and trivialises later play
Boss design: visually cool but irrelevant and buggy at the end
Audio/vibe: music mismatched with the game
Mechanical depth: jump, dash and ultimate add more than typical horde-likes
Polish/completeness: feels unfinished for a full release
Uniqueness: first-person view sets it apart

community.one_liner: A first-person roguelite 'survivors' shooter from Gamecraft Studios where you stack up to ~14 guns and abilities while mowing down endless undead hordes across 30-minute stages.
community.consensus_summary: Vampire Hunters is well liked by Steam players (about 90% positive across ~2,200 reviews, Very Positive, though recent reviews dip to roughly 75%). It is a cheap (about $4.49-8.99) Unity game that left Early Access on Oct 30, 2024 after an EA start in July 2023. Fans love the novelty of a survivors-like in first person with real aiming and a huge arsenal; detractors say it becomes a flat camp-in-a-corner loop with weak weapon synergy and repetitive music. Critic coverage is almost nonexistent: Metacritic has a single critic review (PlayStation Country, 80) so no aggregate score, and a 7.0 user score from only 5 ratings. Several players note updates have slowed, and one complains of no more updates, but others praise the devs for frequent content additions, and the studio lists PlayStation, Xbox and Switch versions.
best_things: First-person survivors-like concept: you actually aim, so it feels more engaging than top-down auto-fire bullet heavens (often compared to Vampire Survivors crossed with Doom, Serious Sam, Painkiller or Unreal Tournament)
Huge weapon and ability pool with absurd stacking builds (many guns at once, guns attached to guns), letting players feel very powerful
Big unlock and achievement list, multiple characters and lots of maps with different enemies and bosses
Level design inspired by Quake/Unreal, with shortcuts and platforming routes; bosses with map-specific gimmicks
Cheap price and strong value on sale; some players report 60-130+ hours
Retro PS1-style look and chaotic, silly tone, plus a story/ending some players found charming
Developer kept adding content in and after Early Access (one reviewer even complains about 'too much content')
worst_things: Gameplay collapses into camping in a dead end or single-direction chokepoint and holding fire for 30 minutes per stage
Weapons feel unbalanced: many are weak, small magazines, and debuffs like bleed/freeze/poison are underwhelming; a couple of guns dominate
Little synergy between weapons; ten machine guns mostly just add raw damage rather than creating interesting builds
Enemy AI is simple (mostly melee walking straight at you) and enemy variety is limited, so aiming rarely matters
Music is repeatedly called repetitive and grating
Unity performance issues: stutters on good hardware, described by one player as poor optimization
Some glitches such as enemies stuck in walls in Classic mode making them unkillable
Despite the huge gun count, the power fantasy feels flat to some: upgrades do not feel impactful and the game gets easy, then boring (one of the most-upvoted negative reviews)
Bare-bones feel: nothing is explained, systems feel arbitrary, and only a handful of maps exist
improvements: More map and mode variety, with unique mechanics or events per stage so each 30-minute run plays differently
Real weapon synergies (per-debuff scaling, cross-effects) and rebalancing so more weapons are viable
Characters and playstyles that interact with weapons differently (movement-based or stationary-based bonuses)
Better tutorial or in-game explanations of keywords, systems and the endgame win condition
Smarter and more varied enemy behavior (flankers, chargers, ranged) to discourage camping, plus cleaner spawn/pathing in Classic mode
More content/updates and DLC; some players also ask for multiplayer/co-op
unique_things: First-person shooter take on the survivors-like formula (aim yourself, not auto-fire)
Two modes: Survivor mode (endless waves, 30-minute stages) and Classic mode (more traditional FPS pacing with rebirth levels)
Stackable loadout of up to ~14 guns plus artifacts with absurd, genre-mixing arsenal (miniguns, shoulder lightsaber launcher, magic frog)
Constellation-style run modifiers where harder settings give more score/XP, with online score leaderboards
Retro Unreal/Quake-flavoured arenas and a goofy steampunk and mythology bestiary (lizards, cat people, evil trains, insect bosses)
tedious_or_disliked: 30-minute stages with long stretches of just standing and shooting before a boss appears
Repetitive loop and repetitive music after a few hours; players say they have 'seen it all' in the first 30 minutes to 10 hours
Grinding unlocks and rebirth progression, including restarting character progression, and repeating the same locations
Confusing win condition: after defeating bosses, a late objective to close enemy portals while enemies become very tanky was unforeshadowed
Score/XP tied to difficulty modifiers in Survivor mode, making safe play feel punished and leaderboards farmable through camping
divisive_points: Survivor mode versus Classic mode: some find Classic more satisfying, others prefer the trailer-style Survivor mode
Depth: fans say build variety and player power are a strength; critics say builds do not matter and only a few weapons work
Update cadence: some praise frequent content, others say content stopped and only a handful of maps exist
Value: 'hidden gem worth it even at full price' versus 'get it on sale, gets repetitive'
community.reception_notes: Early Access began July 26, 2023 and 1.0 launched Oct 30, 2024 on Steam (Windows only on Steam; studio site also lists PS4/PS5, Xbox One/Series and Switch). Steam reception has stayed Very Positive, with positive reviews continuing to come in during 2025-2026, but recent reviews are more lukewarm and a couple of reviewers say updates have stopped. Metacritic: no critic aggregate (only 1 review, 80) and 7.0 user score from 5 ratings. OpenCritic page could not be found or confirmed, treated as null. Priced around $4.49-8.99 with frequent deep discounts. The web search budget was exhausted during this task, so Reddit discussion and patch-note detail could not be retrieved; community views rely mainly on Steam reviews and forum topics.

games.name: WizardChess
games.short_description: What if chess was invented by silly cosmic wizards? WizardChess is a turnbased roguelite where all the pieces have insane abilities that came to us in a shamanic vision. Fight chaotic-yet-tactical encounters with magic powers out of a fever dream! Defeat the FaeQueen and Claim Your Wish!

other_scores.score: Steam owners est. 0-20,000 (SteamSpy); calculator shows $0 revenue estimate, not reliable

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put it as a, uh, as a pretty fun B tier.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Wizard Chess is a turn-based, board-centric roguelike strategy game loosely inspired by chess, made by a small team and now out of early access. You pick a world, build a squad of minions around a king-like player character, and fight through boards. He loves the huge roster of very different units, the big-band jazz soundtrack and the 2D-sprites-in-3D look. The main drawback is pace: one action at a time makes larger boards and some boss fights slow. He calls it a pretty fun B tier and the last game placed in the video.
praise: Huge roster of unlockable minions that each play drastically differently, giving strong replayability
Every run feels different because of unit variety
Big-band jazz music is a standout, and characters' idle animations feel like dancing to it
2D sprites in a 3D environment look unique and fitting
Higher difficulty on replayed worlds introduces new mechanics rather than just bigger numbers
Fast team-building mode with limited moves or time is a fun, low-commitment extra that still unlocks things
Elemental traits and stat upgrades on units meaningfully change how they play
criticism: Strictly one-action-at-a-time turns make the game very slow, especially on big boards
Endgame situations can turn into back-and-forth shuffling with a single enemy
Boss fights can be trivial with the right team, or stall for several turns with nothing to do
Cannot choose which units from the roster are present in a fight or where they spawn; it seems random to him
Roguelike elements and run events (shops, events, side quests) are not very deep
unique_points: Chess-like movement and attack patterns turned into many distinct minion designs, with the player acting as a king-like piece
Higher-difficulty replays add new mechanics rather than stat inflation
Timed/move-limited team-building mode as an alternative to full runs
commentary.quote: I'm going to put it as a pretty fun B tier.
design_criteria: Unit/minion variety: the core strength, each piece plays very differently
Replayability: driven by roster size and differing runs
Pacing/turn structure: one action per turn feels slow on large boards
Player control: cannot choose fielded units or spawn positions
Roguelike depth: elemental traits and stat upgrades exist but stay shallow
Difficulty scaling: higher tiers add new mechanics
Boss design: can be trivial or stall depending on the team
Audio: big-band jazz soundtrack is highlighted
Visuals/charm: 2D sprites in 3D world with lively idle animations
Run structure/variety: side quests, shops, events and an alternate fast mode

community.one_liner: A turn-based tactical roguelite from Australian studio TwoPM Studios where you recruit, upgrade and sacrifice 50+ odd 'chess-like' units on a grid to beat the FaeQueen.
community.consensus_summary: WizardChess is a small, niche indie with a Mostly Positive Steam rating (about 75% of 94 reviews in the local snapshot; the store page fetched showed a higher, Very Positive figure from a smaller sample). Players who like it enjoy the silly tone, jazzy music and the wide variety of weird units. Critics have not covered it: Metacritic shows 'tbd' for both critic and user scores and no OpenCritic entry was found. It left Early Access on Dec 14, 2024 (1.0), and some recent reviewers believe it is no longer being updated. The most common complaint is hidden information and lopsided balance, plus the name, since it has little to do with real chess. Evidence is limited to the Steam review file, Steam store, forum thread titles, dev site, itch.io and Metacritic; sample sizes are small.
best_things: Charming, silly tone and writing, with a fever-dream wizard theme
Unexpectedly jazzy, lighthearted soundtrack that reviewers singled out
Large roster of 50+ distinct units with their own stats and abilities, so encounters feel varied
Distinct, readable pixel units and an easy-to-control camera
Procedurally generated rooms, enemies and rewards vary each run; runs are fairly short (~30 min sessions per the dev's itch.io page)
Recruit/upgrade/sacrifice/trade loop lets players experiment with odd combinations
Steam Deck and full controller support, Steam Cloud and achievements
worst_things: Much information is hidden: many piece rules and permanent buffs can't be seen until accepted, and temporary buffs/debuffs are not clearly shown
Balance: stacking every buff on one or two mobile units creates an unstoppable mega-unit, making strategy shallow
Runs can start in apparent no-win situations because you don't choose which units enter a round and can be handed weak units (e.g. 0-attack chickens)
Reports of frequent bugs and crashes, including one just before a first final-boss win
UI is clunky; the in-game selector lags behind the mouse cursor, so clicks can land on the wrong square with no misclick protection
Content feels thin to some (one reviewer noted only 3 bosses)
Rewards cannot be rejected, so weaker forced pieces enter the army
Reviewers say it is not meaningfully chess, so the title feels misleading
improvements: Let players reject or choose rewards (a Steam thread asks this directly)
Show all rules, buffs and temporary effects in tooltips, and keep a visible log of permanent buffs
Cap or rebalance stacking onto a single unit
Add mid-run save and exit (requested in reviews and a Steam thread)
Add misclick protection and fix cursor/selector lag; fix bugs and crashes
Improve the tutorial and make it skippable; clarify vague achievement descriptions; add more bosses; Linux support was also requested
unique_things: Chess-flavored grid tactics (moving orthogonally/diagonally) but with bizarre wizard units rather than standard pieces
Cards/units are bought and recruited like a deckbuilder, yet play is pure tactics, not a card game
Unit sacrifice and trading as a core progression mechanic
Three stats (ATK, DEF, SKL) with 50+ unit classes and elemental interactions
Whimsical shamanic-vision framing and a light jazzy score, unlike most grim roguelikes
Arcade (quick run) and Story (exploration) modes
tedious_or_disliked: Writing buffs down externally because the game doesn't track them
Required tutorial parts that players say many never finish (one reviewer cited low tutorial completion stats)
Early encounters some feel unwinnable, making runs feel unfair and swingy
Being unable to save and exit mid-run, and the diagnostics prompt reappearing on every return to the title screen
Too many units in Arcade mode was raised as a forum complaint
divisive_points: Whether the name and chess framing is misleading clickbait or just loose inspiration for a fun tactics game
Whether the chaos and randomness is a feature (experimentation, unpredictability) or simply bad balance and hidden info
Difficulty: some find it frustrating and unfair, others rate it around 4/5 and 'feels good' even without liking strategy games
community.reception_notes: Launched in Early Access in October 2021 and reached 1.0 on Dec 14, 2024 at $14.99 (Windows and macOS; no Linux). Review volume is small, and recent reviews in 2026 are a mix with a noticeable negative thread on balance and hidden info, with at least one reviewer believing development has stopped. No mainstream critic coverage found; Metacritic page shows 'tbd'. Sales data is unreliable; SteamSpy puts owners at 0-20k. Limitation: web search budget was exhausted, Reddit was not fetchable, and OpenCritic search returned nothing, so community evidence is mostly Steam reviews and thread titles.

games.name: Deep Rock Galactic: Survivor
games.short_description: DEEP ROCK GALACTIC: SURVIVOR is a single player survivor-like auto-shooter. Take on hordes of lethal aliens, mine riches, and unlock powerful upgrades to survive, as you wield the full arsenal of Deep Rock Galactic. It's one dwarf against all of Planet Hoxxes!

other_scores.score: 90/100 (as cited on the Steam store page)
8.7/10 (as cited on the Steam store page)

placements.verbal_evidence: this is going to be another solid B or low A. I think I'm going to put it under Dome Keeper for now

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Deep Rock Galactic: Survivor is a top-down horde-like (survivor-like) set in the Deep Rock Galactic world, with a digging-for-minerals mechanic and heavy roguelite meta-progression. He says it has an insane amount of content versus most of the genre, including four characters with subclasses that play like about sixteen, equipment, and a new payload mode. Gameplay is fairly generic and number-driven, and some weapons lack satisfying feel. He calls it one of the better ones after about 70 survivor-likes, but not top-10 material, and slots it just under Dome Keeper.
praise: Huge amount of content and permanent upgrades, including equipment that can be put on different characters
Always something to do in a run: digging for minerals, a mission objective, swarms, and a payload
Runs are short, which suits the heavy roguelite focus
Weapon evolution system adds mechanical upgrades and some strategy in choosing upgrades
Fantastic visuals, befitting the IP
Four characters with subclasses that play very differently (effectively ~16)
criticism: Gameplay is fairly simple and generic; nothing crazy unique beyond the digging
Upgrades are mostly numbers rather than mechanical changes
Unlucky low-value upgrade rolls can feel really small
Some weapons feel unsatisfying or not crisp early on despite great art and animation
Levels sometimes feel too short
Prefers the original mode over the newer payload campaign
unique_points: Digging for different minerals that gate permanent upgrades
Per-level mission with a reward adds an extra goal within a run
Advocates rarity tiers (common to legendary) on level-up upgrades, tying into luck
commentary.quote: this is going to be another solid B or low A
design_criteria: Content volume: rates the amount of unlockables and modes highly
Meta-progression: mineral-gated permanent upgrades and equipment
Upgrade design: numbers-heavy versus mechanical, rarity and luck, weapon evolutions
Weapon feel: guns must be crisp and satisfying
Run pacing: short runs with constant activity and objectives
Uniqueness: weighed heavily, and the game loses points for being generic
Visuals and charm: strong art from the IP
Character variety: subclasses create distinct playstyles
commentary.rerank_note: Placed under Dome Keeper 'for now'; he played both early access and the 1.0 release.

community.one_liner: A single-player top-down survivor-like auto-shooter spun off from Deep Rock Galactic, where a dwarf fights alien hordes on Planet Hoxxes while mining minerals and escaping to a drop pod.
community.consensus_summary: Players and critics rate it well: Steam sits at Very Positive (about 86% of roughly 48k reviews) and Metacritic shows a Metascore of 86 from 11 critic reviews, with PC Gamer at 90 saying it dethrones Vampire Survivors. The praise centers on polish, the DRG weapon/overclock feel and the mining-under-pressure twist. Critics and players alike flag endgame grind and balance, and the Metacritic user score is a much lower 7.2 (Mixed) (64 ratings, a small sample). It started in Early Access in Feb 2024 and hit 1.0 on Sep 17, 2025; the 1.0 gear system is the most contested change, and paid expansions (Heavy Duty, Knockout) have followed, so it is actively supported rather than abandoned.
best_things: Polish and presentation: colorful, glowing minerals and enemies, satisfying explosions, runs well on Steam Deck up to Hazard 4
Mining adds real risk/reward: standing still to mine valuable loot while swarmed, and digging new paths through maps
Weapon variety with overclocks that change how a weapon behaves, plus 12 subclasses that play differently
Optional side objectives alongside the main escort/return-to-ship goal make each run more strategic than a pure survive-the-timer loop
Good value at $12.99; many reviewers report 50-100+ hours of play
Carries the DRG humor and feel, so fans of the main game feel at home without needing prior experience
Deep meta progression and lots of unlocks (weapons, classes, biomes, hazard levels) for completionists
Hazard levels give a clear difficulty ladder; higher hazards feel tense and punish greedy decisions
worst_things: Weapon balance: a large share of weapons are described as weak or even harmful to have, while a few carry whole runs
Visibility problems: isometric camera hides enemies behind terrain, the escort vehicle and crystals, and weapon effects draw over enemies, causing unseen contact damage
Permanent upgrades are mostly small flat percentage bonuses that players feel little impact from
Shallow in-run build variety and few synergies: many upgrades are just more damage, and many weapons (drones, beams) feel alike
Large gaps in artifact strength push players to pick the same few upgrades every run
Hazard 4-5 difficulty spike leans heavily on luck (the Luck stat, gear drops) and on a narrow set of meta builds
Some bugs reported: supply pod getting stuck, freezes between levels or at launch
Single-player only, which many reviewers (and Game8/GamingBolt) call a missed opportunity given the original's co-op identity

Run-to-run variance is thin: the variety is pushed into the meta-progression, so a run feels much like the last (top-upvoted negative reviews, e.g. 'extracted all the run-to-run variance into its over-long meta progression')
Steep difficulty walls between hazard levels that are cleared by hours of grinding 1% stat bumps rather than skill or strategy
improvements: Add co-op multiplayer, the most frequent request in Steam reviews
Rebalance weapons, artifacts and underperforming classes (the Driller is named as weak)
Streamline or reduce the meta-progression grind, e.g. let progress accrue on more than one weapon/class/biome at once
Fix visibility: show enemies behind obstacles and stop weapon effects obscuring them
Add tooltips for character/weapon attributes and make upgrades more build-defining with real synergies
Add an endless mode and more late-game content or sinks for excess resources; allow separate move and aim direction (requested by one reviewer)
unique_things: Mining is integrated into a survivor-like: you must stand still to extract resources while enemies close in
Escort/extraction structure: reach a randomly located ship or drop pod, with a timed escape after boss kills, rather than a fixed 30-minute survive timer
Level-capped runs with a capped weapon loadout (max 4 weapons) and choose-one-of-three upgrades
Overclocks that modify weapon behavior, borrowed from the main DRG game
Gear system with randomized stats and per-subclass loadouts (12 subclasses, each with its own gear slots) layered on top of mastery progression
Tunnel-digging that reshapes the map, which can rescue you or backfire
tedious_or_disliked: Late-game grind: one reviewer counts roughly 42 weapons x 12 classes x 5 biomes each with 5 mastery levels, meaning up to ~295 repeated missions
Gear management chore: 12 subclasses each needing 8 items, limited inventory, risk of selling needed gear if not favorited, and mostly boring stat-stick gear
Escort missions and the 30-second escape timer after a boss are cited as stressful or unfair
Cheap-feeling deaths: chip damage from environmental hazards, exploding-enemy waves after bosses, enemies tuned to be just faster than mining speed
Rare gear drops and luck-gated achievements make completion feel like rinse-and-repeat
Early menus require clicking through several screens of locked modes and characters before the first run
divisive_points: The 1.0 gear system: long-time Early Access players say it cut their rating (some from 8/10 to 5/10), while others enjoy the extra customization and loot chase
Difficulty: some call it too hard and unfair at Hazard 5 or on escort missions, others say the right gear makes it easy and that it is a fair challenge
Depth vs relaxation: some call it the most polished but shallow and grind-driven survivor-like, others find it both intense and chill and their second-favorite in the genre
Critics (86 Metascore, PC Gamer 90) are notably warmer than Metacritic users (7.2) and the more negative Steam reviewers
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched Feb 14, 2024; full 1.0 released Sep 17, 2025 at $12.99 on Windows only (no Mac/Linux), developed by Funday Games and published by Ghost Ship. Early Access reception was warm and players asked for co-op and an endless mode. After 1.0 the new gear system, Luck dependence and Hazard 5 balance drew complaints from veterans, though overall Steam score stays Very Positive. Paid DLC (Heavy Duty and Knockout expansions, plus cosmetic packs) has been released, and a reviewer in 2026 says the devs delivered what they promised. Estimated sales: SteamSpy ballpark 1-2 million owners; steam-revenue-calculator estimates about $20.7M gross and $6.1M net (Boxleiter-style estimates, not audited). OpenCritic score could not be retrieved (web search budget exhausted and the guessed OpenCritic page was the wrong game), so it is null.

games.name: Die in the Dungeon
games.short_description: Fight your way through a mysterious dungeon in this deck-building, turn-based roguelike game where you don't use cards, but dice! Deal with enemies by combining powerful dice on your board, boost their effects with magical relics, and risk it all hoping for a good roll on unexpected encounters.

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put this as a high B tier for now. I could see this going up in its final release.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Die in the Dungeon is an early-access, turn-based roguelike dice game where you place unique dice on a board and combine their effects to fight through floors to a final boss. He finds it genuinely unique and has had a blast, noting a huge amount of content and regular updates. However, it is overwhelming for new players, the small-text art style hurts readability, balance is uneven, and runs can drag. He places it in high B for now, with potential to rise at full release.
praise: Every die has a unique effect and adjustable numbers, giving deep customization of dice and board
Three characters with different boards, starting dice and passives make each run feel like a new adventure
Lots of content and regular updates keep it fresh on return visits
Passive relics and newly added potions add variety and distinct playstyles
Events have unique sprites and animations, immersing the player in the dungeon crawl
Enemies interact with your board by placing things on it, adding strategic depth
Dice design works around the luck handicap of dice games in an interesting way
criticism: Overwhelming at start due to many keywords and specific mechanics
Art style is great but small, scattered text makes dice icons and descriptions hard to read and track
Finding new dice later in a run is less satisfying than finding rare cards in Slay the Spire
Defensive or weak builds do not die but make runs extremely long, e.g. 15-minute boss fights
Some mechanics like terrain dice are inherently overpowered, showing balance difficulty
Elites are just multiple waves of normal enemies, which wastes time versus one bigger, scarier enemy
unique_points: Dice as the core deckbuilder-like resource, placed on a board with enemy-interacting board effects
Every die has its own effect and numbers rather than standard d4/d6/d8
Events presented with bespoke sprites and animations rather than plain text
commentary.quote: I'm going to put this as a high B tier for now.
design_criteria: Luck vs strategy: how a dice game manages randomness in a turn-based format
Customization/build variety: unique dice, board, passives, relics
Character diversity: different boards, dice and passives per character
Readability/UI: art style and small text hinder understanding
Balance: certain dice like terrain dice are too strong
Run length/pacing: defensive builds drag, multi-wave elites waste time
Reward satisfaction: new dice feel less exciting than rare cards
Content and updates: amount of content and freshness
Events: visual and thematic effort in events
commentary.rerank_note: Early access rating; he says it could move up at final release.

community.one_liner: A turn-based roguelike deckbuilder by ATICO where you use dice instead of cards, slotting attack, defense, healing and booster dice onto a character-specific board and boosting them with relics, starring cute pixel-art frogs fighting insects.
community.consensus_summary: Players like it a lot: Steam shows Very Positive (about 92% of roughly 3,600 reviews) and the developers and publisher (HypeTrain Digital, Sidekick Publishing) got it through Early Access (started Feb 21, 2025) to a 1.0 launch on May 1, 2026, with Switch also mentioned. Critics coverage is thin (two OpenCritic reviews, both very positive, and no Metacritic score). Praise centres on the dice-on-a-grid puzzle, pixel art and music, and an approachable on-ramp for genre newcomers. The recurring complaints are slow, long runs, builds converging on the same few strategies, enemies that do not scale so stalling or full-blocking works, and a lack of character and build variety. Reviewers who stay long (endgame players) are markedly more positive than those who bounce in the first hours.
best_things: Swapping cards for dice placed on a shaped board turns each turn into a spatial optimisation puzzle; reviewers call it a fresh take that changes how you plan, not just a reskin
Pixel art and character/enemy design (cute frogs vs. bugs) are the most universally praised element, along with a well-liked soundtrack
Combos can get very deep, for example once you can change faulty dice; long-time players say the synergy space is expansive
Approachable: tooltips get new players going quickly, and it is described as a good gateway into the genre
Four characters with different board shapes and sizes, plus artifacts and curses that alter how dice, board and enemies interact
Events can be played around with your dice and many can be skipped if your dice are strong, which players find more engaging than event screens in peers
Active, community-minded dev team: enemy design contests and community lore writing, regular Early Access updates, free Origins demo
Good value at $14.99 with lots of hours of playtime reported by fans (some with several hundred hours)
worst_things: Runs and individual fights drag; many reviewers report runs of 60-90+ minutes, with enemies that have very high HP and low damage and no pressure to end fights
Board readability degrades late: stacked effects on one tile and huge boosted numbers become hard to parse, to the point of not knowing what happened in some fights
Builds converge on one or a few viable strategies, often stacking block and infinite or near-infinite combos; many dice offered in early acts feel like they make your deck worse
Balance swings between trivial and brutal: some players finish with block in the hundreds and lose almost no runs, while others hit a wall at the higher ascension levels (D3 to D8)
Characters feel too similar to some players, especially the two block-focused ones, and there are few non-attack/block dice types in practice
Relics are seen as either underwhelming or game-solving, with weak payoffs for build themes such as glass or gold dice

Accessibility gaps: constant looping animations that cannot be turned off triggered migraines/motion sickness for some, and the pixel font is hard to read for some; Steam Deck controller support was reported as poor
Lore is thin in game with much of it reportedly living in the Discord
Several negative reviewers say it lacks staying power or 'sauce' compared with Slay the Spire, Peglin or Astrea: numbers just go up, decisions repeat each turn, and progression feels flat
improvements: Add a fast mode or option to skip or speed animations to shorten long runs
Improve readability: clearer display when several effects share a tile, and a breakdown view showing how relics and modifiers change each die's numbers
Rebalance so more builds are viable, and so blocking every turn or rejecting all dice rewards is not the dominant approach; make enemies scale or add pressure to long fights
More dice types, characters, relics with bigger build-around payoffs, and more run-to-run variety
Add an accessibility mode (toggle for wiggling animations, readable font) and proper Steam Deck controller support
Reduce the grind of levelling every character for unlocks and 100% completion, and make higher difficulties less reliant on cheesy infinite combos
unique_things: Dice rather than cards, placed into a per-character grid board where position and adjacency matter
Attack, defense, healing and booster dice colour-coded, with boosters and copy effects that feed off neighbours
Starting gear and dice that are worth keeping all run, unlike the disposable starter cards in many Slay the Spire-likes
Began as a 2021 game jam entry and itch.io demo and grew into a Steam release with a community-involved development style
Frogs-versus-bugs presentation with a gambling-flavoured risk/reward layer on events
tedious_or_disliked: Long, slow combats and runs with simple decisions repeated every turn
Levelling characters to unlock content and pursue completion, which fans themselves call grindy
Having to re-read dice descriptions and edge cases each turn, which makes it feel like homework to some
Late-game number inflation and high-difficulty negative modifiers that push toward infinite-combo builds
Persistent animations and small pixel text for motion- or migraine-sensitive players
divisive_points: Difficulty: some say it is far too easy and easy to break, others find the ascension levels brutal
Run pace: some enjoy the calm, strategic tempo; others compare it unfavourably to 30-minute Slay the Spire runs
Build variety: fans praise the combo depth while critics say choices are an illusion and everything converges
Longevity: players with hundreds of hours love it, while a notable minority lose interest within 5-10 hours
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched Feb 21, 2025 on PC after a 2021 game jam and itch.io demo history. Review counts grew from about 2,900 (92%) during Early Access to about 3,600 (92%) after the 1.0 release on May 1, 2026. Dev updates continued through Early Access (for example an update called Challenges on March 3, 2026), and later additions such as potions and boss objectives got mixed responses because some objectives lengthen fights. Some reviewers who replayed after 1.0 said their earlier complaints about slowness and sameness still stood, and the accessibility request for reduced animation appeared unchanged at 1.0. Platforms: Windows and Mac on Steam, GOG version, and a Switch release is referenced by Rogueliker. Metacritic has no critic score; OpenCritic lists only two reviews with no aggregated score returned.

Build, farm and defend your village as you push deeper into goblin-infested territory. Unlock powerful upgrades and craft your environment to survive the endless goblin horde

other_scores.score: 94-95% positive (1,756 positive / 91 negative), Overwhelmingly Positive per Steam data; store page showed Very Positive 94% of 1,773
about $158k gross, about $46.6k net to developer (Boxleiter method, order-of-magnitude only)

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm gonna put this as a good B tier. It's just that there's no bad B tier.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Gnomes is a tower defense map-building roguelike where you place and reposition gnomes, walls, crops and other structures to protect a house from goblins arriving from varying directions on an open map. It was sent to the channel by a viewer and he went in with zero expectations. He found it a surprisingly strategic, unusual take on tower defense that demands attention every round, so it is not a casual chill game. The minimalistic art and hard-to-read chaos hold it back somewhat. He settles on B tier, phrased as a good B.
praise: Unusual fusion of tower defense and roguelike where units and structures can be moved every round
Open map with enemies spawning from different places each round forces constant re-planning
Strong pregame variety: roughly 16 starting loadouts plus different biomes (forest, swamp, desert) with distinct enemies
Rerollable shop every round with lots of crops, nodes and passives supports wildly different builds
Limited relic slots that can be expanded with money create meaningful choices
Runs feel different each time and stay fairly short in round count; appeals to hardcore build-crafting fans
criticism: Not for casual players; slow-paced and requires patience because of constant shopping and repositioning
Minimalistic art makes it hard to tell which goblin does what when things get chaotic
Chaotic moments are less satisfying than in Kingdom Rush or Bloons Tower Defense
He feels he would need much more time to get the best out of it
unique_points: Moving gnomes and structures every round instead of place-and-forget inverts the usual relaxed tower defense loop
Player shapes enemy pathing by building walls in a fully open level rather than defending a fixed lane
Tower defense and roguelike elements are aligned better than in many genre hybrids, per his view
commentary.quote: it's a very unique take on the tower defense gameplay
design_criteria: Genre synthesis: how well tower defense and roguelike elements are integrated
Strategic depth: decisions required every turn and repositioning
Build diversity: starting loadouts, biomes, crops, nodes, passives
Shop/economy: infinite rerolls and heavy buying between rounds
Pacing: slow and patient versus casual relaxation
Visual clarity and art: minimalist style and enemy readability
Run length: short round counts with lots of between-round activity
Meta/relic constraints: limited relic slots expandable with money

community.one_liner: A turn-based, maze-building tower defense roguelite by the two-person studio DYSTOPIAN in which you place and move weapon-wielding gnomes and plant crops to stop goblins reaching your garden shed.
community.consensus_summary: Gnomes (Steam, April 2025, $9.99, Windows only) is very well received by players: about 1,850 Steam reviews at roughly 95% positive (Overwhelmingly Positive), with the last 30 days around 91%. Players call it a tight, replayable throwback to classic mazing tower defense (WC3-style) with Vampire-Survivors/Balatro-style roguelite build variety and short runs. Complaints centre on RNG-dependent shop and relic offers, degenerate dominant builds (cactus, economy plants) and a sweaty, laggy endgame, plus the per-turn chore of moving every gnome. It is not early access; the two devs keep shipping free updates (1.3 and 1.3.2 in 2025, 2.0 with 4 maps and 8 guilds in early 2026, 2.1 balance and performance, 2.2 controller beta) and have since announced a new game, ALLFATHER. No Metacritic or OpenCritic entry exists for this game, so the signal is player reviews, plus a few small outlets and curators quoted on the Steam page.
best_things: Classic maze-building tower defense where gnomes physically block paths and you funnel goblins past them; players compare it fondly to Warcraft 3 TD maps and Plants vs. Zombies

Deep build synergies between gnomes, crops, buildings and relics (crops double as economy and buffs, e.g. coffee plant for attack speed), with items that change core rules like fertilising from dead goblins
Short runs that encourage experimentation and quick pick-up-and-play sessions; run structure compared to Balatro with an endless mode after wave 16
Distinct guilds act like character classes with different starting kits, and maps have different biomes, spawn points and music
Charming lo-fi, arcade look and a soundtrack that many reviewers single out as excellent
Excellent value (frequently bought around $5 on sale), runs on very low-end hardware, custom engine
Responsive devs who keep adding free content (new maps, guilds, relics, languages) and act on feedback
Procedurally generated maps and modifying the terrain give each run a different puzzle
worst_things: Shop and relic RNG is heavily influential; some players restart repeatedly until they get the upgrades a guild needs to function
Balance: a few items, economy plants (e.g. cactus, yawn/root combos) and mazing strategies dominate, so late-game builds converge and strategic variety shrinks
Late game / endless mode becomes sweaty, slow and laggy, with huge numbers of entities, path-visualisation clutter and very long late runs
Some guilds feel like meme or challenge starts rather than solid strategy foundations, per a critical review after an update
Only a single save/run slot at a time, even across modes
Steep learning curve early on with little in-game guidance for people unfamiliar with classic TD
Reviewers who bounce off it find it simple, repetitive or shallow: same loop with slight variations, little variety in artifacts, and runs too short for meaningful economy decisions
Gnome class synergies are weak; most runs stick to one gnome class because of gold cost and class-specific artifact slots
improvements: Rebalance dominant economy builds and underpowered guilds so more builds are viable in the 20+ day late game
Reduce RNG dependence (shop rerolls, guaranteed access to guild-relevant items) or add more ways to mitigate bad rolls
Bulk or group movement of gnomes and other quality-of-life for repositioning, and multiple save slots (both requested on the Steam forum)
Better onboarding and tutorial for newcomers to mazing tower defense
Polish controller support (beta added in patch 2.2) and further late-game performance optimisation
Add a proper soundtrack release (a reviewer wished for one) and requested features such as multiplayer
unique_things: Towers (gnomes) are movable every turn, making it a positioning puzzle rather than fixed-node placement, unlike most modern TDs
Crops and plants are both the income engine and the buff system, so farming and defense are one loop
Goblins and waves can alter the map (e.g. sappers leaving holes in your maze) and tile effects can redirect enemy waves
Roguelite meta-loop with guilds and stages unlocked by play, pick-from-options choices and rule-bending relics, described as bringing Vampire Survivors/Brotato-style build craft into tower defense
Endless mode after beating wave 16 with escalating waves, Balatro-style
Turn-based pacing with unlimited placement per turn, in a compact, low-spec custom engine
tedious_or_disliked: Having to move every gnome every round is called tedious and frustrating by several negative reviewers, and it is the main dealbreaker for players who prefer fixed-tower TD like Kingdom Rush
Endgame grind: planting thousands of cacti or crops and still not clearing a level; very time consuming and punishing
Restarting maps repeatedly to fish for a workable RNG shop
Repetitive opening turns at the start of every run
Short-lived fun for some: negative reviewers say the loop is simple and repeats the same strategy every run (plant as much as possible, build houses, brute force), so interest fades quickly
divisive_points: The movable-gnome mechanic: praised as the game's defining twist by most, hated as a chore by a vocal minority
The roguelite layer: some love the variance and variety, others say it would be tighter as a straight campaign TD with an optional endless mode
Endgame difficulty and sweatiness: hardcore players enjoy the challenge and optimisation, others see degenerate builds and lag
Depth: fans praise mastery and synergy depth, critics find strategy shallow and solved (plant economy plus maze)
community.reception_notes: Launched April 4, 2025 at $9.99 with strong positive reviews and grew steadily on word of mouth. Mid-2025 updates (1.2 with 17 new languages via Gamersky/AllCorrect, 1.3 with 4 new maps and relics) brought waves of new players, and the devs reported about 15,700 new players in one month after 1.3. After a break of well over a year of seven-day weeks, they returned with 1.3.2 QoL (game speed resets to 1x each day, multiselect building tweaks, late-game performance). Update 2.0 (around March 2026, free) added 4 maps (caves, Niflheim, City, and a combined Portal 2 final challenge), 8 guilds and many relics. Patch 2.1 followed a TD Fest feature and a Daily Deal that brought roughly 20,000 new players; it nerfed degenerate builds (cactus and dynamite cost up and made uncommon, Green Thumb now adjacent only) and improved late-game performance, which a minority of reviewers say hurt late-game build variety. Patch 2.2 added controller support in beta. The devs nominated the game for the Steam 'Best Game You Suck At' award in late 2025. In late September 2026 one of the two devs announced a new project, ALLFATHER, so future content support is uncertain. Windows only (no Mac or Linux). A different 2012 iOS game named Gnomes exists on Metacritic but is unrelated. Web search budget was exhausted mid-session, so community reading is based on Steam reviews, the Steam forum and official patch notes rather than Reddit threads.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Hollow Survivors is a fairly traditional action roguelike where you climb a tower out of hell, with a Hades-style hub between runs and survivorlike hordes of enemies in the rooms. He was drawn in by its vibe and art style, and he enjoyed the journey to the ending thanks to meaningful meta progression. After completing it, though, he finds content and replayability thin: boons are the only thing that changes a run, and there are no shops, events or weapon-specific upgrades. He places it in the low-to-middle B tier for now and hopes for more content updates.
praise: Great vibe and art style, with visually distinct biomes
Hub world with characters and permanent upgrades between runs, Hades-inspired
Fast-paced, hectic core gameplay, especially after unlocking the double dash
Infinite wall-less arenas feel immersive
Starting weapons each have their own move set
Meta progression makes the path to the ending a satisfying adventure
Challenging bosses and difficulty before meta upgrades are unlocked
criticism: Little content: few unique events, NPC interactions or unique floors, and mostly the same hordes
Room rewards are weak; boons are rare and the only thing that changes a run
No shop or mid-run currency, so little player choice during a run
Many boons are not impactful, and weapons lack unique upgrades so runs feel alike
Replayability is weak after the ending; hard mode gives no real reward once everything is unlocked
Could lean harder into the survivorlike aspect with far more enemies
unique_points: Blends Hades-like hub and structure with survivorlike horde rooms
Endless wall-less floors where you never run out of things to fight
Design lesson: mid-run currency and a shop would add player agency and reward choice
commentary.quote: this is going to be a middle B, I guess low B, for now
design_criteria: Meta-progression: important and satisfying, but runs out once everything is unlocked
Replayability: weak because runs feel similar and weapons lack unique upgrades
Run variety and events: too few unique events, floors or NPC interactions
Player choice and rewards: no shop or mid-run currency, rare boons
Boon impact: some exciting, many not very impactful
Visuals and vibe: strong art style and distinct biomes
Combat feel and pace: fast, hectic, especially with double dash
Difficulty: hard bosses early, hard mode lacks incentive

community.one_liner: A top-down action roguelite from solo dev Danny Deer (published by PlayWay/Gameparic) where you fight up a tower of about 20+ floors of monster hordes, picking soul-card upgrades and building up a settlement between runs, in a Vampire Survivors/Hades hybrid style.
community.consensus_summary: Players rate it Very Positive on Steam (82% of 201 reviews) for its snappy, fast combat, art, and quick meta-progression, but many recommend it only on sale because the content runs thin after a few clears. The few critics who covered it echo that: Worth Playing scored it 75 and said the loop is fun but does not sustain interest beyond a couple of hours. Negative reviewers find the combat clunky (contact damage, forward lunge on attacks, non-invulnerable dashes) and the meta-progression grindy. It is a full release (not early access), launched 10 Apr 2025, and at least one 2026 reviewer asks whether it was abandoned since Aug 2025. Sales look modest: one estimator puts it near 19k USD gross.
best_things: Fast, fluid, snappy combat when kiting hordes; several reviewers enjoy the roguelite-deckbuilder plus bullet-hell mix
Pixel art and grim atmosphere praised even by players who dislike the gameplay
Progression feels smooth and quick, with a steady ladder of unlocks so you rarely feel stuck
Bosses, weapons (scythe, great axe and others) and spells give variety; spell-based upgrades are the ones with real synergies
Story has a grim opening and a Loop Hero-like tone that one reviewer found enjoyable
All achievements obtainable through normal play with no guides needed
Difficulty described as fair, not too easy or too hard, for a cheap indie; controller support and Steam Cloud included
worst_things: Clunky combat: touching enemies deals damage, attacks lunge you forward into enemies, and dashes lack full invincibility so you often dash into damage
Shallow content: only a handful of unlockable weapons and subweapons, and the same power-ups recur
Most upgrade picks are generic stat buffs or simple triggers; few meaningful synergies outside spells
Confusing boss hitboxes and inconsistent drops (a run with no health orbs, then four or five in one stage)
No in-game encyclopedia or explanation of upgrade-card mechanics; weapons can only be judged from panel stats
Price feels steep for the amount of content (about 10 USD) according to several reviewers
Higher difficulties scale weakly, so post-game replay value is limited
improvements: Add an in-game codex and clearer explanations for upgrade cards and curse mechanics
Fix contact-damage and forward-lunge combat, and give dashes real invincibility frames
Add more content: more weapons, subweapons, enemies, stories or quests per character, and stronger endgame difficulty scaling
Rework upgrade pools so there are fewer dead cards (curse cards need their enabler) and more build-defining synergies
Make unlock and material acquisition less grindy, since rare materials come only from late bosses and boss rewards are random
Post-launch support: a player notes no updates since Aug 2025
unique_things: Survivors-style auto-fight fused with a per-stage reward pick (alternating essence currency and upgrades) instead of XP-gem levelling
Hades-like camp where you invest currency in permanent stat upgrades (one reviewer calls this artificial friction)
Fixed-length tower (about 20 to 24+ floors) with a handful of set bosses rather than endless survival
tedious_or_disliked: Grind for meta upgrades: one reviewer with 4 hours and thousands of coins said the game still felt like its first five minutes
Alternative weapons and spells are a grind to unlock and some are no better than the starter weapon
Rare materials and keys come only from the latest bosses, punishing players who usually die around floor 17
The per-floor reward alternation produces a linear, boring power climb
Repetitive enemies and same-feeling moves become monotonous after about an hour for some
divisive_points: Whether combat feels fast and snappy or jerky and clunky, especially the forward lunge and contact damage
Whether it is a worthwhile 10 USD buy or only a discount pick for its amount of content
community.reception_notes: Launched 10 Apr 2025 as a full release on Windows, macOS and Linux at 9.99 USD; a prologue and demo also exist. Steam has a very positive label but small review count. Metacritic lists it with only one critic review and no user ratings, and no OpenCritic entry was found. Developer/publisher team posts pinned suggestion and bug threads on Steam, but a 2026 reviewer says no updates since Aug 2025, suggesting support has wound down. Reddit and other outlets could not be read; community detail comes from Steam reviews and Steam forum. No major controversies found. Sample of local Steam reviews is small (19 texts); forum-sourced claims were dropped as unverifiable.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Jotunnslayer is a Diablo II-inspired survivors-like with striking visuals, where you pick god paths and character skills that produce wildly different spell effects. He finds it very satisfying and replayable, with mechanical (not percentage) upgrades, varied maps and big Diablo-style bosses. It does not revolutionize the genre, and readability and a few meta-progression annoyances hold it back. He places it in high B tier.
praise: Impressive, satisfying visuals and spell effects (e.g. a level-one ghost ship sweeping the map)
Gods and character skills give drastically different abilities, and each character plays differently
Upgrades are mostly mechanical changes rather than flat percentage boosts, so they feel impactful
Seeing how a god ability changes visually at its final level 18 is a highlight
Maps feel distinct and the big end bosses look cool and satisfying
Lots of meta-progression, mini quests with risk/reward choices, and community events; developers listen to feedback
Many character/god combinations give strong replayability
criticism: Hard to see what is happening on screen; damage sometimes comes from unseen sources, making losses feel bad
Player character is less visible than in other games, worse on some maps
Switching god paths requires refunding and reallocating skill tree points every run (unless meta is maxed)
No luck stat or rarity-style random upgrades, so repeating the same character/god combo feels samey
Some bosses are too close to Diablo II; the game does not revolutionize the genre
unique_points: God-based spell system where each god offers radically different, visually distinct abilities
Upgrades that change mechanics rather than numbers
Optional mini quests with varying difficulty and reward during runs
commentary.quote: It doesn't revolutionize anything, but it just by its visuals
design_criteria: Visuals/charm: major draw, Diablo II-inspired art and spell effects
Upgrade design: mechanical changes over flat percentages
Synergies/diversity: gods times characters give many combinations
Readability: hard to track threats and player model
Meta-progression: plentiful points, but respeccing gods each run is inconvenient
Randomness: wishes for a luck/rarity stat
Enemy/boss design: cool but too Diablo II-like
Level design: maps feel distinct
Replayability: high due to combinations

community.one_liner: An isometric Norse-mythology horde-survivor roguelite (Games Farm / ARTillery, published by Grindstone) where you pick a class plus up to three gods for boons, clear map objectives and bosses, and grind meta-progression trees.
community.consensus_summary: Players rate it Very Positive on Steam (about 82.5% of roughly 7,800 reviews), and critics are lukewarm-to-favourable (Metacritic PC 79 from 8 critics; Switch 2 76 from 12). It is seen as a polished, good-looking, solid survivor-like that does not reinvent the genre. Praise centres on the art, class and god variety, and boss and map design; criticism centres on shallow content, weak late-game scaling, and a few dominant skills. It launched in Early Access on Jan 21, 2025 and hit 1.0 on Sep 3, 2025. It has kept getting updates since, including an endless mode, balance changes, a Conan DLC, a post-1.0 roadmap (Nov 2025) and console and Switch 2 ports. Console ports drew some technical complaints.
best_things: Strong presentation: dark, Diablo-like isometric art, detailed environments and enemy designs, and a powerful soundtrack that stands above typical pixel-art survivor-likes
Six classes each with a signature gimmick plus subclasses unlocked about ten levels into a run, giving more variety than generic +damage/+area/+crit picks
Hades-style god system: choose up to three Norse gods whose boons have real interactions rather than plain stat sticks
Distinct maps with objectives and missions that reduce aimless circling, and cool boss fights
Short 10-20 minute runs suit quick sessions, and meta-progression gives that 'numbers go up' satisfaction
Local/split-screen co-op, full controller support, and ongoing developer support with balance patches
Per-character meta-progression resets and higher difficulty tiers give optional challenge (praised by Rogueliker)
Many players call it a cheap, addictive 'brain-off' game with a long tail (one reviewer has 70+ hours and keeps returning)
worst_things: Low run-to-run variety: many reviewers say runs feel the same and basic attacks feel as good as skills
Limited content at full price: few maps and enemies, and many players say they got their fill in 10-15 hours
A few dominant skills (Frost Ring is named) and god powers crowd out class abilities, so builds converge
Combat lacks impact: weak hit feedback, 'invisible' damage, skills that feel unsatisfying
Skill trees and meta-progression can be maxed quickly and lack depth, so progression ends early
Performance: FPS drops in long sessions or on busy maps, large install size, and Steam Deck complaints despite Verified status
Balance swings: some builds are impossible while others are a 'screensaver', and higher difficulties have been called too easy
Endless mode runs out of skill choices around level 60, which pushes all-in no-healing builds
improvements: More maps, enemies and bosses, plus more late-game content beyond maxing the trees
Rebalance dominant skills and give class abilities a bigger role relative to gods (players want more class slots or stronger class flavour)
Deeper meta-progression, such as branching trees, gear or loot to chase, and better endless-mode scaling after level 60
Better combat feedback (damage numbers, impact) and optimisation for FPS, Steam Deck and consoles
Fix manual-aim options, which some say do not work right, and improve translations of in-game descriptions
Online co-op (currently local/shared-screen only) and a harder top difficulty
unique_things: Norse setting with a Hades-like choose-your-gods structure layered on a survivor-like
Class plus subclass system that changes the run mid-way
Story-mode maps built by hand with objectives rather than pure open arenas, plus boss encounters
Higher production value and art direction than most pixel-art genre peers
Per-character meta-progression reset option and a Conan DLC crossover
Comparisons players make: Vampire Survivors x Diablo, Hades x Vampire Survivors, or 'Death Must Die in 3D'
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding skill trees and stones for 100% gets repetitive after about 10 hours
Repetitive music and samey runs in long sessions
Early maps described as barren, open arenas that can feel sleepy or slow (some wish for a speed-up option)
Endless mode's dry skill pool after level 60
Enemies that teleport or catch you instantly, which makes kiting and repositioning feel ineffective
Conan DLC seen by some as minimal and not worth the price, and DLC detection bugs reported
divisive_points: Difficulty: some say it is tougher than peers, others say Insane is trivial once you have upgrades
Build variety: fans praise god and subclass interactions, detractors say a couple of skills dominate
Value: worth it at a sale price or under $20 for some, too thin for the price for others (10 hours vs 70+)
Originality: 'derivative but well done' versus 'feels uninspired'
community.reception_notes: Early Access started Jan 21, 2025; 1.0 released Sep 3, 2025 with endless mode added, priced around $15 list at launch (Steam showed $8.99 at snapshot time). SteamSpy estimates 200k-500k owners; the revenue calculator estimates roughly $2.27M gross and $670K net, with no copies figure. The OpenCritic page could not be confirmed, so it is left null. Steam: 82.5% positive overall; recent reviews were about 80% positive in the store snapshot. Metacritic headline 76 is the Switch 2 page; PC is 79 from 8 critics. User score 6.7 is based on only 6 ratings, so it is not reliable. Post-launch: a Conan DLC, skin pack, a post-1.0 roadmap (Nov 2025) and Switch 2/console ports. Switch 2 port criticised for framerate and crashes by Gaming Nexus and Nintendo News PL, and the Steam Deck build has negative feedback despite its Verified badge. PC (Windows) only on Steam. A few early reviewers say the game got easier after balance patches.

commentary.summary: Keeper's Toll is a Vampire Survivors-style auto-attacker that wraps its runs in an adventure campaign with quests, NPC events and quest-specific bosses. Discovery of secrets and puzzle-like mysteries, which he feels most survivor-likes fail to capture
Characters feel drastically different from one another

commentary.quote: I'm going to put this as a as a low midb tier.
comparisons: Dungeon/Soul Slayer-style survivor-likes (the game covered just before)
design_criteria: Discovery/secrets: quest-based campaign and mysteries are the strongest aspect
Replayability/build diversity: only two paths per character, weak
Synergies and items: few synergies, bland passives, no rarity
Meta-progression: powerful but per-character XP feels unfair and unflexible
Enemy design: good variety and attention, Souls references
Boss design: single big creatures with no adds hurt horde-focused builds

community.one_liner: A dark-fantasy pixel-art survivors-like (bullet heaven) from Stingbot Games that mixes Vampire Survivors-style horde survival with ARPG elements and Dark Souls-flavored bosses, with six very different hero classes.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate it Very Positive (about 89% of roughly 800 reviews), but the praise is often lukewarm: many positive reviews describe it as a cheap, chill, brain-off auto-shooter and then list major flaws, and many negative reviews say it is fine but loses out to Halls of Torment or Vampire Survivors. Critics barely covered it; Metacritic holds a single critic review (Softpedia, 75/100) so no Metascore is computed, and there is no OpenCritic entry that could be found. It spent time in Early Access (from May 2023) and launched 1.0 on 28 Oct 2024 at about $6.99, with versions on Switch, PlayStation and Xbox. Reviews written through 2026 show the developer is still remembered as supporting it with updates, though the same balance and variety complaints persist.
best_things: Six classes that play very differently (fighting-game-style combo inputs for the Shadow Monk, minion-based Necromancer, tanky dodge-based Bogatyr, etc.), and the cast is praised as unusual versus the standard fighter/mage/assassin set
Detailed pixel art and a well-liked dark fantasy soundtrack
Boss fights and enemy design with Souls-like flavor; bosses are more than plain damage sponges (though some call them not especially intricate)
Cheap price (about $7) and a 10-20 hour campaign make it an easy casual recommendation, described as a relaxing shut-your-brain-off game that suits short 20-30 minute sessions
ARPG touches: limited healing potions, in-run merchants, a minor quest system, per-character skill trees and a global skill tree that forces choices
Curses that impose a penalty but can reward you if you survive them, which is a twist on the genre formula
Skill tree and progression are called fun by some finishers, and quick early power growth suits casual play
Challenging for the genre, which some players welcome
worst_things: Severe class and skill imbalance: Blood Maiden, and to a lesser extent Archer/Pyromancer/Summoner, are described as far stronger, while Monk and Bogatyr are called weak; melee classes can take tens of minutes to kill bosses
Poor run variety: only 4 maps (one a small square arena), a limited merchant pool, and upgrade options that let you pick up nearly everything, so runs with the same class feel identical
The power fantasy fades or never arrives; there is a clear ceiling on how strong you become, and several reviewers said they never felt powerful even with talents maxed
Stat and mechanic opacity: curses, defense value, pickups such as yellow crystals and XP sources are poorly or never explained, and there is no codex or visible list of active curses
Clunky movement and dodging, and only left/right aiming, which is an odd fit for a genre where enemies surround you
Visual clutter late in a run hides dodgeable hazards; some players turn effects off to see traps, and certain curse hazards look like background effects
Seen as derivative: several reviewers say enemies and bosses are very close copies of Dark Souls designs, and that it is a weaker Halls of Torment
Endgame and story disappoint: the final boss is called underwhelming compared with the third boss, and the story is called nonsensical or almost non-existent
Frustrating RNG: too few rerolls and upgrade choices that are often poor or junk actives, which reviewers cite alongside balance problems
improvements: Rebalance classes so weaker ones (Monk, Bogatyr, Archer, Necromancer) and melee builds are viable, and so one or two classes do not dominate
Add more maps, stages and a bigger item/merchant/upgrade pool so runs differ from each other; more levels was a direct request from finishers
Add in-game information: a codex or index for curses, clearer defense/stat effects, a detailed character sheet with damage and bonus breakdowns, and visual indicators for XP sources and elites
More rerolls or better upgrade choice control, and reduce randomness that hands out junk actives
More meta-progression depth and unlockables (only six characters, all unlocked from the start, reduces the chase); players also ask for more XP sinks late-game and more tome drops
Polish controls and sight lines: dodge/aim improvements and clearer hazard telegraphing; one player also requested co-op on the Steam forum
unique_things: Hybrid of survivors-like and Diablo-style ARPG: each character has its own full weapon/skill set rather than a single starting weapon
Souls-lite tone and boss homages layered on a bullet-heaven loop, with bullet-hell style bosses
Class mechanics that break from the norm, such as the Shadow Monk's directional combo inputs and the Necromancer's corpse/minion play
Curse system that gives both debuffs and potential boons, plus a minor quest system and limited healing potions
Individual per-character talent trees on top of a global skill tree where you cannot unlock everything
Kindled (harder) runs that grant extra XP and are used to advance character talent trees
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding the same four maps repeatedly to level each character's talent XP and to see late-game bosses, then restarting the loop with every new class
Achievement grind: some achievements (for example 1 million kills) are called tedious, and several reviewers say most of their hours after the first 4-15 were achievement grinding
Hard kindled runs on fresh characters are described as near-impossible until perks are unlocked, which forces the XP grind
Repetition sets in after roughly 10-15 hours; one reviewer says only about 3-4 hours felt like discovery
Learning curses and unexplained pickups by trial and error
Three of the four maps are infinite in all directions, which one reviewer found disorienting and wished had a constrained layout or map
Character talent XP is slow to earn, which negative reviewers call a drag on progression
divisive_points: Difficulty and challenge: some enjoy it as more challenging than most survivors-likes, others find bosses and kindled runs frustrating, especially with weak classes
Power fantasy: dad-gamer/chill reviewers love quickly getting powerful with AoE and big numbers (especially maxed Blood Maiden), while others never feel powerful
Value: a low price and roughly 10-hour campaign make it a fair buy for some, while others say wait for a deep sale and buy Halls of Torment or Vampire Survivors instead
Souls homages: praised as flavor by some and criticized as too close to copying by others
community.reception_notes: Early Access began May 2023 and 1.0 shipped 28 Oct 2024 on PC, with versions listed for Switch, PS4/PS5 and Xbox; the Steam community has a thread asking whether console is up to date with PC. Steam is Windows-only (no Mac/Linux). Some players also reported Steam Deck performance issues. Launch and current Steam sentiment are both Very Positive, and the low price is repeatedly cited as a reason players forgive the thin content. Several 2025-2026 reviewers say the developer has kept up with updates, but balance, variety and explanation gaps are still cited as unresolved. One review mentions that design discussions once explored other directions such as a Golden Axe-style beat-em-up, and a few vestiges of the original Souls-lite ARPG design remain (for example the Ebon King boss). Commercial performance appears modest (roughly tens of thousands of owners), and critical press coverage is minimal. Web search budget was exhausted during this task, so fewer outside outlets and no Reddit threads could be consulted (Reddit fetch is blocked); Softpedia review page returned 403, so its content is taken from the Metacritic summary.
