games.name: Star Renegades
games.short_description: Star Renegades is a dimension spanning rogue-lite strategy RPG. Outsmart uniquely generated adversaries, forge bonds between heroes and end the cycle!

other_scores.score: DualShockers 90, GamingTrend 90, The Digital Fix 90, RPG Fan 87, Edge 50

placements.verbal_evidence: right now I'm going to put this as a like a mid B tier, which I know is going to disappoint a lot of people

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Star Renegades is a turn-based strategy RPG roguelike with a party of up to five characters, a timeline bar for turn order, and heavy Darkest Dungeon inspiration. He finds the core combat satisfying and strategic, with great art and animation, but is deeply frustrated by a messy UI and unclear information. After about 10 hours he is still confused by mechanics, and runs can drag. He places it mid B, says a UI overhaul would make it much better, and plans to return to it.
praise: Core tactical combat is satisfying, enjoyable and fairly strategic
Timeline/time-bar mechanic, where you manipulate enemy turn order and crits, is unique and strategic
Art style and animations are excellent, with unique animations per enemy and attack
Characters play drastically differently and there are many party combinations
Solid story with attention to characters and camp relationship systems
Items add roguelike variety so runs feel different
criticism: UI is a mess: no quick inventory, information is unclear, and enemy intentions are hard to see
Basic quality-of-life gaps, e.g. needing to press a button then click to inspect an enemy instead of hovering
Overwhelming and confusing to start; unclear why some attacks are automatic and turn order can trigger accidentally
Runs can be very long, with fights taking many turns of repeating the same few abilities
Starting a new run feels like a drag; characters have no roguelike progression and level identically
unique_points: The timeline bar, where positioning before enemies and pushing them back enables crits, is its most unique part
Turn-based RPG roguelikes are rare despite the genre's roots, making this a notable entry
Gameplay is more complicated than Darkest Dungeon, which he is unsure is good or bad
commentary.quote: I hate this game's UI so much.
design_criteria: UI/information clarity: his biggest issue, poor presentation of enemy intent and menus
Strategic depth: timeline mechanic and turn-based tactics are the highlight
Visuals and animation: strong art and per-attack animations
Character diversity: distinct movesets and party combinations
Run length and pacing: long runs and slow early game drag
Roguelike variation: items provide variety but characters lack roguelike progression
Quality of life: small missing features add up to frustration

community.one_liner: A pixel-art sci-fi turn-based tactical JRPG roguelite by Massive Damage (published by Raw Fury) where you chain attacks on a timeline, break enemy turns, and fight an invading empire across dimensions over multi-hour runs.
community.consensus_summary: Star Renegades is received as a flawed but distinctive and deeply tactical roguelite. Critics landed at a Metascore of 77 on PC (40 reviews on Metacritic), with many 85-90 scores praising the art, combat and variety, and a few lukewarm ones (Edge 50) citing overwhelming systems and difficulty. Steam players are more positive than Metacritic users: 82.6% positive across about 3,083 reviews (Very Positive), while Metacritic users sit at a mixed 6.6. Long-time players say it has been effectively left as-is by the developer (bugs and balance issues remain), and it is frequently discounted to under $5-10. Players who bond with the timeline system sink hundreds of hours in, while many others bounce off the run length, RNG and writing.
best_things: Timeline-based turn combat: chain attacks, delay enemies, and 'break' them so they forfeit their turn and take crits; reviewers call it innovative and puzzle-like, often comparing the feel to Into the Breach
Very strong pixel art with modern lighting and effects, plus an energetic synth soundtrack, highlighted by critics (Digital Chumps, GamingTrend) and players alike
Deep build variety via classes, weapons, perks and skills, with lots of synergies to discover
Nemesis-style system where escaped or victorious mini-bosses return stronger with new modifiers, giving runs memorable loops
Camp and affinity system between party members produces cutscenes and unlocks alternate appearances and movesets; progeny system unlocks new characters
Escalating difficulty ladder (Harsh up to Entropy levels) and new-game-plus style restarts where unlocks carry over give strong replay depth for dedicated players
Great value on sale; several players report 200-700+ hours played
Runs on Steam Deck and is praised as a handheld game despite minor lag when fast-forwarding
worst_things: Runs are very long (commonly 2-4 hours, some report 6+), so a death late in a run feels punishing
Heavy RNG layering (rewards, enemy backline placement, nemesis modifiers) can invalidate a build through no fault of the player
Timeline predictions are sometimes inaccurate or ignore certain moves, which can cause run-ending surprises; mechanics are poorly explained in tooltips
Writing and tone are a frequent complaint: irreverent, cliched, fourth-wall-breaking dialogue that clashes with the world; thin story with no Hades-style narrative progression across runs
Bugs: soft locks when returning from the map view, chests or looting ceasing to work, stuck end-of-run states, and autosaves capturing broken states; heavy CPU use reported
Weak tutorial and steep learning curve; players often need outside guides to understand time manipulation and statuses
Meta-progression is slow or uninspiring and many players unlock the important items within a few runs, while higher difficulties effectively force a narrow set of builds
Too few regions, so repeated runs feel samey; map navigation is point-and-click and slow, especially during night backtracking
Full price ($24.99) is widely called hard to justify: several top reviews say it feels unfinished, like early access, and recommend buying only on sale
improvements: Shorter or more modular runs, or mid-run save points and healing options, to reduce the cost of dying
Reroll or refresh systems for rewards to mitigate bad RNG
More accurate and complete timeline predictions and better in-game explanation of mechanics and statuses
More regions, bosses and content variety so later runs differ more, plus richer meta-progression
Rebalance difficulty tiers and weak synergies or combo skills so more than a handful of builds remain viable at high difficulty
Bug fixes and stability work (soft locks, looting, performance); players also ask for a sequel that addresses the feedback
unique_things: Timeline combat where pushing enemies off the timeline breaks them and forces crits, mixing tactical-RPG puzzle logic with roguelite runs
Nemesis-system-inspired boss and mini-boss memory across attempts, with special dialogue on revisits
Dimension-hopping sci-fi JRPG setting (Star Wars meets cyberpunk flavour) with mech and pixel-art aesthetics
Progeny and relationship system that generates variant heroes and unlocks characters through affinity rather than simple currency
Alternating male or female sibling protagonist between campaigns, and a true-ending chain that restarts you at higher difficulty with all systems scaling
tedious_or_disliked: Multi-hour runs that must be restarted from scratch after failure; several reviewers say it would be better as a linear JRPG with saves
Night-time backtracking and clicking through empty map segments
Grindy, repetitive structure: similar fights and few regions across runs, with small incremental upgrades between runs
Learning phase of reading about elements and statuses, and dying to unexplained mechanics
Cringe character banter, and a perceived janky UX and controls that several reviewers say bury a good core game
divisive_points: Roguelite structure: some love the long, high-stakes runs and depth while others say the game would be better as a standard JRPG
Story and humour: seen as charming and funny by some, unbearably cliched or off-tone by others
Difficulty and RNG: 'perfect information' and cerebral puzzle-solving to fans vs unfair and luck-driven to detractors
Value: a steal at under $5-10 on sale, but many feel it is unfinished at the $25 full price
community.reception_notes: Launched on PC on Sep 8, 2020 (Switch and Xbox One Nov 19, 2020; PS4 delayed to Mar 10, 2021 over technical problems), then added DLC and expansions (Star Renegades: Total Lunarcy, Prime Dimension, Enter the Dragoon on Steam). Critic reception was generally favourable at launch; Switch performance was the weakest (Metacritic 67). Steam sentiment has held at Very Positive for years, and recent reviews call the game slept-on but note the developer appears to have moved on, leaving bugs and balance problems unaddressed. Steam owner estimate is 200k-500k with an estimated gross revenue of about $2.3M (third-party estimate, not audited). Windows only on Steam (no Mac or Linux), Steam Deck reportedly works. OpenCritic could not be retrieved, so no score is given. Note: web search budget was exhausted, so community detail comes from Steam reviews, Steam discussion titles and Metacritic pages rather than Reddit (Reddit fetch was blocked).

games.name: The Royal Writ
games.short_description: Sacrifice creates stories in this medieval roguelike deckbuilder. Watch your cards march to glory or permanent death as they battle toward the enemy. Each fallen hero becomes part of your kingdom's legend. Command wisely... some sacrifices are necessary.

other_scores.score: Very Positive, 83.1% of 539 (448 positive / 91 negative) per local data

placements.verbal_evidence: this is going to be a very high B tier

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: The Royal Writ is a board-centric deckbuilder where placed cards advance up the board and score points, using a Balatro-style system of additive (blue) and multiplier (red) units. He finds it unique, charming and build-diverse, but it is complex and poorly explained, so it is not casually approachable. He recommends it to experienced deckbuilder and Balatro-like fans. He places it in a very high B tier.
praise: Very unique scoring: units add or multiply, with blue additive and red multiplier pieces
Extensive build diversity; every run plays out completely differently
Unique, fun, cute visuals with cool cutscenes and attention to backstory
Lots of map options: betting, a wheel, shopkeepers with unique traits, tinkering to convert multiplicative/additive and add effects
Bosses have unique mechanics that are shown ahead of time so you can adjust
Great vibe, audio and visuals; satisfying once you understand the systems
criticism: Complicated and not easy to pick up casually; many mechanics, keywords, temporary vs permanent cards and stats
Insufficient tutorial and information beyond hovering over things; some events unexplained even after heavy play
Dying to something you did not understand feels bad
Cards can be too niche in later runs, leaving offered cards unusable for a specific build
unique_points: Balatro-like scoring layered onto a board that cards march up, with permanent statuses and cards that die and need replacing
Tinkering can flip a card between additive and multiplicative or add teeth/extra effects
Heavy effort put into out-of-combat map options, which he values for player agency in deckbuilders
commentary.quote: this is going to be a very high B tier
design_criteria: Uniqueness of gameplay: rarely seen scoring/board combination
Build diversity: completely different runs each time
Accessibility and onboarding: tutorial and information clarity lacking
Synergies and card design: some cards too niche late in runs
Map and run options: betting, wheel, shops, tinkering give player choice
Boss design: unique mechanics telegraphed in advance
Visuals, audio and charm: strong vibe, cutscenes, backstory
Complexity: many keywords and mechanics that take time to learn

community.one_liner: A medieval roguelike deckbuilder from Save Sloth Studios (published by Yogscast Games) in which your cards are animal characters that march down lanes toward the enemy base, and any card that reaches the base is permanently lost from your deck.
community.consensus_summary: Well received by players (Steam Very Positive, about 83% of 539 reviews) and by the handful of critics who covered it (Metacritic 80 from 5 reviews). Praise centers on the art, music, charm and the card-synergy puzzle; complaints center on unclear rules text, RNG swings, and above all a steep difficulty and mechanic jump in Act 2. It is a small-scale indie (Steam revenue estimates around $96k gross) that players repeatedly say deserves more visibility. It is not abandoned: patches 1.1.0 (balance) and 1.2.0.2 (Act 2 boss eased) shipped, and a recent review mentions an announcement of a sequel (single-source, unverified). It has also come to console (Metacritic lists Switch, Xbox Series X and PS5).
best_things: Storybook hand-drawn art, detailed animations and character design are the most consistent praise, often the reason people bought it
Soundtrack and whimsical medieval tone, with lore-heavy card flavor and historical references
Card-synergy experimentation: building absurd engines from odd characters, transformations, hidden interactions and events is the core joy
Two distinct acts with different mechanics and card pools, which some players describe as two games in one
Permanent card death gives runs memorable stories and meaningful stakes, distinguishing it from Slay the Spire style deckbuilders
Blend of Inscryption-like board logic, Balatro-like blue damage x red multiplier scoring and Slay the Spire-like map with events and bosses
Challenge modes, custom seeds, an option to disable timed boss fights and strong accessibility options, plus 41 achievements to chase
Good value and strong 'one more run' pull; players report anywhere from about 5 to 100 hours
worst_things: Act 2 is widely described as a brick wall: new bullet, honor/morale and poison mechanics plus a huge-HP final boss (reported around 444k HP) made many players quit
Heavy RNG: a run can collapse from card draws or an early card death spiral with little player agency
Rules and ailment text are unclear; players guess what cards, bosses and keywords do and can lose cards permanently through misunderstanding
Many cards and relics feel weak or must-pick, so balance feels uneven
Bullet mechanic and unit death in Act 2 compound each other and are called frustrating or add-nothing by several reviewers
UI gets cluttered in busy battles; base power vs current power is not clearly shown, and misclicks can put upgrades on the wrong card
Some critics and players report repetition over extended play and fairness issues where a run is killed before you can react
improvements: Clearer tooltips, keyword explanations and on-card display of base vs current power and health
Rebalance Act 2 (boss HP, bullets, poison cleansing) and the weakest cards and relics; 1.2.0.2 reportedly already helped
More ways to reliably build around a synergy and reduce feast-or-famine RNG, especially as more unlocks dilute the pool
Better controller support and UI polish (one reviewer wanted easier controller play; Steam lists full controller support)
More character cards with hidden unlockable abilities, which a reviewer specifically wanted more of
Better onboarding so the opening hours are less confusing; more content after the main acts was requested by a couple of reviewers
unique_things: Cards are characters that advance column by column toward an enemy base, gaining buffs each column, and die if they hit the base
Every card is disposable and your deck is repaired and swapped after each battle rather than steadily built up
Act 1 and Act 2 play by different rules and use different card sets, with some Act 1 characters reappearing with new abilities and art
Score is blue damage times red multiplier, Balatro-style, plus gambling and shady-bargain sacrifice events
Character cards with hidden abilities that reveal their text only once triggered
Stun and corpse mechanics where stunned cards become corpses when trampled, and a cover system and projectiles in Act 2
tedious_or_disliked: Constantly replacing dead or injured party members makes it feel like deck repair rather than deck building to some players
Grinding through failed attempts at Act 2 bosses hoping for good cards, with the huge final boss HP bar seen as a slog
Opaque interactions that require trial, error and wiki/community lookups
Rising score requirements while your deck strength drops, producing a downward spiral
Unlock bloat: more unlocked cards and relics can make it harder to reliably find fun builds
divisive_points: Act 2 difficulty: fans see it as the real challenge and a second game; a large share of negative reviews say it ruins the experience
RNG vs synergy: some love adapting to chaos, others say wins feel like luck and there are too few mechanics to reliably synergize
Permanent card death: emotional storytelling for some, punishing and tilt-inducing for others
Length: some finished both acts in around 5 hours while others put in 100 hours, with opinions split on post-game content
community.reception_notes: Released Aug 7, 2025 on Windows via Steam at $14.99 with a demo available; Steam user reviews settled at Very Positive with a consistent split over Act 2. Patch 1.1.0 rebalanced cards and 1.2.0.2 reportedly made the Act 2 boss far more manageable (per player reviews, not verified against patch notes). Metacritic shows 5 critic reviews (score 80) and no user score yet; it lists PC, Switch, Xbox Series X and PS5, and The Outerhaven review is dated Sept 2026. No OpenCritic page could be found. Third-party estimates put Steam gross at about $95.6k and net about $28.2k (Boxleiter method, order-of-magnitude only; SteamSpy owners 0-20k). A Steam community thread shows players praising the option to disable timed boss battles and asking for Act 2 boss help; one boss (Bombardier Sorbus) was alleged buggy. Research caveat: the web search budget was exhausted, so Reddit and other outlets could not be read and community findings rely mainly on Steam reviews plus fetched pages.

games.name: The Spell Brigade
games.short_description: Survivors-like with ONLINE CO-OP for 1-4 players. Team up with your wizard friends to slay hordes of dark creatures. Complete team-based objectives, unlock new upgrades and create overpowered spell synergies. Friend nor foe is safe in this friendly fire bullet hell!

other_scores.score: 86% positive overall; 81% positive last 30 days (Very Positive)

placements.verbal_evidence: Currently, in its early access is going to be a low A tier.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: The Spell Brigade is a top-down, movement-only survivor-like in early access, built around finding and upgrading spells and combining elements onto them. He finds it very satisfying and enjoyable at its core, especially for its movement feel and multiplayer, but wants more content (spells, elements, relics, maps, bosses) and balance work. He places it in low A for now and thinks it could climb as updates land.
praise: Movement-only gameplay is a confident choice and the movement feel is excellent, possibly better than Brotato's
Elemental combos on spells (fire, lightning, frost, acid, dark) create chaotic, varied builds with unique visuals per combination
Randomized upgrade numbers based on luck
Exploding enemies chain reactions act as a catch-up mechanic for players behind
Revive system that works even in single player
Mini quests during runs add variety
Multiplayer is a blast and clearly the design focus; straightforward meta progression and many unlockable characters keep him playing
criticism: Only four maps and they feel repetitive, with not enough to do on them
Characters feel too similar; unique stats are minimal
Relic chests are oddly designed, small and specific, and annoying to find in single player since looking for them costs XP
Mini quests are unbalanced, some trivial and some nearly impossible
Some spells are weaker than others, feedback on damage and friendly fire is unclear, and only two final bosses with uneven difficulty
Fourth spell choice feels useless and muddies the upgrade pool; wants a choice of spell count and more rerolls

Enemies slow slightly when near the player, making weaving between them feel badass
Explosive-enemy chain reactions as a catch-up mechanic
Designed primarily for multiplayer with friendly fire and generous revives
commentary.quote: Currently, in its early access is going to be a low A tier.
design_criteria: Movement and mobility: core to a minimalistic survivor-like, praised highly
Synergies/build variety: elemental combinations on spells
Content diversity: wants more spells, elements, relics, bosses, maps
Map/level design: four maps feel repetitive
Character diversity: characters too similar
Balance: uneven quests, spells and final bosses
Player feedback: unclear damage and friendly-fire signals
Catch-up mechanics and revives: explosive chains, revive system
Meta progression: straightforward currency upgrades and unlocks
Multiplayer design: fun, friendly fire, primary design focus
Visuals: unique spell looks per element

community.one_liner: A 3D survivors-like (bullet heaven) from Bolt Blaster Games where 1-4 wizards fight hordes together online, with friendly fire, team objectives and elemental spell infusions.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate it Very Positive (about 81% of ~16.9k reviews in the local data; the live store page showed 86% overall and 81% in the last 30 days), driven mainly by co-op chaos, charming art and a satisfying core loop. The full 1.0 release on Apr 29, 2026 (after Early Access from Sep 16, 2024) sharply split the community: the most upvoted negative reviews blame a 3-5x increase in grind, costlier permanent upgrades and wizards locked behind gold instead of achievements. Critics are more lukewarm, with a Metacritic score of 69 (Mixed) from a handful of mostly PS5 reviews that praise the multiplayer but flag limited enemy variety and slow progression. Overall: a fun, friend-oriented co-op survivors-like that many feel is thin on variety and too grindy.
best_things: Online co-op for up to 4 is the standout; friendly fire, spell combos and accidentally wiping teammates generate the fun, and reviewers call it the game that makes or breaks the experience
Art style, animation and cute wizard designs with cosmetics and skins are widely praised as polished and welcoming
Easy to pick up, chaotic 'brain off' gameplay that works for chill sessions with friends; several groups report returning weekly
Elemental infusions, augments and spell synergies allow varied, sometimes overpowered builds
Team-based map objectives and quests add some structure beyond pure survival (Metacritic critics cite novel map design and quest systems)
Regular developer updates and receptive, community-oriented devs during Early Access
Runs well on Steam Deck and has cross-platform multiplayer, solo option and controller support
Low price (about $13) and a long-lasting time sink for some players, with several reviewers logging 100-280 hours
worst_things: 1.0 grind spike: gold rewards reduced while prices of permanent upgrades, enchantments, prestige resets and covenant unlocks rose sharply; reviewers say unlocking everything would take hundreds of hours
Wizard unlocks moved from achievement/challenge-based to gold purchases, removing a beloved mechanic and adding tedium
Limited variety: same enemies on every map, only a couple of bosses, and about a third of spells described as weak
Shallow progression: hour 30 plays like hour 1 with bigger stats, so runs feel repetitive after a dozen matches
Netcode and connection problems: no reconnect after a disconnect (a dropped player cannot rejoin), and lag with players matched from distant regions due to no region lock
Performance: endless mode gets very laggy as the screen fills up
Music is seen as basic, repetitive and poorly fitted to the game
Patch cycle perceived as fixing one thing while breaking another (e.g. controller problems after patch 1.1.4 reported on the Steam forum)
improvements: Reduce the gold/grind economy and restore cheaper or achievement-based ways to unlock wizards and covenants
Add more enemy types, bosses, maps and spells, and better balance across augments and elements
Add reconnect-to-session support and region locking or region filters for multiplayer matchmaking
Optimise endless mode and late-run performance; players also ask for split-screen multiplayer (a popular forum thread)
Add rerolls for build-defining traits and infusions, and clearer stat descriptions with exact numbers
Better teammate communication tools and deeper multiplayer synergy; Metacritic critics say co-op can feel like playing next to each other
More music and soundscape options
unique_things: Online co-op first design for 1-4 players in a survivors-like, with friendly fire so teammates can hurt each other
Team-based map objectives and quests (e.g. football/sheep/torch-style minigames) layered on top of wave survival
Elemental infusion system combined with spell augments for build crafting
Covenants as unlockable run modifiers with prestige-style resets of wizards
Full 3D camera with a colorful, cartoonish wizard aesthetic and cosmetic skins, unusual in a genre dominated by 2D pixel art
Cross-platform multiplayer, with a console release (PS5) alongside Steam
tedious_or_disliked: Gold grind needed for permanent upgrades, wizard unlocks and covenants; a single 45-minute multiplayer match may only afford one upgrade
Prestige resets and max-leveling a wizard repeatedly just to unlock one covenant
Some objective minigames (especially the football one) described as boring or impossible to complete with a swarm around
Quest/achievement difficulty is uneven; a third of achievements are pure time sinks, and some Early Access quests were RNG-locked (e.g. needing specific infusions without rerolls)
Hardcore mode outcomes hinge on early trait rolls (lightning/shadow good, acid/dark bad), forcing restarts
Endless-mode lag and the screen becoming unreadable as spells pile up
divisive_points: The 1.0 overhaul: some say the UI redesign, polish and added wizard/boss made it better, while the top negative reviews say it made progression worse and less fun
Solo play: some find it fine, others say it became much less playable solo after the grind increase and that the game only really works with friends
Difficulty and build variety: fans enjoy the chaos and scaling difficulty, while roguelike veterans find builds shallow and spells unbalanced
Visual chaos: a feature for some ('unreadable screen adds to the fun') and a problem for others
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched Sep 16, 2024 and was generally well liked, with frequent content updates. The 1.0 launch on Apr 29, 2026 brought a UI overhaul, a new wizard and boss, but also an economy rework that triggered a wave of negative reviews (the top two negative reviews have 350-400 helpful votes), leaving the recent review window weaker than before; the dev team was noted as receptive, and later patches (1.1.x) continued. Some players say it has improved since and praised the UI redesign. Metacritic shows a Metascore of 69 from 6 mostly PS5 critic reviews (PC 73 from 4; the page did not clearly state which platform the headline score refers to), and no user score yet. games.name: Void Crew
games.short_description: Void Crew is a Chaotic, Co-op Roguelite game for 1 to 6 players: Outfit your spaceship and crew for thrilling quests, brave fierce enemies in Space Battles... and try not to panic!

placements.verbal_evidence: I think I'm going to put this as a solid B tier.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Void Crew is a first-person spaceship management roguelike built around multiplayer, where each player fills a role such as pilot, gunner, engineer or spacewalker. Runs move sector to sector with varied missions, and progression comes entirely from upgrading the ship rather than the character. He had a great time with friends but found the single-player experience much weaker and more frustrating. Unclear information, janky clipping and underwhelming relics hold it back. He rates it a solid B with lots of potential, noting he would need more hours for an accurate rating.
praise: Multiplayer is chaotic, funny and well designed, with friends causing comedic disasters like jumping to hyperspeed while crewmates stand
Distinct crew roles (pilot, gunner, engineer, spacewalker)
Missions feel different from each other (combat, exploration, defending ships) across varied biomes
Visually beautiful, with a cool look and feel
Nerve-wracking fix-everything-on-the-ship moments when under fire are fun
Purely cosmetic loot box customization with no microtransactions
criticism: Information is unclear: port/starboard relic effects, hidden rules like energy cost not going below one, and stat displays that do not match module text
Help menu has many tabs and no search function
Some crew roles feel far less important than the game implies
Janky character clipping through walls
Relics are underwhelming and rare, giving only small stat tradeoffs
Single player is a drag with long, slow tasks, and runs cannot be quit midway because the game is built for multiplayer
Little ship customization early on
unique_points: Character never gets stronger in a run; all progression is ship upgrades (modules, relics, guns, installations)
Deliberately slow installation and repair mechanics so nothing is automated and players must fix things
Meta progression is small numeric stat and ability tweaks
commentary.quote: I think I'm going to put this as a solid B tier.
design_criteria: Multiplayer design: roles and cooperation make the game shine versus solo
Information clarity: poor tooltips and hidden rules frustrate
Mission variety: missions differ in focus and biome
Visuals/charm: beautiful look and cosmetic customization
Item/relic impact: relics feel underwhelming and too rare
Meta-progression: small numeric upgrades only
Run length and pacing: long, slow runs that cannot be quit midway
Polish: clipping and jank

community.one_liner: A first-person co-op roguelite for 1-6 players where a crew of pilots, gunners, engineers and scavengers runs a spaceship through procedurally chosen missions and space battles, with permanent character and ship-gear progression between voyages.
community.consensus_summary: Void Crew is well regarded, especially as a chaotic-with-friends co-op game: Steam shows Very Positive (about 86% of roughly 8,500 reviews) and Metacritic has an 80 from four critics. Reviewers and players love the role-based teamwork and the tension of keeping a ship alive, but the recurring caveats are thin content and repetition after a few runs, a rough solo experience, and run-ending bugs. It left Early Access (launched Sept 2023) with its 1.0 on Nov 25, 2024, and came to PS5 and Xbox with crossplay in Sept 2025. Recent Steam sentiment reads noticeably weaker than lifetime sentiment, driven by complaints that updates added bugs and that the loop hasn't deepened enough; the developer is still actively supporting it, though some players ask whether the game is fading.
best_things: The four-role crew structure (Pilot, Gunner, Engineer, Scavenger) forces real simultaneous cooperation, with the pilot positioning the ship for gunner firing angles while engineers patch damage
Emergent chaos and comedy when a crew of friends panics, argues over ship setup or sabotages each other, which Steam reviewers say is the game's main draw
Tension and difficulty at higher levels that make coordinated crews feel rewarded when they pull off a boss kill or narrow escape
Ship and module customization, including picking hardware and tactics before a voyage, which players like if they enjoy loadout planning more than pure shooting
Ongoing developer support and expansion, which players contrast favourably with publishers that abandon multiplayer titles
Feels like the first polished, popular take on the multi-crew-ship niche, though some reviewers fault the submarine-like flight and inconsistent ship-interior visuals
Works with 1-6 players and with random matchmaking, so it is playable beyond a fixed friend group
worst_things: Content depth is thin: several Steam reviewers say they saw nearly everything (enemy types, bosses, mission/base layouts) within 5-8 hours and call it demo-like for the price
Run-ending bugs in longer runs, such as objectives spawning inside asteroids, astral map interaction breaking after events like Interdiction, and seat/interaction failures that force rejoining
Multiplayer desync and crash issues in long sessions (over an hour or past about 10 jumps), including players who crash but linger in the lobby and freeze it
Some players say it runs worse now than it did a year ago, i.e. updates introduced regressions
Solo play is punishing and widely described as not designed for it, which one critic said undercuts the game's identity
Flight feels slow, submarine-like and fails to convey zero-gravity (called out by Try Hard Guides and in other coverage)
Always-online requirement even in solo, multiple EULA prompts and opt-out analytics drew complaints from some Steam reviewers
Enemy variety and gunplay feel samey; level-up perks such as small fire-rate boosts do not feel like new content
Generative-AI voice acting and content (added or disclosed after launch) drew complaints from some reviewers, including one who felt misled after the refund window
Small active player base: recent reviewers say public lobbies are scarce and mostly private even with crossplay
improvements: Carry blueprints or unlocks across voyages; one 20-hour player found progression too slow for hardware variety and boss loot meaningless because runs end at the boss
Add more enemy, boss, weapon and mission/base variety so runs differ beyond the first few levels
Fix long-run stability: desync, seating/interaction loss, lobby freezes and stuck objectives
Give the Scavenger role a clearer, more engaging identity (criticized in reviews for being ill-defined)
Improve solo and small-crew balance or scaling, plus difficulty spikes seen on continued saves
More cosmetics, endless or post-boss endgame options and more ways to mess with friends
unique_things: Multi-crew spaceship management in first person with real seats and stations, often compared to FTL in 3D or a Firefly-style misfits-in-space fantasy
Players physically move around the ship to repair, man turrets and route power, rather than controlling a single pilot avatar
Spacewalk/EVA scavenging missions and boarding tasks happen alongside the ship combat
Roguelite structure built around 'voyages' where ship gear is found and lost per run while character careers level permanently
Often contrasted with Jump Space (more focused on flying the ship) and Wildgate; Void Crew leans harder on crew management and ship upkeep
tedious_or_disliked: Repetition: the same early-level content and enemy types loop over many runs, described as just the first few levels repeated
Long runs that can end abruptly to a bug, making the time investment feel wasted
Slow XP progression that leaves players on starter gear for a large share of their playtime
Piloting and basic point-and-click shooting feel shallow to some, especially in two-player crews
Low-value rare drops and boss loot that can only be used for one or two missions
Roguelite depth is shallow: few build-defining items or synergies and single-tree character progression, so runs feel alike
divisive_points: Difficulty and solo play: some call the solo experience brutal and unfair, while others respond that it is a co-op game and solo complaints are misplaced
Depth vs. fun: critics and some players say it lacks long-term depth, yet many still rate it highly as a friends game and recommend it on a sale
Price: some reviewers feel full price is too much for the current content, others consider about 25 USD fair for the co-op fun
community.reception_notes: Early Access began Sept 7, 2023 from Danish studio Hutlihut Games (Focus Entertainment publishing); 1.0 launched Nov 25, 2024 at $24.99. Launch critics were uniformly positive (4 Metacritic reviews, all in the 76-90 range) while flagging weak flight feel, difficulty and solo play. A surprise PS5/Xbox Series X/S release with crossplay followed on Sept 4, 2025, ported with Piktiv; a pinned Steam hotfix post mentions lost console progress with compensation offered. It won Best Multiplayer Game at the 2025 Unity Awards and NYX Game Awards honors, and was nominated for Best Debut and Best Game Design at Denmark's Spilprisen 2024. Steam all-time reviews are Very Positive, but a Steam page snapshot showed the most recent 30 days as Mixed (about 65% positive on few reviews), and recent reviewers complain of increasing bugs. Steam revenue estimate (Boxleiter-style, unaudited) is about 4.5M USD gross, roughly 1.3M net, with SteamSpy owners at 200k-500k. Windows only on PC. OpenCritic could not be confirmed, so it is left null.

games.name: BALL x PIT
games.short_description: BALL x PIT is a brick-breaking, ball-fusing, base-building survival roguelite. Batter hordes of enemies with ricocheting balls and gather the riches of the pit to expand your homestead, generate resources and recruit unique heroes.

placements.verbal_evidence: to me, this is just going to be a a fine B tier

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Ball x Pit is a brick-breaker roguelike with a city-building management layer between runs. He finds it very unique and loves the ball fusion and evolution system, which he says is most of the fun. He is less taken with the slow early game, heavy RNG, lack of player control and the tedious hub building. He knows he is in the minority and lands it at B tier, having replayed it after updates without changing his view.
praise: Fusion and evolution of balls lets players build their own synergies every run, roughly 80%+ of the enjoyment
Characters feel different from each other at the start of a run
Late-game builds are chaotic, satisfying and can one-shot everything
Each biome has its own music, visuals, enemies and bosses
Visuals and overall vibe are strong, with plenty of content
Very unique concept, and short runs (about 15 minutes) let you progress both halves of the game
criticism: City building and resource management add tedium, with poor information, unclear buildings and stat effects, and weak quality of life
Pacing is off: early game feels unwinnable without meta progression, and the fun part arrives too late
Heavy RNG in upgrades, including random numbers of upgrades on evolution, leaves little control over winning a run
Gameplay is chaotic and idle-like with little skill expression; mechanics like re-catching balls become useless
Some passives are boring and the hitbox is unclear
Dual-focus design makes both halves feel weaker than dedicated games

Brick-breaker combined with hub city building is an unusual genre blend
Design lesson: games split in two halves often leave each half underdeveloped
commentary.quote: it was a bit of a chore to get to the good part

Run length: short (about 15 min) runs enable two-part loop
Player control/skill: low, chaotic and idle-like

games.name: Below the Crown
games.short_description: Explore the dungeons Below the Crown, in this love letter to Roguelikes, Dungeon Crawlers, and Chess. Prepare for strategy, game-changing spells, psychological tests, and challenges from your fellow players. From the award-winning creators of Duskers & A Virus Named TOM.

other_scores.score: Very Positive, 94.5% of 109 (local snapshot); store page showed 96% of 64

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put this as a high B tier to me, probably more to a lot of people.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Below the Crown is a small, strategy-focused chess roguelike where you command a wizard who summons pieces onto a board inside dungeons. He feels it is the first chess roguelike that truly captures real chess, since good chess play matters more than wild mechanics. Roguelike elements are tiny per-encounter boosts that never overshadow the core chess thinking. He admits he would not play it a lot himself and it may feel repetitive, but he recommends it to chess fans and places it at high B.
praise: Captures the feel of real chess better than other chess roguelikes; chess skill genuinely makes you better
Tutorials teach basic chess tactics like pinning, so players learn something
Smart AI, with gold rewards for strategic plays like checkmates and pins rather than just clearing pieces
Small, simple roguelike elements (easier placement, one-time freeze, one-time transform) fit the game's goals
Limited pieces and a sparse board keep turns slow and deliberate
Unexpected story with fourth-wall-breaking elements
Rooks look like frogs
criticism: Gameplay can feel repetitive, like chess itself
Slow turns and long individual encounters due to heavy thinking
Not a game for everyone; requires careful step-by-step play
He would not personally play it a ton since he is not a strong chess player
unique_points: Roguelike upgrades stay modest so the run is still about playing chess well, even at the final boss
Rewards strategic chess play (checkmate, pins) with gold
Avoids the common trap of piling on crazy rules that erase the chess feel
commentary.quote: it's finally a chess rogike that I could honestly recommend to chess players.
comparisons: Other chess roguelikes (unnamed, one to be discussed afterwards)
design_criteria: Fidelity to core genre (chess): strategy must remain central rather than gimmicks
Roguelike element restraint: small upgrades that do not break the core loop
Reward design: gold for checkmates and pins encourages strategic play
AI quality: smart opponents demand careful thinking
Pacing/run length: slow turns and long encounters, potential repetitiveness
Teaching/accessibility: tutorials on basic chess tactics
Charm/story: frog rooks and fourth-wall-breaking narrative

community.one_liner: A chess-flavoured roguelike puzzle/dungeon crawler from Misfits Attic (Duskers, A Virus Named TOM) where you control a wizard-king, summon and upgrade chess-style pieces, and clear room-sized tactical puzzles.
community.consensus_summary: Players are very positive: Steam shows Very Positive at roughly 94-96 percent across about 110 reviews (103 positive, 6 negative in the local snapshot). It entered Early Access on Nov 10, 2025 and reached 1.0 on Apr 21, 2026 at $14.99, Windows only. The one critic review found (GameGrin, 80/100 or 8/10) calls it creative and fairly balanced but more of a side-activity puzzler than something for long sessions. It is a small, niche title with thin critic coverage, so most of the signal is Steam user reviews. Early Linux crashes and some puzzle-state bugs were reported and at least the Linux crash was later reported fixed. Note: web search quota ran out during research, so Reddit and outlet coverage could not be checked; this summary relies on Steam and one critic review.
best_things: Approachable even for people who are bad at or indifferent to chess: moves are explained, and a danger-tile button shows which squares are threatened
Fair, well-designed puzzles: failures usually feel like your own mistake rather than cheap unfairness (echoed by reviewers and players)
Fresh take on chess roguelikes: you start with no pieces, must move the wizard before placing pieces or casting spells, forcing long-term planning instead of just building an overpowered board
Pieces stay mostly standard with a few restrictive variants, so the game feels 'not too chess but enough chess', with spells, hazard tiles and non-chess pieces adding variety
Retro neon vector/scanline presentation, hum of old electronics and a tense-but-relaxing atmosphere inherited from Duskers
Daily challenge leaderboards, shareable replays and community challenges give short-session replayability
Short runs that can be resumed anytime and multiple win conditions (capture everything or checkmate, board shrinks over time) keep pace brisk
Interesting meta layer: odd psychological-assessment questionnaires and a mysterious emperor narrative that some compare to Inscryption
worst_things: Some players find it shallow or just 'worse than playing chess with generic roguelike mechanics bolted on' (mostly short-playtime negative reviews)
Technical problems at launch/EA: a Linux crash with heavy memory use, invalid game states, a hopper capture not ending a level, a boss turn that would not end, and achievement tracking glitches
Board can feel chaotic once more than about five pieces are in play
Performance issues mentioned in an early negative review
No mid-puzzle restart: failing means leaving the room without bonuses or upgrades (per GameGrin)
Minimal animation; the presentation is stylish but sparse
Narrative is light, especially in the early access build
improvements: Controller support was requested on Steam discussions
A campaign mode built around the Hopper King character was suggested
A way to restart a puzzle mid-room without forfeiting rewards
Bug fixes for stuck boss turns, level-completion triggers and achievements
More depth or content so it holds attention beyond short sessions
Linux stability: early Linux crash with heavy memory use (reported fixed later), although the store page lists Windows only
unique_things: You are a wizard who starts each level with zero pieces and summons them within the wizard's line of sight, unlike drop-anywhere chess roguelikes such as The Rookery
Shrinking board and alternative win conditions remove the need to actually orchestrate a checkmate
Psychological-test questionnaires interleaved with play that affect the runs
Undo tokens, a good-move hint and saved/shared replays make it puzzle-forward and forgiving
Dungeon-crawler framing with RPG-style piece upgrades and spells layered on real chess tactics (forks, pins, skewers)
tedious_or_disliked: Losing a room means losing the run's upgrades from that room with no mid-puzzle restart
Crowded boards with many pieces can become hard to read and calculate
Some situations are perceived as unfair, particularly at the highest difficulty
Players who dislike chess-like thinking find the core loop not engaging
Not a game for long single sittings; better as a second-monitor or between-chores game
divisive_points: Chess as foundation: fans love that chess knowledge is optional, while a few critics say it is simply worse than playing chess
Depth vs shallowness: long-playtime players find deep synergies and builds, short-playtime negative reviewers call it shallow
Session length: praised as bite-sized and flexible, but criticised by the critic as unable to hold focus for a full session
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched Nov 10, 2025 to strongly positive feedback from fans of Duskers and chess games, with praise for the daily challenge leaderboard. 1.0 launched Apr 21, 2026 (publisher Shochiku alongside Misfits Attic) and sentiment stayed Very Positive. A Linux memory/crash bug present in early builds was reported fixed a few weeks after launch by a user. Also distributed in a Humble bundle (Checkmate! A Chess Games Collection) per a Steam review. Metacritic shows no Metascore yet (only one critic review, needs four) and OpenCritic had no findable entry. Steam owner estimate is tiny/unknown (SteamSpy 0-20k). Windows only; Steam Deck/controller support was a player request.

games.name: Dandy Ace
games.short_description: Dandy Ace is an over the top action game that follows this fabulous magician seeking to combine and use his magical cards, fighting and looting his way to defeat the Green-Eyed Illusionist and free himself from a cursed mirror.

other_scores.source: OpenCritic (per Wikipedia; numeric average not retrieved)

placements.verbal_evidence: So, I'm just going to put this as a a B tier.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Dandy Ace is a top-down action roguelike that is essentially Dead Cells with a magician theme, where you escape imprisonment by a jealous rival magician. Its one distinctive hook is card fusion, letting you slot a spare ability as a passive on another piece of equipment. He feels it copied the surface elements of Dead Cells without the depth that makes that game work. Combat is okay but clunky and repetitive, biomes look alike, and there is little left to do after the first win. He still had a good time, beat it on his third attempt, and recommends it to people wanting a different Dead Cells-style experience, placing it in B tier.
praise: Card fusion mechanic (using an ability as a passive on another) allows customization and is the game's unique twist
Enjoyable and satisfying once you get comfortable with dashing and learning enemy movesets
Funny story and opening cinematic with a magician antagonist narrating
Strong meta-progression with gems given to NPCs for permanent unlocks and a sense of growing stronger
Distinct biomes with different bosses and a fitting magician theme with magic references

Fusion passives are too simple, static, and do not improve during the run; abilities lack randomized passives, only level differences
Gameplay is clunky, slower than Dead Cells, and stiff animation; basic attack gets spammed with no combos

Narrator voice lines in every room get to be too much; little content or secrets after first win; off-screen projectiles in late game feel unfair

Magician theme could have been pushed further into distinct environments like a circus or Las Vegas world

design_criteria: Build customization and synergies: fusion system is interesting but too shallow
Item/ability variety: abilities lack randomized passives, reducing loot excitement
Combat feel: clunky, slower, repetitive basic attack
Level and biome design: biomes and rooms too samey, lacking adventure
Visual theme and charm: magic theme underused, biomes not differentiated

Narrative/tone: funny narrator but overused

community.one_liner: A stylish isometric action roguelite from Brazilian studio Mad Mimic in which a flamboyant magician trapped in a cursed mirror palace fights through branching runs using a deck of stackable magic cards as his moves.
community.consensus_summary: Dandy Ace is a well-liked but modestly sized indie roguelite: Steam shows Very Positive (about 87% of roughly 1,300 reviews) and Metacritic PC is 80 from 12 critics, with no negative critic reviews. Critics and players praise the art direction, humor, and the card-slot combat system, and compare it to Hades and Dead Cells while noting it lacks their depth. The recurring complaints are low enemy, boss and room variety, a repetitive narrator, and cooldown-heavy, sometimes clunky combat. It is a released (not Early Access) game, launched on PC/Mac in March 2021 and on Switch, Xbox One and PS4 late 2021; a recent Steam review mentions a late update adding an earlier healing flask to soften difficulty, so it still seems to receive some support. Players who bounce often do so within the first 1-2 hours.
best_things: Card-slot combat: cards fill dash, main attack and special slots in any combination, and each card also grants a secondary modifier effect, which produces a large number of build options
Art style and colour use are the most consistently praised element (Shacknews, Steam reviewers, Metacritic critics)
Fast, responsive movement and fluid action feel once a build comes together
Humour, personality and a memorable cast of characters (Cultured Vultures, PC Invasion)
Branching palace routes lead to different boss fights so runs are not identical
Short runs plus three extra difficulty tiers above Normal give replay value for those who like a challenge
Full voice acting and stylish music that add charm for many players
Good value when discounted; several players say it is worth picking up on sale
worst_things: Low enemy variety, with many recolors and variations, and only around four bosses in total
Rooms and scenarios feel samey; route choices make little practical difference
Narrator has a small pool of voice lines, repeats often, and some find the delivery grating (many mute him)
Combat can feel underwhelming or clunky: ability cooldowns make chaining moves hard and enemy density in small arenas is high
Some cards, trinkets and skills are weak or trap picks, so experimenting feels stale and poisons the unlock pool
Progression pacing: players can finish the game before unlocking half the cards and trinkets
Mac release problems reported: poor controller support on an M1 Mac and a generic OS cursor instead of the in-game cursor
Reviewers compare it unfavourably to Hades for depth, variety and presentation polish
Active skills and passives are unevenly balanced, with some players saying most of them are not worth using and enemies feel strong for the balance
improvements: Make dash a baseline ability instead of consuming a card slot
Let players keep shards between runs, or otherwise speed up unlocks, so progression is not lost on death
Add more enemy types, bosses and distinct room/scenario types; make path choices more meaningful
Rebalance weak cards and trinkets and reduce cooldown friction so combos chain more easily
Widen the narrator's line pool or make him less intrusive; better voice direction for secondary characters
Improve controller support and cursor handling on macOS; Steam forum threads also mention achievement bugs and crashes
unique_things: Weapons are replaced by a four-slot card system where any card can go in any slot and each slot also takes a secondary modifier, rather than a fixed weapon plus upgrades
Even movement (dash) is a card you equip, so you can build around unusual kit such as all dashes
Bright, colourful, comedic magician theatre aesthetic, lighter in tone than typical dark roguelites
A live narrator comments on your performance, which is a Supergiant-style device with a comedic bent
tedious_or_disliked: Repetitive narrator lines wear out quickly, with multiple reviewers muting him
Clearing near-identical rooms of the same small enemy roster becomes a slog, with some levels feeling like a dash to the boss
Losing shards on death makes unlocking cards and trinkets feel slow, while weak unlocks dilute the random pool
Cooldown-gated abilities make crowded fights feel restrictive
Normal difficulty is seen as tough by some, with new players needing several attempts for a first win (about 10 runs for one reviewer), though a later update eased the early game
divisive_points: Difficulty: some call it brutally hard even on Normal, others find it fair and like the higher tiers
Voice acting and narration: praised as charming and fully voiced by some, described as stiff, nasal or cringe by others
Hades comparison: seen as a solid budget alternative by some and a weaker, shallower copy by others
Build depth: some find limitless card combinations, others find no real strategy beyond making initial cards' numbers bigger
community.reception_notes: Launched March 25, 2021 on Windows and macOS, then Switch and Xbox One (Sept 28, 2021) and PS4 (Nov 15, 2021). Critics were generally favorable: 9 of 12 Metacritic critic reviews positive, 3 mixed, none negative, with scores between 70 and 90. Great visuals and vibe

community.one_liner: A Spore-creature-stage-meets-survivors-like action roguelite (Odd Dreams Digital / Secret Mode, PC, $9.99) where you eat prey to level up and pick evolutions that visibly mutate your creature over roughly 20-minute runs.
community.consensus_summary: Players and critics agree the core loop (eat, evolve, bonk, one-more-run) is charming, addictive and great value for $10, with an adorable art style and funny animal flavour. The recurring complaint is thin content: one map, repeating biomes, a small enemy roster, about five bosses, and a few dominant builds, so many players felt they had seen everything after 5-10 runs, especially if they had played the demo. Steam sits at Mostly Positive (about 76.6%, 7.4k reviews at snapshot) while Metacritic shows a Metascore of 74 from 11 critics and OpenCritic a 78 top-critic average (60% recommend). It launched May 8 2026 as a 1.0 (not Early Access) and has since sold 500k+ and received free updates (1.1 June 2026, 1.2 Aug 2026 with mid-run saves), so it is actively supported, not abandoned.
best_things: Intuitive, accessible core loop: eat prey, level up, choose evolutions; short ~20-minute runs make 'one more run' easy
Very charming pixel art and the visual mutation of your creature, plus a feature to save your creature as a GIF to share
Humour, animal facts and puns, and strong Spore nostalgia for the creature stage
Several playstyles exist on paper (tank/damage, charm-army, pacifist/dodge-and-survive), though many reviewers say only about three builds actually work
20 pressure difficulty levels plus challenge modes give a skill ceiling for dedicated players
Great price/value at $10; runs fine on Steam Deck and has full controller support and adjustable difficulty
Developer is responsive: free content updates, Twitch integration, mid-run saves, new Tracker archetype added post-launch
worst_things: Low variety: effectively one map with three similar biomes that blur together, a handful of regular enemies and about five bosses that repeat every run
Builds converge: most winning runs stack physical/plating/size/food-speed upgrades, so 'different' animals end up looking and playing alike
Higher pressure levels mostly add enemy HP/damage and player debuffs rather than new content, so progression feels like a number change
Biomes barely matter: hazards like cold and heat damage only the player, and there is little incentive to leave the plains or invest in resistances
Charm/ally, ranged and pacifist builds are widely seen as weaker than big bulky physical builds
Bosses are seen as damage sponges with predictable patterns; late-run difficulty swings between snowballing to near invincibility and losing early
Released as 1.0 but includes 'coming soon' placeholders and feels like Early Access to many; paid DLC on the roadmap while base content is thin annoyed some buyers
Demo players felt the full game added too little beyond the demo
Most upgrades show up within a single run and the between-run progression does not unlock new biomes or change gameplay, so runs feel samey after 5-10 attempts
improvements: More biomes, maps and enemy types, ideally with biome-specific enemies and rewards that give a reason to travel and adapt
Randomised or mutated enemies/alphas so the evolution theme applies to the world, not only the player
More and more varied bosses beyond the current basic set
Rebalance so ranged, charm and pacifist builds compete with physical tanks; nerf the dominant bulky physical build
More meaningful meta-progression and higher-pressure modifiers that change gameplay rather than inflate stats
Quality-of-life asks: ability to banish evolutions, more UI customisation (damage numbers, enemy HP), mod support, seeded run sharing and more social/multiplayer features
unique_things: Spore creature-stage fantasy fused with a survivors-like/action roguelite structure
Your creature visibly changes with each evolution; a run ends as an eldritch chimera you can export as a GIF
Win by killing the boss or simply by surviving until the timer or cataclysm ends, so dodging and pacifism are real strategies
Charm/social builds let you play like a summoner with an army of charmed critters
Ecosystem framing: predators, prey, alphas, points of interest, day-night cycles and mutually exclusive evolutions (e.g. antlers vs horns, tentacles vs legs)
Twitch integration lets viewers vote on evolutions and appear as named enemies
tedious_or_disliked: Repeating the same map, enemies and five bosses at ever-higher pressure levels
Restarting runs at high pressure to roll a good early attack and scaling ability, since early rolls predict the whole run
Late-run hordes and chaos where balance reportedly breaks down after about pressure 10; some argue the game wrongly tries to be a survivors-like
Invulnerable turtle-shell enemies that are best avoided rather than fought
Environmental damage over time that affects only the player, making resistance upgrades feel like wasted slots
Slow unlock rate and a limited ability pool noted by critics
divisive_points: Whether 76% Mostly Positive and a Metascore of 74 mean a 'good short-session indie' or an under-contented game: many reviewers recommend it while listing the same content complaints
Value: at $10 many say it is a steal, while others feel it ran out of content in under 10 hours and should not have DLC planned yet
Build variety: fans praise 125+ evolutions and distinct archetypes, critics and many players say a few builds dominate and runs feel samey
Difficulty/balance: some find it challenging but fair, others see the post-pressure-10 balance as broken or the early game as too easy
community.reception_notes: Launched May 8 2026 at $9.99 on Windows only (no Mac/Linux); a well-played demo and playtest built hype, and streamer coverage (one reviewer cites NL) drove sales. Early Steam reviews were high but slid as players hit the content ceiling, leaving a Mostly Positive rating at snapshot (a search snippet quoted 87% Very Positive, likely an earlier or different window). Controversies: 1.0 release with 'coming soon' placeholders and a paid DLC announced on the roadmap before the base game felt full. The studio has sold 500k+ copies and shipped free updates: 1.1 (late June 2026: Tracker archetype, Lick Wounds ability, Twitch integration) and 1.2 (Aug 2026: mid-run saving, Jet dash evolution); a community-designed update and premium DLC are planned for autumn. Metacritic user score discrepancy: fetched page showed 8.4 from 18 ratings while a search snippet said 9.0; 8.4 used. Metacritic critic count was 11 and OpenCritic 15 reviews.

games.name: Galactic Glitch

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Galactic Glitch is a fast, top-down bullet-hell action roguelike where you pilot a spaceship through bubble-shaped rooms inside a simulation. He considers it a really solid, satisfying standard action roguelike and highly recommends it to action fans, even though its physics hook is more marketing than substance. He praises the fluid feel, readable chaos, art and bosses, but finds meta-progression weak and room rewards/currency lacking. He places it at the top of B tier and is surprised it got so little recognition.
praise: Extremely satisfying, fluid, fast-paced core gameplay (dash, jump, shoot, grab, throw)
Bullet-hell action stays readable despite heavy visual effects
Shooting feedback and visual effects feel great; distinct glitch-verse art style
Every passive can be upgraded multiple times with impactful effects, enabling cool builds despite limited inventory
Distinct bosses and great music; biomes feel different
Rooms are traversed in seconds, giving a Dandy Ace-like but better Cells-style vibe
Ongoing unlocks (biomes, final bosses, ships, weapons, upgrades) give a real sense of progression; weapons feel different from each other
criticism: Story was not interesting or easy to follow
Physics-as-weapon angle feels more like a marketing pitch than a deep mechanic
Every room is a bubble, which gets somewhat repetitive

design_criteria: Game feel: fluid, fast and satisfying shooting and movement
Readability: bullet-hell chaos remains easy to follow
Visuals/art: distinct glitch-verse style with satisfying effects
Build variety: multi-level passives in limited inventory space
Level design: bubble rooms are fast but repetitive
Boss design: distinct and fun, with strong music

Balance/difficulty: skill-reliant and somewhat iffy balance

community.one_liner: A physics-driven twin-stick action roguelite from Crunchy Leaf Games where you grab asteroids, missiles and even torn-off enemy parts with a gravity gun and hurl them back at swarming enemies across a collapsing galaxy.
community.consensus_summary: Players rate it Very Positive on Steam (about 89.7% of roughly 990 reviews) and call it a surprisingly polished, addictive sleeper with a genuinely novel throwing mechanic and tight controls. Critics are more mixed: Metacritic shows a 74 from 7 critics (scores from 90 down to 50), and the low end faults the repetitive loop and slow upgrade pace. The recurring complaints are thin build variety, uneven weapon and power balance, and progression that slows into a grind after the first hours. It left Early Access (launched July 2024) on June 3, 2025 and has kept getting substantial updates (v2.0 Infinity's Edge in March, Steam Deck Verified and performance work in spring), so reviews from late 2025 onward describe a living game rather than an abandoned one.
best_things: The grab-and-throw gravity gun is the standout hook: tossing asteroids, reflecting missiles, flinging small enemies into others and ripping weapon parts off enemies feels satisfying and is actually powerful, not just a gimmick.
Fast, snappy, responsive controls with generous dash i-frames that make you feel skilled rather than hit by cheap bullets.
Combat pacing: enemies and bosses are not spongy, rooms are bite-sized and the gap between encounters is short, giving a one-more-run compulsion.
Large weapon and ship variety, with starting loadout choice noticeably changing how a run plays, plus a lot of achievement and challenge-run content.
Strong audiovisual presentation: gorgeous readable visuals, meaty weapon feedback and a well-liked soundtrack (one player wished it was sold separately).
Fair-feeling structure: you can win from the very start, with no artificial time limits, so success comes from skill and execution rather than meta stat checks.
Very active, responsive developer who ships large free updates and acts on player feedback.
Great value for the price (around $13, often heavily discounted) and works well on Steam Deck after the spring update.
worst_things: Build variety feels thin: per-run upgrades are dominated by a few basic choices (attack, armor, throw) and players report too few meaningful choices to craft and evolve a build.

Balance problems: a few weapons (the void dagger is named repeatedly) and some powers or drones are clearly superior, leaving most other options as wasted space, while some weapons reportedly deal bugged extra damage.

Difficulty is inconsistent: multiple reviewers find normal rooms too easy once a semi-competent build comes together, even on harder settings, while bosses rely on bullet-hell patterns that a slippery ship handles imprecisely.

Performance and stability: lag and framerate problems, including on Steam Deck at launch of the Deck mode, and some crashes; a player said the game became near-unplayable before the May update fixed it.
Opaque systems: unclear item and glitch-bomb effects, a thin guide, and inconsistent resource drops (for example lifegain items bunched in one stage and absent in another) leave players confused.
Some critics and players find the core loop repetitive, with upgrades arriving too slowly and the driving motivation weak (Cubed3 gave 50).
Story is called subpar by some players, and a minority call the throwing mechanic mostly a gimmick without much depth.
Minor bugs reported: pickups needing multiple button presses, and portals or progression occasionally failing to trigger.
improvements: More meaningful per-run build choices, for example Hades-style weapon-modifying upgrades or multi-beam weapon evolutions, instead of mostly generic stat branches.
Rebalance weapons, powers and drops so more options are viable and the standout picks stop trivialising rooms.
Better in-game explanation of item, bomb and power effects (clear tooltips or a real guide) so experimentation is less confusing.
Smoother economy and progression: shop prices that scale sensibly with what a zone earns, and less forced map-clearing to be strong enough for bosses.
Continued performance and Steam Deck polish, including UI for handheld play.
Faster, more rewarding early and mid-game upgrades so runs do not stretch longer and longer and stall progression.
unique_things: Gravity-gun physics combat in a twin-stick space roguelite: hurl asteroids, bounce them off walls, catch and return missiles.
Enemies are multi-part and can be dismantled, letting you rip off weapon parts (such as a laser emitter) with unique properties and use them yourself.
Throwing is a powerful primary option alongside your chosen weapon, with upgrades like turning thrown objects into homing missile bundles.
Blueprint-based meta progression: new weapons and ships are found as blueprints and bought, with powers largely unlocked through achievements rather than raw stat upgrades.
Infinity's Edge endgame mode with Quantum Powers, Corrupted Upgrades and extra final bosses, plus run challenges and story progression.
tedious_or_disliked: Grind to unlock everything: much of the long-tail content means defeating bosses with every character and repeating challenge runs, which some players describe as a slog.
Runs and mid-to-late progression slow down, with hours of map clearing needed to collect upgrades before bosses are manageable.
Shop prices that feel far out of step with income per zone.
The final boss (Serenity) forcing maximum difficulty frustrated at least one heavy grinder.
The Infinity mode was called drawn out by a player with close to 100 hours.
divisive_points: Difficulty: some say it is too easy and shallow, others say the bosses and grind are punishing or cruel.
The throwing gimmick: praised by most as the best thing in the game, dismissed by a minority as mostly a gimmick.
Meta and in-run progression: described as a pleasingly restrained, skill-first design by some and as underwhelming or lacking synergies by others.
Content volume versus repetition: many see a huge amount to do, others see the same loop repeated.
community.reception_notes: Released in Early Access July 15, 2024 and 1.0 on June 3, 2025 (Windows only; priced about $13). Steam is Very Positive at about 90%. Metacritic has only 7 critic reviews (74) and 4 user ratings (6.3), both tiny samples; OpenCritic has no findable entry. Steam update log: v1.88 (Jan) run challenges and economy rework; v2.0 (Mar 14) Infinity's Edge mode with 8 new weapons, 8 new powers and 3 final bosses; v2.1 (Apr 4) final-final boss and balance pass; v2.2 (May 1) Steam Deck Verified at a stable 60 fps, memory leak fixes and two new room types; v2.22 (Jun 22) bug fixes. Reviews from mid-2026 say performance was poor for a stretch (lag, slideshow on older laptops) and that the May 2026 performance updates fixed it for at least some players, while a minority still report lag or crashes. Developer is praised for listening to feedback. Third-party estimates (Boxleiter-based, order of magnitude only) put gross revenue around $149k and under 20k owners.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Gambonanza is a chess-based roguelike often described as a Balatro-like chess game, with blind-style boards, a shop for jokers-equivalents (gambits), new pieces and board upgrades. Some builds where everything clicks feel great

community.one_liner: A Balatro-style chess roguelike where you fight on a tiny board, buy rule-bending Gambits (joker equivalents), board tiles and pieces, and must capture every enemy piece rather than just the king.
community.consensus_summary: Gambonanza launched May 1, 2026 (Steam, iOS, Android) from Blukulele, co-published by Sidekick and Stray Fawn, and sits at Mostly Positive on Steam (about 74-76% of roughly 1,700 reviews; recent reviews ~73%). Critics are split: Metacritic shows a 64 Metascore from 5 reviews, ranging from 90 (DualShockers) to 40 (Destructoid), with a user score of 7.3 from a small sample. Fans enjoy the addictive synergy-building loop, the presentation and the chess-meets-Balatro hook. Detractors find it shallow and unbalanced, with a weak AI, permanent piece loss that discourages trading, and a few dominant builds. It is a full release that still has an active Steam forum with bug reports and difficulty-balance questions, not abandoned, but I found no concrete patch notes in the pages I could read.
best_things: Strong high-concept hook: Balatro-style run building applied to chess, with Gambits that change piece and board rules (150+ advertised)
Slick, polished presentation: CRT pixel-art look, smooth animations, catchy music and a clean interface
Addictive 'one more run' synergy building when a combo lands, e.g. mass-producing pieces or chaining skipped enemy turns
Easy to pick up for people who only know basic chess moves, and some players say it quietly teaches chess tactics
Unlockable Gambits and higher difficulties extend replay beyond the first win
Tiles, enemy modifiers and boss fights add tactical puzzle variety; some reviewers call bosses and tile upgrades the highlight
Short-session friendly, especially on mobile and Steam Deck
Mobile and PC versions exist, and several players like the low mobile price
worst_things: Enemy AI is weak or effectively random unless it can capture, so the optimal play is often to burn turns and wait for it to blunder a piece
Permanent loss of captured pieces across the run means trades and sacrifices, the heart of chess, are punished and the economy drains on replacing pieces
Balance: queens outclass other pieces, duplication and skip-turn Gambits are overpowered, phantom-to-gold tile combos dominate, while many Gambits are weak or rely on 1/3 to 1/5 random triggers
Crumble mechanic (tiles falling away to end stalling) and some enemy modifiers feel random and can decide or ruin a run
Unskippable animations and boss cutscenes with no speed-up option make the game feel slow on PC
Repetition: identical starting board layouts per stage, builds locking in early, low variety in pieces and tiles
Heavily derivative of Balatro in art, UI, sound and loop, which some reviewers saw as near copy-paste
Bugs and rough edges reported: achievement and Gambit interaction bugs, lost progress in one review, resolution shared across devices, no cross-save
Price: several top-voted reviews (85 and 161 helpful votes) say $14.99 on Steam is too high for the content, especially since the mobile version is about $6 and includes a PC copy
improvements: Add an animation and game speed option or skippable boss cutscenes
Make the enemy AI play to win and rework the stalling meta (for example make piece loss partial or chance-based, or restore pieces between stages)
Rebalance the economy, especially strain 2 price and income changes and queen-strain perishable Gambits
Buff or redesign weak Gambits, reduce low-probability triggers, and nerf the dominant queen/duplication/tile combos
Add more pieces (e.g. fairy pieces), upgrades, tiles, board layouts and music for replay variety
Add an undo or confirm-move option, larger or clearer text for tooltips, and cross-save between platforms
unique_things: Win condition is capturing every enemy piece, not checkmate, which removes check and pin logic
Gambits rewrite chess rules and piece behavior, and a reserve system lets you deploy pieces from off the board
Pieces are a permanent run resource: losing one removes it for the whole run, tying chess tactics to a shop economy
Tiles on the board (trap, gold, ghost, blessed) plus a crumbling-board timer that forces action
Gacha, pachinko and slot-style mini-games for acquiring pieces and items
Mobile-first origin (simultaneous iOS/Android release with a port by Ateo) with a Steam version that has controller and Steam Deck support
tedious_or_disliked: Waiting moves and passing turns until the AI hangs a piece, which some players describe as effectively AFK play
Long unskippable animations, especially the roughly 15-second boss intros, plus a gacha opening delay
Rerolling the shop and chasing specific pieces or Gambits via gacha RNG to complete a build
Repetitive runs because stage layouts repeat and the same strong Gambits get picked every time
Higher difficulties (queen strain and above) that feel more like RNG or forced resets than tactical depth, with Gambits expiring
Text is small and hard to read on Gambit tooltips
divisive_points: Whether a chess game should lean on chance: fans say it's a chaotic synergy builder, not Stockfish chess, while others say randomness removes skill
The Balatro comparison: some love it as 'Balatro but chess', others say it is only a thin clone or that it is a different game entirely
AI difficulty: some call it easy and dumb, others say reviewers did not get past stage 3 and later stages punish mistakes hard
Price: $14.99 Steam feels too high to some given a cheaper mobile version and Balatro's price, while others call it a fair buy, and Steam-specific discussion notes mobile is cheaper
community.reception_notes: Launched May 1, 2026 on Steam (Windows/Mac/Linux, $14.99) alongside iOS and Android. Steam ratings stayed steady at Mostly Positive (about 74-76% overall, about 73% recent), so reception has not collapsed or recovered much. The most-upvoted negative review (about 390 helpful votes) and several others complain about slow unskippable animations, economy balance and AI, and many positive reviews recommend it on sale. Several reviewers note the mobile version is cheaper and feels better suited to short touch sessions, and a few Steam reviews mention needing a speed option on PC. The Steam forum has 291+ topics with bug reports (achievements, specific Gambits, graveyard, Steam Deck) and questions about difficulty plans; I could not confirm specific patch notes or developer responses. OpenCritic could not be verified, and Reddit was not accessible to fetch. Steam revenue estimates from the local dataset are zero/unavailable, so no sales figure is stated.
