community.one_liner: A pixel-art dark-fantasy action roguelite from straka.studio (published with SUPERHOT PRESENTS) where you slide the floating floor tiles of flooded ruins Tetris-style while fighting in stamina-based, souls-flavoured combat.
community.consensus_summary: Loot River landed as a 'fascinating idea, uneven execution' game. Critics were mostly positive (Metacritic 74 from 21 reviews, with scores ranging from 100 down to 40), praising the tile-sliding hook, art and music, while Steam players are Mixed (about 67% positive from roughly 464 reviews) and Metacritic users are lower still at 5.1 (only 13 ratings). The recurring split is between people who click with the soulslike parry/stamina combat and block-shifting puzzle layer, and people who find it clunky, shallow in loot and meta-progression, and buggy. It is a finished 1.0 release (May 2022, Windows only; also appears on Game Pass per a Steam reviewer), but a Steam community thread asks whether it is still being developed, so post-launch support looks quiet. It is now regularly bought for a dollar or a few dollars on sale, and reviewers tend to say it is worth that, not the $25 launch price.
best_things: The tile-sliding mechanic: pushing floating landmasses to bridge gaps, isolate enemies, create chokepoints or escape is praised as a genuinely fresh twist (God is a Geek, Hardcore Gamer, many Steam reviews)
Dark, atmospheric pixel art and an intense soundtrack are the most consistently complimented production elements
Combat, once learned, is described as engaging and well-paced, with parrying and dodge timing rewarding skill
Bosses are said to have distinct mechanics instead of reskinned patterns
Build variety: many weapons, spells and armour pieces plus multiple routes through levels encourage experimentation
An easy/accessibility mode lets players learn the unusual controls and difficulty curve, and modifiers can raise difficulty back up
Short, replayable runs (roughly 5-10 hours to beat, 10-15 for 100%) and a low sale price make it easy to recommend as a change of pace
worst_things: Combat is frequently called clunky, with janky collisions and sloppy hitboxes; one Steam reviewer called it some of the worst combat they had played
Bugs can ruin runs: enemies that lock platform movement can stay in effect after they die, and a boss was knocked outside the arena barrier, forcing restarts
Loot and weapons feel samey (many weapons differ mainly by element and scaling) and meta-progression is very shallow for a game named Loot River
Not much content: several players felt they had seen nearly everything in one or two runs, and Screen Rant scored it 40 saying it feels like an Early Access product
Story and lore are described as boring or forgettable, and endings unfulfilling
Visual clutter and poor visibility during fights make it hard to read the action and spot drops (LEVEL, Metacritic user reviews)
Stamina and parry-heavy design irritates players who wanted fast, fluid roguelike combat
Floating-block mechanic sometimes leaves no route forward, and most weapons are slow, so players feel pushed to abuse parry or die often (Steam negative reviews)
improvements: Fix the soft-locks and bugs (persisting platform locks, bosses leaving arenas, controller remap double-inputs) and keep polishing; players ask whether development is still active
Make loot more interesting and weapons more distinct, with deeper meta-progression
Add more content and gameplay variety, especially mid-run, which GRYOnline.pl and Steam users both allude to
Improve combat readability, hitbox cleanliness and enemy attack/parry timing; some parry-only enemies are said to be nearly impossible to hit
Fix level layouts where the floating mechanic leaves no route forward, and reduce time lost to block-puzzle stalls
Better regional pricing and storefront reach (Steam users ask about Argentina pricing and a GOG release)
unique_things: Tetris-like shifting floor: the map itself is an active weapon and puzzle that you rearrange in real time while fighting
Marketed and reviewed as Dark Souls meets Diablo meets Tetris (The Games Machine, Hardcore Gamer)
You control character movement, attacks and platform pushing at once, which makes controller play close to mandatory
Flooded-ruin setting with procedurally generated labyrinths, a narrative thread and multiple routes
Soulslike stamina/parry combat inside a fast roguelite loop, with easy mode and modifiers to tune difficulty
tedious_or_disliked: Block-shifting puzzles can stall the pace when you are stuck trying to progress, especially when repeated across runs
Stamina management and the delayed parry window frustrate players who find it punishing for any misstep
Unlock/meta loop feels thin, so repeated runs can feel repetitive once the hook wears off
Needing five keys to open gates and other progression gates feel grindy to some players (Steam community thread)
Keyboard and mouse play is widely called awkward, so a controller is effectively required
divisive_points: Is it a souls-like or a roguelite? Players who expected fluid roguelike combat bounced off; those expecting deliberate soulslike combat loved it
Difficulty and easy mode: some say easy mode is essential to learn it, others say hard mode is only frustrating, not rewarding
Length and price: fine at $1-4 on sale, but many say too little content at the $20-25 launch price
Critics scored it far higher (74 average) than Metacritic users (5.1, just 13 ratings) and Steam players (about 67% positive)
community.reception_notes: Launched May 3, 2022 on Steam (Windows, $24.99) with SUPERHOT PRESENTS as co-publisher; critics were generally warm on the concept while Steam settled at Mixed and Metacritic user score ended at 5.1. Metacritic's 74 comes from 21 critics; user reviews there cite clunky combat, poor visibility, repetitive puzzles and an unfinished feel. Steam reviews continue to arrive years later (through 2026), often praising it as a cheap, short, flawed-but-interesting pick from a first-time studio, and commonly noting it was picked up for about $1-4 on sale or via Game Pass. The Steam discussion board shows reports of many bugs, a controller-remap double-input bug, requests for a GOG release and regional pricing, and a thread asking whether the game is still actively developed. One Steam reviewer says expectations were set wrongly by a souls-focused YouTuber recommendation and that the game is a shallow-progression roguelite, not a souls-like. OpenCritic score could not be retrieved: web search budget was exhausted and the direct OpenCritic URL guesses did not resolve, so it is left null. Reddit and several outlet URLs (PC Gamer, Screen Rant, Game Informer, IGN) were blocked or 404.

community.one_liner: A 2D pixel-art side-scrolling RPG platformer by solo dev Sean Young (SmashGames) with permadeath, randomly generated underground dungeons, combine-any-two-items crafting and local/online co-op.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate it Very Positive (about 85% of roughly 7.6k reviews) and many describe it as a charming, replayable, challenging roguelite with great music and crafting. The big caveat is that development stopped years ago, and the late updates left game-breaking bugs (final-boss/victory-screen crashes, chicken cooking freezing the game, multiplayer false-loss bugs). A vocal share of the negative reviews are about abandonment and the developer's shift to Roguelands rather than the core design. No professional critic coverage exists (no Metacritic critic score, no OpenCritic entry found); Metacritic has only a small user score (7.3 from 32 ratings). A community fan patch and a 'Rewritten' project keep interest alive, but the player count is tiny (around 12-13 concurrent).
best_things: Addictive 'one more run' loop: each death leaves you slightly stronger through unlocks, giving clear short-term goals
Crafting by combining any two items is fun to experiment with and rewards discovery
High replayability through unlockable races, hats, companions and randomised stats/builds
Satisfying, challenging difficulty with a real sense of accomplishment on beating the final scourge levels
Excellent music and sound design, plus charming pixel sprites
Co-op where the run continues as long as one party member survives encourages teamwork
Good pacing, enemy and map variety; fast, ninja-like movement and combat
Strong nostalgia and loyalty among long-time players, some calling it a childhood favourite
worst_things: Abandoned: no official updates for years, with the developer having moved on to Roguelands
Late-game bugs that can make the game unwinnable, such as crashes at the final boss or victory screen
Specific known bugs: cooking raw chicken freezes the game, forced wolf riding with no jump-off, shopkeeper interaction icon disappearing
Multiplayer is buggy: false 'all players downed' game overs, players falling through the floor on restart, desyncs
Multiplayer lacks Steam integration and in-game communication tools, so people rely on third-party workarounds
Mouse cursor flicker bug reported since 2021 and never fixed
Some players consider it overpriced or mediocre compared to many modern roguelites
Some unlocks are obscure and hard to figure out
improvements: Add a tutorial or early guidance; new players get little direction on doors, recipes or systems
Let players choose their starting attributes instead of repeatedly clicking 'roll stats'
Save discovered crafting recipes so players don't have to write them down
Fix the long-standing game-breaking bugs (final boss crash, chicken cooking, multiplayer false losses)
Add Steam-integrated online multiplayer and communication tools
Explain or fix obscure unlocks
unique_things: Combine-any-two-items crafting as the core progression system rather than fixed recipe trees
Side-scrolling Terraria/Spelunky-style platforming blended with RPG stats, races, hats and companions
Co-op permadeath where the run only ends when the whole party is down
Inspired by Monster Hunter and Spelunky per the store description, unusual for a 2D pixel roguelite
Persistent unlocks (races, hats, companions) that change how each run plays
Active community-made fixes (MagiciteFanPatches, Magicite: Rewritten) extending the life of an abandoned game
tedious_or_disliked: Repeatedly rerolling stats until a desirable combination appears
Early game feels punishing and opaque until the mechanics click
Writing down crafting recipes because the game doesn't record them
Hunting for unlock conditions that are not explained
Working around broken bugs (shopkeepers, wolf mount) mid-run
Co-op sessions ending in frustrating false-loss resets
divisive_points: Value: fans say it is a hidden gem worth it despite bugs, while others call it abandonware to avoid at full price
Difficulty: described both as infuriating and as deeply satisfying
Multiplayer: some love the co-op, others find it the most frustrating and buggiest part (and it is local/3rd-party rather than Steam-integrated)
Reviewers disagree on whether abandonment should drag down a game they otherwise enjoy (several negative reviews are explicitly about the developer rather than the gameplay)
community.reception_notes: Launched June 9, 2014 (Steam, $9.99, Win/Mac/Linux) and built an enduring audience, with a Very Positive Steam rating that has held even as the review count grew past 7.5k. The developer stopped supporting it years ago to work on Roguelands, and players say the final update introduced game-breaking bugs, which fuels many recent negative reviews and some resentment toward the developer. The community is small but still active on Steam forums (matchmaking threads, 'Anyone still plays?' posts), with unofficial fixes like MagiciteFanPatches and a 'Magicite: Rewritten' effort. Metacritic shows only a small user score (7.3/10 from 32 ratings, no critic reviews). Note: my WebSearch budget was exhausted so no Reddit or outlet reviews could be read; Reddit and Fandom wiki fetches were blocked. Estimated sales figures come from third-party models and are not audited; the revenue calculator gave no explicit copy count (price math suggests roughly 200k+ units, but that conflicts with SteamSpy's 500k-1M owner estimate, which likely includes keys, bundles and free copies).

Loud, flashy presentation with ridiculous guns

community.one_liner: A top-down roguelite shooter from solo-ish indie studio Bearlex Games (Steam Early Access since Nov 2022) where you pick a character, dig through large cave stages, mine crystals and fight swarms and bosses while stacking weapons, mods and perks.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate it Very Positive (roughly 90-92% positive across about 220-300 reviews), but it is a tiny-audience title (Steam estimate of 20k-50k owners, only a handful of concurrent players) with no Metacritic or OpenCritic critic coverage at all. The sampled top-helpful English reviews skew heavily negative and are remarkably consistent: a great-feeling base (pixel art, music, humor, gameplay loop) that runs out of variety quickly, with the same maps, enemies and bosses repeating and very sharp difficulty spikes. The game is still in Early Access almost four years after launch. The developer kept shipping updates through mid-2025 and published a revised roadmap in Feb 2026, but has slipped the full-release target more than once. Critic-style validation is absent, so the verdict rests on players and on the developer's own update trail.
best_things: Strong pixel-art look, music and humor that land in the first runs (a reviewer who still gave a negative verdict praised all three)
Fast, satisfying core loop of shooting swarms, leveling up and stacking perks, in the survivors-like / twin-stick tradition
Low price (about $5.99) makes it feel like low risk; several reviewers say the price softens the disappointment and that it is worth trying for genre fans
Weapon modding and a perk/gem system give room for theorycrafting and min-maxing builds (one 15-hour reviewer says it is fun for chasing a specific build)
Several playable characters with distinct mechanics, e.g. a bear with a tank companion, Team Mischief as a group you drag around, and an auto-aim/auto-fire character for less precise players
Local co-op, full controller support, global leaderboards and a competitive scoring angle for players who like chasing ranks
Developer is visibly active and communicative: regular patch notes, new biomes (Enveloping Rime), new characters and a public roadmap
Random events add some variety inside runs (called fun even by a critical reviewer)
worst_things: Repetition: same large cave-style maps, same enemy set and same bosses recur across runs and even within a run, so runs feel alike after a few hours
Content is thin: reviewers cite about 3 characters and one repeated map at the time they wrote; several reviewers say it feels like a demo or tech demo at the current price
Upgrades feel flat: mostly plain stat boosts (damage, attack speed, accuracy) without real trade-offs or interesting interactions between weapons and skills

Steep difficulty spikes: enemy power jumps after the first level, elites are bullet sponges, and late-game enemies or modifiers (e.g. exploding enemies) can nearly one-shot even heavily defended builds
No real ending or goal to finish a run, so the game is scores and upgrades with no payoff; one reviewer contrasts it with Binding of Isaac for this reason
Stability complaints: reports of crashes during runs (including losing a long run while chasing an achievement), and one reviewer says it heavily taxes their PC
Levels look bland (walls, floors and crystal veins) and rooms can feel empty
Early Access has dragged on since Nov 2022; the full-release estimate of 2025 has passed (store page, not reviews)
improvements: More enemy and boss variety, including biome-specific enemy sets, so deeper floors do not just mean more of the same enemies
A real ending or win condition (and more biomes) so that runs and meta-progression have a finish line
Upgrade and build design with trade-offs and synergies rather than plain stat bumps; make weapon and ability choices feel meaningfully different
Rebalance difficulty (early ramp, ice biome, boss timer that fills too fast, elite damage) and make defense stats stay useful late
Fix crashes and add run recovery; make the no-upgrade score mode's rules and lack of unlocks clearer on the store page
Clearer communication on development pace and release timing (the Feb 2026 roadmap moves in this direction with a town hub, reworked upgrades, gear system and more biomes)
unique_things: Digging and crystal mining are built into level traversal; the crystal-wall mining is the one thing reviewers say sets it apart from other shooters (though some find it pointless or annoying)
Weapon modding plus a gem system on top of perks, rather than only passive pickups
Team Mischief character, a squad you lead and drag with a distance slider, and Orso with a tank companion and HQ assistance

Two distinct modes at launch: a roguelike mode with upgrades and unlocks and a score-focused mode with leaderboards, weekly/daily challenges (weekly mode slated for removal in the Feb 2026 roadmap) and a planned speedrun mode
Rover-style mining vehicle abilities and industrial weapons such as a sawblade launcher; Steam Inventory cosmetic drops
tedious_or_disliked: Meta-progression reads as grindy: one reviewer says grinding upgrades pushed the point of being overwhelmed back but added little new fun
Slow start and boring early perks; first few minutes of a run lack excitement
Being one-shot or killed by a single hit in an otherwise slow-paced run
Leaderboard-first-place achievements (later changed to top 5) were seen as unattainable and as a sign of priorities; suspected cheating on the boards was also mentioned
Digging through walls is called annoying by some players
Steam community threads complain about an ice biome that slows and punishes players and a boss timer that fills too fast
divisive_points: Auto-aim/auto-fire versus manual aiming: one reviewer found aiming too hard without auto-aim and auto-fire unsatisfying, others enjoy the survivors-like feel
Mining/digging: a signature feature to some, pointless busywork to others
Price vs content: praised as a cheap fun roguelite by some, called not worth it (compared unfavorably to Vampire Survivors at similar price) by others
Difficulty: some want a harder roguelike challenge, others find the spikes and one-shot deaths unfair
community.reception_notes: Launched into Steam Early Access on 4 Nov 2022 at a very low price with Windows only and no Mac/Linux. The store page says price will rise about 50% through Early Access. community.one_liner: A 2013 side-scrolling action-platformer rogue-lite from Cellar Door Games where each death passes the castle to a randomly generated heir with quirky traits, while gold spent between runs permanently upgrades the family.
community.consensus_summary: Rogue Legacy is received as a genre-defining, highly addictive early rogue-lite. Critics scored it in the mid-80s (Metacritic 85 from 43 reviews, with 9/10 from IGN and Polygon), and Steam players rate it Very Positive at about 92% of roughly 18.9k reviews. Praise centres on the heir/trait system, the permanent progression that softens permadeath, and the 'one more run' loop. Modern players are more split: many call it dated, grindy and clunky next to newer roguelite-metroidvanias, and often point to Rogue Legacy 2 as the better version. It is a finished, fully released game (Steam 2013, later ported to consoles, Switch in 2018, iOS in 2019), not early access.
best_things: The heir system: each death gives a choice of three randomly generated children with different classes, spells and traits, which turns failure into a comic, varied start to every run.
Permanent progression softens permadeath: gold spent in the manor upgrades stats and unlocks gear and runes, so even failed runs feel productive.
A highly addictive 'explore, fight, upgrade, repeat' loop with short runs (20-30 minutes) that suits casual sessions.
Bosses stay defeated and their castle locations are fixed, so progress is permanent (one Steam reviewer who dislikes roguelites called this the deciding factor).
Humor and charm: quirky traits, jokes and a colourful retro art style give the game personality.
Smooth retro combat and a trait system regarded by some players as one of the best in the genre.
Plenty of content, including New Game+ with escalating difficulty, and a 100% completion goal.
Critics gave it near-unanimous praise (42 of 43 Metacritic reviews positive), and it is remembered by players as a modern classic that helped start the roguelite craze.
worst_things: Controls and movement feel loose or clunky to some players, described as sliding on ice, while the game expects precision against many projectiles.
Repetitive content: room layouts and enemies recur, and critics and players say many enemies are reskins or upgraded variants of a small set.
Upgrade costs climb steeply, so a lot of gold farming is needed to keep up with enemy scaling.
Difficulty comes more from enemy quantity and cheap room setups (being swarmed in the first room, awkward platforms) than from smart level design.
Some traits are poorly explained or are just visual effects with little gameplay impact, and classes can feel negligible in practice.
The randomness does not always synergize with the platforming, which can produce unfair runs.
Aged mechanics: players compare it unfavorably with the many modern indie metroidvanias and with the sequel.
Many reviewers say the sequel, Rogue Legacy 2, improves on the original so much that the first game feels hard to go back to.
improvements: Tighter, more responsive movement and platforming control (a recurring complaint from critics and players).
More enemy variety and less reliance on reskinned foes.
Better explanation of what traits do, and more traits and classes that change how the game plays.
A way to respec or reset upgrades to try different builds (a Steam reviewer specifically asked for this).
A gentler or less grind-heavy upgrade cost curve and more meaningful upgrades than raising attack or health.
A modern refresh: several players say the sequel already delivers this and that the first game deserves a proper revisit.
unique_things: The genealogical premise: you play a family dynasty, and every heir has randomized traits such as colour-blindness, ADHD, vertigo or dwarfism that change play.
Gold does not carry over unspent: it is lost on entering the castle, so every run opens with a spending decision at the manor (the game's signature loop, sometimes criticised as a lock-in).
The architect can lock the castle layout and bosses have fixed locations, giving rogue-lite procedural rooms with metroidvania-style permanent boss progress.
Dark Souls and Spelunky-inspired design goals but with 'forgiving and accessible' persistent progression, which made it a template for later rogue-lites.
New Game+ scaling and a humorous tone set it apart from grimmer roguelikes.
tedious_or_disliked: Gold grinding: farming money run after run for increasingly expensive upgrades, especially when stuck on a boss.
Unspent gold being lost each run annoys some players who do not want to be forced to spend it.
Repetitive rooms and enemies after many hours.
Having to play an unwanted class or heir when the three options offered are not appealing.
Clunky controls, particularly keyboard and mouse default bindings, where controller is advised.
Harsh, unwelcoming onboarding for newcomers, with a few players also citing projectiles or enemies passing through walls and unreliable downward-thrust attacks.
No way to reset upgrades, and enemy scaling makes the grind feel mandatory rather than optional.
divisive_points: Grind: some see the gold/upgrade treadmill as central and rewarding, others see it as a time sink.
Controls: Steam reviewers disagree, with some calling them very tight and others calling them floaty or clunky.
Difficulty: critics said it rides the line between frustrating and fun, and its difficulty may put off less patient players.
Worth playing today: some say it still holds up, others recommend skipping it in favour of Rogue Legacy 2 unless on sale.
community.reception_notes: Launched June 27, 2013 on Windows and sold over 100,000 copies in its first week per Wikipedia; development reportedly cost about $15,000 and was recouped within an hour of launch. A third-party estimate puts lifetime Steam gross revenue around $11.5M (Boxleiter-method estimate, order-of-magnitude only) and Steam owners at 200k-500k by SteamSpy. It won PAX 10 and IndieCade finalist recognition and placed on several 2013 best-of lists. Ports followed: Linux/Mac Oct 2013, PlayStation platforms July 2014, Xbox One 2015, Switch 2018, iOS 2019. Rogue Legacy 2 released April 28, 2022 and is generally viewed as the improved successor. Note: OpenCritic could not be retrieved, and the session's web search budget was exhausted, so community detail comes mainly from Steam reviews plus fetched pages; the Steam storefront page showed a slightly lower 91% of about 10k reviews, likely a locale/language filter difference.

community.one_liner: A fast, free-moving 2D pixel-art roguelite platformer by Flying Oak Games and E-Studio where Kyhra dashes, slashes, parries and stomps through five realms of machine enemies and hand-made bosses.
community.consensus_summary: ScourgeBringer is well regarded for its movement and combat feel. Steam is Very Positive (about 86% of roughly 3,300 reviews), and Metacritic critics average 76 from 13 reviews, with the top scores around 90. Players and critics agree the flow and the soundtrack are excellent, and that the game is brutally hard and fairly thin as a roguelite, with little build variety, few items and five repetitive realms. The Metacritic user score is a much lower 5.8 (Mixed) from only 29 ratings, and difficulty and grind drive most of the negative Steam reviews. It left Early Access in October 2020 and later reached consoles and mobile. Recent Steam reviews from 2025-26 are still mostly positive, and the game is often discounted to very low prices.
best_things: Movement and combat feel: fluid dash, slash, parry, stomp and projectile-smashing that reviewers compare to Celeste, Hotline Miami and Mega Man
Enemies only hurt during actual attacks (no contact damage), which players like in a fast game
Skill-based bosses: players say they can't be beaten by raw stats or a lucky build, so wins feel earned
Soundtrack by Joonas Turner is widely called a standout, and several reviewers bought it separately
Pixel art, effects and Kyhra's character design are praised, as is the story's mystery and the quirky EULA with a pizza recipe
The permanent skill tree is satisfying to upgrade and gives a sense of progress between runs
Realm-specific mechanics and cool weapons such as lasers add variety within the five realms; players like discovering mechanics without tutorials
Accessibility options (slower game speed, slower bullets, extra health drops) let more players enjoy the game
worst_things: Extreme difficulty: many negative Steam reviews from experienced players say they stalled at realm 3 or the first boss after 7-20 hours
Shallow roguelite variety: few in-run items, little synergy, so runs feel alike
Only five realms that must be replayed from the start every run, which leads to repetition
Screen chaos: many enemies, bullets and heavy effects make it hard to see your character or threats, especially in the later realms
Health is a scarce resource and getting hit cuts your blood multiplier, which pushes play toward no-hit runs
Some players report clunky or unfair controls: a slow heavy attack and parry, auto-aim on dash and shots that can't be disabled, enemies dragged along by a dash, and hitstun
Late skill-tree unlocks feel weak, and maxed players pile up blood currency with nothing to spend it on
Smaller complaints: some controllers are not supported natively, and one long-session crash report on a modern PC
improvements: More in-run items, weapons and synergies so runs differ more, and more realms or level variety
Fairer defensive tools: i-frames on the dash, a faster heavy attack and parry, or a bigger or upgradeable parry window
Clearer combat visuals, such as toned-down effects and better enemy readability in realms 3-5
More frequent or reliable healing, and options to disable dash and shot auto-aim and to remove hitstun
A structure with fast travel or a more connected, metroidvania-style world that unlocks abilities through progress (one reviewer suggested this)
More meaningful skill-tree upgrades so maxing it out is not anticlimactic, and better communication of how hard the game is
unique_things: A free-flying, Celeste-style movement roguelite where parrying and smashing bullets matter more than build luck
A skill-over-loot design: power comes mostly from player mastery, with the permanent skill tree adding smaller boosts
Hand-designed boss fights, unlike the procedurally generated bosses in the developers' earlier NeuroVoider
A blood resource with a kill-streak multiplier tied to health, which makes the health bar a risk-reward currency
Accessibility sliders for game speed and bullet speed
tedious_or_disliked: Redoing the same early realms after every death, with no shortcuts, to reach the harder later content
Grinding blood for the skill tree early on, and feeling gated until you unlock key skills such as deflection
Runs becoming repetitive after a few hours because of limited items and enemy/room variety
Dynamic or adaptive difficulty that some players find confusing, or that does not make the game easier enough
Late realms where chaotic screens make fights feel like mashing buttons
Short-lived progression: the skill tree is fun until it is maxed out quickly, after which the game feels like pure 'git gud' repetition
divisive_points: Difficulty: fans call it fair and rewarding while others with years of roguelike experience call it unfair
Roguelite depth: some love the arcade purity and skill focus, others want more builds and progression
Metacritic critics (76) and Steam (about 86%) are far warmer than Metacritic users (5.8 from 29 ratings)
community.reception_notes: Early Access began in February 2020 and the full release was on 21 October 2020 (PC, Xbox One, Switch), followed by PS4/Vita in April 2021, PS5 in April 2022 and iOS/Android in September 2022 (per Wikipedia). Critics praised the fluid controls and combat from the start but noted thin progression and depth. Metacritic PC critic score is 76 from 13 reviews; the Metacritic user score of 5.8 has only 29 ratings. Steam reviews are still arriving in 2025-26 and mention an adaptive or dynamic difficulty system added after launch that not everyone finds helpful. OpenCritic could not be located and is left null. Steam price is $16.99 but it is frequently on deep sale ($2). Revenue estimates from steam-revenue-calculator.com (Boxleiter method, rough) put gross at about $301k and net about $89k on Steam alone. Its copies field is empty, and SteamSpy suggests 200k-500k owners, which likely includes bundles and giveaways.

community.one_liner: A turn-based chess-roguelike where you play a lone black king with a shotgun against a full white army, picking paired buff/debuff cards after each stage.
community.consensus_summary: Shotgun King is a well-liked indie: Steam shows about 91% positive across roughly 7,450 reviews (Very Positive), and the store page lists 93% overall at the time of fetch. Players praise the absurd-but-working premise, the card system and the short, replayable runs. Critics are fewer and more lukewarm: Metacritic's PS5 page shows 75 from 5 reviews (Wikipedia lists Switch at 82 from 4), with criticism aimed at difficulty spikes and limited replay value. Metacritic users are noticeably harsher (6.6 from 25 ratings) than Steam players, mostly over RNG-driven card pools and balance. It is not early access; it launched May 2022, got console ports in Aug 2023, and was still being patched through 2025 with the 1.6 Bad Company update and later 1.62x fixes.
best_things: High-concept premise (chess king with a shotgun) that keeps chess's planning and tactics while feeling fresh and funny
Buff/debuff card system: each stage you choose one white card (enemy buff) and one black card (your buff), which keeps runs different and builds interesting
Strong card interactions and synergies, with many builds on both sides of the board and some combos rewarded with achievements
Short runs (about 20 minutes) and a low price (around $10), so it is easy to pick up; a demo exists
Accessible to chess novices and often described as more fun than regular chess because of the roguelike variety
Fitting retro pixel art, sound design and music
Lots of content and life: 20 difficulty ranks, endless mode, Chase and Charnier modes, 100+ achievements, Workshop/mod support, free updates
Developer returned with a large free update years after launch (v1.6, about 30 new cards, 2 shotguns, 5 ranks), which players welcomed
worst_things: Heavy RNG in card offers; at high ranks the draws can be anti-player and runs feel decided before you can build anything
Enemy scaling outpaces the player: enemy health and buffs stack while shotgun damage barely grows, so late ranks feel unfair
Discovered checks and self-inflicted deaths from firing and opening a line are instant losses and feel cheap, even with blunder shields that only cover some cases
Card pool bloat: prerequisite cards and large pools make it rare to find synergies you want
No mid-run saving in a roguelike, which players find painful for long high-rank runs
Some cards and unlock paths are weak or hidden, and several shotgun unlocks are very hard to earn
Achievement hunting relies on luck and specific multi-card combos, not skill (a recurring complaint from 100%-ers)
Some mechanic interactions are undocumented and must be discovered by trial and error
improvements: Restore or add a proper toggle that highlights dangerous/check tiles (the middle-mouse highlight was removed in an update and moved behind a cheat/mod, which players see as an accessibility loss)
Give players more control over draws: card banishing, more rerolls, or smarter offers so the pool does not bloat
Rebalance late ranks and some cards/units so player scaling keeps pace with enemy scaling
Add mid-run saving
Improve progression and unlocks (especially alternate shotguns) and make achievements less luck-dependent
Better in-game explanation of card interactions and warnings for discovered attacks; fix controller/Steam Deck issues such as grenades
unique_things: You are a single king with a shotgun versus a full chess army, so the chess rules stay intact but your only weapon is the shotgun
Dual card picks that simultaneously buff you and empower the enemy army, so difficulty is part of the build rather than a separate slider
Reviewers and players describe it as playing like a turn-based tactics game as much as chess: managing ammo, spread and damage matters more than chess openings
Shotgun mechanics on a chessboard: firing pushes you back, killing pieces can expose your king, and the AI sets traps with queens, bishops behind pawns, etc.
Steam Workshop and Lua modding support plus many modes (endless, Chase, Charnier raiding mode)
tedious_or_disliked: Repetitive loop: commentary from critics and Metacritic users is that you see most of the game's content within the first ~20 rounds
Slow, stressful board-scanning at high ranks when you can no longer easily see which tiles are dangerous
Hitting a hard wall around rank 7-9 or 10+ where losses feel RNG-driven rather than earned
Achievement and codex grinding that depends on drawing specific card combos
Losing a long run with no save to a single misclick or discovered check
divisive_points: Is the difficulty fair? Many Steam players say losses feel deserved and skill-based, while others say late ranks are pure luck
Replayability: Steam players praise it as highly replayable, while critics (PLAY, Push Square) and Metacritic users call it repetitive
Update direction: the 1.6 content update was celebrated, but the removal of the check-tile highlight and a censored tutorial line drew negative reviews from some longtime players
Whether it is really chess: some say it becomes a turn-based shooter rather than a chess game
community.reception_notes: Launched on PC May 12, 2022 to very strong Steam reception; PC Gamer is quoted on the store page calling it a supremely addictive turn-based roguelike. Console ports (Switch, PS4/5, Xbox) followed Aug 24, 2023, with physical Switch/PS5 editions shipping Apr 25, 2025 after delays (per Wikipedia). The v1.6 Bad Company update (April, anniversary update) added roughly 30 cards, a Charnier raiding mode, 2 shotguns, 5 ranks and 10 achievements; v1.62x patches through summer fixed softlocks, AI bugs, Steam Deck and macOS control issues. Some recent negative Steam reviews cite the removed check-tile highlight, card-pool bloat and a censored tutorial line. Steam lists no Metacritic score (the PC version is not scored); Metacritic only has console scores. Steam-revenue-calculator estimates about $1.89M gross and about $556k net; SteamSpy owner estimate 200k-500k (order-of-magnitude only). Publisher is listed as PUNKCAKE Delicieux on Steam and Headbang Club on Wikipedia. OpenCritic page could not be located; WebSearch budget was exhausted, so the score is null.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Spelunky (2008) is the classic exploration-focused roguelike credited with helping revive the genre in the modern era. PepperHead openly admits this is a controversial take: he is not a fan. He wants meaningful variation between runs, and feels every Spelunky run plays similarly. Exploration-only style is not what he wants from a roguelike
unique_points: Focus is on exploration, worlds and secrets rather than build variety, which was its original goal
Mastery comes from learning each trap and avoiding one-shot kills
commentary.quote: I'm not a huge fan of this game there I said it
design_criteria: Run-to-run variation: wants different builds each run, which Spelunky lacks
Purpose of randomness: random elements need a reason to exist
Difficulty: brutal one-shot deaths he finds frustrating
Exploration and secrets: acknowledged as a strength but not his preference
Historical influence: respected for reviving the genre

community.one_liner: A procedurally generated 2D platformer by Derek Yu (freeware 2008, HD remake 2012 on Xbox 360 and 2013 on PC) in which you descend cave levels collecting treasure and rescuing damsels, with permadeath and no persistent upgrades, widely credited as a foundational roguelike-platformer.
community.consensus_summary: Critics and players treat Spelunky as a landmark of design. The HD version carries a Metacritic PC score of 90 (as listed by Steam), and the Metacritic Xbox 360 page shows 87 from 54 critics; Wikipedia also lists Vita 88 and PS3 83. Steam users are Very Positive at about 92 percent of roughly 16.7k reviews. Praise centres on tight controls, systemic interactions, fairness of the core rules, and extremely high replay value (Daily Challenge, co-op, deathmatch). The recurring complaint is brutal, instant-death difficulty with no difficulty options, plus RNG-dependent bad runs. It is not early access and is not abandoned, but the PC port is old: recent Steam reviews report launch trouble on Windows 11, no Steam Cloud, and a few reports of lost saves. Many players now suggest Spelunky 2 as the next step, though some Steam reviewers prefer the original.
best_things: Tight, responsive movement and a huge skill ceiling; players describe moves becoming muscle memory and runs feeling earned
Systemic, emergent chaos: enemies, shopkeepers, damsels, bombs and traps all interact, producing memorable stories (for example an angry shopkeeper or an exploding frog wrecking a run)
Short runs (typically 30 to 45 minutes) with no meta-progression, so skill and knowledge are the only progression
Daily Challenge gives a shared seed and leaderboard that some players have used as a nightly ritual for over a thousand hours
Lots of hidden secrets, items and areas (Black Market, hell/Yama run, journal, skins) that reward curiosity and experimentation
Fun local co-op and deathmatch; co-op revives via coffins add social chaos
Strong audio-visual charm: cute art and music contrasting with a ruthless game
Critics compared it to a manual of game design; GamesRadar gave it 5/5 and IGN gave 9.0 with an Editor's Choice
worst_things: Many threats kill or stunlock instantly (spikes, ghost, mantrap, black knight, UFO, shopkeepers, yetis, explosions), so one small mistake can send you back to the Mines
Some runs are decided by RNG rather than skill, for example a Black Market entrance next to a shopkeeper or no bomb merchant when a golden chest is walled in
No difficulty setting or assist options; newcomers find it punishing with little on-ramp
PC port technical problems: crashes when changing resolution, needing multiple launches on Windows 11, and Windows-only (no Mac or Linux)
No Steam Cloud support; a few reviewers report losing progress after a failed launch and reinstall
Controls can feel cramped or quirky to some (complaints about no auto-run toggle, cramped hands); critics also flagged control quirks and a throwaway multiplayer
Some reviewers with mixed feelings called the game a poor grind because one death costs 15 or more minutes of progress
improvements: Steam Cloud saves and more robust save handling, given reports of deleted progress
Better compatibility and stability on modern Windows (Windows 11 launch failures, resolution-change crashes)
Optional difficulty or assist features, or a gentler on-ramp for first-time players
Safeguards against the most unfair RNG placements (Black Market entrance near a shopkeeper, bomb scarcity) without removing the challenge
Mac and Linux builds, or official ports to more current platforms (a Switch version exists per Wikipedia, but not on PC storefronts)
unique_things: Permadeath with literally no persistent power-ups: the only thing that carries over is player knowledge and unlocked shortcuts
A platformer built on roguelike principles, inspired by Rogue and Super Mario-style movement, which helped define the roguelike-platformer subgenre
Levels assembled from hand-designed room templates in a 4x4 grid that guarantee a path, so generation feels authored rather than random
Fully simulated world where shopkeepers, damsels, and even you can be killed or turned against you; killing or robbing a shopkeeper has lasting consequences in that run
A time-limit ghost that punishes slow play, pushing players between careful and fast styles
Daily Challenge with a global seed, and deep speedrun/score-chasing culture (hell runs, 'no gold' and speedrun achievements)
tedious_or_disliked: Dying to a trivial mistake late in a long run, then restarting from the Mines
Stunlock chains from arrow traps, tiki men, boomerang throwers and shopkeepers that feel unfair even to experienced players
Unlocking the secret path (shortcuts, Black Market, City of Gold, Yama) is obscure and convoluted when playing blind, which some compare to The Binding of Isaac
Completing all achievements and journal entries can take hundreds of runs (one reviewer was at 920 runs), which some see as a grind
Jank on modern PCs: needing relaunches, resolution crashes, missing cloud sync
Co-op and multiplayer can be frustrating if friends are not on the same skill level (one reviewer called it not fun with friends)
divisive_points: Fairness: fans call it tough but fair and say every death is your fault; critics of the game say the stacked instakills and RNG make it unfair
Original vs Spelunky 2: some Steam reviewers say the sequel is better in every way, while others say the sequel did not improve on the first
Metacritic user score is only mixed (7.4 on the Xbox 360 page from 216 ratings) even though critics rate it 87 to 90, reflecting players who bounced off the difficulty
Whether the game is a replayable perfect roguelite or a frustrating grind depends on tolerance for permadeath without progression
community.reception_notes: The 2008 freeware original already had a cult following; the 2012 Xbox Live Arcade HD remake was a critical hit and the PC/PS3/Vita/PS4 versions followed in 2013-2014, with a Switch release in 2021 per Wikipedia. Wikipedia notes it passed 1 million sales by 2016, sold 61,408 copies on Steam in week one, and about 577k Steam copies lifetime; PC Gamer UK named the 2013 remake its Game of the Year, and it ranks highly on Eurogamer's Games of the Generation and The Guardian's 50 Best Video Games of the 21st Century lists. Steam-revenue-calculator estimates about $10.6M gross and $3.1M net on Steam (Boxleiter method, treat as order of magnitude); SteamSpy lists 1-2M owners. The game is not in active development, but remains popular (the Steam listing showed around 60 concurrent players at the time of the data pull, with reviews still arriving in 2026). Known PC issues: Windows 11 launch trouble, no Steam Cloud, Windows only. Spelunky 2 (2020) is the follow-up. Note: my web-search quota ran out mid-task, so OpenCritic could not be confirmed (null) and Reddit, IGN and Eurogamer pages could not be fetched; scores for Metacritic come from Steam's listing plus fetched Metacritic pages.

games.name: Below the Stone
games.short_description: Below the Stone is an extraction roguelike about dwarves on the quest for the deepest depths. A place where each and every descent will lead to new adventures -- and where only the most determined dwarves with many lost lives will be rewarded by the hidden world lying below the stone.

other_scores.score: about $150k gross / $44k net (Boxleiter-style estimate, order of magnitude only)

placements.verbal_evidence: none

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Below the Stone is an Early Access Terraria-style digging roguelite: you descend underground, mine gems and minerals, return to the surface for upgrades, and repeat. He was excited to see a real roguelike built on this traditional formula but came away very disappointed. He found the content shallow, repetitive and quickly exhausted, with little reason to keep exploring. He sees potential if the developers add much more content and mobility, and will revisit after updates. He never states a tier letter in this segment.
praise: Enjoys the general dig-and-upgrade exploration loop and is a big Terraria fan
Likes exploration and discovering new biomes in principle
Sees real potential if it receives substantial content updates
Design is straightforward and can be satisfying when exploration feels purposeful
criticism: Gameplay is very repetitive; he felt he had found everything almost from the start
Underground quests never change (kill X bats, kill X ooze)
Biomes are essentially the same with different, merely upgraded minerals
Armor and weapons are the same items with better stats, nothing unique
Combat/movement is basic, with no dash or roll, just swinging a sword
No goal to work towards, so he maxed things out and lost motivation to explore
unique_points: Uses a traditional Terraria-like mining formula as a roguelite structure, which he found promising in concept
Design lesson: exploration only works if new finds are meaningfully different, not stat upgrades
Lack of other activities (unlike Stardew Valley's mines) leaves the loop hollow
commentary.quote: it's not a game that I really had a great time with personally
design_criteria: Content variety: biomes and items feel identical beyond stats
Exploration motivation: needs goals and reasons to keep digging
Gameplay depth: basic combat lacking dash/mobility
Item uniqueness: gear should do something different, not just bigger numbers
Quest design: static repetitive objectives
Replayability: boredom set in quickly

community.one_liner: A pixel-art mining/extraction action roguelike by Strollart (published by Apogee) in which dwarves dive into procedurally generated caverns, loot and craft, and risk losing carried gear if they die before extracting.
community.consensus_summary: Below the Stone is a modestly successful Early Access title (Steam, Nov 2023) with a Very Positive Steam rating of roughly 84% across about 440 reviews. Players like the cozy dwarven presentation, pixel art and ambient music, and the risk/reward loop, but many describe it as thin, repetitive and unfinished, with progression that stalls once you pass the early layers. It has no Metacritic or OpenCritic scores and almost no outlet coverage beyond news and roadmap posts, so reception is driven by Steam reviews. It is still in Early Access: sources say the developer is working toward a final update (Layer 3 plus bosses on Layers 2 and 3) in summer 2026, and the Steam page lists a planned exit around Nov 2026 that depends on feedback.
best_things: Charming dwarven fantasy setting and pixel art that reviewers call cute, chill and easy on the eyes
Ambient soundtrack (over an hour of music) praised for atmosphere, though one critical reviewer calls it generic
Core loop of mine, loot, craft, extract, with a risk/reward tension around what to carry down and what to leave safe at home
Gear progression through ore tiers (tin, copper, iron...) gives clear power increases, and gem socketing and potions add prep depth
Hub-building and unlocking vendors, NPCs and quests keeps some players going despite the lack of a big goal
Responsive, community-driven developer with Discord engagement, playtests and regular content updates (combat update, new biomes, Kingdom o' Quests)
Relaxed, cozy feel for short afternoon sessions; some reviewers compare it to Core Keeper but on a harder setting
worst_things: Too little content and no ultimate goal; several reviewers say it feels like an early alpha despite five years of development
Weak progression: no levels or real meta-progression, only ore-tier crafting and a simple 'resistance' armor stat, so dying mostly just sets you back
UI described as a nightmare and frustrating, plus reported freezes when buying or selling and unfixed bugs
Combat is called clunky, with weapon animations not matching enemy hitboxes; one critic says there are few real threats or challenges
Harsh death penalty: carried items are lost unless you pay to keep them, which some find punishing for a game with limited depth
Seen as too expensive for the current content at about $15-20 in Early Access
Economy and quest balance problems, e.g. bar-repair missions costing more in materials than they pay in gold, and many items with no use
Bugs and unanswered bug reports: reviewers report freezes when buying or selling and community-reported game-breaking bugs left unfixed for months
improvements: Add a long-term goal, more biomes, enemies, bosses and equipment (Layer 3 and boss fights are the announced final update)
Build real meta-progression and chase items so runs feel cumulative instead of just repeating ore tiers
Quality-of-life fixes: item pickup filters (auto-ignore tin, for example), better UI, less fiddly picking up of plants and mushrooms
Fix combat hitboxes and balance difficulty, and squash reported crashes and freezes
Rebalance crafting ingredient availability and quest rewards (for example missing ingredients on layer 2, gold rewards lower than crafting cost)
Add localization (Japanese, Chinese, French requested) and more reasons to use the many currently useless items
unique_things: Extraction-style structure applied to a dwarf mining roguelike: choose what you keep safe at home versus what you wear and carry into the dive
Gem socketing for magical buffs and pre-dive potion brewing/crafting as part of preparation
Dwarven kingdom hub used for crafting, storage, trading and recruiting NPCs (10-12 planned)
Dark caves where you must hold a torch, which shapes exploration
Combat update added secondary melee attacks and armor set bonuses with biome-specific armor recipes
tedious_or_disliked: Slow, repetitive loop of mining ore to craft the next tier, with little variety once the early layers are learned
Early-game grind: the first missions demand large amounts of materials (for example glowweed) and the start is described as a challenge
Fiddly item pickup and inventory clutter, including aiming at plants and picking up junk you cannot filter out
Losing everything carried on death unless you pay, which makes failed runs feel like a setback rather than progress
divisive_points: Extraction structure: fans enjoy the tension, while one negative reviewer calls extraction a mistake that strips the meta-upgrade feel of action roguelikes
Difficulty: some call it extra-hard Core Keeper, others say it has very few real threats and the challenge is mostly tedium
Value and content: many positive reviews accept the early access state and recommend it for potential, others say it is overpriced for what exists
community.reception_notes: Launched into Steam Early Access on Nov 17, 2023 (also GOG and Epic listings) at $19.99 with a launch discount, now listed at $14.99. A full release across PC, PS4/PS5, Xbox Series and Switch was once planned for 2024, and the 2024 roadmap listed a Fashion update, Caves Awaken parts 1 and 2, and a Layer 3 update by mid-2024. Later coverage says the combat update is the penultimate Early Access update, with a final summer-2026 update adding Layer 3 and bosses on Layers 2 and 3, so the schedule has slipped well past the original roadmap. Steam lists the game for Windows only and the store page expects a flexible exit from Early Access around Nov 2026. Metacritic has a page but shows no critic or user scores yet; I could not confirm any OpenCritic entry. Some reviewers complained about old bug reports going unfixed before and after launch. Data from SteamSpy and the revenue calculator are rough estimates.

games.name: Cavity Busters
games.short_description: Cavity Busters is a roguelite toothpunk bullet hell where you bite and chomp cavity infested enemies. Run on the walls, dodge through bullet filled rooms and stomp baddies. Collect power ups, contract powerful diseases, and carve your way through a bloated body kingdom.

placements.verbal_evidence: "I'm going to put this as a as a high SE tier" (ASR garbled; could be high S or high C)

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Cavity Busters is a top-down bullet hell shooter roguelike where you play as a tooth with a huge pile of overlapping mechanics: throwing and recalling your tooth, a health-fuelled auto-shotgun, a zoomed-out jump, and wall-dashing with slow-mo. Items are plentiful, often carry big downsides, and you can spend health to dig new rooms and extend floors almost indefinitely. He finds it inventive, content-rich, funny and strong in its boss fights, but thinks the sheer chaos and mechanical overload drag it down. Verdict is a tier placement that sounds like 'high S' or 'high C' (the ASR says 'high SE'), which is ambiguous.
praise: Boss fights are really cool and the boss designs are interesting
Bullet hell gameplay feels great
Many viable ways to approach any fight
Huge amount of content and plenty of secrets
Funny, fun story with lots of humor
Passives that radically change how the character plays, with five to six found per floor
criticism: Too many mechanics; takes forever to get comfortable and is overwhelming
Because all options are viable and usable constantly, it is unclear what to do
Overall chaos across gameplay, mechanics and run structure is too much
Health-based digging can make a single floor last around 40 minutes
Passives with massive downsides that you are pressured to take, and removing them is slow and not guaranteed
unique_points: Tooth throw, recall, and mid-air recall with special effect, alongside jump, wall-dash and slow-mo
Spending health to dig new rooms lets you expand floors nearly infinitely
Items have upsides and heavy downsides, and skipping them triggers other negatives, echoing Blazing Beaks
commentary.quote: it's a game that I think deserves a little bit more work and a bit less chaos
design_criteria: Mechanical complexity: too many overlapping systems overwhelm the player
Boss design: praised as interesting and cool
Combat feel: bullet hell experience feels great
Item/passive design: many impactful passives with strong downsides
Content volume: lots of secrets and content
Run length/structure: health-digging can stretch floors very long
Humor/story: fun and funny

community.one_liner: A solo-developed toothpunk roguelite bullet hell in which you play a single tooth (Gummy The Soft) who shoots and recalls himself as a boomerang, dashes, parries, and runs along walls through a bloated body kingdom.
community.consensus_summary: Players receive it warmly: Steam shows Very Positive at roughly 96% across about 125 reviews, and several reviewers call it underrated and say they prefer it to The Binding of Isaac. Critical coverage is thin, with one OpenCritic review (6.1/10, Nindie Spotlight) and two Metacritic-listed reviews (80 and 75), which is too few for Metacritic to show a score. The recurring themes are inventive movement and mechanics plus a large item pool, set against a steep, overwhelming start and poor item readability. It began Early Access on Steam in August 2020, went 1.0 on 18 March 2022, and reached Xbox, PlayStation and Switch in April 2023 via JanduSoft. The dev keeps updating it, and the Steam page cites ongoing content updates.
best_things: Movement and skill expression: dash with i-frames, bullet parry, wall-running and sliding, stomping enemies from above, all chainable
Tooth-as-weapon boomerang: shooting the tooth and recalling it deals damage both ways, making gunplay feel inventive and satisfying
Large item pool (Steam lists 317 upgrades; console listings say 280) that can make a run wildly strong, weak or both, with diseased upgrades as risk/reward
Playable characters feel mechanically different rather than like stat-modifier reskins
Wall-digging mechanic adds risk/reward and is seen as well balanced: helpful but not a cheat button
Reviewers praise boss and enemy design and the amount of content for the price ($14.99)
Music and gross-but-funny audio/art style praised, including many tooth puns
Steady post-launch content updates; reviewers say each update brings new content; runs well on Steam Deck
worst_things: Overwhelming onboarding: many mechanics are thrown at the player at once, and key information gets lost in rapid-fire tutorials
Item descriptions are hidden or vague; some items are unidentified and some set HP to 1, which can unknowingly end a run
Stability complaints: crashes, freezes and audio bugs reported on Windows and under Proton/Linux (Windows-only on Steam)
Clunky feel to some early weapons: one requires picking up the ammo you fire, the other auto-aims
Samey colour palette makes enemies, items and props hard to tell apart (IndieGameFans review)
No autosave mid-run reported by a player, so a crash costs the whole run
Critics and some players see it as a close Isaac/Gungeon derivative that does not surpass them
improvements: Introduce mechanics gradually with a better tutorial or pacing, so runs start simple like Isaac and complexity builds through items
Make item descriptions clear and show what items do, especially HP-altering ones, instead of hiding them
Improve visual clarity and colour differentiation between enemies, pickups and environment
Fix crashes and freezes and improve Proton/Linux compatibility (no native Mac or Linux build)
Add a mid-run save or resume safety for crash cases
unique_things: You are a tooth: a boomerang-style shoot-and-recall attack that damages enemies on the way out and back
Wall-run and wall-dig mechanic adds a second traversal layer unusual for top-down shooters
Disease upgrades you can contract and cure to keep the good effects, as a risk/reward item twist
Mouse-and-keyboard-first design with bullet parry and i-frame dash, more fast-paced than tank or twin-stick Isaac clones
Dental/body-horror toothpunk theme with pun-heavy humour and a 'bloated body kingdom' that changes each run
tedious_or_disliked: Steep learning curve and a punishing early game; one reviewer took several attempts to beat the first boss
Too many systems to juggle at once (parry, roll, wall-run, ammo pickup, stomp) feels cumbersome to some players
Constant dodging, rolling and wall-running reads as more bullet hell than roguelike to players who expected an item-driven game
Decoding unidentified items by trial and error is frustrating
Technical crashes interrupt long runs
divisive_points: Mechanical density: some see layered systems as deep skill expression, others say less would have been more
Bullet-hell vs roguelike identity: praised as fast and skill-based by some, disliked as too dodge-focused by others
Isaac/Gungeon comparison: several players say it beats Isaac, while one critic says it fails to meet the legend that inspired it
Difficulty: some find it hard to master but rewarding, others find it tough and cruel, though accessibility options soften it
community.reception_notes: Early Access on Steam from 12 Aug 2020, full release 18 Mar 2022 at $14.99; Xbox One/Series, PS4/PS5 and Switch versions launched 20 Apr 2023, published by JanduSoft, with Steam left as SpaceMyFriend. Launch-era Steam negatives (2022-23) focus on overwhelming pacing, hidden item text and crashes; more recent reviews (2025-26) are largely positive and call it underrated, though Linux/Proton crashes are still mentioned. The Steam page still cites active dev updates. Metacritic has no score yet (2 critic reviews, needs 4) and OpenCritic has a single review, so critical consensus is essentially unavailable. SteamSpy estimates 0-20k owners, and the revenue estimate site shows $0 (no usable data). Steam is Windows only.

games.name: Cursorblade
games.short_description: Cursorblade is a bullet hell game where you play as the cursor, fighting your way through waves of enemies. Combine weapons and items to become more powerful with your own unique builds. Slash, dodge, upgrade, and repeat!

placements.verbal_evidence: I do feel bad to put it as a c tier it's not because it's a bad game

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Cursorblade is a cute, very simple top-down bullet-hell-ish game where your cursor is both hitbox and weapon; you damage enemies by touching them and dodge by not getting hit. He finds it satisfying and charming but basic, with a game-jam feel. Upgrades arrive once per wave but barely change how you play. He places it in C tier while stressing it is not a bad game, just not something he would replay.
praise: Cute and satisfying to play
Very straightforward concept that does what it sets out to do well
Does not over-reach; restrained content suits the game
Could be a fun, easy intro to basic roguelike action for a younger audience
criticism: Upgrades (rockets, spinners, fire damage) are not impactful, so runs play the same regardless of picks
Gameplay loop of hitting then evading is very repetitive
Pace is so fast it feels random, like swiping without thinking
Would be more interesting slower, leaving room for more attacks and mechanics
Feels like a game jam project; he would not play it again
unique_points: The cursor is both hitbox and weapon, dealing damage by touching enemies
One upgrade per completed wave keeps the structure minimal
Design lesson: slowing the pace would allow richer enemy attacks and more thoughtful bullet-hell play
commentary.quote: it's just super cute and super basic with a very straightforward concept
design_criteria: Upgrade impact: upgrades should meaningfully change gameplay; here they do not
Pacing: too fast makes it feel random and leaves no room for depth
Repetition: same hit-and-evade loop throughout
Scope/simplicity: straightforward design is appropriate but shallow
Charm: cute presentation
Enemy attack variety: wants more attack patterns via slower pace

community.one_liner: A cheap Windows-only arcade bullet-hell roguelite by solo-ish studio RealPeach in which you are the mouse cursor, slashing waves of cute enemies and picking weapons and passives between waves.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate it Very Positive (about 85% of roughly 1,045 reviews) and treat it as a short, satisfying, cheap ($4.99) arcade score-chase with an original mouse-only hook. The most common complaint, even in positive reviews, is thin content: few weapons, enemies and upgrades, one boss, one map, and most people see everything in 1-3 hours. There are no professional critic reviews; Metacritic shows no critic score and too few user ratings for a score. Content additions since the demo appear minimal and a Steam discussion thread raises worries about the project being abandoned.
best_things: Novel concept: the mouse cursor is both character and weapon, with one-to-one mouse-only control that players say they have rarely seen in a bullet hell
Fluid, responsive, fair arcade feel; difficulty is described as challenging but fair by many, and as a good nice timekiller or relaxing pause
Wave structure with a choice of one of three random weapons after each wave and a passive every few waves, giving simple survivors-like build decisions
Cute art and animation (goofy-eyed monster sprites) and satisfying sound and visual effects
Very cheap, short, easy to pick up and addictive for quick runs; some players lost track of time
Achievement hunting and the wave-50 boss give a clear goal; some players pushed to wave 57 and beyond chasing high scores
worst_things: Very little content: roughly 6 weapons, about 12 upgrades, fewer than 10 enemy types, one map and a single boss at wave 50, after which waves continue endlessly with the same enemies
Builds feel bland and a handful of options dominate, so runs feel identical; many upgrades are just 'X appears more often'
Almost no meta progression: currency only unlocks new swords/cursors, so there is little reason to keep playing after unlocking everything (several say you have seen it all by the third game)
Late waves become cluttered, so skilled dodging matters less and play turns into slowly picking off stragglers
Looping, short and generic music gets grating; a few players mute it, though others praise the soundtrack
Technical bareness: no Steam Cloud saves, essentially no graphics options (no resolution or FPS cap), some reports of bugs and slowness
Some unlockable cursors/characters are seen as weak or useless, and right-click abilities have a slight activation delay that makes them unappealing
Shallow, barebones feel: several negative reviews call it unfinished and Flash-game-like, with no saving and little build diversity
improvements: More weapons, items, enemy types, bosses, maps and characters; players note little has been added since the demo
Real meta progression or build-diversity systems (and a save feature) so unlocks matter beyond new swords
Make cursor-specific active abilities more useful and responsive
Options: FPS unlock, resolution/graphics settings, Steam Cloud, and more music tracks
Modding or Steam Workshop support (repeatedly requested in Steam discussions), plus community translations
Clearer developer communication about the project's future and fixes for balance issues such as a blade bypassing invincibility frames and concern about the round-80 boss
unique_things: You play literally as a mouse cursor, using mouse motion alone to move, attack and dodge
Bullet hell blended with survivors-like level-up choices but with no persistent stat meta-progression, closer to an endless arcade high-score chase
Cursor-themed characters/blades each with a right-click active ability
Combo meter and score-driven unlock points, where raising wave difficulty earns unlocks faster than perfecting combos
Tiny runs and a playable free demo on itch.io (v0.27f), making it a pick-up-and-play desktop toy
tedious_or_disliked: Content exhausted within 30 minutes to 3 hours, making repeat runs feel padded and monotonous
Some players say runs feel like chore-like work, one comparing it to cleaning windows
Reliance on RNG weapon offers to carry runs
Difficulty spikes: a minority find it too hard from the start, and demo players say it gets annoying past wave 10
Endless post-boss waves repeat the same enemies with nothing new
Looping music and lack of settings options
divisive_points: Difficulty: some call it fair and even easy (100% in a couple of hours), others call it punishing and unfun
Value at $4.99: fun short game for the price versus not worth it for the content, with some recommending alternatives like 20 Minutes Till Dawn
Roguelike versus roguelite label: debate over whether the lack of meta progression makes it a true roguelite
Music: praised as awesome by some, called repetitive and grating by others
community.reception_notes: Released Nov 6, 2023 on Steam (Windows only) at $4.99 after a free itch.io demo; Steam has held steady at Very Positive since launch (85-86%). Nodal.gg reports average playtime of about 2.2 hours with 65% of players reaching 1+ hour. No Metacritic critic or user score (only a couple of user ratings, below the 4-rating threshold) and no OpenCritic entry found. The last itch devlog found was a balancing and bug fixes post from Aug 2023, reviewers say little was added beyond the demo, and a Steam discussion thread (about 12 comments) worries the game is abandoned. Workshop/modding, FPS unlock, extra powerups and translations are popular requests. Family Sharing and achievements supported.

games.name: Necrosmith 2
games.short_description: Like a dead man reanimated by dark sorcery, the necromancer simulator is back! Give the undead the ability to fly over mountains and swim across rivers, explore a fully generated world at night and fend off enemy hordes during the day. Start a new, uhm, life.

placements.verbal_evidence: "this one's going to be a high SE tier for me" (ASR, likely 'high C tier')

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Necrosmith 2 is the sequel to an auto-battling undead-army roguelite where you craft minions and let them fight on their own. He was looking forward to it because the first game had obvious quality-of-life fixes to make, and it does deliver better visuals, better AI and more mechanics such as the Titan. Overall he finds it a step down from the original. The separate small worlds and the overpowered Titan strip out the exploration, adventure and strategy he loved, and he beat the game far faster than the first one.
praise: Visuals are improved over the first game
Better minion AI and more quality-of-life improvements
More mechanics and more things to do with the different undead
Titan creation (assembling collected pieces into a huge unit) is cool and awesome to have
criticism: Lost the sense of adventure: multiple separate worlds (only three) replace one big world to push through
Each world is beaten quickly; he finished the whole game in a handful of runs, about four times faster than the original
Starting later worlds with powerful minions makes them feel less impactful
Map is small and its outline is revealed very fast, so there is little exploration
Titans are overpowered and trivialize base defense; park one at base and ignore it for ~20 minutes, reducing strategy
Overall feels less free and loses the charm of the original
unique_points: The Titan mechanic: collect pieces to build a huge unit, limited to one or two
Design lesson: more systems and better AI do not compensate for removing exploration and strategic tension
Separate selectable worlds per run change the pacing versus one continuous expedition
commentary.quote: I personally have a more fun experience from the original than this one
design_criteria: Exploration and adventure: the original's single expanding world is valued over small separate maps
Strategy and decision-making: overpowered Titans remove the need to manage the base
Power curve and pacing: starting with strong minions dulls progression impact
Run and game length: beating the game very quickly is disappointing
Visuals and quality of life: improved, but does not offset the lost charm
AI and mechanics depth: more mechanics and better AI are noted as positives

community.one_liner: A real-time necromancer tower-defense/auto-battler roguelite from Alawar/Amber Jam where you stitch undead minions from monster body parts, send them out to explore a procedurally generated map, and fend off enemy hordes and bosses on a timer.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate it Mostly Positive (about 78% of roughly 1,500 reviews, steady in recent reviews too), and most positive reviewers frame it as a cheap, chill, silly minion-builder that is worth buying on sale for 10-25 hours. The two critic reviews on Metacritic (GameGrin 8/10, Movies Games and Tech 7/10) are friendly and stress humor, Steam Deck suitability and the fun of combining parts. Negative reviews focus on a grindy meta-progression, a steep jump in difficulty between the three maps, Titans that make normal units irrelevant, weak inventory/recipe UI, no mid-run save, and late-map FPS collapse and memory problems. Many players see it as an incremental upgrade that could almost have been a big update or DLC for Necrosmith 1. It is a released 1.0 game (Mar 27, 2024, Windows/Mac) with a developer bug-report form on Steam, but several reviewers say known bugs and performance issues have gone unfixed for months.
best_things: Build-a-minion loop: mixing body parts from different fantasy races and discovering secret recipes is the hook most reviewers enjoy
Humor and style: sarcastic cat narrator, pop-culture/other-universe creature references, nice pixel visuals
Improvements over Necrosmith 1: manual control of a single unit, pause to think mid-battle, better part sorting, area-defense orders for minions, more maps/biomes
Controllable Titans are a fun, pretty power fantasy and a big new mechanic
Artifacts and body-part variety allow different builds and keep runs interesting
Chill, low-stress pacing and low PC demands; good on Steam Deck according to critics
Great value: cheap base price ($7.99) and frequent deep discounts; completionists report around 17-20 hours for 100%
worst_things: Severe performance problems in big maps: once most of a map is explored, FPS can fall to single digits or near zero and memory use balloons, sometimes making runs unplayable
No save during a run; long runs mean leaving the game open, and several players report softlocks that erase ~30 minutes of progress
Difficulty and upgrade costs spike hard from map 1 to map 2 and 3, forcing repeated grinding (upgrades cited at 15,000-45,000 gold versus ~10,000 gold earned per run)
Balance: Titans trivialise or dominate fights while normal units are weak against bosses, so unit design matters less than having a Titan
Recipe/inventory UI is poor: no search, filter or species sorting, constantly shifting part list, and scrolling hundreds of recipes
Bugs and unfinished details, e.g. mislabeled abilities (two different weapons named Steam Saw), reported unfixed for months
Audio: units spam loud ability sounds, with several Pharaohs making the game unbearable without muting
improvements: Add a mid-run save or resume, or suspend feature
Optimise performance and memory for large explored maps
Add search, filters and sorting for body parts and recipes (including show only craftable recipes)
Rebalance map-to-map difficulty and upgrade costs to reduce forced grinding; add a game-speed-up option
Rebalance Titans versus normal units and make unit composition and recipes matter more than artifact stat stacking
More maps, challenges/handicap modes, new buildings and upgrades, and more story content; some players want a sequel with more variation or multiplayer
Fix sound spam and mislabeled items
unique_things: Necromancer-simulator framing: you play the villain, reanimating monsters from parts to conquer the land
Five-part minion crafting with set bonuses across fantasy races and 300+ hidden recipes, discovered by experimentation
Hybrid of tower defense, auto-battler, resource gathering and light management/idle elements, with a countdown timer that ends in a boss fight
Direct control of one unit at a time plus area defense orders, with giant Titan units as elite constructs
Day/night style exploration of a fully generated world with lairs to attack and areas to defend; three mini-worlds with story
tedious_or_disliked: Mandatory meta-progression grind, described as mobile-game style, with very expensive upgrades before world 3
Long stretches of waiting while minions gather resources; the game can turn into an idle/clicker game
Crafting becomes repetitive: pick five parts and go, and random picks work nearly as well as careful builds
Secret recipes are hard to discover by trial and error and often feel underwhelming or pointless compared to artifacts; many players just look recipes up
Being one part short of a desired recipe (also noted by critics)
Runs take long and cannot be paused by saving, so casual play is hard
Game feels small and repetitive across its few maps
divisive_points: Difficulty: some players find it much more challenging than the relaxed first game and like it, others find the map-to-map jump unfair
Value and scope: many call it a great cheap game, others say it should have been DLC or an update to Necrosmith 1 and that Necrosmith 1 was better
Titans: praised as fun and controllable, criticised as overtuned and making normal minion crafting irrelevant
Length: some like that it does not overstay its welcome (about 10 hours), others want far more content and replayability
community.reception_notes: Launched Mar 27, 2024 (Windows, Mac) at $7.99 with a free demo and a separate soundtrack. Early critic coverage (Mar-Jul 2024) was positive. Steam reception settled at Mostly Positive and has stayed there, with recent 30-day reviews around 78% too. Steam reviews posted through late 2025 and 2026 still complain about FPS drops, memory leaks, lack of saving and unfixed bugs; the community forum (about 284 topics) has threads on late-game lag, OBS issues, unreliable saves, and a pinned developer bug-report form from Amber Jam, plus a fan thread asking about Necrosmith 3. Metacritic has only 2 critic reviews and 2 user ratings, so no official Metascore or user score is shown yet (needs 4). No OpenCritic entry was found. Note: the WebSearch budget was exhausted in this session, so research relied on Steam data, Steam reviews, Metacritic, the two critic reviews, the Steam store and community pages; Reddit could not be fetched.

games.name: Slime 3K: Rise Against Despot
games.short_description: Welcome to Slime 3K, an unhinged roguelite bullet-heaven set in the Despot’s Game universe! Build a deck of crazy weapons, grow stronger and devour hordes of pink puny humans as a murderous jelly blob on a warpath of death, violence and pretzels.
