commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Slime 3K is a horde-survival, single-level-layout roguelike that closely mirrors another game he already covered, reusing characters, enemies, animation and art. You play a very slow slime and buy weapons that just stack into an inventory, with little depth beyond that. He finds it fun at first but repetitive and shallow, since builds barely change how you play. The cute, funny art style rescues it, and he feels it needed more development time. He places it in a high tier, which the ASR renders as 'high seat tier' and most likely means high C or B.
praise: Charming, cute and funny art style that he says saves the game
Enjoyable and fun in the first runs
Satisfying to find different weapons that kill things
A few build directions exist, such as shotgun-style versus other weapon effects
criticism: Shallow inventory system: you just buy weapons and stack duplicates to level them
Very repetitive, and different builds do not change moment-to-moment play
Extremely slow slime with no mobility, unlike the genre norm where movement is key
Found an infinite-money exploit that he could repeat consistently from the fifth run
Camera sits awkwardly low, leaving the character close to the screen edge
Feels like it needed more time in development
unique_points: Being slow and tanky with no mobility is an unusual twist for the horde genre, making it all about whether weapons out-damage incoming hits
Mechanically it does little that is new, relying on its sibling game's formula
commentary.quote: the art style does save this game quite a bit
comparisons: The earlier auto-battler-style horde game from the same art lineage (name forgotten, likely Brotato-adjacent)
design_criteria: Mechanical uniqueness: little that differs from its sibling game
Build diversity: builds exist but do not change gameplay
Inventory/equipment depth: only buy and stack weapons
Movement/mobility: absent, slow character
Replayability/repetition: gets repetitive quickly
Art style/charm: cute and funny, the main strength
Economy balance: exploitable for infinite money
Camera/UX polish: awkward low camera

community.one_liner: A pixel-art roguelite bullet-heaven from Konfa Games and tinyBuild, set in the Despot's Game universe, where you play a murderous slime and build a deck of weapons and passive-tag synergies to survive escalating hordes across about 20 levels.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate it Mostly Positive (about 80% of roughly 1,700 reviews) and it is a modest, cheap ($4.99) indie hit that has not broken out; third-party estimates put it at 50-100k owners and roughly $120k gross. Fans love the art, animation, weapon variety and the deckbuilding and tag-synergy layer, which they say makes it more strategic than a typical Vampire Survivors clone. Detractors say the meta-progression is slow and grindy, builds get narrow, and later levels feel like stat checks or difficulty spikes, so the game runs out of surprises around the mid-game. It left Early Access (launched Nov 2023) with a 1.0 release on Oct 31, 2024, and recent reviews are slightly better than the all-time average (86% positive on a small sample). I found no professional critic coverage: Metacritic lists the game but has no Metascore and only a couple of user ratings. Note: the task brief says 2023, which is the Early Access date; the full release is 2024.
best_things: Pixel art, character design and animation are widely called masterful and are the most consistent praise, including from players who otherwise bounce off the game
The deckbuilding layer (choosing which weapons can appear in a run) plus a tag-synergy system gives builds real strategic weight, unlike idle-feeling survivor-likes
Weapons are varied, funny and have satisfying sound design (one reviewer singles out the shotgun audio)
Upgrades, both in-run and meta, are described as large and intuitive rather than many tiny percentage bonuses, so there is little 'number soup'
Enemy hordes flowing around obstacles and the general action/effects feel polished and fast
Every level differs and pushes you to adapt your deck, which keeps the campaign feeling fresh and gives achievement and challenge hunting to do
A soundtrack that some reviewers call top-tier, and a low price that many consider good value, especially on sale
Decent playtime for the price: a top-voted review reports nearly 30 hours and full completion
worst_things: Grindy meta-progression: upgrades and new cards are expensive and gated behind very specific unlock conditions (e.g. finish a level with several level-3 weapons of one type)
Difficulty spikes and stat-check levels, with level 10 and the later levels called out repeatedly for chaos, tanky mini-bosses and slowdown
Performance: frame drops and lag in late levels, particularly when many enemies and projectiles are on screen; a Steam discussion complains of freezes at the end of level 10
Builds feel limited: players report being pushed to a single exact deck per level, and many unlockable cards or tags feel cosmetic or weak
Weak-feeling weapons early and long stretches of repeating the same loop; one reviewer says hour 20 has little more than hour 2
Bugs and platform issues: a level-10 crash report, a macOS launch failure thread, mouse/controller input conflicts, and poor Steam Deck input handling
Boss-kill loot spawns on top of the player, which can break the 'No Hands' achievement, and boss rewards are seen as near worthless because the run ends right after
Some find the loop repetitive and unfun compared with Vampire Survivors, calling it 'mid' or boring after a few hours
improvements: Raise the five-deck save limit; players say it forces constant rebuilding and discourages experimentation
Better in-game explanation of mechanics (tags, synergies, why you are dying), since many negative reviews come from players who never discovered these systems
Rebalance difficulty spikes and the tankiness of late-level enemies and mini-bosses so not every hard level requires one specific build
Speed up or flatten the meta-progression and relax narrow unlock conditions so diverse weapons arrive before the campaign ends
Fix late-game performance, boss-loot placement, and controller/mouse/Steam Deck input options (including a setting to replace the hold-to-exit-shop button)
More powerups, loot and variety in level content (some levels feel like empty arenas with nothing to do)
unique_things: Deckbuilding bolted onto a bullet-heaven: you build a deck of weapons pre-run and levelling up opens a shop instead of offering random picks
Tag-synergy passives that reward stacking weapons of the same tag, tied to meta-upgrades that change mechanics (such as contact damage)
Weapons merge in tiers (two tier-1 weapons give a tier-2 weapon, up to A-tier), per a Metacritic user review
Roughly 20 hand-designed levels with distinct enemy waves and bosses instead of one repeating arena, and predetermined waves so skill rather than RNG decides outcomes
Twin-stick aiming with manual shooting, rather than fully auto-attack, plus optional map activities that make you roam
Dark, edgy humour in the Despot's Game universe with a murderous jelly protagonist
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding DNA/XP and resources to unlock upgrades and cards, with players repeating a farm level such as level 10
Hold-button prompts (especially to leave the shop on a gamepad) that are used very often with no option to change
Screens crowded with projectiles and enemies, making evasion hard and triggering lag
Replaying short runs against special levels (e.g. slowing-bullet level) that can instakill you
Rebuilding decks repeatedly due to the limited number of save slots
Shop-centric economy: money comes mainly from shops and drops, so weapons feel weak until you build up
divisive_points: Difficulty: fans call the bottleneck levels good forced experimentation; critics call them unfair stat checks
Deckbuilding: some see it as the game's best feature and the source of strategic depth; others find it constricts variety or simply dislike it, and one left after seeing the deckbuilder tag
Depth vs. repetition: some say every system has a purpose and rewards learning; others see the same loop executed repeatedly with shallow meta-progression
Comparison with Vampire Survivors: some call it their favourite survivor-like, others say the older game does everything better apart from the visuals
community.reception_notes: Launched in Steam Early Access in November 2023 and reached 1.0 on Oct 31, 2024, when it also appeared on consoles (Metacritic lists PS5, PS4, Xbox Series X, Xbox One, Switch and PC, published by tinyBuild). Metacritic currently shows no critic reviews and no user score (2 ratings). No OpenCritic page was found in my checks. Steam reception has stayed Mostly Positive, and recent reviews trend somewhat higher. Community discussion on Steam centres on crashes or freezes on level 10, macOS launch trouble, controller/mouse input conflicts and grinding strategies. No notable controversy found. Limitation: my web-search quota was exhausted, so I could not reach Reddit or press reviews (Reddit fetch was blocked); community findings rely on the Steam review sample and Steam community thread titles.

games.name: SpellRogue
games.short_description: SpellRogue is the ultimate tactical turn-based roguelike! Draft from over 350 powerful spells to assemble the perfect combination and crush your enemies in 70+ unique encounters. Face brutal choices, adapt to impossible odds, and strike back at the horrors that destroyed the world.

placements.verbal_evidence: currently it's going to be a c tier for me

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: SpellRogue is a dice-based deckbuilding roguelike where spells trigger on specific dice rolls. PepperHead likes the art style and finds the randomness less punishing than in most games of its genre. His main problem is that the roguelike layer is thin: only about five or six spell slots, limited upgrades, few passives and events, and almost no change in build from one floor to the next. He finds runs slow and repetitive, and he got bored quickly. He thinks it could improve with more content and places it in C tier.
praise: Appealing art style
Handles dice randomness better than most deckbuilding dice games; low rolls are still usable
Spells keyed to specific roll values let you build a deck that covers low and high rolls
Core mechanics are pretty cool
Has room to grow with future updates
criticism: Very few spell slots and all spells are found quickly
Spells can be upgraded only once and upgrades are often not very impactful
Few passives, events and unique things to find during a run
Slow pacing and repetitive fights; build barely changes by the third floor
No permanent roguelite meta-progression, so every run feels the same
Only about three characters, with starting decks that must be unlocked
Dice randomness still favors high rolls (sixes) and undercuts the strategy side
unique_points: Spells activate on particular dice values, so deck building means covering low and high rolls
Many spells scale with how high the rolled value is
commentary.quote: currently it's going to be a c tier for me
design_criteria: Randomness vs strategy: dice luck in a turn-based strategy game erodes strategic depth
Build variety: few spell slots and quick convergence limit choices
Upgrade depth: single, weak upgrades
Run pacing: slow and repetitive within a run
Meta-progression: lacks permanent unlocks to make runs feel different
Content variety: few events, passives and characters
Visuals: art style is praised

community.one_liner: A turn-based roguelike from Guidelight Games where you roll mana dice each turn and slot them into a loadout of spells (an engine-builder more than a true deck-builder) to fight through corrupted regions and three acts.
community.consensus_summary: SpellRogue is a well-liked but under-the-radar Slay the Spire-style roguelike, sitting at Very Positive on Steam (about 87% of roughly 1,650 reviews). Players who like it praise the dice-plus-spell system for giving more control than a draw pile, the depth of build variety, and the clean art and UI. The main complaints are grindy meta-progression, slow late-game difficulty tiers, balance swings and a feeling that it runs out of surprises. Critics are sparse: Metacritic lists only two reviews (Softpedia 85, Gaming Age 70), so it has no Metascore. It was in early access from February 2024 and left it with a full 1.0 launch on 24 April 2025. Steam review dates suggest players are still posting well into 2026, though Steam forum threads mention a thin player base and some bugs.
best_things: Dice-driven spell casting keeps the variance of a card game but gives players more agency and skill expression; many compare it favourably to Slay the Spire
Huge build variety: 350+ spells with branching dual upgrades, shards/badges, 145+ artifacts, and several viable archetypes per character
Four elemental characters (fire, earth, water, wind) with their own mechanics and multiple starting loadouts
UI and information display are praised as adaptive and clear, and the game plays well on mouse, keyboard and controller
Runs are fairly short and do not overstay their welcome; some reviewers find the pacing of progression and achievements satisfying
Strong art direction (board-game-like tiled maps and figurine characters), good graphics and card/spell design
Long-term replay from daily challenges, the Descent difficulty ladder, mutators and meta-progression unlocks
Good value on sale; a demo with carried-over progress was appreciated
worst_things: Meta-progression and unlocking feel grindy, with some calling the unlock structure bloat rather than meaningful new content
Higher Descent/difficulty tiers are described as a slog, with semi-random modifiers undermining build experimentation
Combat rules are hard to grasp at first, and some players find few synergy paths so building up power over a run is difficult (the most-upvoted negative review)
Balance: some enemies and forced debuffs hard-counter builds, offered spells are often weak, and scaling is hard to come by in some runs
Late-game and some runs feel luck-dependent; a few players say you can tell after two fights whether a run is viable
Repetitive enemy variety and a feeling that you have seen everything the game offers after a while
Combat screens carry a lot of effects and information, which is overwhelming and hard to parse at first
Audio/SFX mixing criticised by some; Steam Deck battery drain and performance mentioned in one review
Some reviewers find it competent but unremarkable (a '5/10') and say it lacks the choice impact of Slay the Spire
improvements: Offer clearer onboarding for the combat rules and more reliable ways to build synergies and scaling
Add more enemy variety and more varied encounter/path design
Allow swapping spells in and out before a fight for more flexibility
Make spell and artifact offers less often useless, and strengthen scaling options such as runes
Reduce reliance on grinding for unlocks and rework difficulty modifiers so they are less punishing
Improve the audio mix and polish remaining UI/icon rough edges and controller dice-selection bugs
unique_things: Not a draw-pile deck: you equip up to 7 spells on the field with extra in reserve, and power them with dice
Mana dice can be rerolled, duplicated, split and enchanted, turning dice manipulation into a build axis
Each spell has branching upgrade paths plus shards and badges, giving layered customisation
Enemies actively disrupt spells and dice (curses, ignite and spreading debuffs), so you are managing your own toolkit as well as the enemy
Board-game presentation with tiled maps and figurine-like characters
Descent difficulty system and mutators for escalating challenge
tedious_or_disliked: Grinding character levels and unlocks, called out by the Gaming Age critic and several Steam reviewers
High-difficulty late game repeated runs described as a horrific slog
Friction of rolling dice and placing them into spell slots every turn wore some players down over many runs
Lots of on-screen effect and information tracking each turn
Runs with weak starting loadouts or useless offers feel like you should just restart
divisive_points: Dice luck versus control: fans say dice manipulation gives consistency, while others say you mostly win when lucky
Difficulty: some find it too easy early yet dragged out, while others call it dull and punishing
Meta-progression: praised as a deep well of content by some, dismissed as padding or a grind by others
Versus Slay the Spire: some say it improves on StS, others say the devs did not grasp what made StS great
community.reception_notes: Launched in early access in February 2024 and reached 1.0 on 24 April 2025 (Windows only; $19.99 on Steam; publisher Ghost Ship Publishing). Metacritic has 2 critic reviews and 3 user ratings, below its threshold for a displayed score; OpenCritic search did not surface a listing. The Steam store page quotes TechRadar praising the dice-and-deckbuilding mix, though I could not open that review. SteamSpy-style estimates put owners at 50k-100k and steam-revenue-calculator.com estimates about $496k gross and $146k net (Boxleiter-method estimates, not audited). Steam forum threads mention bugs (controller dice selection, dodge, a mutator combo) and worries about a small player base, while recent positive reviews show continued play and appreciation. I could not retrieve patch notes or Reddit discussion (Reddit blocked, WebSearch budget exhausted), so post-launch update history is not verified here.

games.name: Star of Providence
games.short_description: Star of Providence is a top down action shooter with procedurally generated elements. Explore a large, abandoned facility in search of incredible power, fighting dangerous foes and gaining new weapons and upgrades as you progress.

placements.verbal_evidence: none

commentary.label: Tier list Part 2 (2024)
commentary.summary: Star of Providence is a fast-paced top-down bullet-hell shooter where you pilot a small spaceship room to room killing enemies. PepperHead was excited going in but came away disappointed, mainly by the gameplay itself. The tiny screen and high speed make it feel like trial and error, especially on later bosses, and he found it unfair and punishing from the start. He still appreciates its content, secrets and charming pixel art, and may keep playing. No tier letter is stated in this segment.
praise: Lots of content, hidden stuff and secrets to discover
Variety of different worlds and bosses
Charming SNES-style pixel art that looks great
Strong intrigue that makes him want to keep playing
criticism: Screen is very small and gameplay very fast, so you must memorize enemy move sets or take damage
Bosses feel like trial and error with almost no reaction window, which feels unfair
Dash does not give invincibility; rolling into a bullet still hurts, odd for such a fast game
Teleport instead of dash is an upgrade rather than core mechanic
Health is very hard to regain, so every hit feels permanent and punishing
Not enjoyable enough from the start; too punishing early
unique_points: Finding health only raises max health, so damage is effectively permanent loss
Dash replaceable by a teleport upgrade, which he thinks should be baseline
commentary.quote: it is important for games to be enjoyable from the start
design_criteria: Fairness: trial-and-error boss learning with little reaction time counts against it
Difficulty/punishment: too punishing early on
Core mechanics: dash without i-frames feels wrong for the pace
Health economy: scarce healing makes damage feel terrible
Content and secrets: large amount of hidden stuff is a plus
Charm/visuals: pixel art praised
Onboarding: game should be enjoyable from the start

community.one_liner: A top-down twin-stick bullet-hell shooter with roguelite runs through a procedurally generated abandoned facility, by Team D-13 (originally released in 2017 as Monolith, now published with Bigmode).
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate it Overwhelmingly Positive (about 97% of ~3,375 reviews), and the recent reviews I read are almost uniformly glowing, with many describing it as a sleeper that got a second life after videogamedunkey's Bigmode picked it up. Critics were positive but few: Metacritic lists 6 reviews (Metascore 84) mostly from 2017 plus one 2025 review, and the Metacritic user score is 8.5 from only 37 ratings. The praise centres on tight game feel, huge boss and enemy variety, and deep post-game challenge layers; the complaints centre on steep skill-check difficulty and on weak or unexciting roguelite upgrades and meta-progression. It is not early access; it has been substantially expanded since launch, and the large Relics of the Past expansion is now included free on Steam.
best_things: Extremely responsive, polished controls and game feel; many reviewers call it one of the most satisfying shooters they have played
Huge amount of content for a tiny install size, with many bosses and lots of enemy variety and new attack patterns still appearing deep into endgame runs
Skill-based progression: players improve by learning patterns rather than by finding broken builds, which they find more rewarding
Layers of optional post-game challenge (difficulty levels, looping, trials, secret superbosses and multiple 'final' bosses) give very long replayability; several reviewers logged 100-270 hours
Soundtrack (chiptune) and pixel art praised as charming and well made
Unlockable ships such as the sword ship change how a run plays and are described as making it feel like a different game
Helpful accessibility options, such as a hitbox marker setting, and hitboxes some players find forgiving
Weapon variety (13+ weapon types with 50+ modifiers per the store page) and an exploration-and-secrets feel reminiscent of older shooters
The large Relics of the Past expansion is now bundled free, and reviewers say it is what makes the game shine, with secrets and discovery driving them to keep pushing
worst_things: Roguelite upgrades and perks are seen as bland: mostly small percentage boosts to damage or reload that do not change playstyle
Meta-progression between runs feels thin or slow to some players
Weapons have very limited ammo and swap often, so players rarely get to enjoy the interesting guns
Dash gives no invincibility frames, which some find a poor design choice in a dodge-heavy game
Many mechanics are unintuitive and must be learned by dying repeatedly
Difficulty ramps very hard for some players, especially trials and boss gauntlets with low damage output, and base difficulty feels too high to them
Technical nitpicks in recent reviews: a blue-tinted black shader that prevents true OLED blacks, and fullscreen stutter reported by one player
improvements: Make perks and drops more impactful so runs can feel powerful or distinctive rather than just incrementally stronger
Add ways to extend weapon life, such as ammo min-maxing or reroll options, to reduce forced weapon swapping
Speed up or deepen meta-progression and unlocks, which some find slow
Better onboarding and explanation of mechanics so players do not have to learn everything by dying
Add a setting to disable the black-level shader for OLED displays
Community requests on Steam include arcade stick controls, better game-over screen detail, aspect-ratio options and workshop or modding support
unique_things: Hybrid of shmup/bullet hell and twin-stick dungeon crawler with roguelite runs, often compared to Enter the Gungeon but with much more shmup-style dodging and skill expression
Lots of hidden depth: secret bosses, multiple final bosses, looping difficulty and trials buried under the main game
Exploration element compared by one reviewer to Guardian Legend, plus a surprisingly involved narrative and lore
Ships and characters that substantially change playstyle (for example the sword ship)
Small file size but very dense content; publisher Bigmode is co-founded by videogamedunkey, who helped bring it new attention
tedious_or_disliked: Dying repeatedly to learn unexplained mechanics, which some find frustrating rather than fun
Forced weapon swapping with scarce ammo
Losing uncollected drops if you accidentally leave a room while dodging leftover bullets
Slow upgrade pace and unlock grind that leaves some players feeling their time is wasted after a single hit ends a run
Boss-heavy sections that feel punishing rather than exciting for some players
divisive_points: Difficulty: fans call it the hardest yet most rewarding roguelike, while others say it is too brutal or too easy depending on skill and mode
Art style and direction: praised by most, called subjectively bad by at least one negative reviewer
Roguelite depth: some love that skill beats build luck, others find the upgrades shallow and the roguelite layer a perfunctory afterthought
Comparisons to Isaac or Gungeon: one positive reviewer warns it should not be played like those games, while a negative reviewer says it shares Gungeon's flaws
community.reception_notes: Launched on Steam in June 2017 as Monolith to positive but modest attention; Steam revenue estimates (Boxleiter-style, unaudited) put gross at roughly $1.19M and owners at 50k-100k, though the owner figure likely undercounts recent growth. It was renamed Star of Providence for console releases (to avoid confusion with Monolith Productions) and published with Bigmode, the label co-founded by videogamedunkey; several Steam reviewers say they found it through Dunkey. Wikipedia's sources give somewhat inconsistent dates for console launches (PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch, between 2024 and February 2025), so treat exact dates as unverified. The large Relics of the Past expansion (two extra floors, 2,000+ room layouts, looping difficulty, rare weapons, blessings and hacking) is now free on Steam, and recent reviews are near 100% positive. Steam store is Windows and Linux only; no Mac. OpenCritic score could not be retrieved: the web search budget was exhausted and the guessed OpenCritic URL pointed to a different game, so null is reported rather than guessed.

games.name: Go Mecha Ball
games.short_description: Load up and roll out, in this twin stick shooter with roguelike progression! Blast your way through arcade-style levels, using pinball-style physics mixed with an arsenal of devastating weapons. Defeat waves of enemy bots, battle big bosses, and upgrade your mech between runs.

other_scores.source: Steam user reviews (Very Positive, about 86% of 461)

placements.verbal_evidence: to me, Go Mecca Ball is going to be a Ctier. ... for me, Go make a ball as a Ctier.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Go Mecha Ball is a fast-paced action shooter roguelike where you shoot and can curl into a ball to dash and roll around large arenas. He found the core movement and VFX fun but was disappointed, feeling the roguelike layer is thin and many small issues accumulated. Runs are a standard structure of clearing waves, a shop, and bosses across two worlds. He finds it punishing and under-rewarding, and he hit serious frame drops. He places it in C tier, saying that means not a game for him rather than a bad game.
praise: Core gameplay of dashing and rolling into enemies feels good and enjoyable once comfortable
Visuals and VFX are really solid
Enemy and boss designs are great
Launch pads and boosts hint at cool movement options
Some players will connect with the crazy gameplay much more than he did
criticism: Little roguelike depth: guns have no upgrades or variance, character and grenades stay the same every run
Upgrade choices after levels are generic (more damage, more health) and don't change play; new abilities can be useless with a two-ability cap
Bosses give no reward beyond a bit of health; not enough rewards throughout runs
Very hard and punishing with no healing outside the shop; some enemies, like a homing dashing ball, are hard to evade
Movement focus is underused since fights happen in single rooms with little exploration
Severe frame drops by the third world, down to 4-5 fps
Flying up feels awkward since you can't descend quickly
unique_points: Transforming into a ball to dash and roll between areas is the core gimmick
The slam-down area attack ability should have been a core mechanic to make vertical movement feel complete
Design lesson: a strong movement hook needs level design and roguelike variety that make use of it
commentary.quote: Once again, Ctiers are not bad games. They just are not games for me.
design_criteria: Core movement/feel: dashing and rolling is fun but underused
Visuals/VFX: strong and chaotic
Roguelike mechanics: too little variety in guns, upgrades, character
Upgrade quality: generic stat bumps that don't change play
Rewards: bosses and runs give too little
Difficulty: punishing, no healing, unkind to new players
Enemy/boss design: great but some hard to evade
Level design: rooms too confined to exploit movement
Performance: frame drops hurt the experience
Meta-progression: only permanent additions, nothing interesting

community.one_liner: A neon arcade twin-stick shooter roguelite by Whale Peak Games (published by Super Rare Originals) where you switch between a shooting mech and a fast rolling pinball-style ball to smash, bounce and blast enemy bots.
community.consensus_summary: Players like it: Steam sits at Very Positive (about 86% of roughly 460 reviews) and critics landed at a Metacritic 70 from 10 reviews (range 60-85), so the split is 'superb feel, thin roguelike'. Nearly everyone praises the movement, physics-driven collision combat, bosses and presentation, while the recurring complaint is that levels and enemy spawns are fixed, so runs feel samey and content runs out fast (4 zones, 4 bosses, 4 mechs). Metacritic users are noticeably cooler (6.6 from 25 ratings). Launched January 2024 as a full release (not early access); several Steam reviewers say the developers have stopped updating it, leaving bugs such as a pause-menu lock, broken key rebinding and a memory-leak lag unfixed. It is a small commercial success rather than a hit (Steam revenue estimates around $140k gross).
best_things: Movement and game feel: rolling, bouncing, boosting and transforming mid-air feels weighty, snappy and 'juicy' rather than floaty, and is the most-praised element across Steam and critics
Collision combat: building speed to deal contact damage (which also drops ammo) and launching enemies into each other or off the map is widely called satisfying
Fusion of genres: pinball physics plus twin-stick shooting plus roguelike progression is described by critics as a combination nothing else quite matches
Bosses: multiple reviewers (Game Rant, Inverse, Steam players) single out the boss fights as exhilarating pattern-learning set pieces
Presentation: bright neon art style, fluid animations and a dynamic, interactive soundtrack draw frequent compliments
Level furniture (bounce pads, boost pads, fans, tubes) feeds into mobility and gives arenas pinball-table character
Easy to pick up and play: Steam reviewers note the simple core loop and good controller and handheld PC play; runs are short arcade-style sessions
Solid enemy variety in the moment-to-moment sense that forces use of ball dodging, abilities and weapons together
worst_things: Levels, enemy spawns and boss order are the same every run, so as a 'roguelike' it lacks the randomness the genre is known for (the most repeated Steam negative and echoed by Inverse, GameCritics and Game Rant)
Thin content: only 4 zones, 4 bosses and 4 mechs; unlock lists are long on paper (25+ weapons, 20+ abilities, 50+ upgrades) but many weapons and upgrades feel incremental or same-y
Higher difficulties mostly add enemy health/armor rather than new enemy types or layout changes, so progression feels static
Stability and bugs reported on Steam: pause menu that cannot be closed mid-run, key rebinding not working, and lag attributed to a memory leak after 30-60 minutes
Seemingly abandoned: players report the developers said no further work would be done, so known bugs persist
Some players find the visuals and audio fatiguing, with reports of eye strain and watering eyes and an 'overstimulating' soundtrack over long sessions
Steam reviewers also cite little meta-progression beyond unlocks, limited power-up choice (perfect builds feel rare) and burnout after a few hours
improvements: Add procedural or shuffled level layouts and enemy spawns (a 'true randomizer') so runs differ
Clearer upgrade descriptions showing actual stat changes, since players often cannot tell how an option will improve a build
Higher difficulty tiers that change enemies, bosses and layouts, not just health and armor
More content: additional zones, bosses, characters and more build-altering weapons and upgrades rather than small stat tweaks
Deeper meta-progression than the gacha-style unlock system that critics say feels disconnected from progress
Fix pause menu, rebinding and memory-leak issues, and add accessibility options (GameCritics noted no colorblind mode; some players want a clearer crosshair and less screen strain)
unique_things: Instant transformation between an on-foot twin-stick mech and a rolling ball, where ball speed is itself an offensive weapon and ammo source
Pinball-style arenas with ramps, bumpers, fans and boost pads that turn level geometry into a movement and damage tool
Arcade structure of three themed levels then a boss, repeated across four worlds, with short runs
Dynamic, interactive soundtrack and a saturated neon aesthetic; one Steam reviewer likens the hectic pace to an easier ULTRAKILL
Hub that functions as a small playground with permanent upgrades and unlocks in a gacha-like system
tedious_or_disliked: Repeating identical level layouts and spawn patterns every run, which some call a slog after 2-3 hours
Unlock-only meta progression: once you finish unlocking everything there is little to do
Repetitive tutorial prompts (noted by Checkpoint Gaming per Metacritic's summary)
Chaotic, visually busy screens where it can be hard to read what is happening or track the crosshair, which put some players off entirely
Difficulty jumps between normal and harder tiers that mainly inflate enemy health
Slog after the first 2-3 hours once the main activity is just unlocking everything (Steam reviewer, with complaints the base price, about 19.49 EUR, is too high for the content)
divisive_points: Whether it counts as a true roguelike: fans accept it as an arcade run-based game, others feel misled by fixed levels
Price vs content: Steam lists $7.99 (may be a sale price; one reviewer cites a 19.49 EUR base price), and some call that overpriced for the content while others call the core loop worth it
Sensory intensity: praised as thrilling by some and exhausting or eye-straining by others
Metacritic users (6.6) vs Steam users (86% positive) disagree noticeably on overall quality
community.reception_notes: Released on PC (Steam, Windows only per Steam) on January 25, 2024, with console versions via Super Rare Originals; critic reviews clustered around launch (Jan-Apr 2024) and were mostly positive-to-mixed (60-85). Steam users rate it better than Metacritic users do. A Steam reviewer claims the game was overshadowed by Palworld's launch in the same period and that the small team moved on after a few updates; this is one player's account and was not confirmed from a primary source. Multiple recent Steam reviews (2025-2026) repeat that it feels abandoned with unfixed bugs. Steam concurrent players are near zero, and third-party estimates put it at roughly 50k-100k owners and about $140k gross revenue (Boxleiter-based estimate, not audited). OpenCritic page was not found. Search budget ran out during research, so Reddit and Steam community thread contents could not be read. Metacritic also lists console scores: Xbox Series X 81 (9 reviews), PS5 72 (4 reviews).

games.name: Moon Watch
games.short_description: Bullet heaven, deckbuilding, and strategy – Moon Watch is a wild new mix from the creators of Backpack Hero! Master your tactics, not reflexes: stop time at will, craft a killer deck, stop the horde in their tracks!

other_scores.score: Mixed, 49 positive / 28 negative of 77 (63.6% per local data; store page showed 57% of 56 at fetch time)

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put this as a high C

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Moonwatch is an early-access deckbuilding, turn-based real-time action roguelike from the Backpack Hero developers, where time only moves when you move, in a Superhot-like fashion. You play abilities from a hand built over the run, spending mana that regenerates faster the less you move. He loves the core concept and the space zombies-and-vampires vibe, but finds it unbalanced, thin on content and with unsatisfying bosses. He places it in high C, with real potential to climb to B or even A as it gets tweaked and expanded.
praise: Very unique concept: a Superhot-style time-stop mechanic fused with deckbuilding
Mana regenerating faster when you stand still creates a cool gameplay loop of move, cast, wait
Characters have different starting decks and feel drastically different from each other
Runs feel unique between characters and builds
Funny overall vibe of fighting zombies and vampires in space
Developers (Backpack Hero) have a track record of unique concepts, and he is excited about where it goes
criticism: Currently unbalanced and finicky, feels early even for early access, with exploitable mechanics and underwhelming ones
Each character has only about three builds that do not fuse well, so runs feel similar once tried
Few abilities and items, so duplicates show up often and chaos or breakage results
Polarizing boss items can make you overpowered or instantly dead after a bad start
No good way to discard or reshuffle a bad hand
Most bosses cannot be fought directly (for example activating towers) and none has a DPS check, a wasted opportunity
Visuals feel minimalistic and he is not a fan
unique_points: Time only advances when you move, yet you can trigger hand abilities while time is stopped
Mana regeneration tied to standing still forces a tension between positioning and casting
Boss items act like cursed items, e.g. no mana gain from moving but mana from kills, making it all-or-nothing
commentary.quote: I'm going to put this as a high C
design_criteria: Concept uniqueness: rewards a novel time-stop deckbuilding hook
Balance: currently exploitable, with some mechanics overpowered and others weak
Build diversity: only about three builds per character, limited cross-fusing
Content depth: too few abilities and items, leading to duplicates
Boss design: bosses lack DPS checks and feel unsatisfying
Risk vs reward: polarizing boss items swing between dominant and dead
Visuals/charm: minimalistic visuals but funny space-horror vibe
Character variety: distinct starting decks make each character feel different
commentary.rerank_note: Early access evaluation; he says it could move to B or potentially A as content and tweaks arrive.

community.one_liner: A time-stop bullet-heaven/horde-survival roguelite with deckbuilding from Jaspel (Backpack Hero team), published by Pretty Soon, set on the moon in an alternate 19XX against vampires and cybernetic undead.
community.consensus_summary: Moon Watch has Mixed Steam reviews (about 49 positive vs 28 negative, roughly 57-64% depending on snapshot) and no critic coverage on Metacritic or OpenCritic. Players who engage with it like the Superhot-meets-Vampire-Survivors hook and card synergies, and the itch.io page rates it highly (about 4.7/5 from 112 ratings). The dominant complaint by far is that the Early Access project looks abandoned: the store page promised 8-10 months of EA at the Dec 4, 2024 launch, but there has been no substantive update since then and no developer communication, and recent reviews are overwhelmingly negative on that basis. Content is thin (3 characters, 80 cards, 43 relics), so even fans say it is short. Net: a promising concept that is stalled, hard to recommend at $9.99 beyond a few hours of play.
best_things: Core hook of pausing/stopping time inside a bullet-heaven format, described by players as Superhot plus Vampire Survivors in one
Fun card and relic synergies that reward combo-building
Runs are replayable in short bursts; some players keep looping back for a run or two
Multiple modes (Classic, Horde, Wave, Challenge Runs, Infinite Loop/Endless) and progressive unlocks of cards, relics and starting decks
Nice, fun little game with a few good synergies despite short length (recurring sentiment in positive reviews)
worst_things: Perceived abandonment: no meaningful updates since Dec 2024 and zero communication from Jaspel or Pretty Soon, which drives the most-upvoted negative reviews (33, 22, 15, 11 upvotes)
Early Access timeline of 8-10 months was blown far past; roadmap items like the tech-tree meta-progression have not appeared
Thin content for $9.99: 3 characters, 3 acts, 80 cards, 43 relics, 23 enemies and mini-bosses; one reviewer valued it at about $5
Gameplay described by some as basic and repetitive
Bugs: starter decks reportedly not working properly, unlock progress not persisting for some, card selection bugs, crashes with certain card combinations
No Steam Cloud saves and Steam Deck achievement tracking problems
improvements: Communicate a roadmap or at least confirm whether development continues
Add the promised content: more cards, characters, stages, enemies and the tech-tree meta-progression
Fix the unlock/save persistence, starter deck and card selection bugs; add Steam Cloud
Add windowed resolution options and more control customization (requested in Steam discussions)
Rework build strategy depth: weapons and items are both temporary, pushing players toward just spamming as much as possible
Better balance between movement and build power so dodging matters across the whole run, not only late
unique_things: Time-stop as the central weapon: stopping time lets you plan and set up combos in a horde-survival game
Hybrid of three genres: bullet heaven, deckbuilder and tactics, which players say is doing something new
From the creators of Backpack Hero, bringing a deckbuilder-flavored design sensibility to the survivors-like space
Setting and tone: a moon in an alternate 19XX fighting vampires and cybernetically enhanced undead
Modes including Wave, Horde, Challenge and Infinite Loop rather than a single run structure
tedious_or_disliked: Dominant strategy is to spew out as much as possible to offset everything being temporary, described as boring and time-consuming
Movement can feel superfluous: when the build is strong you can stand still, when weak no dodging saves you, and few things need dodging until late
Repetitiveness and short length drain replay value after a few runs
Lack of meaningful new content means players hit the same ceiling quickly
Unlock progression and bugs that interrupt runs
divisive_points: Whether the concept and itch.io-demo-level quality justify buying now: itch.io players rate it 4.7/5 while Steam reviews are Mixed
Whether the time-stop plus deckbuilding mix is a fresh hybrid or two genres that clash (one reviewer says Loop Hero does the deck/auto-battler blend better)
Whether the game is truly dead or just quiet: some supportive posts say keep going, devs, while many call it abandoned
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched on Steam Dec 4, 2024 at $9.99 with an 8-10 month EA estimate; the itch.io version had earlier builds (Act II in Sep 2024, Endless Mode demo update Oct 2024) and was well-liked there. Steam reviews turned sharply negative from about Sept 2025 onward as players noticed the absence of updates and communication (a Steam thread titled around 'STILL NOTHING' dated 7 Nov 2025). Top negative reviews had dozens of upvotes for calling it abandoned; a few players still recommend it for the few hours of fun it offers. Metacritic has a page but no scores; no OpenCritic entry found. Revenue data is unreliable: the steam-revenue-calculator estimate shows $0 and the owner estimate is under 20,000, so sales were likely small. Caveat: the WebSearch budget was exhausted during this research, so the picture rests on Steam store/community pages, the itch.io page, the local Steam reviews file and Metacritic; Reddit and outlet reviews could not be fetched.

games.name: Wizard of Legend 2
games.short_description: Face perilous magical trials in the fast-paced rogue-lite follow-up to the acclaimed original, featuring co-op and vibrant new 3D visuals. Master new Arcana and elements, experiment with spell combinations, and become the next Wizard of Legend!

other_scores.score: Mixed, about 52-53% positive (1,340 positive / 1,238 negative in the dataset; Steam store page showed 53% from 1,972)
Mostly Negative, 36% positive from 11 recent reviews at time of page fetch
about $1.08M gross, about $318K net developer revenue (Boxleiter-style estimate, order of magnitude only)

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put it as currently a low C.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Wizard of Legend 2 is an early-access fast-paced hack-and-slash action roguelike where you play a wizard with a variety of elemental spells. It is a sequel, made by a different team, to a game he rated very highly. He is disappointed, feeling the new team missed what made the original special and leaned toward a Hades-like formula instead. Visuals, VFX and moment-to-moment gameplay are fine, but structure, pacing, tone, balance, clarity and meta-progression disappoint him. He places it at a low C for now, hoping updates improve it, though he doubts it will match the first game.
praise: Visuals look pretty good to him, despite fan complaints about departing from the original style
VFX are good
Core gameplay feel is pretty good
Developers patched many of the specific issues from his earlier rant
The original Wizard of Legend is a fantastic hack-and-slash game he may rate even higher now
criticism: Elemental masters are reduced to mini bosses; the same biome every run with a random boss at the end, losing the original's randomized-biome hook
Pacing is much slower and enemies feel weaker/less interesting than the original's fast play
Voice-acted, overly serious characters constantly talk, making the game hard to take seriously
Unbalanced, inconsistent, unclear information, and buggy roguelike elements
Meta progression is not very interesting
Elementalist fights are less fun and interesting than the original's
unique_points: The original's twist: each biome was randomized based on the elemental master fought at the end, making elemental masters the core point of the game
Design lesson: a sequel that chases a more mainstream formula can lose the specific identity and speed that made the original special
commentary.quote: it feels like they missed the point of what made Wizard of Legend one a good game
design_criteria: Identity/core hook: whether the sequel keeps the original's defining randomized-biome elemental structure
Pacing: fast and snappy versus slow and mainstream
Enemy design: enemies feel weaker than the original
Boss design: elemental master fights less fun and interesting
Meta-progression: not very interesting
Clarity and balance: unclear information, unbalanced, inconsistent behavior, bugs
Tone/narrative: heavy voice acting and serious tone undermine the charm
Visuals/VFX: good and acceptable despite differing from the original
Run variety: same biome every run reduces variety
commentary.rerank_note: Early-access re-evaluation: he rated the first game very highly previously and made a separate rant video on the sequel; current low C is provisional, pending updates.

community.one_liner: A 3D, up-to-4-player co-op action roguelite sequel to Wizard of Legend, built by a different studio (Dead Mage) in Unreal, where you mix elemental Arcana spells across runs through the Floating Lands.
community.consensus_summary: Mixed on Steam (about 52-53% positive across roughly 2,000-2,600 reviews; recent reviews lean Mostly Negative). The moment-to-moment combat, spell variety and 4-player co-op are the consistent bright spots, but original-game fans see a stripped-down, less polished successor with far fewer spells and relics, plus buggy online co-op. Critic coverage is thin: Metacritic has only 3 PC reviews (scores 100, 80, 60) and no Metascore yet, and user score there is 5.2/10 from 15 ratings. It left Early Access (launched Oct 2024) and hit 1.0 on June 12, 2025, but many players say updates stopped around July 2025 and call the game abandoned, which heavily colours recent sentiment. The steady refrain is that it is fun with friends on a discount, while solo players are pointed back to the original.
best_things: Fast, responsive combat and character control; several reviewers say it feels smooth and natural, with i-frame dashing
Large mix-and-match Arcana system across six elements (fire, water, earth, lightning, air, chaos) that supports experimental builds
4-player online co-op plus local split screen; friends describe it as chaotic fun and the best way to play it
Good-looking stylised 3D visuals, enemy variety and biomes that do not overstay their welcome
Bosses are fun and have combo-style attack sets that become manageable once learned
worst_things: Content cut versus the original: one detailed reviewer cites about 71 spells vs about 204 and about 145 relics vs about 315, with only 10 relic slots; many others note fewer Arcana and relics generally
Online co-op bugs and netcode: desyncs, softlocks, crashes that scale with player count, and no ability to reconnect to a run
Campaign is short (reports of about 4-9 hours to beat, one claiming a very fast clear) and only a handful of biomes, so replay feels repetitive
Dialogue and voice acting criticised as excessive, badly directed and miscast, with the player character lacking personality
Boss and enemy telegraphs often judged too short or unclear (few audio cues), plus knockback and fall damage frustrations
Feels soulless and less snappy than the original: several top reviews (including a 1000-hour original player) call it sluggish, derivative of Hades, and stripped of the 2D style's charm
Balance problems: lightning and some builds are far stronger than others, while many upgraded Arcana or trinkets feel weak or useless
$24.99 price judged too high for the content and stability by many
Abandoned after 1.0: the most-upvoted recent negative reviews say updates and developer communication stopped, leaving bugs and missing content unresolved
improvements: Restore cut content: more Arcana, relics, cloaks and possibly more relic slots, plus a gems-to-gold style conversion some miss from the original
Fix multiplayer netcode, add reconnect/rejoin and pause options, and resolve softlocks and crashes
Add more biomes, enemy variety and run variety to lengthen the campaign and reduce repetition
Better tutorials and in-game explanations of spells and mechanics (flagged by reviewers as unclear)
Co-op quality-of-life: option to reduce ally skill transparency/clutter, shared loot from events, and a possible return of a PVP mode
Clearer telegraphs and audio cues for attacks, and ability to bank the ultimate; fewer forced dialogue interruptions
Communicate a roadmap and ship the promised updates, since silence from the developer is itself a top complaint
unique_things: Full 3D take on the Wizard of Legend formula with 4-player online co-op (the original was 2-player)
Arcana system where each spell has variants/enhancements and elemental mixing drives build identity
Dash gives invincibility and enemy contact does not hurt you, changing the feel from the original's harsher rules
Hub with a large cast of talkative NPCs and a Hades-like story framing around the Floating Lands
Spell-combo focus combined with local split-screen and Remote Play Together options, uncommon among action roguelites
tedious_or_disliked: Unlock grind: basic starting equipment and badges are locked behind repeated runs, which some find annoying compared with the first game
Progression feels unrewarding and weakly meaningful; starting strength barely grows between runs
Runs repeat the same enemy order and biome sequence, so variety fades quickly
Constant NPC chatter and lengthy, poorly voiced dialogue during hub and runs
Multiplayer clutter making it hard to read attacks, plus one-person-only event rewards that force loot negotiation
divisive_points: Difficulty: some say it is easier than the original (easy to clear, dash immunity), others find bosses overtuned and punishing
Whether it should be judged as a standalone game or as a sequel; newcomers often rate it fairly while original fans call it a step backward
Solo vs co-op value: solo is called fine by some and not recommended by others, while co-op is the usual recommendation
Art direction: seen by some as attractive and cartoonish, by others as generic and murky versus the original's clean 2D look
community.reception_notes: Early Access began October 3, 2024 and 1.0 shipped June 12, 2025 at $24.99 on PC (Steam; Metacritic also lists Xbox Series X, PS5 and Switch, confirmed by Metacritic's platform listing; the Steam page shows Windows only). Developer is Dead Mage, a different team from the original's Contingent99; publisher is listed as Balor Games. Launch reception was poor-to-mixed, driven by missing content, bugs and comparisons to the original. Players report the last meaningful update was around July 2025 and several reviews from late 2025 through 2026 call it abandoned, with one reviewer claiming the publisher's restructuring gutted the team (unverified, from a user review). Recent Steam reviews are negative mostly about abandonment and unresolved bugs, while a minority still recommend it cheaply for co-op. The Steam store page shows Windows only. Note: web search quota was exhausted during this research, so no Reddit threads or major-outlet articles beyond the three Metacritic-listed reviews were read; OpenCritic data could not be located.

games.name: Bad North: Jotunn Edition
games.short_description: Bad North is a charming but brutal real-time tactics roguelite. Defend your idyllic island kingdom against a horde of Viking invaders, as you lead the desperate exodus of your people. Command your loyal subjects to take full tactical advantage of the unique shape of each island.

placements.verbal_evidence: Even though I am going to put this as a C tier, the game is unique.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 4 (2025)
commentary.summary: Bad North is a real-time tactical roguelike where you command small armies to defend islands from Viking raids. He is drawn in by its cute visuals and vibe, and finds it visually and mechanically unique. However, he feels the core strategy is shallow and repetitive, and that it would have worked better as a non-roguelike. The roguelike layer is minimal, runs are long, and it is slow to get interesting. He still recommends it to fans of simple tactical games, but places it in C tier.
praise: Cute, slightly disturbing visuals and strong overall vibe
Sound design is incredible, including the little splash of enemies dropping into the water
Real-time tactical roguelikes are rare, so it feels unique
Permadeath of units makes close fights very tense
Appealing for players who like simpler tactical games
criticism: Core gameplay and strategy are shallow and repetitive (archers beat shields, lancers beat archers)
Roguelike elements are too small: random islands and items barely change strategy
Very little pre-run customization and the first islands are always the same
Takes too long for things to get interesting, and runs are very long
Unit level-ups are identical every run, so a fixed mission structure would have suited it better
Losing a favorite army permanently 40 minutes in feels bad
unique_points: Rare real-time tactical/RTS-style take on the roguelike genre
Permadeath of army units adds tension, a double-edged pro and con given the long runs
Each island is a self-contained small level with house-protection objectives that feed currency and upgrades
commentary.quote: Even though I am going to put this as a C tier, the game is unique.
design_criteria: Visuals/charm: cute and atmospheric, a major draw
Audio/sound design: praised as incredible
Uniqueness of mechanics: real-time tactics twist is valued
Strategic depth: too shallow and repetitive
Roguelike elements/replayability: minimal variation between runs
Pre-run customization: too little
Run length: too long, slow to become interesting
Permadeath/stakes: creates tension but can feel punishing after long runs
Progression: fixed unit level-ups undermine roguelike variety

community.one_liner: A minimalist real-time tactics roguelite by Plausible Concept (published by Raw Fury) where you command up to four squads to defend procedurally generated diorama islands from Viking raiders, with permadeath for your commanders.
community.consensus_summary: Bad North is widely liked by players (Steam 'Very Positive', about 93% of roughly 14.4k reviews) mainly for its striking minimalist art, readable terrain-based tactics and quick, low-stress sessions. Professional critics were more lukewarm: Metacritic sits at 72 (Switch page; PC 74, Xbox 65) and OpenCritic at 71 with only 46% of critics recommending, spanning Nintendo Life 9/10 down to Destructoid 5.5/10 and TheSixthAxis 5/10. The recurring verdict from both camps is 'brilliant core, thin content': it is short (roughly 4 to 12 hours), has few unit classes and enemy types, and little reason to replay. The free Jotunn Edition update (July 2019) added commanders, traits, items and skills and improved replayability, but the game is essentially finished and has had no major content since; newer Steam reviews still ask for more classes, a harder difficulty and a level creator.
best_things: Minimalist low-poly diorama art and sound: islands stained with blood as battles go on, small details like shields turning toward incoming arrows
Broad-stroke control scheme: you position squads, not individual soldiers, so it is easy to learn in minutes yet still tactical
Terrain matters: cliffs, ramps, chokepoints and beaches on each procedural island shape where you defend
Rock-paper-scissors between infantry (shield), pikes (anti-brute) and archers, with special skills, produce tense and satisfying last-second saves
Slow-motion / pause-friendly flow feels more relaxed than typical RTS games
Short, jump-in-jump-out sessions; a campaign does not overstay its welcome and suits Steam Deck / Game Pass play
Emotional attachment to named commanders whose permadeath carries weight
Jotunn Edition's extra commanders, traits and items added welcome variety for free
worst_things: Very little content: only three troop classes with a single skill each and a limited enemy roster; many players say they saw everything in a few hours
Low replay value for a roguelite; one campaign clears most of the content and there is no other game mode
Late-game giant archers / ballista-like units are a common complaint because they out-range and crush most units with no clear counter
Difficulty curve is lopsided: the early campaign is trivially easy and the late game spikes sharply
Perceived randomness (enemy landing spots, item and commander luck) can make late losses feel unfair
Minimal unit control leaves you unable to fix AI behaviour, such as odd target choices and chasing fleeing enemies; hard to notice squads dying
Full price ($14.99) is often judged too high for the length; widely recommended on sale or via Game Pass
Shallow upgrade and preparation options: several reviewers say there are too few meaningful ways to spend coins, so it feels like a 'mini game' for the price
improvements: More unit classes, skills per class and enemy types, especially on higher difficulties
A difficulty beyond Very Hard and/or a hold-out / endless style mode
Larger unit caps (players suggest 6-8 squads instead of 4) and bigger maps
More meaningful upgrade and preparation options so coins buy real choices
A counter or rebalance for the late-game heavy archer, plus more island variety
A level creator / mod-style tooling and DLC-style content expansions
unique_things: A real-time tactics game stripped to its bones: four squads, no base building, no resource micromanagement
Procedurally generated tile-like islands where geography is the main tactical resource
Permadeath campaign of commanders across an archipelago with a pursuing fleet, a roguelite structure applied to RTS
Houses you can lose or save: coins come from protecting villages, tying score and economy to defense
Serene, meditative tone contrasted with brutal, blood-stained outcomes
tedious_or_disliked: The first quarter of a run is easy and slow, with little challenge and upgrades only after several coins are earned; restarting after a loss means replaying that stretch
Repetition sets in after a few hours because of limited enemies and units
Abilities must be placed the instant enemies land, which some find restrictive rather than strategic
Feels 'like a mobile game' to several reviewers (it has iOS/Android ports), with lots of unused screen space and vague mechanics
Losing to late-game archers after a long run, where skill cannot fully compensate
divisive_points: Simplicity: praised as accessible and elegant by some, called shallow and 'mini game'-like by others; one critic said it streamlines strategy into something that does not wholly satisfy either casual or veteran fans
Randomness versus skill: some feel mastery is rewarded, others feel RNG decides late runs
Length and value: a tight 5-10 hour campaign is a virtue to some, a dealbreaker at $14.99 to others
Jotunn Edition balance: some felt buffed archers made pikemen less needed and skewed balance
community.reception_notes: Launched August 2018 on Switch, PS4, Xbox One and PC (Xbox Game Pass at launch; Steam store lists release as Nov 16, 2018), with iOS and Android ports about a year later. Launch critic reception was mixed (Metacritic 65-74 by platform; scores ranged widely), and the launch build was called 'bare' in retrospect. The free Jotunn Edition (July 2019) added hero traits, extra commanders, items, skills and harder content, and Steam players rate the game much higher than critics. Nominated for Strategy/Simulation Game of the Year at the 22nd D.I.C.E. Awards. Steam revenue estimate (third party, Boxleiter method) is about $8.1M gross and $2.4M net, owners roughly 500k-1M; treat as order of magnitude. Still getting positive Steam reviews in 2026 (recent ones cite 4-190 hour playtimes) though players say it deserved more content. Mac supported, no Linux build.

games.name: Breachway
games.short_description: Explore the galaxy in this deckbuilding, sci-fi roguelike where ship upgrades and crew management are key to your survival. Optimize resource generation, engage in intense turn-based battles, and take on ever-growing threats as you seek out The Signal.

other_scores.score: 2 to 5 reviews listed (sources disagree), no numeric scores, Metascore not yet calculated

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put Bridgeway as a low C tier. Uh that could honestly go up to like a high B or even low A once the game comes out.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Breachway is a deck-building roguelike that mixes FTL-style ship management and galaxy travel with Slay the Spire-style card combat. Cards are split across ship slots, you can target parts of enemy ships, and you manage fuel and energy. He enjoys ship building, the map and the visuals, but finds the combat loops repetitive, the card design uninspiring and synergies limited. Bugs, frame drops, long loads and crashes after about two years in early access hurt it further. He places it in low C, with potential to rise to high B or low A after polish and a full release.
praise: Ship building and customization is enjoyable
Travelling the galaxy map with events and fuel management is cool
Visuals and art style look great, with a 3D space environment and changing background
Mixing FTL and Slay the Spire is a concept he likes
Targeting different parts of the enemy ship adds interest
Lots to love, and he may return after polish
criticism: Core combat is repetitive: enemies run short fixed loops (missile, block, recharge; or burn, block, burn)
Once the build is set, battle outcomes depend on the build rather than on play
Used cards go on cooldown and back to the draw pile, so key passive or power cards can get stuck undrawn
Card design is basic and uninspiring (lasers that deal a bit more damage), with no crazy scaling
Synergies are limited because energy types split play across three or four decks
Early access bugs, frame drops, long loading and crashes
Small, boring font and wordy dialogue in a reading-heavy game
Little meta progression; unlocks mostly add new things to play with
unique_points: Cards are attached to different ship slots, each with its own energy type, which adds complexity but fragments deck building
Cooldown cards return to the draw pile instead of discard, creating an unusual draw dynamic
A 3D animated space backdrop makes a deck-builder feel more alive than static screens
commentary.quote: I'm going to put Bridgeway as a low C tier.
design_criteria: Combat variety: enemy loops are too repetitive
Card design and synergies: basic cards, limited synergy across split decks
Build customization: ship building is fun but outcomes depend mainly on the build
Complexity vs depth: complex energy and slot systems yet simple card effects
Visuals and art style: 3D space setting is a strong point
UI and readability: small, boring font in a text-heavy game
Meta progression: minimal, only unlocks of new options
Polish and stability: bugs, frame drops and crashes in early access
Exploration and map: galaxy travel, fuel and events are appealing
commentary.rerank_note: Not a rerank, but he says it could rise to high B or low A after full release and fixes; it has been in early access about two years.

community.one_liner: A turn-based sci-fi deckbuilding roguelike from Edgeflow Studio (published by Hooded Horse) in which you fly a modular ship through sectors, managing power, heat, crew and per-weapon card decks in FTL-meets-Slay-the-Spire fights.
community.consensus_summary: Breachway sits at Mostly Positive on Steam (about 76% of roughly 1,500 reviews; recent 30-day sample around 75%). It is still in Early Access two years after its Sep 2024 launch. Players who like it call it a fresh FTL-with-cards hybrid with a distinctive cooldown-based deck system and a developer who patched often. Since roughly mid-2026 the most upvoted negative reviews say progress has stalled: the run still ends after the second sector, the promised next map has not appeared, and some users suspect the game is abandoned. Critics are few and mixed: Metacritic lists only a few critic reviews but has no Metascore yet (it needs four scored reviews), and the reviews I could see carry no numeric scores.
best_things: Distinctive take on deckbuilding: each weapon and module acts as its own mini-deck, and played cards must cool down in the discard pile before they can be drawn again, so burning through your deck is a real risk
Strong FTL plus Slay the Spire feel; several reviewers call it a better spiritual successor to FTL than Into the Breach
Power allocation, heat management and crew abilities add a layer of decision-making beyond plain card play
Weapon types feel different from one another (for example pulse lasers and railguns that snipe components, flak against missiles or drones), and loadout variety supports different builds
Sci-fi presentation, Expanse-like tone, ship design and music get frequent praise from positive reviewers (though some negative reviews call the ship designs generic)
Developer has been responsive and patched frequently during Early Access, and many reviewers say the game improved a lot since launch
Good value and replayability for $19.99 according to positive reviewers, with ascension-style difficulty levels unlocked by winning
worst_things: Progress has stalled: the run still ends after the second sector with no resolution of the story, and the long-promised third map has not shipped, so some players think the game is abandoned
Stability and performance: crashes after combat or on load, lag spikes and input lag even on high-end hardware (RTX 5070 Ti/5080 and similar), with reports that save progress is lost after a crash
Many bugs around card interactions, tooltips and heat, and some players cannot tell what is a bug and what is a badly explained mechanic
Combat becomes repetitive: shoot, shield, shoot, repeat, with long fights against high-health, high-shield enemies
Shallow content: little enemy variety, repetitive bosses, few ships, four factions that barely differ, and very thin story or motivation

Balance problems that cut both ways: easy for most of a run, then spikes from the final boss and the second boss (overheat, heavy shielding, hacks); raw damage often beats the hacking, brittle and overheat systems
UI and clarity problems: tooltips that overlap and block equipping items, hard-to-read health and shields, and a tutorial that does not explain the fuel and yellow-path movement costs
Weak metaprogression: reviewers say you carry little between runs, and most runs are a slight variation of the starting gear
improvements: Ship the promised additional sectors and an ending; one reviewer also suggests an endless or procedural mode
Fix the crashes, save issues and performance stutter before adding content
Add more enemy, event, quest and boss variety so the map stops feeling sparse
Improve tooltips, card descriptions and the tutorial so mechanics such as heat, fuel and movement costs are clear

Rebalance difficulty and resource scarcity (starting fuel, deck-thinning costs, heat builds, the second and final bosses) and make the hacking, brittle and overheat options competitive with raw damage
Strengthen metaprogression and add more ships and weapon variety; some players also ask for ship visual customization
unique_things: Per-module mini-decks that combine into your hand, with a cooldown in the discard pile, unlike Slay the Spire's shuffle-the-discard loop
Three resource colors (power types) plus heat and overheating as a core tradeoff
Node-map navigation where path colors spend different resources, and fuel that is scarce and only found at stations
Crew and subsystem management with enemy component targeting and hacking, plus faction relations and 4X-flavoured space trade
Hard sci-fi tone in the style of The Expanse rather than space-fantasy
tedious_or_disliked: Long, drawn-out early fights where damage per turn is low (roughly 4-8) and enemies carry about 50 HP plus shields
Fuel scarcity (only 2 starting fuel, refuel only at stations) that limits exploration and pushes grinding sectors
Hard-to-predict negative node debuffs and enemy hacks with no counter unless a station offers security systems
Calculating multi-card damage combos with shred, brittle and other modifiers is cumbersome
Deleting or upgrading cards is expensive, and weapon decks can be full before you get a chance to upgrade
Reinstalling or restarting after crashes and the general sense of being railroaded toward a loss
divisive_points: Difficulty: some players find runs and bosses too easy, others find the later bosses and scarce resources punishing
Whether the roguelite loop is engaging or a slog: a minority call the combat great, while highly upvoted negatives (150 hours, 6 hours, 30 hours) say decisions feel low-impact
Whether the dev is still committed: earlier reviews praise frequent updates, while 2026 reviews cite two years with no new map
Deck size strategy: Breachway rewards bigger decks than most deckbuilders, which some see as innovative and others as unintuitive
Visuals and ship design: positive reviewers praise ship design and the sci-fi look, while a 14-upvote negative review calls the ships generic and the battle visuals pointless
community.reception_notes: Launched into Early Access on Sep 26, 2024 at $19.99 (Windows only) with Hooded Horse as publisher. Early Steam reviews (around patch 31 and after) were warm and stressed rapid patching, a live Discord and a stated roadmap. By 2026 the tone on the most helpful negative reviews had shifted to frustration: crashes and lag persist, the game still ends after sector two, and promised content has not arrived. A reviewer also notes it appeared in a 2026 Tacticon showcase and questions that given the lack of progress. Steam forum counts show a large bug-report backlog (about 536 threads). Third-party estimates (Boxleiter method, not audited) put it at 50,000-100,000 owners and roughly $725k gross and $214k net revenue. Steam revenue calculator lists roughly 1,000 reviews. I could not verify the current development state, patch cadence or official roadmap because the Steam news page returned no content to my fetch.

games.name: Cubic Cosmos
games.short_description: Cubic Cosmos is a thrilling fast-paced roguelike card game. You have been trapped in a deadly game. One wrong move could see you reduced to a plaything of the goddess. Can you free yourself from the endless cycle and escape your fate?

other_scores.score: Very Positive, about 92% of ~1,003 reviews positive (923 up / 80 down)
about 68% positive of a small recent sample (16 reviews at time of fetch)

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put Cubic Cosmos as a mid low B tier.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Cubic Cosmos is an auto-battler-style deck-building roguelike where you place up to five units on a board and they attack on their own, with most cards granting permanent buffs for the rest of the run. He enjoys the big-number combos and the feeling of understanding the systems well enough to break the game. The runs become repetitive, the art style, music and sound design feel weak, and information and keyword clarity are poor. He recommends it to people who like the concept but places it in mid-low B.
praise: Permanent buffs from nearly every battle make progression feel big and unusual for the genre
Building broken combos is super satisfying, especially the first few times
Lots to do between battles, plus triple and fuse mechanics to duplicate effects
VFX are satisfying: explosions and flying tokens
Rewarding to learn, since system knowledge directly produces crazy effects
Different champion classes change things somewhat
Developers were not afraid to use huge effects
criticism: Game is very easy to break, so it often ends up as one card then waiting for animations (his Steam review: the deck played itself)
Repetitive and redundant after a few runs
Art style feels uninspired, almost AI-generated in vibe; music and sound design are weak
Too much on screen, enemy effects are hard to track, and player info is meh since you usually just kill everything
