unique_points: Permanent run-long buffs on most units and cards are the core hook, which also makes balance very fragile
Triple-and-fuse of units duplicates permanent effects, allowing runaway builds
Pro and con: extreme breakability is both the fun and the weakness
commentary.quote: I'm going to put Cubic Cosmos as a mid low B tier.
design_criteria: Balance/breakability: permanent buffs make it easy to trivialize the game
Replayability: repetitive gameplay loop after a few runs
Synergies/combos: big satisfying combos are the main draw
Charm/visuals: art style feels uninspired, VFX are good
Audio: music and sound design are weak
Information clarity: cluttered enemy info and unclear card effects and keywords
Meta/run progression: permanent in-run progression is the core system
Skill/knowledge reward: understanding systems is rewarding

community.one_liner: A fast-paced roguelike deckbuilder with tower-defense-style lane combat (monsters attack back to front) from Inkstone Atelier, built around run-long stat stacking and explosive combo chains.
community.consensus_summary: Cubic Cosmos is a low-profile but well-liked indie: Steam shows about 1,000 reviews at roughly 92% positive (Very Positive), with recent reviews noticeably weaker (about 68% of a small recent sample). Players praise its permissive, break-the-game synergy building, the run-long scaling of cards and a generous amount of content (12 heroes, 240+ cards). The main sources of negative sentiment are undisclosed generative-AI card art, a sense that the game is easy/repetitive once a build snowballs, and unclear UI/keyword explanations. It launched in Early Access on Sept 16, 2025 and had its 1.0 launch on Apr 28, 2026, with the dev apparently still patching (an earlier reviewer flipped to positive citing steady improvements). No critic coverage exists on Metacritic (page has zero critic reviews) and nothing turned up on OpenCritic.
best_things: Anything-goes synergy building: players love assembling absurd, over-the-top combos and scaling to huge numbers, and like that the game does not try to cap power the way Slay the Spire-style games do
Stat boosts from spells, monsters and events last for the whole run, so cards genuinely grow and you plan around growing specific units
Selling cards in shops (about 50% value) instead of paying to remove them eases RNG pressure and encourages pivoting builds
Lots of content and variety: 12 heroes across 3 classes with distinct synergies, 240+ cards, 50+ relics, multiple modes and 10+ difficulty levels
Strong 'one more run' pull; several reviewers report 25-60 hours and one 260+ hours
Satisfying combo chains with lots of animation and effects going off; the game feels powerful from the very first run
Doll Code system lets you export cards and share/receive others' pawns and replays, adding a light meta layer
Low price ($12.99) relative to the amount of content, frequently cited as great value
worst_things: Undisclosed generative-AI card art is the top complaint: the two most-upvoted negative Steam reviews (93 and 125 helpful votes) cite odd fingers, repeated poses and 'obviously AI' cards, and people say they feel misled
Game is easy and repetitive for some: one reviewer beat the top difficulty with every character without a loss, with decks effectively locked in by the first boss
Heroes are said to play too similarly, with hero abilities easy to ignore (only a couple felt truly distinct to that reviewer)
Stat stacking has little downside, so builds converge on a few stat enablers plus a few hard hitters
UI/readability gaps: card types (artifact vs sorcery etc.) are unclear, keyword phrasing is odd, and many things are left unexplained
Chain reactions can be too fast or opaque to follow, leaving some players confused about why their board was wiped

Technical rough edges: game freeze when starting a new run (pinned Steam workaround), buggy controller support, poor text on Steam Deck, a Linux launch failure (no native Linux build), a reported crash
Repetitive, looping music mentioned by a reviewer
improvements: Disclose or replace the generative-AI art and be transparent about the art pipeline
Better in-game explanation of keywords, card types and monster effects, plus general QoL and UI clarity work
Add downsides or tension to stat stacking and make higher difficulties and late-game builds more varied (late-game builds called limited)
Differentiate heroes more so their special abilities meaningfully change play
Improve controller and Steam Deck support and fix the new-run freeze; community also asks for ultrawide support and more languages (Russian, German)
More Steam achievements, and clearer purpose for the dolls/meta systems (one reviewer collected dolls without knowing what they do)
unique_things: Monsters attack from back to front in a lane/tower-defense style layout, so reaching enemy backlines is a real strategic lever
Most attribute boosts persist for the entire run rather than one fight, pushing a 'grow your cards' play pattern
Tension between prolonging fights to buff cards and finishing fast to earn more lucre (currency)
Selling cards for lucre instead of paying to discard
Doll Code system for exporting cards, sharing pawns and battle replays with other players
Hearthstone/Battlegrounds-like creature-and-spell feel mixed with roguelike path choices; reviewers compare the card-modifier depth to Inscryption
tedious_or_disliked: Undisclosed AI art (some buyers refunded or wrote negative reviews purely over this)
Feeling the run is decided early, then just watching the deck play out
Long chains of auto-triggering effects that some find hard to follow
Having to learn unusual keyword terms (mobility, auto, death, lasting, charge) before the game clicks

Steam-page tags/marketing: players who expected a roguelite with persistent power-up meta-progression felt misled, since the dev reportedly said it is not meant to have that (though the game does have XP-based unlocks of cards/characters)
divisive_points: Is it a roguelite or a roguelike? Some say the tag is misleading because there is no permanent power meta-progression, while others note unlocks/XP and Doll Code carry-over count as meta progression
Difficulty and balance: fans love that it is wildly breakable, while critics find it too easy and shallow once you learn the stacking loop
AI art: some players call it a dealbreaker that warrants a negative review, while others say they enjoy the game regardless and dismiss the complaint
Hero diversity: one reviewer with hundreds of hours found some heroes 'world enders' with very different styles, while another felt they mostly play the same
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched Sept 16, 2025 and 1.0 released Apr 28, 2026 on PC (Windows/Mac; Steam lists Inkstone Atelier as developer and publisher). Steam priced at $12.99. Reviewers describe it as an under-the-radar sleeper ('best roguelike deckbuilder nobody is talking about'), and one early negative reviewer later rewrote their review positively after learning the systems. Since late 2025 the AI-art controversy has dominated negative reviews and is now the most upvoted criticism, which likely explains the softer recent score. Steam community has a pinned workaround for a new-run freeze and a FAQ. Sales estimates from third-party Steam trackers were empty/zero at time of check so no reliable copies/revenue figure was obtained. Metacritic has no critic reviews and only a single user rating (9/10; user score needs 4 ratings); no OpenCritic entry could be found. Note: web search budget was exhausted, so Reddit and outlet reviews could not be retrieved; conclusions rest on Steam data, Steam reviews and discussion pages.

games.name: Inkshade
games.short_description: Inkshade is a turn-based tactics game carved out of strange wooden miniatures, wrapped in a web of locked rooms, and orchestrated by an otherworldly game master. Victory is not guaranteed, and the only constant is the cruel black ink that flows within the pieces.

other_scores.score: No user score yet (needs 4 ratings; 2 ratings: 1 positive, 1 mixed); 0 critic reviews

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put as a low B.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Inkshade is an Inscryption-style game that swaps cards for pawns placed on a small tactical board. He loves the haunted-house exploration, narrator, story and puzzles outside combat, but found the combat itself boring and shallow. Strategy is limited, pieces are near-identical, and progress leans heavily on meta-progression stat upgrades. He finished it out of curiosity, describes the experience as mixed, and places it in low B, recommending it to Inscryption fans who can tolerate the gameplay.
praise: Out-of-combat vibe: a house that slowly opens up, with a narrator who guides and sometimes misleads you
Unlocking new rooms feels exciting, with puzzles that are solid
Story and mystery hold him in from start to finish
Spooky atmosphere, with some genuinely freaky moments
Combat boards look cool and each has a small story setup
Captures Inscryption's vibe, which is hard to replicate
criticism: Combat is boring: only movement and attack, with little strategy
Most pieces are nearly identical and enemies differ mainly in health, damage and range
Heavily dependent on meta-progression stat upgrades, so some fights are mathematically unwinnable without them
Dominant strategy is to buff a single unit and have it carry everything
No real builds during a run; fights are predictable from start to end and the same board repeats
Ending was less satisfying than hoped; low replayability as a one-time adventure
unique_points: Copies Inscryption's vibe without its card gameplay, which is harder to clone than typical mechanics
Only two damage and defense types (magical or physical)
Acts more like a one-time adventure than a replayable roguelike
commentary.quote: I can definitely recommend Inkshade as long as you're okay with the gameplay.
design_criteria: Strategy depth: combat has too few actions and options
Build variety: no builds beyond pre-run planning
Meta-progression: over-reliance on stat upgrades makes fights depend on them
Enemy design: enemies are near-identical beyond stats
Atmosphere and vibe: a major strength outside combat
Puzzles and exploration: rewarding room unlocks and puzzle design
Story and narrative: compelling mystery and narrator
Replayability: a one-time experience with modes afterward

community.one_liner: A first-person, dark-atmosphere turn-based tactics roguelite by Studio Vezelle where you command wooden board-game miniatures against a malicious game master, with locked-room escape puzzles between battles.
community.consensus_summary: Steam players rate Inkshade Very Positive (about 87% of roughly 636 reviews, Steam listing as of the data pull), driven by its atmosphere, sound and art, and the creepy, sardonic game master. The common caveat is that the tactics are shallow and the roguelite loop is grindy: units differ mostly by stats and a few broken-strong upgrade paths trivialise late fights. It is constantly compared to Inscryption, usually unfavourably on depth but favourably on vibe. There are no critic reviews: Metacritic has a page with zero critic reviews and only 2 user ratings, and no OpenCritic entry was found. The game is a finished 1.0 (not early access) that got several post-launch patches in Aug-Sep 2025 (lantern toggle, contrast slider, walk speed, new challenge mode), and still receives positive reviews into 2026.
best_things: Atmosphere, art direction, lighting and sound design (the wooden 'bonk' of pieces, battle themes, end-credits track) are the most consistently praised element
The game master is a memorable, sardonic and malicious narrator whose worldbuilding and banter give the run a sense of story
Escape-room style puzzle sections in locked rooms give a satisfying break from combat and several reviewers found them clever and tough
Tactical board is simple and readable: pieces cannot pass through each other, so bottlenecks, shielding and elevation matter
Collecting and upgrading new pieces feels rewarding, and tense battles where you could lose your whole roster give real dread
Strong Inscryption-like vibe with different mechanics (mid-run recruiting of defeated enemies, hex-grid tactics) that some find a fresh spin
Steam Deck works well per at least one reviewer (minor remapping), plus accessibility options like adjustable difficulty and colour alternatives
worst_things: Tactical depth is shallow: units are differentiated almost entirely by five stats (movement, health, range, damage, defense) and only a few have special abilities
Balance is exploitable: stacking armour/attack on one or two pieces (the Wretch is repeatedly named) makes most enemies and bosses trivial, so strategy falls away
Enemy AI is passive and only engages when a piece is in range, enabling simple luring tactics
Very dark visuals; even with lantern and brightness options, some players cannot see enemy units and felt unfairly killed
Performance and stability complaints: low fps on mid-range GPUs, some maps heavy, and one reviewer reported frequent crashes on an older Win10 PC (fine on a newer machine)
Controls can be clumsy: passing a unit's turn with a triple click is easy to trigger accidentally, no clear attack-range preview for ranged units before moving, unit names hard to see
The narrator talks a lot and dialogue cannot easily be skipped even after many repeats
Story and character connections are thin and the ending left some players unsatisfied; limited replayability after finishing
improvements: Add more unit abilities and build variety (area attacks, taunt, summons, status effects) so pieces differ beyond stat numbers
Rebalance upgrade costs and scaling so one maxed piece or armour stacking cannot trivialise the game, and so early grinding feels less punishing
Improve brightness/visibility and add camera options (decouple camera from mouse, manual camera toggle) to address eye strain and motion sickness
Fix the unit-pass input (allow un-passing or use a less accident-prone control) and show attack range and unit names more clearly
Let players skip or shorten repeated narrator dialogue
Optimise performance and stability, and consider modding/community map support or more backstory content (suggested by one reviewer)
unique_things: Combines first-person escape-room exploration of locked rooms and an airship setting with a turn-based tactics board game run by a hostile game master
Pieces are wooden miniatures on a physical-feeling board with hex grid, elevation and height effects
Roguelite meta-progression through spending scrip on permanent upgrades to a collected roster, plus a mid-run recruitment system for defeated enemies
A post-campaign challenge mode (including a Monomanipulation mode for single-unit runs added in Sep 2025) that players say is closer to a classic roguelite
Unlocking new pieces is tied to solving puzzle rooms, and opening rooms is tied to progressing through battles
tedious_or_disliked: Grind: you need upgrades to win fights and need to fight (and often lose) to earn upgrade currency; reviewers cite only about 15-20 scrip per failed run versus 50 for a single point of damage
Dying can send you back large sections, keeping pieces and upgrades but losing run progress, which feels heavy in mid/late game
Enemies and early encounters scale with progress, so knowledge and skill matter less than how many upgrades you bought
Spreading upgrades across many pieces is a trap; new players may have to restart or soft-lock themselves on harder settings after a reset
Long runs with repetitive combat and a chatty narrator during tutorial/first-hour failure scripting
Darkness and camera behaviour causing eye strain or motion sickness for some
divisive_points: Inscryption comparison: some see a worthy atmospheric cousin, others call it a shallow imitation without Inscryption's mechanical depth
Difficulty: some enjoy brutal early hours and tense fights, others find it grindy early and then trivial once an overpowered build is found
Puzzle rooms: praised as a highlight by some, called shallow or unclear by others
Narrator and story: charming and creepy to some, repetitive and flat to others
community.reception_notes: Released Aug 14, 2025 on Windows only (no Mac/Linux) at $19.99, developed and published by Studio Vezelle. Post-launch patches: The Lantern Update v1.1.010 (Aug 30, 2025) made the lantern toggleable and added a contrast slider and brightness button, directly responding to visibility complaints; v1.1.011 (Sep 6) added Monomanipulation challenge mode; v1.1.012 (Sep 17) added faster unit walk speed and fixed keymapping bugs. A soundtrack was released Sep 29, 2025. Reviews continue into 2026 and stay mostly positive. Metacritic had 0 critic reviews and only 2 user ratings at fetch time and no OpenCritic page was found, so there are no aggregate critic scores. SteamSpy-style owner data was not informative (0-20k), so copies sold is unknown; $193.9k estimated gross at roughly $12-20 average realised price implies on the order of 10-15k copies, which is my rough inference, not a sourced figure.

games.name: Blazing Beaks
games.short_description: Roguelite - where too much greediness can be fatal. A colorful world with armed birds blazing their way through piles of mutants, monsters and creepy creatures. Lots of mysteries to unravel, secrets to discover and levels to explore.

placements.verbal_evidence: not a huge fan I'll put it as a d

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Blazing Beaks is a top-down shooter roguelike where you play as birds with guns. Its hook is that enemies drop cursed items with only downsides, and you choose how many to carry to the shop, where they can be swapped for beneficial items. He loves the concept, art and sound design, but finds the actual game suffers from design and balance problems. He never feels powerful, dies often on first visits to new areas, and puts it in D while respecting it.
praise: Cursed-item-for-shop-exchange mechanic is a really cool concept and gimmick
Art style is appealing
Sound design is amazing and very cute
Some cursed items have unique, interesting negative effects
He respects the idea and says it is fine if others like it
criticism: Never feels powerful or satisfying when progressing through a run
Shop items are random and often not game-changing, sometimes all useless
Only two to three health, so new areas usually kill you until you learn enemy attacks
Learning patterns per new area forces restarts
Runs feel not very impactful between characters or weapons
Curse design got more effort than the rewards, which were underwhelming
unique_points: Enemies drop downside-only cursed items that you trade in at the shop for useful ones
The push-your-luck question of how many curses to grab before the shop
Design effort seemed concentrated on the curses rather than the rewards
commentary.quote: not a huge fan I'll put it as a d
design_criteria: Power progression: run should feel increasingly powerful and satisfying
Risk vs reward: curse collection traded for shop rewards
Item quality and randomness: rewards need to be impactful, not useless
Difficulty and health: very low health punishes unfamiliar areas
Run variety: characters and weapons should make runs feel different
Art and sound design: charming and cute, strongly praised

community.one_liner: A pixel-art twin-stick roguelite where armed birds fight through randomized rooms, hauling back cursed artifacts that carry debuffs, with solo, local co-op and local PvP tournament modes.
community.consensus_summary: Blazing Beaks is well liked but a niche, under-the-radar title: Steam sits at Very Positive (about 83.5% of roughly 2,600 reviews), and critics on Switch landed around 80-81. Reviewers and players praise the charm, art, music, tight controls and the risk/reward artifact loop, and it shines in local co-op. The main complaints are a lack of meaningful meta-progression, heavy RNG (weapons and artifacts), uneven balance, and a sense that runs get samey; many negative reviews come from players expecting Nuclear Throne or Enter the Gungeon depth. Several recent Steam reviewers describe the game as effectively left dead on PC, though a mod/Workshop scene exists and a dev Discord community is still described as alive. Steam owner estimates are low (under 20k by SteamSpy; about 13 concurrent players), and revenue estimates are modest (around $265k gross / $78k net per a Boxleiter-style calculator).
best_things: Charming, clean pixel-art style with distinct, readable characters and enemies
Risk/reward artifact system: treasures carry debuffs (for example cannot shoot while moving) and you must survive to a shop to cash them in for a big power spike
Music repeatedly called out as some of the best in the genre
Tight, responsive twin-stick controls and a satisfying 'nuclear throne-like' feel
Fun local co-op for two players in story mode plus a four-player local tournament mode with five sub-modes
Eight birds with distinct stats and quirks (chicken accuracy that drops when moving, platypus extra loot, penguin cloning)
High replay value through randomized rooms, items and secrets, and a looping endgame that can go on indefinitely; Steam Workshop character mods
Good value and varied enemy behaviors; bosses need specific strategies
worst_things: Little or no sense of meta-progression: unlocks mostly dilute the item pool and nothing builds toward a long-term goal
Heavy RNG: weapons are scarce and random, artifacts cannot be planned around, and some runs reach the first boss with no artifacts
Balance is uneven: some guns and artifacts are strictly worse, many items are plain HP ups, and a couple of birds (Blue Bird, Chicken) outclass others (Duck, Seagull)
Some enemies and rooms feel unfair (for example unclear charge-up attacks, hitboxes and momentum-based movement) while bosses can feel easier than regular rooms
UI problems: some menus cannot be used with the mouse, gamepad aiming is called imprecise, and there are remote play/focus glitches and a launch failure report
Levels are small and repetitive with one boss type per biome; runs feel samey after several hours
Often viewed as a weaker clone of Nuclear Throne or Enter the Gungeon
No online multiplayer; it is local only, and PC is Windows only
improvements: Add real meta-progression or goals (for example a relic checklist or a good ending for collecting everything)
Make artifact drops more consistent, and rebalance weapons, artifacts and the weaker characters
Add online play or better remote-play support
Fix UI: full mouse support in menus and better gamepad aiming
Give more control over builds or weapon upgrading rather than pure RNG
Improve boss difficulty curve and late-game power scaling, and add more boss and level variety per biome
unique_things: Cursed-artifact economy: you carry debuffs and must reach a shop to exchange them for permanent buffs, so greed can kill you
Anthropomorphic bird cast with per-character positive and negative traits
Campaign plus a four-player local arena tournament in the same package
Looping endgame that can go on indefinitely
Steam Workshop character mod support
tedious_or_disliked: Runs feel samey and repetitive after a few hours because of small levels and predictable enemies
Forced RNG reliance: a good run can feel one in a million because of unfair environments
Weak upgrade system, for example tiny percent bonuses per coin, and filler items like plain HP ups
Steep learning curve and unforgiving difficulty; more frustrating than fun for some
Solo play is seen by some as much less fun than co-op
Frustration and rage moments: even fans say it can make you rage out, and players note the game depends on overcoming frustration
divisive_points: Difficulty: fans say it is fair and skill-based and you die from mistakes, detractors call it unforgiving and luck-driven
No meta-progression: a purist 'true roguelike' feature for some, a dealbreaker for others
Comparison to Nuclear Throne and Gungeon: some call it a great alternative, others call it worse in every way
Solo versus co-op: best with friends, but solo experience is judged weaker by some
community.reception_notes: Critic scores (Metacritic 80 from 9 reviews on Switch, OpenCritic 81 from 11 reviews, mostly Nintendo-focused outlets) come from the console release; Metacritic user score was 7.4 from 56 ratings on the page fetched (a search snippet showed 7.9 from 37, so it may have shifted). Steam lists a May 10, 2019 release (the game had earlier 2017 roots; the Steam date was not verified as early access). Early Steam community threads show Applava promising boss and artifact rebalancing and a weapons review, but recent Steam reviewers (2026) describe the game as dead/left without updates while still praising a dev Discord. It has Steam Workshop mod support, Steam trading cards, and is also on Switch, PS4 and Epic. Price is $14.99 and it is often on sale. Note that Metacritic and OpenCritic pages could not be confirmed from Steam, which lists no Metacritic score.

community.one_liner: A spaceship-builder arcade roguelike (officially licensed re-imagining of the browser classic Captain Forever) where you blast randomly generated enemy ships, graft their parts onto your own, and push through the Solar System to beat King Kevin.
community.consensus_summary: Critics at launch (June 2016) were warm: PC Gamer called it a stately, affectionate overhaul of the original with more structure and customization, and Rock Paper Shotgun was positive but noted the campaign can feel like a grind and suits short sessions. Steam players are Very Positive (about 80% of roughly 380 reviews), with the loudest praise for the chaotic build-as-you-fight loop and the art and music. Negative reviews cluster on the forced post-fight build timer, brutal late sectors where a stronger enemy wipes your hard-built ship, and lack of persistent progression or difficulty options. Recent Steam reviews (2025-2026) show the game is effectively static: long-time fans say it needs balancing, more content, even multiplayer, and the developer appears unlikely to add much. Not early access; a physical Collector's Edition also exists.
best_things: Build-while-fighting ship construction feels improvisational and creative; every piece you attach changes movement, armor and firepower
Scavenging parts from randomly generated enemy ships keeps each encounter a new puzzle (PC Gamer: improvisational, gleeful and brutal; Retromation: action-FTL meets Legos)
Weapon variety (ScatterBlasters, MegaBoom rockets, RipSaw blades, lasers, a healing module) and unlockable Power Bulkheads give room to experiment
Bright 90s Saturday-morning-cartoon art style and sibling-rivalry framing (girl as Captain Forever vs little brother King Kevin) are charming
Mellow electropop soundtrack is singled out by reviewers and sold separately as an OST
Easy to pick up, strangely addictive, with a sandbox mode and Steam Workshop support for free-play ships
worst_things: Timed build phase after a fight: leftover parts vanish when the teleport timer ends, so you arrive at the next sector half built
Brutal difficulty spikes: a much stronger enemy can shred your ship in seconds, making effort feel pointless (reviewers describe one-tap deaths even with a shield)
Dying loses everything from the run, with no resource saving or meta progression to soften it
Combat reads as shallow: mostly orbiting an enemy with clunky controls; many weapons just get outranged by lasers
Enemy parts are always a tier above what you can build, so farming and scaling feels futile
Seen by fans of the original as more restrictive than the seamless Captain Forever; some say to buy the Trilogy or Reassembly instead
Reported as needing keyboard and mouse for best control
Builds feel pointless: after a long build, a random much stronger enemy can wreck the ship, so the creativity is rarely rewarded
improvements: Option to shorten, lengthen or disable the build timer
Let players store higher-tier parts or carry some resources between runs so the start is less punishing
Selectable difficulty or a balance pass on enemy tier jumps and one-shot deaths
More content and goals (quests, objectives) because killing ships and grabbing parts gets old by the time all characters are unlocked
Multiplayer, requested by a long-time player
Better controls and less obstructive dialogue
unique_things: Real-time modular ship building on the fly in the middle of a roguelike run, rather than menu-based upgrades
Licensed re-imagining of a cult indie classic by a different developer (Pixelsaurus with Future Crayon) than the original Farbs trilogy
Ten-sector trip across the Solar System with a sibling-rivalry story wrapper and cartoon tone
Teleport after killing the highest-tier enemy makes each sector a fight-then-scavenge-and-rebuild cycle
Steam Workshop and sandbox mode let you reuse constructed ships outside the campaign
Physical Collector's Edition on USB cartridge with manual, soundtrack CD, watch and stickers (reviewed by SLUG Magazine)
tedious_or_disliked: Rushing to attach parts before the timer expires, often with little time to build anything usable
Repeatedly restarting after losing a long run with nothing carried over
Fine-motor precision needed to attach parts while under fire (Common Sense Media notes this and later-level frustration)
Harvesting parts from the same kinds of enemies becomes repetitive over a long session (RPS: can feel like a grind, best in short bursts)
Devs' standard advice to find time-extension components is seen by some as not addressing the complaint
divisive_points: The build timer: some see it as the tension that defines the game, others call it the main flaw
Art and humor: praised as nostalgic and charming by some, criticized as plain immature by others
Remix vs the original trilogy: Remix is more structured and accessible, while purists prefer the seamless, slower original ship-building
community.reception_notes: Launched June 3, 2016 on Windows, Mac and Linux at $9.99 with quotes from PC Gamer, Rock Paper Shotgun and Retromation. Metacritic has only two critic reviews so no Metascore is shown; the user score is 8.0 from just 5 ratings. Steam Revenue Calculator estimates about $61.7k gross and about $18.2k net, and SteamSpy owner range is 50,000 to 100,000 (estimates, not audited). The negative reviews from 2024 to 2026 show the timer complaint is long-standing and unaddressed. No evidence of a major controversy or recent big patches. Steam data lists the release as 2016 even though the ranking lists 2015.

community.one_liner: A dark-fantasy deckbuilding roguelite/RPG from AYGames in which a cast of antiheroes explores a camp-and-map world fighting turn-based card battles where played cards turn to ash and must be paid back with health to reuse.
community.consensus_summary: Deck of Ashes is received as a mixed-to-decent, niche deckbuilder. Steam sits at Mostly Positive (about 72 percent of roughly 1,070 reviews), while critics land in the 6-7 out of 10 band, with a Metacritic score of 66 from 4 reviews and outliers at both ends (Gamer's Palace 93/100 versus Xbox Hub 2.5/5). Nearly everyone praises the art, voice work, character writing and boss fights; nearly everyone dislikes the slow, padded combat, the housekeeping after battles, and uneven polish. It spent just over a year in Early Access (April 2019) before a full PC/Mac release on June 9, 2020, then reached Xbox One, PS4 and Switch in 2021-2022 as the Complete Edition. Recent Steam reviews (2025-2026) still complain about broken controller/menu handling, and the game is now regularly bought very cheaply on sale.
best_things: Hand-drawn, original art direction and distinctive, instantly readable card art
Four likeable, flawed antihero characters, each with their own mechanics and story campaign
Voice acting, music and sound design are strong for an indie, especially Magnus and the Ash Master
Boss fights feel epic and puzzle-like, rewarding adapting your strategy
The Ash Deck risk/reward system (spend health to renew used cards) creates real tactical tension
Badlands mode offers a streamlined, Slay the Spire-style pure card-battle roguelike run
Dark, grimy tone and narrative give it more story weight than most roguelike deckbuilders
Good value when discounted; some players report being happy with 7+ hours at a few pounds
worst_things: Combat is slow and spongy: trash fights take too many turns even on easy difficulty, and balance is conservative
Ash (the resource that gets you new cards) is tightly limited, so card acquisition is a bottleneck; other resources feel meaningless until late
The node/map and camp exploration feel repetitive and boring, with repetitive events and little sense of going anywhere
Early chapters repeat almost identically across characters and runs, hurting roguelite variety
Persistent bugs reported since launch: NPC upgrade failures, visual glitches, sound mixing, and debuff balance problems (one debuff reportedly distorts crafting by a large margin)

Controls are broken for many players, with controller confirm prompts getting stuck and the ESC menu sometimes impossible to close (one reviewer says the problems go away with the gamepad unplugged and mouse used)
Presentation inconsistencies: awkward font choices, localization/translation errors, uneven voice acting and disproportionate character designs
Dodge chance and monster first-turn speed advantage feel arbitrary in an otherwise deterministic system, with no action log to review
improvements: Fix and polish controller and keyboard/mouse input, menu handling and save loading
Add more playable characters beyond the current four and more variety in early-game encounters
Speed up combat and reduce spongy enemy health so ordinary fights do not drag
Make non-Ash resources matter earlier and loosen the card acquisition bottleneck
Improve the map/node events and camp progression so exploration feels purposeful
Add a combat log and clearer information about speed, dodge and debuff effects
unique_things: The titular Deck of Ashes: cards used in battle are temporarily consumed into an ash pile and must be renewed by paying life points (strain)
A camp/survival-expedition structure with resource management layered on top of card combat, rather than a pure node-map climb
Card recipes and crafting instead of straightforward card rewards, with persistent negative cards entering your deck
Each character has a unique story campaign, alongside the separate Badlands roguelike mode
Visual cues often compared to Darkest Dungeon combined with Slay the Spire mechanics, with a narrative-first angle
One Steam reviewer compares it to a smaller, lighter Gordian Quest (single mention, not a broad consensus)
tedious_or_disliked: Paying to renew and housekeeping your deck after every battle is slow and laborious
Wandering around camp repeatedly gathering resources until a boss shows up
Long trash fights and padded boss encounters that require extra map traversal
Camp upgrade system that overwhelms with analysis paralysis
Recipe-based rewards and unpredictable negative cards that dilute decks instead of giving the satisfaction of picking a card
Grinding battles early because other resources are irrelevant until endgame
divisive_points: The ash/strain system is praised as a clever tactical layer by some and called a terrible, counterintuitive extra chore by others
Conservative, methodical balance: good for newcomers and slow-play fans, but experienced deckbuilder players say the fun (speed, synergy, randomness) is sucked out
Price: fine at a deep discount, but several players say the full price (around 16 pounds or 20 dollars) is too much
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched April 2019 and lasted just over a year before the 1.0 release on June 9, 2020 (PC/Mac; Steam lists Windows and Mac only). Console versions followed in 2021 and the Complete Edition reached Switch in April 2022. Launch critics called it solid but uneven, and a Turn Based Lovers review flagged lingering bugs, balance and localisation issues at release. Revenue estimates are low (Steam revenue calculator about 67.7k gross and 20k net, SteamSpy owners 50k-100k), consistent with a small niche hit. Steam currently shows about 872 recommendations and very low concurrent players; recent 2025-2026 reviews still report controller and ESC-menu bugs, and the game is commonly discounted to a few dollars. Paid DLC includes a soundtrack, artbook, skins and the Tome of Dimensions.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Downwell is a minimalist roguelike where you fall down a deep well instead of climbing, using only left, right and jump, with the jump button also firing your gun downward. He thinks it is amazingly well designed and feels like a game-jam idea turned into a fun game. It is punishing and purely skill-based, and it becomes repetitive because there are no distinct builds. He finished it once and does not plan to return, so he places it high in D tier, explicitly not counting its low price.
praise: Very minimalistic yet amazingly well designed
Unique gimmick of descending as fast as possible rather than advancing forward
Simple controls: left, right, jump, with jump again shooting downward
Different weapons and upgrades found across runs
Skill-based: progress comes from mastering the mechanics, never from feeling overpowered
Feels like a quick game-jam idea turned into a really fun game
criticism: Gets very repetitive since there are no unique builds
Progress is only about how far down you can go
Very punishing: you have little health and take damage easily

Single-button-combo design where jumping and shooting share an input
Pure skill-based roguelike with no power fantasy
commentary.quote: it's actually really amazingly well designed
design_criteria: Personal entertainment: rated on how much he enjoyed playing it, not on price
Build diversity: lacks unique builds, making it repetitive
Skill vs power: purely skill-based with no overpowered moments
Difficulty: punishing with low health
Replayability: he felt done after one completion
Minimalism/controls: simple three-button scheme

community.one_liner: A one-man-made (Moppin) vertical arcade roguelite where you fall down a procedurally generated well, using gunboots as both jump and weapon, in a stark black/white/red pixel style.
community.consensus_summary: Downwell is received as a small arcade classic: Steam sits at Overwhelmingly Positive (about 96.5% of roughly 8,600 reviews), OpenCritic at 83 (84% of critics recommend) and Metacritic PC at 81, with stronger scores on iOS (91) and Switch (88). Critics and players praise the tight, instantly readable controls, the one-more-run loop and the style/module variety. Complaints cluster around high difficulty and run-to-run luck, thin long-term progression and power-up pool, and a few missing quality-of-life options on PC. Metacritic user score is notably lower (6.8, Mixed) than Steam, suggesting a split between fans and people who bounce off the speed. It is a finished, cheap game (about $2.99 on Steam) that has been ported widely (iOS, PC, Android, PS4/Vita, Switch, PS5) rather than an early-access or abandoned title.
best_things: Extremely responsive, simple controls: left/right plus one button that both jumps and fires the gunboots, so movement and combat are the same verb
Addictive short runs that invite 'just one more try'; good for quick sessions and works in a vertical display mode on Switch
Distinctive, minimalist look (black, white and red with swappable palettes) and a strong soundtrack, including the music cutting in the moment you land
Deceptively deep mechanics: combos, gem collection, ammo management and stomping enemies reward skilled play
Styles, modules and perks that change how a run plays, giving variety within a very small game
Bargain price and heavy replay value; many Steam reviewers report owning it on several platforms and playing for over 100 hours
Hard mode and a meaningful final boss give a reason to keep going for players who master it
Polished feel for a solo-developed debut; awards included Destructoid Best Mobile Game of 2015 and GDC Best Debut nominations
Plays well as a low-commitment pick-up game: several Steam reviewers play it while waiting in queues or alongside podcasts, and some own it on multiple platforms
worst_things: Very punishing: tiny health pool and fast pace mean one or two mistakes end a run, which many players find unfair or overwhelming
Runs feel luck dependent (level layout, upgrade offers, shop items), so skill cannot always rescue a bad run
Enemy density late in a run can make it hard to spot your character and produces deaths players call unavoidable
Some color palettes reduce readability, since gameplay relies on three colors and a few palettes only have two
PC port lacks basics: no proper options menu, no jump remapping on keyboard, no screen shake toggle according to negative Steam reviews
Hit detection and movement complaints from some players when the screen is busy
improvements: A full options menu on PC: key remapping (jump cannot be rebound), screen shake toggle and other accessibility settings
Stronger persistent progression or meta-unlocks so repeated runs feel cumulative (Game Informer cited lack of long-term incentive)
A larger and better balanced perk and weapon pool; reviewers note a few options are clearly stronger than the rest
Better readability in busy rooms and in alternate palettes, with gameplay-critical colors kept distinct
More difficulty options or an easier entry ramp for newcomers who find it too hard
Better support for widescreen/horizontal displays, where the vertical aspect ratio is awkward
unique_things: Gunboots: the jump doubles as the weapon and as a fall-slowing tool, fusing platforming and shooting into one input
Vertical, downward-only descent structure with short runs, closer to an arcade score-attack than a typical exploratory roguelike
Strict limited palette (black/white/red, blue for water) with many unlockable palettes that act as collectible skins
Combo-and-gem economy where stomping chains without touching ground drives both score and currency
Originally designed for mobile and vertical play, and it still plays well on phones and rotated displays
Soundtrack that kicks in on landing, tying audio directly to the core movement loop
tedious_or_disliked: Reaching proficiency can feel like grinding through many quick deaths with little carried over between runs
Repetitive runs despite procedural generation, noted by Game Informer
Random level, shop and upgrade rolls that some players feel do not reward learning from mistakes
The pace is too fast and stressful for some, who describe it as nearly unplayable without inhuman reactions
Forced screen shake and missing accessibility/control options on PC frustrate a few players
divisive_points: Difficulty: fans call it tough but fair and mastery-driven, while detractors call it luck-heavy and overwhelming (Steam 96.5% positive versus Metacritic user score 6.8)
Depth versus repetition: Eurogamer and Nintendo Life describe real depth, Game Informer and others find the run structure thin after the first hours
Minimalist presentation: praised as charming and stylish, but the limited palettes and audio bother some players
Whether the game suits PC: PC Games felt it was cut to mobile needs and felt odd with PC controls, while many Steam players love it
community.reception_notes: Launched October 2015 on iOS and Windows (Android January 2016, PS4/Vita May 2016, later Switch and PS5) to broad acclaim, winning TouchArcade Game of the Week and Destructoid Best Mobile Game of 2015 and earning Game Awards and GDC nominations. The critic scores are strongest on iOS and Switch and lowest on PS4/PC, consistent with its mobile-first design; PC Games was a notable dissenter at 70% over the PC feel. Metacritic user reviews are mixed (55% positive, 29% mixed, 16% negative on about 198 ratings) while Steam remains very high, and recent Steam negatives in 2025-26 still focus on speed, luck and missing PC options, suggesting no major control/options patch has resolved them. Steam estimates (SteamSpy 200k-500k owners; steam-revenue-calculator about $817k gross and $241k net to the developer) are rough Boxleiter-style figures across Steam only and exclude mobile and console, where the game sold widely.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Doomspire is a Hearthstone-style deck-building roguelike that tries to recapture Hearthstone's PvE modes such as Catacombs. Between fights you pick cards, passives and removals, but the game pushes only a few builds and is badly unbalanced. He describes infinite loops, ramping so strong a turn-one full board is routine, and thin enemy and content variety. He thinks the developers did not play enough Hearthstone or deckbuilders. He creates a D tier just for it, the only game placed there.
praise: Respects the amount of work that went into it
Hearthstone-like core (mana, trading minions, hero damage) is straightforward and readable
Generous reward choices between fights: cards, passives, card removal
Premise of reviving beloved Hearthstone PvE/Catacombs-style play is appealing
criticism: Extremely unbalanced; builds like plants are broken and can go infinite
Very few viable builds, with only a handful of good cards per archetype
Ramping is even stronger than in Hearthstone and duplicating passives breaks the game
Few enemies with repetitive decks; needs roughly three times the content
Each enemy has many passives that are tedious to read, unlike Hearthstone's single impactful hero power
No real events; rewards feel like the same shop every time
Visuals are weak and generic standard fantasy

design_criteria: Balance: core mechanics are easily broken and ramping is overpowered
Build variety: only a few builds and few worthwhile cards per build
Enemy design: few enemies, many passives, lacks a single defining mechanic
Content volume: needs roughly three times as much for this genre
Run structure: no events, rewards feel like repetitive shop
Visuals/charm: generic fantasy, lacks Hearthstone's personality
Card design expertise: developers seem inexperienced with deckbuilders

community.one_liner: A casual single-player roguelike deckbuilder by Crater Studios, heavily modeled on Hearthstone's Dungeon Run/Solo Adventure, where you pick a faction (allegiance) and climb an endless tower of ever-harder boss fights.
community.consensus_summary: Doomspire has Mixed Steam reviews (about 56% positive of roughly 160 in our data; the store page showed 54% of 139). Launch (Sep 19, 2025) was poorly received: players called it a demo-like product with a bloated random card pool, too few bosses and enemies, and an unfair difficulty wall after around floor 15. Sentiment among reviewers improved after the v1.1 Allegiance patch, which let players pick a faction with its own starting deck, and later patches; several reviews are flipped or edited from negative to positive. It is still viewed as thin on content, repetitive at depth and overpriced at $14.99 (some paid more at launch). Critic coverage is almost nonexistent: Metacritic shows a single 70 from Gamesurf, who felt it should have launched in Early Access, and no OpenCritic entry was found. It is a full release, not labeled Early Access, but it plays like one.
best_things: Hearthstone Dungeon Run-style loop is fun and low-stress; several reviewers say it is a good chill game after a long day
Allegiance (faction) system added in v1.1 gives focused starting decks and clear archetypes, widely credited as the patch that fixed the worst of launch
Fun to discover synergies and find what is overpowered; one reviewer likes that it favors fun over balance
Good visuals, animations and sound for an indie; 3D heroes and blocky minions are liked by some
Developers ship frequent patches (balance, 60+ new cards, deck reshuffling, faster progression) and are seen as listening to feedback
Progression unlocks passives, hero skins, card backs and powers; some players sink 70 to 270+ hours
Easy to pick up with no city building or meta-management, just cards and depth
worst_things: Very small content pool: only around 9 bosses, few enemy types and roughly 8 cards per faction, so runs feel samey quickly
Endless-run is the only mode; there is no real ending, and deep runs (depth 40+) become long, same-feeling fights against boss HP in the thousands
Difficulty spikes and feels rigged after roughly floor 15; AI enemies get strong stacked passives and multiplicative buffs while players get additive ones
Heavy RNG in offers: reviewers complain of being offered off-synergy cards and passives that dilute decks, and of clunky power cards that clog the deck
Enemy AI is simple (trade 1 for 1, otherwise go face) and enemies have no special mechanics, just more passives
Missing basic quality-of-life: no tutorial, no glossary, cannot inspect your deck or opposing passives when choosing fights, no animation speed-up
Technical issues: Windows only, runs poorly on Steam Deck (about 20 fps, no controller support), a reported GPU renderer-timeout hang, and odd bugs such as a huge negative floor number
Reports that updates wipe saved runs
improvements: More bosses, enemy types and cards per faction (the most repeated request, even in positive reviews)
Ability to buff or upgrade specific cards outside combat (items on cards, like Monster Train or Legends of Runeterra) and more ways to customize or thin a deck
Percentage-based or more plentiful healing, since flat heals are useless at deep floors with very large max HP
Starting-deck and build variety, plus a real run structure or ending, not just endless scaling
Animation speed options, tutorial, glossary and deck/passive viewing during route selection
Steam Deck and controller support, and saves that survive updates
unique_things: Essentially an entire game built around the Hearthstone Dungeon Run / Tavern Brawl idea, with minion-board combat instead of hand-management card play
Faction (allegiance) identities such as dragons, thorns/silverthorn, undead/death knight, poison and archers, each with leveled unlocks
Enemies and bosses use the same passives the player can unlock, so the passives you see bosses use are what you later collect
Infinite depth scaling where bosses get increasingly silly stats
Deck reshuffling so a run does not end when your deck empties (added in a late patch)
tedious_or_disliked: Long deep runs where every fight looks the same but bigger, with no animation speed-up; several players quit around depth 40 to 50 from boredom
Starting over with the same weak starting cards each run in earlier versions; progression that mostly unlocks things you already saw a boss use
Switching faction requires abandoning a run
Grinding to unlock key passives and factions before higher floors feel manageable; about 30 achievements seen as grindy
Constantly having to skip offered cards because the growing unlocked pool is off-synergy
divisive_points: Post-allegiance-patch quality: many say it is now good or decent and recommended, while others still say it feels like a demo or early access
Difficulty: some find it too easy once a broken combo is found (ramp bundle, silverthorn plus taunt), while others find it brutally unfair after floor 15
Price: some say it is fine at current price for the content, others call $15 (or more at launch) too steep
Marketing: complaints that the developer spent on streamer sponsorships while the game lacked basics
community.reception_notes: Launched Sep 19, 2025 to Mixed reviews after a demo that many thought was more fun than the release. Patches per the Steam news page: v1.0.2 (Sep 22, 2025) sped progression by 37% and nerfed a passive; v1.0.3 (Oct 1) cost/undead fixes; v1.1 The Allegiance (Nov 28, 2025, per the page) added allegiances and 60+ cards and removed a boss passive; v1.1.2 (Dec 18) did a boss balance pass and added deck reshuffling; later a v1.2 (Jan 26) restoring allegiance unlocks and UI polish and a v1.3 Fire & Ice (May 4) with shared passives, scaled boss difficulty and a new arena. The fetched page's years for the later entries were garbled and likely refer to 2026. Some reviews note an earlier month-long gap without updates. Windows only; Steam Deck not supported well. Metacritic has only 1 critic and 2 user ratings so no score is shown. The Steam ratio is unlikely to move much because many reviewers update after patches but the overall total is small (about 160).

games.name: Withering Rooms
games.short_description: Withering Rooms is a challenging 2.5D horror RPG set in a procedurally generated Victorian mansion that changes each night. Explore Mostyn House to collect the perfect items for your build and face a huge cast of overgrown undead, invisible ghosts, devious witches, and more.

commentary.label: Top 10 of 2024 (#7)
commentary.summary: Withering Rooms is a 2.5D action horror roguelike mixing stealth and soulslike mechanics in a surprisingly large adventure. You play a young girl who starts out weak and hiding from monsters, then grows into a fighter or wizard. He calls it the most surprising and interesting game on his list, feeling more like an action horror adventure than a typical roguelike. Despite UI, repetition and weak-boss complaints, he highly recommends it to anyone wanting a different roguelike experience.
praise: Surprising scope: keeps expanding until it feels like a massive adventure game
Intentionally slow, simple, clunky gameplay that supports the vulnerable start
Progression from helpless hiding to becoming a true fighter or wizard
Hardcore death system that sends you back to chapter start, making combat risky and frightening
Remembrance shrines let you pay to permanently keep items, an interesting player decision
Curse rot mechanic changes visuals, audio and gameplay, with fantastic effort put into the changes
Strong sense of adventure and unique monsters
criticism: Map and inventory UI could use better filters and player feedback
Late-game fast travel is lacking
Gets repetitive by the end despite its size
Player became so overpowered as to be near invincible
Many bosses look cool but are mechanically uninteresting, and infinite lives in boss fights reduce the threat
unique_points: Permadeath treated as a hardcore chapter-reset death system rather than a full run reset, keeping levels and permanent items
Curse meter that rises with horrifying events and transforms the world and mechanics
Roguelike elements (random loot, rings with randomized stats) serve an action horror adventure

Meta-progression: remembrance shrines to permanently keep items
Atmosphere/visuals/audio: curse-driven changes to the world
Boss design: visually cool but mechanically shallow, infinite lives reduce threat
UI/usability: map and inventory filtering and feedback
Pacing/repetition: large game that gets repetitive late

Exploration/adventure feel: sense of expanding world

community.consensus_summary: No community or critic consensus could be established. The local Steam dataset has no appid for this title, and Steam store searches for 'Magic Book Autobattler' and 'Magic Book' returned no matching autobattler (only unrelated titles such as Amanda's Magic Book entries, Book of Demons, Slime Rush: Leshy and the Magic Book). The only grounded information is from the ranking video (Part 3, about 2:03:57-2:04:28): the reviewer says he found the game's Steam page had been rebranded, that the game no longer exists under that name and can no longer be bought, and that viewers will not know what it is until a newer version comes out. He gave no tier or opinion on gameplay. The title may also be a rough chapter label rather than the official name. The general web search tool hit its session budget, so no reviews, Reddit threads, Metacritic or OpenCritic pages could be retrieved.
worst_things: Delisted/rebranded on Steam, so it cannot currently be purchased under this name (per the ranking video)
unique_things: The reviewer called the situation unique: he said he had never seen a game vanish from its Steam page through a rebrand like this
